Dungeon Keeper was my most favorite game of all time, and I've been waiting a little under 14 years for the sequel that never came, until now that is.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who appreciates the older, finer games that were common place a decade ago.
-Edit-
Now that the game has been fully released, I'll give it my 1.0 day 1 launch review. I'll review it again once there is a more stable patch.
This game captures Dungeon Keepers essense without question, it is everything you can expect from a Dungeon Keeper sequel and more. It's unique style sets itself apart and is a breath of fresh air, but you cant help but think you're playing Dungeon Keeper. For this I can give the abiance, theme, gameplayand atmosphere no less than 11/10
Now onto my problems with the game.
The game feels very rushed, the skirmish mode is limited to 3 maps, limited to 2 players with a smallish map with little to it. It seems like they are placeholder maps, and it's not like the sandbox map is a small as the skirmish maps. I feel like for launch, 3 small sized 2 player maps doesn't cut it.
In multiplayer, it is extremely buggy as the minions don't fight each other properly, the game is prone to crashing, I noticed when destroying another players dungeon heart, damage doesn't appear to be dealt either.
The campaign is very prone to FPS drops, no matter the persons computer specs. It first appears in mission 3, or in any game where the enemey can attack your dungeon heart, as for whatever reason that drops FPS to unplayable levels, That isn't the end to the FPS drops as from mission 4 on, FPS drops are common and on mission 4, happen right at the end as you're mousing over the inhibiters and shrines and for the rest of the game once you have vision of that area.
These will all be patched so I will edit this post once it has been fixed, but for those expecting to buy this game and play it over the weekend, this post is to warn you that the game is having a troubled launch as most games do.

If you enjoy X-COM, you will probably like this turn based strategy game. The story starts slow and requires some patience in the learning phase like many games. As the story progress, you quickly appreciate the strength of various soldier class, the importance of positioning, the differences in making use of environment.
Coupled of growing challenging scenarios, the story is quite touching (though Dialouge is a bit lengthy). Most map have some variations / twist on its own, and you won't feel like "Äww, its the same map like previous..".
Summary:
- Well Balanced Game Play, game difficulty goes up as you level. Excellent for games who like challenges to their tactical mind
- Players are free to spend their experience on any class and level according to their game play style (Sniper, Assault, Scout, Anti-Tanks)
- Skirmish mission & story mode available. Experience from Skirmish mission can be brought into story!
- High-replayability. Didnt get Rank A for the map ? Play it when you complete the game. Try the Skirmish difficulty challenges to test your deployment skills!
This game is a must have for Strategy game lovers.

This game is the largest stakeholder simulator ever created. Make sure to keep your vassals and court happy to avoid revolutions or any sort of a turmoil. I have enjoyed the game so far. In particular, I liked the random events that take place throughout the game. For example, your son’s wife can get possessed by a demon and slay half of your family or your younger son will decide to assassinate you and all his older brothers to inherit the crown. Equally, sometimes you are that very person who coldly murders most of your family while being driven by hunger for power. In any scenario, you will have plenty of fun while rewriting world’s history. It feels like a game with a storylines alike Game of Thrones – intrigues, assassinations, betrayals, seduction and other joys of life.
I would personally advise to play this game on Ironman mode only, as it forces you to embrace all the chaos you have caused and all challenges that have emerged in the game, forging your mind to be more strategic next time and also not trust anyone.

I love the art, the theme, the story, the puzzles, and the humor. This is a very well done game and, though it is somewhat short, it's well worth the price of a movie ticket (at least where I live).
Basically, it's a point and click adventure game with a bit of an X-Files flair that's not too terribly difficult, but just right, in my opinion, for a nice casual gaming session. I recommend you click on everything and everyone not because of puzzles, but because some of the dialog is hilarious.
It's kind of like a throwback to the old Sierra adventure games, but with a more modern touch. I cannot recommend it highly enough.
Hopefully, the devs will sell enough copies that they'll make sequels, because I want more McQueen and Dooley!

This kickstarter game project is set out to make a game that will hopefully be a successor to 'Dungeon Keeper' by Bullfrog Entertainment.  It has even been given the thumbs up by 'Peter Molyneux'.
The aim of the game is to build up your dungeon / minions and conquer the other dungeons while playing in a top down view.. or FPS if you have a possession spell to take over one of your minions.
If you want an idea of the game concept then I'd recommend checking out "Dungeon Keeper" (not Dungeon keeper2) and then imagine it revamped to today's graphics.
Edit: The game is still being updated with multiplayer now working (occasionally buggy)  and a map editor expected in the future, however right now there is the campaign mode and 'extra' unlockable themes which you can change the look and feel of your dungeon.

An average run of the mill cRPG that is vastly inferior to Pillars of Eternity.
If Steam allowed a neutral rating this would get one from me, but alas Steam doesn't, so it gets a negative vote.
The bads...
Ambiguous quests - finish out of sequence, don't clear from log, don't update correctly, allow the sales of mission critical items, allow the killing of mission critical NPCs without warning.  While it's acceptable to think and be responsibile for your actions a warning should be in place.
Map is useless, UI is basic, pathing stinks, travel is terrible on large maps.  The view is pretty bad too, needs to zoom out much farther.
AI always has more AP than you, and will break LOS constantly even though you can't.  Be prepared to take group damage even when you're spread out far.  (Richocet comes to mind)  The converse is not true, your range is much smaller.  Combat is affected because of that and is left boring and flat.  The physical and magical shield concept might be good but if Youtube fanboys suggest taking hydro/geo/pyro/aethero in your party you're pretty much fighting yourself.
Character creation is too ambiguous and stat allocation is affected by that.  Are you a tank?  Great, just take strength and constitution, but don't forget wits, memory, leadership, and many more to be effective.
The good
Kill everyone in sight, take their loot or goods depending if the NPC is a trader.  Story is tossed aside by the fact you can kind of get away with killing everyone - less reason to do the right thing.
Other than that not much.  If I reroll a new story I will forego the Origin characters as they're nothing special, and focus on a single damage type.

Completed act 1 three times now, and have just completed the game.
For me, the first 2 acts were really great. Lots to explore, fun battles and many choices to make, all of which felt like they were important. Character creation and leveling was great fun, as could build however you wanted. I really didnt like my character at the start and was thinking about restarting, but after I started getting gear that improved my other scores, and let me learn spells from other schools of magic I started to really love it, in the end having a Elementalist Staff wielder, making for great moments of being able to summon ice storms and lazor beams.
However, it all goes downhill near the end. Arx is where the final act takes place, and looks very promising at first. That is until you have to spend many many hours searching for anything to move your quests along, or spoil it all by looking at a walkthrough.
(Spoilers!) I think many will agree with me that finding Arhu is the hardest part in the game, not because its a good puzzle, but because you get so little infomation to go on. If this is the sort of game you like, or you think you might be interested in this game: buy it. It's amazing. The turn-based combat is fantastic. It actually feels tacitcal and when you figure out a clever way to approach a battle and then win, it is very satisfying. If you play for tactical combat, you'll love it. If you play RPGs for an engaging story and world, you'll love it. If you love tinkering with builds and different class comps, you'll love it. If you love reactivity, freedom, and choice and consequence - you will love it.
If you think you might possibly enjoy this game - buy it, you will not regret it. This is the best RPG since Witcher 3.

Good premise and atmosphere, but some of the gameplay is mediocre.
It's basically an interactive story point-and-click game but with a mainstream 3rd person view, some basic stealth and QTE mechanics, and a larger budget to make it more appealing to the masses. This combination of niche and mainstream works well enough, if you have modest expectations. The story is quite enjoyable, but a bit short. Voice acting is decent, and the music fits the mood well. Graphics are fairly modest on a technical level, but some environments still manage to look beautiful, and the effects look slick. While I was expecting some rough edges with gameplay, the core mystery solving mechanics also have some flaws - the answer was sometimes too obvious or seemed inconsistent or illogical. As a console port there are some issues - flawed mouse sensitivity, clunky PC controls you cannot re-bind and a prohibitive autosave system. All these issues are annoying, but they don't ruin the game completely. Possessing cats and solving crimes as a ghost was pretty cool at times.
This game reminds me a bit of Alan Wake and LA Noire. While not as good as either of those games, it was better than I thought it would be after seeing the professional reviews. Its sad the developer went bust one month after making this game.
If you have modest expectations and some patience, its an enjoyable interactive-story game.
Recommended, at sale price.

A deeper game than what I thought it would be. I suggest it a lot.

Visuals: Lots of effort and love was put into the animation and level of detail in objects, environments, etc. The "cut scenes" are put together really well, there's no guessing as to what's-what. EASILY some of the best sprite-work I've ever seen.
Music: Solid. It helps create the atmosphere the developers were going for.
Story: Characters are mostly forgettable, save for Otus (he is the protagonist after all). Story has some weight to it, but often times there's a difference in what I feel (eh) and what the game wants me to feel (despair).
Controls: Twin-stick, though it supports WASD+Mouse. Standard 2D Platforming fare otherwise, with flying being really easy to use. Overall, pretty solid, but it took me some getting used to using the LT/RT buttons for the picking-up/throwing mechanics.
Gameplay: A bit lacking for my tastes. Not a whole lot to explore except for finding hidden chests and what-not. I didn't find the puzzles challenging. The Boss Fights: some may find challenging but not in a way that tests your reflexes as one would expect from this kind of game. It's more of a "what the hell do I do" kind of thing. Most players should have no issue figuring out what to do, which doesn't leave much in terms of an actual challenge.
Overall: Good game, but the drawbacks mentioned above keep it from greatness.

This game gives me THAT feeling... The one that can be commonly associated with indie titles. You know the one. No? Let me elaborate.
After breezing through Owlboy in 7 hours, I can safely say that I was not satisfied with the game, and only artsy indie-only ♥♥♥♥♥♥s will come out of the game thinking "yeah, this was worth my money. Poor Indie devs took like 10 years man!". I got this game at the lowered price of $20, and even at this price I will warn you that Owlboy is not worth anything higher than say, $10. Now that I have prefaced this, let me get into some of the issues.
First off, this game controls like garbage. This astounds me, because there are not that many controls in the first place. The worst thing I had to deal with during my boring journey was that YOU HAVE TO ♥♥♥♥ING ROLL FIRST IN ORDER TO SPRINT. This ruins so many things by extention. Because your movement speed is worthless, you will unfortunately be encouraged by the game to spam rolls constantly, inhibiting precise movement and making a really, really ♥♥♥♥ing annoying sound. Once you begin to move about the world this way or as slowboi, you'll notice something else.
This game feels... Empty. This is due to many things, such as:
1. Few Enemies
2. Low Enemy Diversity
3. Pointless NPCs
4. Weak Worldbuilding
5. Few Collectibles (Coins and ♥♥♥♥ discs)
6. Lore = Three ~5 page books* (like 10 words per page), and some dumb♥♥♥♥ lorenerd.
7.. Gorgeous open areas... With nothing to do in them.
About that "feeling". This is what causes it, and is the second largest reason for my not recommending this game. It is the feeling you might get from, say, a unity built game that looks pretty, but lacks purpose and substance. You feel alone. It feels wrong, Owlboy! Don't do this to me!
Those two problems are by far the worst, but this game has plenty of other issues.
Combat - Can be quite boring, and tends to be floaty. The bosses in this game are meh. Of the companions you will pick up, only one is really quite effective for combat. Others are either backup, waiting for this other companion to reload, or primarily used to get through lazy metroidvania style blockages in the world.
Characters - You won't get attatched to anyone in this game, and you certainly won't care about their mortality. All of them are either painfully boring, total♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or don't get enough screentime to be used effectively. When I started this game, I really wanted to care about these characters. But, by the end, I didn't care about any of them.
Story - SPOILERS
Now that everything else is out of the way, let me say something good about the game. This game is similar to a lot of indie games coming out these days, in that it banks on pixel art to draw people in. And truth be told, this game is actually quite gorgeous. Not as good as something like Hyper Light Drifter (a game that actually plays well AND has good art), but still pretty nice to look at. I guess most of those 10 years in development were spent drawin trees, aye?
And, though somewhat generic, this game does actually have a decent soundtrack. It's orchestral, and can sometimes aid the world in feeling large, even sometimes managing to make your journey feel "epic". It is not, do not be fooled by the good music.
Owlboy is not worth $20. Pick it up if it goes on sale for $10 or less. It suffers from bad controls, an empty world, weak combat, bad characters, and a dull story. However, it does have good art and music.

This game seems to be doing so many things right. And I do like it. I really do. It does a great job of producing a legitimately creepy atmosphere. The characters are good, and the visuals are great. The "monsters" are creepy, but not so otherworldly as to make you go "oh, ha-ha. Tentacle monster. Meh."
There are serious problems, though, and I don't mean from a technical standpoint. To go over it without giving away anything:
Your one weapons, such as it is, is more difficult to use than it should be.
The hit detection for the enemies is spot on. For my one defense? Not so much. I once used it three times on one enemy (admittedly a boss) to no effect. That's not cool.
The reasoning for the weapon's value and for why you can do what you can do is not well established, especially early on.
There's an In Media Res intro section that should juts plain not be there. It's got spoilers, and it serves no purpose. Basically, you get thrown into stuff, plot points are spoiled, and then you get taken to the actual start of the game and the story. There's no point to it, and it actually detracts from the atmosphere and suspense building the rest of the game is really good at.
I recommend it, but the developers should work on the issues.

The soundtrack is awe-inspiring and it hasn't been been since I was a young boy playing Chrono Trigger on the SNES that a band of pixelated heroes had felt so... real. There are times in the game that you will be reminded of the classics from yesteryear; there are hints of Zelda, Rayman, Metroid, Castlevania but Owlboy always feels distinctively it's own thing. There are a few questionable mechanics in the game. One of your companions has a recharge rate on their weapons that can be absolutely maddening. Though I'm not quite sure whether this is a bug or a feature as it lends to every single one of your companions being indespensible, never being able to rely completely on one single companion. The story remains the single best thing about this game. It covers themes of loss, failure, inadequacy, and learning to have hope in hopeless times in ways that no other medium could. If you enjoy SNES era games or story-rich indie titles Owlboy is a must play. 9.5/10

This is a tough one to review because it's difficult to say who this game is for.
I could say that strategy buffs will love trying to tackle the puzzle of defeating an enemy non-violently, but this doesn't typically offer the type of options that strategy fans are used to and then sometimes it's impossible to defeat your opponent non-violently in this game.
I could say that this game is for all those who are either frustrated with or enthralled by modern day political strife and uprisings, but this game takes such a neutral point of view on political issues, that anyone looking for it to cater to their personal views is going to be sorely disappointed.
Regardless, this game is something unique and special. It's art style is downright beautiful, which I say as a person who never understood nor cared for the popular pixel art style utilized by other games. The sound is immersive and I highly recommend playing this with headphones for that reason; it might just cause you to be more emotionally invested in the well being of your sprites.
For the sake of helping people make their purchasing decision, here are some negatives I noticed:
-There's zero tutorial or direction as to how to use any of the options at your disposal or what most police items do.
-There are some bugs that seem to negate items you've just chosen or at least no indication as to why they didn't active.
-The game gives no weight to losing your sprites or promotes protecting them. Just a "oh no, they've killed someone."
-Contains four "campaigns" with two playable perspectives, roughly giving an hour of playtime each; is there any replayability once you've finished? Hard to say at this stage, but it seems not unless the game gets expanded on or the community heavily gets behind customizing levels.
Summary: If those negatives don't turn you off right now and you're willing to throw $12-13 behind such a unique, beautiful concept, then I'd say the money is worth it; already I feel like I've gotten my money's worth and that the wait for this game has been worth it; hopefully you'll be able to say the same.

Even if you've been waiting on this one for years now, like I have, I'd recommend that you chill on it for a few more months until it's more enjoyable to play. As of right now, it's unintuitive, unoptimised, buggy and generally difficult to play.
I'll start with the things I enjoyed about the game. Starting off on the rioter side in the Arab Spring scenario, I found that the game succeeded in evoking a strong emotional response while also being suitably challenging. It was genuinely disturbing to watch the police units fire indiscriminately into my crowd of peaceful protestors, and even though I ultimately won the scenario, I was still left feeling morose at the thought of the number of people who had died for that victory. I suspect that that's exactly the sort of emotional response that the game is going for, and in that regard, it succeeds.
However, for everything the game has in its ability to evoke the emotions associated with the scenarios it portrays, it lacks far more in its actual design and gameplay. In designing the controls, I suspect that the developers wanted to simulate the chaos and disorganisation in trying to direct people in a riot, but it comes off as feeling sluggish at best and outright random at worst. Targeted abilities, such as projectiles, can either land directly on their mark or fall completely flat, seemingly at random - I'm not expecting a one-hundred percent hit rate, obviously, but any indication at all of factors that could affect my unit's accuracy would be appreciated.
The various items and abilities you can confer onto your units are not sufficiently explained and lack almost any feedback when they're used - I can give my protestors laser pointers to 'slow down' police units, for example, but there's no feedback to indicate whether the ability actually landed or had any effect, and even if it did, what's the use in making a single hostile unit move slower for a few seconds? Slingshots are supposedly a more potent way of harming police units at range than the rocks and random debris that all mobs have the ability to throw, but targeting them is an exercise in guessing, as is working out if they had any effect whatsoever. The same goes for many other items, and the only way to discover which ones are actually useful is to play and lose a few times before you hit on a winning combo.
This lack of feedback is unfortunately a running theme on both sides of the protest line. Police units can be individually outfitted with different gear, but there is no indication
of the pros and cons of different kinds of gear versus one another. What's the difference between a 'crude long baton', a 'wooden stick', and an '18in plastic tonfa'? How is 'Gasmask 2' better than 'Gasmask 1'? Why do my ballistic units have a choice of five different smoke grenade launchers, and again, how do they differ? Why, after I threw aside my moral values in total frustration and gave every ballistic team lethal ammunition, did they kill
people than when they were using less-than-lethal rubber bullets? The game makes no effort to answer any of these questions, and even after a solid hour of trying different bits and pieces of cop gear to no visible effect (the first hour being spent playing the protestor side), I'm left no closer to finding out.
The game attempts to model the media outlook on a protest event and supposedly punishes the more violent side by giving their opponent a bonus in the next mission, but once again, precious little information is given on how gameplay is affected. After a particularly bloody day in Cairo in which over a hundred of my protestors were shot dead, I was told that my side would have a 'massive advantage' in the next mission. How that manifested, however, is a mystery to me. I was given fewer units to field, a more difficult mission to fulfil, and the police were no less armed or brutal when they turned up to once again to - quite literally - shoot my peaceful protest down.
Bugs, too, are rife in this game, which is odd after the huge period of delay it was subject to before launch. Protestor mechanics mostly work well, but the police side is barely functional. Riot shield-clad tactical units occasionally flee their positions and concede ground to peaceful, non-aggressive protestors for no discernible reason. Assault units sent in to strategically separate and arrest vulnerable protestors, proceeding to drag them off-screen, sometimes disappear from the map for up to a minute at a time before trickling back onto the field in disarray - were they indulging in police brutality where I couldn't see them or something? Shotgun-toting ballistic units occasionally only fire one or two of the ten guns available to their squad, and whether or not they hit anything is up to factors that the game makes no effort to inform the player of. Units tasked with throwing stun grenades into the crowd will often seemingly have a seizure and flicker from left to right on the spot, trapping their entire squad in inaction until given a new order. When pushed to it, enemy protestors seem to either phase directly through my testudo of riot shields or merge together into one single super-protestor, making them impossible to dislodge from a map area in either case.
The relatively static camera has trouble following the action in some maps, and I lost one scenario as the protestor side when a police unit charged off the corner of the map, leaving me unable to target them with attacks or abilities even though they were still counted as being inside the 'objective zone' for the game's purposes of resolving the scenario. As for protestor mechanics, I haven't once been able to get the 'build barricade' ability to work - a frustrating problem, as it's the only way that units in the 'aggressive' stance can attempt to hold a position.
There's a few extra modes to toy with in the 'Custom' section of the game, but I had even less luck getting those to work properly. I gave 'spectator' mode (also called 'journalist mode' when you unlock it, for some reason) a go and attempted to pit 400 furious, heavily-armoured, molotov-tossing guerrillas against 120 equally well-armed officers of the law. When I started the game, I was surprised to find that only four rioters showed up. They promptly ran off-screen, handing an immediate and anti-climactic victory to the police. I figure the cops must've been more confused than I was.
The game's performance, particularly for a two-dimensional game with deliberately low-res graphics, is surprisingly poor, particularly when aiming abilities - it goes without saying that trying to drop a molotov on top of a charging police line before they run out of its landing zone is already challenging, and it becomes impossible when the framerate drops into the low single digits. To its credit, the game didn't crash at any point, though it still escapes me how a 900mb game that seems quite undemanding in terms of system requirements can run as poorly as this one does at times.
To conclude: it's a great concept and it certainly succeeded in evoking the emotional response it was surely aiming for, but as a game - as a collection of interlocking mechanics that responds to player input - it has a long road ahead of it. Hopefully, most of the negative points mentioned in this review will be obsolete after a few months of tuning and polishing from the developer(s?). At present, though, I'd advise putting your purchase on hold.

The essence of RIOT can easily be summarized into 2 words: unrest simulator.
It basically puts you in charge of one of the 2 opposite teams, the police and the protesters, with objectives ranging from occupation of public soil (a highway, a square or a construction site) to the disband of a peaceful/violent protest.
The game lets you decide, before each start, what kind of equipment you want to give to your angry mob (from megaphones to rocks to firecrackers and molotovs) or the squads of policemen you want to deploy (there are 3 types, tactical, assault and kinetic squads) and their equipments and veichles.
To complete the objectives it is usually required to push or disperse the opposite team away using various tactics and equipment to support your advance (or your defense).
Very interesting is the mechanic regarding the escalation of violence and the exploit of social media, both simulated into the game.
First of all, all the squads have two "modes" that can be switched during the game: harmless or violent. Depending on your playstyle you can decide to follow the "harmless way" (protesters sitting in the middle of the road, policemen just pushing people) or the "guerrilla" style (with molotov, barricades, tear gas, flashbangs and even guns shooting each other), using then the social media (aka cameras and cellphones) to depict yourself as the victim persecuted by the other side or call reinforcements.
The game counts 4 campaigns, each composed by 4 missions playable as one of the 2 sides:
-no-TAV protests in Italy
-the arab spring in Egypt
-the protests in Greece
-the Indignados protests in Spain
Plus, each campaign unlocks a series of scenarios ranging from the Kiev protests of Maidan square to France, USA, Colombia, hoping that more will come in the future.
The graphic is clean even if sometimes it can be difficult to follow the action (especially if the situation escalates violently) and it can be very laggy when there are 2-300 people on screen at the same time.
The sound, on the contrary, is perfect with the sounds of bombs, firecrackers and screams very well reproduced in game. There are even the original chores of the protesters taken by the the public footage.
I definitely recommend this game as it simulates pretty accurately how a protest or a riot developes nowadays, with a high level of challenge at higher difficulties.

Crusader Kings II (CK2) is best described as a medieval political simulator, which doesnt really sound very exciting or do the game justice. This is a different breed of strategy game, where it isnt about building the biggest army and going round painting the map your colour. You can 'win' the game without fighting a single battle, you can topple empires through sheer use of intrigue, and win wars without fielding a single troop.
CK2 lets you pick any point between 769 (with DLCs) and 1453 and then pick any living character in that time period to play as - from great historical figures like Charlemagne or Ragnarr Lofbrook, to a random baron in middle francia with just a humble castle to his/her name. You (the player) play as the dynasty of that character, so when he/she dies, you continue playing with their heir, who will (hopeully) inherit a lot of the titles that daddy owned. I say 'hopefully' because exactly what you stand to inherit depends on things like the inheritance laws in your budding empire, not to mention different marriage rules and other factors. Some government types are restricted to specific inheritance laws - if you are commanding a disorganised tribe then there is a very good chance that it will break off and fracture, meaning that successfully 'unifying' the tribes needs to be done within the lifespan of one character. Unfortunately you may then be blessed with a king with horrible traits who everyone hates, who clings onto life desperately, refusing to drop dead. This is a game where you will probably at times WANT your character to die so you can start playing as the next of kin - a younger, perhaps more suitable ruler.
Yes, CK2 is a rather complex game to put it mildly, and there isnt much in the way of a tutorial. Therefore it is STRONGLY recommended that you check out some youtube videos aimed for beginners. While you are at it, check out the video of someone conquering the world playing as a sentient horse. Yes, historical accuracy is rife here, but with an understanding of a couple of the more amusing loopholes in the game, you too could become an immortal horse emperor. But I digress...
CK2 is a rather unique game, and one that other large scale strategy games (such as the Total War series - which I also love) could really learn a thing or two from. The level of intrigue, diplomacy and 'cunning plans' available here is one that I have never seen any other game come close to. Want to go to war? You gonna need Casus Belli (cause for war) buddy - and what you stand to actually gain from that war depends on that justification used. A system of 'claims' is used for the various provinces in the game. If your character (or one of his vassals/courtiers) doesnt have a claim on that piece of land, you cant go to war for it.
Final thing worth mentioning here are the mods. CK2 has mod support, and some of the total conversion mods that I have played are excellent. The mechanics and style of the game lend themselves superbly to the political, scheming landscape of Game of Thrones - and you will be pleased to know there is a fantastic total conversion mod that turns the world into Westeros, with various start dates depending on whether you are up to date with the books/TV show or not. As a prince of the Iron Islands, I successfully captured Daenerys and forced her into becoming my salt-wife and bear my children - and thus my firstborn pirate son inherited the Iron Throne in one fell swoop. Or was that just a dream I had the other night?
There is also a Lord of the Rings conversion mod available which I am fond of. All sorts of traits and 'features' are introduced to mimic middle earth, so Elves are immortal and Treants cannot reproduce, and neither can marry filthy orcs.
Anyway, back to topic, this is an excellent game and quite unlike anything else you are likely to play. The game is a bit dated, but it isnt really a game that relies on graphics whatsoever, and it is still fully supported with fresh DLC still being released. All I can say (other than the above) is watch a couple of tutorial videos on Youtube and see if it looks like your cup of tea. Hard Reset is a cyberpunk FPS that is labelled as "old-school". These days there are a couple of such FPS games out there, notably Shadow Warrior, a remake from the same developer team. Hard Reset really delivers the old school: you have dozens of enemies sent against you at once, countless of objects you can destroy in the surrounding area (the game counts and rewards these environmental kills). What's more, the protagonist has weapons that do not require reloading - you just press and hold the button till all your foes are eliminated.
Weapon-wise Hard Reset follows an interesting concept. You have two weapons and instead of mapping them to the numbers you can switch between them with the use of Q and E which are usually for "previous" or "next" weapons in the genre. As you make progress in the game the more nanocells you can pick up - these allow you to upgrade your two best friends thereby granting them extra firing capability. This is how you turn your rifle into a shotgun, then grenade launcher, RPG etc. The number keys are now unlocked and you can easily switch between these "functions" during a battle. It is an interesting concept, certainly.
Graphics-wise Hard Reset looks stunning. Some of the effects are beautiful and if you look around you can easily notice the inspiration of various sci-fi authors such as Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥(to give you a hint: there are shuttles in the air with huge neon advertisements). The story is somewhat mediocre - there are comic book style cutscenes between the various chapters telling you the story of a major who wages a desperate battle against machines. These "custcenes" could have been better with a more appropriate voice acting.
Do note that the game is very difficult. Many of the bigger enemies can easily kill you; using environmental kills is highly recommended due to the splash damage you can do with them. Running and jumping will be your best asset sometimes and even then you'll perish several times - the creators knew this that is why they included an achievement for not dying on a level.
The game is short - 5-6 hours is enough to complete it. It is commendable that the developers released a free DLC that continues the story throughout 3 extra levels. You have the usual new-enemies-new-boss-new-environment deal here.
Hard Reset is a very good game. If you miss the old school style FPS games you can give this one a try as it offers you top-notch graphics, achievements and replayability in case you want to try the higher difficulty levels, too.
PS: Wow! I did not know Philip K. D.I.C.K's surname would be censored! :D

The basic Hard Reset experience is arcade-shooting action in a nutshell. You have only two guns, a gun that uses bullets and one that uses energy. However, the base guns (basicly rifles) have additional shotgun, gernade, mine-throwing, and various single power-shot modes that can be unlocked with points earned from kills and from scavenging yellow-glowing-box-things scattered throughout the levels. The varitions between similier modes for each gun are minor (the bullet-gun shotgun is slow and single-shot, the energy version is a wide spray of electricity for as long as you hold down the trigger), but the differences do add up.
Your only enemies are machines, which is good and bad. It's good if you like watching your target's armored body fall apart, but bad if you don't like bullet-spongy enemy. Several large foes take forever to kill. However, the degree of bullet sponge was acceptable to me, as per the enemies. The enemies themselves are limited for the first part of the game, which I liked because it made it easier to learn patterns, especially for large groups of enemies (there are several). The Enhanced content adds some new foes, however, and a flying version is both very deadly (it shoots back) and extremely annoying.
The combat in Hard Reset is the meat of the game, and is intense and demanding (many enemies focus on melee, meaning they throw themselves at you in large masses). Impediments to progess are all extremely basic keypad interacts that are thankfully less annoying than keycards. There is an extensive story, but I got sick of it early, and when the extended content shows up I'm pretty sure the whole thing stops making much sense, anyway.
If you like the momentum and skill required by games that utilize healthpacks over regenerating health, you will probably like this game.

Like, shoot this with that weapon, use the other one upgraded to something to kill that thing, and then use a different upgrade for other weapon to do this and then finish the enemy off with that. Hard Reset is a very, how do I put it, interesting unique take on the genre of shooters. It seems more like the outset of a butterfly. Looks wonderous on the outside, extremely vague and odd on the inside. Starting off, the game tells me the controls of the game. I don't mind that at all. Does that well so far. I also thought it was pretty innovative how if you hover your cursor over a nearby screen it starts up the little video for you so if you want to watch it you don't have to wait for it to start all over again, just move your cursor away if you are not interested.
Then I get to what appears to be a larger robot than all the other little ones that come in clusters. These appear to be bullet sponges but I thought I had to have a special way of taking them down with the alternate plasma weapon I had. Of course not knowing this I tried everything but the bullet spongey method and frustrated myself unnecessarily. Finally, it worked sinking mass amounts of bullets into it and got it killed. It told me how to do everything else but not how to handle the big boys? I was so confused I thought I broke the game.
Also the game has a VERY obscure way of explaining things. Some things it will show you directly, others it will just say figure it out yourself. It seems like this game wants to be too many things for a 3000ish MB type game and I am actually quite disappointed. To be fair I did not expect much from a game this size its just that if you plan to make a tutorial for your game, explain things properly. Certain actions like jumping are clearly explained. Other very vague things like pickups and even when you first visit the upgrading station. It's incredible how much work was put into this but not enough work to explain what all this is. I was stunned. Not to mention that you don't have enough to DO anything when you get there. You figure at least they would give you enough currency to start off with to demonstrate how the buying process works but that never came into play.
Long story short: I do not recommend buying this game. A lot of things are bullet spongey, other things are very obscure and you have no idea what to do, a lot of things are just blindly there being picked up and you don't know if you should pick it up or not. If you cannot make a decent tutorial, how are you gonna pull in your playerbase? If I am offput on how a tutorial explains things, there's a problem with your game.
A more fleshed out tutorial needs to be made for the customers. If you are planning to innovate the FPS genre, might wanna flesh out how your game works first so people aren't wandering around blindly, asking themselves "What is this? What's this? What's that thing? What do I do? I'm so confused!"
Sorry guys I do not recommend this as a purchase. That's just who I am.

27 hours in the game and I haven't even left Fort Joy. Literally... I haven't broken out. I convinced my best friend to join me and we have been hacking away at anything and anyone who seemed like a bad guy. Breaking the game mechanics is legitamately half the fun here. We managed to sneak our way past Magisters by using the teleport spell. Somehow... we always managed to take the back door into every dungeon.
We couldn't stop getting ourselves in trouble at every turn. By the way, getting into trouble is just part of the fun. Speaking of which, be ready to quick save a ton. The developers were kind enough to give 5 quick save slots along with auto saves and unlimited hard saves... Unless you're playing on that insane 4th difficulty, in which you have just the 1 save and a total party kill is very very bad. You basically get your save erased on the hardest difficulty if everyone dies.
Pros:
-Break the game dammit. Just do it! I swear finding ways to navigate and utterly cheese your way around a level is amazing. We saved a paladin just by teleporting everyone up to the second floor of the castle, then knock down the ladder, and then sneak to the front door... only to get prepared for a massive fight just before the doors swing open and  a Knight and Battle Mage just flat out turn into hulking battering rams that decimate the first guy they see. The amount of planning that you can make for a battle is amazing... I even got a chance to set up environmental hazards for the enemies by moving poison barrels and oil barrels ahead of a fight.
-The sneaking system is hilarious, but well maintained. Seeing a lizard tail poke out from under a barrel makes me giggle. The enemy vision scales down with higher thievery skills.
-The turn based fighting system is the best I have seen yet. It really feels like a ton of heart and effort has gone into this portion of the game. You need to see it to understand just how much it is like a legitamate DnD pen and paper style turn based system. It brings that niche genre to an immediate resurrection and breathes new life into it. Trust me, if you get this game for any reason, and you like turn based strategy, this is the very reason to get giddy like a damn school girl. The battle system alone is a game changer and was an insta buy for me and my friend.
-Choices, choices, choices. Choose wisely or shoot yourself in the foot... or shoot your friend in the foot... or shoot that annoying cat and feed it to the elf. I'm not joking, that cat is in the way all the time. I can't go 5 seconds without accidently lighting it on fire. The dialogue system is very well done and the choices you make will certainly matter. You can miss massive side quests that actually are very important to the overall story and your well being. Other mission and quests are just there to get your butt into a ton of trouble just because you said "what's the worst that could happen?". Everything... Just be careful with your choices. You may also live with any and every choice you make. Bad decisions can follow you and from the looks of it, can have consequences on the quests that get closed off because someone had a bad attitude with you or they got shanked unsuspectedly when you were looking the other direction. However, even bad decisions seem to lead down some interesting paths.
-Dialogue is absolutely amazing. Every character and NPC I have met so far is voiced and has a good feeling to their emotions. They always feel genuine, so far. I have yet to meet an NPC that had seemed overly annoying or out of place. The voice actors have done a really good job. My favorite part is the narrator, who has a soothing englishman's accent and doesn't feel snobby. Once again, props to the voice actors.
Neutral:
-Have yet to experience the Game Master mode, yet the tutorial makes it out to be a true Dungeon Master style with 4 players under the control of the DM. You can make full campaigns and there are a literal sh*t ton of options. Just look up Game Master Tutorial on YouTube, which was made by the devs, and you'll see what I mean.
-If you don't pick one of the Main Characters, you may be missing out on massive parts of the story. Do not worry. If you create a custom character, you still have the option of taking 3 of the main characters along in your quests. Each main character has their own story and ambitions. Be sure to pay attention to them as they may lead you down some very interesting paths.
Cons:
-I am legit am coming up short for things I do not like. There were some minor bugs when the game first released, but the devs seem to have a fast response time and are working diligently on most of the problems we were experiencing. In fact, most of the major issues disappeared on the first week. Sooooo... these are not the cons you are looking for...

I was a bit hesitant to buy this game after reading the reviews about the map scaling being wonky compared to ETS2. I actually waited a week or so after release, then decided to go ahead and buy it. I have zero regrets. This game is absolutely enjoyable, as it is an entirely different experience driving in ATS than it is ETS2. I still play ETS2, and will always have a fond love for that game.
The graphics are gorgeous, the trucks are even more so, and if you're new to ETS/ETS2/ATS, then I highly recommend you buy this (even ETS2, while you're at it). I have few gripes about the game, including the map scaling which really doesn't bother me all that much; the on-ramps on freeways are extremely short and not at all realistic, but again it doesn't detract from the game as a whole. Perhaps my biggest gripe would be the lack of states out of the gate. I understand there is a lot behind this game already, however, Arizona is the last free DLC that will be added to the game, which is still a few months away from release. It would have been nice if SCS would have done the entire Western United States as free DLC, maybe Arizona, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Wyoming, Idaho, Washington, and Oregon. Then had gone from there, just so there is quite a lot of distance to cover while they work on cranking out the paid DLC.
Regardless, I love this game. While I have low hours played on it, don't let that deter you any. I play a variety of other games and love to give them equal attention. If you're able to, I suggest getting a steering wheel with pedals to add to that realistic touch. I play on a gaming laptop, so I have to use the keyboard which if you don't have the option of getting a steering wheel, still get this. Keyboard is still fun and the only thing you may have trouble with is backing the trailer up into position.
I know this review is a bit scatter brained, and I apologize if it is a hard read. I hope with the paid DLC that they do it in regions, such as Mid-West, Eastern, etc., and not state-by-state. The game itself is $20, so I am hoping that the paid DLC stays under that price range. Get this game. You'll enjoy it, and have a blast.

I've had a lot of fun with Chivalry. In its golden age, there were always players looking to improve, clans to scrim against and tournaments which were rare but kept the competitiveness growing.
Those days are long over. If you're looking to play casually with some friends or by yourself the game is a good pickup, but taking it any further than that is a mistake.
The servers, for instance, are horrible. Chivalry truly shines in 1v1 up to 5v5, but the servers you will find popular these days have over 40 slots, causing massive instability. There are some duel servers around, but even they have flaws, such as poor hosting, manipulative admins and low tick rates.
While the experience you will have while playing chivalry will be massively influenced by your connection, many players are ignorant in this regard and will play with packet loss, which causes a lot of issues within chivalry. This is surprisingly common among players who consider themselves "high level" and is extremely frustrating to play against.
The community is extremely against feinting, likely due to the huge amount of third person players who believe playing without feints is more skillful, which is absolutely not the case. There are no Mercs (Mercenaries) servers in Australia because of this, which is a mod created to balance and change the game around the feint mechanic, increasing the quality of high level play.
If you like the sound of Chivalry and wish as i do that there was a decent melee fighting game, check out Mordhau. The game is being developed by experienced players from the chivalry community to create the game we've all been longing for.

Owlboy is one of my favorite games of the year. This game features some of the most beautiful artwork of any game I have played in recent memory. The soundtrack is awe-inspiring and it hasn't been been since I was a young boy playing Chrono Trigger on the SNES that a band of pixelated heroes had felt so... real. There are times in the game that you will be reminded of the classics from yesteryear; there are hints of Zelda, Rayman, Metroid, Castlevania but Owlboy always feels distinctively it's own thing. There are a few questionable mechanics in the game. One of your companions has a recharge rate on their weapons that can be absolutely maddening. Though I'm not quite sure whether this is a bug or a feature as it lends to every single one of your companions being indespensible, never being able to rely completely on one single companion. The story remains the single best thing about this game. It covers themes of loss, failure, inadequacy, and learning to have hope in hopeless times in ways that no other medium could. If you enjoy SNES era games or story-rich indie titles Owlboy is a must play. 9.5/10

For a game with such an incredibly action packed, electryfying soundtrack, the gameplay itself it rather slow. Usually exploring a level will follow the same rhythm: See a small group of enemies charge at you from a certain location on the map,  find cover and take care of them, gather the loot they dropped and repeat until you accomplish whatever your objective was on that mission and move on to the next one. Some levels are "special" in that they deviate from that formula. One in particular makes it so that if you take too long to beat a level, you self destruct, plain and simple; And as crazy as it might sound, i honestly think this should've been every single level in the game. Because only that time limit is the only thing in the game that lets you feel the emergency and adrenaline the soundtrack tries so desperately to convey.
Although the developers have been listening to their community during early access and have adressed some issues, one problem that never felt like it was properly tinkered are the boss and how crushingly difficult they are. It's very easy to get instantly demolished by a boss that uses a certain attack pattern that takes you completely off guard, and in my experience the only way to deal with them in a consistently efficient manner is to use all of the money you get throughout your run to buff your weapons and equipment to the max, and just play as aggressively as possible against the boss to bring its health to zero as soon as possible. This makes it so that bosses never feel unique like they do in games like Nuclear Throne, they just feel like the same big machine just with different guns and grunts every time.
I really wish steam reviews had a neutral rating for games like this because despite all of its flaws it's still very fun to play. But i feel like half of that fun is just listening to the game's soundtrack. Like seriously, before you argue please try to play the game with the music off. It's a whole other experience, and not in a good way.
To conclude: if you're the type of person who can put up with an game's flaws and enjoy it for what it is, neurovoider is not a worse game than any other roguelike on steam. But from my point of view, the only thing that really separates it from every other roguelike that's come out on steam recently is the amazing music. Sadly, that's not what i'm reviewing.

Hard Reset provides a sugary love letter to fans of the no holds barred, 12 gun carrying, wall to wall shooting and explosions shooters of the past; however in doing so it still maintains a modern identity of its own.
In a market teeming with ironsight, cover system and squad command based first person shooter games (which are all of very high quality), it's intreresting to see a game chisel away the layers of peripheral gameplay features that have been slowly added one by one to make modern shooters what they are today and deliver a no nonsense fight-to-survive action rollercoaster. There's no aiming down sights, no taking cover or even crouching for that matter, no huge expansive environments, no mediocre plot that's trying to hard. There is a story and some really nice graphic novel-esque FMVs, but it's clear that this is a game all about playing.
Imagine anything from the family of original first person shooters like Wolfenstein or Quake, just with high end graphics and a weapon modulation and upgrade system. But the core of the game is just you, your gun and a boatload of mechanical gribblies that want to saw you to pieces. This is a very neat game.

After completing my first playthrough of this game, I must say it is one of my favorite games I highly recommend it.
Pros:
- The art style is fantastic, this is an example of a game that doesn't need realistic graphics to be amazing.
- It is a challenge, while some missions are easy, some of them require a ton of planning and working with multiple strategies on the off chance something goes wrong, which will likely happen.
- Engaging story, the story, for the most part, is very immersive, you'll grow to like some characters, and hate others.
- A ton of play styles, other than the limited class amount, you can play with almost any style that you wish.  Do you want to have only machine gun carrying troops, you can.  Do you want to play with only a tank and a sniper, you can.  You aren't forced to play a certain style, while some styles may be more effective than others, any strategy is possible.
- Option between having the characters speak Japanese or English.  While some may not bother switching the spoken language, it is an option.
- No level grinding required, there hasn't been a point in the game where I required playing the optional missions to beat a level, and I didn't ace every mission before hand, in fact, over half of my missions were C rank, which is normally the average rank for taking out every enemy before getting the end objective.
Cons
- The game doesn't explain stuff well at certain points.  During my full playthough, I have gotten two game overs due to the fact that unless you are the very observant, you can completely miss some required parts that either makes your mission very difficult, or just lead to an instant game over.
- Random Number Generator, while you can heavily influence many things randomly generated, it still exists, there are many times where I have had to hold back a turn instead of advancing because the troops are horrible at aiming.
- The game rewards rushed strategies more than safer.  The game's ranking system is very weird, due to the fact that you can rush the end of the level with a scout and get an A rank while taking out every enemy and eliminating many threats will reward a lower rank.
While this isn't technically a con, there is an achievement that is difficult to get, not that it is actually difficult to get, but because late game, where you are attached to your squad (and the possibility of the achievement opens), the choice of which unit to sacrifice for it is one that I myself personally refuse to get, I will achieve everything else in my multiple playthroughs though.  Unless of course, one person in your squad ends up costing you a mission and you want them to suffer, but who would ever do that.
As a result, this is a game that you will put many hours into, unless you aren't a fan of the game, but there will always be those games to some people.  I've honestly had less fun playing games that cost $50 while this is $20, and I will be going back to this for multiple playthroughs.

It's wrong to say that Hard Reset is bad; I just personally cannot recommend it.  It does have several good points - i like the setting, it provides a decent challenge at higher difficulty levels, and it actually doesn't look too bad.  Also, the environmental kill system is pretty fun - the game actually encourages the player to go more for these kind of kills, rather than going for accurate, individual kills.
In saying that, there are many things I am not fond of: not least of which is the movement - the feedback from movement makes Hard Reset seem like a mid-90s game. In fact, the basic structure of the game feels like that. After every level (there's not a huge number of them) you are given stats of how many of the enemies in the level you killed, how many of the secrets you found in the level, and such.  To me, it felt slightly lazy, as if there was no real interest in providing something new.  The other thing that bothered me, being a player hugely interested in narrative, was that the story was largely forgettable - in fact I'm still not sure what went on!
One final word - the addition of the extra content makes this a slightly better package than it would have been, but still, in my opinion, it remains largely mediocre, and that is something I cannot recommend

First off, If you're not a fan of anime, this is probably not the game for you. However, if you do enjoy it or just don't mind it, then there’s a lot to love here. Think if X-Com and Code Geass had a very drunken one night stand, and you'll get an idea of what this game is.
Pros:
-Very engrossing story, especially if you enjoy WW2 history
-Great main characters, with a surprising amount of depth
-Minor Characters with layered back stories, which make you feel bad for letting them die
-Beautiful art style
-Interesting tactical system, with all unit types having uses throughout the story
-Character perk system leads to having to tailor your squad to the mission. Or just roll with an all Waifu army. Whichever floats your boat
-Deals with some heavy **** really well
-Hitting that last ditch shot across the map feels so very good
Cons:
-The A.I. Is not the best, and can make stupid decisions at times. Nice if it helps you win a level, but could be disappointing for strategy buffs
-Some missions contain high amounts of BS (Units that appear from nowhere, invincible enemies, etc.)
However, you can cheese the game right back, so there's that)
-You have to play inventory Tetris for tank upgrades (Not too bad, but I really hate it when games do it)
-Rankings based on turns to complete mission rather than a better metric for skill
-Tank controls can be terrible. Sometimes you'll spin around for no reason, or get stuck on nothing. Not game breaking, but can be annoying nonetheless.
-Voice acting can't be muted via the menus, even though Music and FX can. (Another pet peeve. I like to listen to my music while skirmishing)
-Save system is a little clunky
In summary, it's a really great story and characters, with combat that’s a bit clunky, with occasional sections of BS, which in the end is a really enjoyable game.

Can't stop playing! It's too good! I haven't been this engrossed in a video game since Witcher 3.
The various systems of the game are so well crafted, and open up so many possibilities both in terms of combat and how to deal with quests.
The tag system and large dialogue options allow for proper roleplaying.
There's a TON of things to do, and none of them are of the "icon clearing" variety found in your typical open world GTA/Ubisoft AAA bore.
The writing is very solid, it doesn't take itself too seriously and it's very funny, but deals with serious subjects (racial tension, faith, abuse of power etc...) in a mature way.
The music is also seriously underrated.
The graphics are good in terms of the environments, but I guess I'm a not a big fan of the character models. The faces are quite ugly, and the fact that every "finesse"/rogue armor pieces are baggy pants and sleeves kinda irks me, it doesn't look very light and stealthy. A very minor gripe however, since we don't spend too much times looking are our heroes up close.
I've read that some people have encountered broken quests, and I guess it can be expected at launch given the insane number of them and unlimited possibilities (you can literally kill any NPC, steal any item etc...), but personally the only issue of that kind that I've encountered was just a completed quest (I got the item rewards for it) that didn't clear out from my quest log (The Imprisoned Elf).
I'll just finish by going back to how good and fun the combat is, the interactions between the different elements is a fantastic sandbox to play, and sometimes horribly fail, in. The AI is not exempt from that, I cried laughing last night when an enemy rogue went invisible and promptly revealed himself by falling on his butt after sliding on an ice patch he had created moments before!
There are so many builds to be created and ways to approach a fight (including not fighting it at all sometimes, either through dialogue or sneaking/thievery), I can't see myself getting bored anytime soon!
The replayability seems huge as well, since you can have very different questlines depending on who you bring along in your party and who you're playing as your main character.
TLDR:
Fantastic RPG, breathes fresh air into the genre, most fun turn based combat this side of XCom, gives you a ton of freedom and fun with it's system. Serious GOTY contender!

Conan Exiles,
Seems to have recieved quiet some bad reviews upon launch. Are they valid? Let's see,
As soon as my install got done I launched the game, watched the intro and couldn't wait to unleash the barbarian within me. The very barbarian I saw jumping across the screen when I was just a kid when Schwarzenegger played the role.
Those where the days, those where the heroes and that same feeling got hold of me again.
So, I couldn't be bothered with online teensitting. Time to go solo. Barbarians don't need no backup. I will show the world what it means to be Barbarian..or not..
So, before you embark there's this character creation system. It's more fleshed out than the one that comes with Ark and fits the Conan the Barbarian (80's) theme just right.
You can even choose a deity, although it isn't really clear if that plays a major role or not. You do get some bonus if you choose a god, but not all descriptions are that clear. Probably only to those who're really into Hyboria lore.
Anyway, on with the game.
As soon as you spawn you get this familar feeling that you've seen this and done that in Ark, or other good survival games. Than again, you see things which are just better than in Ark.
What? is that possible!? yes, it is. As a matter of fact, I like the GUI much, much better in Conan if I compare it to Ark's. It provides me with more info and looks more pleasing. Also, almost all items have an information button. That is pretty nice, since I'm a sucker for lore and story.
But, alright, who cares what i like, how does the game play?
It plays Unreal Engine Pre-Cooked.
If you don't know what that means, read it up and stop complaing about lag spikes.
The reason why the game jitters or hangs from time to time has nothing to do with bad quality, bad design or you having a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ rig. Its'due to loading pre-cooked data. Check your install directory and you'll see what's happening.
Does that make sense:
Hell yes that makes sense. It makes for easier and faster updating and patching from the developers side. meaning: "We work on this game and we do our best to deliver" Later, they're going over to cooked versions, just as with Ark, Rising Storm, or any other big Unreal Engine game. But, for now, it's prefectly legit. Epecially because it's Early Access.
How does it look:
The game looks good. There's a pretty clear direction along the design and the game world is interesting enough to keep exploring. Even if it's a bit small right now. Not very small, but too small if you want to do all out clan wars with big groups of players. For solo and co-op it's fine.
Are the graphics as good as the screenshots? Almost, I cranked it all up to maximum and got pretty close to the screenshot quality. So, that's okay in my book. Even more than okay.
How does it sound:
Just awesome, there's some serious sound engineering going on within Conan Exiles and it shows that a pro company is behind it. From the cutting down of a tree to the beheading of an unfortunate soul. It sounds great. Nothing wrong here.
How does it feel?
Oh..hmm..here it comes..
"Hey, this feels like a total conversion mod of Ark"
What I mean is that many things are just 1:1 the same (By execution) They don't seem to be copied, just kept in. That's also why I'm not sure if this is really a Conan / Hyboria worthy game at the moment.
Because, let's face it; playing as weapon swinging barbarian means you know how to do combat. Well, the combat is to basic. Block, attack, dodge bla bla. Nothing technical here. Just a button smasher. Not engaging enough if you ask me.
I need directional sword control like in Dark Messiah. Technical and fast. That's what defines a warrior. Not just some crude button smashing.
And due to that messy, too simple fighting I find myself playing just another survival game.
But, okay, besides of that I think the game is well on it's way to become a nice mix between a role playing and survival game. Especially with the many options to host your own server straight out of the box. Adjust anything to your liking and hit play. Yes, you can use scripts and such, but this is just better service and more friendly.

I highly recommend this game! It's free to play, with multiple endings; you will get the most out of this experience if you play it all in one sitting. Although the concept is really nothing new (a tale of unrequited love and the anguish it can cause), the game presents this concept in a unique way. I would love to see this game expanded upon because it really leaves you wanting more.
The sprites are adorable and the sound/music really helps set the tone. The writing, despite a few grammar errors here and there, is simple but adds realism in the dialogue between characters (and the inner thoughts of the main character). The humor is a nice touch, which juxtaposes very well with more disturbing elements later on. This game doesn't rely on blood or jumpscares to frighten you. The sense of fear is cumulative; like a chill slowly running up your spine which gradually increases as the game progresses.  If I had to compare it to another game, I would say it reminded me of "Hello?...Hell...o?"
Confess my Love involves a lot of experimentation, perfect timing, close attention to minor details, interesting puzzles to solve and plenty of trial-and-error gameplay. The entirety of the game takes place in a single setting, with only three characters. The minimalistic approach and seemingly innocent story really lulls you into a false sense of security. You think you know what will happen next, or you think you know exactly what to expect. But there's a lot more beneath the surface!

It can get a little repetitive if you play enough, but mixing things up with custom settings usually makes for a really fun, albeit frustrating, experience. And as more maps are added it gets better. Definitely worth it for the price, even if you don't play it too often

It really is awful and makes the game very frustrating, the map design probably isn't helping with it either.
OVerall it is an okay game, but it's worse than ETS 2. So if you don't own ETS 2 already I suggest you purchase (and play!) that before you buy this one.

When I first started playing Mass Effect 2 I hated it. I had just finished the first game and the changes were jarring: levelling works differently, all the controls have been overhauled, and I found the first hour of the game pretty dull. I'm not sure why I stuck with the game, but I did, and man am I glad. Turns out Mass Effect 2, while weaker in many areas than the first one, is a great game. Yes, its RPG elements are dumbed down, yes there is a greater focus on FPS elements, and yes the opening chapter is a bit lame, but it pulls everything together beautifully in the end and makes for a great, entertaining, solid entry into the franchise. If you're like me, and you loved the first game, but after an hour of playing you still don't feel like the second one is for you: stick with it. It's worth it. And you will be rewarded for your patience.

In the end, seriously worth giving a try.  Even if every mechaninc doesn't gel for you, theres still a ton to look at and explore here.

I will recommend Hand of Fate, but certainly not without qualification.  Many elements of this game involve the RNG - the success/failure card picks, the combination of enemies you face in a given encounter (and the environment in which you face them), the weapons/magic/blessings/armor you have access to in a given game.  All of this can lead to a very frustrating experience.  You may desire to complete a "quest," only to find that you can't seem to get the "success" card multiple times in the card game. Sometimes, you won't even see the quest card that game.  Perhaps I should've seen all this coming? I enjoyed the Arkham Asylum-esque combat, and the ability to create both your equipment and encounter decks. My main recommendation would be simply to quit after you finish the campaign. Tying up the lose ends, even if you enjoy the game, may be more trouble than it's worth.

Owlboy is a game developed and published by D-Pad Studios. Owlboy is an adventure in the truest sense of the word. You'll explore, fight baddies, gain power-ups, and make friends all throughout a wonderful world and story. The art direction is gorgeous, the animations of the characters and enemies are fun to watch, the music is a treat to listen to, and the story is a great mix of silly fun, abject terror, and heartwrenching moments. When I say that Owlboy is a great game, I really mean it
That being said, the game is not without it's faults, by far the biggest being it's difficulty, which is all over the place. You'll breeze through some sections of the game only to be utterly crushed by others. While checkpoints are liberal, you'll be tearing your hair out through some sections of the game trying to figure out what to do, and the lack of difficulty options certainly doesn't help. Exacerbating the issue is that while cutscenes are skippable, some mid boss fight conversations are not, and the aforementioned emotional scenes rapidly lose their luster as your forced to watch them over and over again as you die repeatedly to the more difficult bosses
Also, don't be fooled into thinking this is a metroidvania game. While it is heavily exploration focused, and you can be rewarded for revisiting previously visited areas, the game is actually quite linear, and there isn't much reason to play it multiple times if you aren't going for 100% fully finished game
Owlboy is a modern day classic, and other indie developers need to loot to it as a gold standard for what can be done with both the platforming genre and pixel art. Owlboy is an indie classic!

Crusader Kings II (CK2) is best described as a medieval political simulator, which doesnt really sound very exciting or do the game justice. This is a different breed of strategy game, where it isnt about building the biggest army and going round painting the map your colour. You can 'win' the game without fighting a single battle, you can topple empires through sheer use of intrigue, and win wars without fielding a single troop.
CK2 lets you pick any point between 769 (with DLCs) and 1453 and then pick any living character in that time period to play as - from great historical figures like Charlemagne or Ragnarr Lofbrook, to a random baron in middle francia with just a humble castle to his/her name. You (the player) play as the dynasty of that character, so when he/she dies, you continue playing with their heir, who will (hopeully) inherit a lot of the titles that daddy owned. I say 'hopefully' because exactly what you stand to inherit depends on things like the inheritance laws in your budding empire, not to mention different marriage rules and other factors. Some government types are restricted to specific inheritance laws - if you are commanding a disorganised tribe then there is a very good chance that it will break off and fracture, meaning that successfully 'unifying' the tribes needs to be done within the lifespan of one character. Unfortunately you may then be blessed with a king with horrible traits who everyone hates, who clings onto life desperately, refusing to drop dead. This is a game where you will probably at times WANT your character to die so you can start playing as the next of kin - a younger, perhaps more suitable ruler.
Yes, CK2 is a rather complex game to put it mildly, and there isnt much in the way of a tutorial. Therefore it is STRONGLY recommended that you check out some youtube videos aimed for beginners. While you are at it, check out the video of someone conquering the world playing as a sentient horse. Yes, historical accuracy is rife here, but with an understanding of a couple of the more amusing loopholes in the game, you too could become an immortal horse emperor. But I digress...
CK2 is a rather unique game, and one that other large scale strategy games (such as the Total War series - which I also love) could really learn a thing or two from. The level of intrigue, diplomacy and 'cunning plans' available here is one that I have never seen any other game come close to. Want to go to war? You gonna need Casus Belli (cause for war) buddy - and what you stand to actually gain from that war depends on that justification used. A system of 'claims' is used for the various provinces in the game. If your character (or one of his vassals/courtiers) doesnt have a claim on that piece of land, you cant go to war for it.
Final thing worth mentioning here are the mods. CK2 has mod support, and some of the total conversion mods that I have played are excellent. The mechanics and style of the game lend themselves superbly to the political, scheming landscape of Game of Thrones - and you will be pleased to know there is a fantastic total conversion mod that turns the world into Westeros, with various start dates depending on whether you are up to date with the books/TV show or not. As a prince of the Iron Islands, I successfully captured Daenerys and forced her into becoming my salt-wife and bear my children - and thus my firstborn pirate son inherited the Iron Throne in one fell swoop. Or was that just a dream I had the other night?
There is also a Lord of the Rings conversion mod available which I am fond of. All sorts of traits and 'features' are introduced to mimic middle earth, so Elves are immortal and Treants cannot reproduce, and neither can marry filthy orcs.
Anyway, back to topic, this is an excellent game and quite unlike anything else you are likely to play. The game is a bit dated, but it isnt really a game that relies on graphics whatsoever, and it is still fully supported with fresh DLC still being released. All I can say (other than the above) is watch a couple of tutorial videos on Youtube and see if it looks like your cup of tea. Speaking of which, I took so long writing this that my own tea is now stone cold. And I only did it for that cursed Steam awards completion. Bah.

Valkyria Chronicles commits one major sin as a strategy game: it expects you to follow a certain order of steps in order to complete any given map. You *can* beat the maps in a variety of ways--and the game will rate you poorly for it. Setting up chokepoints with scouts, blitzing with soldiers, sabotaging enemy tanks with Lancers... you can be as smart as you want, VC won't like you unless you play how *it* wants.
If you can get past that, you'll find an amazing title here. Lead artist Raita is a little odd in how he draws women (boobs do not work that way, good sir), but there's no faulting the amazing visual style and setting for this game. For something set in as mined-out a concept as World War II, Valkyria Chronicles is far more engrossing in its visuals and music than its concept will make you think. Gameplay-wise, Valkyria Chronicles is also quite inviting in its combination of real-time third-person action and turn-based gameplay.
Many of the fun content in Valkyria Chronicles--different weapons for recruits, for example--are hidden in out-of-the-way areas and will need a guide to be found, and the odd sense that you're not playing as the game wants you to will haunt you, but Valkyria Chronicles is a game that is definitely worth your time and money.
