Summary:
An old-school shooter to the core with beautiful cyberpunk environments, challenging combat, waves of enemies and a unique weapon system. Held back by awful voice acting, awful music, cheap cutscenes and a half-hearted story that explains little. Unfortunately, you often feel powerless against the chaos because there are no effective ways of dodging, it's easy to get trapped in a corner or have one of the countless explosive hazards set off a deadly chain reaction. Defeating certain enemies is very difficult without specific weapons which you may not have bought earlier. But if you're here purely for the vintage shooter action, you won't be disappointed, as it offers plenty of challenge.
The full story:
Hard Reset is a real mixed bag, and certainly not for everyone. It's an old-school shooter to the core, featuring only minimal controls and no extra bells and whistles, just you and waves of robotic enemies. The enemies, even on normal difficulty, can be quite challenging and are good at dodging attacks. They love to ambush you at every turn, flank you, and can quickly whittle down your health if you don't keep moving; you must always be ready for a battle and think on your feet to survive. There are different types, some which explode in your face, others which charge at you, and some that stay at a safe distance and snipe away... with rockets. The few boss fights are challenging and old-school as well, involving glowing weak points and waves of minions, but when you learn their pattern you feel unstoppable. For the most part, combat is challenging, but fair; if you fail, you know it's your fault. On the other hand, the little guys are a lot more troublesome because they love to hide and ambush you, get right in your face and when they die, they cause damage if you're that close. Every single room in the game is filled with destructible objects which either explode or cause electrical damage, so you can imagine that one stray bullet, even from the enemy, often sets off a chain reaction of things exploding in your face. At times like these, the game feels unfair. Dodging or jumping doesn't always save you, enemies sneak up behind you with ease and it's easy to get trapped in a corner, so many situations turn into trial-and-error. Some enemies love to hang out at a distance behind cover and are difficult to destroy with anything but one or two weapon types which you can't even buy until later on. Rockets and mortar shells constantly fly at you and FPS logic tells you that if you're behind cover or sprint several feet away from its impact, you'll be safe... but not always. Enemy projectiles' splash damage has a ridiculous reach.
Your own weapons are still formidable, however. You get only two (with separate ammo types), but a whopping five firemodes apiece, each of which is designed for certain situations. You have the minigun, grenade launcher, rocket launcher, railgun, shotgun, proximity mines and my favorite, the smartgun which detects enemies and shoots through walls. You can also upgrade your weapons, health and armor through seamless first-person terminals, using experience you collect from combat and finding secret areas. But even if you fully upgrade your health and shield, it's not by much; Hard Reset doesn't hold your hand and the only assurance you have is frequent checkpoints and no game over. The only guidance you have is a vague objective and the occasional voiceover communication.
Speaking of which... the voice acting is awful. With the exception of one guy, it's just ingenuine and unenthusiastic. The music is also total crap, consisting of the occasional ambient pad and a bunch of random futuristic drilling noises, like a robot dentist's equipment. Apparently, the composer didn't care either, but at least it lets you know when you're entering a fight. There is actual music when action begins, but it's your average, generic attempt at sounding futuristic: lots of synths, breakbeats and the occasional guitar. Completely forgettable at best, grating at its worst.
The sound on the other hand, is great. Every little object you bump into sounds real, the sound of robots exploding into piles of scrap is satisfying and the weapons sound appropriately futuristic and cool.
The visuals are gorgeous. That should be obvious considering it's on the Unreal 3 engine, but the environments look amazing. The dystopian city of Bezoar stretches out around and above you, massive and intricate, triggering memories of Blade Runner or Hong Kong from Deus Ex: Human Revolution. So many scenes in this game deserve that you stop and just take a  look around. It's such a shame then, that this game is fast-moving and direct by its very nature. The models and textures are beautiful; things that anyone would be proud to put on their resume. Most props fully utilize the Havok physics engine and behave realistically, never once glitching for me. The layout of certain objects in certain places doesn't always make sense, but it's still cool to see things fly everywhere in the heat of battle.
I'll mention the story last because it's not important. In fact, it's barely there at all. In between levels, what little plot there is is expounded through cutscenes which look suspiciously like rough draft cinematics; you know, a comic book of moving sketches designed to give an idea of what the finished, pre-rendered cutscene will look like. But there's a difference between stylish, comic book cutscenes (see: Beneath a Steel Sky, Max Payne 2) and a rough draft someone never finished. Anyway, the story has something to do with a network of digital personalities, the big, faceless, evil corporation that controls it and robots that want it. Very little is ever explained, leading to more confusion. But again, it's not that important because when you're playing, you only get a vague objective to strive for and the occasional voiceover telling you what to do next, very little context or exposition. And that's another thing: The environments, visuals and sound design make me want to explore this world, understand it, spend some time in it, but that just ain't gonna happen.
It's a very short game too; if you spend no time collecting secrets and are better at staying alive than me (which is likely), you'll blaze through it in no time and wonder what the Hell just happened. The Exile DLC is included, although it's more like "almost half the game the developers didn't have time to finish before release". Seriously, it's a continuation of the main game, and if you don't have the DLC, it ends abruptly after a boss fight with no explanation. Still, it's free, so you can't complain too much. It also takes you outside the city, into outdoor environments like a machine scrapyard full of encroaching greenery, introducing a few new pesky and challenging foes in the process. Still, it's quite short and (at least for me) becomes a grind, repetitively blasting away, clicking a panel, walking forward, rinse and repeat. Once you complete normal, more difficulties open up along with a survival mode.
But like I said, this game isn't for everyone. If you love old-school shooters but want a modern presentation, if you want a good challenge and can stomach some unforgiving mechanics and if you love cyberpunk settings but can deal with a minimal story, this should be right up your alley.

Let me say that first, I love everything about this game. It has everything I could possibly want:
1. House building
2. Boats of various kinds with naval warfare and fishing
3.Variety of mounts from traditional horses to cars
4.Variety of vocations
5.Classes are very nicely done, easy to switch and combine to make one that meets your taste.
6. Large open world
7. Plenty of companion animals
However can I recomend this game? No. There's three main reasons for this:
1. Labor system. The labor system is set up where pretty much anything cool you want to do requires it. Go fishing? Need labor. Mine resources? Need labor. Here's the thing: If you arent part of their "patron" status, where you purchase the monthly subscription, the amount of labor you regain is miniscule and only gained when you're actually playing. If you arent playing or just leaving your toon logged in, you dont gain labor.
Patron status however? Labor isnt an issue. Heck, get patron status and you'll even get exp buffs, etc... in short making the game where if you truly want to enjoy it, you need to get the subscription.
Case in point, my friend has played the a fraction of what I have and has already far surpassed my level because he has patron status allowing him to do things I had to wait to do. Happy as I am for him, its still insulting that because I don't spend money paying for this subscription, even if I put in double the amount of game time he does he will still surpass me just because of what a huge difference that subscription offers.
I'll be honest, I have no issues with subsciptions for F2P games, heck I did it on SWOTOR and I've never regretted it. I understand a company needs to make profit of some kind. But the labor system alone is what kills the whole thing.
2.Grind: I knew going in that MMOs always have a serious grind to them. But with Archeage and the labor system it takes it to the max. Building ships, house building, leveling; all of it is a huge grind after another.
3.Credit Car Warriors. Again, I have nothing against a company making profit, whether its through subscriptions or their online market. But on this? Doesnt matter if you spend a load of time working for something like that new piece of armor; someone can just use their credit card and bam, that stuff you worked hard for has been blown away.
Look at the Ollo Server for example: the largest guild KGB and its subsidaries are known for this.
Synopsis: I love the game, it has everything I could possibly want. However this is all ruined by greedy business practices. Will I still play the game? Yes. Though to the extent which I want to? No. Nor can I reconmend it. If you're looking to kill some time and spend quite a bit of money, then by all means, go for it. As for me, I'll stick to the F2P content.

Owlboy is a 2D puzzle-platformer about an anthropomorphic owl named Otus who finds himself unknowingly in the midst of a cataclysmic disaster millenia in the making. With the assistance of friends he makes along the way, Otus solves puzzles, shoots enemies, defeats monstrous bosses, and unearths dark secrets about the world he lives in.

In terms of gameplay, the only thing that sets it apart from other platformers is Otus' ability to carry one of his companions while in flight. Over the course of the game, you encounter 3 friends who accompany you on your adventure, each of which has a unique ability that can be used to gain access to previously inaccessible areas, solve puzzles, eliminate enemies, and avoid or circumvent obstacles. Although a novel mechanic, it is utilized in generally uninteresting ways, resulting in a gameplay experience that falls a bit flat.

The puzzles presented in the game aren't difficult in the slightest, and your companions' abilities are only used in the most surface-level puzzle-solving. Oftentimes, the puzzles come down to: use a companion's ability at this point to progress. Had more of the game's puzzle-solving revolved around switching between companions or combining their abilities in unique ways, the gameplay would have been much more enjoyable. However, this would have required fundamental changes to the story beats and progression as the first two companions are introduced in the first couple hours of the game. The third (and final companion) isn't unlocked until you are in the throes of the game's climax. To make matters worse, over the course of the game you periodically lose a companion, meaning that you only have a full party for what seems like the last hour or so. Despite the narrative justifications for this, it's frustrating that  one of the defining mechanics of Owlboy can only be fully utilized for the last hour or two of the game.

The story itself is filled with the charm and whimsy that you would expect from a game like Owlboy. The game's narrative follows Otus as he attempts to save his people from a cataclysmic event which gets increasingly dire as the game progresses. There are some unexpected turns in the story that kept it from being completely predictable, but at the end of the game it was a pretty standard "save the world from X because ancient people did Y" narrative you might expect from an animated children's movie. Although it falls victim to some fairly common narrative tropes, the story was compelling enough to keep me engaged and interested for its entirety.

Artistically, Owlboy is a masterpiece, and I struggle to think of a more perfect example of pixel-art done right. Whether soaring through the sky towards a floating continent, or dashing through lava-filled caves, every frame is a beautiful pixel-art painting. The environments teem with life as birds fly off into the distance, stars twinkle in the night sky, and the background and foreground slide along in some of the best examples of parallax scrolling I've ever seen. The character sprites and monsters are beautifully animated and brimming with personality that would make even Nintendo green with envy. The entire game is filled with screen-shot worthy moments that were composed with almost absurd attention to detail. Although the artwork in Owlboy is second to none, the soundtrack itself is a wonderful composition of scores that perfectly complement every scene. Lilting clarinets, violins, and cellos accompany Otus on his journey to save the world, instilling a sense of mysticism and serenity that is not often found in games.

Unless you're one for scouring every inch of a game in order to collect every single coin imaginable, once you're done with Owlboy there's no reason to come back. There is no "New Game+", unlockable content, or multiplayer. That isn't to say that it would need any of that. The journey is a short one at roughly 6-8 hours, but considering the overall shallowness of the gameplay, any longer and it would have been a slog. There's no question as to when the game will come to a close as the story ends in a textbook climactic fashion. With most of the narrative threads being wrapped up in the game's bittersweet conclusion, the ending of Owlboy feels nothing short of satisfying. It's not disappointing, nor is it powerfully moving. Instead it feels absolutely appropriate, a perfectly competent bookend to what was overall a thoroughly enjoyable experience.

Despite the lackluster gameplay and the occasionally frustrating traversal segment, Owlboy has stuck with me. From time to time I'll find myself whistling the main menu music or imagining the blue skies and gently swaying foliage of the introductory area, and I'm immediately reminded of the games from my childhood. 16-bit vibrant landscapes, colorful characters, and comical villain archetypes. Owlboy serves as a rose-tinted lens through which I retrospectively view the games of my childhood. It's nostalgic, charming, and beautiful.

Would you read or watch a trilogy and then stop right before the end? Do you like cliffhangers that will never be resolved? Do you like to having the feeling you are in control while playing a game, only to be railroaded into doing something stupid later on? No? Then this game is not for you. Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 are solid, if not excellent games. They have their flaws, but I can live with them. But it is a continuous storyline that runs across three games, not two. Mass Effect 3, the third installment, not available on Steam, but only on Origin, has a very controversial ending that ends the trilogy on a sour note. If you've somehow missed the controversy, just google Mass Effect 3 ending, read some of the many things that have already been said about it, and weep. Weep for the loss of something that could have been epic. Weep for the hurt feelings of countless gamers. Weep for the sorry fate of a couple of epic fictional characters, that felt like friends to so many of us.
If you think you will be able to live with the above and also love RPGs, and especially if you liked Mass Effect, then by all means, buy this game now, no hesitation, just make sure to get the Digital Deluxe Edition and the various add ons. Or just keep reading and then make up your mind.
Mass Effect 2 continues the story that began in Mass Effect, but with some changes. You need to assemble a new crew and won't be able to play with your friends from Mass Effect, with two exceptions, although there is DLC that will allow you to play, briefly, alongside Liara as well. A very large part of the game is spent assembling a team for a mission that will determine the fate of the Galaxy. Although it is a roundabout way, it does allow you to make new friends and new enemies alike. With a better game engine, the game looks far better than Mass Effect and is much less dated. You can now select additional actions, good or bad, to determine how your character, Shepard, is viewed. The various classes are structured differently from the first game and you no longer get a new weapon every 10 metres, there are far fewer flavours availble. But although it is certainly different from Mass Effect, it is not vastly different. The voice acting is excellent, the music is good, the storyline could be a bit better and straightforward, but is still very good. In and of itself, it is arguably the best game in the series.
The only real drawback of this game is the lack of a satisfying ending in Mass Effect 3. So be aware of that before you purchase this game.

Actually CK2 at its core is a good game. I played hundreds of hours offline and own most of the major DLC. But my gripe with this game is the poor quality of the recent DLC (and associated patches), each of them introducing (partly game-breaking) bugs and/or unfinished features which are hardly dealt with or not at all.
Examples includes the Decadence system introduces in one of the first DLC (Sword of Islam) which was not working as intended for (3?) years or the Converter for EU4 which was sold long time even it was known to be not functional . While the first few DLC are quite nice or at least ok, the quality of recent releases rapidly dropped i think with "Rajas of India", then "Charlemagne" and finally "Way of Life".
The latter one is just the most recent example of bad practise: Released just few days before Christmas "Way of Life" just not delivered poorly balanced features (e.g. insanely overpowered intrigue or seduction) but also introduced the so called "dismiss levies bug" which rendered the AI unable to declare war not only for the owners of the DLC but also for everyone else(due to patch)! That's a borderline rip-off considering that most people cannot play the game during the holidays until the developers choose to come back from their own around 6th of January.
EDIT: A patch was released which solved the levies bug and other major issues on 17th of January 2015.  Still, the bug forums are full and a lot of glaring issues remain untouched.  While admittely these bugs are minor compared to the levies bug, overall they are a serious annoyance (e.g. undisposable anti-popes and continous religious unrest) and the game is faaaaaar away from beeing stable or polished!
This is especially outrageous as a few days (Feb.2015) ago a total of 3 new DLCs for 2015 have been announced BUT the patches which should fix the old bugs have been tied to those patches. SO as the next DLC has not been announced in detail we are looking forward to even more months in which the game remains broken on so many levels!
TLDR: This is a negative response to Paradox bad practise of  constantly releasing hardly polished DLCs which introduce new (partly game breaking) bugs and/or features instead of addressing these issues! This full-price game (albeit costing 150 EUR with all DLCs and already about 3 years old) has become something that plays like a bug-ridden EARLY ACCESS title or BETA with many features not yet working as intended!

Initially, Glass Wing failed to live up to my already low expectations, but all that changed once I found the scythe. The primary use of the scythe is to hack away tall grass which, paired with the pots and the health icons, makes it clear that the game was heavily inspired by the Legend of Zelda series.
Glass Wing alternates between tricky platforming sections and "find the proper tool for the job and figure out how to use it" puzzles. Some of the platforming sections took me more than one attempt, but they weren't frustratingly difficult. As you progress through the game, you gain new platforming abilities, and since the developers know you have the ability, they designed the rest of the game with them in mind which makes things trickier as you go.
As for the puzzles, some took me a while to figure out and started to cause frustration, but once I figured out the solution they seemed rather clever. There are also monsters and they can be killed, but there is little point in doing so and they do not go down easy, so it's best to do as the game says and avoid them.
There are no collectibles or extra routes, so you're likely only going to make one run through and that should only take a few hours (less than 5). Still, I had fun during my time with the game, so if you aren't scared off by the visuals being what they are or the risk of finding the puzzles to be "too obtuse" rather than "clever," Glass Wing may be worth a go.

If you want a short review go to the bottom for a summary.
Glass wing is a 3D puzzle-platformer game where you play as a little fairy type creature called Mayfly. The game seems to be influenced from classic titles such as Orcarina of Time on the N64.
The game took me about 3-4 hours to finish, although short I do highly recommend purchasing this game.
It seems basic at first but give it a chance and you find yourself pleasently suprised with what it offers you.
So after starting (I won't ruin the other thing that happens :P) you will find yourself feeling like Link, minus the green, the sword, the flute, and you seem to be a bigger version of his fairy.
Alot of the beginning if traversing through some basic landscapes and getting introduced to the controls and certain elements of the game you will be seeing.
After a while you will notice you are picking up some glass wings that Mayfly lost in the beginning, collecting a number of these will start to give Mayfly some interesting abilities. A good point to make it once you acquire a new ability, you will find you need to use it quite often, unlike other typical games where you may only use it for the area you are in and then barely ever again. I find it nice where the game will build on what you have and force you to use everything to get further.
Using 'tools' you will find along the way you will be required to use them to help you solve some puzzles and continue through the game. You cannot put away items and you can only hold one item at any given time. Be aware that certain moves will cause you to drop your weapon, which is a nice feature.
Puzzles in the game are pretty clever and fun to interact with, I found myself rather impressed by a few of them. They will make you uses tools as often as possible, one in particular has a feature I didn't expect.
The landscape has some elements that will block your path or try to hinder you in certain scenarios, you will come across electric orbs and flooring, sludge, thorns and a couple of others. In certain scenarios they will be more annoying that others.
Monsters in this game are all dino-like, and they vary a little bit. Every monster is this game has aim hax (not kidding xD), stay clear as much as you can, although they will come for you within a certain distance. You can kill monsters (more effort than it's worth), but after a while you do get a nice health bar, also there is plenty of health around so you shouldn't die to monsters really.
The game's landscapes and levels are very nice and well thought out. The music is very nice to listen to and I found that each track suited the part of the game it was assigned to. Also I found the boss monster to be very impacting on this game, it made me want to run away all the time, maybe due to the first encounter you have with it.
Overall I think this is a very nice game to play and you really feel you are playing something from the 90's, if you grew up in that period of time you will really enjoy this.
Pros
+ Simple game that feels like a blast from the past.
+ Will keep you playing, keeps adding new elements to stop the repetitive feeling.
+ Interesting move set which you will enjoy using.
+ Easy controls
+ Great soundtrack
+ If you grew up in the 90's you should enjoy this
Cons
- Monsters hack :(
- The big monster also hax ;__;
- I got some slow down, usually when initially running the game, doesn't ruin the experience though.
- A single glitch is on the 3rd last section, there is an error message and you will not lose progress.
- If you are a graphics gamer (you know who you are) you might not appreciate this game.
8/10 :)

Valkyria Chronicles is among the most sombre jrpgs I've ever played. It's not depressing, but it is muted, by jrpg standards. Its characters speak in a constant concerned tone, even in moments of victory. The number of anime cliches it borrows can be counted on your fingers. Its colour pallett consists almost entirely of gun metal grays and desert sand browns. Its humour is often matted in irony, like Alicia's allusion to draft dodging every time she activates her ability Undodgable Shot - "Don't even think about dodging!"
Despite that, Valkyria Chronicles has a certain vibrance to it. The character design is where most of the charm comes from. To put this into perspective, Edy is a character with not even one line of dialog in the plot who is subject to permadeath if she goes down in battle and is one of over 30 avaliable characters you can have join your squad. Edy got her own DLC. That's honestly just how charming the average character is in this game - they don't all get their own side stories, but they could. Almost none of them look like capable soldiers, but that's all part of the story. Keep in mind this all takes place at the tail end of the war.
Once you take control of your soldiers, you've got a blend of turn based strategy games and a real time tactical shooter, the type where you go down in one or two shots if you get spotted. Since every unit in the game is ranged, most of the strategy revolves around finding cover and cutting off the angles so that the enemy can't advance. Valkyria Chronicles is at its best when, in the course of a larger battle, you're forced to hold a position until you can eek out an advantage by diverting the enemy's attention or landing a decisive blow. Occasionally it shoehorns you into these situations rather than letting them happen naturally, and these missions are a drag. It's also got a few battles that are overly scripted for story reasons which are too linear to really be called strategy, but there are a few scripted battles worth remembering, too.
It does not seem like bad game. It's easy to lose time in it.

DreadOut is a very cheap version of Fatal Frame, and it's sad because it could have been better. The problem is the lack of plot. If you want to fool around, killing evil spirits, it's perfect for you. But if you're searching for a game like Fatal Frame, you might be disappointed.

If you are the type that enjoys exploration and creative combat, there's a lot of value in this game. When I say a lot, I mean A LOT. I've sunk over 400 hours into this and there are still unique things to test and do. Story and the world itself has been quite interesting as well so the game is not just an encounter-after-encounter dungeon simulator with nothing else. There is a lot of replayability to the game, not to mention the online component and the potential there (ymmv depending on how much you like playing with others and who's available online).
Either way, D:OS2 is a steal at its asking price, considering how much you'll get out of it. It has a number of bugs here and there and can use a few more quality-of-life updates, but it's an incredible experience even now. Extremely highly recommended.

Fun game, but can be really frustrating, so best played in short bursts.  The  SURVIVED (i.e. You Win) screen  tells me I played for 114 minutes and died 433 times, but it honestly felt a lot longer than that.
This is one of those twitch/punishment platformers, though it's not exactly a platformer since you control a floating ball that can move about freely without worrying about gravity.  The goal is to make your way to the end of each of the levels without dying.  There are no checkpoints, and but the levels is pretty short.  Unlike other twitch platformers, you have a healthbar and most hazards will not kill you in one hit - being squished between moving walls/ is the common exception.  Your health also decreases over time, so it serves as an implicit time limit even in the relatively few levels which don't have a huge moving wall (or Boss) chasing you.  Boosting (i.e. "running") makes the health decrease much faster, so it's best used only when needed.
Each level has collectible "krebs", and getting all of these greatly increases the challenge, but they are only useful for high scores and achievements.  After the first few levels, I stopped even trying collecting them all and focused instead on just surviving.
The game is HARD, and controls take a lot of getting used to.  The keyboard offers the most precise controls, but unfortunately a bug keeps you from being able to boost (speed up) while moving diagonally up-left, which makes a few levels impossible.  So yeah, that's definitely a minus.  But the rest of the game makes up for it in my opinion.   The gameplay, though frustrating, is still fun, I found the retro graphics quite nice, and the soundtrack is great.  After finishing it, I spent some time going back to a few levels to unlock some achievements, and see myself coming back over time to unlock more.

Righty, felt that now would be the best time to write an actual review with the release of act 2 and stuff. Never really written a review before but i felt to give a try, why not? So before we go any further, if you dislike indie games, horror games, cameras, or anything relating to those things; proceed no further! This game is filled with every single 1 of those things. Now for the pros/cons:
Pros:
Fatal Frame inspired gameplay
Very, Very Atmospheric and tense filled
Scary!
Neither pro or con:
Cheap jumpscares (besides the atmosphere which is done well, they throw in some cheap jumpscares to scare you, not something i enjoy in horror games but that is me, thankfully it is kept to a minimum)
Weak game length (5 - 8 hours but could be a solid time)
Cons:
Story is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(Starts off good then falls apart in act 2)
Gameplay can be repetitive (Horror games fix this with puzzle elements, this game has very little)
Graphics are meh (for those that care about visuals)
Characters aren't fleshed out well
In-depth review starts here, shorten review near the bottom with my score.
OVERVIEW: If you are expecting a top quality game, you will not find it here. However, this little gem is in a league of its own. Done by an indonesian company, Digital Happiness, this game takes elements from Fatal Frame, and silent hill and combines them to make Dreadout. You got the setting of Silent Hill and the gameplay of Fatal Frame, what more could you want!? Sounds so great and I have to say, the execution is solid and sound. While they were limited with what they have, they made more out of the little. When I first played this game, it was last year in like June when Act 1 was out on Steam. I bought it, played it and wanted more. I loved Fatal Frame and was happy to see another game use that same gameplay style.
GAMEPLAY: In this game, you don't "charge up" your camera to do extra damage, you find weakspots on ghosts and aim for those to do more damage. Ghosts aren't pushed back when you attack them, they merely appear elsewhere and can attack in 2 ways: Physical or Mental. Unfortunately though, that is pretty much the extent of gameplay here. You use a camera to attack weakspots and not much else. Puzzles are kept to an absolute minimum meaning you won't be doing much besides running around from point A to point B and snapping a couple ghosts. Their are some bosses that are unique in their own way but felt half done honestly. The "only" difference you will feel between ghosts is the number of shots it takes to kill them. Some take a couple, some take a lot. The only unique ghost i saw in the game that differ itself from others is when you had to use the environment to find him or use mirrors.
STORY:
EDIT: I will hold on to my previous review here of the story but it seems the developers took a route with an abstract story. Piece together the pieces scattered about and understand the whole picture. That seems to be what they intended for instead of just throwing everything at you. A nice touch but until more is understood properly, my view of the story will not change.
Another thing about horror games is the amount of files/documents you find to give you sense of backstory. In this game, that isn't possible. Their are FAR too few files to find in this game and most of them don't tell you exactly what happened at all before your arrival in town. I think I only found like 2 files that gave a hint to something about murder in the town but that is it. In Act 1, you get a decent amount of story that brings the characters into town and lose each other to Silent Hill. In Act 2, this is immediately forgotten and you have no clue what the heck is even going on. The story is no longer developed properly and the characters are completely forgotten (figuratively, not literally).
GRAPHICS: Not something I really want to go much into because unless you love visuals, graphics are on the low end for me. However, I won't leave it out. I have a decent machine so I can easily max this game out. Graphics, currently, are on the weak side because they have to be downgraded for 32-bit machines. They are expecting to release HD textures for 64-bits so I cannot judge properly on the asthetics.
ATMOSPHERE: Lastly, the thing that consitutes a good horror game is the type of atmosphere it delivers to its audience. I have to say, the atmosphere is spot on here. I felt very scared during the whole ride and couldn't help but be actually scared at some parts. The Silent Hill theme was good to give that sense of a ghost town as you walk through, not knowning what was going to happen. Unfortunately, that gets dropped for a night time travel for the rest of the game but that didn't bother me too much. I was walking slowly throughout the game, taking in my surroundings and watching my step. A couple characters gave that eerie feeling along the way like "did she do it or WTF WHAT THE HECK IS GOING ON WITH HER!?". Overall, the atmosphere is spot on, tension was everywhere, and the entire ride i didn't know what to expect, getting that wtf moment when everything got spooky.
Overall rating: 6/10
If you are looking for a game that delivers on atmosphere and a solid Fatal Frame type gameplay, by all means dive in. Its completely worth your time and money to be able to enjoy a solid Indie-developed horror game. I would highly recommend it over a lot of other AAA type out there (but if you had to choose between alien isolation and this, go with the former). You can tell the developers tried their best to make a solid horror game so for me, I hope they continue to deliver on other horror games of this type in the future.
Otherwise, i recommend moving on. The story is weakly developed, very few puzzles and not much is developed beyond the atmosphere part.

The mix of abstract rogue-like events drawn from a virtual deck of cards that is then played out in a Batman-esque fighting game makes Hand of Fate an easy game to recommend. The graphics are colorful, the sounds great and the voice over narration achieves something I've not seen in another game: an adversary that breaks the fourth wall and speaks directly to the player.
The Dealer concept works for several hours of play as a sort of mentor, antagonist, peer and philosopher, making all manner of observations and acidic quips. This masked character sets up the field of play, composed of upside down cards arranged in a variety of formations. You move a simple, game-board style pawn, like if Monopoly went all Dungeons & Dragons, navigating a limited number of routes to find the stairs to the next level.
The Dealer both taunts and encourages you along to a particular confrontation, completing a story-mode mission; or, in the case of endless-mode, the script runs short and he quickly begins repeating himself.
While the game offers a fair amount of loot and situations to encounter, and the developers do seem to be adding more of both, it is limited not just by this single narrator, the Dealer, but by a total lack of customization of your character. Every time you play, you look like a background character from Ragnar's troupe on Vikings. While the Dealer is faceless, your character is stamped with one single solitary, indelible look. Seeing options for both, even in the form of a DLC that included more encounter cards and such, would enhance the replayability and deepen the experience.
The combat keeps things fresh with relatively simple controls and a rock-paper-scissors structure of moves and counter-moves. Adding in the variety of effects such as freezing, cooldown reductions, stunning etc allows for a great many synergies to discover through repeated play. I did find the documentation of just how all these different statuses and statistics interacted to be lacking, but I don't think it ultimately effected my enjoyment of Hand of Fate.
For me, combining the abstract fantasy tropes of the encounter cards with the fun, colorful and continually improved-upon combat, hit that sweet spot of allowing for my own imagination (excepting for being trapped with the one skin) to exist alongside the developer's sense of imagination. Hand of Fate helped me imagine many fun, pointless, rollicking and satisfying fantasy beat'em ups, so I give this both thumbs up.

The killer problem, for me, is that the game is stuck in 600x400. I have tried everything I can think of, and have read all support pages, the developer's FAQ page, and in addition every Steam and Google page I can find containing the words "Hand of Fate" and "resolution." There have been lots of issues with this by other players, and also with windowing, wrong monitors displaying, and so on. Other people have complained about being stuck in resolutions HIGHER than 600x400 (wish that was my problem). None of the fixes work, at least for me. The steam launch option to select resolution does not help, in that the only selection available in the resulting launch menu is 600x400. This is true no matter what my computer's screen resolution is set to prior to launch - I have tried many different ones. Starting and switching out of windowed mode still only allows 600x400.
The 600x400 resolution makes it very hard, and at times impossible, to read the text on the cards. Plus, it just looks bad.
I should add that the very first time that the game played, it tried to display in higher resolution, but the graphics were too wide for the monitor at the higher resolution and the sides were cut off. I opened the in-game resolution settings, and as I was selecting alternative settings, the setting went to 600x400, and no other options since then will appear. I have deleted and downloaded the game and its local content again, to no avail. I can't delete or clear any save files or profiles, since they can not be found in the locations documented by the developers, maybe because I am running Windows 10, or maybe because there has been a recent patch, or maybe because they are now in Steam's cloud. Who knows.
I do understand that for most people, the resolution is not stuck.
I get the sense that the developers really cared about this game, and really tried hard, but I think they lacked the technical expertise necessary to make the game function well across so many different computer set-ups. I know this is a common problem. I'm glad I bought this on sale, because I lost only $8 instead of $25.

What's wrong with the game has to do with how Trion treats its playerbase, which is like complete and utter garbage. I'm not really going to say anything that hasn't already been said, but don't commit yourself to this game without being ready to shovel out a respectable amount of money-- probably more than you'd pay for an episodic series of any AAA title, when all's said and done.

This is actually the first review I've ever done for a game on Steam, and probably one of the first reviews I've ever done for a game period.
I can remember about 7-10 years ago I watched the first trailer of this game on Youtube and I thought, "meh, it'll probably just become abandonware like the Underside or something." I was thought it was cool, but I had no idea that they had been working on the game all this time. Then when it finally came out, words could not describe how excited and eager I was to buy and play. I was trying to save up some extra money for Christmas shopping and all that, but I couldn't fight temptation, so I payed for the game and was happy. My Christmas shopping went well but that's beside the point.
Anyway, playing this game, I have a lot of good things to say, but there's also things that did disappointed me.
STORY - 4/5
The story was interesting to say the least and you could definately see the humor here and there. It definately makes me happy that I played the game blind. I espeically loved the Buccanery scenes - just hilarious. The game as a whole is kind of like a good Disney movie when you think about it. I would go more into this, but I'd probably give spoilers and I really don't want to ruin the game for anyone. Besides, I'm lazy.
GRAPHICS - 5/5
The biggest eye catcher of this game (for me anyway) was the stunning graphical design. The details put into both the background and foreground create a very strong atmosphere for the curious adventurer. I really enjoy fantasy games a lot, and this is one that makes you feel like you've stepped into a beautiful movie and you want to see everything it has to offer, prompting you to explore every nook and crannie. Every new area makes you feel excited to pass through.
MUSIC - 3/5
There's a lot of good music in this game, but a lot of it isn't very memorable. Still though, it does help add to the fantasy atmosphere of this game. Overall, I'd say the soundtrack is very nice, but it's not enough for me to have an interest in paying for the soundtrack DLC.
DIFFICULTY - 2/5
I'm not a very good game player, actually. But the thing is, I beat this game with minimal effort and only a couple of the bosses gave me trouble before I figured out easy ways to beat them. I beat the final boss while getting a freaking PERFECT on him. No damage. Beating this game shouldn't be any challenge for veteran players. The story and the graphics are where this game shines. The real challenge for me was the collectables. There were some items I couldn't figure out how to get and I plan to play it again to try and get 100%.
GAMEPLAY - 3/5
The gameplay has a tendency to be a bit monotonous but ultimately works well for this sort of game. I wish I could have seen more content but I guess that's what you get from 10 years of work where the main focus seems to have gone into the story and graphic design. I'm not a game maker so I wouldn't know the difficulty in it so whatever. There are some very interesting parts of the game and they mix it up well, but much of it doesn't feel very new or innovated.
CONTROL - 4.5/5
The controls in this game are very easy to get the hang of and make for very easy gameplay. You shouldn't have much trouble figuring this game out. My only problem is that if you have a partner too close to an item you're trying to pick up, you'll end up picking up your partner instead. That can get a little annoying but overall it's not that much of an issue for the most part.
LENGTH - 2.5/5
This is my only serious problem with the game. While the story is drawn out reasonably, it took me longer to finish Undertale than this game, and that only cost me $10. I essentially beat this game into what could be considered... 24 hours, I guess? Not sure, eitherway, the game feels short but the detail helps to make up for it. Maybe I put too much time into playing it or something, but the story just feels a little rushed. Not that bad, but it makes me wish the game had more content to it.
OVERALL - 4/5
Owl Boy is a fun game with a good degree of replay value. The graphics, story and music will take you on an adventure that you will love being a part of, but don't expect anything too expansive or original other than the overall theme. The polish made the game shine, but when you get past that it just feels like there should be more to it. Maybe someday we'll get to see sequel with more to it, but looking at how long they took to complete the first game, I don't see that coming anytime soon, and if they try to do it too quickly, it probably won't have the quality that the first game did.

“Not all missions go as planned.” This is the phrase that lights up your screen before you crash land on the stormy, unforgiving planet of Mars. Your mission is no longer to collect planetary data, but to survive. JCB Pioneer: Mars by developer Atomicom and publisher GamesCo is gritty, tough, and difficult, and because I played it before its official release, I encountered some technical issues that were at times incredibly frustrating. But the originality is there, and both the impressive setting and complex story allow you to completely immerse yourself in the moment of the game.
Because your character is stranded and your one and only goal is to survive, there is no time for leisurely exploration of the planet. In fact, time is a limited and precious resource: the only oxygen available to you is the supply in your astronaut suit, and every second that supply goes down. From the very beginning, you are racing to get back to the base and replenish your tank, then repair your power systems and vehicles, then restock your weapons and refill your oxygen tank again, all while dodging lava eruptions and explosive meteors. Needless to say, playing JCB Pioneer: Mars is an intense experience, and even just a few minutes can leave you breathless. That said, the high stakes give you an adrenaline rush as your basic survival instincts kick in, and the desire to not die propels you forward in the game. Even when you do die from an empty oxygen tank or a meteor blast, you feel compelled to try again and beat the harsh elements. Also, I would like to note that I played at the “extreme” level of difficulty, but you can also choose to play at “easy” or “regular” levels.
One element that adds to the chaos of this quest for survival is the ambiguity of directions. True, you are provided with a mission log that constantly updates you with the next task, and the game controls are as simple as pressing different keys to move and function. And finding locations and objects is not difficult, for you have arrows that pinpoint their exact area and distance. However, it is entirely up to you to figure out how to do everything. For instance, I never knew my oxygen was decreasing until it was critically low, and then I had to run around my base opening every single crate looking for oxygen canisters, then figure out how to transfer it from the crate to my suit. May sound easy enough, but the stormy landscape obscured my vision, and the pressure of finding it in time severely affected my ability to think clearly and calmly. I thought it was interesting to observe how much harder everything became when I was under a time limit and could not see, and I think it really added to the realness of the game.
My one complaint is purely technical: maybe because the game has not been officially released yet, or perhaps my network connection was too weak, but the game often lagged or was extremely slow. When I had to get in a vehicle and drive to the main base at the beginning of the game, it took me almost 10 minutes because it seemed like I was crawling one inch per second. And when the main challenge of the game is to operate under a time limit, this could be very stressful. Also, something that bothered me personally was the inability to minimize the game on my desktop; if I needed to do something else on my laptop, I had to completely quit the game and then reload it, which took several minutes. But other than these minor technicalities, I fully recommend JCB Pioneer: Mars!
Rating: 7/10

This game is one of the best RPGs I've ever played. The gameplay is challenging but fun, the music and the artwork are beautiful, and the story is emotional and well told.
You play the game as the character Otus, who, like many video game protagonists, never speaks. Most games do this to allow the player to project themselves onto the main character, but Otus' mutism separates him from the player, distinguishing him as a distinct character with his own thoughts and feelings. The game makes it clear that his mutism is a disability, which makes him an easy target for abuse. Despite this, Otus makes friends who help him accomplish great things, and the game manages to keep the player rooting for him the whole time.
The music and artwork are absolutely beautiful. The orchestral score is brilliantly composed and puts most film scores to shame. And the sheer level of detail put into the pixel art and the animations throughout the game is legitimately astounding. It's no wonder it took ten years for this game to be developed. And if that weren't enough, Owlboy doesn't simply rely on the nostalgia generated by its retro-style artwork -- it brings its own unique creativity and charm to the table. Certain puzzles have to be solved by letting a fire-eating lantern creature follow you around, or by picking up a cloud and squeezing the rain out of it. I was consistently impressed by how thoughtfully everything was put together.
The controls are relatively simple, and the gameplay remains challenging throughout the game mostly because your abilities never really change. Once you finish the tutorial portion, you've pretty much got all the abilities you're going to have for the remainder of the game. Because, instead of a vast array of magical powers, you gain friends. Friends with guns. And I think that actually enhances the message the game's trying to convey.
Ultimately, Owlboy is about overcoming disability, and a large part of that is establishing a solid support system of friends and/or family to help you when you can't do everything yourself. And this is a good message! Otus doesn't have to be some ultra-powerful chosen one to save the world. He's just himself, and that's all he needs to be.
Overall, this game quickly became my personal all-time favorite. Everything from the art style, to the gameplay, to the thrilling story captured my interest and left me wanting more. Kudos to everyone who made this game, you did such a great job.

It has everything I could ever want in a game and more: Customization possibilities through the roof, a character for every play style and modification for strengths and abilities, fast paced intense combat that can last hours or matches that take micro seconds to burst through, parkour and movement mechanics are stupidly fun, weapon customization, consistent updates, it's third person, cooperative space grind-a-thon, and T H I C C  waifus. Honestly I've been shying away from this game for years and I regret ignoring it for so damn long. To think something like this with all this interesting and amazing features is packed away in a nice tight little free-to-play package astounds me. I'm not a big spender for games, I honestly despise the concept of throwing money at a screen as it's an impulse I have that derails me from the game itself. Warframe takes that annoying feeling of having to spend money to compete with others, burns it and has it hanged by an oak tree for the townsfolk to watch.
It's exactly what I'd envision a free-to-play game to be, you have the option to blow through practically everything with a couple bucks sure, but everything is there in front of you to take if you just play the game, and the feeling of obtaining items that in no way you'd ever expect to get unless you gave up around 100$ is magical, leaves a good feeling all around you and makes you appreciate the work and effort you put into it. It doesn't demand too much from you, this game is a grindfest no doubt but doesn't make it so painful to endure that you want to log out and contemplate your life choices, it actually has randomly generated template areas to adventure through and increases in difficulty every planet you hop on over to with even better materials and loot to acquire, you could do the same thing for hours and still feel like you're playing on a new area, despite some of the rooms and buildings you enter being familiar.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often made the reviews too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery page. Shouldn't happen here, but I've always been one for both consistency and efficiency.
Gameplay: Krunch is one of those games which you can pretty much sum up all of the gameplay in a serntence. It's a game where you have full vertical and horizontal control of a sphere in which your objective is to get to the goal without dying. You also have a run button, but this should only be used sparingly or whenever you are confident in your current health, since "running" consumes HP. After a set point of HP loss, you can't run anymore, so you need to use it intelligently.
It's also rather difficult to talk about the levels without an initial comparison to Super Meat Boy, since the levels are pretty challenging and pretty short. While the game doesn't immediately show you initial times after you beat the levels, they are visible once you go to the level select screen, so it's not too much of a hassle. Also within these stages are Krebs, or what are basically coins that you can collect for additional score. They aren't necessary and are only there for the challenge, but I can appreciate it nonetheless. Regarding the challenge of the levels and also comparing it to Super Meat Boy, the game starts off at roughly Light World Hospital and ends up about halfway through Light World Hell. So basically, the game is challenging, but never to the point where you'll want to stop playing. Much like Super Meat Boy, there are plenty of obstacles within the four worlds and are generally used pretty creatively without ever really feeling cheap.
One of the things that a reviewer complained about in this game is the fact that once you run into a wall, you bounce off of it. I don't have a problem with that, as it encourages precision gameplay over reflexes. That's not to say that reflexes aren't useful, but the game does force you to play a little more carefully than you may expect. The only thing that I can kinda complain about is that the hitboxes sometimes felt a little finicky, specifically with the bombs. Other than that, pretty much every death in this game will be your fault. Just the way it should be.
Overall, I can see a lot of both replay value and speedrunning potential for this game. Even for a normal person, it's a nice time killer. $10 may be a bit much given the fact that it can be beaten in an hour and a half, and I do somewhat agree (I picked this up in a Humble Bundle a while back), but on sale for something like $5 and I'd definitely say this game is worth the asking price. 8/10.
Story: There really isn't much here, but the comic you do get with the Digital Collector's Edition is quite nice. Not worth reviewing.
Graphics: A lot of effort has been put into this game, and it shows. The graphics style is basically if you take a Gameboy game and apply different color filters to it. The pixel art is great and has a great deal of detail, the boss design is great, and the game just looks all around great. In fact, my only gripe is that level names can be hard to read at times. That's really it. As far as the technical things go, the game launches in a 1280x720 splash screen and then fullsizes to your native resolution. You can play this game in windowed mode if you're into that sort of thing simply by pausing and pushing Y on your 360 controller (don't know the corresponding keyboard command, although I'd imagine Alt-Enter would work just fine). Overall, there was a lot of work put into the graphics for this game, and it's one of those games that just looks good irrespective of the visual style. 5/5.
Sound: Pretty much just music here, and I've gotta say that the music is pretty rad. A couple of standout tracks are the Boiler track (Ignition) and the last track of the soundtrack (ESCAPE). I'd give these a listen on Youtube beforehand to decide whether or not you'd be interested in giving the five dollars extra for it. I find it hard to say, since I once again got it in a Humble Bundle. However, irrespective of what version you get, the soundtrack is pretty good with more than a few pretty memorable tracks out of the bunch of 11. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 8/0/5/4; cumulative score of 8.5/10. A pretty rad game overall, although the price may be a bit steep for you. Just use your discretion, folks.

Valkyria Chronicles was originally a PS3 exclusive, however the port to the PC works quite well, with the exception of non-effecient tank driving.
For a game that relies heavily on plot it rarely drops you into a battle. But when you fight you have to fight hard if you wan't to make effecient progress.
Core concepts of the gameplay are balancing troops with draw-backs and buffs as well as grouping people who 'like' eachother together. Grouping friends together gives them certain boosts like damage, some troops however have major drawbacks like the character Susie Evans. Susie is a pacifist which means theres a chance in which you order her to attack she'll simply aim and say 'I can't do it!' then end her turn, this is a heavy drawback as Susie is a scout, a class that is good at moving into open space to attack and then run to cover. If 'pacifist' activates you either need to spend another turn getting Susie to cover or let her die.
The game has a few balance issues such as the inability to hit a target at point-blank range with a tank cannon however because the deviation of your projectile is based on RNG it also means you can pull insanely stupid stuff like sniping a tanks engine from half way across the map because RNGsus said your bullet was 100% accurate.
With my experience with this game I've found it extremely hard to take down armored targets because Tank cannons and Lances (Or RPGs) are extremely innacurate in compairison to other weapons. However this only seems to be true for myself, as the enemy can fire an Lance from on top of a cliff and hit a soldier.
If you're a Japaboo you'll wanna play the game in Japanese however the english subtitles are more or less completely innacurate to the actual diolauge. The english dub of the game is... questionable. To me it felt as if certain characters lost quirks while they gained others, however there's always a daimond or two in the dirt so a few characters fit their voices.
Other elements of the game include leveling up your troops, giving them better equipment, upgrading your tank and a lesser known function visiting the graveyard. If you have lost no soldiers in combat (Your troop falls than is 'tagged' by an enemy) an old war veteran will teach you certain orders you will not learn by training your troops. However these orders cost large ammounts of exp so you must balance between getting new orders and training your troops.
Personally I feel as if one of the major problems with the game are ids difficulty spikes. Some levels are crazy easy others are mad hard. One example of this may be the battles you play in the 'Barrius Desert' in which the first battle is as simple as crossing a plane while the game introduces a 'sandstorm' effect, To which the second fight has you fighting not only a tank that does not take damage every time you hit it, but also has a pair of giant cannons on the front and rear that insta-kill the Edelwiess if you're caught in its cone and a grand total of 6 machine guns that will attempt to mow down any infantry that try to get close, and while you can destroy these guns you have to hit the gun mantlet, if your shot so much as lands five inches to the left of the gun- no damage. All the while a second boss comes in that you are unable to kill whom wields a weapon that anhialates infantry.
The long and short of this review is... If you enter VC with expectations of plot and engaging gameplay, You'll get plot. If you have busted luck and RNGsus is always on your side- play on EX mode to get the same experience as me. The game tells a better story than the anime and has less cliche'd romance♥♥♥♥♥♥but if you're not prepared to pour blood sweat and tears into balls to the walls insane fights...

TL;DR: There are very little strategy or tactic components in VC; it is more like an animate visual novel that allows players to re-enact the battles following a pre-written script. Watch the animated version if you don't have time to spare.
I actually somewhat don't hate this game, especially given the fact that it's first published on PS3 in 2008.
The graphic is ok, the fully animated and voiced cutscenes shows good effort, the plot is kinda cheesey but still acceptable ( just like most of the Japanese animates), it also offers a good variety of weapons and skills to choose from, it's somehow an acceptable turn-based strategy/tactical game. However, I still cannot recommend it.
The biggest problem VC has is it doesn't really have any AI system in it's NPCs and enemies.
All enemy units just move to their predetermined positions and using specific skills every turn regardless of the situation, and will sit there until the end of the world if you don't bother to get in contact with them.
There is little (or next to nothing) "creative" or "your own way" of playing this game except following the walkthrough.
Almost every stage can be solved in less than 5 turns if you follow the walkthrough to the very extent (by that I mean: move the specific character to a specific location and doing exactly what the guide tells you to), otherwise you will have a quiet difficult fight and receive low score.
It's somewhat sad to see how this game fails to deliver more tactic or strategy essences to its players. I mean, it has a decent basic system and good graphic (2008 standard) with full voice cast, and will be a great game if you can play it like XCOM, Shadowrun, or Heroes of M&M.
BTW, if you really are interested in the story of VC, but don't want to go through the whole game following guides, I would recommend you to watch the animate version of Valkyria Chronicle. It has 25+1 episodes that basically follow the plotline in game with some minor variation and additional stories.
ps: as a Japanese speaker, I must say the translation of English subtitles are horrible, although they somewhat make senses by themselves, the meanings are often way off the original voice casts. ex: Selvaria is a Colonel, never a Brigade General, and she was almost always being addressed as "Daisa"(romanji pronunciation for Colonel in jpn) by her comrades and soldiers instead of her name.

Hard Reset is a game with great high-level ideas and infuriating moment-to-moment gameplay experiences. I am generally so busy asking myself questions like "Why am I getting hurt?", "Why can't I jump over this foot-high railing?", "Why is it so hard to switch to the right weapon/mode combination when I'm getting swarmed by sawblade-bots?", "Why can't I jump over this foot-high brick?", "Why do I have to turn on a generator to turn off that energy barrier?", "Why did that energy barrier randomly turn back on after I went through so much trouble to turn it off?", or "Why can I jump onto this two-foot high box, but then once on it can't jump over the three-foot high wall next to it?" that I can't really appreciate the strategic depth of the upgrade system, the old school nonlinear level design, or the treasure hunt for all the secret caches. Those are things that generally excite me, but the experience of the game for me is mostly fumbling with weapon controls and slamming into invisible walls.

I had this game in my Steam Library for nearly a year, and didn't get round to playing it until recently due to having so many other games to play, but also because I didn't expect to much from it. When I finally played it, though, I found it hard to pull myself away. This isn't so much a 'gameplay' game since you don;t really do that much, but it is more like an interactive movie, and has a great story that I found kept me gripped until the end. It probably won't be something I'll replay, since I know how the story goes now, but it's a great game for a single play-through if you really like a deep immersive story, and a nice relaxing game-play style. I completed it in around 11-12 hours, so it's not super long, and part of that time was hunting down bonus stuff to unlock extra 'stories' within the game, but what you do get is good quality.
Its a nice little game to play with your friends. If you have any....

JCB Pioneer: Mars (JCBPM for short) is the debut title from developer, Atomicom, working closely with one of the world's largest construction machinery manufacturers, JCB.
In JCBPM, you play an early Mars colonist whose descent to the planet goes awry. You wake up next to your escape pod and a helpful AI (?) introduces you to your suit's functions and directs you to nearby salvation: an electric vehicle from JCB, the X-18. Not only does the X-18 move pretty quickly compared to your plodding steps, it also protects you from the dangerous weather of Mars and, importantly, has its own Oxygen supply.
After recovering the X-18 and navigating a few more hazards you soon find yourself at a deserted and not-quite-operational habitation unit ('hab'), presumably the home of an even earlier colonist. From there the AI leads you through basic missions to restore the hab to operation, making you self-sufficient for water, food, and all-important Oxygen.
You're then introduced to the trade interface, where you can take on new missions to extend your base to further support the colonisation efforts. In the future JCB seems to have expanded into interplanetary colonisation, as for these missions and other tasks you're awarded JCB credits and research points, which you can spend on researching and upgrading your suit, vehicle, and buildings, as well as buying other vehicles from JCB.
JCBPM's graphics are full 3D from a first- or third-person perspective.
The landscape looks suitably Mars-like from my point of view, though I'm no expert. There are reddish-brown rocks and lots of dust, weird rocky formations, and jagged hills. It's desolate and unfriendly looking, as it should be. Vehicle and building models look suitably rugged and realistically futuristic -- no crazy pulsing plasma fields and black-hole generators -- though the giant holographic-style 3D printers and the nano-rifle are perhaps a bit of a stretch. There's a good range of buildings and once they are built they become part of the world, with power conduits making cool little speed bumps for your vehicles and larger buildings allowing you to climb external ladders.
There's a model for your character when playing in third-person view: a realistic-looking, if somewhat boring, EVA suit. Animations seem a bit wonky and I didn't like the fixed camera position, though, so I played in first-person instead. The AI has a very pretty portrait when she's speaking to you.
Special effects are impressive, with dust clouds, meteor strikes, and other cool weather and hazard effects. Oxygen venting from damaged buildings looks great, too. The lava looks terrible compared to everything else, though, and there are very rigid boundaries around some of the hazards; take one step outside the boundary and meteors disappear, for example. And for some reason we never see the sun or either of the moons.
The interface is mostly very nice looking, but is not very pleasant to use. The map sometimes moves when you want it to and sometimes doesn't. Connecting buildings to power sometimes works and sometimes doesn't. There are also a couple of places where text is too large for the available area and gets cut off.
The game uses Unreal Engine 4, so there are plenty of graphics settings. I didn't encounter any graphical performance issues running, but it did run rather hot.
The game has very sparse music, but it's well produced and fits well. The initial loading music reminds me of something from 2001: A Space Odyssey, with slow light melodies interspersed with deep reverberating BOOMS. It's very nice. I noticed only one other ambient background music track.
Sound effects are good, with suitable sounds for an electric construction vehicle throughout. The X-18 motor sounds are particularly good. Interface sounds are appropriately futuristic.
The AI has a lovely female voice to match her portrait.
The basic gameplay is similar to most survival-crafting games: find resources, take them back to your base, and turn them into stuff to either help you survive or allow you to more efficiently make better stuff. JCBPM differs from most other games, though, in that a lot of the focus is on your trusty steed: the X-18. Without this you have no hope of survival, so you need to frequently return to the garage to restore its health as well as its Oxygen and power reserves.
There's a set map that's the same each time you play; there's no procedural generation here. Though I quickly became familiar with most of the landscape near the base, it's still fun to explore new areas.
Your part in the Mars colonisation seems decidedly unglamorous, as you'll spend most of your time driving to resource pits, mining resources, driving them back to your base, and dumping them into whatever 3D printer is currently making or upgrading your next building. There's crafting of items you need to survive, though they mostly (all?) are single-use items, which really doesn't fit with the 'realistic colonisation' goal, where everything should be recycled. There's also refining, very basic trading, and a large number of missions that make the whole game seem like an extended tutorial, as they direct you through building up basically everything from scratch. There's no multiplayer or combat yet, but both are planned for the future.
Back at base you control placement of new buildings, connections to the power grid, and upgrades. There's a good range of buildings and upgrades, but the interface makes it all harder to manage than it should be. If I hadn't had to restart so many times and experienced so many crashes I'm sure I'd be a lot further on than I am now, but even so it looks like there's enough here to keep even the most even-tempered would-be colonist busy for a long time -- at least until the rather limited basic resources run out.
As is the case with many Early Access titles, JCBPM has many bugs and other frustrations. The developers seem to be fairly active and a new patch was released very recently. Here's a short list of the issues that most got to me, but there are many, many more:
- Very common "Fatal Error" CTD around base
- Very long loading times
- X-18 can get stuck inside world geometry
- Gain RP by completing EVAs, but that's impossible with the crashing and geometry issues
- Partially built buildings sometimes reset to 0% built after a reload
- When you reload, everything you've scanned on the map disappears
- No pause, making it very easy to die of asphyxiation while you're taking care of a real-world need
- 'Drop item' is actually 'destroy item'
- %-based resource pools don't work like they should: a 100-unit 70% Fe, 30% Mg deposit may give you 99 Fe and 1 Mg.
- Other assorted bugs: power connections don't always work, tutorial sometimes gets stuck, some missions require other missions to be completed first (e.g. the alternative refinery requires the upgraded refinery)
Pros:
+ Mostly excellent graphics
+ Excellent sound and voice acting
+ Very cool setting
+ Solid core gameplay
Cons:
- Very buggy
- No pause
- Long load times
- Lots of backtracking and it's the same each time you play (except for the random resource pools)
I've experienced alternating emotions while playing this: frustration first, then enjoyment, and now frustration again. I've decided to start over yet again after a series of crashes caused me to lose far too many resources, but my frustration levels are high enough now that I need to give it a break for a while -- at least until the CTDs are fixed. If a mostly realistic survival game set on Mars sparks your interest and you're not quick to anger then by all means give it a shot. It's a great start, but it still has quite a way to go.

Mass Effect 2 is commonly regarded by fans as the best of the 3 in the series, and with good reason. While the first and last games are by no means wanting for story, Mass Effect 2 delivers a story - and most importantly, a climax - where the choices made throughout the game are truly felt as meaningful.
The skill system is heavily simplified from Mass Effect 1, but I didn't miss the added complexity. The change from an ammo-less weapon system to the more standard ammo-restricted game was a little disappointing due to my personal playstyle, but serves the game well. This system carries over almost completely unchanged into Mass Effect 3.
Like many fans I was slightly disappointed that key teammates from the first game only make small appearances in Mass Effect 2, but those who remain, and the new characters that join them, come alive with excellent writing and top-notch voice acting. Liara fans in particular will definitely want the Lair of the Shadow Broker DLC if you want to spend any amount of time with her.
Jack Wall delivers his best work on an incredibly memorable soundtrack, an achievement that is even more notable by being superior to the arguably bigger-name (but more forgettable) Clint Mansell soundtrack of Mass Effect 3. Many of the tracks have been on my workout playlist for years.
Buy it. But not before buying and playing Mass Effect 1 and importing your save file to set up the galaxy you'll continue to explore. Then consider carefully how well you look after your crew mates, because you choices here will affect what you see of them when you import your save into Mass Effect 3 - if they survive at all, that is.

In my opinion, the best action RPG ever made. While the overarching plot of the entire trilogy develops the least over the course of this game compared to the other ones, Bioware made a smart decision and used ME2 largely as a opportunity to give your companions massive character development. The real gem in this game isn't the main questline, although the final mission really does leave a good taste in your mouth given you took your time beforehand. Where the game really shines is the side "loyalty" missions and the aforementioned character development. They really did a good job of making you care about your crewmembers. My main gripe is that compared to ME1, they really dialed back on the exploration side of the game, i.e. landing on and exploring uncharted worlds and stations. Fortunately they really fleshed out that part of the series in Andromeda. Also, they simplified a lot of the RPG elements that were already fairly barebones in the first game.
Also I miss the mako.

I have not played Mass Effect 1- but I still found this game to be amazing. The characters, the story, the gameplay - it is pure fun. The cover-based squad combat works great. The downsides to this game are that you have very limited options when it comes to choosing weapons- there is often one clear weapon to choose over another when picking a shotgun, pistol, SMG, etc. Also, the game seems to get into the end-game very quickly- just when you think you're just coming together as a team, you hit the last level. Finally, it seems that choosing different squadmates has a very small impact on gameplay- it makes little difference who I choose to bring with me. This game is very well done; it does one thing, and it does it really well.
The combat is skill based and rewards timed attacks and blocks as well as accurate hits.
There is a progression system which involves acquiring new weapons, but none of these weapons are blatantly overpowered and/or give experienced players a huge advantage over newer ones. Skill with your weapon is vastly more important than tier of that weapon. However, it should be noted that the majority of players are experienced and therefore good at the game, making it incredibly hard for a new player to learn the mechanics of the game. A bot mode is available (but honestly not very useful) for practice.
The microtransactions are purely cosmetic.
Map design and game design (that is, the design of the team objective and other game modes) are both done very well.
I recommend the team objective game mode, it is the bread and butter of the game modes (free for all, team deathmatch, last man standing, and various other game modes are available as well).
Bugs I have thusfar encountered (this will be updated if I find any game breaking bugs) have been mostly glitches in the bodies. For example, a corpse's teeth, fingers, and big toe might be suspended three feet above the ground, pulling parts of the body along with it.
I have had a couple crashes occassionaly, which should not be ignored, but it has not happened enough to really get on my nerves. All the crashes happened while I was in the server browser, but more than that I cannot say about why they happened.
UPDATE: These crashes have suddenly become very frequent and annoying. As for the cause, I still know nothing but that they always happen in the Server Browser. So watch out for that.
The biggest thing to watch out for in this game is the community. The community is highly toxic, angry (that is, they tend to rage at the other team a lot), and generally rude. The general community insults, taunts, and harrasses each other at a level comparable to the community of League of Legends (for reference).
I highly recommend you disable the chat in the options menu. That will solve most of your problems.
However, be wary of random vote kicks. I have seen several people, and myself been, vote kicked for no apparant reason.
