This is a visual novel about a man who wakes up in a strange room with no memories of who or where he is.
The mechanics of this game are, like most VNs, pretty simple. You follow the dialogue and make choices to progress the story into either 'good' or 'bad' endings. This is a short-medium length game that probably won't take more than 10 hours to finish. As well as the usual dialogue, there are many simple puzzles that must be figured out to proceed in the game.
I say 'simple' as in their design, but actually some are quite difficult to complete and will cause a 'game over' if you fail, forcing you to either start from the beginning of the game or back to your last save point. As there are no autosaves, you should save the game often, or else get familiar with the skip button. There are also some very good guides for this game made by the community that can help you solve the puzzles if you're stuck or just want to play casually (like me...).
In terms of endings, there is only one 'main/good' path to choose. There are many choices that can lead you off of this path, but they are short and always lead to your death. There are also some choices that you make in the early game that have consequences in the later parts of the game, the community guides can also help you make choices here.
The art, while not revolutionary, is well done for the most part. Although some backgrounds are certainly done better than others, I wouldn't consider any of them to be of poor quality. The characters, especially Christina, are very well done and have a nice style to them. The music is very good and fits the situations nicely, but I found the tracks a little repetative toward the end of the game.
For the story, the beginning of the game feels very stretched and almost boring, with dialogue explaining seemingly every little detail of the surroundings. But this wordy dialogue quickly fades away as the real story begins to unfold into many complex and interesting events involving the protagonist and his past as he discovers the secrets of the world he finds himself in. I mean, some parts of the story are quite cliche and you can guess some of the plot right from the beginning of the game, but there are also a lot of unexpected events that unfold that keep it interesting and create a sense of wonder and suspense.
Overall, I would recommend this game to any visual novel fan due to its interesting story and nice artwork.

TL;DR: There are very little strategy or tactic components in VC; it is more like an animate visual novel that allows players to re-enact the battles following a pre-written script. Watch the animated version if you don't have time to spare.
I actually somewhat don't hate this game, especially given the fact that it's first published on PS3 in 2008.
The graphic is ok, the fully animated and voiced cutscenes shows good effort, the plot is kinda cheesey but still acceptable ( just like most of the Japanese animates), it also offers a good variety of weapons and skills to choose from, it's somehow an acceptable turn-based strategy/tactical game. However, I still cannot recommend it.
The biggest problem VC has is it doesn't really have any AI system in it's NPCs and enemies.
All enemy units just move to their predetermined positions and using specific skills every turn regardless of the situation, and will sit there until the end of the world if you don't bother to get in contact with them.
There is little (or next to nothing) "creative" or "your own way" of playing this game except following the walkthrough.
Almost every stage can be solved in less than 5 turns if you follow the walkthrough to the very extent (by that I mean: move the specific character to a specific location and doing exactly what the guide tells you to), otherwise you will have a quiet difficult fight and receive low score.

If you are a fan of visual novels with compelling stories, this game is for you.
The good first. The game has a deep and interesting story. I won't spoil much, but the plot unveils itself rather nicely and smoothly. Although the game could have been longer (and with a better ending :,( or a sweeter ending), the story was very good. There are also a series of puzzles that you have to complete in order to beat the game, which may be challenging, but are quite interesting and fun somtimes. The game also has very well drawn art. There are few characters that are drawn, but the ones that are drawn are drawn with spectacular detail and style. The backgrounds fit in as well. When I judge a visual novel, I often do care a lot about the art because I feel like that is an integral part of the game. Additionally, the music of the game is very nice, it get repetitive sometimes, but it is really relaxing and fits very well.
The bad now. Sometimes you get really lost what to do. Like you actually can get really lost what to do next, especially when there are no blatant hints or clues, and it may take you a long time to figure out just what needs to be done. Additionally, the game really punishes you for messing up. I got bad ending after bad ending after bad ending. Be prepared to save and load the game :) The last bad thing about this game was the that English translations were okay, but started to get worse and worse. The first few parts of the game, the English was almost flawless, but the later you got into the game, the more and more scrappy and mistakes were everywhere. None of the mistakes were bad enough to be game impacting, but as an example, one time he was mistakingly used for she and I became confused for a bit.
I can only write reviews this long for games that I truly enjoyed enough to see both the strengths and flaws to, and this visual novel is a very good one. I would highly recommend any and all visual novel fans to pick this up and try it. Even for those that aren't visual novel fans, give it a go!

I had no idea what this game had in store for me when I bought it. I wanted a strategy game that made me feel good when I figured stuff out. I wanted a strategy game that made me want to mess with the mechanics to create a "high-level gaming experience." I wanted an RPG that made me feel the progress I made. I wanted an RPG with good writing that isn't super big, like Witcher because monies. I got a good scratch to that itch here in Valkyria Chronicles. It's got likeable characters, a solid story, and enjoyable and effective gameplay.
Give it a spin. You might like this one, even if you aren't a fan of strategy games. It's plenty forgiving, but challenging if you want it to be.
___________________________________
War breaks out. Two nations clash with the neutral Gallia in the middle. Welkin Gunther, the son of a renowned general, is a young biologist at university, called home to help his sister, Isara, relocate because of encroaching forces from the East. The war reaches his hometown of Bruhl faster than expected, forcing him into service.
I had my fun with this story. It's clean and to the point at times with just enough backstory/lore/mystery to keep you going forward with anticipation. It is a JSRPG (Japanese Strategy RPG) so there are noticeable Japanese elements present. Some of it is welcome, like interactions and quirks of characters. However, the story appears to be part of the excuse for the gameplay here. Often times I feel that the character reactions/thought processes were not good - it wants you to play more than feel sometimes. I suppose that would be a good thing, but here, I wish that they sat down and fleshed out details to make it that much more satisfying.
Each part of the story is broken up into chapters (literally) of a book. It lets you go at your own pace: rocketing through the story, or stopping to smell the roses called side stories. I like this alot actually; this is player-agency over story that I think is done rather well.
You have a battalion's worth of characters. Not exaggerating. Not much is actually detailed about them at first though. It is through use of those characters in the game that unlocks more of the backstory - sort of proving their worth then finding more about the person behind the soldier. I'm not going to cover much about them because there are so many. Though, I feel that because there are so many, you don't really get a feel for a large chunk of them; it's a "knee-deep ocean" of characters with a few deep trenches for only a handful of 'em. There are definite anime tropes at the surface though - look beyond and find some of the pearls underneath.
It's WW2 with a new country, mysticism, resource struggles, and anime tropes. All done rather well actually.
Ever play Eternal Sonata on PS3/XBOX360? Yeah. It's kinda like a hybrid of that and Advance Wars/Fire Emblem/DND.
You play using a top-down, drawn map overviewing the area of combat on a turn-by-turn basis. You use this map to select units and perform actions. But you don't just select, drag-and-drop, and end. You have a number of points which allow you to use units - one point lets you move an individual character, while two points lets you move a tank. When you select a unit for use, you enter a third-person scale environment, controlling that character. You can direct them to do an infinite number of minor actions with one major action. Be wary though; in third-person mode, as long as you control the character without entering "aiming mode," you can be fired upon by a majority of the enemy units.  You can, however, do the same against the enemy when it's their turn.
It's really fun if you like strategy games. Positioning, timing, planning, (and of course bull-rushing) are all important aspects of the game. It's also rather forgiving, but merciless to reckless players. Good for those gamers who don't really play strategy games often. Or you can make it hard on yourself with self-imposed challenges or skirmish maps in-game.
KBM controls are adequate. They aren't intuitive, but they are effective. There's something funky when using KBM though. Your actions, particularly movement, aren't as refined or just goof up completely. For example, moving a tank using KBM may end up stalling you, wasting your points, as you control the camera with the mouse. This is another game where controllers seem to have an edge.
The game runs around 45 fps on my non-gaming laptop constantly, occasionally hitting 60 (no noticeably broken physics when done so). It only dips below when processing a few tiny segments with lot of scripts for retaliation, shooting during player/enemy movement, tons of pieces/parts on the entire map. There are no crashes for me, and on a rare occasion will minimize; no negative effects though as it will halt all actions (except music) until you maximize it again.
Reminds me alot of the Saving Pvt Ryan/old CoD soundtracks. It's generic at times, but it's more than sufficient at pleasing your ears. Otherwise, it just didn't cut it for me.
Not much humor to be found here.  There are a couple of cards, however.  If you didn't get this in a bundle or a giveaway, shame on you.

I can't recommend this game enough or say enough good things about it, but I'll try to narrow it down. The story, the graphics, the music, the attention to detail, the amount of freedom and choice, the challenge, even just the feel of it... the nostalgia... it feels like a love letter to old pencil and paper RPGs, this game has it all, including a team of developers that obviously poured their hearts and souls into the game.
I've never played any of the other Divinity games, but a friend bought this for me so we could play together at launch and I fell in love with the game instantly. I love that even small little side quests and side characters have an insane amount of detail and work put into them, items found in one area of the game and choices you've made have lasting effects on other areas, items and people throughout the game. This game has impressed me beyond belief, especially in a time where gaming has felt dull and cheapened by unfinished games filled with DLCs.
This is easily a contender for game of the year and possibly best RPG of all time. I highly recommend this to any fans of the original Fallout, Wasteland, Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, etc, even pencil/paper D&D, with it boasting a vast and well designed Game Master mode where you can take on the role of a DM and run a campaign or even create your own campaign and play along with your friends, taking control of anything in real time while a party is running through it. I have spent 3 hours in this mode alone, just making maps and having a blast doing so.
Best of all, this game is an absolute bargain... no reason to wait until a steam sale if you're still apprehensive (you shouldn't be). At only $44.99, when you'd be spending double that on a game with much less, split between rip-off Season Passes and other DLCs, this game is a steal!
TL;DR: Like RPGs? Stop reading the reviews section and buy the game.

Anime style story-driven tactical RPG about courageous Squad 7 of militia fighting a hostile nation that invaded beautiful and peaceful country of Galia.
PROS:
- Beautiful comic book style graphics.
- The game uses fictional countries and nations, but definitely has a WW2 feel. If you like WW2 themes (I do), the game is great.
- Fine character development and touching story.
- Good voice acting.
- Good music.
- Lots of tactical options. Every unit serves its purpose. Multiple options to win every battle.
- Some levels are challenging, but as a person that sometimes has to refer to tutorials and FAQs, I was able to complete all by myself.
MEH:
- AI moves might be better. There are times when enemy is able to ruin you, but instead of destroying one tank, delivers equal number of attacks on both your tanks. So you have a feeling that AI goes easy on you. There is no difficulty setting.
- Japanese dev had to squeeze a cute winged piglet there. It serves no purpose at all.
- There are times where it is sort of naive, but it's still good.
CONS:
- Controls are sort of clunky, definitely prepared for gamepad, not a mouse.
- Your tanks get stuck.
- Some parts are unskippable, which may be painful, because sometimes you know you royally screwed up after enemy's first move and you'll need to reload from save for sure, but surprise surprise, you have to wait for enemy's all moves to do anything (it can take 2-5 minutes).
As you can see, important stuff in the game is really good. There are some nuissance bugs and glitches, but it's all within norms. I recommend Valkyria Chronicles wholeheartedly.
GAMEPLAY 8/10
GRAPHICS 9/10
AUDIO 9/10
STORY 9/10

Stop reading reviews and just buy this game! It's absolutely worth the full price, and being on sale makes it a no-brainer!
This is an amazing game to keep you busy between larger games, or just as something to play to unwind before bed. There's not a ton of over-arching story, which makes it ideal for dipping into for a few minutes at a time, even if you let weeks pass between play sessions.
The general mechanic is that you've died, and are playing a card game against death. Death deals a set of cards that create a dungeon for your character to play through. Each card is a different room or event for you to play through, with everything from gambling events to stores to story-driven events to combat. Each dungeon you play through unlocks new cards -- both equipment for your adventurer as well as rooms and events to play through.  The next time Death deals a dungeon, it will be slightly longer than the last one you played through.
One of the best mechanics is that when you hit a "combat" room, you actually "dive into" the card and control your adventurer as he fights the minions from the card. The combat mechanics are simple, but surprisingly fun. The minions have enough variation in attacks and style that combat never becomes dull, even though you have to fight several mobs per dungeon.
The devs are also great people. They've added a ton of new contenet since the games release, and as you play through you'll notice their little DLC expansions peppered through -- you always have the option to dive into DLC from the main game. I hope they keep releasing these expansions!
So all in all, this game is a no-brainer. It isn't likely to be one that you sit down an play through entirely without breaks, but it makes a perfect distraction between larger games or just for a short session at night. Add it to your collection now!

-*90% of loot in containers (corpses, chests, drawers, etc.) are randomised each time you load a save file if the container hasn't been inspected, except for fixed loot (key items and other certain equipment)

CONS:
- A couple of bugs are still left (hopefully it will get patched and fixed soon ^^)
- Sometimes the AI can be a bit derp, and at other times it can be uber smart xD Thus, I recommend your first playthrough to be on classic difficulty max, if not explorer :)

Although a very simple story that we've all heard many times in some matter, Owlboy still manages to pull off something beautiful with quite potent underlying themes. Otus, an owl, struggling to prove his self-worth to the owl community of Tropos, becomes the only hope for them and the rest of the world they live in when their village and others are attacked by a group of evil sky pirates. Otus sets out on his adventure and must traverse mysterious environments and dungeons and will encounter  dangerous enemies. With the help of some odd friends along the way, Otus's journey only gets much more dark and adventurous.
Beautiful graphics, scenery, music, animation, and sprites. Nothing falls short of amazing. Puzzles aren't difficult, but the appeal of them is to remind us of old dungeon puzzles from Zelda and older RPG's. Nothing 'hard' in the sense a child couldn't do it. Levels are well layed out and fun to explore. Bosses are very unique and different, again nothing hard about them, just fun simplicity. Characters have very rich detail and humor to them, as well funny personalities.
Owlboy focuses on how friendship and coming together can vanquish evil. It's the tale of how even the smallest and least likely  of people can make the biggest difference and change history.

I've been playing this game since the Beta.This is by far one of my favorite games and I absolutely recommend it, with a couple of caveats:
1) THE LABOR SYSTEM
The cap on LP for a free-to-play account is 2,000. You need labor points for literally everything in this game. Harvesting plants, taking care of animals, harvesting resources, opening coinpurses, weapons and armor dropped by mobs, and crafting anything all takes LP. On a free-to-play account you are given 5 LP for every 5 minutes of game play but if you're doing anything besides questing you can blow through that really fast.
2) FREE-TO-PLAY VS. PATRON
Up until last month, I've always been F2P. I broke down and bought myself a patron subscription for Christmas. There are definite advantages to being a patron:
-You get 10 LP for every 5 minutes of game play and 10 LP for every 5 minutes that you're offline.
-Patrons can own land and they get a buff just for being a P2P player.
-Patrons get an extra daily log-in reward that you can spend in the Marketplace.
3) THE LAND SYSTEM (P2P ONLY)
There are housing and farming districts in every zone on the map but whoever zoned those districts must have been drunk or high when they did it. Every house or garden plot you can get has square edges but there are several places where the devs put rounded edges on the zones. Also, the plots don't snap to the plot next to it. You can just put your plot down wherever you please so there are several places where a spot between houses or gardens will be just small enough that you can't put anything down. And when you own land you have to pay taxes. This sucks LP REALLY fast.
4) PVP
If you like PVP, feel free to ignore this one. This is a PVP-based game and they reward you heavily for killing other players. For example, if you kill enemy players during war time or in a war or hostile zone, you get Honor Points which you can use to buy cool stuff in the Marketplace. And there's nothing stopping a level 55 player from going into a level 10 questing zone and killing newbies for easy Honor Points. I've experienced and witnessed this happening many, many times. It's possible to kill members of your own faction and once you do you become a pirate, which in itself offers a variety of perks. There is a trial system but it's mostly a joke. And you take to the ocean at your own risk because the entire ocean is a PVP zone. I cannot begin to tell you how frustrating it is to be sport fishing alone and be attacked by a boat-load of pirates who proceed to kill you, steal your fish and destroy the boat you spent tons of money and resources building. So, yeah. I'm not a fan of the PVP.
There's something in this game for everyone. If you like it enough, pay for patron and get the perks. If not, it's a lot of fun that's free. I hope this review helped.

I have not played Mass Effect 1- but I still found this game to be amazing. The characters, the story, the gameplay - it is pure fun. The cover-based squad combat works great. The downsides to this game are that you have very limited options when it comes to choosing weapons- there is often one clear weapon to choose over another when picking a shotgun, pistol, SMG, etc. Also, the game seems to get into the end-game very quickly- just when you think you're just coming together as a team, you hit the last level. Finally, it seems that choosing different squadmates has a very small impact on gameplay- it makes little difference who I choose to bring with me. They all do about the same amount of damage- the only thing that changes are your abilities, which means that teammates with the more useful abilities should ALWAYS be chosen over those that don't have useful abilities. Other than this, everything about the game (except for the mining mini-game. Don't get me started on that) is phenomenal- there is a universe here that is meant to be explored, and boy is it fun.

This game was 10 years in the making and it looks gorgeous. The pixel artwork is fantastic and they took great pains in animating all the stuff. Absolutely phenomenal artwork. But sadly artwork does not simply sell a game. This game has done nothing innovative in terms of gameplay. The gimmick here is that it is a platformer but you can fly. The main character can fly and has a spin attack and a dash attack which I think was only useful to break some walls. You can carry your pals one who has a shotgun and can burn things,the other who has a gun which shoots pellets and the third who has kind of a websling. You get these pals are various stages of this 8-10 hour game. So they basically shoot for you and the controls use the mouse to shoot,WSAD for movement and double pressing W makes you fly. The level design is average at the most with you mostly shooting enemies and solving very trivial puzzles which involve button pushing for the most and nothing else. This is the most uninspiring gameplay I have ever seen. It is not fluid at all and the main character moves so slowly. It becomes a pain navigating the levels with such a slow character. The levels are also dungeon like so there are celings to stop you and there is not much use of the vertical flexibility that could have been achieved. The boss fights are very simple with very easy to figure out patterns. The last    boss gave me some trouble but I finished that in 3 tries after figuring the pattern. I generally do not care about a game story and completely ignored that one but you can talk to folks and figure out whats happening. I found the cutscenes very annoying and they sometimes popped up randomly which was very annoying. Also there is a level the last one which is very annoying as they do not ley you fly and it is absolutely the worst level designed and is completely against the flow of the game. I would not recommend this game. it was an absolutely chore to play with nothing innovative in the gameplay and a very slow moving character. Also the character switching is clunky where you can get the pal you want to use teleported to you. Absolutely boring gameplay.

If you overcome the scary learning curve, you'll feel like the King in you Castle. Or the Emperor. Or Duke or Count, if you like an even harder challenge.
This game is a perfect mixture of empire management with a side of economics, law and an approach to war that no other game has --with the exception of Europa Universalis, from the same studio--.
You'll have to plan your wars carefully, keeping in mind you need a valid casus belli, craft alliances with historical medieval leaders and kingoms to avoid the extinction of your bloodline and raising its prestige. Oh, and if you think your enemy is just the one outside your borders, think again: your courtesans and vassals are willing to do anything to the their arses in your throne: murder, civil war, the pretendership of your brothers, pressure to change the laws, revolts of peasants.
Whether you prefer to plot your way from count to king, to win the Reconquista with the Kingdom of Castille or to ravage the land with the mongols, there is only one true ruler of the real-time strategy games and that is Crusader Kings II.
It is highly recommended to purchase the expansions that allow to play as the oriental powers and the ones that add different eras to play.

Great Early Access Game! I am playing single player or private server, no public server just so you know. The game is challenging but yet fun and very immersive for me. I am a huge fan of Robert E Howard and a huge Conan fan. So this soemthing I have been watching for some time. Having been a avid Age of Conan fan this fit right into my wheel house.
Probably the biggest annoyance is losing all your stuff when you die, it can be recovered so not all bad. I know it makes it harder but it  seems silly to reappear naked again.  There is a setting on server to change that so I may go update that at some point but for now I will leave it.So far I have been playing with the default server settings with no issue.  Speaking of server settings, the single player server is highly confgurable, I looked through it but thought I would play a while before I changed anything. At some point I will setup a server for friend and will tweak it when that happens.
So far the building is good, needs more content but that will come as we go through the early access. The combat is hard, I have not mastered it yet so running away is the best option. A surprising enough there is a story, there are books and letters you can collect, each with its own tragic tale. Plus I met a freindly NPC today, he did not do much but talk to me but cool...there is more to come.
The other surpising thing is it is very performant for me, I have a gaming machine from a few years about (nvidia 560m) and it runs like a champ. There is a setting to allow the game to chose the settings and it is. It looks good, runs fast and is very responsive.  I have very few lag issues, I account those more to the machine then the game (since I see it in other games).
One of the best parts is the music. It is a combination of the music from the orginal Conan movie (the one with Arnold) and peices from Age of Conan. Very fitting and very thematic for me.
I can see how public servers would be an issue, the game is hard enough without the trolls. It seems to me it would be very easy to troll in this game, camp over bodies, destroy others buildings and steal others stuff for starters. I will probably never on a public server.
All in all well worth the 30 dollar price, I will get my money out of it

I give Valkyria Chronicles a
BUY NOW - if your a fan of turnbased games
SALE- if your not sure of the genre or you wanna play an engaging game in between AAA releases
Didn't expect much from this game but I had extra steam points so i thought i would buy it.
This is my first JRPG so i cant be a good judge in terms of the JRPG genre but if you are new to the genre this review is for you
PROS
-Interesting turnbased combat system that doesnt destroy the pacing
-The setting is a alternative world war 1 era
- Challenging campain scenarios
- nice cast of side characters and main characters
-Engaging narrative
- rouge like mechanics
- relevant character classes that can suit your style
Cons
- there is a learning curve if your new at this genre
- english voice acting is a bit cringey (recomend the japanese)
- story near the end got a bit wonky in my opinion but nothing too bad.
Final thoughts
Valkyria chronicles os a very enjoyable strategy game that mixes the turn based combat and live action gameplay very well. Think of this as a third person turnbased game. Honestly i was never a fan of the 'god view' turn based stratefy games that JRPG's are known for but when i saw the gameplay footage of this it caught my attention.
One last thing about the narrative of the game. While the main story is a bit lacking I find the mix of rouge like elemnts like permanent character death very refreshing to a story driven game. All the minor characters can die if you pass the mission ( if all of your team dies i think it will revert like nothing happened.) This is similar to the xcom style where the units you build can die permanently. This one time I had a unit who was in critical condition and i had a choice to continue attacking the objective or save her. Thinking I was about to win anyway I went for the objective but i didnt destroy it. So when it was the enemy's turn they killed of one of my units and there was a very sad moment where I realized the consequence of my move. It doesnt help that all of the side characters have there own personalities and unique character models so i was genuinely attached to my team.

Cant stop playing. Great team based game. If you are playing it alone you are missing out on being able to divesify and lean on the skills of your friends for survival. Alone is fun also but can get grindy as you have to provide for all your own needs.
The Lighting and graphics look great. And you really get that feeling of scale when you get to a high point and are looking down on it all. The area to play in is HUGE and that element of suprise is there when you unexpectedly fiind something interesting to explore as you round a corner. With the promise of future biomes I can see myself putting many hours into this.
I have played many FUNCOM games and they seem to have finally found that area between what MMO's are missing and multiplayer sand box. I have said it many times. Sandbox survival and building games are the future of MMO or Multiplayer type games. About time someone with experience in massive internet gaming came to the table and added there experience!
The Conan setting is one the of best Fantasy Settings IMO. It does everything right. Magic is not common and the Mythical beasts are rare. Seeing the Fantastic elements in game seem more visceral and exciting beacause it isnt drowning in it. Which in most games of this setting fail at because it becomes common place and meh... whatever.. Unexciting.
The combat is difficult and not flashy. This is a plus IMO. You can see the action and arent blinded by it. It Becomes very tactical and party position is very important. I dont even mind the friendly fire as it makes everyone better when you have to school up your pals. LOL. I can see that the PVP element of this game will be quite competitive for clans as it will focus on tactical party gemeplay and not a bunch of group spamming. That said... Its not perfect and I think there is room for improvement in the area of weapon deflection and movement. For example; Dodge needs to be able to bound by a double tap and strafe should be added. Defending with the shield to striking your target seems unwieldy at the moment. I havent really tried deflecting with weapons yet. If that mechanic exist, I am not sure. All in all I do enjoy the combat and having the right gear makes a big difference.
I wont get into the crafting experience other than to say it is on par with any other good survival game and does feel like an accomplishment when you are able to craft some cool stuff. The same goes for leveling up.
I do like the fact that there is a story line. They did this one right for a multiplayer game by not making it about you but the area you have been thrust into. Discovering different aspects of the Exiled lands is a nice bonus! The delivery feels unique when you talk to different NPC's about the exiled lands as a first hand account and not just the same story the poor bloke standing next to you is also the hero of. Well Done!
Getting in on this Early Access will not be a dissapointment! If they can keep up this kind of gameplay down the road with Exiles, it will have a long life as a highly rated game!

I was really looking forward to this game and I had a lot of fun with it, but my God did it try to ruin that fun at every turn.  I don’t know if it is because of the recent update or what, but my experience with the game consisted of about 50% fun and 50% glitch.  Some ghosts don’t show up even when all of the requirements for their appearance are meet, and when they do show up they are immortal.
Now, yes, there are some ghosts in this game that are designed to be immortal, but I’m not talking about those.  I’m talking about regular, average ghosts that I can absolutely defeat but who simply won’t die no matter how many times I take a photo of them or their weak point.
Another glaring issue is the camera’s range.  The way it works in-game is that when a ghost gets a certain distance away from you the camera’s screen gets all glitchy and then you can take their photo and deal damage.  But it appears that in order for the static to manifest the ghost has to cross some sort of invisible threshold that only exists when the camera is up.  So, if you pull the camera up too late or if the ghost manifests in your static-zone, the static will not appear and you cannot do damage to it.  For the most part this is not an issue, but there is one boss fight in the school that takes place in a very small room and the ghost started to bum-rush me or manifest just a few feet away.  Even though he was in the camera’s screen and I could take his picture, none of them did damage and he would hit me.  I would run from side of the room to side of the room, pulling the camera up and taking a photo, but there was no static, no damage done, and he would soon kill me.
Dying due to glitches is bad enough, but to then see a dying-screen message of, “maybe you should consider switching to casual gaming,” is just infuriating.  Add to this a bunch of achievements not triggering even when you meet their requirements exactly, and this game can become very frustrating very quickly.  There were other glitches that I encountered, but they hardly effected gameplay as badly so I won’t mention them.
All of that being said, the core mechanics of wandering around a haunted town, defeating ghosts with your camera, finding articles/notes that reveal more of the plot, and finding items to increase your powers are all a lot of fun. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes survival horror games where you can actually fight back but aren’t unstoppable.  I’d almost compare this game to the better Resident Evil titles in that you can defeat nearly all that stands against you, but just a few mistakes and you will die.
tl;dr – Good game, but tons of glitches that, if encountered, can make the game almost impossible to play.  Wait till the next patch comes out and then look to see what people are saying.

Will say shortly - This Game Amazed Me. 10/10
EDIT (Act 2 released): Feelings are same, game really amazed me, it have really good atmosphere, interesting story and interesting way you can play it, it's done in classical style Horror games (understand and explore things by your way), but in modern way to do it. (yes exactly, here no one will tell you where to go, what to push, when to turn atc... here every single thing can be important, things that happen in the beginning can be used in the end part of the game and not as in modern games where every single thing showing you what to do, here you must remember, think and try everything).
Dreadout is not an easy game, but it's easy in same time, here you need to think and explore things, sometimes you will lost, sometimes you can be confused in what to do, but most Puzzles have very easy way to complete them and exactly this is confusing, when you're not waiting that easiest way can be the right way.
Dreadout is the game about girl Linda who fall in to unknown world, another world, where every thing can be hostile, from where no one comes alive. Linda knows nothing about this world, about its creatures, ghosts and people that are living there, she knows nothing about the rules of this world. So yes, player knows same that Linda know about it and you must find, explore and understand all this things with Linda and you must help her to find and explore right answers, tweaks, things and stories of the world about you and Linda know nothing and there is no one to tell you, no one to take your hand and say - "Hey! There is the right answer!". Yes, all this things you and Linda must understand and find by your own. You must find way out.
Good sides for me:
* Atmosphere.
* Story.
* Exploration.
* Puzzles that are challenging.
* That you must find right answers by yourself and not when game drags you like a kid.
* Many ways to scare you and not focused on just one element.
* Ghosts (enemies), each one have it's story and are made in quite unique and interesting way.
* Dreadout is specific game, it can remind many classical horror games, but released in it's own way and have many specific elements that are interesting to explore.
* Gameplay and way how you play it.
* Game hardness, it's hard and easy same time, also sometimes confusing (in a good way), what makes you to search and find right decisions.
* Limbo system, when you really don't want to die... Someone find it annoying, but for me it was part that makes me to afraid of death, when you will be punished for your fault.
Bad sides for me:
* Game needs Optimization, not a critically, but have performance problems.
* Repetitive AI (enemies), on second turn you will know any move of the enemies what makes them easy for me.
It's just my opinion, of course someone will and someone will not agree with me, I played many Horror games before (more classical style one), but just some of that games was really interesting for me to explore their world, and Dreadout now, is new one in my favorites list.
I Recommend Dreadout if you love Atmospheric-Horror games where you must explore things by yourself, where no one is explaining you what and where to do and if you're tired of modern horror-puzzles when game explains you every single thing, here even story must be explored, you must finish the game to understand it, but it's not the fact that you will and for each player story can be different not because it have alter, but because of the experience you will get from it.
And I Recommend it if you love Atmospheric games, if you love exploring and if you just love specific games, games that have Soul and games that are made with Love.

I'll start by saying i've not played all that far through the story - I've had multiple starts due to purchasing just prior to release and a Co-op partner who seems to enjoy playing several classes before sticking to one.
Interestingly enough, this has had the positive of showing me just how different the game can be with different class combinations. We've played combos where it seems that no matter how careful we are, the battlefield inevitably becomes a blanket of different elemental affects indiscriminately maiming everybody on it and we've had more tactical groups that have more control over such affects, without the volatile power behind their attacks.
We've settled on a slightly more understated group, methodically using status affects to control the flow of battle and tip it into our favour.
The game is beautiful looking, it's as deep as you wish it to be and the sheer amount of detail in the world is amazing. The UI is simple without being restrictive, the game will guide you without holding your hand and through that allows you to make your mistakes, or genius discoveries and whichever it be, you're left with under no illusion: That was your doing, for better or worse.
I always want to like games like this but often find the world doesn't feel alive enough, is to linear or awkwardly open to its own detriment - the balance is never quite right, but here, for me at least it has been struck and i've really enjoyed exploring and experimenting.
tldr:
The game is generally well polished, fun and of good depth. Looks beautiful, with an interesting story and the world feels richer for it. Worth a buy from any RPG fan, especially if like me, an rpg feeling like an MMO with no players in it just feels like an empty experience to you - you wont find that here.

- While the graphics are not astonishing the overall aspect of the terrain is what you could expert from a martian type planet surface, apart from the obviously shaped bridges and tunnels that allows you to pass through mountain ranges.
On the negative side:
- No pointers are given which makes the first attemps difficult. Pressing needs such as oxygen and water should be better managed in the first phases.
- This game is also ergonomically deficient, inventory management is prehistorical (manual transfer of items and a ridiculously low capacity of storage for every container), individual interfaces are neat but it remains tedious to juggle between all of them
- Controls are horrible, in particular the vehicles where 90% of the time is spent. Between the inability to reverse when needed, getting stuck in certain places, and the really capricious excavator arm which has the shortest reach possible, this renders the exploration and mining experience frustrating, which is the core of the game.
As a conclusion i do not recommend the game at this stage but the content is promising and if some major works are done on the gameplay aspects (this should really be sorted out before making any new content) then this game can be a good one.

A game with a serious identity crisis.
It starts steep and has heaps of bugs.  But that's just being in Early Access, and there is proof they are being quickly addressed by the devs. So no need to hang up on them.
The bigger problem is the uncertain genre of the game, which will most likely take a PVP MMO direction.
Right now, the game is unfinished, with lots of content missing, and as such tries to appeal to explorers and builders. While their cash is welcome, they will likely get disappointed soon, as the planned direction is:
"Frontier Gameplay - related to rival corporation narrative with a gameplay involving shooting"
The game has started off with a plan to be an MMO. Great investment in stunning scenery and realistic machinery (designed by actual JCB engineers) that are extremely fun to drive around in the environment. Really.
The team has probably ran out of money, or for any other reason had to do an earlier start, resulting in cutting corners and releasing whatever they had ready. The bugs are fine, as they are being corrected.
The bigger problem is that due to such repurposing the concept has gotten lost, and the genre became extremely fuzzy and inconsistent.
A game with an identity crisis.
So how well is the promise "a hardcore blend of survival and construction gameplay" met?
"Survival" ?
Taking place on Mars, and trying to be more or less realistic there are no zombies, cannibals, dinos or other mythical monsters to survive against. The only realistic challenge here is exposure to the environment. Since that probably did not seem to be interesting enough for gameplay, it has been spiced up with some meteor showers, acid clouds, geysers, tornados, glaciers and radioactive sites filling up the majority of the space that is not prohibitively difficult to drive on. Practically turning the game into a 3D "super mario" where you need to dodge the various obstacles the team could come up with and throw you at. (Or discover and learn the "long-cut" getting to the resources driving around in relative safety.)
Main aspects of survival (O2, food and water) are easily covered after the first few missions, and stop being interesting.
Other more realistic aspects of the Martian environment are missed out (temperature, radiation, seasonal weather and daylight changes).
We do not really know much about our avatar, and his/her physical state of "survival", skills, resilience or anything like that.
There is no growing threat that you should build your armor, base and defenses against, something to keep you challenged.
Unless of course, you add rival companies, who will start to kill you in your quest ripping The Red Planet off of its resources.
(Why else would we go there, really?)
"Adventure" ?
There is a lot of exploration to do.
The map is made up of a mix and match of real Martian geographies stitched together, which is actually pretty much fun to drive around in the cool vehicles (a couple upgrades are advised though).
Driving in the canyons, flats, bumps, craters, edges and cliffs while trying to discover more and more resource ponds is fun. Not hundreds of hours fun, but a couple dozen for sure.
"Construction" ?
You can build your base made of pre-designed buildings, which can be upgraded and specialized. You can refine the minerals you mine and sell them to cover your expansion.
The purpose of this expansion, however is unknown at this point. There are no potential directions to take, no broad set of buildings that you can build. You cannot choose your preference what you want to build or your strategy how to get there. Instead: you are constantly being bombarded with "missions" - which are practically just the game telling you what to build next. And these missions seem to be the primary way to get advancement (financially and in XP). The only _choice_ you can make is in what order you build the buildings the game is telling you to build. Well, such level of handholding may pleasure some players, but not all. Not me for sure. Of course, later it might be more open: to build the buildings that help you better in a PVP combat, but that seems quite far away yet, and is a very different direction from the current "builder/explorer" shape.
"Role Playing" ?
Your player seems to be gaining XP, and get level-ups.
There is however complete mystery about what that means, how that impacts your gameplay (if at all) and what you can do about it.
No choices, no skills to select, no specialization, no unlocking of new possibilities. Nada.
Maybe something interesting comes here later on, but most likely related to the shooting aspect. That's just a guess though.
"Simulation"?
Well, driving around the JCB machines custom-designed for this game in the beautifully crafted map is fun. Really fun.
"Management"?
The game at this point seems to be about discovering resource pools, using the minerals to build up your base, refine them and sell the surplus to (partially) fund your endeavours.
At this point you have to do all this manually: Drive out, dodge the obstacles, discover the resources, mine them, transport back, and move them between your backpack, your vehicle, storage, refineries and 3D printers.
That means a lot of taxiing and packing the resources from A to B. This actually takes up 80% of the gameplay.
There seem to be plans to add workers later on, who might hopefully do some of this grinding for you, but how that's done is unclear.
I am especially wondering how workers will drive around with the resources dodging the "super mario" style obstacles scattered between the resource ponds and your base. What paths will they be taking and how their driving skills' results (the damage to or destruction of the vehicles) is going to be managed.
I do not really think the current design of the game supports this "management" type of direction too much.
All in all, I think a lot of work has gone into the game, great design and working engine (apart from the bugs that you also need to count with at this point).
As a simulation/exploration game it is already quite fun. But I'm not sure if that's enough.
In the future, it might become a great PVP MMO, if you are into that. Right now there is no content supporting that direction.
At the moment it seems more like being a building/exploring game, but with limitations to content, too much handholding, and lots of grinding and silly obstacle-dodging in gameplay. And, if the direction changes, it might be disappointing for current players.
A beautiful and promising game, but with a serious identity crisis.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a mystery adventure game played in the third-person perspective of Detective Ronan O'Connor a career criminal turned cop, who is hot on the trail of the notorious "Bell Killer" in the quiet town of Salem, Massachusetts. The opening scene will introduce you to an elusive killer, Detective O'Connor and an unknown teenager. The failed capture of the Bell Killer leaves Detective O'Connor dead, the girl missing and the killer still at large. It is now up to you to solve your own murder and find out what happened before your soul can move on.
It should be noted that none of what I mentioned above is, in any way, a spoiler. This occurs minutes into starting a new game. However, it stands as an interesting premise, one I honestly can't recall playing in the past. With that being said, Murdered: Soul Suspect has been a very difficult game to pinpoint. I found myself motivated by the main storyline, but often pulled astray by lackluster side missions and shoddy combat junctions. The end was worth the time invested, but getting there was one of uncertainty; let's start from the beginning.
For those that don't know the history of Salem, Massachusetts, it is infamously known for the capture, trials and executions of accused witches circa 1692-1693. The game takes place entirely within a small suburb of Salem and the lore of the game is derived from such [so much so it practically beats you over the head with it]. While previous knowledge of these events aren't necessary, as the game will give you over two-hundred collectables that provide details of such events, it is interesting to see what was influenced from the town's history or forced to make deductive conclusions from seemingly illogical perspectives.
During the course of your investigation you'll meet others [both dead and living] that will help you on your journey, providing clues that propel you closer to the truth. Here is where I had mixed feelings about the game. You see, the main story I found compelling and the script did a wonderful job of teasing you with tiny, minute details without giving you much of anything to go on. Then, however, you're side-tracked with boring side missions and dreadful combat.
As you were warned, you must occasionally fight demons whose sole purpose is to consume your ghostly essence, but luckily Ronan has the ability to banish these demons with the power of obnoxious QTEs; where he gets these powers is never explained. Whenever I was forced to fight these demons I found it painfully annoying. These encounters felt forced, stuffed into the fabric of the game where the suspense waned and a hole needed to be plugged. I hated the combat to the point I chose to simply die each time I got caught and reload as opposed to actually killing the demons.
Demons aside, Soul Suspect suffers from several other shortcomings: repeating dialogue between NPCs, useless abilities like "Poltergeist", which gave me the ability to possess electrical devices during plot convenient sequences, the ability to read minds when it was necessary and the ability to teleport. Even with all of these powers I still felt like a poor excuse for a ghost, the store brand product of something better. The game gives you these abilities, but then severely limits you to what you're able to do with them. Even as a ghost, I couldn't indiscriminately walk through walls, forcing Ronan to avoid "ghost walls" or spiritual residue from old structures and objects, all of which prohibited walking through; Invisible walls for ghosts you might call them. It is never explained why they exist or the reasoning behind them.
The strangest thing about the game isn't the main story, which is surprisingly solid, but the extras the game throws in to expand its own longevity. The side missions were dull, the collectables were seemingly unnecessary outside achievement hunting and the combat was utterly pointless. Woven between these shortcomings was a tapestry of mystery that could have been so much more if the effort was put elsewhere. Instead were given bits of possibility only to be disappointed.
Forgo the extras and put that effort into Ronan's murder and you have a great murder mystery to solve. However, you never really feel like a true ghost, nor really even a mediocre detective. Murdered: Soul Suspect is a case of trying to do too much and spreading your content too thin. The phrase "less is more" fits this game all too well.


Overall, Murdered: Soul Suspect is good, but not great. It has a lot of hiccups that, if you can look past, has something interesting to offer. The story is intriguing, the voice acting is well done and some of the characters are interesting. I'd cautiously recommend it if you can find it on sale, but don't except a masterpiece if you pick it up. Case closed.

I wanted to like this game, but then I played it.  Pretty much every mechanic in the game is handled poorly.  Most of the puzzles in the game consist of you searching the crime scene to collect a pool fo mostly useless clues and then picking the correct one out of the list when prompted.  Hmm, which clue is related to the Bell Killer?  Could it be the one that just says "Bell Killer"? Yes, yes it is.  Every time.   90% of the "puzzles" are exactly this.  No creative or deductive thought is required to finish this game.  The only other major mechanic in this game is demons.  They are one of the worst mechanics of any game I've ever played.  Basically they are like wandering sentries that you have to sneak up on to destroy.  If they spot you they chase you around for a couple of minutes.  They are never fun.  They are only annoying hinderences that stop you from continuing the story.  They were obviously slapped onto the game to make things more "difficult" and drag the game out.  Without them you could probably finish the game in a couple of hours.  Most of which is walking back and forth between the various crime scenes in the absolutely tiny town of Salem.  There are a bunch of collectibles to find throughout the game, but unless you collect all of them of a given type you don't get anything out of it.  And when you do finally get them all you are rewarded with a crappy little short story about someone's death.  The overall story of the game is ok I guess.  It has some serious problems, but relative to how bad the rest of the game is, I guess it gets a pass.  It does not however make slogging through the rest of the game worth it.  I'll give the game some credit though, the title is sort of clever.

First off, I don't hate this game.  I just feel there were better choices that could of been done in its creation.  I think I'm upset because I didn't get what I expected in the game.   I'm accusing this game of trying to appear to be more than it really is.  Like a good spymaster, you look at it on Steam and it intrigues you.  There is no other game quite like it from other developers and you believe you're going to get wrapped up in some non stop Game of Throne like challenges.   You get those situations, but you really do grow older waiting for it to happen.  IF you read about the game, and must have it, I recommend waiting for the Steam sale.
Seeing how you really can't lose the game, the threats that are opposed upon the player are empty.  It's not really a game.   You decide what is winning or losing.  If world conquest is your thing, don't expect it to happen in this game during your life time unless this game is all you do.   The computer can just create a large random army out of nowhere anytime it wants to humiliate you for such ambition.   Unlocking achievements can also be something to strive for.
This may just be me, but I am not patient with this game.  Some of you may love waiting for a pop up that says something like, "Rome is getting into Christianity.", to click something like, "Not our concern.", but not for me.  I am also accusing this game of having thin content.  The calender ticking away is just to spread the little content it has out.  Example, "We have a hundred and twenty new pop ups in this expansion with twenty new art pieces, that may pop up over seven hours of play." I think they need a larger pop up programming staff.  I play a game to kill time, not to watch a game kill time.   I bought most of the expansions during the Steam sale to try and thicken it up, which probably isn't a good thing.  I feel fifteen bucks for one of these is too much.  You are really buying a few new menu selections, some pop ups, and the ability to read the history of characters from other lands.
You will read the history of the character you are playing to have the same static menu's in your face, with the same random occurances any other character will have, and he will never follow the path you read about, or even try.  I played an interesting guy and read that he started the school of Astronomy.  That's awesome, I would love to play through the struggles the guy had to go through to get such a school going during his historic time.  Unfortunalty, all I could do was marry him to some random girl and press claims for territory, and he even randomly slept with another girl, thus goes the only history the game would allow me to create for this guy.   Once started the school of astronomy, now reduced by me to a land wanting, a#% crusher.
You'll be remarrying,playing matchmaker, and assigning duties.  Once people start dying, I stopped caring who replaces them, because the personality traits that could cause problems on those jobs rarely do.  I tried to hire greedy characters to start stuff, but they collected taxes and died.  Battles will be decided by whomever raises the biggest army.  You know you're going to lose or win after the vassels are raised.   If your numbers are smaller, you lose the Risk portion of the game( if you choose to quit after this .)
The art department on this game rocks.  Also, whomever looked into the history of these characters did their part.  A historically accurate game is a great idea, and it made my money jump into the grand Paradox pocket.
It would of been better as a "Choose your own adventure" over a map than one with menu's and a pop up clock.  The menu's are not necessary.  Example, "Your sister has betrayed you, you should arrest her?"  This is a "Yes", or, "No" question.  I don't really want to be guided to a menu that has, "Imprison" on it amongst choices like, "Send a gift.", or "Arrange Marriage"
This is another gripe, you get little symbols that pop up at the top of the screen that guide you to MENU's( some of these menu's are hard to figure out, and if you're new, you won't figure out what to click, so you just ignore it, to most likely have whatever is happening have no effect.)  If you're going to have pop ups, then guiding me to a menu is unneccesary.  I'm micromanaging, to micro-results to micro-events.  I also believe this game could guide you a little better.  Instead of watching days tick by, I'd rather just skip to the day something happens, or something needs to be taken care of.   This game could be made so much better.

This game has less to do with encountering ghosts and more to do with solving difficult puzzles. Don't get me wrong...I love puzzles! Instead, I end up being frustrated.
Also, the game lacks balance. The first ghost you encounter is a violent giant pig that apparently CAN'T BE KILLED! Why is this the first creature I encounter? Why not start with a very basic enemy to help you get a hang of the controls? I don't know! Makes no sense. Also, the first boss you encounter is nearly impossible. You fight a ghost with scissors in a small space that requires you to have impossible reflexes in order to even have a chance at victory.
At the end of the day, this game isn't fun or scarry, but frustrating. I'm hoping that the developers take all these things into consideration before they release Act 2.

I had read all the negative reviews for this game and wanted to give it a try because sometimes people can be a little over the top when it comes to writing something bad about a game, but in this case, every single one was justified. It doesn't matter how mad or wacky the developers said they tried to make the game, it is a lie. There is no effort put into the making of this at all. I truly feel sorry for the developers if it took them longer  to make than the twelve minutes I put into getting all of the achievements.
In ADventure Lib you play a hero who has to find a great treasure to prove himself to the king. There is a pool of words that are scrambled into the game and will be randomly assigned to certain items. These are words like 'key, butter, Charles, plunger, knife etc.'. Every time you begin a new game everything will be re-randomized using the same pool. The story remains the same, the characters remain the same, the only thing that changes from playthrough to playthrough is which item gets called what.
Being a point and click this makes ADventure Lib a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to play. Point and click games rely on you combining different items with each other, as does this, except these items are randomly named so the entire game is trying every single item with something else until something works. All future playthroughs will be boring as once you know where you find the item you'll know what it is meant to be and where it is meant to be used.
Every achievement can be found in one single playthrough and can be gotten within 15 minutes with ease, though there is nothing to make you want to get them besides the fact you actually wasted money on this and feel like you NEED something in return.
The voice acting is poor, the graphics are basic and the story is terrible. There is no re-playability, and no fun to be had the first time you play either.
There MAY have been a good idea somewhere here but the lack of effort from the developers have left this game completely worthless.

This game is an interesting concept that would potentially be a fun free flash game that could garner some mild interest. It is NOT, however, anything worth paying money for. There's maybe 20 minutes of gameplay at best, the voice acting is sub-par, the alleged "wackiness" and "comedy" is one joke repeated over and over again, and the actual gameplay is pretty horrendous. First things first, because there's a lot to cover here. Metro Last Light Redux is a post-apocalyptic first-person shooter set in underground Moscow. It continues the story of Metro 2033, and does so very nicely. If you've played 2033 Redux, then there aren't a ton of new mechanics or gameplay features. All the guns that were in 2033 are in Last Light, as well as plenty of new guns to try out, and mods to improve them.
As for the story and setting, both Metro games pass with flying colors when creating the worldspace. If I didn't have to worry about air filters and mutants, I'd spend time casually strolling through the Metro and Moscow. The world is absolutely beautiful in terms of post-apocalyptic worlds.
Combat isn't the focus of the game, survival is. Pro tip: thoroughy check every nook and cranny for spare ammo or filters. You'll thank me later. There are sometimes multiple ways to progress, and stealthing your way through a room of enemies can have its benefits.
My favorite part of the game is the bonus content. There are two sets of levels, the story missions and the bonus missions. My advice is to do the main story before you start doing bonus missions. The bonus stuff is often stuff that's already in the main story, just from a different angle. There's also two levels that aren't linear and that are more focused on killing time and also exploring a beautiful world.
Side note: once you finish the main story, do yourself a favor and play the Developer Pack. Just do it. Please.
Overall, beautiful world, great combat and stealth mechanics, a satisfying story and characters, and plenty of content that will keep you coming back to the game after you've beaten it.

Hard Reset is very much like Painkiller or Serious Sam.  You have to manage plowing through waves of little bad guys in each area, while keeping your ammo and heal counts up, especially for when the big guys come out.  It's like those other modern shooters in terms of the level design being very linear and corridor-like, except that the combat is actually fun thanks to some clever weapon design.  There's also loads of completely inexcusable invisible walls that you will never get used to, both in secret hunting, and in trying to deftly maneuver in combat.
The visuals are reminiscent of a shooter that's several years older, but they get the job done in terms of providing an appropriate and unique atmosphere.  I find the comic-book style cutscenes to be both moderately well executed and out of place.  The writing is bad, the story is pointless, but killing things in a cyberpunk city is fun.
Honestly, I prefer Hard Reset to Painkiller and Serious Sam.  I prefer the level-up choices that the game offers me and it provides some choice-driven context to a genre (corridor shooter) that generally  has none.

This review is based on Hard Reset at the price point of $2.50 USD.
Hard Reset is an interesting FPS game - it is similar in feel to Serious Sam 3, both in the type of weapons you can use, as well as the hidden secrets. However since it is single player, I found myself expecting more of a storyline than a Serious Sam game. There is a story, but it is so convoluted, and told poorly through a series of comic strips. After about 3 hours into it, I found myself not caring much about the story - the combat is the only really interesting part.
The combat for the most part feels tight and you do feel some sense of progression as you can upgrade various parts of your character/weapon, however I would have really preferred more customization i.e. more RPG aspects. The level of customization was similar to a Bioshock game.
The enemy encounters were pretty intense at certain points, but on the whole after about half-way through the game, the fights don't get any more difficult - they just get more annoying. You will be fighting the same types of enemies, just in larger numbers and in more difficult battle areas.
Despite the flaws, the combat and the upgrading/secrets were enough to keep me playing until the end. Just don't expect to really enjoy the story much. That being said, for $2.50, it was pretty enjoyable. I'd recommend it, but its not worth more than $5.

What can I say about Hard Reset: Extended Edition?
Its a great throwback to the 'run and gun' games of the past, I personally think Serious Sam's latest effort does a better job in that regard but Hard Reset has something Serious Sam doesn't... Upgrades. New weapons can be unlocked and upgraded by finding 'Nanites' that are scattered around a level, of course most of the high value amounts are found in secret areas.
I greatly enjoyed playing through the game and was really enjoying the plot, right up to the point where it just cuts off abruptly. There is potential for a sequel but who knows if thats even in the works. Take a look at Rage for a great example of wasted potential in regards to a continued story.
Between some of the levels (I was going to say all but thats not the case) you're treated to a semi-animated comic book to explain the plot. This is a touch that I loved because it gives the game a greater feeling of depth and you want to explore the world this story is set in. Sadly this is where the game falls flat, while playing I found my character getting stuck on invisible walls and not being able to jump over or climb on things that I really should have been able to. It broke the immersion of the game quite badly especially since finding the aforementioned secrets quite often means having to explore the world around you, increasing the likelihood of running into these issues.
I would recommend this game, for some nice 'run and gun' fun. But don't expect anything too deep and try not to be upset by the abrupt ending. I really hope that Flying Wild Hog create a sequel to this rather than let it die off.

I never played the original Metro Last Light, so I can't offer a comparison. All I can say, however, is that the graphics are still impressive today, taking full advantage of its surroundings, ranging from dark sunway tunnels, the catacombs of a dead church and the grimy radiation covered Russia it all lies in.
The combat is incredibly satifying, allowing you to go from brilliant stealth, blowing out lamps and shooting out bulbs with my lethal air rifle to further wrap myself in darkness for that easier knock-out, to going full Rambo with a minigun and laying waste to all that dared face me.
However, the game is far from easy, as when you finally need to go above ground, it's much more terrifying than being surrounded by skeletons with only a lighter to stave off the darkness. The reason why being that the mutated monsters of the wasteland always try to overwhelm you, and ammo is scarce in a world where few humans dare to go. Additionally, damage to your gas mask causes it to crack and make things even harder to see. Essentially, its one of the few games where I was excited to descend into the darkness of the underground.
One other point, simply because its this that makes me love this game so much than other FPS's: The immersion. Due to the HUD fading away whenever you don't need it, it makes the game so much more immersive and, in my opinion, better. It truly feels at this point that you are just a russian soldier trying to survive in a unforgiving metro.
So, the bad things?
The sound design can be slightly irratating at some point, with the same stock grunt used whenever you pump a air rifle, or knock out an enemy, and the lip syncing falling just out of match now and then. Also, the main character Artyom can feel just like a blank slate, which I suppose is intentional. Also,  the story, while overall alright, is only that. I never knew why I was doing half the things I was aside from "He's a nazi. Nazi bad. Kill".
But, overall, still a fantastic game. If you can, play it. Play it now.

If you've played Original sin 1, then this will feel extremely familiar.
A mistake many bigger companies seem to make is to simplify and gut a mechanic without much improvement added, if at all. Unlike these companies, Larian Studios actually kept and expanded on nearly all the good mechanics, skill variation and gameplay (races, attribute and skill redesign, etc.), improving the game in almost every aspect and redesigning a few things to make them more complex, streamlined or interactive, rather than oversimplfying.
If I had to pick one improvement to praise above all the others it would be the new way skills are managed. This new system is the shift towards "skill slots" managed by a memory attribute. Instead of having each skill limited to X numbers of abilities based on your skill in this ability, every ability learned is stored and can be made active for 1, 2 or 3, skill slots based on it's power. As such, you can choose to make all your skills of the same school, or mix and match as your leisure. I'll draw a comparison here to a wizards spellbook in dnd. Rather than having a limited selection of "spells", such as a sorcerer in dnd, and having to unlearn and re-learn abilities if you want something changed (Which could have become a hassle if there were skills you wanted to have purely for out of combat situations), you can now simply switch your skills around based on your current needs for the next encounter or to help overcome terrain obsticles. And if you want to have a broaded skill selection in combat, you have to devote points or feats towards this purpose. (Though you get enough that it's not really needed unless you want to generalize rather than specialize, since as stated above, you can select which abilities you want to use before a combat encounter anyway)
As with Original sin 1, there is a lot of content and side-quests here, allowing you to go trough the game at your own pace. One thing I found really interresting, is the "pre-made" characters as they get a unique story arc that opens up more options for how you tacle quests, all of them seem to have a unique quest line attached to them and almost every conversation of importance seems to have it's own line for the created characters to use. You can choose to play as one of these, or choose up to three of them to act as your companions with their own agenda while playing your own custom character, even making them the "main character" for the main plot, should you so choose. You can also select all of their initial classes, allowing for great customization and allows you to construct your party completely around your own playstyle and needs.
While the crafting system has had several things added to help expand the system, such as the new rune system which allows for further customization of items, there does not appear to be as many recipies for crafting your own gear beyond the first few levels. Though crafted items does conform to your level when you crafted them, but from what I can tell, you can't really make them magical for instance and improve resistances by adding orbs, such as you can in OS:EE. As this is something that got improved upon and added in Original Sin's enhanced edition, I suspect it will be the case for Original Sin 2 as well, depending on player feedback. (Or it could just be me that never figured out the new recipies for crafting and combining unenchanted gear to make it magical etc. It's quite possible.).
Another GREAT addition is the Game master mode. This allows you to create campaigns for your friends and make your own unique stories, encounters and quests to help expand on the games longevity and replayability. The addition of mod support, the ability to share these campaigns online and creating new assets is simply fantastic. Bioware did this for Neverwinter Nights back in 2002, and it's still got a strong community and unique player made campaigns. If Larian Studios continue down this road with this IP, I think it's going to stick around for a long long time!
There is also a new arena mode, where you can go head to head with your friends or people online in various 1v1, 2v2, etc. matchups to test and improve your own skills, and bragging rights for owning your friends with a cheesy build ;)
Larian studios manages to meet and exceed expectations and did a great job keeping kickstarter and early access buyers updated with the development process and progress, listening to player feedback and communicating with the playerbase. This is an example I wish more devs would follow, as it's greatly helped improve their game and makes the community feel like their opinion matters.
I'd strongly reccomend any RPG fans to buy the game. Not only will you get a game well worth the asking price with plenty of hours of playtime for each dollar spent, but also help support a developer that is no doubt going to keep doing great work into the future as well, as long as we players keep on rewarding such great work and their dedication to their playerbase.
