So many negative reviews so I'll just say this.  I stopped playing this game twice, only because it took up my whole life.  I have far more hours on it than my steam says, truthfully, I've hardly played on steam and I have 434 hours logged.  There is one thing I'd like to say.
THERE IS NOTHING YOU CANNOT DO IN THIS GAME EVEN IF YOU CHOOSE NOT TO OPEN YOUR WALLET.  THIS GAME IS 100% F2P.
I have seen far worse in games than the pay system in this one.  This one is only hindering on your ability to own housing/crafting, but thats easily managable.  As you advance in a craft, the labor costs decrease as well, making some things that where not effective earlier, something you can sell to make money now.
People say you can't make money when your not patron(subscriber) and I disagree.  I always have enough money for patron status within a week using the formula at the bottom of this review to craft via buying and selling things from the AH.
Now it is true, when you first start playing, you cannot access the AH without an AH license.  My first playthrough I saved up money for 2x APEX and bought patron which removes the need for the AH license, but I still picked one up later.  That one barrier is a hinderence but does not make that game unplayable, as by the time you reach max level, or maybe even halfway to max level, you should have enough money from fighting alone to get a single apex for an AH license.  I'll post the formula for making money at the bottom.
HIGHLIGHTS
_______________________________________________________________________________
TRUE OPEN WORLD
1.GLIDERS!!!!  This game has so many fantastic design elements I've never seen anywhere else.  First of all GLIDERS!  OMG GLIDERS...Every game I've ever played since this game, has me trying to double jump to pull out my glider.  You are MEANT to explore every nook and cranny of this game.  There are even "achivement" awards for finding specific areas and even if nothing is in a place, how do you know another player isnt hiding a large tree farm hidden behind that mountain.
2.Naval Warfare!  They did a fantastic job with ships and boats, to fishing boats etc.  Gameplay is VERY smooth over water and each component on a ship is destructable with its own HP bar.  I wish there were a lot more types of ships as well but they did a fantastic job there.  The physics on ships can make you laugh sometimes too when they go to right themselves.  Although I wish there was more of a reason to leave a ship out and/or docked.  There's a button that makes it so no one can steal your ship, but it only lasts a minute after you disembark.  10mins when in town would be a lot better, and 1 minute at sea would still work.
3.  It is a true open world.  As for some loading screens, the only loading areas I'm aware of is dungeons, and those are no PVP group events anyway.
4. Multiple Islands/Dialects.  The world is very large, and sadly I wish it were bigger still.  You will have to learn other langauges if you wish to speak with anyone from the other faction and that can take some time and money but is still a fun aspect of the game.
PVP
The PVP aspect is a part of the game I wish they knew how to address better.  PVP starts around level 30 areas and is pretty much open after that point.  PVP as it is now is very, very fun.  I'm not really a huge PVP'r, but the threat of danger is always around which is fun.  As the game currently stands, you can opt out of PVP by simply sticking to your homelands.  Passed level 30 areas, you just have to watch for criminals from your own faction, but I personally have never really had too much to worry about.  There's 3-4 areas, per Continent, that you cannot be attacked in and those areas are quite large.
Two things would make this game A LOT better imo though.
1.  Create a server that has a 100% unkillable rate on home Continents, like they do for levels 1-30 but make it for all areas.  Still able to get jacked on the high seas and opposing Continent but thats a risk you take.  (Easy Mode)
2.  Create a server that has a 100% no protection rate on home Continents allowing only the guards to protect you. Then make it so when you die, you drop ALL your items including some of what you have equiped or possibly all of what is equipped.(Hard Mode)
THIS would remove the entire pay to win PVP aspect of the game and fix the only real problem with the "Credit Card Power" system and at the same time, a lot more items and gold would shift hands via AH as well as a lot more crafters being needed.  The creation of these two servers would solve a good majority of the complaints and negative reviews.
Here is the forumla for making money.
SP() x (AHT) = G ()  //Selling Price(SP) x AuctionHouseTax(AHT) = how much Gold you get back (G)
G() - MC() = SP()    //G - Material Cost(MC) = Single Profit(SP)
1000/LC() = TC()     //1000 / Labor Cost(LC) = Total Crafts per labor potion(TC)
TC() x SP() = TP()   //TotalCrafts x SingleProfit = Total Profit(TP)
TP() - LPC() = NP()   //Total Profit(TP) - Labor Potion Cost(LPC) = Net Profit(NP)
If your Net Profit is in the positive, your making money effectively without using any labor of your own.  I also believe the AH takes more tax if you are not patron, but i dont think its much more, its 10% from patron or (0.9) in the formula above.

This game lives and dies by how much you enjoy listening to the dealer and how much you can roleplay.  I don't mean roleplay like in an Elder Scrolls game where you make a backstory, I mean roleplay that you're dealing cards in some candle lit basement with a creepy weirdo that has a particularly soothing voice.  If you can't get down with that then this game is gonna suck.
The combat is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥.  No other way to describe it.  It's a poor man's Batman, complete with the little spidersense signs above enemies to let you know when to counter attack.  At least Batman let you go stealthy when you wanted to.  Here every combat encounter is the same "mash the attack button then counter when it tells you to".  There's no weapon variety either.  All weapons, from hammers to axes to magic swords, play the exact same, save for some activated abilities that work on cooldowns, and getting those is up to the RNG.
Your player character is also awful.  He's this weird mowhawk barbarian dude that looks terrible.  For a game about roleplaying I would've loved to see some kind of character creator.  Even if we couldn't get some way to choose between warrior/rouge/mage, at least some option to choose to play as a girl or a black dude, or someone that isn't ugly as sin.  Thank God for the DLC styles giving you masks and helmets so you don't have to look at your character's face.
Everything else in the game is done through cards.  Move from card to card, get little blocks of text from cards, choose cards to see if you win or lose non-combat encounters.  It's a little dull after a while and you stop seeing the cards and the stories and start seeing numbers.  Once you get to that point, the game becomes a lot less fun.
I still recommend Hand of Fate, but it's clearly better than the sum of its parts and only if you can really get into that DnD style roleplaying mindset.

This is a premiere strategy game.
It is NOT tactical.
Let me repeat that.
Tactics are NOT NOT NOT involved.
I see too many people try this game expecting something akin to Total War only to get turned off by the lack of tactical decisions. "Strategy" games are more akin to simulation games in essence. You plan your course of action through dangerous circumstances to achieve the best victory possible. Strategy is knowing when to fight, where to fight, how to take advantage of your situation for long-term benefits, and other similar questions. Tactics is "how to fight" and this game does not cover that. It is a question of logistics rather than tactics. Do you have enough troops, rather than are your troops fighting at optimal efficieny. Do you have the defensive high ground, rather than whether or not this unit happens to be in good terrain at any given time. Do you catch the enemy army off guard, rather than using flanking to decimate part of the army.
If you expect a Civilization-esque game, or something like Total War. Check your expectations. Go online, and watch gameplay before buying. You are probably in for a surprise.

Summary: Oh NOW I get it.
Mass Effect 1 was a promising game with really groundbreaking ideas, but it was deeply flawed and just not that fun. I was very disappointed with it and considered it one of the most overrated games around. But colour me impressed. Mass Effect 2 improves on its predecessor in nearly every aspect. While ME1 was a frustrating experience, this game is compelling and actually drew me in and urged me to finish it, and I can even see myself playing it again not to pinpoint its flaws but to, y'know, play it some more because I like it.
The single best thing about this transition is that the filler that plagued the first game has been almost completely dug out. No more obnoxiously long empty corridors, lengthy elevator shafts or drawn-out loading screens. Shepard can run at any time now, and areas are much more compact while maintaining a sense of scale. You might be a bit disappointed at first with the new Citadel, but think about how LONG it took to get around that place and you'll get over it quickly. This obviously makes the game more accessible and better paced. Oh, and the Mako and those pointless, infuriating open planet sections are completely gone, praise the Enkindlers.
It seems accessibility and simplification were the name of the game during development, as something else that has been gutted out are a lot of the RPG elements, to the extent that there's no longer even an inventory. Loot you find on the field is transferred to your ship, including raw elements and blueprints, and there you can choose which to invest in. Even the amount of available attributes for characters has been halved. It's not a perfect change, and I've heard people bemoan the loss of ME1's 'hardcore' RPG elements. But ultimately, ME1 provided an illusion of complexity. All those acid and synthetic rounds, armour types, every weapon type for every character even though some of them can't even use a sniper's zoom? A mess. There was really no need for the loot system and it quickly became an inconvenience, an unidentifiable list of numbers and letters you must occasionally stop your adventure for and muddle through, automatically taking clearly the best items and melting down everything else. In ME2, you just grab everything in the field and choose whether you want to use it during your downtime in the ship. This series' strength is its story, world and characters, each of which you customise to more effect, and the inventory system was a good thing to cut and it keeps the pace up nicely. You'll still end up stopping for hacking mini-games though, and unfortunately these are a weakness as while they're smooth enough, they're never challenging. Fail a combat encounter and you might find yourself autosaved before a hacked terminal, and this quickly becomes an irritance.
Another area that's seen a massive overhaul, and one I didn't really expect, is the combat. Sure, it's still a rather typical cover shooter with invincible waist-high ledges and doesn't exactly reinvent the wheel. But the mechanics and encounters have seen excellent improvement. Areas seem much better suited for combat now, and there are some genuinely great set-pieces. Combat is more frequent, and there are more enemies with better AI. Weapons are no longer energy-based; they have ammo now (a simple one-clip-fits-all system) and have to reload, and it's easy to underestimate how effective that is in determining how a player strategises how they use their weapons. Strategic use of powers is regularly called into action and now easy to grasp too; warp barriers and armour, overload or drain shields, hit the weak spots with health. Combined with all those pace improvements mentioned before combat just feels so much faster and more intense. Misgivings include that enemy types are still a bit repetitive.
It seems like the gameplay and mechanics are finally living up to the first game's realised world and characters, but even this area has seen progress. The game invests so much more in its characters, actively encouraging you to get to know them, favourite them, involve yourself in their personal matters, all to productive ends; even not favouring a character can see repercussions in the endgame. It's still rather staunchly militaristic and as such Shepard is rarely 'you' and rather a rough-and-ready military man you happen to control, but the story takes an appropriately darker, seedier turn away from the stuffy politics of the original that makes it a bit more rogueish and interesting. There's some really interesting locales and places to explore in this game too, and a couple of cool new aliens to meet. Like the first game there aren't that many actual 'levels', but certainly more than the first game, and it feels less deceptive with the disappearance of the Mako levels.
Visually, ME2 has been polished and not much more, not that it needed it; same big beautifully designed world and intricate character models. There is noticeably less texture flicker and artifacting. Uncanny valley moments and lipsync strangeness are apparently unavoidable but greatly reduced. Characters popping out of scene and missing dialogue cues still happens unfortunately, but it's not as obvious now. One very entertaining out-of-bounds glitch I discovered on Illium aside, the game ran without a hitch.
I'm relieved that this series has some substance to the ridiculous hype that follows it around. ME2 is a very memorable game. Its beautifully realised world and characters can now finally be shown off with solid combat, refined mechanics and a hefty dose of pace. It's a much tighter experience and one I can get excited about. I'm looking forward to finding the time to play through again, maybe to fine-tune my choices from the first game, or maybe play through as a Renegade this time. Point is, I'm looking forward to it.
ONE FINAL QUESTION REMAINS: DO you play the first game before this one? I DID find that having played the first game had me in the know about certain things and in some ways enhanced my experience with some callbacks to my actions there. I could say my experience of ME2 was improved then...BUT if your question is, "What is the hype about these Mass Effect games anyway?" - PLAY THIS GAME FIRST. If you fully intend to play each of the games regardless, perhaps pick up the first one, just bear in mind it's not a particularly good game. There we go, a letter to my former self.

My personal review of the game:
Positives:
1) Asian take on Fatal Frame.
2) Javanese / Indonesian mythology and folklore.
3) Good ghost graphics.
Negatives:
4) Doesn't progessively guide you on what and where you need to go.
5) Scissor Man battle is unfair.
6) You won't know there was powerups till you die (many times) in the game.
7) Sobbing ghost battle is unfair. You won't know that you need to shoot her back.
8) Have to shoot countless times to know something is wrong with the photo?
Overall:
A good game, but is let-down by not providing a clear and progressive stages to acquiring information and power-ups. Got this cheap in a sale. For that price, it's a decent enough game, but there are a few things holding it back. Some of the times I died, I wasn't sure what killed me, or you could get jammed into the corner by enemies and then meleed quickly to death. In some places you're deliberately shoved into tiny areas with large monsters... which I tend to find irritating rather than a fair challenge.
The upgrade system was kinda fun, though I'm not sure what the point of having two guns was - in this game 1 gun can have 5 functions, which are all the different weapon types you need. Seems a better prospect to use just one of the gun types rather than both... I stuck with the mechanical gun throughout. Played through on Normal mode... though if the harder modes requrie more ammo, you may want to have rocket launcher/shotgun/machinegun combo on both. The enemy HUD upgrade I think should've been a default feature rather than an upgrade tbh.
The game is pretty short, but if you're buying this in a sale, the length doesn't matter as much... but the ending is definitely cliffhanger'd, which was disapponting for me. I think they could have written a bit more on it, even if they left a challenge open at the end of it, just to add to the sense of completion. In general, the plot could do with a little more beefing up, just to get a better sense of the world and what the heck is going on. You're not going to find a groundbreaking plot here, but I don't think it's the kind of game that needs a unique plot.

I'm going to be as honest as possible about this game without coming across totally scathing, but this game is just not up to par. I would even say that it's not really a passing grade.
Let me start with what is good. The sound was amazing. Music and musical changes as well as ambient noises make for a great deal of atmosphere and scare-factor in these games; clearly the developers and designers of this game realized that. The models used for the creatures and ghosts also struck me as unsettling and scary.
The price is also affordable which is a bonus.
But I guess that's it.
Graphics were sub-par. I can foregive this however and would encourage you to look past graphics when making a purchase in the horror genre. I think too much emphasis on graphics can actually ruin a well designed game.
But this game didn't strike me as well designed. My first frustration was centered around the inarticulate communication of what is seemingly the first real puzzle. A help screen can be accesssed in the games menu and when all else fails, the main character also keeps a journal that can be referenced at any time. Presumably, to help with solving puzzles. As you might have guessed this was not the case with the first puzzle. You are left to wander the halls aimlessly looking for anything to help you. The only clue from the journal? I need something sharp. The rest of the puzzles mechanics are just "dropped" on you with the anticipation that you'll piece together what the developers were driving at. I can appreciate this approach to puzzle/horror games (Riven and Myst were both fun and did similar things) but I became frustrated with the pig/key puzzle and its abstruse and very obscure "picture of what could look like bad graphics on the ceiling" solution.
After spending so much time pacing the hallways to figure out this puzzle, the fright of the game had become entirely deflated. With my frustration now outweighing the atmosphere, I carried on with the puzzle in to a room where I need something sharp. The first item I see of notable worth in the room? A pair of scissors. I don't just get the scissors though. I need to go over to a crib (for what reasons I'll never understand since I'm not looking for a crib) and trigger a boss fight. Okay. Bosses are usually another side of a game that can be fun and interesting.
Nope. The pairing of cloogy controls and a constrained space (you fight in an enclosed room) are the only reasons this fight can be considered "challenging". The space was a good idea. The controls were not.
You spend a great deal of game-time in third person following the main character with a pretty typical control scheme. Moving the mouse moves the camera while you use the keyboard to interact (E) and move (WSAD). The flashlight on your phone is turned off/on with (F) while the right mouse button puts you in "first person" mode where you look through the camera of the phone to snap a picture with the left mouse button. Doing so to a ghost deals damage to them. You cannot move quickly while taking these pictures. Why? Because screw you. That's why.
Those controls are reasonable. But it leaves you impared when attempting to swap between third and first person modes and quickly line-up a snap-shot of anything.
And guess what this fight demands of you? You guessed it. So here you are, in a tight space, moving from third to first person, which in turn slows you down or speeds you up, attempting to take pictures of a ghost that is phasing in and out of existence around you. All that was truly needed was a bit more indication of where this ghost was going to appear next or maybe slightly more space, but there is no way to "quickly" look behind you and check all angles. You  have to run in short circles in the middle of the room whipping the camera around just enough to line up a snap-shot and hope you don't get so much as nicked by the boss, because then you'll be locked out of recovery and defeated.
What's so bad about being defeated? Well, when defeated (killed) you are sent to a spirit world. Your task here? Wait for your character to pick her sorry butt up off the ground then run a soul-crushing distance (about 20 or so seconds) back to the light and re-enter the frustrating game that sent you here to begin with. Every time you are defeated. Wait for her to get up ~sigh~ Run for a mind-numbing 20 seconds to the light ~sigh~ Try again.
Look. I know many are not  going to take well to my review. Haters gonna hate. But more of my time was spent running to the light, wandering hallways aimlessly, and doubting my purchase than was spent enjoying the game. I never finished the first boss. Like many other games that frustrate me, I will likely return and complete the game; a kind of "due diligence" on my part. I did so with the original Red Faction game as well (also a terrible game).  But I ultimately don't recommend this title. It lacks both polish and necessary (not even good... just necessary) design elements.

THE GRIND

There is some customization in this game, you can customize the colors of pretty much anything ranging from your spaceship to your Tenno. I feel the lore of the whole thing is a little lackluster, and the story is very bare bones. It is easy to follow and is sufficent but I do not recommend this as a story game, this game is here purely for the gameplay.
MULTIPLAYER

A fun game with a good amount of content, but gets repetitive after a while.
In Recettear, you're a shopkeeper trying to pay off your father's debts. Every week, you need to pay a set amount of your loan, and you need to pay more and more every week.
To earn money to pay said debt off, you sell items to customers. Items are acquired by either adventuring into dungeons, or buying them from the market.
You've got a shop with a certain amount of counters where you can sell items. You'll be bargaining with your customers for the best price, as each customer has budgets you'll learn.
You can decorate and expand your shop, and the way you decorate influences who comes to your shop. You can also influence who comes into your shop using the window display, which is the counter in front of the window.
There's also a merchant level, which is raised by selling and buying items from your customers. As it is raised, you can do more things to your shop, such as expanding it, unlocking vending machines, getting new items for sale in the market, etc.
The prices for things also fluctuate. There might be a shortage of food, for example, so you can sell your stock of food for twice their base price. If there is low demand for weapons, you'll have to sell your weapons for a much lower price.
This actually makes things very interesting, as you can buy items from the market while their price is low, to make an even bigger profit.
Adventuring is when you pay an adventurer to go into a dungeon to kill monsters and get items. There's eight adventurers, each having different abilities and attacks. In dungeons, you're going to be finding chests and monsters, along with occasional bosses.
These adventurers are unlocked over time, some by fighting them as a dungeon boss, others with more specific requirements, such as talking to them in the Town Square, or selling items to them enough times.
When you kill monsters in dungeons, sometimes they'll drop crafting materials, which you can use to craft items you can sell for a large profit.
There's a few big problems with Recettear. Most importantly, the way markets are handled.
In dungeons, there is a small chance you'll actually get something worthwhile, something you'll make a profit with that is worth the large amount of in-game time you'll take to get it.
Dungeons take a large amount of the day to enter, which could be better spent having your shop open to sell items.
You'll make much more of a profit if you buy items in the market and sell them yourself for a higher price. Doing this, you'll have plenty of time in the day to sell what you've bought for more of a profit for what you'd get from your dungeon findings.
The problem lies with large the profit from the market and the guild is. A big part of this is how cheap items that are currently raised in price are.
Say an item has a base price of 8,000. If this item is in high demand, you can sell it for 200% of its base price, or 16,000, plus whatever else you'll add to the price according to your customer's budget for a profit.
The market sells this item for 5,500-6,500. Right there is a pretty big profit of roughly 2,000, but in high demand, this item is sold for around 8,000-10,500.
At the least, that is around a 5,000 currency profit, without raising the doubled base price for a profit.
That really makes the whole "fluctuating price" thing not really worthwhile, if you don't have to worry about loosing money when buying an item in high demand, and yet you can still make such a big profit off of it afterwards. There's no reason to buy things from the market during low demand, since there isn't enough of a profit to warrant waiting until items are low in demand to stock up.
Trying to beat the game through dungeons isn't really possible. As some point, you're going to be relying on the market for profits.
The game also gets very repetitive because of this. While going into dungeons would spruce up the gameplay, your days are going to be spent either going through the market menu or having your shop open. Selling
enjoyable, but it gets tiring when it is one of the only two things you're going to be doing.
Dungeons, while adding variety, are kind of tiring and boring after a while. While the different adventurers can make things interesting, it is just a simple top-down dungeon with enemies. There aren't really enough dungeons in this game either, totaling at 5, with one in endless mode, but they do last until the endgame, with the last one unlocking at merchant level 100.
You're going to be spending a lot of time fighting the same enemies and collecting the same items, during the time between just unlocking a new dungeon and trying to get a new one.
There's a decent amount of content in this game, from crafting all the items to getting all of the adventurers. There's also your merchant level, which, in New Game +, carries over, so you can get to higher levels and unlock items then you couldn't a single playthrough. There are five weeks of payment in this game, with the last week's payment being 500,000.
There's also an Endless Mode which is unlocked by getting to the end of the game, in which the game doesn't end and the debt keeps getting bigger and bigger until you can't pay it.
Despite all the negativity, this really is a fun game. Running the shop is enjoyable, crafting new items is fun, and trying to unlock all of the adventurers is very entertaining.
One of my big positives is the varying budgets everyone has that you'll learn as you play. As your customer reputation increases, which is accomplished by giving them a good deal, or selling an item on your first price, their budget will increase, so they can buy more expensive items. You'll get Merchant Level EXP bonuses for knowing the budgets and price ranges of your customers, so learning each of them is useful. Your reputation is also lowered for haggling too much or scaring away a customer with a high price, so you need to be careful with how much you're asking for.
Another thing I like is how many items you can craft. There really is a lot of items, and you'll often craft weapons and armor for your adventurers stronger than anything you could buy from the guild for them.
Overall, I definitely think this game warrants a look, as it is a fun game with a decent amount of content, but just gets repetitive after long periods of play. Lots of items, interesting customer budget/reputation system that is very interactive, lots of unlockables, and is actually pretty difficult.
Markets are too strong and kind of dwarf dungeons, and you'll be repeating the same daily schedule for a while, but otherwise, this game is enjoyable and interesting.

This is primarily a thoughtful game.
As you progress, the cards you gain relate to the choices you make earlier in the game. There are times when you must do battle (i.e., the "twitchy" parts), and during such battles you might perish, but they do not constitute the bulk of the game. I consider this more of an unfolding story than an FPS hackathon. If you either play only or absolutely cannot abide the latter, you are not likely to enjoy this game.
One aspect of this game I found amusing is how it reminds me of
(a game I played over 1000 hours). One mechanic of the game is balancing the purchase of food against the purchase of other useful items and resources. Without sufficient food, you will start to take damage as you explore, and ultimately starve. You are not likely to die of starvation since you'll probably have an encounter before then that kills you.
This is not a turn-based game. Using a controller, you will press the "accept" button the vast majority of the time to advance the story. During battle, the left joystick and buttons are all necessary to vanquish your foes. I haven't used it with a mouse but, according to the "controls" menu, it accepts mouse input.
Overall, I like this game because it has both thoughtful story elements and interesting battles. I believe I have completed about 20% of the game, but the difficulty increases so I expect it will take longer to complete the game than five times the amount I have already played.
I suggest you take a look at
. As he says, the artistry provides an enjoyable atmospheric RPG experience. It is "rogue-like" in that you progress "down" levels but this is a far cry from an 8-bit 2D Rogue knock-off. It is a 3D (based on
) immersive adventure. I applaud the creators for conceiving of such a blend of genres.

So, obviously it's impossible to ignore that there are two major 6DOF shooters with bigger budgets also in development - the multiplayer oriented Descent: Underground and the singleplayer focused Overload, the latter made by lots of ex-Parallax people - i.e., the people who pioneered the genre.
Geocore's focus is somewhere in-between the competitors mentioned above, designed by a long-time competitive Descent fan it nails the feel of the movement of one of these games. It's primary focus does seem to be multiplayer, and goes for a bit more of the pure old school Descent feeling, avoiding Descent: Underground's different ship classes and progression mechanics. Everybody starts with the same stuff - at the moment you even start with every single weapon on-board from the get go, though I wouldn't be surprised if that changes down the line. The multiplayer really hasn't caught on as of the time of this writing though, and you're unlikely to find any other players unless it's during a developer hosted event. The times I've managed to find matches, it's been running well, though currently the weapon feedback leaves a lot to be desired. Projectiles kinda just vanish when they hit something, leaving very little indication of if you're doing any damage or not.
The game also has a singleplayer component called patrols, which is fairly basic though a decent diversion and a way to test out your settings, these missions mainly consist of narrow corridors punctuated with mini-boss arenas and color coded keys, not really offering any of the intricate and vast tunnel networks of the original Descent nor Overload.
The environments in general are pretty drab looking, mostly just consisting of metallic surfaces with occasional machinery, colored lightning and the odd rock surface every now and then. The visual sameness sometimes makes it hard to make out enemy robots from the backgrounds. I think a little visual variety could go a long way in making this game stick out a bit more, though I wouldn't expect it to ever quite get the polished look of D:U nor Overload considering their respective budgets.
There's a pretty good soundtrack in there too. Nothing particularly revolutionary, mostly going for the same kind of vaguely Front Line Assembly or Skinny Puppy sounding tunes that you'd find in the Descent series.
All in all, with the two big competitors in mind it's hard to recommend this, especially in this early access state, to anybody but the biggest fans of 6DOF shooters, but there is a pretty good foundation in here, however in need of more refinement, especially on the visual side in terms of environment variety and shading. I'm still giving it a thumbs up, but I'd recommend you check in on it's development over time before making up your mind.

A little background:  I have been an active and dedicated player of the 6dof game DESCENT since it came out in the 90s.  I still play competitively in the 1 v 1 Descent community on the DCL (Descent Champsions Ladder)
I have had the fortune of being able to watch this game progress from it's infancy on in to it's current state and I will tell you this.  The guy making this game is a gaming pilot from the Descent days and still plays.  I think that's a critical component to making a solid 6dof game.  He understands what made Descent so attractive to the competitive community and to the casual FFA players and is successfully translating that into his game.
The programmer listens and asks for feedback.  He is continuously improving this game and it is clearly moving in the right direction.  His attention to detail is borderline OCD and it's paying dividends.
I think it's important to know that this game isn't 'done'.  This game is evolving and maturing on the daily.    For those that know me....they know I say what is on my mind and I don't pull any punches.  I have been critical of certain aspects of this game and the programmer took my advice and worked hard to incorporate my ideas for improvement and persisted until he succeeded.  I appreciate the effort and can't imagine the amount of work that he's putting into this thing to give us a finished product that will be enjoyable for years to come.
If you haven't tried this game out yet and you appreciate 6dof games....give it a try.  Feel free to give feedback knowing that it will be considered seriously.

I first played this game close to eight years ago as the time of this writing, and when I first tried that demo I got the impression of a good, albeit short, game. That impression was wrong, this is definitely a GREAT game.
Owlboy is an adventure in the truest sense of the word. You'll explore, fight baddies, gain powerups, and make friends all throughout a wonderful world and story. The art direction is gorgeous, the animations of the characters and enemies are fun to watch, the music is a treat to listen to, and the story is a great mix of silly fun, abject terror, and heartwrenching moments. When I say that Owlboy is a great game, I mean it.
That being said, the game is not without it's faults, by far the biggest being it's difficulty, which is all over the place. You'll breeze through some sections of the game only to be utterly crushed by others. While checkpoints are liberal, you'll be tearing your hair out through some sections of the game trying to figure out what to do, and the lack of difficulty options certainly doesn't help. Exacerbating the issue is that while cutscenes are skippable, some mid boss fight conversations are not, and the aforementioned emotional scenes rapidly lose their luster as your forced to watch them over and over again as you die repeatedly to the more difficult bosses.
Also, don't be fooled into thinking this is a metroidvania game. While it is heavily exploration focused, and you can be rewarded for revisiting previously visited areas, the game is actually quite linear, and there isn't much reason to play it multiple times if you aren't going for 100%.
Don't let that dissuade you though, Owlboy is a modern day classic, and other indie developers need to look to it as a gold standard for what can be done with both the platforming genre and pixel art.

Great game. Although the story is kinda cliche at times, it has many emotive moments, and the plot twists keep it interesting. The characters are quite likeable, you may encounter a few anime stereotypes here and there, but most of them are pretty good.
Gameplay-wise is where Valkyria Chronicles shines. The game is some kind of mix between action rpg, strategy rpg and shooter, and plays perfectly. You control a squad of gallian soldiers, each one associated to a class. There aren't many classes, but they all play differently, and they are really cool (there's a class with explosive lances, just saying). You have a bar which determines how far you can get during the turns of each of your soldiers. Moving an unit costs a command point, and when you run out of them your turn ends. The AI is decent, it reacts to your actions quite well. The missions may have similar objectives, but they aren't repetitive at all.
The aesthetic of the game is incredible, it looks as if the game was made with watercolors. The graphics hold up quite well too, and the animations are detailed, even if some of them are reutilized. The soundtrack is mainly orchestral, and the themes fit with the atmosphere of the game.
The game has a decent length too, it took me 40 hours to finish it, so you don't have to worry about the amount of content.
I definitely recommend Valkyria Chronicles. It's a flawless game, and you'll probably enjoy it, even if you aren't into anime. So don't be afraid of giving it a try, it's worth it.

ADventure Lib is a very entertaining, funny and short experience.
A Gameplay & Review video showcasing the features I'm about to talk about:
When you start the game, all objects and characters in the world are shuffled with the game's database of objects.
That means the character you play as could be a potato, and you're trying to save toilet from a fire-breathing plunger.
The gameplay is incredibly simplistic. You have a "Look" action that gives you a hint what the object is meant to be used for. E.g "This rope is very sharp" so you know to use it as a sword. You also have your primary action which is to use or talk to objects/characters.
There's the option to have voice acting, which is decent and funny. Accompanied by some fun music.
The puzzles are incredibly easy to solve, so don't expect anything harder.
A cool feature is the ability to import your own objects and characters into the game. You can import any picture you like, accompanied with an audio file of you choosing (or you can record it within the game using your microphone) so that the game will pronounce your object during voice acting sequences. You can also upload your created objects into Steam workshop. Obviously this helps refresh the game a few times if you want to have a laugh with a friend.
Again, if you go into this game knowing that it's very short, but its main purpose is to make you laugh, then you'll have a good time.

This is a premiere strategy game.
It is NOT tactical.
Let me repeat that.
Tactics are NOT NOT NOT involved.
I see too many people try this game expecting something akin to Total War only to get turned off by the lack of tactical decisions. "Strategy" games are more akin to simulation games in essence. You plan your course of action through dangerous circumstances to achieve the best victory possible. Strategy is knowing when to fight, where to fight, how to take advantage of your situation for long-term benefits, and other similar questions. Tactics is "how to fight" and this game does not cover that. It is a question of logistics rather than tactics. Do you have enough troops, rather than are your troops fighting at optimal efficieny. Do you have the defensive high ground, rather than whether or not this unit happens to be in good terrain at any given time. Do you catch the enemy army off guard, rather than using flanking to decimate part of the army.
If you expect a Civilization-esque game, or something like Total War. Check your expectations. Go online, and watch gameplay before buying. You are probably in for a surprise.

Spoiler Alert: The main character dies. The good news is that it happens right at the start of the game. Then the game gets going. However, unlike some God of War clone this isn't a revenge fueled bloodbath of carnage and destruction. There isn't an ocean of "enjoy to destroy" cannon fodder to kill/loot on the way to the final boss. This is a supernatural redemption story in the vein of Ghost or Always with a dash of The Frighteners thrown in for a bit of fun.
The bulk of the game will be exploring mutliple crime scenes as you piece together not only the reason for your own murder, but the deaths of many fellow spirits that you encounter along your main quest. In some regards I am reminded of the forensic analyst role from Heavy Rain. Once you have gathered enough clues in the crime scenes you can attempt to discern the next location that your journey takes you. The good news is that, unlike Heavy Rain, this game does not rely on timing based quicktime events to tell the story.
However, the only real combat in the game does rely on a tried and true quicktime mechanic. This involves sneaking up behind the occasional demon and performing a stealth kill sequence to banish it. This involves a random quicktime sequence where you a flashed a direction to press along with an appropriate button/key. Not that deep.
TL;DR version: If you are a casual gamer that isn't looking to mindlessly button mash your way through a plotless demon horde this is a nice change of pace. If you want some thing procedural like the Kings Quest, Monkey Island or Quantic Dream created games (Indigo Prophecy, Heavy Rain, Beyond) then you'll enjoy the storytelling. It would really fit in nicely with that friend that owns all the Telltale Games titles. Just don't expect a lot of white knuckle fragging.

Ah archeage,
An interestingly invented MMORPG with elements that not alot of games can boast about. However here are some things to consider before spending money
- Is there any land available for your house?
- Do you have enough time to prioritize farming?
- Can you afford 2 Apex per month without Real Life payments?
If you can't answer these questions with a straight forward yes then you may end up paying real life money just to get patron status and find either you have no land to use your blueprints, you don't have enough time to farm on your land and/or don't have the time to afford status.
If you are considering dlc or "mounts" here are a few other points to consider:
- Does the mount go faster than 10m/s without items?
- Do you already own a car in the game?
- Are you specifically just getting it for it's looks rather than it's utility?
- Are you just getting a mount because it can turn invisible?
- Is the mount going to be any better than the current horse, elk, etc you own?
- If you are just getting a mirage donkey have you considered that every other mode of transport has more than just 1 slot to carry packs?
- Are the items you're considering getting your horse, elk, etc better than the ones you can get straight from the Burnt Castle?
Alternatively you can try earning money using other skills but no doubt you'll end up farming due to the labor generation problem.
For all those who aren't aware labor generates over time which means you have to keep your computer on, with the game running and stay online if you are not a patron which for some of you electricity bill complainers is a no go. If you have the time and can earn patron status then you can avoid this problem with very little effort after your first 2 apex.
Money management is essential for learning when to spend and when to save for your apex whether it be labor potions that you get from the AH or materials which you can use to craft packs. You can keep telling yourself that you won't need to train commerce but the fact of the matter it is the only way without having to look up guides, train your other skills, research mob spots, etc.
After that long disclaimer out of the way let's get on with the review!
The game from the start is overloaded with cutscenes, voice acting and great visuals however, the game unfortunatly makes this too easy for you no matter which class you start off with you'll find that almost all the mobs in the area are easy to kill some. one hit kill. This gives you a false sense of sercurity when facing higher leveled mobs, in fact you'll find you'll still have it even at level 55. One tip I can give you guys is to check the health of the mob to see if you can kill it before it kills you.
Otherwise the strange yet fun experience of zooming up to lvls 30 is quite exilirating most players can manage this within a day or two of gameplay however it does not take long, please don't take this as a sign to skip past content by doing so you miss out of gilda stars, essential weapons, xp, tutorials that you'll end up asking players about (like a noob) and more importantly soup: soup is litterly your bread and butter of this game - without mana, there is no kill, there is no heal, there is no spell and your health bar will plummet as a result of you only doing 300 damage whilst the mob drains you right down to the last cm of health.
Death on Archeage is not important: you will lose xp and your armour might be slightly damaged but you can easily earn back the xp you lost and you can repair at a blacksmith, there are xp restores and you can spend labor to restore at a nui statue but when you only end up gaining back a small percentage it doesn't seem worth it. The best way to make sure you don't waste the "restore xp" is to wait until lvl 50 when you will definitely need it to speed through the leveling process.
Best way to get xp? Quests, do not waste your time on crafting for levels because that is a waste of labor, labor of course you should be using to get apex and/or items you need and nothing else.
After explaining all this you'll be wondering what is PvP like? And well I can only answer it as honestly as possible: It is quite unbalanced, certain classes such as "the shadow class" allows you to sneak around invisible, jump back meters and gain an incredibly unfair speed/attack speed boost that will make everyone on the game that tried to kill you whine.
Then there's the cleric class, like the song class their focus is healing, buffing and most importantly reviving this makes the song class seem inferior some people will combine the two in hopes that it makes the class worthwhile but I found that you either want the cleric class for healing or you want the song class for speeding up your mount. You never want both because that is a waste of a skill you can keep it if you REALLY need the extra heals but if your focus is healing please do everyone a favor and just pick cleric. The song class is more for speed and buffs and stuns it is not meant to be played as a cleric it can however be very useful for quicker heals but has a high mana cost.
Then there's the mage classes... PRRRRRRFHAHAHAHAHAHA! Oh my god are you serious? You can't move whilst casting spells? Oh ho hohoohohoho! (Use with caution) You get to be invincible but lol that is so not worth it just to watch the pvp happen AFTER you lose your invincibility.
Then there's the battlerage class again, this is a really unfair combo with shadow class combined because of the ridiculous combos, the smashes the range the damage the quick initiations the jumps the spins the cooldowns the stuns and to top it off if you add this to archery this becomes ridiculous it makes the game seem like it didn't take into account all the problems this class gives others in pvp combat and now you have boneyard there's not even an escape so have fun dying whilst the OP character stuns you to death.
The Archer class is the only class I can recommend to all players, it's skills and diversity allows for some of the toughest mobs to be taken down with ease alot of players bash this skill but it is actually the most useful skillset in the game instant hover in the air whilst you shoot down your enermies, stuns, endless arrows and to top it all off the only stat you need to care about is agility and the rest is just down to preference.
Defence - Are you tired of walking around with your trousers down? Did you get given the worst drops since goblin armour in runescape? Do you die everytime you try to say hello to your fellow party members? Take Defence today! No longer will your shield seem like a slot wasted, gone are the days you have no buffs to help you and remember: Braum will keep you safe! Disclaimer: Braum is not responsible for any deaths dismemberments of any limb or torso, he is not responsible for launching players into the air at your enermies, if you think you seen Braum please contact Riot services we've been looking for him for days and we still can't find him!
(Besides that they need to change the symbol to a shield a blue cross is very confusing and looks too much like the battlerage skill)
So now you know the reasons why PvP is all over the place some players being overpowered, others underpowered and some pay to win I'll let you decide which is which.
When you push aside the faults of the Pvp and the incredibly unfair trade routes to the enermy gold trader (see shadow class) you can actually have fun with the rest of the game there are some things to watch out for:

Besides that the game is easy to get into and can be quite casual, some people claim it's farmville but that is only one element of the game, what is the thing missing in most MMORPGs? Variety and Customisation: Archeage has both.

Owlboy was the only game I have actually looked forward to playing in a long time, and one of the few games I have bought at release.  Overall,  Owlboy is worth it.  The game has been in development for 9 years, and the effort definitely shows.  Easily one of the best soundtracks of the year, and probably the best pixel artwork out of any 8-bit game.  The flying mechanic felt extremely fresh and new for a 2D game, and Owlboy executed it perfectly.  I have not felt immersed in a game in a long time and Owlboy gave me that feeling.  When I stopped playing Owlboy, I honestly could not wait to start playing again, something I have not felt towards a video game in a long time.
The only negatives for me is how short the game is (however, I did not 100% the game), and the relative easiness of the game.  The game never felt particularly hard, with only one memorable platforming challenge, and only one boss fight that took more than 3 tries.  One of my favorite games of all time is CaveStory, and if you are looking for a challenge similar, you will not find it in Owlboy.
Overall, Owlboy is a lot of fun, with a very interesting game mechanic that no other game has done (or done well), and the story and characters were fun and immersing.  The major stand out points for Owlboy are definitely the art and the soundtrack.  8/10

After playing the totally amazing ME1 (how did I miss out on that one for so long?!?!) I just had to continue the story and get ME2.
It's such a great idea to be able to import a savegame from the first game in order to have some continuity with shepherd (if necessary, google for a guide on how to do that, it's so much more immersive to "use the same Shepherd", as this is a continuation of ME1)
The game DOES feel different than the first part. Sure, the graphics are quite a bit better, and stuff like shooting from cover works better this time around... I am encountering way less problems with that than I did in part 1, where sometimes, you'd try to shoot but couldnt.
However, some of the changes take a while to get used to. Reloading (better reload before the clip is empty, otherwise you might run out of ammo while you use a chance to fire off a long burst at an enemy) and collecting ammo (yes, you can actually run out of ammo, so you need to switch weapons or use powers), and also, you really have to be more tactical even on the easier settings this time around. No "stand outside of cover and shoot away", you'll die quickly. Fortnately, health and shields recover quickly once you're in cover again.
At first, I wasn't sure whether I enjoy the changes to combat (on harder settings, you REALLY need to use your team-commands and special powers, even though the AI of your team is working pretty good, apart from some silly moves sometimes), but eventually, I started getting into it... when you win a battle, it does feel more satisfying, and the fights are quite a bit more immersive altogether imo.
The story...what can I say? Just as immersive as part 1, and a great continuation to it. SOme of the decisions you have to make will make you think hard, and the writing reminded me of great SciFi-shows such as Babylon 5 (and I do think the devs DID watch that show, as the collectors remind me a LOT of the Shadows, visually)... I really wanna see how the story develops, where it leads. That's one thing that Bioware totally nailed with these games.
The team is really cool, so are the dialogues, and I found myself smiling a lot at some of the cut scenes and team-comments.
Graphically, its obvious this is a few years old, but it does look better than ME1, and I don't mind the slightly dated graphics at all.
Pros:
- Graphics are better than ME1
- Story is even more immersive than ME1
- Combat requires a more tactical approach, which makes it more immersive and "realistic"
- Did I mention the great writing?
- Digging the characters
- Great music by the guy who composed "Requiem For A Dream"
- Gathering resources for upgrades is fun, MUCH better than ME1...no more driving around with Mako, you scan the planet from the Normandy, keep an eye on a graph, and once there are peaks, you fire a probe. Not difficult, but much less grindy (IMO!) than ME1
- Some familiar faces from ME1, starting early on!
Cons:
- Some changes to combat, ammo, etc. So if you "binge play" and go from ME1 to 2 straight away, some adjustment time is necessary
- You MIGHT not like the combat as much if you loved ME1, as it's a bit more difficult, yet I did give it a chance and it won me over, feels more satisfying IMO
- No more Mako. If you liked that aspect of ME1, it's gone, but thats ok.
- UI sometimes feels a bit clunky (accessing journal, codex, achievements), and research can be a bit confusing
Verdict: ME2 picks up where ME1 stopped, continuing a VERY well-written and interesting story, making you feel very immersed. The game has quite a few improvements, even though not all changes are for the better IMO. If you liked the story in ME1, you owe it to yourself to continue and see what happens next.
EDIT: I just finished the game. Game time is 20 hrs, yet I didn't do quite ALL of the side missions. I did a LOT of them, and all loyalty missions, didn't get into any romance-situations.
And I am changing my rating from 9.0 to a 10.0. The story picks up even MORE eventually, fights become even more fun, and the storyline, dialogues and cutscenes are totally AWESOME.
I was on the edge of my seat throughout, I was laughing quite a bit at some of the snarky comments by my team mates (Joker rules), I was saddened when I lost a member of my squad (even though I predicted it).
Both ME1 and 2 have hteir merits. I still love the first part a lot, but this one is even better, if you can deal with the changes made to the gameplay.
Don't miss out on this, and even though it's been said a lot, if you can, play the whole series.Installing ME3 while typing this.

Pro's

What it lacks in combat depth, Hand of Fate (HoF) certainly makes up in presentation.
Don't be fooled by the cards on the table, essentially HoF is a dungeon crawler with perma-death and the cards just represent the the various rooms, like in Binding of Isaac for example. Content seems to be no problem, the developers are actively still working on the game, adding new content (for free & DLC) and fixing bugs. It is very atmospheric and manages to pull you into it's strange world, masterfully narrated by the card-dealer, who you are playing against.
The only thing that could be made better would be the combat system, it strongly reminds me of the Batman Arkham games (Arkham-Combat), however due to money limitations, the devs couldn't afford the mo-cap equipment necessary to execute it well. The animations sometimes seem clunky, and the difficulty is simply determined by the number of enemies on screen, as they sometimes grow in numbers so much, you can't really counter the single hits or ranged attacks thrown at you anymore. However, the combat encounters are short enough to not make it stand out too much, so it's more of a small annoyance than a real problem.
Additionally, since your rooms are technically cards, you have to build a deck full of encounters and weapons, all with different effects. This adds another layer of depth to the game, so choose your cards wisely!
In the end, Hand of Fate is a masterfully presented rogue-lite, which makes you more interested in it's world and the people (or monsters) that live in it. Combat is dull but scarce enough to not make it stand out too much. If you played it to the end, no worries, there's an endless mode.
C'mon, it's probably one of the Top 10 games of all time. If not that, it's got one of the strongest stories in all of video game science-fiction. Nearly flawless.

This is a premiere strategy game.
It is NOT tactical.
Let me repeat that.
Tactics are NOT NOT NOT involved.
I see too many people try this game expecting something akin to Total War only to get turned off by the lack of tactical decisions. "Strategy" games are more akin to simulation games in essence. You plan your course of action through dangerous circumstances to achieve the best victory possible. Strategy is knowing when to fight, where to fight, how to take advantage of your situation for long-term benefits, and other similar questions. Tactics is "how to fight" and this game does not cover that. It is a question of logistics rather than tactics. Do you have enough troops, rather than are your troops fighting at optimal efficieny. Do you have the defensive high ground, rather than whether or not this unit happens to be in good terrain at any given time. Do you catch the enemy army off guard, rather than using flanking to decimate part of the army.
If you expect a Civilization-esque game, or something like Total War. Check your expectations. Go online, and watch gameplay before buying. You are probably in for a surprise.

This game is a few different things rolled into one.  RPG and Turn Based Strategy.  The story is interesting enough and after every few segments you watch, you participate in a campaign, where the turn based gameplay comes in.  Valkyria Chronicles is a lot like the new X-COM, with one exception... I think it is a ton better!  The story has more depth and there is more backstory.
The one thing which would make this game way better than what it is, is if the maps and unit placement was random.  Unfortunately, once you learn a map, the unit placement, and their routes, it pretty much becomes easy to conquer the map.  This does take time, however, and you may find yoruself playing the same map a few times before learning the trick.  I think it took me 5 or 6 times trying to defeat the Super Tank.
All that said, I feel the replayability will be decent enough, between the skirmish maps which you can play trying your hand with different units and strategy.  As the game progresses you may also work towards upgrades for your tank and units.  Just about 24 hours of gameplay in and I feel as if I am not even half way through the game.
This title, I feel, is one of those gems out there.  Engaging and fun.  The game plays very well and I have not encountered a crash or glitch yet.  If you like Turn Based unit tactic games... with exception of X-COM 2, I do not believe I have played any other as good as Valkyria Chronicles.

Developed by: Fancy Fish Games
Achievements: Yes
Steam Workshop: Yes
Story:
ADventure Lib is set in a medieval world and you are a hero who embarks on an adventure to save the kingdom; however who/what you and every other thing in the kingdom is/are is totally shuffled when you start playing causing some hilarious moments.
Gameplay:
Start the game with a shuffle button; every character and item is randomized but still keeps their assigned roles. (IE. In my first play through the king is a butter knife and the hero is a potato)
Classic adventure gaming returns with looking at items, collecting items, combining items and using items. At least in this game the ridiculousness of that classic system is highlighted but the completely insane randomization
Because of this most of the game play is just trying to find the right tool for the job at hand, whether it’s fighting the PLUNGER or helping the CHICKEN. Results may vary.
There are secrets to be found, from the charming Easter Egg/Throwbacks in the backgrounds or the collectables that are a little tougher to find, sometimes.
One of the coolest features of ADventure Lib is the ability to create your own assets to put in the game! An easy to use interface lets you provide the image (I used a transparent PNG and it looked great) record the word yourself and it gets added to the game with everything else.
Steam Workshop is also integrated so you can share your creations with everyone. Whatever they may be. We all know what’s coming.
The game is admittedly on the shorter side but that actually works for me; the best part of this game is shuffling the entire game into a new experience and playing with new crazy stuff going on. That said, the ending I received initially was fairly abrupt and I am not 100% sure if there is a “good” ending that you can receive on subsequent plays.
All in all there isn’t much that you wont be able to figure out with a light application of intelligence
and patience. This isn’t Dark Souls; this is a lighthearted adventure and just a good bit of silly fun.
Graphics:
ADventure Lib, for being a simple 2D exploration game, manages to look really clean and well put together.
It looks they way you would expect, being light on the animation side with stuff bobbing around the screen. This helps when you add your own content it fits in perfectly.
Able to change character’s two main color schemes anytime
Sound:
Music and SFX: The sound effects and music are just fine. No problems with them; nothing special in that regard.  It all blends into the game play well.
Voice Acting: This game is fully and independently voice acted. It is half of the charm, really! Its nice that they took the time to do this even if it was done by people who are new to the industry. Only a couple lines came off as recorded out of place but it was hard to notice amongst the crazy dialog. Also: If you add an asset to the game you can count yourself as a voice actor as well. 😀
Final Verdict:
ADventure Lib is a light-hearted and loving tribute to the “use X on Y” genre. While it is small in scale I had no technical issues playing it and had a lot of fun working out the puzzles (basic as they are). Adults and kids alike would have a fun time with all the goofy situations that arise in this game and at the price it’s damn near risk-free to give it a try. It is a little short but it’s fun to replay (especially after adding new characters/items to the game!).
Disclaimer: I was provided a copy of this game for review purposes.  My opinions are my own.

Kingdom Wars 2: Battles has a great premise, yet results in quite shoddy execution. While the mechanic of sieges hasn't been looked at in this kind of way since the golden days of Stronghold, it is quite lackluster regarding complexity and will end up being a zerg-fest about who can push more bazillion troops to suicide against enemy walls than the defender being able to mass produce defenses and bowmen alike.
The gameplay being a bit on the simple side could have been overlooked if it wasn't for pseudo-MMO crafting grinds which are desperately required to unlock even the most basic of building progressions for multiplayer battles. There's a little diehard community, but masses wise, Kingdom Wars 2: Battles could soon be considered abandoned.
I'm not going to lie, I did have fun times with this together with a friend, but for every hour of fun I was frustrated by random crafting drops, not finding any matches or just plain slow progression that can even put JRPGs to shame.
All in all, this product is stitched together from ideas of many other games, all of them greater than this result of mashed up ideas.
While I did spend a lot of time in this, there's no way I can recommend it to anyone. Play Stronghold instead. Any of them, really.

This the first review I've written on steam and with good reason... first of all let me clarify that I'm a CONAN fan since childhood and I've never have played this kind of game before (I'm not familiar with Ark, Rust, Forest or any other survival PVP).
This game is simply amazing, the atmosphere and immersion are overwhelming, the combat is similar to Skyrim (although a little rough around the edges), the crafting is simple and intuitive, the soundtrack is right on spot and the world is ruthless and unforgiving. I've been playing on a private server on my own for 9 hours now and I haven't have a dull moment yet, and I'm just scratching the surface of this behemoth of a game... The map is huge, full of interesting scenery and creature, there are fully voice acted friendly NPCs which I didn't expect and it brings you completely into the CONAN mythos from the start.
Probably the biggest surprise for me was the performance, I have an "OK" pc (AMD phenom II x4 965, a GeForce GTX 760 and 8 GB of Ram, nothing fancy) and the game run smooth with a mix on Ultra, high and medium settings.
I can't really speak for the multiplayer aspect of the game since I've just played single player, but I'm really confused by the "mixed" respond on steam, especially for and early access release and with the huge support that the developers have gave us in just a couple of days.
If you like CONAN this is a no-brainer: The game feels like CONAN, sounds like CONAN and plays like CONAN.
If you like don't-hold-your-hand RPG or immersion this game is definitely for you: It make you feel exactly like a prehistoric nomadic caveman, it's full of mysterious and awe inspiring scenery, and it test your will to survive in a really extreme way.
If you like surviving games this is your game: Like I said this is my first step into the genre and I think it was the right one, the first time I die it was from hunger/thirst just a few steps from a river and it was very intense and realistic, it made me value more the half empty water skin and handfull of bugs that you have at the beginning.
If you had a bad first day of release experience, due to server problems or FPS drop, take a deep breath and try it again:
I really don't understand the negative reviews, it's just plain weird for an early access, this is by far the most polish one I've encounter.
Again, for me the whole experience has been fantastic to say the least and I think the developers deserve a round of applause!
I really hope they continue the good work and give of more lore oriented content from the great source material in the upcoming months, and keep giving great support and feedback.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a game with a really cool idea, but with terrible execution. Even on sale, I couldn't recommend this game. (overall worth? about $5.00).
The idea of being a detective ghost, and getting the chance to investigate your own death is very cool. The writing is surprisingly good, and it didn't really feel cheesy. Likewise, the voice acting was pretty good and I didn't find myself hating any of the characters. Usually teen girls in games can be a little, overacted?
However, that's all that is good about the game. Any writing that isn't related to the main story was terrible. The little story snippets that you get are not scary, nor interesting.
This is compounded by awful, and I mean awful, level planning and game design. Your ghost powers, which could be AWESOME, are hindered by invisible walls. In this case, invisible ghost walls that have no reason to be there, prevent you from taking better shortcuts, or are there just to make you weave through the miniscule levels in a particular way.
And then there are the demons, an utterly pointless addition to the game. All the way done with the investigations in a level? Well, lets just add some extra demons on your way out, to annoy you. Oh, how about some demon hand pits that you have to avoid. The only reason I can see for these being added to the game? To make the game feel longer. To make the final scene completable. Whoever planned this game, and designed the levels and town should be fired. This game is a perfect lesson in how NOT to make levels.
Then there are the pixel hunting items. Where you'll spend a few extra minutes per level scrounging around to find half invisible items that don't do much but give you a codex and a short voiced story after finding them all. Without these items, some of your ghost powers would be utterly useless. And many of these items don't contribute to the main story. Those items are real world items that don't use your powers. They could have done so MUCH with the reveal and teleport powers, but after getting them you use them maybe once or twice. But mostly only to get those silly little trophy items.
Also, any action in the game is dumbed down to quick time events. Yes, quick time events that don't even register your keypresses properly. It's a game of chance if the game decides to excorcise a demon. On top of this, you often have to kill multiple demons in a row. Failure to kill, sometimes resulting in death, makes you have to start all over again. Meaning if there are four demons, and you kill three, but your kid happens to distract you... Then you have to start the whole process of killing all four OVER again.
What a terrible game mechanic.
There were also still a number of bugs. The most noticeable were the freezing bugs, where when you go to "peek" through someones eyes, the game will not let you click anything. So, you have to restart and hope the same bug doesn't happen again.
It's one of the most atrocious amalgamations of horrendous game design and mechanics on the market.

Recettear takes an interesting concept (running an rpg-world item shop) and makes an entertaining game out of it. Charming is a good way to describe the game itself - the characters are adorable and endearing, the gameplay is like a neat mini-game, and the overall atmosphere is comfortable and relaxing. As someone who mostly disliked Metro 2033, I was pleasantly surprised when I found myself genuinely enjoying Last Light. I liked the greater emphasis on stealth-action combat against human enemies. I liked the story of Last Light better than 2033's. And the atmosphere, oh boy the atmosphere! Especially that of the outdoor wasteland settings, which were just breathtaking to experience.
But then the game had to screw it all up with one particularly enraging boss battle. See, I was almost done fighting my way through the swamp level. As I was crossing a narrow stretch of water to get to my friends waiting just on the other side, one of those giant lobster things ambushed me. "Okay," I thought, "I'll kill this thing and then I'll be safe with my friends." Upon defeating this mutated abomination, I discovered I was all out of gas mask filters!
So there I was suffocating on the toxic air of the Russian wasteland while those idiots who were supposed to be helping me stood there talking! A few seconds later and I was a dead man. So I restarted and what do you know? IT STARTED ME AT THE BEGINNING OF THE BOSS BATTLE AGAIN. So now I'm at a point where I cannot progress because by the time I kill the boss, I'm out of filters and there's unskippable dialog preventing me from getting to a checkpoint in time.
As much as I disliked 2033 at least nothing like this happened to me in that game. Last Light could have easily gotten a recommendation from me but instead I have to say no.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a rather unique cutesy blend of a item shop sim and a dungeon crawler. You have to try and raise about
within a 36 day cycle by buying and selling itemsfrom people, or you can try your luck, and sell items you find in the dungeons.
Why choosing Recettear?
Its a cute, little game that does a very good job combing the two genres it tries to represent. The dungeon crawling even has its own little side story line that you can explore all the way into post game. The item shop portion is just the base story and you can just keep to the shop to finish the game, if you wanted.
Graphics   7/10
Nothing really big in this department. Just your 2D with some basic shadowing to make it appear slightly 3D. Still, for what it is, rather cute and simple. Its a nice break from the games that are currently main stream.
Music and voice acting  5/10
Voice acting can get REALLY repetitive and, at times, you just want to put the game on mute. Its okay to start off with, but, expecailly in the item shop, your MC really likes to hear herself talk. The music, however, isnt too bad and its a nice relaxing backround noise that keeps things flowing rather nicely.
Game play 10/10
Controls are really simple and it does a very good job at teaching everything you need to know about them, within the first day (or two). Each adventurer has a unique feel to them and the only thing that i had issues with, was that some of the later dungeons, seemed rather repetive and it got to the point of me wanting to skip the loot and GTFO. There are only 4 dungeons you will have access too, without endless mode, and its reccomended that you keep going to the last dungeon you have availible to you, inorder to get better things to sale. Bag space is a BIG issue, but a nice challenge, to deal with as you can only carry so much with you while out adventuring. This means that you have to sell any items you want your adventures to wear, in order to free up bag space.
Yes I'm looking at you Charme... If they try to do that, either go for the money, or super price the item they want so they go away for a bit.
User interface/Game Mechanics 9/10
The user interface is rather simple and easy to figure out. you only have 5 buttons you need to worry about and most of the information you need, like keeping track of your orders or keeping track of the news, is easily accessible whenever you need it.
Game Mechanics, on the other hand, is deviously clever. You will get random news events that will dramtically change how you run your item shop and even dungeon crawl. The game will even keep track of what you are taking advantage of, and react to it.
Also each npc that visits your shop, there are barely any if you dont dungeon grind and unlock more adventures, has a particular budget and you can "level up" how much they have by  buying and selling items from them around where they think its worth. The table below is a good  and relible way to get the most out of your store while trying to level up their pockets. One last thing, if a customer wants to buy something off your shelf, they will automatically have enough to buy that item, regardless of how much their budget is. The budget is only really implimented when they ask you for an item (like a book) or orders.
Difficulty- what you expect from a game like this
With the table above, it was rather easy to almost finish the game with my first run. I had issues on the second to last week, but just bought a carp load of candy, and spent everything else i had on items for the second run. Game over isn't a big deal, since you reset to day 2 with almost everything you had when you failed a payment. I have heard some of the later dungeons can be rather tricky, but as long as you try and keep your adventurers gear reasonable and you do some runs with them, it shouldnt be too bad. I mostly stuck with Charme due to her speed and the fact that she crits like someone trying to roll a 4 on a d4.
Price
I got this game rather cheap off of the steam summer sale, but i wouldnt pay the full price for it. If you can find it under the $10 or even the $5 I would go ahead and get it. Its a decent game, but a little pricey to just pick up if you are bored and wanting something different to play. (why i originally picked it up xD )
Conclusion
All in all, its not a bad game, just a small and cute game that can easily become a guilty pleasure  to the point that you are asking yourself, "why am I playing this game and why can't I stop?"
