As most MMOs go, it can be pretty attractive at first. The crafting is interesting enough, the combat keeps you in the game with both a unique way to combo your abilities and the over-the-shoulder perspective, and the intricate class system makes sure you feel unique.
The biggest hook would be the sandbox feature which, hey, it manages to pull off mostly. Its combat really isn't that bad either and neither is the class building.
But realizing that the same thing you're doing at level 20 is going to be the same thing you'll be doing at 55 is, while sadly pretty common, is also pretty shattering.
Now this is the part where someone will step in saying, "But the PvP, raids, STUFF WITH GUILDS!!" As nice of a thought that is, it's not very feasible with this game considering just how dry and toxic the comminity is, which is one of the major issues with the game. Of course most MMORPGs never really have that big welcoming vibe to them, but I can compare Archeage's community to that of drama club in high school: it's full of people with the mentality of a teenager who aren't socially repellent outcasts because they are shy or misunderstoon but rather they are so willing to go out of their way to instigate petty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t purely to save their online honor.
If your are reading that last bit and are offended, of course not the entire community is toxic. Sometimes I can get a laugh out of the faction chat and have a good time, but I never really had a moment where I haven't though to myself "I would hate to be their friend." If you decide to play, right off the bat you'll be witness to little feuds between guilds and players who still think insulting your mom is fashionable. The community as a whole has the same effect as /r/fatpeoplehate on Reddit or that seriously awkward kid from school that you always avoided because he was both a terrible person and probably had some sort of personality disorder that his parents never bothered to take a good hard look at.
The bot issue is not any better, by the way. If you want a game to macro your way to the top, the developers will let you do just that. Unfortunately, this is probably the ideal way to enjoy this game and the fact a lot of people can get away with it is so disheartening to the point you'll ask, "why should I even bother?" The lengths of unfun you need to go with this game to actually get to the fun is lame. Again, even more dissappointed consdering that to cap out requires very little grinding, mostly just the fetch-bear♥♥♥♥♥quests will get you to 55.
On top of all that, the game seems to have gone stagnant with little stirring by the developers. Playing it, you'll have very few moments with the feeling that you having your time invested here will be worth it in the long-run. Again, you'll mostly be doing the same thing as you would be at lower levels to cap and the environments get stale real fast. Really, once you've seen about 4 different themes around your continent, you've seen it all. Unless you have a large group of friends or you fit in with the rejects that make up the community, then you may not find your time worth it.
I should also probably mention the sleazy p2p methods, too. You're going to be pressured into getting a subscription to the game (Patron) so you can get enough 'labor' to do anything that isn't combat-based. For those who do not know, labor is essentially the energy bar from those old Facebook games your mom used to play 5 years ago that would corner casual gamers to pay real money so they can make any progress. If you want pespective, about 3/4ths of that playtime you see up there is purely spent AFKing so I could rack up enough labor to do about a total of 2 hours worth of activities (though to be fair, I'm a bit green to this game anyways). The only big difference is that they manage to streamline it enough so the community thinks it's HARDCORE GAMING material.
There are still some postivies going for this game, and if you find those valuable enough then you can likely find yourself enjoying this. In fact, I believe a lot of people can enjoy this for at least a week not knowing too much about the game going in. But after you hit that point where it all comes at you with a switch-blade, you will most likely be dejected. The cons greatly outweight the pros in this game, but if you can find more value in what little benefits it has then maybe you'll find yourself enjoying it for the long haul.
Also not to be a Tumblrina but the objectifying of women in this game is pretty hilarious; the developers almost had no shame in perpetuating the Eastern MMO stereotype.

I have (off of Steam) over 3,000 hours on this game and another 1k and change here. I’ve played this game since closed alpha, so I've seen it through its good and bad times. I stopped playing from October 2014-September 2015 and just quit as of 9/2016. I uninstalled the game and blew up all of my gear before quitting. I will not return.
Pros:
This is BY FAR the best mmo for PvP that I have ever played. I’d almost say that a huge portion of my life became this game just because of the PvP. It is, after all, completely fantastic. I’ve alpha/beta tested many MMOS from GW2-ESO and believe me; this one did a lot of things right. The PVP is amazing and the combat system is extremely fluid.
So, PvP and Naval Combat would be the best pros.
**HOWEVER**
To PvP AT ALL, you need to spend hundreds of dollars on the cash shop to even get close to the gearscore that you need to be. You also would need to spend hundreds to get a ship geared to the point that it needs to be. Which brings me to...
Cons:
1). It’s a money/gigantic time sink
For starters, I’ve dropped over $3,00 USD into the game over the 4 years that I've played it. At the end I had a decently high gear score @6.2k (there were many people in the 7-8k+ range though), and was to constantly PvP just about anywhere. If I had tried to get that by straight grinding, I would have had to put more hours in than a full time job. Not worth it at all either, since most of the content was boring as hell.
2). Arena System
Completely broken. Once you get past a certian rank, you'll spend 30 mins looking for a single fight or wont find one at all. The new arenas (Blood and Sand) are no better at all and have encouraged more pay to win power.
3). What are we gearing up for?
The lack of endgame is astonishing. You basically run around doing the exact same "endgame content" day after day, looking for the opportunity to wave your epeen everywhere and claim dominance over the people who don't have credit cards. You no pay? You no win.
Overall, the game is a pay-to-win trash heap of what could have been an amazing mmo. Trion completely ruined the game and I won't be surprised when this dies out completely in the next several months. They'll probably do another server merge before then and ruin everyone else's land/lives.

When I first played this game I was blown away by the design, graphics and interesting story elements that you don't typically see in a strategy game as this. However the more I played the more I began to dislike this game.
The over all issue is there really is no sense of strategy to this "strategy" game. Oh yes, there are instances where you can go an try to scout an area, set up snipers on roof tops and what not, but the game does punish you for it. All battles are ranked based on how many turns you take to complete a mission which consist of mainly of capture a certain check point (capture the flag style), defending an area, or eleminating certain foes. The more turns you take, the more you recieve a poor ranking. Thus most "strategy" is just to run and gun foes down until you get to your objective.
Further, you are basically going to spending the majority of your time level grinding.
In all it is a shame that I was disappointed. I was hooked by the different classes of troops, a very interesting story element that would play out (despite it being your typical anime wifu element), and good graphic design. If you do want to purchase this, I would recommend doing it when it is on sale or for finding it cheaper from another store.

This the first review I've written on steam and with good reason... first of all let me clarify that I'm a CONAN fan since childhood and I've never have played this kind of game before (I'm not familiar with Ark, Rust, Forest or any other survival PVP).
This game is simply amazing, the atmosphere and immersion are overwhelming, the combat is similar to Skyrim (although a little rough around the edges), the crafting is simple and intuitive, the soundtrack is right on spot and the world is ruthless and unforgiving. I've been playing on a private server on my own for 9 hours now and I haven't have a dull moment yet, and I'm just scratching the surface of this behemoth of a game... The map is huge, full of interesting scenery and creature, there are fully voice acted friendly NPCs which I didn't expect and it brings you completely into the CONAN mythos from the start.
Probably the biggest surprise for me was the performance, I have an "OK" pc (AMD phenom II x4 965, a GeForce GTX 760 and 8 GB of Ram, nothing fancy) and the game run smooth with a mix on Ultra, high and medium settings.
I can't really speak for the multiplayer aspect of the game since I've just played single player, but I'm really confused by the "mixed" respond on steam, especially for and early access release and with the huge support that the developers have gave us in just a couple of days.
If you like CONAN this is a no-brainer: The game feels like CONAN, sounds like CONAN and plays like CONAN.
If you like don't-hold-your-hand RPG or immersion this game is definitely for you: It make you feel exactly like a prehistoric nomadic caveman, it's full of mysterious and awe inspiring scenery, and it test your will to survive in a really extreme way.
If you like surviving games this is your game: Like I said this is my first step into the genre and I think it was the right one, the first time I die it was from hunger/thirst just a few steps from a river and it was very intense and realistic, it made me value more the half empty water skin and handfull of bugs that you have at the beginning.
If you had a bad first day of release experience, due to server problems or FPS drop, take a deep breath and try it again:
I really don't understand the negative reviews, it's just plain weird for an early access, this is by far the most polish one I've encounter.
Again, for me the whole experience has been fantastic to say the least and I think the developers deserve a round of applause!
I really hope they continue the good work and give of more lore oriented content from the great source material in the upcoming months, and keep giving great support and feedback.

This is an instant-recommend.  For this low price, you CAN NOT go wrong here. I played for over an hour in my first session, and the time flew by.  This is one of those "one more try" sort of games, where you're SURE you can do better if you just have one more run and try harder.  Plus, I'm sure the multiplayer will be a blast the next time I can get a friend to come over.
Do any of you guys remember a little game called "Ragdoll Masters" from like 10 or 15 years ago?  It's kinda like that, but better, and cheaper.  Seriously, that game still costs 10 bucks and you can't even get it on Steam.  This is $3 (or $2.09 if you bought it during the first week like I did) and I would have gladly paid $10 for it.
The Basics:
--
So the premise of this game, (and RM, which I'm sure served as some inspiration) is that you control a floppy ragdoll of a character in a zero-G arena.  The way you move determines your rotation and the positioning of your limbs based on a simple but elegant physics engine.  The goal is to beat your enemies to death, while keeping yourself from getting hurt too much.  Blows to the head are the key to victory, and you certainly want to keep your own head out of harm's way as much as possible.
What's new:
--
So I said that this game seems to take a lot of inspiration from "Ragdoll Masters" but what makes it better?  Well, the biggest thing is the armor and weapons.
Armor makes you slower and clumsier, depending on what type you wear, and how many pieces.. but it will soak up some hits for you, before it gets too damaged and falls off.
Weapons come in 1-handed and 2-handed varieties.. you can carry any combination of 2 1-handed weapons if you desire (such as two swords, a shield and a mini-crossbow, an axe and a magic wand, etc), or a single 2-handed weapon, such as a large melee weapon, a bow and arrow, a magic staff, or a freakin CANNON.
There are many types of armor and weapons to unlock, each with their own playstyles and strengths (particularly the weapons).
Perhaps the coolest thing about the armor and weapons is that it adds variety to the enemies you face in the singleplayer mode.  Instead of just 1v1, 1v2, 1vGiant, 1v2 harder dudes, 1v3, 1v2 giants, etc.. you get a bit more variety because their armor and weapons will be randomized each time.  The enemies in a given round might spawn with completely different weapons than last time, which will greatly alter how you fight them.
Conclusion:
--
This is kind of a big review for a very inexpensive game.  You don't need me to sit here and ramble on any further.  I think it's great, I think you should try it, end of story.
I mean, it's not some epic end-all-be-all game of the year 2016 or whatever.. but will you get a lot of casual fun for your couple of dollars?  I think so, definitely.
Yes, it had a rough start, but still a lot better start than most EA games nowadays. I am recommending this game due to the very active dev team and how much fun it already is in its current state.

A smashing evolution of an old formula. People who've played and enjoyed Ragdoll Masters, Ragdoll Kung Fu, Hammerfall, and other turn-of-the-century physics-based beat-em-ups will recognize the excellence of this title immediately.
For the uninitiated, you control a ragdoll character in a puppet fashion, flailing their weapons toward enemy weak points. In this game, armor provides some resistance to damage before falling off entirely, and further damage to un-armored limbs will result in dismemberment. Armor can provide offensive capabilities as well, which one-ups previous titles of this kind. An armored boot beats a bare skull, and even limbs holding weapons can be lopped off for proper disarming. Ranged weapons are included, and seem pretty fairly balanced with their limitations of reload speed and aiming precision. You can block with your weapons, as well as equip shields in your off-hand.
There is some character customization available, aside from gear you can also customize hair/skin/facial features and their respective colorings. The weapons and armor can't be recolored, however. Weapons can be held in reverse grip as well as standard, adding more depth to the loadout. Customized loadouts can be saved and loaded as the situation demands.
Single player is a 10-match affair, your custom character versus ten assorted combinations of foes in varying gear and sizes. Wins unlock keys, which unlock more gear. There's no storyline, no excess reading, just heavy metal and the clash of steel.
Upside:
Quick and painless to drop in or out of
Simple to learn, truly impressive when skill meets talent
Great advances over previous niche titles
Local MP includes some different modes, as well as customizable gravity and move speed
Plenty of weapon variety/possible loadouts
Dirt cheap game, I paid $2.09
Downside:
No female floppies
Can't customize gear appearance, just character
AI is fairly easy, didn't see difficulty options
Game is short, All achievements in first day/3hrs ingame
Music is repetitive, limited selection of tracks
Graphics are a bit like Flash games on Kongregate or Newgrounds in style (YMMV)
*Damage is not affected by movement speed, damage dealt is based on gear vs weapon. So a weapon that deals three damage to an unarmored head, will always deal three damage, whether rebounding lightly off the opponent's sword or being swung down with the wrath of heaven.
In the end, Floppy Heroes totally delivers at its price point. I highly recommend this as yet another way to smack your friends around the house, and I hope the developer continues to hone their talents and release either updates or sequels, which I'd be happy to invest in.
Note: Other games you might like include the original, Ragdoll Masters(10$ from dev site), Swordy (E.A.15$), Hammerfight (5$ on steam, abandonware, formerly called Hammerfall), and Rag Doll Kung Fu(10$ on steam).

+One of the only games that lets you run a shop, and does it well.
+Fun, engaging characters and story.
Cons:
-The dungeon crawling could be done better.  It's primitive, but fine enough to not hurt the game.
-The game puts you on a kind of time-table of how much money you have to make per day.  This is nice for giving the game some urgency, but it forces you to worry about efficiency, which can be a little stressful.  I would appreciate being able to have more of a sandbox atmosphere where I can take my time.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is an interesting game. The gameplay mechanics are quite unique but the premise is fairly typical of a story with paranormal themes; a ghost partners up with the living to solve a series of murders. It's not mind-blowing but the way its handled in Murdered works quite well, mainly due to the decent voice acting, the supernatural abilities, and the clever art style that blends reality with a ghostly dimension.
The majority of the game is quite fluid and offers little challenge (in a good way) but I have to say that the action sequences feel forced and really bring down the quality of this game. They break the flow of the story and the combat itself is often imprecise and sloppy for what are essentially quick time events. I figure that what happened to Murdered is the same as with Deadly Premonition in which this is something that the publisher demanded of the developers, who reluctantly and haphazardly complied by shoehorning in some janky action sequences in the final hours of development.
If you're aiming for 100% completion I suggest collecting everything BEFORE entering the abandoned and decrepit house near the end of the game, as the final sequence will prevent you from collecting any more items within its level and there is no free-roaming afterward. I found this out the hard way, fortunately you can start a new game, collect what you've missed, and the relevant achievements will still unlock even if the collectibles counter has reset to zero.

I'm not entirely sure what to think. On one hand, this is certainly a more playable, more accessible, and somewhat more entertaining game than its predecessor. The side missions here provide a bit more depth, and I think that for the parts that were streamlined, mainly in terms of replacing the constant inventory management with a somewhat universal upgrade system, it was an improvement.
My problem is with how many of the imperfect, but still working features of the first game were cut out. For example, vehicular exploration does not exist in ME2. Granted, it was pretty annoying to spend considerable chunks of time wandering the planets only to be told, upon discovering some salvage, that I don't meet the minimum skill requirements to gather it, but I don't think that this warranted removing such elements entirely. How about giving me enemies to fight during these trips, or allowing me to gather the items, but just not use them? Nope, just cut it out entirely, and replace it with a planet-scanning minigame that is somewhat enjoyable, once I get past the fact that having to hold down the right mouse button for these sequences seems completely pointless. I mean, if I'm going to be in scan mode, then there is no reason that I'm ever not going to be scanning.
However, I think that the biggest actual downgrade from ME1 is the dialogue. The dialogue wheel, and all of its problems, still exist, but its ugliness is only intensified by some very awkward acting. The VAs do an okay job, but the words themselves can sometimes be downright cringeworthy, mainly due to the requirement of the paragon and renegade speech checks, which are often required to succeed at any matter of diplomacy. In the first game, this existed, sure, but that was when Shepard actually had a personality. and a clear set of goals. Here, that unified personality has been chopped into two pieces, each of which always seems exclusive to the other. The player can either do more paragon speech checks, which involve being the most upstanding human being ever, or more renegade speech checks, which involve berating others and throwing insults at them whenever possible. This might have worked if every character was not a walking cliché whose personality clearly suggests that they would be more prone to one type of persuasion than another. This is where the awkwardness happens, when I am given the option to charm someone who clearly cannot be charmed, or intimidate someone who clearly cannot be intimidated, and it ends up working anyway.
The game is prone to quite a few glitches. There's too many to go into explicit detail, but basically it consisted of ammo that cannot be picked up, and squadmates who disappear from both cutscenes and gameplay.
Whereas the first Mass Effect felt like more of a tactical RPG with shooting as an afterthought, its sequel feels more like a shooter, with RPG mechanics as an afterthought. It is still a fun game, even if removed so much from the original. Next, I am going to play Mass Effect 3, which I'm sure is going to be the best. Hopefully, it will bring back the depth, improve the writing, and not be a disappointment, right?

Archeage, Archeage, Archeage, why did it have to go so wrong?
I'm not going to ramble on about every single detail of this game, plenty of other people have. I'm just writing this for the sake of personal closure.
Archeage could have been THE MMO. THE WoW killer. The be-all-and-end-all of MMOs. I'm well aware that the title I just said has been given to MANY MMOs, (SWToR, ESO, TERA), but if you have played Archeage (And I do recommended playing the first 15 levels, then you'll truly understand what this review is saying) you'll know that Archeage was destined to be the real WoW killer. THE MMO.
So where did it go wrong?
It's funny how just a small little thing can ruin such a magnificant example. The fact that this game is free killed it. In order for this game to be free, Trion had to burden it down with microtransactions.  And what a mistake that was. In order to fit in with the crowd of free to play MMOs, Trion felt it would be a good idea to make the game free, when a simple $15 per month sub fee would have been well justified with how much content and opportunity this game had.
Everything in this game either costs money to enjoy or isn't worth doing. The housing system? Costs money. Auction house? Costs money. Farming? Costs money. simple things such as crating and getting loot? Costs money.
Even the things that don't cost money aren't worth doing because this game has no hope for it left. Its playerbase is gone, and whoever is left is either a new player or a bot.
Hopefully someday soon another game like this will pop up without the colossal failure of what this game did wrong.

Idle questions drift through my mind sometimes (normally when I’m at work and supposed to be having more productive, less idle thoughts).
There are a few questions that always plague me when I settle at my desk in the mornings
Questions like:
“What am I doing here?”
“Why isn’t it lunchtime yet?”
and the classic
“Is there a microscopic black hole under my desk because I think time has slowed down?”
(There isn’t by the way, I’ve checked, although if it really is microscopic I might have missed it).
I recite these musings to myself like a kind of depressing mantra every morning, but it’s the afternoons when my thoughts really go off on a tangent.
For example, have you ever wondered why we have two letters in the English alphabet that make the same noise, C and K?
I have....
And whilst we’re talking about C, why do we use it to make an S sound in some words?
(Circle, I’m thinking of you here)
We’ve already got a letter that can make "Sssss" Sounds, it’s the letter S, why is C stepping on S’s toes?
If C did step on S’s toes, and it turned into a fight, which one would win?
Which one would I want to win?
Don’t get me wrong, it’s not always that insightful in my mind, that was a good afternoon.
Thankfully a slightly more relevant question occurred to me today, relevant because I was sitting at my desk subtly checking for black holes
(I have to be subtle or my colleagues might think I’m weird).
Anyway, as I was eyeballing a shady corner of one of my draws for suspicious gravitational anomalies my mind wandered towards thoughts of home (as it often does) and my plans for the evening, plans which included playing American Truck Simulator.
Now, it’s no secret that I like to zone out with a good long session of European Truck Simulator 2 when time allows so I was looking forward to getting behind the wheel of a “Good Ol’ Big Rig” and trucking in a Zen-like trance across the US of A.
It was then that it occurred to me that I didn’t know which was bigger, geographically speaking, Europe or America.
As this question was obviously much more important than any actually work I was supposed to be doing, I immediately turned to my friend Google to investigate.
The problem was Google didn’t seem to know the answer.
Keep in mind that whilst at work I have to be just as subtle in my clandestine internet activities as I am in my black hole survey, so I could only really scan the results (whilst the boss wasn’t looking) without opening up any actual web pages.
This led to a list of links with snippets of information like “Europe has a slightly larger landmass” and “America is much larger than Europe, France is smaller than Texas”.
I decided that as I couldn’t investigate this properly whilst being watched by “the man” (and I was aware that whilst it seemed like a burningly important question when compared the dullness of actual “work” it wouldn’t matter to me in the slightest once I was at home and had more interesting things to do).
Anyway, due to the lack of an immediately accessible answer I decided that they were probably about the same sort of size, a decision which has now become fact in my mind, a fact I’ve made up myself, but a fact none the less.
It made sense to me, If SCS had made a trucking game which spanned most of Europe then American Truck Simulator would probably be on the same sort of scale, therefore America must be the same sort of size as Europe, you can’t argue with science like that.
These thoughts were still with me when I finally escaped the shackles of work and settled down in front of my PC.
Steering wheel and pedals at the ready, I fired up ATS ready for some “Stateside Trucking”
For the uninitiated, American Truck Simulator places you in charge of your own haulage company (as does its sister game Euro-Truck Simulator 2). You start out by choosing where you want to set up your first little base of operations and then you’re master of your own haulage destiny.
Unfortunately you don’t start with any money, driving skills or even a truck of your own, you’re going to need to earn, learn and buy these things as you play.
The “earning and learning” elements initially come from the successful completion of “quick jobs” which you’ll find available to you from the various locales scattered across the map.
These jobs vary in length and payment; you’ll find yourself hauling all sorts of cargo across the states.
You’re working for the metaphorical “Man” with these jobs though so you won’t earn as much as you would if you were your own boss, but as you haven’t got your own truck when you first start out, running these contracts in the loaner rigs provided is the only way you’re going to earn a buck.
When you’ve finished browsing the list of jobs currently available to you, you’ll pick a contract you like the sound of (whether that’s because it pays well, you like the idea of hauling a particular cargo type, or you think it might push some interesting scenery past  your windows).
A click of a button later and you’ll find yourself sitting in your borrowed rig; trailer hooked up and destination already set in the sat nav.
It’s time to get trucking!
Now you’re sitting behind the wheel of a big rig, trundling along the byways and cruising down the highways it’s important to keep in mind that this is a simulation title, not a joy ride in Grand Theft Auto.
You’re being paid to complete a delivery job.
Running red lights, racing past speed cameras and smashing other vehicles off the asphalt (as tempting as it might be) could result in some hefty fines, if you’re saving up to buy your own rig, this is not a good thing.
Traffic transgressions aside, you’ll eventually reach a point where you’ve got a tidy sum of money burning a hole in your pocket. Whether this is through the diligent completion of delivery jobs or the quick fix solution of a crippling bank loan is up to you, but sooner or later you’ll find yourself touring the dealerships to pick out a truck of your very own.
When you’ve got your heart set on a rig, the dealer is going to tempt you with a wealth of optional extras from the cosmetic to the mechanical and like a kid in a sweetshop; you’re going to want them all.
With your chest full of pride and your wallet empty of money, you’ll now be the proud owner of your own truck. It’s time to stop making money for “The Man” and start making it for yourself.
You’re no longer tied to the “quick job” market, you can take contracts directly now and cut out the middle man.
The downside of this is that now you’re using your own vehicle; you’re going to need to look after it, give it petrol to drink and pay to have it fixed up if it gets “poorly”.
You need to look after yourself too, drive for too long without rest and you’re going to get drowsy. Falling asleep at the wheel can really ruin your day (and your truck) so rest stops in lay-bys are a must on long drives.
As well as getting rich from completing all these contracts, there’s also the added bonus of increasing your own driving skills, this is done with an almost RPG like experience levelling system.
Complete a contract quickly without smashing up your truck and you’ll gain experience; gain enough and you’ll ... [snip]

Forget sniping or cover (there is no crouch key) mobility is the key in this run and gun linear shooter. With a checkpoint system that opens the new area while sealing the last the levels feel more like a series of confined arena's packed with a mixture of heavily scripted spawns making for a very hectic style of arcade gameplay.
With old school secret areas dotted around containing power ups, and intermittent upgrade points players can spend any nanites (experience) they're collected to upgrade different aspects of defense or offense. Such customisation will alter difficulty and play style allowing some longevity for re-runs.
The graphics are nice and with an environment full of destructibles the game encourages the use of stategic misses to take out the enemy hordes in a more imaginative manner then simply clicking on them repeatedly. Another nice touch is the hit zone allocation to enemy allowing the player to strategically cripple or desperately reduce enemy constructs 1 part at a time, resulting in different animations and behaviour.
The comic book style interludes add atmosphere and story to an otherwise shallow in-game experience.
Summary: Good looking frantic fun with short bursts of fast and reflexive gameplay between bouts of leasurely safety.

"tutorial island" or act 1, took me about 20 hours to complete by myself when i had absolutely no idea what i was doing, and about 10 the second time when i knew exactly what i had to do. Act 2 seems to have taken somewhere between 35 and 50 (played with a friend) hours for my first time through, and i missed A LOT of quests and content. I do like how this game rewards exploration though, so many places youll find a random key, or a dead body with a note that can help you in a dialogue later and allow you to pass enemies or unlock something.
by far my favorite addition to this game is the option to respec whenever you want, even your civil attribute points after act 1. I can play an aerotheurge, then get bored of it and switch to pyro or geo without much work. Definitely adds a lot to this game, as one of the issues i had with the first game was getting stuck in one boring playstyle and using the same moves over and over.

I love this game. The art style is cute and the game mechanics are simple. The game is a little out of the box for an RPG. It is both a sim game as well as a dungeon crawling game instead of just the latter. You are an adorable (yet annoying and too cheerfully trusting girl) that gets left with her dad's massive debt. She is guided by her fairy (the very serious loanshark) to open up an item shop to help repay it. Now the game is simple to understand. You have the day broken up into four parts. You decide what you want to do for the day whether it be shopping for items to stock, adventuring with a hero for loot, or stocking you store and opening it to the public. Ultimately it's all about the money. Or pix I should say. One part of the gameplay is the shop. You end up haggling with customers to get the best price and stocking it to attract the most customers. The second form of gameplay is adventuring with the hero. This is where the "little out of the box" ends. This is your typical RPG where you go around killing monsters picking up loot and equipping or using items. Definitely appreciate this portion of the game because when I get bored of selling things to people (or running low on items AND being bored) I get to change the scenery in a sense. It's really a great game with just enough to keep you going.

I understand that combat, of any sort, should be a last possible option in any survival horror game. It's not scary if you can just shoot an enemy or whack them with something heavy until they resemble a fine red mist. I get that. However, you need other options if that is the case. Either running away, or at least enough of a combat mechanic not to die every time something scary pops out.
Now, I'm not saying the basic enemies are difficult or anything. Not that I have much experience beyond what you meet in the school. Though even with those, hit detection feels buggy. My problem is the boss in the school. It's been quite a while since I've encountered such an amazingly unfair fight.
First of all, it relies on quickly bringing up your camera. This would be fine, if Linda understood the concept of urgency. If you're moving even a tiny bit, she won't raise the damn phone when you hit the button. Or it might be because she has to face the direction the camera is in, which is also terrible as a mechanic in a fight that requires quick reactions. Early on this is not an issue, but the boss only gets faster and 'barely in time' soon becomes 'raise the phone when I tell you to, you bint!'
This would not be a problem, if there was room to dodge. Nope. The boss can hit you no matter how hard you hug the wall as you try to run by. And you have try to pass the boss because, guess what, if it corners you there is no way to get out of that. Considering the fight is in a very tiny room with an invisible wall in the corner thanks to the desk, this is just not fair. Especially considering you litterally have a boss who vanishes after taking a hit an can move through walls. Oh, and did I mention a single hit stunlocks you? If you get hit, prepare to eat at least 1 one more attack or even 2 if you're in a bad spot. That's not so bad, until the boss suddenly goes all Sonic the Hedgehog on you and its speed doubles. You can't run from that and odds are you'll be looking in the wrong direction when it comes out of the wall.
Which brings me to the next issue. Linda is so damned slow. I understand certain items make her faster, but bloody hell. I get it. The place is dark, scary and there are dangerous beings roaming around. I wouldn't practice free running there either, but pick up the pace a little would ya? Even her sprinting speed would cause obese kids to point and laugh.
All of this just made me feel like dying was not my fault, and I shouldn't feel that way. When I die, it should be because I ♥♥♥♥ed up or wasn't doing the right thing. It should not be because passing the boss without getting hit requires divine intervention and a particularly large rabbit's foot. I'm not asking for matrix reflexes and an arena to fight in, but I am asking for a character with more of a sense of urgency and more space than a bloody walk in closet to fight the hyperactive evil spirit.
What finally made me quit, though, was the punishment for death. Guys, one of the most important things in gaming is being able to quickly return after dying. Making it take longer and longer each time you die is not an effective punishment. I have tried everything I could think of. I stood in the center and spun around. I died. I huddled in a corner and waited. The boss came through the wall right next to me, stunlocked me and I died. I hugged the contours of the room and ran in circles, hoping to put enough distance between Linda's slow♥♥♥♥♥and the enemy to raise the camera in time. Guess what, I died. And each time I woke up in limbo and had to walk further and further before I could come back to life.
That did not make me think 'Darn. Well, I deserve this. At least I know what to do now.' Instead it made me judge the mind numbingly long and boring walk and think 'You know what? No. I'm not walking all the way over there to get my♥♥♥♥♥kicked again.'
I wanted to like this game, I really did. I still want to know what was going on, but the gameplay is not worth learning what happens in the story.

I personally don't favor this game a whole lot and I wouldn't recommend it to people who are accustomed to Western RPGS (such as myself, despite playing JRPGs). The game, despite being very flashy and action packed, can get bland quickly, and once you complete your Second Job Change, for me, it feels like the end of the game. I know there's Transcendence, El Resonance, and a whole lot more to become stronger, but to attain said aspects are ludicriously difficult (if you buy your equipment with K-Chings, you're a successful trader, you've got a monster computer unlike me, or all of those three, good for you). And sure the combat mechanics/styles are very interesting, but sometimes the monsters/bosses can be a massive nuisance (Ran, I hate you to no end) and the dungeons can be a whole lot more difficult than one would guess (don't always trust the recommended "Average Level Equipment"). Then, dear God...why does Arena even exist...? For me, it's the most frustrating part of the game. Even though I'm more of a dungeon-farming player, I sometimes have the urge to do PvP, so I used to go in expecting to be paired up with someone that's around my level, but I get paired up with people that have disgustingly powerful equipment. This game becomes frustrating once you've experienced, perhaps, 100-300 hours of this game.
Foremostly, the game has a lot to offer to the point that it becomes tiring to focus on each and every part of it. If you focus on just one part, you'd be lagging behind in dungeon difficulty. Each region comes with, I believe, two sets of gear that give set bonuses and you can upgrade them. That sounds dandy and easy until you realise you have to add enchantments and effects (although only on weapons) to the equipment. So, you're stressed with getting the equipment (although, now they give you cubes that give the set, though separating weapons from armors), leveling them up, enhancing them with "magic stones", and adding effects. Not to mention, +5 is not the max (I think it's +13), and each time you upgrade it, chances of it
increases, risking you losing the set bonus effect. It can be restored, but its difficult/expensive to obtain the item to restore them as well.
Job changes are simple: you become level 15 for the first, complete it, then become level 35, become the third tier of that character. But, when you want to become a Transcendent, not only do you have to be level 70, but you need to go through dungeons of the same level (by the way, the difficulty jumps to a massive height, making it difficult for soloists) and you need to go through Secret Dungeons (which, as well, are very difficult). The easy part is being level 70. The tough part is getting through the Secret Dungeons and, even though it's not relevant to Transcending a character (I believe), Henir. To get through these Secret Dungeons/Henir, you have two options: play with a party and (if you have a horrible computer) let the others carry you through OR become a merchant, with not enough ED, and earn money by farming in easier dungeons to buy gear and items adequate enough to go through the dungeon by yourself (which takes a whole lot longer than a new player would guess since most of those adequate items are more than 20M ED). Now, you COULD wait for events and they tend to give good gear. They're just like Secret Dungeons (again, if you're a new player); getting the event items can be a pain since they might be for rent and to get the permanent gear you need to grind so hard in those dungeons that may be as difficult as Secret Dungeons. All in all, the process of becoming a good or great player takes extremely long and you may have to prioritize this game and spend loads and loads of actual money for in-game money.
Arena is extraordinarily bad. When I first began playing this game, arena didn't seem so bad. But, they once had a level jump event and it broke the matching in arena. Matchmaking is based on ranking (obviously), but some of these people that were Rank D or Rank B jumped to level 70 and it was so common going up against them (I'm guilty for doing the same thing). Although it didn't give good equipment to those that level jumped, it was still frustrating going up against them. I don't think they do level jumps anymore, but, it's still broken being matched up based on ranking. I recently came back to the game and I decided to do a little bit of PvP after playing again for a few days. My first opponent was level 96, Transcended with El Resonance, and my third was level 99, only Transcended. I was level 60. The match was completely one-sided; no way of me bringing them down to 3/4 of their health. I did go against a level 27 (my second match), but even then, that proves unbalanced match making. It's not just the matchmaking that peeves me, but it's sort of the combat style of Elsword itself. Some would say there's skill involved, others say that you just get good stats and mash buttons. Honestly, that's what I think. I've been against someone my level before and I was playing Luciel. Luciel has skills with so much hitboxes it's not even fair. The player complained about "Luciels needing to run away and mash buttons" and I agree with him entirely, albeit I think every character has to. The majority (and if not, all) of the characters have skills with a a hand full to massive amount of hitboxes and if your MP regain is high, you can keep your enemy staggered (unless they Mana Break out of there). But, even though there's Mana Breaking as a possible trait, some skills won't allow the character to Mana Break, making it a pointless feature. Basically, arena is broken. I don't mess with it as much as I used to anymore.
There's probably more (or less) of what's distasteful of
that I don't know, but I'd say these are the major problems of the whole game. This is purely opinionated; I've never reviewed a game before and I see it as it is, never deeper, thus undermining my rights to even discourage other people from playing this game, but there's one thing I can definitely say for sure:
If you're used to Western RPGs and want to try something similar to JRPGs or you want to play a game that doesn't require too much time or money to become good at, this game is most certainly not for you. But, if you want to play it because its art-style (which I cannot deny) is brilliant and you want to get some "waifu" (yes, there's a marriage system), then, power to you, go ahead.

Owlboy is a fairly good game; my problem is that it isn't worth the price.  Most especially due to the fact that it is being touted as a metroidvania, when in fact the game is extremely linear.  Don't be misled as I was:  this game is actually just an ARPG.  What little exploration there is to be had usually amounts to nothing more than an occasional short branch in the path, and the rewards for such exploration are generally no more impressive than a few coins.
The game world is beautiful, and the characters are fun.  Sadly about ten hours is all you'll get to enjoy those aspects of this very short game.  Combat can be a bit awkward when compared to other action games, due to the fact that you spend much of it hauling around your gunners (the only way to damage the majority of enemies).
It's possible that I might have been more impressed with this game had I experienced it in a vacuum, but unfortunately it comes on the heels of Ori and the Blind Forest.  By comparison Owlboy is shorter, more expensive, less immersive, less challenging, offers less chance for exploration... I could go on, but I think the point is clear.  My conclusion is that while this is not a bad game, I wouldn't pay more than $10 for it had I the chance to do things over.

Archeage, Archeage, Archeage, why did it have to go so wrong?
I'm not going to ramble on about every single detail of this game, plenty of other people have. I'm just writing this for the sake of personal closure.
Archeage could have been THE MMO. THE WoW killer. The be-all-and-end-all of MMOs. I'm well aware that the title I just said has been given to MANY MMOs, (SWToR, ESO, TERA), but if you have played Archeage (And I do recommended playing the first 15 levels, then you'll truly understand what this review is saying) you'll know that Archeage was destined to be the real WoW killer. THE MMO.
So where did it go wrong?
It's funny how just a small little thing can ruin such a magnificant example. The fact that this game is free killed it. In order for this game to be free, Trion had to burden it down with microtransactions.  And what a mistake that was. In order to fit in with the crowd of free to play MMOs, Trion felt it would be a good idea to make the game free, when a simple $15 per month sub fee would have been well justified with how much content and opportunity this game had.
Everything in this game either costs money to enjoy or isn't worth doing. The housing system? Costs money. Auction house? Costs money. Farming? Costs money. simple things such as crating and getting loot? Costs money.
Even the things that don't cost money aren't worth doing because this game has no hope for it left. Its playerbase is gone, and whoever is left is either a new player or a bot.
Hopefully someday soon another game like this will pop up without the colossal failure of what this game did wrong.

When I think about fantasy RPGs they tend to involve a whole lot of fighting and the occasional tavern break to play some dice or card games against the locals. In Hand of Fate you play cards with the occasional break for fighting. The combat is a little repetitive but encounters never last very long and is still fairly enjoyable.
The card game itself, though, is great - a sort of progressive deck-builder with dealer-supplied cards thrown in to shake things up. You move across a randomised map of location cards, resolving the conflicts on each as you pass them, and gaining (or losing!) loot and resources as you make your way to the boss for the level. Then you start again for the next level... but with a couple new cards, a few new story items and a new item or two up for grabs.
The style, story and narration are also quite charming and really add to the overall feeling and aesthetic of the game.

Ahhh Warframe. A strange love hate freemium game. One of the few Freemium games where they do try to make it better(and the devs do fail,and often with spectactular results)
The game itself? Runs great. It's clear this game has had some effort put in,even with the new Plains of Eidelon update,I still was running fairly well(until the Door of Friendship was a thing)
The gameplay? It's strange,because it fits a few different niches. It's basically a fast paced horde shooter/basher. And it's *fun*. You can mod your weapons to your taste,but DE needs to balance the mods so that way you can have some more flavor or utility instead of the same fit for every weapon.
The art style is a nice mishmash of East meets West. The lore is all over the place,and can easily be ignored,so if you want something you can turn your brain off,hang out with friends and show off how pretty you can make yourself this is it.
But where does this game falter? The grind can be excessive at times. The Hema and Gara are way too hard to get. But everything else isn't too horribly bad.
A few of the major quests are kinda bleh(looking at you Chains of Harrow)

I'll start by saying i've not played all that far through the story - I've had multiple starts due to purchasing just prior to release and a Co-op partner who seems to enjoy playing several classes before sticking to one.
Interestingly enough, this has had the positive of showing me just how different the game can be with different class combinations. We've played combos where it seems that no matter how careful we are, the battlefield inevitably becomes a blanket of different elemental affects indiscriminately maiming everybody on it and we've had more tactical groups that have more control over such affects, without the volatile power behind their attacks.
We've settled on a slightly more understated group, methodically using status affects to control the flow of battle and tip it into our favour.
The game is beautiful looking, it's as deep as you wish it to be and the sheer amount of detail in the world is amazing. The UI is simple without being restrictive, the game will guide you without holding your hand and through that allows you to make your mistakes, or genius discoveries and whichever it be, you're left with under no illusion: That was your doing, for better or worse.
I always want to like games like this but often find the world doesn't feel alive enough, is to linear or awkwardly open to its own detriment - the balance is never quite right, but here, for me at least it has been struck and i've really enjoyed exploring and experimenting.
tldr:
The game is generally well polished, fun and of good depth. Looks beautiful, with an interesting story and the world feels richer for it. Worth a buy from any RPG fan, especially if like me, an rpg feeling like an MMO with no players in it just feels like an empty experience to you - you wont find that here.

Think of "Papers, Please!" but with
- cooking
- cheerful colors
- dead potatoes
- potato gods
- potato puns
- cannibalism
- more culture pop references than carbs
The gameplay is easy enough in the beginning. Drag potatoes with a big red bar to the red food processor, drag the yellow one to the yellow machine etc. The difficulty quickly picks up when more conditions are added. Red to red but only if the number of red is smaller/higher than X, and you'll only receive a bonus if the number is between y and z.
The hungry gods won't be happy with one simple dish for long, they want five of them, with x ingredients and a specific quality, you need ingredients of that quality to get the dish right, if you don't you might need add boosters, those cost in-game money ($tarch), but the clients won't wait forever, if you don't want to lose favor give them drinks.
You turn dishes into drinks but don't miscalculate the ingredients you need, and don't give the gods too many drinks or they'll leave. Also, some machines only work efficiently when the potatoe you throw into them has a certain weight or age or high. And some potatoes don't belong in hell, you better add the number of their sins to make sure you show mercy to the right one, and better don't miss the sinful potatoe one of the gods has asked you to look for...
Yes, it gets pretty busy soon enough. Add boosters for everything and it gets even more chaotic. Especially if you choose an unfortunate combination...
This could become difficult as there are many little things to forget but thankfully, all informations and requirements are easy to find any time while you play. Everything is explained and by clicking or hovering with the cursor over icons, you always get an information of the meaning. Also, you have the option to pause (or even enable auto-pause) the timer to carefully look at all the given information and numbers. You know, for a casual-casual experience, when the stress shouldn't become greater than the fun.
It's a nice, silly game if you want to waste some time and like to focus on micro-managing your casual sim. It can become stressful when you don't like making mistakes or deactivate the auto-pause but all over all, it's rather easy. I've yet to see if there's something like a Game Over screen.
Once you fall into the right rhythm for your current level, it won't matter much if you make a mistake now and then. It won't hurt your results much, only your pride.
There's not much to say about the music from my side. It's nice, not overly annoying, but I turn it off anyway.
The story is simple and obvious and relies mostly on the humor.
If your humor occasionally falls into the "This is so dumb, I love it!" category, you'll love this. If you don't like silly, sometimes painful puns, you'll hate this.
The biggest strength and also biggest problem with the story and humor are the countless pop culture references. Be it celebrity cooks, Overwatch, popular movie characters, singers... It's funny if you're somewhat up-to-date with what the cool kids talk about on the internet but even if the jokes don't fly over your head, it's the kind of humor that won't last. This game's story and humor is doomed to be dated sooner or later without any potential to be a timeless classic.
But right now it's fun, the gameplay is enjoyable if you like this stack-on difficulty kind of game. It's just the right amount of pressure and stress to stay focused without getting frustrated. The graphics are pleasant enough for this kind of game if you like bright colors and potatoes as your heroes and gods. And frankly, who doesn't?
I bought it in a bundle and definitely recommend it if you can grab it during a sale.

Hard Reset is a game made with old school FPS sensibilities. It comes from the Serious Sam/Painkiller mold, where you have to run around like a maniac to kill baddies that are bigger and faster than you. Plus it's a cyber-punk game, but Deus Ex this ain't.
The game has a lot going for it, even with some of its budget title sensibilities. The shooting is intense and satisfying, and the game features a variety of difficulty levels to match your skill level. You're equipped with two guns that can change forms to become 10 different weapons total. Learning the special features of all the weapons is key to surviving the fights that Hard Reset throws at you. Guns can be upgraded and unlocked at numerous kiosks strewn throughout the game, with credits picked up from enemy bots and secret areas. Here's where one of the game's flaws show up; there is no New Game Plus mode where you get to run back through earlier levels of the game with your upgraded guns, which would have been a lot of fun.
The game is pretty to look at but short, even with the added DLC they give you for free, and the story never makes any sense. Even then, the price is right for a good, fast and fun shooter experience. These are the same guys responsible for the 2013 revamp of Shadow Warrior, and while the experience here isn't as polished as what you'll find there, it's still got a lot of bang for your buck. Worth it if you catch it on super sale!

DreadOut was an interesting experience and as warning to players out there, an incomplete one. Writing a review of this game is a bit odd at this juncture for a couple of reasons: One being that DreadOut, at least the Steam version, has only recently made available to the Mac. This new version that was used to write this review so it might have a few kinks yet to work out.
The second reason why reviewing DreadOut is a bit awkward is that the developer doesn’t really clearly announce the game as an episodic game. In fact, if a player wasn’t expecting it, the way the game currently ends with a lackluster “To be continued” might be a bit like a slap to the face. However, after a bit of digging, there are statements that the game is intended to receive “updates” in a similar fashion to episodic games sometime in the future.  Announcements of this are a bit skimpy on detail however and not really forthcoming enough to prepare player on when to expect anything, including basic patches and DLC releases. What this means that as of the release of this review, this game is fun and playable but by no means 100% complete. As it stands now, the experience only took this reviewer only four hours of play to casually stumble through without making any real effort.
For those who no nothing about this game, the story centers around a high school girl named Linda who is on some kind of trip with four other classmates and her teacher when they discover that road they took was cut of from a destroyed bridge after a bit of reckless exploring by some of the more rebellious classmates a sort walk leads them of rough terrain to the other side of the bridge and into an abandoned town, then to the abandoned school…and crazy stuff happens leaving Linda alone in the dark with nothing but her cell phone and a bunch of ghosts.
It’s creepy, yes, but mostly because of the sound design and the fact that Linda’s only real defense is her phone. If one mutes the sound, however the whole game seems a lot less intimidating and a bit sillier, more like the main character is in a haunted house rather than in any real danger. If Linda “dies”, for example, she just runs toward a light in this place called limbo and she wakes up where she fainted.  The ghosts come from Asian inspirations, but again without sound a lot of them seem almost goofy. Linda gets chased by a pig demon or has to take pictures of a creepy ghost with scissors to complete a puzzle, but both of these dangerous beings seem a bit laughable. The only real shocking event seemed to be the unending jump scare that was a whaling undefeatable ghost that would follow the player around while invisible if not viewed through Linda’s phone.
Mechanically the game was hot and cold as well. The game seemed to react much slower than the player at times and were a few instances when Linda seemed to be defeated by stun lock (the animations taking any control from the player) more than anything else, but again on the flipside, this was counter balanced by the game’s atmosphere, sound and lighting. It was much easier to accept the any clunkyness in the controls when the player is under the impression that he or she is supposed to be playing as a normal, scared, slightly clumsy teenager, fumbling in the dark by the light of her cell phone. Switching between third and first person camera also adds to the sense of confusion and vulnerability rather than coming across as clunky or slow reacting. Only rarely did the faults in the slow reacting controls make themselves obvious when they encounter a situation where fast reflexes seemed to demand too much from the control scheme.
Still, credit goes to where credit is due. DreadOut was entertaining and the game’s intro was interesting enough to make an audience to wonder what happens next, despite the shortcomings in the games length and content. Will it be worth waiting for? Only time will tell, but it certainly looks to lean toward a positive outcome.The review gave it thumbs up because it was easy to see the potential in DreadOut and what was playable was enjoyable, but how the story, sound and other content will shape up later is still up in the air.

Holy Potatoes! What the Hell?! is a colourful, hell-themed cooking management sim. You play as Sweeny Tots, an amnesiac potato chef who is trying to cook his way through the nine levels of hell’s kitchens and get into heaven.
It’s the third instalment from local game developers Daylight Studios. The first game, Holy Potatoes! A Weapon Shop?!, was a puntasy business sim where you played as a entrèe-preneur forging hundreds of different weapons; the second game, Holy Potatoes! We’re in Space?!, had you managing a battle spaceship while you went on a space adventure.
The gameplay harkens back to the studio’s first game, which revolved around completing quests via time/task management and pleasing ‘customers’ versus the second game which added an element of space battles and had you trashing everyone in your way.
The game’s learning curve is well thought out,  albeit plodding in the first few levels. It’s easy to pick up the gameplay and create a simple strategy.

While on the surface, it may seem like another generic JRPG going for a cutesy art style, the Recettear is actually a completely original RPG that puts you in the place of someone you barely think about: the item shop owner. As Recette, you buy and sell various items to pay off your missing father's debts. Aided by the fairy Tear, you two team up and open a shop together. The actual selling of items is done through a barganing system where you can haggle your customers to get a higher price. You can get items by either buying them from a market, or hiring an adventurer to collect items for you. That is where some of the more traditional game mechanics come in as it plays kinda like a 2D top down adventure game. Though the tutorial can be a bit long, it is worth it to experience a truly unique game that will leave a lasting impression on you.

Alright where to start... Elsword has some fun aspects to it.
I personally found the art,charcters,customization, powers, and gameplay are amazing.
However this game suffers from a sever case of Pay 2 Win.
Let me start with the co-op dungeons is a blast and typically aren't that bad for the fix couple of group of dungons. In fact I never really had pronbems with the dungeons at all until the lastest (when I played) dungeons set preety late in the game. (Level 81)
The issue occurs when you attempt to do PVP.
No matter how well you play and how you set your charcter up and how you know it you will most likely lose to someone with gear they payed for along with the best gear at the time (TIme/Space gear when I played) If you had any gear that wasn't grandized Secret dungeon gear then you where going to have a HARD time getting any wins at all. Espcially against range spammers.
Now I gave a bit of leway here and worked hard to get Grandized Secret Dungeon gear which takes about two weeks of contant play to get when I worked on my set. This fixed the issue of being dominated for a little bit you would still see it here and there but you could hold your own if you had the skill and not the gear.
Sadly though after I got my Grandized SD gear the devs decided to revamp SD gear a few days later and made my gear compeletly useless (Powercreep).
After that I left the game on my PC and only played it once after six months. As you can see I did put in some time into this game as the co-op is a blast and the art, charcters, and powers are really fun and unique.  I had first played this game in 2013 and started again around christmas 2015 so I've seen the later development stages of this game in two diffrent eras.
To sum up:
Pros:
-Good Soundtrack
-Good Charcter design and backstory
-Good level's
-Community is rather helpful really vetran players like to help newer/new charcters out / show off (wont lie)
-Powers are cool and combos as well
-Constantly new events going on
-Great concept
-Free to play*** (Besides the pay to win)
Con:
-Pay to Win  (in PVP)
-Powercreep
-the basic enamies get reskinned after the first few stages (Look diffrent act the same)
-etc
This game is fun and to be honest if I was a say in the direction of this game... I would rebot it and focus on removeing the Pay to Win aspects of it. The PVP is really fun when its fair and I could see it being rather compeative to an extent. Personally unsure on how to fix the Powercreep. That was mostly an issue for me since it happened like days after I got my gear that I came home and worked on for an hour or two every day.
If you go for co-op sure have fun and sure the heck did.
But as of what I know now the PVP isn't the best place to be heading at the momment.

tl;dr Just download Xonotic instead.
They took an arena FPS that was slightly popular on PC, bought the rights to the name, and then proceeded to strip away everything that made the original game great and create....well this.  They used an engine that can't handle the type of fast-paced gameplay that Nexuiz was known for.   They came up with a weird mutator power up system that should have just been a special game mode, and then made that a core game mechanic.  The netcode is just bad, so the online play isn't worth your time.  It's crazy how much they managed to change the game for the worse.
This game also split up the original community because of the drama caused by the whole thing.  The guy who made the original game engine sold the Nexuiz name without asking the community.  Since people in the community helped develop Nexuiz, and since the Nexuiz name then became the property of THQ, people dropped it and made a new game based on Nexuiz gameplay called Xonotic.  Many of the players were unhappy and went over to play Xonotic after that.
Support for this game has ended.  It was a flop to begin with, but when THQ went under, this game disappeared for years.  People just kind of wrote it off as a lost cause.  Even if it had ongoing support I still wouldn't recommend it just because you can get Xonotic for free.  Xonotic is just a better game for so many reason.  Better online play, better engine for fast gameplay, better weapons, more content, and the list goes on.  It doesn't have the Cryengine graphics that this game has, but it does keep true to what made the original Nexuiz game great.  I've spent hundreds of hours in Xonotic and don't regret a minute of it.

Edit:
I got busy and had to put the game down for a while.  Came back after a few months and decided to finish it, so these are my final thoughts on the game.
I love the art direction of this game.  It's one of, if not the best looking pixel art games I've ever seen.  There are a few areas and animations that aren't as good as the rest of the game, but you have to really pay attention to pick most of these out.
The music is outstanding.  The composer and orchestra did a phenominal job creating beautiful and memorable music (I actually bought the soundtrack).
Gameplay is good, but frustrating at times.  The movement feels responsive and fluid, but combat can be a bit overwhelming at times when you're trying to move, dodge, shoot, and switch characters all at the same time.
The puzzles are in general relatively easy and I would've personally preferred a bit more of a challenge, but they were still fun.
Plot is good.  Nothing amazing and a bit predictable, but interesting enough to draw me in and keep my attention.  My only real criticism of the plot is that the end seemed a bit rushed.  Great dialogue though!
I would have liked the game to be longer and bigger, but I realize that there's only so much that a small studio can do.  Hopefully they'll be able to get more funding and expand their team for Owlboy 2 (fingers crossed).
I was also frustrated by the lack of a map.  It was easy enough to find my way around, but a map would've been nice so that I could see any places where I might've missed some coins (and getting myself oriented after a few months of not playing).
Overall, I love the game but it does have its flaws.

For those of you who would rather watch my video review, here ya go:
What this game did well was make a very replayable game with an interesting story that makes you want to keep replaying it. It does this through the side stories in the game. For a lot of cards, when you land on them they will give you a side quest that you can complete. If you do complete it then it will unlock another card that keeps driving this side story into multiple play throughs. This really helps in making the game not stagnate the more you play it, because it is constantly adding new cards for you to interact with and furthering the stories at the same time.
On the subject of RNG, this game is not always fair because a lot of it comes down to RNG. Most of the time you can handle what the game throws at you, but sometimes you will have a game where literally nothing goes your way. If you do not enjoy games that have RNG elements like this, then you will probably not enjoy this game. However, I feel like for the most part the RNG is not that bad.
The main problem that this game has is the combat. The combat is fairly simplistic, where you mainly just dodge and counter enemy attacks, similar to the Batman Arkham games, but less polished. Something about the combat just isn’t very satisfying. The enemies usually take a good bit of hits before they go down and when they do go down they don’t really have any kind of death animation, they just go full ragdoll which isn’t very gratify.
But, this game is still very enjoyable to play and I recommend checking it out.

You choose your equipment and some of the encounter cards to build each match, and then the story setup you've selected adds cards. It's clever and works well.
Most cards are choices rather than combat, with semi-random success, others are static choices that you can learn and rely on in future games. This creates a great mix of surprise and predictability.
Combat is fairly basic but engaging - not the highlight of the game, but it doesn't hurt it either.

This game is super AWESOME and fun!
And it gets increasingly better value for money as time goes on!
How is that even possible? you may ask: well this already fleshed out fully immersive game, keeps having more content added into it every month or so:
I stopped playing for a couple months, come back and start playing, die in a dungeon yet again and am rewarded by unlocking 2 new DLC that got added without my knowing, Fantastic!
The narrator/dealer of the game makes it such an awesomly immersive experiance, each step has a chance to get further dialogue.
GAMEPLAY:
Before statring a run;
You have 2 decks of cards you can change up with your unlocked cards: 1st your equipment, 2nd your exploration/encounters. The dealer adds further encounter cards based on the level, of which there are 12.
3rd deck option if you paid for it (which is a must, so worth, so good): is picking a class/difficulty for you character, that can affect combat and exploration, including unlocking more encounter cards.
Each run attempt you can select different things for those 3 options, and each attempt will unlock more cards for your main 2 mentioned decks.
3 resorces that needs various degrees of management and affect you are; HEALTH, FOOD, GOLD.
Exploration:
the cards are aranged face down in a path, you move 1 card at a time, flippping it over and selecting options to get through it. could be a fight, merchant, chance, or choice based options.
The results can be anything from many of these cards, most of them have a chance to unlock further cards for future attempts, if you select correctly/choose well. Through these is the main way of drawing from your equipment deck and affecting your 3 resorces.
The whole time the dealer has awesome dialogue based on the cards and your options as well as banter, this makes the atmospher of the game awesome.
Combat:
Is fairly simple but fun and can be heavily affected by equpitment, blessings and curses you have got hold of during that run. You have attack, combo damage, block,counter, stun, dodge roll, weapon ability, artifact ability.
This from an overall perspective is a very unique and fun game, plenty of loot and replayablity, and you gain more options even on failing a run, so your time never feels completely wasted.
VERDICT:
There's nothing about the game I dislike or feel is badly done, so a full recommendation from me :)

Given my huge income of 100+ gold from all my vassals, I decided to upgrade Constantinople and many of my holdings. Hours later, I mended the Great Schism by conquering Holy Lands and declaring them mine. Most of Europe became Orthodox and I removed the Pope from his seat, leaving no Christian rulers. I was then known as "The Saint", and gave birth to a long line of Byzantine Emperors who ruled with iron fists, seeking to return the Legacy of Rome.
After years of crusading and aggressive expansion into Italy and the Middle East, I reclaimed the old Roman Borders. The Roman Empire was once more established, but Rome was not done. All the land from Constantinople to Egypt, Egypt to Spain, Spain to France, Germany, parts of Russia, and all of Scandinavia were to be conquered. I gained the S.P.Q.R achievement for restoring all that belonged to Rome and more. Much of the Middle East was conquered and pushed back. With an income of 500+ gold a month and trading posts spanning around the entire Empire, I was set.
Until it all changed, the Golden Horde formed and attacked me after I just finished off the 10th civil war to lower crown authority. The Khan stole a great chunk of land, and I was seriously low on man power. The Golden Horde continued to push foward, while my army was busy fighting off civil wars and religious rises. I finally managed to win my civil wars, and was left with a few years time to rebuild my army. 600K+ troops later with a personal levy of 80K retinues, I took back what was mine and destroyed the Golden Horde.
With less than 30 years left until end game, I was looking forward to saying I conquered most of the world without cheating. Yeah, not so much. My cousin forms the Kingdom of France and fights for independance, and somehow most of my Empire flocks towards him to rebel against me. My army is cut in half, and I am busy trying to fend off France while also being attacked by mysterious figures that start assassinating my bloodline.
I eventually murder all of my cousins children, excommunicate him, and then murder him. I am victorious, the Great Emperor Buoso II. Little did I know, I had a falling out with the rest of my bloodline for killing a family member. My title is usurped, and I am forced to watch as my Uncle begins to lose Kingdoms worth of land to vassals rebelling against their liege. I assassinate him and try to marry my child into power, but before I can do that his son is also killed by that mysterious assassin. This leaves no rightful hier to the Empire of Rome, and it splits apart again.
Every duchy, county, kingdom, and what have you in the entire world splits up into over 500+ independant states. Everyone starts fighting for power, and I sit there having just lost a game I spent over 50+ hours on. My jaw drops. My computer couldn't handle the entire world fighting and I eventually just gave up on that game. Crusader Kings II can change in the blink of an eye.

Ok, so clearly there is a rabid fan base for this game and the ratings are generally positive - thus I bought the game. The graphics are solid and the overall UI looks appealing... but after playing for two afternoons I'm a bit stunned there isn't more of a balance in the reviews. For the positives, read the others. This review is going to point out just a few of the negatives of this game that will save you a few bucks.  I'll start by saying I love these kinds of games generally. I've played Civ since the first, all the total wars, and hang around with my kids setting up armies once in a while. I love war strategy games and the more complex the better... this is not one of those.
- Deceptive advertising: This game is for historical simulation buffs, not strategy game buffs. The rule set and complexity of the game will only add to the fun for a very, very small number of snobbish gamers that like to argue over ducal claims to Leon. (They also like to write reviews apparently). The action posed knight on the cover art + total war like game map is deceptive. This is a game of endless spreadsheets, stats, and family trees that are eternally obscure.
- The tutorial is poor. Before even pointing out your primary goals, (still not sure what they are), you have to find the impossible wife ("Healthy" was not one of my options, but part of the instructions), and fabricate a claim on a muslim island.  What?!?  Then they just leave you like a bad habit with hundreds of buttons that don't mean much. Good luck sucker.  Somewhere in the distance I can hear some putz designer saying, "Scaling, we don't need to stinking scaling!" So if you finish the tutorial, go ahead, and try to whip up a "normal" game... how's that going for you? Did you really learn to play in their tutorial?
- Choices. Complexity should amount to more meaningful decisions to make. This game boils down to 1) keep vassals happy, 2) fabricate/push claims on territories, and 3) make babies and waaaaaaait for them to grow up. Tech trees? bah. Strategy? bah. Defences? Not needed.  Just play matchmaker and bribe people.  No need to actually give the player something to consider and plan for...
- Game Balance. Wait, why is the person that I just gave a duchy to still mad at me?  Why should I care? Looking carefully I am apparantly a "Tyrant" (-70) because a turn ago I removed a title from someone that just led a rebellion... Tyrant? Really?!? and -70 essentially overrides ten or so positive elements... seriously, just one example of preposterous rule sets that whack the game out regularly.  Some may thing this is interesting, realistic, detailled, or something, but the emperor simply has no clothes on people! This game is lame, boring, and frustrating... and far from realistic.
- Fun.  Oh yeah, that counts for a computer game too!
Still, I may just not be as smart as the folks that gave this a good rating, or they may have thought it would be funny to give you bad advice and see how many might still buy this.  You may enjoy games that have you looking at charts and meaningless attributes all day so that you can watch the computer tick off random events. To each their own. This game is not for me.
