What can I say, this game would be awesome if:
1. It was balanced.  Right now even the easiest setting is a blood bath!  You are always out numbered at the start and it seems every encounter has atleast one or more npcs which either summon adds, or the game just cheats and throws more adds in as the battle progresses.
2. NPCs played by the same rules as the characters.  an NPC the same level as your character will always have more HP, will always have more Regular Armor and more Magic Armor (these are two seperate things in this game) will always have more skills and more resists and this is at the easiest setting.  Also NPCs can cheat and shoot arrows and cast spells through things that block your attacks. Like wise human like NPCs seem to have infinite special ammo (like fire arrows and poison bombs) and Monstrous NPCs constantly spam their AOE/status altering attacks.
3. Every battle ground is staged against you.  The enemy always has the high ground for ranged attacks, requiring you to navigate 2 or 3 turns to get on even footing and away from the preplaced barrels of fun that get exploded for your enjoyment er uhm death.  All the while your enemies, enjoying all this carefully placed stuff are wearing you down and spamming the entire battle field with fire / ice / poison etc..
4. Even if you are the kind of person who enjoys reloading and trying the same battle over 10 times or more to figure out how to beat any particular fight, you will still be upset when the game crashes while your doing one of those reloads, or the save you have been reloading over and over again gets corrupted and cant be loaded, Or you finally win the fight only to discover that one of those negative status effects that got applied during the battle, never comes off afterwards, oh and the quest that was supposed to be updated / completed doesnt get updated or completed either.
All that said, there is a real diamond in the rough here.  Graphics are amazing, Music / sound is nice (i havnt been tempted to turn it off yet,) and what little i have been able to see of the quests / roleplaying part of the game has left me wanting more and more (which makes me ever more frustrated with all the above that keeps me from persuing the actual game.) I'm gona take a few days to cool off, then let a few weeks pass by and see if they have had a chance to work on their bugs and balancing issues.  IF your considering buying, I'd wait too.

Some first impressions playing in tactician mode.
Safe to say, this is a best of class game.  Addictive and very rewarding.  Challenging and sometimes frustrating, but the game (so far) offers a solution to every problem if you persevere.
Stunning graphics and music.  Lot's of voice acting, some of it excellent (eg. Fane) though the Narrator can be a bit of a ham - which is a pity given it is such a large part and has such a big impact early on.
The environments are amazing.  Beautifully rendered and inventively designed.  Baccus's Labyrinth and Vault are an enormous pleasure to explore and overcome.
The story becomes immersive over time, though I would say the writing is not as strong as other elements and lacks the emotional punch and humour of, say, EOS Online.
A few irritating bugs.  For example, the screen will sometimes stop following your movement if you switch to another character.  The only way to fix this is to talk to an NPC or save and reload.
Combat takes a while to get used to.  There are a couple of key innovations which I initially found very frustrating.  1.  The aoe effects are unpredictable, prevalent and fairly deadly until you get a bit of magic armour.  Over time you get better at understanding what will make an aoe effect spread (or diminish).  However, there remain times when a normal melee attack or ranged attack cause aoe effects to spread to nearby melee characters randomly.  2.  Armour is split into magic armour and physical armour.  Most damage AND crowd control is resisted by one or other type.  This means that if the other side has an armour advantage (as they do in tactician mode), their crowd control is available from the get go and yours is postponed until you have already won the fight.  It also means that emphasising one or other damage type can be a winning strategy if you want to cheese it.
That said, the encounters the game gives you force a constant rethink and require a willingness to adapt.  Fighting the undead particularly the Incandescent mobs is very challenging if you have narrowed your options.  Overall combat is deep and satisfying.  So far there has been no sign that this will be a game where you fall into using the same series of spells every fight.
There are a few things I wish could be fixed.  1.  When you place a spell or other action, the characters affected are highlighted, but sometimes your nearby characters get hit nevertheless.  2.  Melee can sometimes hit you even if you are up on a platform - which seems wrong.  3.
Tooltips could do with some work.  The tooltip for Blind, for example, does not say it is resisted by magic armour.  The tooltip for some spells mention that they hit only enemies.  The tooltips for other spells that hit only enemies are silent.  Maybe past players of the franchise understand these things, but not good to waste gold or upgrade points on something that turns out not to work the way you thought.  4.  Sometimes the game will prevent you from firing a ranged attack because there is no line of sight.  In other cases though it will allow it and the attack fails.  In these cases, there is a small yellow note on screen that the path is obstructed, but it is easy to miss once or twice in a long fight.  Why not just disallow the attack?

Video showing off the game:
Holy Potatoes! What the Hell?! is a cooking sim where you cook potato sinners in hell and use them as ingredients for dishes you serve to gods. It's pretty dark, but it has that Holy Potatoes! charm.
The gameplay is quite simple: sinners have sins that have stats, you choose which means of torture for the sinner based on those stats. The better your equipment for the chosen stat, the better the ingredient that sinner becomes. Those ingredients are used to make dishes, which get you God favor from the Gods you serve. That favor is then used to buy better equipment to get the better ingredients. Rinse and repeat as time goes on.
The gameplay is simple, but the characters and the sins are hilarious. A lot of the fun for me was just reading what the sinners did while I was choosing their horrible ultimate fate.
There's a certain charm about the Holy Potatoes! games that just tickles me. What the Hell?! continues that charm very well.

My 2 friends and I bought the game to play cooperatively, here's what we found out.
Co-op mode is 2 players only.
Survival mode is also 2 players only.
That leaves multiplayer mode, which unfortunately is 4 max players, so that leaves room for 1 A.I. opponent. Which would be fine if the Hard A.I. was any good, but it's not competent at all.
Connectivity is very junky, my friends could see my game, I couldn't see their's. Also Join Game via Steam is not possible.
Our first game was a Total Annihilation victory conditon, which we coudln't complete despite destroying the enemy's main base, because some buildings couldn't fall below 1 HP.
We couldn't deploy trebuchets because none of us had the required tech (which you unlock at the main menu) to build them, maybe thats why those buildings wouldn't fall, still very silly mechanic.
We experienced heavy lag issues during gameplay at random times, the framerate would get choppy for a dozen of seconds and then it would go away. I suppose it's better than desyncing, but still..
The biggest flaw in this game IMO is the terrible unintuitive UI. From a serious lack of shortcuts, to missing common features that you expect to find in any modern RTS (like when you want to add a unit to a group by selecting the unit and then shift+1 to add it to group 1, that doesn't work here), to frustrating moments when you can't find where your units are because:
a) Center on unit doesn't prorperly work in some cases, especially on grouped units the camera goes all over the place.
b) No messages at all of what is happening to your units, if they are under attack, out of stamina, low on health, where are they, what militay units are idle, you are oblivious to what is happening around the map if you are not looking around all the time.
c) The minimap is just BAD. Some colors are hard to see, flare is always off from where you clicked, it's just useless.
Also If a unit is engaged in battle, good luck retreating it. Some of them run properly, but the ones that are closer to enemy units, you literally have to fight against their suicide will by spamming the right click mouse button until they (hopefully) get to your base.
Finally, from the 2 multiplayer games we played, we encountered some bugs, one of them was a very obvious one: 3 units from a larger group suddenly were stuck on a hill where there was no path to it (was pretty funny when it happened though).
From my experience this game lacks some serious standard RTS features, needs a UI rework, better A.I. and tactical unit behaviour. It would also benefit from bigger maps with more opponents (4 players is too low c'mon) and a rework of the Survival mode to allow more players to enjoy some zombie horde slaying.
Honestly most of the positive reviews here were misleading to say the least, whereas the few negatives were spot on.

Get ready for the least sweary episode of Hell's Kitchen you are ever likely to see as Daylight Studios return with more potato based puns and cute characters in another Holy Potatoes! game in - Holy Potatoes! What the Hell?!
A lot of the elements from the first two Holy Potato games return - The cute characters; The slightly cheesy pop culture references and writing; And the same kind of core "craft items to sell them" gameplay loop we've seen previously. Though, this time, it's the potato people themselves that are the key ingredients as we mash, dice & slice the souls of spud-like sinners in fiery pits of hell to create delicious starchy meals.
What has changed slightly is the look of the game. Gone are the flat, 2D comic strip visuals only to be replaced with a 3D, almost cel shaded, look that (personally) I'm still not sure if I actually like. It is still very much a Holy Potato game and maintains that overall bright colorful aesthetic but sometimes I find myself a little distracted by the pill shaped character models especially during the cut scenes as we move from one Circle of Hell to the next.
What's more I did find myself hitting that skip button more often than not during these cut scenes as the writing feels a little weaker than its predecessors and jokes aren't as funny. (But I have to admit I did like the Divine Comedy reference with our fellow chefs being called Dantee and Veggil.)
That said the gameplay is pretty fun. Maybe less engaging and diverse than something like We're in Space but certainly on par with Weapon Shop. And I can certainly see myself sinking a few more hours into this as I attempt to escape the underworld for the great restaurant in the sky.
Overall I'd say this isn't a bad little game. A good accompaniment if you've played the previous Potato games or a nice casual introduction to the franchise. But if you are going to pick one out of the three personally I'd choose Holy Potatoes! We're in Space?! over this one.

Metro: Last Light Redux is a really good first person shooter/ survival game. There is a good amount of weapons and customization in the game which gives you multiple ways to approach situations in the game. The enemy AI is really nice and makes combat really interesting as opposed to some shooter games that have really simple AI. The multiple endings is a nice touch to this game and really makes you think about what you are going to do. Personally I don't think this game can be considered horror except for a couple of jumpscares you can encounter in the game. The graphics look really nice and clear. The survival aspect of this game really adds to the tension of the game. I highly recommend you buy this game if you like survival oriented first person shooters.

For an early access game with the absolute basics it's quite good. The world is very well designed and has enough diversity to set it apart from other survival games like Ark. Speaking of Ark, CE has much better optimization now then Ark has had since its release and it looks better then Ark even on lower settings (I played both on a decent laptop both on low settings and ark was still laggy and looked like it was made of playdough, Conan wasn't laggy and looked good).
That being said, while it is a good looking game that runs well for such an early stage it does have a crudely designed player UI that feels restricting unfinished (which it quite possibly could be). One of CE's most unique features is the slavery and religion mechanics. While exploring you will come across both hostile and non hostile human npc's that you can take as slaves to work for you.
The religion mechanic is in my opinion is CE's strongest feature. You choose a god in the character creator and if you perform acts of said gods desire you get rewarded. Currently you can choose to be a cannibal get rewarded for eating people, sacrifice subjects to your god, force your religion on others or be an atheist. A great feature especially for RPers.
Overall CE is a very EA game with the potential to shape into many things without the restrictions many other survival games suffer from.

Intriguing setting

Not completely liniar

Cons:
Still some minor bugs and glitches

I'd like to eleborate on some glitches I have encountered.
1) During the first part at the bridge, I went back to the main menu to increase graphic quality, however, when I loaded the game back up, I could not speak to anybody and I was stuck in front of the bridge.
2) During the night portion, I went back towards the car and encountered the big guardian. I let myself be killed for him to appear in my Ghostpedia. However, when I came back from limbo I was in a void. I could only see the friend character. After a couple of seconds the school started to appear around me, starting the cutscene you would normally get when walking up to the school. Nothing game-breaking, but somewhat strange and looks ugly.
3) While I was fighting the ghost in the narrow hallway in the school the first time around, I shot a couple of pics of her face, trying to hit her in the back. After a while she just stood frozen. This made it very easy for me to hit her in the back, since she posed no threat.
The rest of the game worked like a charm! I really can't wait to see what Chapter 2 might have in store for us. I do hope it will be (a lot) longer than the frst part, since not a lot of the story has been played out yet. Also, it would be great if the demo gaeplay could be added to the full game, since it acts as a prologue, and you can't have both the demo and the actual game in your library at the same time.
Final verdict for Chapter 1: 7/10     Would recommend (especially now during the sale)

You play as Otus a mute owl as he embarks on an owl-hood defining adventure that will involve navigating through treacherous dungeons. Otus himself has no true combat abilities as he can only stun enemies. This is where his companions come into play. As you progress, you will gain new allies that Otus can carry along with him. Each ally has a unique type of ammunition which has it's own attributes. You can only have one active companion at any given time but you can switch between them on the fly.
Take note that, your companions cannot be hurt and any damage you take from enemies / hazards will be reflected on Otus' health bar. You also drop your companion if you get hit. The only way to regain health is by getting 'health pickups' which usually appear as fruit / vegetables? OR by resting. To my knowledge you can only rest at 2 places in the game - your home and a camp fire nearby the town. The game also has no concept of lives. When your health is reduced to zero, you just respawn at the last checkpoint. Yes, this is an auto-saving game. No manual saves here. You can however manually load from the last checkpoint - sometimes useful if you accidentally entered a new area (e.g. boss area).
Right from the get go, you are introduced to the game's collectible Buccanary coins. This is not in-game currency as there is nothing you can buy in the game. However, at preset coin thresholds you can visit a shop to unlock trinkets which are upgrades for yourself - increase your max health or for your companions - longer range, improved shot. These coins are littered around the Owlboy universe usually cleverly hidden in the dungeons but also sometimes hidden in plain sight.
I think the 'hi-bit' art and music needs no introduction. Feel free to take a look at the videos / screenshots that are available. You can also find some bits and pieces of the soundtrack publicly available on the
/ the
pages. I will only add that the sound effects are really good and many sections / mini-cutscenes have their own music, all of which are really good and help to set the tone with the story.
It pains me to say this but Owlboy is not the great game that I hoped for. The weight of expectation after having waited more than 5 years probably has something to do with it. Having said that I agree with what most of the other reviewers have said about the game.
Long story short : Owlboy is another good game that could have been great.
Hands down the best of the trilogy, it'll grab you and keep you interested all the way up until the final mission.

Played since early 2012, with 1000+ hours put into this game, was too lazy to launch on Steam and used the client instead most of the time. Eventhough I enjoyed this game for its unique mechanics, character designs/aesthetics, and community, there has much that has gone wrong in this game (Although I still comeback for major updates for a short while of time to see if they tried to put effort into fixing this game).
Pros:
- The amazing variety of customization that you can do; albeit the girls has more interesting selections than the guys.
- Eventhough it is a P2W game, if you manage doing marketing well, spending time to invest buying low and selling high, striking good deals with other players, lots of grinding, doing surveys for KC, and taking advantage of events that give free stuff, it is possible to play for free with good gear, but takes a lot of time and effort.
- Memorable OSTS, although I put the music volume at 0 because its very distracting when you play pvp and need to listen to the enemy closely.
Cons:
- PvP: I myself am a PvP main on Elsword, so why would I put this here? In my opinion, PvP was fantastic throughout Season 1 and Season 2. You were placed in the right skill level so that matches would always be mentally challenging by constantly having to read your opponents moves, well-paced with most matches taking 2-4 minutes, and a good learning experience to improve by learning from your mistakes. However now, match ranking has been unbalanced, sometimes placing me against low level new players which is unfair, dying quickly due to +11-+13 geared players who usually use the run and attack tactic or spam one combo/skill to win (I will never understand how people find fun in doing that), and unbalanced skills which make some characters op and others with a disadvantage proves to be frustrating indeed. The lag is also very unbearable, which I blame from the merging of Latin American server with the North American server, as well as when Elsword was introduced to Steam (Eventhough ironically, I was hyped that Elsword was going to be on Steam when it was announced). Most of the time nowadays, I spend playing in sparring, rather than arena because of the less toxicity and more chilled atmosphere.
- Community: Depends on how you play the game. For me, I enjoyed the community of Elsword because I was able to find a guild that was outgoing and made friends who I still occasionally talk to today and recieve compliments in sparring matches (NOT Arena) because of my playstyle. However the community is not always pretty, especially when you get into PvP Arena. In the more recent years, I have yet to experience a day in PvP without being called a noob, cheater/hacker, and verbally harrassed, (Though I never cared about it because I learned to ignore these types of things) which is pretty disappointing. Although I never experienced being scammed before, there have always been a lot of scammers on Elsword because the game is highly dependant on trading with other players.
- P2P: I've spent a well 100-200$ on this game, mostly on cosmetics, but never in enhancing items. Nowadays soloing newer dungeons or to do well in PvP, you need at least +10-+13 in order to survive. It sucks when you put much time and effort in this game, but is limited because you don't have strong enough gear unless you pay. I grinded my way through events and dungeons to get +9 on all of my gear, but it is still barely good enough for the higher end PvE and PvP. Getting +10 or higher through free enhancement events/giveaways requires extremely good luck, or else say goodbye to your wallet.
TL;DR
If you don't want to pay money on this game, good luck spending hours upon hours grinding and waiting for events.
If you do pay money on this game, good luck spending over 100$ trying to get +10-+12 and even more for +13.

During my review of Chainsaw Warrior (also on Steam), I commented about how the computer game port of Chainsaw Warrior was easier to play than the actual card game published by Games Workshop, because it was easier to play a one-player card game with rules as convoluted and dorky as a computer game than as an actual, physical card game. What would happen if someone walked in on you rolling dice and drawing cards all by yourself?
"Oh, are you playing Solitaire?"
"No! I'm not playing Solitaire. I'm playing a game where you have to fight zombies and aliens and disarm a nuclear bomb in 60 minutes or the world will be plunged into eternal darkness."
"...it is okay to masturbate, Jimmy. You don't have to be ashamed of your body."
"But I'm not doing the M-word, Daaaaaaaaad!"
Hand of Fate is like one of those dorky card games. I think the developers realized this when they started development, and so they threw in the card dealer and added all the stuff about life and death afterwards. It definitely needed it - because the Dealer is what really makes this game work. Without the Dealer, the game is you, sitting at a table, drawing cards and hallucinating these battles and these traps and sometimes wrestling with a convoluted camera angle operated by a narcoleptic operator. Plus there wouldn't be all these interesting story crumbs as to who the Dealer is, why you're here playing this game, the big dust-up that will eventually happen between you and him if he draws one more ♥♥♥♥ing Devilish Traps card.
It's not a bad game, but I just feel like it depended on a lot of the momentum from my earlier victories to keep me going, because I got tired of it after I got stuck fighting the King of Scales. Speaking of the King of Scales: This game has a difficulty curve that partially resembles a flat area and then a sudden, large ramp-up in difficulty on the last two stages. The difficulty curve ramps up on the King of Scales because the game forgets to tell you that his henchmen are all invincible while he's around, something that took me ten tries and five minutes in the Steam Community forums to realize. Also there's some fun balance issues that randomly make the game too easy or hard. And I hate when the game makes me have to run through a Traps level, because not only are you trying not to die to a bunch of traps, you're also playing with a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ camera angle that hides some of those traps.
So while it's not a perfect game, it's rather fun while the unlocks keep coming, but when they stop... oh man, this game starts to fall into a RUT.

The good news is that I really like the art style and visual design of the game (it looks great, with lots of little details hidden in the levels on posters and signs and so on, and the cyberpunk theme is a lot of fun), and it mostly feels good to play, like an old school shooter. It's a "hard" game, which in itself can be a good thing, except it's not really hard because it's challenging but because there are situations where you can quickly end up dying for what almost seems to be no reason your first time through because you don't know where the enemies are going to spawn or where the environmental hazards are until you've already seen them. Once you know where everything is, it's suddenly very easy to avoid them all and lead the enemies into traps instead (because they're quite dumb), but it leads to more trial and error than I'd like. Yeah, it's true to the old school spirit of the game, I guess, but I suppose that's not really what I'm feeling up for right now.
Combined with that, it doesn't help that you can kind of paint yourself into a corner with the weapon upgrades if you don't choose well. Hint: AoE/splash damage is your friend.
Something else I haven't heard other people mention, so it may just be me, is that a couple times I got stuck going in circles for maybe ten minutes, completely unable to tell where I was supposed to go next. I wasn't lost or anything; I just couldn't find any door to go through or button to push or anything because it didn't stand out from the rest of the environment enough, which I haven't really had happen with other games much. I will chalk it up to either my partial color blindness or possibly just me being a dumbass.
Anyway, I really wanted to like it, and there were some things about it that I genuinely did think were rather well done, but I had enough frustrating moments that I think I'm going to go back to playing Tower of Guns for my 90s-style FPS needs for the time being.

KW2B is a (partially asymmetric) RTS. It is NOT your typical Starcraft/ competitive melee RTS clone but rather the "enjoy your units and have some fun" kind.
You build your base, gather 4 types of resources, research upgrades and recruit your army. On top, you get to fortify your base with several layers of upgradeable walls so attacking an enemy always ends in a siege battle. There are 3 different races with ample differences in gameplay and base building and each of them gets their own castle.
And at this point you're probably asking yourself: "Wait, I can't build my own castle or what?". The answer is YES. The castle layout is fixed and so is the general landscape beneath your base. You can place your RTS typical structures wherever you want but wall segments, gates and towers are all built on a fixed "addon" location.
However, this doesn't detract from the fun and I'll explain why down below.
As for game modes, it offers a singleplayer campaign which also acts as tutorial, PVP up to 4 players, COOP vs AI (the AI is good enough) and a zombie survival wave mode where you defend your castle (and that of your friends) against ever increasing waves of zombies.
This is a low-budged indie game with all the pros and cons:
The game has anything from crashes and disfunctional addons over a laggy interface which also is not always properly updated to minor bugs which can be summed up as 'lack of polishing'.
This has to be pointed out as well. You can find developers in the ingame chat every day and they do their best to respond and act on every bug report you commit. They also mediate in balance discussions and admit if something has been overnerfed or whatever. In general it's a very pleasent experience with these devs and they put out patches on a regular basis.
Moderators are online almost around the clock and the entire community is small but very helpful.
Well maybe special is the wrong word. KW2B employs a large variety of iconic game mechanics from other RTS (many of which are lost today) and mixes them. The result is compelling to me because a) I get to enjoy all those mechanics again and b) it is simply fun to play.
I'll try to give you an idea (RTS veterans will understand):
There is food, gold, wood and stone. You start with high gathering rate but limited resource patches to kickstart your base and then transition into slower but renewable resource generation for late game. How and what exactly depends on your race. Generally speaking, elves have the most stable renewable resource generators, humans the most efficient and orcs spawn free units instead.
For every player you kill, for every game you win and for every day you log in you get a loot reward. There is a good dozen of items with varying rarity to be gathered and you use those to permanently unlock new structures, units and upgrades for your race to be used in any future match.
Once you've unlocked them all, you can spend those resources on "cards" which are one time boosters you can bring into the next match. For example, you can spawn a blob of additional, free workers or add a ton of food to your bank.
Like in many strategy games you have units which are specialized in killing a specific unit type. However, it's not dead set in this balance. You can still damage cavalry with archers and swordmen for example, but you trade units with less efficiency. Your fortress, good micro or a better economy can easily offset this, though.
As you upgrade your barracks it will train units of higher level. Killing enemy units will grant them additional exp. Unlike the usual veterance system though, it's up to the player to decide which stats are improved on a level up. A leveled unit basically gains stat points like in an RPG that you can apply to one of it's 3 defenses, damage, movement speed, health, stamina (which is also used as mana), etc.
Every race has a bunch of heroes and wizards like in Battle for Middle earth 2. You can train and level them like regular units but they have a higher max level and a whole lot of active abilities. There are also war beasts and mercenary units!
Considering you have everything at home you need (more or less) there is little reason to leave the save embrace of your fort right? Wrong! The maps are littered with capturable pieces like bandit forts, lumber mills, quarries (which provide you additional renewable income) and ruins of old castles which walls and towers you can man like they're your own. These ruins offer choke points, ambush routes and everything the heart of a tactician requires. And then there is a dragon on every map, guarding a treasure (additional meta loot) which the players compete for.
So let me get back to what I said in the beginning. You can man your walls with archers and other units and mount ballistas, trebuchets, oil and a bunch of other machines onto towers and gates like in Stronghold. Unlike stronghold the final layout of your walls, towers and gates is fixed rather than pieced together by the player. Tbh, the layout of the landscape and your base greatly differs depending on which race you play. The concept here is comparable to Empire at War or Battle for Middle Earth 1.
Also unlike Stronghold the devs had the opportunity to carfully craft and balance your foritifcations so the result is more complex and fun than anything you can build with the limited tools in that so called castle simulator (SH). You get access to walls of different heights, you have up to 3 layers of fully seperated, fully mannable (if upgraded) walls. Your keep is always located on a hill which gives you further height and line of sight advantage (both matter for archers) and there is always a backdoor.
Additionally, you're not forced to fully upgrade your defenses every game. Sometimes you want to leave the out wall a mere fence to slow down the enemy an keep your forces together at the base's core. Sometimes you want the out wall asap to better control the area around your base. Thus your castle doesn't necessarily look the same every game.
As an additional source of income you can task your workers to loot the corpses on the battlefield. Yes, the insane gore in this game is part of the gameplay! Even better, not looting them before nightfall means they will rise as zombies which pose a serious threat. The zombies don't fight for any player per se but a good player will know how to use them to their advantage...
This game may fall flat on you if you have too high expectations. It's not super polished and the graphics aren't really up to date. That said, the music, art design and concept are just beatiful and super enjoyable. KW2B can stand on it's own and fill a niche that other RTS have left wide open for the past years.
If that is what you are looking for the stop reading and buy the game already!

1. Introduction
2. Technical review
3. Game review
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.Introduction:
You SHOULDN'T buy the game if you do not understand the concept of "Early Access" or you simply do not wish to engage in a product still in development - which is totally cool and legitimate but it is unfair towards the Devs if people put their frustration into negative reviews here, effectively ignoring the "Early Access" component.
Some people also said that this game is overpriced and/or "Early Access" would just be a cover-up to hide all the bugs etc.
Those people are WRONG!
Conan Exiles gets a posive recommendation and I am going to explain why!
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Technical review
Critized main issue: Server lagging/rubberbanding!
While it is true that - including for me - the game was simply unplayable in the first days of "Early Access" I keep being patient.
Why?
Funcom did not anticipate such a strong interest in the game which overwhelmed the servers of their partner "Pingperfect".
Guys, please be serious, we all know that with many new games server issues are to be expected and the devs are engaged quite closely with the community to resolve this.
They already took action by cutting ties with their former partner "Pingperfect" and are looking for a new appropriate server partner.
Keep in mind that since release we have seen around every 12 hours an update and the devs are constantly working to iron out technical problems.
That is what "Early Access" is all about, developing a game together with the community!
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Game review
3.1 Character creation
3.2 Game concept
3.2.1 Combat
3.3.1 Thrall System
3.3.2 Religion
4. Graphics
5. AI
6. Conclusion
3.1 Character creation:
You choose your sex, race, religion and customize your facial and body features with the help of sliders.
Due to the full nudity, you can enjoy resizing your characters dong to reflect what you wished for in reality or go all humble. Same counts for female breasts - Funcom tradition when thinking about Age of Conan.
However if you are prude there are options to disable or partially disable nudity.
I would never understand personally why someone might be offended from a naked human body but is totally fine with gore but ok, nevermind!
Facial hair for males are greyed out still, something that is going to change very fast surely.
The racial background is purely cosmetic and a roleplay aspect while religion has a deeper sense. More about this later.
Generally it feels very intuitive to create your character, not to overwhelming and not too simple and thankfully you can not create weird mutant like character like in ARK. You are Human and you are going to look like one - great!
3.2 Game Concept:
Like many people already said before me, Conan Exiles does remind me the most of ARK. It uses the same engine (UE4) and the game concept is similar however in my opinion it feels like an updated version.
The menus are more intuitive and they also improved the building system because unlike ARK you can use the terrain, adapt the height of your foundations and build into mountainsides.
Sometimes certain parts do not want to snap in the right place but generally I prefer the Conan Exiles system over ARK, I had far less issues here.
So while generally being another survival game where you have to manage hunger, thirst, stamina, encumbrance and your health it brings new fresh elements into the genre (Soon more about it.)
I noticed a tiny nice feature regarding encumbrance. In other survival games you can freely move until you are encumbered - same goes for Conan Exiles - however the more you carry here, the less faster your Stamina regenerates which will decrease your intervals in which you are able to run!
Another survival aspect is "corruption"
The more time you spend with dark beings and dark places, you gain corruption which will overlap your health bar, effectively reducing your maximum available amount of health.
How to remove it? For this you need dancers! Yes, some nice men and women entertaining you! Read more about it later in the thrall section!
A neat little features!
3.2.1 Combat:
The combat system generally reminds me mostly of TES: Skyrim. Wield the weapons you want and attack your foes etc.
Nice but honestly I wish they will introduce a more in-depth system, currently you can try to dodge enemy attacks but it doesn't work intuitively yet and the possibility to cripple certain body parts is also missing.
You cannot hit someones arms so he cannot wield his weapon or cripple his legs so he cannot chase you e.g.
Shooting arrows at foes also doesn't bother them. They just keep running like they are made out of steel.
I hope they gonna change this however gore is a feature on s.o. death!
3.3.1 Thralls:
A unique aspect of Conan Exiles is the feature that allows players to capture Human NPC's in order to break their will and make them work for you!
Some might think that it is similar to a pet system like ARK in which you tame dinosaurs but I think it is different and it also feels diferent in the game.
The possibility to tame and ride animals is not yet implemented in Conan Exiles but will come in the future, better reflecting the equivalency of taming dinosaurs in ARK probably.
The thrall system currently enables you to capture someone, bring him back to your camp and let him spin around in the hamster wheel - sorry -in the Wheel of Pain.
It takes quite some time but after the procedure is done you can make use of your new thrall.
However, they have certain qualities.
There are archers, fighters, blacksmiths, chefs, dancers and probably more.
There are NPC's with certain abilities out there which you have to find in order to fill in your desired role.
To remove corruption you will need dancers e.g.
3.2.2 Religion:
A new and fresh aspect to the genre!
You choose the deity of your desire during character creation (currently there are four but they plan on bringing in more) and then you are able to build the first tier level of your deity's altar/shrine/etc.
Keep in mind that every deity is unique regarding items you can get but the mechanics are the same, you have to gain their favor!
There are two higher tiers of altars available (three in total, counting the starting one) with more unique religious items which you can unlock once you've reached higher levels!
When you gained the highest amount of favor, your deity will reward you be allowing you to summon his avatar which you can control then for a brief time (1 minute on default I think?) to crush everything in your path!
I am curious to see how much further they will develop the religious aspect!
4. Graphics:
I tried all the different graphics options, all the way from "low" to "ultra" and I can tell you that this game looks gorgeous, the graphics are very well done and manage to transfer an atmospheric feeling. Those sandstorms are gorgeous!
Something I could not test for myself yet required a low end laptop. In the graphics settings is a checkbox wich adapts the graphics specifically for low end laptops, enabling people with less sophisticated hardware to play the game.
The greatest atmospheric "turnoff" currently is the missing AI intelligence as well as NPC animations.
5. AI:
This is one of the priorities of the devs to change (Early Access) however currently, NPC's simply stand around, doing nothing and they feel rather robotic in their behavior and only get active when they spot to attack you.
6. Conclusion:
Fresh, new ideas for the survival genre! My main issues about rubberbanding or lack of AI intelligence and animations is subject to change, so I recommend the game!

This is quite a surprising game. Like if you took a solid fps from 90s, upgraded visuals/sounds to "modern" standards and threw it on the market full of easy faceroll shooters (often filled non-fps features of dubious quality). A bold move.
So, what does the game do well ? It doesn't try to be something else. It's a railroad fps in the best traditions of games like unreal, quake, hexen, halflife and so on - it's a superb journey to genre sort-of forgotten. /But/ - you have to like this kind of games. Not everying is perfect either (see a few highlights below) of course, but then again - what is ?
A few details (all from "insane" difficulty PoV where applicable):
* difficulty
I'm happy to report the game is quite challenging. This is a great refresher after many AAA titles that generally fail miserably in this department. The game will put both your hands and your head to test - and that's great.
* controls
Compared to past fpses, the authors decided to ignore crouching (not a big deal tbh, though it feels strange initially) and the jump is of very limited use (think of it as something a bit more realistic, no practical use during fights).
* saves
No manual saves, though the checkpoint system is mostly well made as far as pacing goes. Probably of little/no issue on easier levels, but on the hardest level you might rarely fell into some short loops skewing a bit towards Dark Souls experience ;)
* story
Well, there's some stuff between chapters (in form of "moving" comic) and to lesser extent during the gameplay. No complaints, but nothing special or extensive. Then again - the game is not about the story ;)
* visuals, sound

Conan Exiles is without a doubt the most promising early access survival game to come out sense ark, Once you get through the bugs you find an extreamly lore friendly and deep story / pve element than all the other survival games on the market.
I highly reccomend playing this game on your own server with friends doing pve for now while they fix issues, this is what were doing and the game runs extreamly well, i'm getting about 90fps constant, everythign works but with just some wonky snapping when you build,
The gameplay is pretty much what you expect but with really useful server editing that you can do to make certain parts of the game much better like xp gain. Standard xp gain is way too little, and 1.5-2 is where you should have it set at if you want to just play this game for a few hours a day, 1 x xp is really for the people who want to play this game all day every day,
The next big pro right now is that the devs are releasing about two patches a day since launch to clear out the bug issues,   and looks like theyre going to be adding quite a bit more to the game content wise in the coming months,
Theres dungeons that you can do and lots of secrets to discover, not only that but the base building is already one of the most interesting ones out there with the thrall and relegion mechanics that are in the game and are being expanded on in future patches.
Content wise think of ark when it was first released and they're about equivelent but with more pve content for conan.
OVERALL i would put Conan Exiles at 8 ENDOWMENT SLIDERS OUT OF 10

After playing this game for a total of twelve hours from large amount of exploration through ghost-hunting, achievement-hunting, decal-hunting, and document-hunting, I realize that there is much more to be said about this game. Hence, I have decided to delete my previous review of the game and rewrite the whole thing.
I first got wind of the game by chance whilst looking through pages worth of games in greenlight district (pun intended), with the some games looking absolutely dreadful... until I saw DreadOut. Upon looking through the page, my first reaction was, "Yes, please!" to which, I subsequently found out about their IndieGoGo campaign, and threw my hard-earned cash at them.
It has been a very long time since anyone used the classic horror formula of the highly praised
franchise. All we have been getting in the recent years are just a bunch of sad excuses for a horror game like
, throwing bags of train tickets at people to Jump Scare Central. Look, I know that
is highly praised by many that probably get a raging hard on whenever they hear the game's name, but the game does not create any sense of agency for me, to which, I will talk about it in the future.
by no means is a perfect game; the game is severely flawed in many different aspects because of its low budget, and one of the first actual PC games being released in Indonesia (as I was told by the developers that companies tend to lean more towards creating applications for mobile phones instead), and because of these two factors, I have cut this game more slacks than the chefs cut New York Strips in an American steak house.
To begin with, the English voice acting is believable, albeit somewhat cheesey. I genuinely felt entertained even after listening to them for the eleventh time. Despite the short and scarce dialogues, I could hear the different personality and manner of speaking in all of the character, though I just hope that I could spend a little more time to get to know them better, as spending so little time with them made them feel more like a bunch of talking paper dolls rather than your friends.
Though admittedly, the characters are pretty nicely designed.
Speaking of looks, though, I have never been much for graphics. Sure, if a game looks photorealistic, it is definitely a plus, but I have never made it an absolute requirement, much unlike many of the graphic hounds that demand everything look like, if not better than,
, regardless of the game's budget and country of origin. The graphics overall are fine, with some noticeable resolution differences between the environment and the characters, though I suppose it is understandable, as most people are too busy staring at Linda's butt, rather than looking closely to the environment's decals.
One thing I absolutely loved about the environment are the decals. I explored the whole game, from edge to edge, just to find all the little references and names on posters, books, and pictures, scattered all over the game. This is also the one thing I keep on hearing people compliment the game about. It was not the whole "super elite ultimate graphics of doom" that mattered, but rather the little bits and pieces the game the developers have carefully placed inside. Unless it is a pile of trash on the ground, those decorations rarely repeat itself, making it that much more interesting to stare at walls for several hours. Think about it, they actually made staring at walls and floors interesting!
On one occasion, I even found my own name as the title of a book, which left a great big smile on my cheeks.
The best part the game has to offer, in my personal opinion, has to be the diversity and lores of enemies, the music, and the atmosphere (to which the music greatly contributes to). I have always thought what it would be like to have eastern superstition and mythology transcribed into a game, and
answered my questions in the first ten minutes I stepped into the school. All of the western horror games consists of zombies, ghouls, and ghosts, and over time, they can become very dull, like the declining fear factors zombies have to people now. Rather than sending me running upstairs and diving into my bed sheets like what
can still do to me, zombies are now more of a plaything for violent acts. The inclusion of oriental beliefs made the once dull experience brand new again, like smelling a fresh burp after chugging down twenty mints. You also rarely deal with the same enemies again in the game. If I were to include the demonstration into the mix, the maximum instance of a ghost appearing in summation is four, two of which, showed different behaviours and wielded different weapons.
Now, I have just about exhausted the good side, now we must take a look at the bad part. The definite downside for me has to be the Scissor Phantom boss fight, and how illogical and ambiguous puzzles can be.
We all know about the dreaded boss fight that made so many of us slam something accross our room (preferrably not the keyboard/controller) after bashing our head against it for a few times. If I were to describe what the boss fight was like, I would say it looks like the result of Nicolas Cage snorting a pound of coke in
and then proceeds to smack everyone's head as he runs around shouting, "Not the bees!" The boss fight is (or at least was) a complete deathwish, and could take some five retries before you get the gist of it, and another five to luck out on the Scissor Phantom not spawning right on top of you. This also made the YOLO achievement as difficult to get as a solid brick of gold.
I never really got what the meaning and purpose of the puzzle was until the result is about to be shown, namely the picture of a small key after finding the group of hanging shadows that decided they wanted a group selfie, and the hanging scissors in the secret room with the scissor phantom, who turns out to be the closet cross-dressing principal of the school. You have to come out of the closet sooner or later, Mr. Principal.
Finally, there are a few points I would like to make for the new update before closing in the review.
The Indonesian voice, despite the fact that I do not understand the language a single bit, sounded pretty good to my foreign ears. However, there are three things I have noticed. First, the movie clip in the very start with the
title showing up, you can hear Shelly speaking in English in the background. Secondly, I do not know whether there is an equivalent for the line, "We clicked right away, didn't we?" in Indonesian, but the part felt very odd due to the obvious seperation between Ira's movements and her dialogue. Lastly, both Shelly and Ira speak like they have their mouth only a few millimetres away from your ear. I am unsure how the voice actresses' voice was recorded, but the way they sounded just felt off. Miss Siska, Doni, and Yayan on the other hand, sounded quite fine.
Lastly, this point may be addressed already, but I can see the foliage floating about in the fog as I walked towards the town.
I had a great time playing
despite some of the frustration it has brought me, but unlike the frustration
brought me, I kept on coming back for more, and made me want to explore and find everything I could. This is one of those rough gems that has the potential of brining the horror genre back on its feet to where it once was, and perhaps explore further into territory unknownst to us. If you prefer defacating your pants through jump scares and chase scenes, this will not be a game for you, but if you like to soil your pants your way through atmosphere, buy it.
TL;DR:
If you like to douse yourself in adrenaline through jump scares and gore, do not play this; if you do not care as much, buy it.

This game's controls are a little odd but they can be adjusted. The graphics are subpar and the character selection is massive and unique. When it comes to what you can do with them or how different they are from each other, it's another story. There's no special abilities or features that would convince you to play as someone else; this makes for close competition with no one person having an advantage, which can be viewed as good or bad.
SpeedRunners does offer lots of gameplayer, as it boasts both an un-interesting but none the less existent singleplayer and a plentiful intense online. Simply put, SpeedRunners is an interesting spin to the racing/parkour scene with little variety, unique graphics, extreme competition, and character differences (mechanics wise) so non-existent that they're sure to make you quickly unenthuastic about their large roster.
As you can tell, I have mixed reviews about SpeedRunners. If you have some money lying around and you're looking for a competitive game to play with friends, get it. But if you're looking for singleplayer content, or unique artwork, or character variety, don't get this.

Okay. Maybe I was drunk on eggnog last christmas or something, I was way too kind to this game.
Don't buy, not even on sale, not for now. I'll set your expectations:
Pros:
Good music and responses
Concept is interesting, at least, as you are encouraged to loot corpses lest they become zombies
Orcs, elves, humans play differently
The fun stops there.
Cons:
Lag and crashes. Read the Community Hub, where great gaming PCs stutter at 3fps for a game that doesn't seem to need bloom, anti-aliasing, or whatnot. Having thousands of units isn't an excuse, as older games handle squads and that many units without lag. That oldergame is BfME2, which is my next point:
Game system feels like a clone of BfME2 that lost its polish. Levelling up structures, the cavalry infantry archer triangle, unit experience, heroes, all feel familiar but poorly executed.
Tech and cards. By face value, cards are basically "choose your God Power" a la AoM. Because of the rarity of certain resources, you can get hit by someone with a free Hydra in multiplayer because he has that card, you don't have a counter.
Tech runs into the same problem that AoE3 had: AoE3 was a great game, but having to play a hundred games while not yet unlocking all the good/necesary cards to WIN just to level up a Home city isn't fun, doing it for all other civs is a chore.
For this game, it's a bit simpler, but it's still a chore to have to run at least 10 Skirmish games to unlock MOST of what a race can have.
Now, some hope. Devs do respond, mostly. They update the game frequently, about once a month. They have a nice concept, and players appreciate it. It's not worth your dollars right now, and not even when it is on sale. When it does, I'll be among the first to sing its praises.

Dreadout is a great freshman effort at crafting a new Indie 3rd person survival horror game. It is not a perfect or even a long game, even with the promised 2nd Act still in production, but what is there is pretty damn unsettling and creepy. You just wish there was more of it.
Going in its favor is the great atmosphere of a small Indonesian village (which you only get to explore a tiny portion of) and a school. The Indonesian language shows up all over the school, lending it just enough familiarity and exotic flair for those of us who grew up on horror games set in the States. Adding to this are the ghosts you encounter, of which there are a small number. It isn't like Fatal Frame where you keep encountering 'filler' ghosts that respawn when you get stuck and are circling throughout a level.
Much has been said of the frustrating bosses in this game, but whether they've tweaked them or nerfed them or I just got lucky, neither of them gave me too much trouble, although the last boss's strategy did get annoying, even with the hints you get upon dying from her to tell you what to do.
Just how does a phone camera have the power to stop the undead? I dunno, but I'm glad it works for the most part. Sometimes you wish it took pictures faster so you could nail a ghost's weakspot, especially the one you do find in the school that wanders around on the second floor.
The graphics range between impressive and late era PS2, which shouldn't be looked at as a flaw. I enjoyed them. The sound design works well and instills more of the creepy atmosphere.
The voice work is miss and hit. It doesn't have any standout lines like "A Jill sandwich", but thankfully it's limited to the beginning when the students are all milling about. It's probably for the best that all the kids disappear; they undermine the horror more than help it.
I hope Digital Happiness continues to make horror games and to refine their experiences. If you want to play this game, play the demo first; the demo is, oddly, a unique experience and works more like a free prologue to the game you buy. The demo's content isn't cut and paste from the main game and works better at instilling horror than the main game does.
If you know what you're doing, the game will last around 2 hours, but there are a number of achievements to track down and collect which can help extend the game's life. It's no Fatal Frame but it earns high marks for trying.

This game. Where to start?
Well I guess first off is to say, honestly this game isn't bad, it's just dead now. In a nutshell Nexuiz is a Unreal Tournament clone, and in and of itself it does the job well enough. At the time this was released, I do believe the gaming industry was in an arena shooter desert where they were far and few between, so we needed this game. However, it never picked up any real momentum due to not having enough marketing, and, well, Cryengine. Cryengine looks pretty, but back then it could alienate alot of your userbase just due to needing so much more power than other engines. Nowadays, I don't think that's as much of an issue unless you're running a 10 year old rig, you should at least be able to play on minimal settings.
Then THQ went under. Due to issues with that, the master server list for this game went down. This game will not start if it sees the master server list down. So for a couple of years it was completely dead in the water. I think you could start up stupid mode or the beta exe and still be able to play, but that would only be with bots, and you could only run stupid mode if you had a really high end rig, it was the same game, just in super graphics mode.
The master server list is back up, and if you are extremely lucky you might see a server, but more than likely it will be no humans, and all bots. This game has been dead for so long, and didn't have enough of a following to start with, that everyone who owned it has all but forgotten it, and any new owner will more than likely give up because all there is to do, is play against bots.
If you don't mind playing against just bots, and you are a fan of arena shooters, it really isn't a bad game. It's a UT clone, and in that regard it does it's job pretty well. It's just dead for players and I don't see that aspect changing anytime soon.

You play as the ghost of Ronan O'Connor as he investigates his murder and attempts to find the identity of the serial "Bell Killer."  There are several investigations you must perform through the game, plus a number of optional side cases where you can help other ghosts resolve whatever issues are keeping them in the world.  The story is really interesting, especially when you discover the identity of the serial killer, but the game is just okay.
Finding clues to solve the investigations is kind of difficult.  There is only a narrow margin in the view angle that will allow you to actually examine each clue, and there is nothing to indicate what can or can't be examined other than the "Examine" option that appears when you look directly at a clue.  Piecing together the clues to solve each case is not at all intuitive, and often doesn't even make sense.  The soundbite clues were my least favorite; the game plays a sound as the menu appears (and the menu has its own sound clip), then you have to choose which object in your sight makes the most sense for the sound you may have not even heard.  There is no way to make the sound replay.
Thankfully, there is no punishment for selecting the wrong clues when solving a case.  Unfortunately, there's also no reward for perfectly solving a case.  After solving a case, the game tells you exactly where to go next, which makes for a very linear experience.  You do revisit a few locations, and you can sidetrack to perform optional cases or discover collectibles, but the game really holds your hand the whole way through.  This makes the game pretty easy to complete, but I didn't feel like it caused me to enjoy the game any less.
The ghost powers are nothing more than arbitrary game mechanics that change for each situation depending on what the game needs to let you do in order to progress.  You have the ability to possess people and listen to their thoughts, which results in you hearing the same small selection of dialogues over and over.  Sometimes cases will make you possess a person and "influence" them to provide more clues.  You are prompted, "What will make this person remember _______ event?" and then you choose something from among the clues you've found thus far.  You also have the ability to teleport a short distance, interact with electronics as a poltergeist (which only draws peoples' attention when the game needs it to), and reveal ghost objects of events from the distant past (which doesn't ever seem to do anything useful except allow you to find optional collectibles).
Each case only requires you to find a handful of available clues, so you need not collect all 362 pieces of evidence (189 of which are for the main story) if you aren't the completionist type.  Failure to collect all the clues will not affect the outcome of the game, so don't expect a Heavy Rain type of game where information you do or do not find affects future revelations.  However, collecting all of the clues does reveal a lot of information about the locations and characters, so you are actually rewarded for picking up the ridiculous amount of collectibles.
Despite these flaws, I did enjoy the game.  It holds up as a solid detective game even if the clues and cases are somewhat arbitrary.  This is certainly not the best detective game I've played but it is far from being the worst.

Owlboy.
The game is an action platformer.
You play as "Owlboy", a mute fledgling owl that is forced to spread his wings and thrust into an adventure like no other.
The art style:
Is wonderful, with its vibrant and colourful display, its locations are wonderful; you can really see that this was a labour of love, rather than a rushed game.
The Music:
The music is truly fantastic, it really helps to create emotion, whether that being melancholy or wonder, it has a track for that; I couldn’t help but find the soundtrack and listen to it again. The fact that it is fully orchestrated helps wonders too.
The Story:
I felt that the story captivated me and kept me well engrossed, making me want to come back to play the rest almost every night. The story took me about 6-7 hours to complete, but I did not get all of the collectibles that are on offer. I was not disappointed.
The Combat:
The combat is something that I enjoyed; you pick up and carry one of three different characters to act as your weapon each with a unique still set that will be useful in your travels. There are a large variety of enemies that you will face and a good amount of boss fights that will engage you. I only wish the boss fights were a little more difficult.
I honestly loved this game and I recommend it to you whole-heartedly.

The game is fun and offers some stratagy based money management as well as requiring a bit of luck.
In standard new game there are only 2 dungeons, one is basically a tutorial dungeon with not a lot to offer the other is a 3 part dungeon with a 4th area allowing you to fight just the bosses over and over again.
Early in the game dungeon crawling is a must to gain pix, however later on, for me it was after just the 2nd week, it no longer seems really helpful.
Often times townspeople will come in selling an item and then before the time segment is even over will buy it right back. One of the best ways to make money is buying for 30% and reselling for 130%.
One of the best items to stock up I found was weapons, in later weeks they get boosts in value and can be sold for as much as 300% base. For me the last 3 days all weapons were increased in value, not sure if it was luck or game mechanics, but in the last 3 days alone I amassed over 300k pix.
The game does have NG+ as well as a survival mode, but for the most part there doesn't really seem to be a whole lot of replay value after you intitally beat it.
I bought it on sale for 9.99, not 100% I got my moneys worth, but it was definitely a fun game. I have a total of around 7 hours in the game including offline time, and that's about the amount of time it took me to beat it with having to start over once. I'd recommend buying it, but definitely on sale for 9.99 or less simply because of how short the game is, and how little replay value it offers in my opinion.

When I was younger, I used to adore the old Mario games for their simple comlpexity. The way a younger person like myself could play the game and enjoy it on a simple level, but once I was older I could return to the game and find new secrets and techniques to play the game. Even as an adult I was able to enjoy those games, and it has been nearly a decade since a game has proved to me that a kid could enjoy and appreciate it just as much as an adult could.
Then comes Owlboy
I had little to no knowledge of this game going in, only that I loved what I saw in the trailer and the promise of "9 years of work" being put into this. I picked it up on day one and I cannot tell you how glad I am that I did so. Merely opening the game and seeing the intro screen made me feel the first sense of childlike wonder I'd felt in years. The art style was stunning even for a pixel game of our day and age.
AND THE MUSIC. If the gameplay, story and art didn't steal my heart right off the bat I guarantee you the soundtrack did. When I first flapped my way into the Tropos area of the game and the triumphant violins began their chant I was brought to tears by the sheer beauty of what I was playing.
In fact, I don't believe I was crying for reason that the game was gorgeous, but that it reminded me why I started playing games in the first place: Because it made me feel something. Something special. I hadn't felt a sense of wonder like it since I'd played Super Mario Galaxy on the Wii.
TL;DR Game made me cry 100/10

Welcome to Velvet Sundown!
You are about to join in on a brand new, original game experience! Unlike most games, Velvet Sundown is not about beating the game but playing with real people behind different characters and roles. Your ability to interact and converse with them is the core gameplay!
Velvet Sundown sets you up with a new identity each time you play. You are someone different, most likely someone rich and famous. You have a history, motives and reasons to communicate.
Velvet Sundown has a running start directly into the best gameplay. There are currently two 45-minute-long scenarios to choose from. Each requires a minimum of 4 players online to play. When the minimum amount of people required is reached, the game will start automatically in 3 minutes.
Velvet Sundown is massively emergent. We've made the storylines, yet you control the story and the twists along the way. We hope you'll have fun playing the varied characters and please, do give us your feedback! You can reach us on the forum or send us email to
or tweet us at @velvetsundown
To ensure everyone has a pleasant and enjoyable time playing the game, we should all try and behave ourselves! There are off-game areas, like the Chat in the menus, where you need to be courteous to others. However, during the gameplay of Velvet Sundown everyone will be improvising their lines, and acting according to their characters, and therefore some rougher behavior is well accepted. The rule-of-thumb here is that you can be harsh when it fits your character and the situation — when it is entertaining and fun to all! Of course not everything is accepted in-game either: spamming, griefing and advertising are never allowed. When controlling the 3D character you are also well advised not to 'break the fourth wall', i.e. do not talk about real life topics that are not relevant to the in-game setting.

Short version: "Meh" It's not bad, especially for $20, I just can't personally recommend it.
The story starts off relatively serious, but very quickly becomes a saturday morning cartoon. Some of the \"Side Stories\" also contain plot critical information, and can be unlocked out of order.
Basically don\'t play this game for the story, especially if you\'re not a fan of Captain Planet.
As for the gameplay, it innovates on the turned based tactical RPG genre a bit by having you personally take control of the characters you want to move, and manually aim when you wish to shoot. It starts off being very fun and interesting but enemies quickly become bullet spongy, immune to headshots, or resistant to exlposions, made worse by the fact your shots can randomly miss despite having to manually aim. I found myself save scumming nearly every mission after the first boss because of how stale the combat became, and because certain missions can quickly become unbeatable if you aren\'t familiar with the level, and objectives.
The game features a progression system, in which experience can be contributed towards one of the 5 infantry classes (You cannot choose a class). Each level will increase health, and at certain thresholds you\'ll unlock a \"Potential\" (Special trait). At lvl 11, you\'ll unlock an elite version of the class, which unlocks a new weapon and usually has a noticable increase to the classes total Action Pool. However this progression is pretty lackluster, even at maximum level the enemy will often still be stronger than you. Some of the alternate weapons are also pretty terrible compared to the default weapon, and should rarely be taken into combat.
I mentioned \"Potentials\" which is unfortunately another missed opportunity, as well as a reason to save scum. Some of the potentials a character have can be incredibly powerful, but most of them are activated randomly. Double Tank Damage for instance, this can lead to your Anti-Armor infantry 1 shotting most tanks if this triggers, but it is entirely random  when it does. This can be infuriating if there\'s an enemy tank that you NEED to kill this turn for whatever reason.
However, as much as I personally HATE this game, I cannot say that it is bad, or that it isn\'t worth $20.00. It\'s just not something everyone will like, and most people will probably find SOMETHING to hate about this game if they play it all the way through. If the idea of a 3rd person tactical RPG set in fantasy WWII Switzerland interests you, then it might be worth checking out, especially if it goes on sale.

Just 100%ed the game and it's dlc wildcards. I'll focus on the main game in this review. This game is well worth the price(although I got it during the winter sale). The replayablity is really high and there are tons of new cards to unlock everytime you play a stage or endless. The main game let's you select the boss for the stage and each one comes with seperate rules(in the form of curses) and encounters to make getting to each boss it's own challenge. You can make your own deck to suit your playstyle or to adapt to certain stages, the cards that make up the equipment and encounter deck are cards you unlock from bosses, tokens, and from the easy and hard mode fates(you also unlock new gain cards from tokens). Equipment explains it's self, but encounter cards make up the floors in the stages, so you are in charge of the events that occur on each floor, it's a really awesome feature of this game. There are three main ways to die, one is from combat, another is from failing chance cards that make you draw pain cards, and last is from starvation.
The combat in the game isn't the best part, but it at least provides a good amount of challenge to the game, this is even more so if you're stuck in basic gear. Some negative things I could say about the game would be some chance cards are really hard to succeed at or survive(looking at you Petward ;c) and some of the most annoying encounters are locked in your deck and can ruin a playthrough. I'll briefly go over endless which is a mode where you select which fate you'll use and every card you unlocked will be in the mode(so no deck building), it's pretty much a mode where you need to survive as long as possible to get a highscore. Endless can be fun, but if you have encounters like Petward still up it could be all for naught. So I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes rogue-likes and action rpgs that have a twist to make it feel like a completely different experience. :)

After years of crusading and aggressive expansion into Italy and the Middle East, I reclaimed the old Roman Borders. The Roman Empire was once more established, but Rome was not done. All the land from Constantinople to Egypt, Egypt to Spain, Spain to France, Germany, parts of Russia, and all of Scandinavia were to be conquered. Alright, I'll start this off by saying,  my experience with the game is only a few hours of play, so I'm not sure I can relate well.  Anyway.  Onto the major points:
- Yes, this game is quite beautiful graphics-wise.  I can't say that enough, the pixel art style is done with so many pretty, flashy effects.  I do love that about it.
-  However, the above point cannot possibly out-do the negatives!
-- I know it's an early access game, and frankly we can only HOPE the devs see the multitude of bad reviews marking the same points over and over!  The difficulty is one of the top points.  I found the second big display you have to pop  with your weapon.  A big purple one.  As soon as I did.. -4- fire-spitting spheres spawned!  Seriously.. 4??  I'm chewed up by just one or two of those guys.. bur 4 at once?  in a locked room with no cover?  Needless to say I died quickly, only to be revived at a checkpoint way back in bum♥♥♥♥t, egypt.  Or in other words.. there's just no way to know where you are, where you're going, where you've been.  It's a mess.
-  Which is the next point.  Lack of direction.  Sure you have that little tap-button to bring up the objective ping.  But really, that system is so broken!  It often points in a direction you really can't even come close to getting to from where you are.  Honestly it needs to take the current surroundings in mind.. sometimes you just -cannot go that way- because of a wall or locked access or something.  And without a map, it's all moot anyway.  Because you can't figure
out what you have or have not done, which is made worse by dying.
-  Some weird red screen with lots of little codes pops up when you die, but there's no way to know what to click on!  But then you have no time, and it just ends up popping up 'Injection Failed'  Seriously.. GIVE AN EXPLANATION WHEN YOU RANDOMLY THROW NEW STUFF LIKE THAT IN A PLAYER'S FACE!  It's not hard to know you need this.. really guys!
-  Did I mention the difficulty?  Stuff takes a lot of shots to kill, while you're fighting with your limited move set to jump over, run under, or otherwise avoid them.  But you have next to nothing for offense.  Heck, you don't even know why they are shooting at you!  Did we really want to pick a fight with them?  Do we even have a choice?  Then there's the scaling.  Some random robots doing various things, then suddenly you come across a - LASER TANK -.  Holy balls, those things are just too massive in health, and damage dealt!
-  Then the upgrade system.  I lost the reflect because I didn't know what upgrade tokens did.  And since it's not dropped by enemies far as I can tell, you lose a major bit of the only advantage you're given as a result.
-  Then there's the level itself.  From the beginning, the entire level is just way too overloaded with boxes that explode into acid, and wires.  Wires everywhere.  Oh gods the wires.  Your gun is already woefully weak to everything you fight.  But then to add into that wires and boxes both that soak up your shots, while the enemy robots have no trouble shooting you right back through them.  That's just inexcusable!  Fine, background objects hanging all over.  If you have to shoot them as much as the bad guys to get -TO- the bad guys, then you're just never going to get anywhere.
- And how about that beginning?  I must have spent 10 minutes after getting the first 'word' that you had to hit 'c' to open a screen to reboot the suit!  NOWHERE is this told to you in game.. I had to find it online!  That's seriously bad design, if you cannot solve a game without resorting to looking it up online, the game has been too poorly designed.
So as you can see, there are a TON of major problems with this game.  I can only hope it doesn't end up moving into a shipping state with this many things wrong with it!  The game shows promise, but these issues and a few minor graphical glitches and such seriously need to be fixed if they expect us to play this.  Get to it guys, you have plenty of people telling you what needs addressed, even how in a lot of cases.  So let's do it.  We didn't buy into a game to watch it burn and die!
Do I recommend it?  Well, I marked 'no' but, I'm not exactly 100% on that idea.  I will say that if the game does not improve from where it is, I will certainly say 'Avoid at all costs!'  Keep that in mind, devs!

Visually, the game is great.  That's about as far as greatness goes with this title.
The combat is slow and very random at the beginning since you have to train your characters accuracy by purchasing better equipment, but even once it's maxed out you'll still find yourself missing impossible-to-miss shots. Which is a shame because at first glance the fps-style aiming for the combat seemed interesting, but it's rarely ever useful as you could just as simply select a target with an auto-aim and no target has more than 2 points to bother attacking.  A more traditional target selecting system for this game may have made the dice-roll of accuracy a bit more palatable too since it doesn't wear the veneer of fps aiming mechanics.
The most annoying flaw in this game was that you could play it with only half of the unit types, since some of them were so utterly useless. I completed the game using only 2 of 5 unit types for the majority of the game, only in special instances needing to include 1 of the other types for a specific target. Finally, the lack of movement options on the maps is very restricting of actual development of strategy as you will have at most 2 lanes of attack.
I came to this game because it was "story rich" but that story is weak and juvenile, filled with simple characters and uninteresting plot elements. The enemy continues to escalate in power despite claims throughout that whatever you are up against is their ultimate weapon. Also, for a "strategy" game, the strategy employed by the characters within makes little to no sense as you come into great power with little consequences to using it, but it is never used.
