Hand of fate is a Dungeons & Dragons inspired card game with hack 'n slash combat. As you progress through the game and solve quests, more cards become unlocked for you to bolster your deck with. Your opponent, or Dungeon Master, sits across you and deals you the cards as the game unfolds, offering comments, threats, and wry observations as you play.
Combat is fast paced and feels good and different blessings and curses you accrue over the course of the game influence your tactics both in and out of combat. As you solve quests, deal with demons, or help the innocent on your journey, the DM awards you with coins. When you die, and you will die, the coins are shattered and give you new encounters, weapons, armour, and blessings to fill your deck with. But beware, for as you grow in strength, so do your adversaries.
Your deck is the permanent feature of the game. The cards you unlock carry over from one game to the next. Each game you play is like a new adventure. In this respect it kind of reminds me of FTL: Faster than Light, although death isn't nearly as certain in Hand of Fate than it was in FTL (unless you play Endless Mode).
It's compelling, beautiful, and very more-ish. As every individual game is highly influenced by chance, very few games are similar. There are weapons I have yet to use because I haven't drawn them in a game yet, even though I unlocked them many games before. No game sees you go through your entire deck, so you never quite know what to expect, or when to expect it.
TLDR Pro's & Con's
PRO:
Great atmosphere
Random factor (no game ever quite the same)
Persistent rewards
Good solid combat
Feels rewarding (even if you don't win)
Multiple questlines that you play through 'simultaniously' over the course of many games
CON:
Random factor (sometimes the deck is just stacked against you)
No direct control over your starting equipment
Mouse hover-over selection doesn't always work quite right (sticks to first option) so you have to make sure you have the right selection highlighted before making a choice
I highly recommend this game. This is the closest I've seen a PC game come to capturing the feeling of playing an actual table-top card game with someone.

Ok, so clearly there is a rabid fan base for this game and the ratings are generally positive - thus I bought the game. The graphics are solid and the overall UI looks appealing... but after playing for two afternoons I'm a bit stunned there isn't more of a balance in the reviews. For the positives, read the others. This review is going to point out just a few of the negatives of this game that will save you a few bucks.  I'll start by saying I love these kinds of games generally. I've played Civ since the first, all the total wars, and hang around with my kids setting up armies once in a while. I love war strategy games and the more complex the better... this is not one of those.
- Deceptive advertising: This game is for historical simulation buffs, not strategy game buffs. The rule set and complexity of the game will only add to the fun for a very, very small number of snobbish gamers that like to argue over ducal claims to Leon. (They also like to write reviews apparently). The action posed knight on the cover art + total war like game map is deceptive. This is a game of endless spreadsheets, stats, and family trees that are eternally obscure.
- The tutorial is poor. Before even pointing out your primary goals, (still not sure what they are), you have to find the impossible wife ("Healthy" was not one of my options, but part of the instructions), and fabricate a claim on a muslim island.  What?!?  Then they just leave you like a bad habit with hundreds of buttons that don't mean much. Good luck sucker.  Somewhere in the distance I can hear some putz designer saying, "Scaling, we don't need to stinking scaling!" So if you finish the tutorial, go ahead, and try to whip up a "normal" game... how's that going for you? Did you really learn to play in their tutorial?
- Choices. Complexity should amount to more meaningful decisions to make. This game boils down to 1) keep vassals happy, 2) fabricate/push claims on territories, and 3) make babies and waaaaaaait for them to grow up. Tech trees? bah. Strategy? bah. Defences? Not needed.  Just play matchmaker and bribe people.  No need to actually give the player something to consider and plan for...
- Game Balance. Wait, why is the person that I just gave a duchy to still mad at me?  Why should I care? Looking carefully I am apparantly a "Tyrant" (-70) because a turn ago I removed a title from someone that just led a rebellion... Tyrant? Really?!? and -70 essentially overrides ten or so positive elements... seriously, just one example of preposterous rule sets that whack the game out regularly.  Some may thing this is interesting, realistic, detailled, or something, but the emperor simply has no clothes on people! This game is lame, boring, and frustrating... and far from realistic.
- Fun.  Oh yeah, that counts for a computer game too!
Still, I may just not be as smart as the folks that gave this a good rating, or they may have thought it would be funny to give you bad advice and see how many might still buy this.  You may enjoy games that have you looking at charts and meaningless attributes all day so that you can watch the computer tick off random events. To each their own. This game is not for me.

There are a lot of technical gameplay issues that need addressing, like pacing and enemy scaling.
Early on in the game you have weapons that simply do not do much damage against enemies that have a relatively large amount of health and hit hard enough to take a full bar of health within a hit or two (purple bullet enemies.) This makes it a game that would be ideal for some sort of shield, evade, or deflect mechanic, yet none exists. You can't even hide behind cover, since the terrain is incredibly destructible by most enemies.
While just about everything about the game is beautiful, it suffers from the identity crisis issue of not throwing itself entirely into one genre or the other. In one sense it has some Dark Soulsian difficulty, a 'bonfire' mechanic (manually activated in-world checkpoints,) and a world that only vaguely tells you sometimes where you should be going. That clashes with the seeming randomization of the game, where enemy placement is mixed up and unpredictable, meaning that the aforementioned problem of not being able to effectively deal with enemies is absurd. At least in Dark Souls you could roll away. The dash in this game is virtually worthless, (it amounts to the body length of ATAI, the main character,) since it covers almost no distance.
If you shoot at something long enough, it does eventually die, but there are so many random enemies everywhere that I have no idea what most of them do until I've either died or lost 90% of my health. It bears repeating, since it is obvious the devs are taking concepts from it, that Dark Souls used pacing very efficiently in the enemy types one faced at various stages of the game. This game doesn't.
I've seen laser cannons, missile launchers, incendiary automatic weapons, and basically everything else on the enemies and I barely played an hour and a half. In most games of this genre, you see smaller, weaker enemies with less dangerous weapons to star. Sure, I'm fine with them doing a bar of health, but when I'm fighting something that can chase me into a corner with all the health in the world, fire almost continuously, and chunk my health with bullets that never end, that's a problem. That's a mid-late game situation in most games of this genre. They do that right. This game... you have every enemy and weapon combination attacking you from the start, but you have access to a peashooter with a couple superficial (read: worthless) upgrades like bounce, penetration, and multiply. Those don't help me kill anything faster, they just let me cheese certain enemies by abusing line of sight and aggro. Not really emergent gameplay.

Good game with an interesting mixture of popular RPG mechanics. 3 diverse and fun to play factions, Humans which are your typical jack of all trades faction with good defense and offense but not the best at either. Elves which are your best defensive faction because of their self-sustaining economy and strong wall fortifications, also invisible archers which are a pain. Orcs which are supposedly good at rushing but it doesn't normally work out for me, thankfully the orcs are also a strong faction in mid game with powerful offensive units, I believe they are the only faction with non-siege units that are effective at breaking gates down (ogres and minotaurs). There are also 3 mercenary unit factions that are fun to play around with (Dwarves, Dragons and now Undead). The gameplay is fun as feels like a mixture of Age of Empires, Stronghold and other classic RTS games. Graphics are outdated but you get accustom to them in time, especially if you are an old-school RTS player. Be warned this isn't a game you should jump directly into multiplayer in, its highly advised you play at least some of the campaign missions and some skirmish games first. As their is a tech-tree system that requires different crafting components you use to invest in. I believe you start with a fair amount of crafting components now to research some of the tech tree but this is an important point because without the tech tree research, you will be at a large disadvantage in multiplayer and unable to build the majority of your units / upgrades.

As someone who is a big fan of Fire Emblem games and also enjoyed playing X-COM, I was hoping this game would be an excellent fit for me.  Unfortunately Valkyria Chronicles is a game that comes very close to being good, but stumbles at pretty much every opportunity.  The game has a weird crouch mechanic that makes headshots ineffective. Bullets farther then a few yards out are often ineffective and anti-tank guns are underpowered and very inaccurate.  This means that the easiest way to win is buffing scouts with commands and rushing.  The game suggests that this is the best way to play and gives low grades on any mission where you didn't rush like a banshee.  This could be forgiven if any other units/strategies came remotely close to being as good as this one.
The level design isn't too bad, but a few feel a little cheap, and one with infinitely respawning enemies is decidedly awful.  The story on the other hand is full of values dissonance and Mary Sue characters.  I'm impressed that they tried to work  key themes into a greater overall narritive, but they come off heavy handed and the sacrifices of many of the characters make no sense in the context of the story.
Valkyria Chronicles tried to do something different, and I have to commend the effort.  With a couple of changes, it could be a great game, but as it stands, it sort of hits a gaming uncanny valley where everything feels off.  As a fan of strategy games, I'm glad the game was successful and that there is still a following for such games.  However, I would be hard pressed to recommend it to anyone.

There is a lot of potential for this game. I've only played in single player mode so I can't speak to multiplayer. In many ways the game in the early stages is much more forgiving than Ark or Empyrion (two survival games I've recently sunk a lot of time into). I've seen many reviwers compare CE to Ark and I think that's a fair assesment.
PROS:
1. Graphics and performance are nice even on my older system. I did see some hitching once in a while and had one CTD.
2. Gameplay is intuative to seasoned players familiar with survival games. New players may need to watch some YouTube tutorials.
3. Very adult themed game with no holds barred. May be a turn off for gentle minded folks so beware.
4. No damage from elements. You won't die of heat or cold something I was glad to see.
5. Base building mechanics are solid.
CONS:
1, If you liked Ark combat then you'll like CE combat. Using bows can be frustrating. Hope they at least add a little spice here to make it more fun. I was disapointed not to see heads and limbs flying.
2. No roaming bands of mobs. At least in single player, it would be nice to have a few bandits show up at your base. Right now not really any reason to build a base other than it is fun. (for single player)
3. Argo range seems a little off. Those little round walking toad looking guys will zero in on you when they are a dot in the distance.
Wishlist:
1. Roaming mobs to attack base. Give you reason to build defenses.
2. Decapatation and other mayhem when fighting. Finishing moves would be nice too.
3. More RPG elements early on. I liked finding that note early on.
Conclusion:
For an early access game it plays surprisingly well. It does seem that CE has tried to avoid a lot of the annoyances that other survival games have which is nice. Single player has enough stuff to do and places to explore that you should get at least your $30 worth fairly fast. I've just scratched the surface and look forward to many hours of fun. Buy it if $30 won't break the bank and you are looking for a fun game that will only get better.

OK, this has been said in many other reviews, but it seems it's worth to repeat it: this is yet Early Access Game. Early Access means often this is not even a beta, so expect issues, glitches, bugs and a vague sense of "not even nearly finished".
So, is it worth to pay for an unfinished product? Maybe.
First of all, you are not paying full. Many of us are fond of crowd funding. See this as a form of crowd funding for the game, you pay in advance a little less, you get access to the developing game, and hopefully you'll like the finished one.
Second, you can contribute to the game, in terms of feedback.
Getting on the game proper, if you enter now expect no tutorial and no "hint" on what to do. It's pure sandbox (literally - for the first mile) and you will have to learn by trial and error.
Some non-spoiling tips.
1. You are in a desert, you'll need to drink very soon. Make water one of your first priorities.
2. Try EVERYTHING. You won't find what you need lying around or popping out of slain creatures. You need stone? Try a pickaxe. You need wood? Try an hatchet. You need meat? Well, make a wild guess.
After two hours of game and half a dozen deaths, I am starting to understand how things work. Map is a bit crappy, and create a bed as soon as you can in a location you can easily find. Apart from that, it's the Hyborian Age, you are naked and bare handed, and ready to rumble. What are you waiting for?

I've played Fist Puncher ALOT on both Windows 7 Home Premium 64 bit and Linux Mint 17.3 Cinnamon 64 bit. I honestly don't understand the negative reviews Fist Puncher recieves. Fist Puncher does exactly what it sets out to do: action-comedy with a crap load of unlockable goodies.

- Younger players might not get Fist Punchers 1980s action movie humor.
A Steam Must-Have.

I'll be damned, this game is actually back from the grave! Now if only all the players would come back to populate the servers...
Whether you like the game comes down to only 1 thing: how much you like the crazy Nexuiz mutators. These change the game drastically, sometimes affecting all players globally. Of course, there are also game modes without these mutators, but this is what makes the game special.
Some examples:
- All players get jetpacks.
- Controls are inverted for everyone!
- 1 random player loses his weapons and becomes a living bomb. You can kill lots of players with a kamikaze (although most of the time it's rather annoying, because you lose your health and armor stack)
- Color blind mutator literally changes everything to a greyscale. You'll have trouble telling teams apart. Friendly fire is on.
- Ground suddenly feels slippery and everyone is sliding (careful around edges)
- Nuke. Everyone dies, then respawns.
- Invulnerability (only you)
- You get Strength (double damage)
- You get your favorite weapon.
- Shooting teammates now heals them instead!
...
There's many more (about 50?). The global mutators take turns in a stack. The stack can be cleared too. Mutators affecting only you take effect instantly when you pick em up, I believe...
Honestly, it's chaotic as hell and a lot of these mutators are rather unwelcome (kamikaze and nuke). But if you like chaos, you will like this game. If the devs would actually put some effort into balancing the weapons and creating a competitive game mode with less ridiculous mutators, it could be great.
100% recommended. Back to the good old survival horror :)

So me and my friend were looking through the games that Adult Swim Games have published on Steam since they have a pretty good selection, (Volgarr the Viking, Duck Game, Headlander, ect.) and found Fist Puncher. We had been looking through Steam to find a good 2d side scrolling beat 'em up since it had been forever since we played one that was really good and new to us. Story: Not much to say about it since we didn't get far but it was harmless enough.
Music: The music was pretty bland. No rock, no weird electro, no 8-16 bit, just really bland uninteresting music that you would hear at a cheap backwater bar.
Gameplay: The real heart of the problems we had with the game so I will try to rapidfire this. The enemies took too long to kill and were not even fun to beat up. The level up system was mediocre. You have to stick with 1 character since the levels are not persistent with all characters (which there are 20 of). We kept dying not because of lack of skill, but because the enemies took too long to die and did so much damage that was unavoidable due to the rather wonky controls. Graphics: This game was released three years ago as of the time of this review but the graphics are very bare bones. Yes it is retro, but that doesn't mean you can be lazy at making a pixel graphics game.

Widely considered by most to be the best in the trilogy, and for good reason. When it hit the scene early in 2010, it was a major step up from the already great Mass Effect. Combat, characters, overworlds, storytelling, atmosphere, Interface, sound quality, choices and side-quests, all of it was greatly improved with this game, and still stands strong to this day.
The story follows two years after the events of Mass Effect 1. Due to reasons I will not reveal in fear of spoilers, Commander Shepard (the character you play as) has gotten off the public eye and is working with the pro-human organization called Cerberus, to deal with a threat the authorities choose to ignore. In order to do so, squad-mates must be recruited for a Suicide Mission to get rid of the threat.  And that's where you come in. Throughout a lengthy 35-40 hour campaign, you will travel to distant and varied worlds, making tough choices that can have devastating outcomes, to gain enough manpower for your campaign.
The main plot of the game is actually really simple. Like, REALLY simple, close to shallow. All you do is find out where the threat comes from, assemble a team to deal with the threat, find a way to get to the threat and then destroy it. The real meat of the game is actually with the squad-mates, in fact there are far more missions centered around recruiting characters and later gaining their loyalty through other missions. It's more of a character study than a traditional RPG (though you still get to explore fascinating locations and all that good stuff). And it works, because these are some really great characters. They're layered individuals from fascinating cultures and backgrounds, with believeable and complex motivations, striking personalities and involving arcs that really invest you in their struggles and the galaxy they inhabit.
It also helps that the conversations have been much improved from the previous game. In ME1, as well as other games, during dialogue characters would tend to stand completely still, maybe move their arms a few times with a bit of a stern, not very emotive face. That still happens from time to time, but often characters will now walk around the room while they talk, or maybe the camera will move around, focus on something or give interesting angles. The much improved camera work in this game is really welcome. Here they use shadows and light, colour, as well as other things to better create a mood, which really improves the quality of your interactions.
There are a lot more things I could say about this game, but what it boils down to, is that I think this is a fantastic game that you should give a try if you are interested in a character-focused game that touches on very real and difficult themes and issues in a very mature and smart way. I recommend that you import a save from ME1, since choices you made there will show up again, either to shake your hand or kick you in the balls. It greatly increases your ability to create your very own Shepard with a unique history, and that is a great experience.
Score: 9.8/10

I'd like to start this review by congratulating the designers, who by and largely succeeded in making one of the most atmospheric, spooky and genuinely fascinating horror games of recent years. I'd then like to move on to saying ♥♥♥♥ YOU, YOU ♥♥♥♥ING MOTHER-♥♥♥♥ERS, for creating such a ludicrously CHILDISH way of "punishing" the player for the seemingly unforgivable crime of...wait for it...DYING IN A VIDEO GAME. What is this punishment, you ask?
Well, the first couple of times it's actually kind of groovy. Your character awakens in a "Limbo" of sorts, lying on the floor of an otherwise featureless landscape surrounded by lit candles. She finds her feet, and soon enough you figure you may as well run towards a coalescing light nearby. Sure enough, you slowly emerge back into the land of the living, and may continue where you left off.  Sounds pretty nifty, huh? TRY DOING IT MORE THAN TEN TIMES IN A SINGLE SITTING.
But wait, there's more! The light...get this, you're gonna love this...the light MOVES FURTHER AND FURTHER AWAY EVERY TIME YOU DIE, until it's eventually, like, a minute or more's running distance away. In other words, not only are you rewarded with a two-minute wait before you can get back to trying to work out just how to get past that tricky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a boss bit, but you can't even walk away for those minutes like you would with a slow load screen, unless you have a pet monkey you can train to SIT THERE FOR TWO ♥♥♥♥ING MINUTES HOLDING THE "SHIFT" AND "W" KEYS DOWN!!!
I can tell the people who made this game are very talented, but apparently they either don't give a damn about public opinion or they don't know how to do STEAM UPDATES. Because given the number of negative reviews I've seen complaining about this particularly "striking" and "unique" feature, I for the life of me cannot understand why the designers haven't decided to PATCH this INSANELY BAD IDEA. Seriously, it's stupid, and insulting, and to add further insult you start getting on-screen comments like "You might want to consider switching to casual gaming" whilst running towards the light for the umpteenth time. Oh yeah, TROLLING people who shelled out good money for your game...genius.
Let us seriously, SERIOUSLY hope that this nonsense is gone - or at least severely lessened - by the time that Act Two of an otherwise excellent game rears its head, 'cause honestly Digital Happiness, it's the only conceivable reason I can see why this game has such an appalling Metascore. Apart from this highly significant flaw, and perhaps one or two puzzles/boss-battles which rely just a little TOO much on obscure solutions, this is top-rate horror gaming. Oh, and a map wouldn't hurt either. But honestly, the main criticism I have is the "dying" system (which you can't even circumnavigate by re-loading, thanks to you getting an auto-save the second said death occurs).
The people who make games this good deserve respect, but you know what? So do the people who PLAY them. Wake up, designers. We're not all uber-gamers who devote our lives to spending sixteen hours a day in front of the computer. By all means make the games challenging, but please refrain from tactics which just make people wanna relinquish their support for your product (and future products) altogether. I'm sure the "Limbo" idea was cute on paper, or in design meetings, but don't make the game-buying public your ♥♥♥♥ing guinea pigs. Cheers.
Verdict: 8.5/10 (subject to improve if the developers grow a conscience and "do the right thing").
LONG OVERDUE UPDATE: Okay, so I finally deigned to play the second and final Act of this game, after finally abandoning my long wait for the devs to return the "new" 32-bit version of the game to its former 64-bit glory (don't even ask...Google it if you gotta). First up, regarding my little rant above...yes, the devs did more-or-less address the infamous "never-ending Limbo" issue, not by removing it entirely, but by adding an option where you could set it at the initial, much shorter running distance. This is obviously a lot less annoying, but still pushes one's patience by the fortieth time that it occurs.
So what do I now think of the game as a two-part whole? Well, I gotta say, despite many reservations I still hold about it, I'm quite happy to raise my Verdict to a 9 (but no higher). It still has a TONNE of problems, but nonetheless easily qualifies as one of the best third person survival horror games to come down the turnpike in a long while. Let's see if the newly-released Keepers of the Dark side-game improves upon the tremendous potential shown herein.
Revised Verdict: 9/10.

Pros:
+ Quick and fun to play
Cons:
- Awkward damage modeling; slow strikes do as much damage as fast ones, and bending matrix-style to swing a polearm can hit someone behind you (when physically it should not be even possible to do this). The end and start of weapon swings do full damage, even though physically this should result in minimal damage due to low momentum.
- Rough around the edges; approaching a ramp from the side can cause you to get stuck in the air. Many other bugs present in the game.
- Awkward hit registration. Strikes that LOOK like they should connect do not connect. Strikes from the side sometimes connect with a shield even when there is nothing in the way.
Verdict: 4/10. It's quick, bloody and fun. But if you are looking for a realistic medieval combat simulation, this is not your game. It's also littered with janky animations and weird bugs all around. And once you have left the noob servers, be prepared for the onslaught of veteran players who know how to abuse 'dragging' (delaying or speeding up swings to catch you off-guard) to ridiculous levels, as well as those who know how to abuse the terrible animations to contort their character's body to dodge weapons in physically impossible ways. Infinitely frustrating when there are these players in the game; and in all honesty, if a game is frustrating to no end because of its broken mechanics which people abuse, then there is probably little point to playing it for fun. Because unless you have some masochistic tendencies, and you enjoy dying a million times over to bug abusers, then you will not find this game fun. YMMV.

While most reviews on games tend to give you a good idea of what the game will feel like when you play it, I don't believe any review I've read has perfectly portrayed what Archeage is. There has been so much negative stigma attached to Trion and this game that I almost never tried it since so many people warned me not to.
To put it into the simplest terms, there is some seriously positive and negative things about this game that people overlook when they hear "pay to win."
To get straight to the point, The list of things I find lovely about this game:
-

This game is very lovely and serene. I'm sure many would have a differing opinion but compared to many other mmorpgs, this one certainly raises to the top in both graphics and the background music.
Aside from the beautiful world, the character customization is fairly detailed and gives plently of options to allow the       creation of characters that are unique and different.
-

This has always been important to me and it's one of the main reasons I couldn't continue to play Final Fantasy XIV Online. Archeage, as far as I've experienced, is completely open world without really any loading screens after you begin playing your character (with the exception of portals). This is great for the feeling of immersion and stops the game from being choppy.
-

Unlike games such as World of Warcraft or Guild Wars 2, there's not exactly a profession system. The best thing about Archeage is that you get free range over crafting, no choosing between leatherworking or alchemy, you can do every single profession without having to stick with just one. This is a system I personally enjoy, especially since each profession tends to go hand and hand with eachother.
-

This seems stupid, but it's a small detail about this game I absolutely adore. In every game I've experienced, you buy a mount from a vendor, hope you get it from a dungeon/raid, or as a reward from an achievement. It doesn't necessarily work like that in Archeage. Yes, you can buy them from vendors, but usually only as little baby mounts which you have to raise by growing food to feed them, giving them water, entertaining them and giving them attention until they've grown full size. It's something I enjoy simply because It helps develop the player relationship with their mounts/companions by having raised them and being able to give them their own names.
-

When you create your character you're given six different classes to choose from, which is a pleasant amount for pretty much any mmorpg, but it gets so much more in depth as you start to level. Once you choose your initial class, you are allowed two more skill sets to create your own custom fighting style and the best part is, you can switch it out anytime you want without losing progress. For example, If you wanted to try sorcery and added occultism as your second skill set, after you get your third (we'll say witchcraft), you can switch any of them out any time you want for a different skill. It basically allows you play and level every skillset on just one character which gives a lot of freedom.
-

While there is a good amount of content around combat and questing, you'll find that there are many small things you can interact with and manipulate. Housing and farming is a huge attraction to this game, and while it's pretty much reserved for subscribers (unless you're in a guild), it's kind of charming to see the many little player farms each decorated to their own liking and sitting cozily next to eachother. With how big the world is, you often get gliders and row boats as well that are equally as charming when you're just floating above towns taking your time to reach the ground.
Unfortunately, with every good aspect to a game, there's always the bad ones, the ones that have been talked about repeatedly in an effort to get you to turn back before you play.
With that being said, there's quite a few issues I've had with this game:
-

What are labor points? Labor points can be thought of as energy that you use on ANY action not pertaining to combat, you know: gardening, planting, crafting, identifying weapons and armor, opening coinpurses, honestly there's not much you can't do without labor points. The problem is, as someone who is free to play, you don't get a whole bunch. It pretty much encourages you to log on and minimize it to the task bar while you go watch a movie or something just to get your labor points up. Usually you get five points every five minutes, and sadly, they don't accumulate while your logged off. However, if you become a patron you get 10 points every 5 minutes, along with a higher labor point cap and they accumulate while you're logged out. It's a really restricting system and can be irritating when you need to craft something that requires 100 labor points and you only have 70.
-
This is a problem that doesn't happen OFTEN, but it has happened enough that it's noticable and irritating. My main issue is that with a game that is released to the public and has been published for quite some time should have these bugs worked out, especially since they tend to be major, like the screen going black when you look in a certain direction or textures from the ground copying and pasting into the sky. Again, these glitches don't happen a bunch but there are definitely some noticable issues.
-

This would not be such a problem for me if they gave you more character slots with a subscription, but they don't. You get two and only two for the entire account and if you want more, you need to buy them with real money. Now usually, with a game like this, I wouldn't complain. You can play every class on one character so why would you need more than one character? But my problem is, there are four different races and if you're like me, you like to at least try out the different starting areas and characters, and this is especially hard with the deletion time when you decide you don't like a character you've made.
My advice, if you make a character and dislike it, try to delete it before you get above level 10, and DO NOT delete two characters at once. The wait time for a character to delete tends to increase with the longer you have them/the higher the level they are and you CANNOT create a new character while you're deleting another one (Unless you already had another character slot open). There is a reason for this, from what I read, it's to prevent the creation of characters just to receive property and then delete them so that their main character can take it. I'm not entirely sure if this is why, but regardless, it's irritating and takes into account that the restriction on character slots makes this process all the more painful.
-
I've read many reviews claiming this game is Pay to Win, and knowing Trion, I don't exactly doubt it, but it's not pay to win in the way people have made it seem. As someone previously stated, it's more "pay to get there faster" than anything. Any gear a pay to win player can get, you can get. This mainly affects PvP and unless you're in arenas trying to conquer everyone, this aspect of the game is really not going to have any influence. I've not personally experienced this and don't believe you should let it stop you from attempting the game.
No review you read will accurately express your own personal experience, I highly recommend that you TRY this game and its pros and cons before you decide if it's for you instead of just taking someone's word for it. <3

One day I was playing the Extended Timeline mod (great mod by the way) for Europa Universalis IV and I got the hankering to see what all the commotion the CK II peasants have been babbling about for so long was about. Considering most of the money from the DLC's is almost completely necessary (twice as long game lenth, twice as large map size, Muslims playable, Nords playable, Pagans playable, Republics playable, the Pope's hat customizable etc.) a $160 price tag for the collection is more than hefty and I would certainly have not bought nor would have reccomended this game had I not gotten it for just $40.
However, this game is incredibly fun - it is about managing your dynasty through nearly 600 years of absolute mayhem, ensuring that out of all your plotting, traitorous subjects not one can murder your children: because you insta-lose if you don't. It's about seeing who gets what title and who gets to manage what provinces or what city, it's about religion, imperialism, feudalism - though far from a cakewalk and with a learning curve even for someone who wasted countless hours of their life playing EU IV, this game is sophisticated yet just simple enough to be remarakably enjoyable.
Every type of nation in this game plays uniquely - sit back and do nothing as Irish peasants, viciously and ruthlessly sail around and pillage with an axe in your hand as a screaming Viking lord, attempt to gradually recoverr the innumerable lost territories for Byzantium/Rome, restore unity and stability so that the Islamic Golden Age can continue, or just simply invade all these fools as a crazed Mongol/Magyar/Cuman/Khazar horde. This game is just fun - I can't exactly name what it is, but something about this game is just extraordinary. Maybe it's the exceptional soundtrack...

If you're into strategy games, you deserve to play this and don't be put off by the initial learning barrier. Because when you're succeeding at this game, there's no feeling like it.

I hate to say this....
...but I cannot recommend this game. I would love to do it, because the game tries to do everything in the right way, but I simply can't, because this time it just doesn't work. It's a shame, because Flying Wild Hog did a bunch of things right. Hell, they nearly headed the perfect direction, but there are a few bad development decisions that have a significant impact in the final result.
As I don't want to give the impression that this is an awful game or anything like that, I will start telling what does this game do right, because it does a couple of things right.
This game is an amazingly beautiful game. It invites to just stop and look at everything. Graphical fidelity is great (really impressive for an Indie tittle), artistic design is UNBELIEVABLE, and it runs like charm (at least on my HD7970). The hand drawn cinematic, similar to those in Mirror's Edge, are really cool and hide the loading times pretty well. This is maybe the strongest feature of the game, it's technical side is amazing. Way better than expected.
The game then wants you to run. Its action it's extremely fast paced, demanding you to aim fast, shoot fast and think fast. It also demands you to search for health, to use objects in the map to cover from fire (sometimes there are so many enemies shooting at you that otherwise is impossible) while enemies moving to get you out of your cover without the regular magical mechanics of AAA shooters which regenerate health and let you stay there for ages. In 2013 all I can say is Hooray for Flying Wild Hog! Even AI is better than usual. It isn't smart, but it's very very aggressive. Even the weapons, which seem to be a bit lackluster at the beginning, are pretty good once you start upgrading them. And there's a huge difference between every weapon, making each of them good or bad depending on the situation. Again, well done.
So, if the game does so much things right, why does it fail? Because there are two important things that it does wrong. First one is the level design. Even if I love all the chances it gives to use map elements to kill the enemies, every level ends up being a corridor with some arenas in between and some secrets here and there. It's very Serious Sam-esque, but the design of every zone (specially in big arenas) is much worse. Sometimes really dull. It's not enough to leave me in an empty place with some objects and throw a bunch of enemies at me. To do that right you need a place that is awesome. For example, the town fight in one of the last levels of Serious Sam 3, or the different fights in the Egyptian ruins, are leagues beyond anything this game achieve.
But is not only the level design what is flawed, but the enemy design. I'm not only talking about aesthetics, but behavior. Some robots are cool (the one that charges on you), but some other are just dull and the game relies too much in throwing lots of them at you. Again, this works in Serious Sam because every enemy presents a different and well balanced threat. Here it doesn't. Also doesn't help that some of them, if they are a bit far from you, look a lot like the environment, making them difficult to be seen.
This two things lead to some very uninteresting fights, which considering this is a shooter is like a capital flaw.
Talking about the story... well, there's not too much to say. It doesn't help the game, neither kills it. Just an average one which is never very important for the enjoyment of the game.
Considering all of this, I cannot recommend it. And it's a shame, because it's a game I wanted to like, but I just don't enjoy it too much. That doesn't mean some other people won't enjoy it, because it still gets many things right, but here the scale is just a binary yes/no, so this one gets a no.
Anyway, Flying Wild Hog looks like a very promising studio. I'll take a look sooner or later at their Shadow Warrior, and I'll definitely wait for their next projects.

Hand of fate is a Dungeons & Dragons inspired card game with hack 'n slash combat. As you progress through the game and solve quests, more cards become unlocked for you to bolster your deck with. Your opponent, or Dungeon Master, sits across you and deals you the cards as the game unfolds, offering comments, threats, and wry observations as you play.
Combat is fast paced and feels good and different blessings and curses you accrue over the course of the game influence your tactics both in and out of combat. As you solve quests, deal with demons, or help the innocent on your journey, the DM awards you with coins. When you die, and you will die, the coins are shattered and give you new encounters, weapons, armour, and blessings to fill your deck with. But beware, for as you grow in strength, so do your adversaries.
Your deck is the permanent feature of the game. The cards you unlock carry over from one game to the next. Each game you play is like a new adventure. In this respect it kind of reminds me of FTL: Faster than Light, although death isn't nearly as certain in Hand of Fate than it was in FTL (unless you play Endless Mode).
It's compelling, beautiful, and very more-ish. As every individual game is highly influenced by chance, very few games are similar. There are weapons I have yet to use because I haven't drawn them in a game yet, even though I unlocked them many games before. No game sees you go through your entire deck, so you never quite know what to expect, or when to expect it.
TLDR Pro's & Con's
PRO:
Great atmosphere
Random factor (no game ever quite the same)
Persistent rewards
Good solid combat
Feels rewarding (even if you don't win)
Multiple questlines that you play through 'simultaniously' over the course of many games
CON:
Random factor (sometimes the deck is just stacked against you)
No direct control over your starting equipment
Mouse hover-over selection doesn't always work quite right (sticks to first option) so you have to make sure you have the right selection highlighted before making a choice
I highly recommend this game. This is the closest I've seen a PC game come to capturing the feeling of playing an actual table-top card game with someone.

Quality over Quantity
To say that this game is short is an understatement.
This game occupies 3056 MB of space. Yeah, go figure.
That's why they decided to not waste a DVD on it.
THE POSITIVES
1. This is a PC exclusive (a rare breed these days) with the fully optimized graphic options. The controls are smooth and responsive. I also found myself being swept over with feeling again and again that I was playing a PC exclusive. It is worth paying money to have that feeling - that's what the consoles are turning us into.
2. Your character is not a mute like in most shooters.
3. I will say that the new engine delivers. The distant vistas, the textures, the physics, the explosions, the graphics in general are great, DirectX 9.0c and all. The details are meticulous especially up close, you can see the tiniest scratches and dents on the objects.
4. True, there is no health regeneration.
5. The game runs smoothly, no FPS spikes, the dozen or so near-simultaneous explosions are an eye-candy.
6. Upgrades for the 10 weapons as well as the gear is always welcome. However, just like in Witcher 2, as soon as you finish upgrading one "tech tree" or one upgradable branch the game ends.
7. Finally, this game has style. Even though the streets and the slums are empty except for the rampant robots, the peculiar sci-fi world where humanity has learned to download its consciousness into the computer is pretty cool to ponder about.
The minuses:
1. No crouching.
2. No melee (I doubt it's useful against the machines anyway but quite often they do get close enough to ram you)
3. You cannot see your legs and you do not cast a shadow.
4. BUT there is SHIELD regeneration - something the previewers failed to mention. So the concept of the old school no-health-regeneration kinda goes out the window.
5. No reloading.
6. The story is kinda blah.
7. The amount of enemy types is very limited.
8. The jump is realistic. And I by that I mean it is practically nonexistent. You cannot jump over the rails and some other objects even when it seems like you can to save time.
9. The game is extremely short. (4.5 hours)
The debatable table:
1. Initially, there is little to no tactics involved. Once you are met by a group of enemies you will tend to just retreat/move in circles and shoot them up. Since there is no reload option, there really is no incentive for you to stop shooting or taking time for aiming. You will also quickly utilize the environment for more efficient destruction. Tesla coils from the consoles, the explosions from the barrels, the gas balloons, etc., it's all there.
2. The gameplay is a cross of Doom 3, Serious Sam, Pain Killer and perhaps Unreal Tournament. Oh wait, all of those games have the same gameplay, that's right you move fast and you blow things away with the hundreds of rounds of ammo. So do not expect this game to make you ration your ammo or even health for that matter since your shield will regenerate.
3. The game is extremely linear [duh, it's a shooter) although there are plenty of secret areas that can be accessed if you blow up one of the adjacent oil barrels. Do not expect these secret areas to hold any secrets pertaining to the game, you will just find extra ammo most of the time.
In the end, I found myself being sucked into this game nonetheless somehow. True, it is short, but on the other hand, you do not have to commit too much of your time into beating it.

A really challenging title for those of you who like action/platformers. Not very fast paced, but difficult nonetheless.
Disclaimer: the game is in early access, so a lot of things are probably going to change/improve. The review is actual for the 4th of May 2017.
In MegaSphere, your character is investigating why are the stars of Solar System are going dark. It is an action-platformer, where you explore massive randomly-generated levels with well-defined objectives and progression.
-	Challenging difficulty. The game feels really skill based. When you die from the enemy attack – you know exactly how you messed up.
-	Plenty of weapons with different shooting patterns and tactical uses. Weapons can also be upgraded by putting special modules in the slots. I.e. reflection that makes bullets bounce from walls. Shooting also feels nice: the weapons you get at  the start are by no means powerful, but it’s a great feeling when you hit something successfully and then finally destroy it.
-	Great lightning and particle effects: the backgrounds are dark, and they make a great contrast with explosions / other game effects, which are masterfully made. These are hands down some of the best effects I’ve seen in a 2d game.
-	The music and sounds are OK. Not exceptional, but not bad: music does not feel repetitive and gives a good background for playthrough.
-	Environment with destructive elements: some parts of the levels can be destroyed, there are also explosive crates which you can use strategically to damage enemies.
-	The beginning is a bit slow and somewhat boring. There’s a good idea about gradually introducing game features by continuously unlocking them to the player (dash -> gun -> upgrade menu -> codex -> map, etc), but right at the start you need to traverse large spaces without much stuff going on. It gets much better when you enter the second location though.
-	No pausing the game when you open codex / equipment window. It’s probably by intention, but it often prevented me from reading codex / equipping stuff when I felt like it.
-	Maybe a bit more explanation about how saving works? I.e. codex record about this: right now even if I reached the checkpoint before boss, died, then respawned at the same checkpoint a few times, then exited the game – I still get thrown one level back to the checkpoint there.
-	Navigation tab could really use a legend somewhere, because icons of the map are not really obvious (i.e. at least in codex, where weapons are described; the game could do the same with navigation icons: icon – description).
-	AI is sometimes easily fooled (especially with destructive environment) – but in all honesty it does not make the game any less challenging
I think the game got my attention by its difficulty. The no hand-holding approach definitely works here, making fights and exploration entertaining and victories rewarding. Due to this, I can strongly recommend the game.

Final Impressions:
The Medal Master achivement appears, presently, to be unachiveable, as no medals seem to be produced from bot matches and there are insufficient players for proper pvp/quick matches.
The issue with speed vs. fire rate for several weapons still seems to apply (not a lag issue) and this is unfortunate and makes, at least for me, a handful of the weapons totally useless.
I would recommend this game if it were picked up in a bundle and/or certainly if it becomes free. As a standalone purchase however, this game has an insufficient player base to justify the expense.
I suggest to the developers:
1. Hold some Nexuiz events to better market this older title
2. Decrease the stand-alone price and/or add in some additional DLC (between your more active projects) to increase it's cost vs. benefit rating
3. Actively seek to include the title in other bundles to increase availability and perhaps expand the player base (I acquired the game via the Cryengine dev pack on Humble bundle for example).
I am changing the rating on this review to a positive one--as I do find myself playing the game and that, unto itself, speaks volumes.
Third impressions:
Nexuiz is slowly growing on me. No real online multi-player (lack of population). Still having issues with aiming--given run/jump speeds etc. I have yet to receive any medals--so I believe this remains glitched and may have to be worked around for the achivement to trigger for pokemon purposes. Fun for short bursts, but still can't recommend it as an individual purchase at this time.
Second impressions:
CTF is definately the best match type so far--such has remained enjoyable.
Hitbox/accuracy remains an issue--the raw/base movement of characters still seems to surpass actual projectile speed (does not seem to be a lag/graphic setting issue, but more play is needed).
Mutators are enjoyable and afford an excellent, and in a couple instances--funny, variation to some of the other arena games I have played.
Tried some online quick matches. Player population remains very limited. One game was fine (albeit a loss) the other has me questioning how prevalent hacking is amonst the minute player base (1-2 shot kills 8 times in a row within 10s of respawning, and whilst on the run, seems a tad high--but then I am new to this product. However, such was not noticed in any bot matches or my other online/pvp matches to date).
First impressions:
Acquired via the Cryengine Humble Bundle.
Maps are generally well designed. CTF is fun, however, DM is, unfortunately, quite bland.
Both CTF and DM suffer, from what is intended to be a feature, by the ADHD style of movement within Nexuiz. Yes it is fast paced, but so much so that it is more about "spray and pray" than actual aiming/accuracy.
The frequency of powerups/drops et al. is also very high on the maps I've explored to date. This makes resource conservation of little value, thus far, and further supports the "spray and pray" style.
If you want arena combat, akin to Speedy gonzales running around with a rocket launcher, then Nexuiz fits the bill.
I remain hopeful I'll see some value, beyond achievement collecting, in Nexuiz and I will update this review accordingly as additional play time is logged.

Quick Summary: Murdered Soul Suspect is a mystery game more than an action game, so if you’re looking for a shooter or platformer, you won’t find much of that here. I haven’t really played many mystery games so the closest that I can compare this game to is the “investigation” portions of the Batman Arkham series, where you’re in a room with crime scenes trying to piece together what happened. The game has a ton of collectibles, both quest related, and for background on the story, making the experience immersive and decently long if you actually stop to read everything.
You play a police detective named Ronan, killed during an investigation into the “Bell Killer,” a serial killer terrorizing the town of Salem. Yes, it’s the Salem with the Witch trials from hundreds of years ago, and the history of the town will play into your investigation. You’re not alone on your quest though, since a local “medium” who can see ghosts such as yourself, has her own investigation to follow and it happens to coincide with yours. Good thing too, since being a murder victim means you can’t interact with most of the living world.
As a ghost, Ronan has access to certain powers such as the ability to move through solid objects, “possess” random people (you don’t really control them), “reveal” memory remnants, and later on you can teleport short distances.  The game is played in third person perspective with a lot of narration by Ronan, giving it a sort of noir feel (reminds me of Alan Wake, but with no shooting). The town of Salem is pretty small in this game, and despite being a ghost, a lot of areas are off limits to you because of walls and buildings being “consecrated.” There are 2 worlds that you can see at the same time, the real world (that you can walk through objects in) and a ghost world (mostly walls and objects that block your movement). The town is also littered with ghosts other than yourself that you can talk to. Some of them have mini quests (investigations) that you can take part in, but most of them are just there for short conversations, adding to the game’s atmosphere. I actually stopped talking to random ghosts about 1/3 into the game since most of them don’t have anything story related to tell you.
As I mentioned before, this is not an action game so you don’t really fight anyone, however there are a number of “demons” roaming the town in story related areas. You can either avoid the demons by stealthily sneaking around, or you can try to banish them by sneaking up behind them and executing a quick time event. You can see the demons through walls, so it’s possible to get around them if you have ninja hiding skills. Frankly, I suggest banishing them all so you can roam freely and pick up all the collectibles in each area.
Pros:
+A decent, slow paced mystery story with some twists and turns. You’re playing this game for the story more than anything else.
+The investigations are kind of fun, searching for clues and piecing together events after you’ve gotten the hang of it.
Cons:
-If you’re mostly into shooting games, you may find yourself bored. There’re some stealth sections, but the majority of the game is puzzle solving and searching for clues.
-The game uses an autosave system that isn’t very well explained.  There are times where it shows the “saving” icon, but if you quit and reload you’ll be missing a bunch of progress/clues.  I recommend completing side quests separate from main story sections (don’t go back and forth between side quest and main quest) and then move on to the story section. The only time I could be sure the game had saved was when I entered a new area in the story.
Overall, I’d recommend this game if you’re looking for a moderately easy “thinker” game, and are taking a break from action/shooting. If you’re just going through the main investigations of the story and not bothering with side missions or collectibles, you can probably finish in about 7 hours.

While most reviews on games tend to give you a good idea of what the game will feel like when you play it, I don't believe any review I've read has perfectly portrayed what Archeage is. There has been so much negative stigma attached to Trion and this game that I almost never tried it since so many people warned me not to.
To put it into the simplest terms, there is some seriously positive and negative things about this game that people overlook when they hear "pay to win."
To get straight to the point, The list of things I find lovely about this game:
-

This game is very lovely and serene. I'm sure many would have a differing opinion but compared to many other mmorpgs, this one certainly raises to the top in both graphics and the background music.
Aside from the beautiful world, the character customization is fairly detailed and gives plently of options to allow the       creation of characters that are unique and different.
-

This has always been important to me and it's one of the main reasons I couldn't continue to play Final Fantasy XIV Online. Archeage, as far as I've experienced, is completely open world without really any loading screens after you begin playing your character (with the exception of portals). This is great for the feeling of immersion and stops the game from being choppy.
-

Unlike games such as World of Warcraft or Guild Wars 2, there's not exactly a profession system. The best thing about Archeage is that you get free range over crafting, no choosing between leatherworking or alchemy, you can do every single profession without having to stick with just one. This is a system I personally enjoy, especially since each profession tends to go hand and hand with eachother.
-

This seems stupid, but it's a small detail about this game I absolutely adore. In every game I've experienced, you buy a mount from a vendor, hope you get it from a dungeon/raid, or as a reward from an achievement. It doesn't necessarily work like that in Archeage. Yes, you can buy them from vendors, but usually only as little baby mounts which you have to raise by growing food to feed them, giving them water, entertaining them and giving them attention until they've grown full size. It's something I enjoy simply because It helps develop the player relationship with their mounts/companions by having raised them and being able to give them their own names.
-

When you create your character you're given six different classes to choose from, which is a pleasant amount for pretty much any mmorpg, but it gets so much more in depth as you start to level. Once you choose your initial class, you are allowed two more skill sets to create your own custom fighting style and the best part is, you can switch it out anytime you want without losing progress. For example, If you wanted to try sorcery and added occultism as your second skill set, after you get your third (we'll say witchcraft), you can switch any of them out any time you want for a different skill. It basically allows you play and level every skillset on just one character which gives a lot of freedom.
-

While there is a good amount of content around combat and questing, you'll find that there are many small things you can interact with and manipulate. Housing and farming is a huge attraction to this game, and while it's pretty much reserved for subscribers (unless you're in a guild), it's kind of charming to see the many little player farms each decorated to their own liking and sitting cozily next to eachother. With how big the world is, you often get gliders and row boats as well that are equally as charming when you're just floating above towns taking your time to reach the ground.
Unfortunately, with every good aspect to a game, there's always the bad ones, the ones that have been talked about repeatedly in an effort to get you to turn back before you play.
With that being said, there's quite a few issues I've had with this game:
-

What are labor points? Labor points can be thought of as energy that you use on ANY action not pertaining to combat, you know: gardening, planting, crafting, identifying weapons and armor, opening coinpurses, honestly there's not much you can't do without labor points. The problem is, as someone who is free to play, you don't get a whole bunch. It pretty much encourages you to log on and minimize it to the task bar while you go watch a movie or something just to get your labor points up. Usually you get five points every five minutes, and sadly, they don't accumulate while your logged off. However, if you become a patron you get 10 points every 5 minutes, along with a higher labor point cap and they accumulate while you're logged out. This would not be such a problem for me if they gave you more character slots with a subscription, but they don't. You can play every class on one character so why would you need more than one character? But my problem is, there are four different races and if you're like me, you like to at least try out the different starting areas and characters, and this is especially hard with the deletion time when you decide you don't like a character you've made.
My advice, if you make a character and dislike it, try to delete it before you get above level 10, and DO NOT delete two characters at once. The wait time for a character to delete tends to increase with the longer you have them/the higher the level they are and you CANNOT create a new character while you're deleting another one (Unless you already had another character slot open). There is a reason for this, from what I read, it's to prevent the creation of characters just to receive property and then delete them so that their main character can take it. I'm not entirely sure if this is why, but regardless, it's irritating and takes into account that the restriction on character slots makes this process all the more painful.

Indie games are often maligned (often incorrectly) by certain people who claim that they are done cheaply, cobbled-together or just somehow "lesser" games. Whilst there might be some games you could reasonably say this of, Hard Reset is a shining example of how this statement isn't always true.
The graphic fidelity shown here is stunning for such a small developer, and the world created is very believable and detailed. As soon as you jump in, you definitely get a Bladerunner kind of vibe going on, and it serves to create an excellent atmosphere.
I personally found the story to be a bit generic and therefore lacking (although I do confess in not exactly being a story person for games), but this doesn't really matter as the game does so well in it's execution. From the very start, the game sets a good pace, along with a fair challenge that never feels cheap or unreasonable. From the very first battle, I found the lovely destructive explosions of the robots expiring along with the smacks and clanks of hitting the machinery incredibly satisfying.
The only real downside I had with the game is in it's length - it's a few short hours, and does indeed feel like it's only getting going when it ends.  I understand this may be mended somewhat with the inclusion of the DLC, but I haven't played it myself so can't comment.
So, on balance I'd say for it's full price of £9.99, you might be better served by looking elsewhere. However, if it comes up on offer for anything less, then it is a worthy purchase.
I think it may end up surprising you!

Created a Battle; Humans Vs Orcs
Hour 1:
All seems well. My peasants are happily gathering materials such as stone, gold and food. I have captured a orc outpost, and have found some gold caches guarded by wolves. I made a stone wall around my castle, some turrets have mounted trebuchets on them.
Hour 2:
The Orcs have attacked me. I destroyed their siege equipment, and now my archers are slaughtering them by the droves. The Orcs have retaken their outpost, which is located close to my base. In both skirmishes i have lost a good amount of men.
Hour 3:
*hear moans* huh, thats some pretty bad orc audio.
From the battlegrounds dead orcs and humans alike are rising from the dead. Undead ogres start to appear out of the fog of war.
Hour 3.5:
I have rung the bell of war. All peasants are now inside my base. All battalions are recalled, and everyone man, women and child armed to the teeth. My palisade wall is gone, and with it some of my hope. Zombies have come from everywhere, my walls are being attacked as we speak. My barracks are pumping out pikemen and swordsman.
Hour 4:
My first gate has fallen. I have sustained heavy casualties, but i think I have managed to stem the flow of zombies. I feel hopeful.
Hour 4.25:
My last gate has fallen. All the hope we had felt quickly turned to horror as men we had fought along turned into zombies.Their corpses re-animated. By making more men to defend against the zombies, we have simply given them more soldiers. I have lost contact with the orcs, I feel that they too are in a dire situation.
Hour 4.5:
This is the last entry, I have a small ring of pikemen keeping the zombies at bay. One by one they are falling, my wizard is exhausted, his spells have long been used up. He quickly stumbles, and is killed by the zombies. The castle is lost, overrun by the undead.

Ok, so clearly there is a rabid fan base for this game and the ratings are generally positive - thus I bought the game. The graphics are solid and the overall UI looks appealing... but after playing for two afternoons I'm a bit stunned there isn't more of a balance in the reviews. For the positives, read the others. This review is going to point out just a few of the negatives of this game that will save you a few bucks.  I'll start by saying I love these kinds of games generally. I've played Civ since the first, all the total wars, and hang around with my kids setting up armies once in a while. I love war strategy games and the more complex the better... this is not one of those.
- Deceptive advertising: This game is for historical simulation buffs, not strategy game buffs. The rule set and complexity of the game will only add to the fun for a very, very small number of snobbish gamers that like to argue over ducal claims to Leon. (They also like to write reviews apparently). The action posed knight on the cover art + total war like game map is deceptive. This is a game of endless spreadsheets, stats, and family trees that are eternally obscure.
- The tutorial is poor. Before even pointing out your primary goals, (still not sure what they are), you have to find the impossible wife ("Healthy" was not one of my options, but part of the instructions), and fabricate a claim on a muslim island.  What?!?  Then they just leave you like a bad habit with hundreds of buttons that don't mean much. Good luck sucker.  Somewhere in the distance I can hear some putz designer saying, "Scaling, we don't need to stinking scaling!" So if you finish the tutorial, go ahead, and try to whip up a "normal" game... how's that going for you? Did you really learn to play in their tutorial?
- Choices. Complexity should amount to more meaningful decisions to make. This game boils down to 1) keep vassals happy, 2) fabricate/push claims on territories, and 3) make babies and waaaaaaait for them to grow up. Tech trees? bah. Strategy? bah. Defences? Not needed.  Just play matchmaker and bribe people.  No need to actually give the player something to consider and plan for...
- Game Balance. Wait, why is the person that I just gave a duchy to still mad at me?  Why should I care? Looking carefully I am apparantly a "Tyrant" (-70) because a turn ago I removed a title from someone that just led a rebellion... Tyrant? Really?!? and -70 essentially overrides ten or so positive elements... seriously, just one example of preposterous rule sets that whack the game out regularly.  Some may thing this is interesting, realistic, detailled, or something, but the emperor simply has no clothes on people! This game is lame, boring, and frustrating... and far from realistic.
- Fun.  Oh yeah, that counts for a computer game too!
Still, I may just not be as smart as the folks that gave this a good rating, or they may have thought it would be funny to give you bad advice and see how many might still buy this.  You may enjoy games that have you looking at charts and meaningless attributes all day so that you can watch the computer tick off random events. To each their own. This game is not for me.

Hard Reset is like some strange and wondrous artifact from an alternate universe, one where technology continued to advance after the 90's, but none of the corridor shooter tropes we see in games nowadays ever caught on.  It combines oldschool FPS gameplay from the Unreal era with shiny modern visuals, then adds a light sprinkling of modern shooter mechanics (a regenerating shield meter, two basic weapons that can be upgraded into several very different forms) that enhance the core gameplay without overwhelming it.  Graphic novel-style cutscenes between levels tell a serviceable cyberpunk tale that provides context for all the shooting, but once the action starts, the story elements have the good grace to step aside and let you get down to business.  The levels are open and reward exploration, with secrets to find and explosive items scattered about that let you set up environmental kills - another nod to oldschool design.
If you have even the slightest interest in oldschool FPS's, you owe it to yourself to check out Hard Reset.

I recommend this game, BUT at a discount.  During a sale or something.
I think the game is pretty fun, but has a few flaws that keep it from beign significantly better.  I've never been really into Dungeons and Dragons, but I've always thought the concept was fun.  Basically, this takes some of the ideas of dungeon exploring from D&D and puts you in the place of the single player of the game, playing against the Dungeon Master.  As a genius add-on, rather than rolling dice to determine the outcome of enemy encounters, you enter a 3D action battle that plays very much like the Batman: Arkham series (which I really enjoyed).  Overall, great idea and production quality.
On the overall card/exploring portion of the game:
The idea is fun and I enjoy running into new cards and seeing the outcome and individual stories as they unfold over multiple playthroughs.   Each run plays similar to a rogue-like in that you play a ~20 minutes session where you start from scratch and progress through a dungeon, trying to become more powerful while maintaining your life, food and gold.  Here's where it takes a turn.
I enjoy hard games.  But I like to have the difficult and whether I win or not depend on my skill, not luck.  The game has multiple difficulty settings, but I feel like it either needs more (preferred choice) or needs to balance them better.  I find normal mode to be incredibly easy, where hard mode is too hard.  I play a run on normal mode and come out with far more life and strength than I went in with, rarely even being hit by enemies, or play hard mode and only make it half-way through the run.  Well, get better!  This is part of it, but often times, as mentioned by other reviewers, you run into an unlucky location and  half of your max life, most of your food, etc...   I would say that combat is about 4x harder on hard mode than on normal mode because: 1. The enemies are stronger. 2. There are twice as many of them.  It would be nice to be able to balance the difficulty with a mode between normal and hard. Maybe where there are twice as many of them, but they aren't stronger.
All-in-all I think the dungeon portion of the game is fun, but can be frustrating when everything goes down the tube over the course of 3 steps.
As far as teh combat:
I really enjoy  the combat style and feel that it complements the game well.  That being said, it could use quite a bit of polish.  After having played the first two Batman: Arkham games on hard mode and mastering the challenges, I feel that I am pretty good at the combat.  That carries over to some degree here.  The Batman games  (at least on hard mode) are heavily combo focused and require you to keep an eye on your enemies, the combo counter and plan your next move carefully.  Trying to attack an enemy that is down or trying to counter when an enemy has not begun an attack ruins your combo.  This is all the same in Hand of Fate BUT it is not nearly as clear what is happening.  When you finish an enemy on Batman, you hear a "Whoosh" sound.  You know he is down.  As crazy as it may get sometimes, you have all of the indicators to know exactly what is happening with each enemy on the battlefield at all times.  In Hand of Fate, collisions are often screwy, it can be hard to tell who is dead and who is not and counters seem to misfire fairly often.  It's pretty regular to attack an enemy you didn't mean to.  With the challenges of hard mode I would feel prepared to take it on if I had better control and awareness in battle.
Overall, I think it is a fun game.  Take the great parts of the rogue-like genre, D&D and the Batman: Arkham games and combine them, but be aware of the significant issues that come along with this.

Kingdom wars 2 is an RTS in the classic style with some intresting intricacies and improvements on the overall formula. There are a few main recources: food, gold, wood, stone, and population. Where the game shines in my opinion is the differeing abilities to gather these recources. For instance, after a battle you can task peasants to loot corpses for gold and valuable loot, and as they do so they will also make sure the soldiers that died dont come back from the dead. Which brings me to arguably the most fun part of this game, the zombies. The zombies are a dynamic RTS threat that I have not seen done anywhere else and they are enough to pick this game up if you see it on sale.
When fighting the zombies you have to take a completely different approach to combat. If you send waves after waves of enemies to get chopped up by them youll only make the situation worse, because those freshly dead corpses will rise up from the grave to haunt you. If they get out of hand they can easily overwhelm you and with a combined effort topple your walls and destroy your recources crippling you completely as they overwhelm your stronghold. Being defeated by the zombies is almost fighting them.
Keep in mind this review is only for the single player, as I have not tried the multiplayer, but even as a solitary experience I found this game worth a buy at sale cost.

I had some concerns after deeply regretting investing in Funcom's other gaming franchises but against my better judgement I chose to give Conan Exiles a chance.
I shouldn't have.
Funcom has been able to demonstrate yet again that they still suffer a curse of terrible decision making. Funcom is known to have conceptually fantastic titles that completely fail to deliver in various aspects but almost all of which can be attributed to someone at the top of the organization chain being entirely clueless about how to operate a AAA title.
The first few days after launch I experienced the very much anticipated latency and rubberbanding issues many others have described. There also is a litany of very frustrating bugs which, although annoying, are understandable with an early-access release.
But why I cannot recommend the game is much more complex than simple gameplay issues. As of right now, Funcom has zero officially hosted servers online. The only servers currently available to play on are servers run and managed by other players. It takes mere seconds and a youtube search for "admin abuse" to see why many players including myself systematically refuse to play games in environments where fellow players can ban you.
The reason for this is simple: Funcom yet again took the cheapest possible route when determining how to host their servers. They chose to cut corners and allow a third-party startup company to brand themselves as an "official conan exiles server host" in exchange for reduced or free infrastructure costs. To nobodys surprise, this host (PingPerfect) was completely and totally unprepared to serve as a host for this game and Funcom chose to completely suspend hosting official servers.
The developers and folks responsible for actually designing Funcom's portfolio do not deserve to suffer the incredibly poor decision making of the management at the top and the players certainly don't deserve it either because the game itself seems to have potential if only it wasn't stymied by the idiots in Funcom's board room.

I ONLY KIND OF RECOMMEND THIS GAME WITH THESE CAVEATS:
I do NOT recommend paying 25 dollars for it (which is the going price as of the writing of this review.)
I've put a good 30 hours into it so far, and I think after beating the final challenge, I'll be done with it until there is more DLC or a HoF2. Once you've completed the encounters, there's really only a few variants in Endless mode that are somewhat interesting, but I don't think I'll be playing through them all, as they consist of encounters I've seen a million times.
The gameplay consists of a randomly dealt and organized map of cards which you traverse. When you complete encounter cards, you get tokens, which unlock new items, encounters, and more, which pertain to the cards defeated. The difficulty of these encounters ramps up very quickly and sometimes seem impossible with their ridiculous requirements, which bank almost soley on your luck in drawing the right encounters previously.
This is a huge problem, as a lot of the encounters rely on luck rather than skill. The bigger problem is, a lot of skill portions rely on how well your luck is at picking success cards in those encounters (if you can't play Four Card Monte and follow the Success cards, you will not enjoy this game). It took me a lot of grinding to finish a lot of the encounter cards, and as of right now, I still have not beaten the main Story mode, because you are restricted by the curses you are given when you enter a level, and the last boss has ridiculously overpowered curses that make the last level about luck rather than challenge.
The combat in this game is similar to the Batman Arkham games, which is cool, and very close to as smooth as those games. But the VERY limited enemy selection and TRUE boss battles (not just better versions of main enemies) makes this tedious over time. The selection of weapons gets bigger as you finish more encounters, but as you are given them randomly during play, a perfect loadout is left to chance, which is mostly ok, considering a perfect loadout would make you practically invincible, but not ok when you end up with nothing at the end of a dungeon because of a poorly placed random chance card.
I purchased this game when it was on sale for 9.99, and I think at that price, it's worth it. If you are someone who enjoys a challenge, this is a very challenging game, but the challenge is mixed in with a fair amount of true unfairness, which I think sometimes is confused for challenge.
Just know that this will be frustrating as all get-out.
