MegaSphere is a futuristic 2D platforming action game developed by AKGames. In MegaSphere you play as ATAI, a special ops combat unit that has been sent to investigate some strange goings on with a few nearby stars. You find yourself in a strange installation filled with deadly robots and strange references to something known as the Half-Dead god.
Full disclosure: A review copy was provided by the developer.
Up first I’m going to talk about my two biggest issues with the game (which will be addressed in the next update though it currently has no expected release time). These issues are the lack of a save system and the lack of any real direction in the game. The lack of a save system is pretty self-explanatory and it means that you have to start over again every time you quit. It can get pretty frustrating (even with the current amount of content) if you have to keep restarting the same area, plus the levels are randomly generated so if you were trying to do something in particular and you have to leave, you might as well give up on doing that since you may not see it the next time you load that area. As I said, my second problem is with the lack of direction in the game, hopefully this’ll be fixed by the addition of quests as well as a chunk of story in the upcoming update I mentioned. As it stands though, MegaSphere ends up feeling like an exploration game more than anything else. I enjoyed wandering through the six different areas currently in the game, killing enemies and crafting new weapons, but after looking around all of the different areas I feel like I’ve seen all there is to see, even with randomly generated levels and that’s a tad disappointing. Once these are addressed in the next update I’ll update my review and re-write or remove this paragraph.
On to what is undoubtedly the game’s greatest strength, its visuals. MegaSphere is incredibly good looking, it has some of the best pixel art I’ve seen in games and its design is consistent throughout. It’s definitely one of the best looking games that uses the Unity engine. The visual effects in the game are also awesome. There’s good variation between all the different weapons and there are some particularly cool effects for when you get close to dying, though with any luck you won’t be seeing much of them! The menus and UI are also pretty good but they’re being streamlined in the next update which should make them even better.
Next to walking around, combat is what you’ll spend your time doing, thankfully it’s pretty good. There are a few different types of enemies each with very different ways of engaging you which makes combat with more than one type of enemy particularly interesting. A couple of the enemy types also have different variations, the different variations have different appearances as well as different attacks, further diversifying the game’s combat. It’s pretty challenging on normal difficulty (there is an easier difficulty if you do find it a little too hard) but once you figure out how all of the different enemies work it does become reasonably easy to predict how they’re going to attack which means you can try and avoid their attacks. Once you’ve figured this out you can also start using the environment to your advantage by standing/hiding out of range of an enemy and shooting at them from there.
Killing enemies always drops health but sometimes you’ll also get weapons, upgrades and shields. You begin with three health segments on your health bar but when you collect health it just adds new segments if you have full health. I’ve only made it as far as six full segments before losing health so I’m not sure what the maximum amount is. A shield simply goes on top of your health bar and offers you more protection, they don’t recharge though so you’ll have to find a new one once yours is fully drained.
There are quite a few different weapons in the game, ranging from the burst rifle you start with to a grenade launcher and even a flaming bear gun! All of the weapons have advantages and disadvantages so they are mostly balanced though the flaming bear gun does seem to be considerably better than any of the other weapons. Sometimes the weapons come with upgrades (the flaming bear seems to always come with all three upgrade slots filled) but they can also come with no upgrades which means you’ll need to find upgrade tokens as well as upgrades to fully upgrade them.
Upgrading weapons currently takes place in the game’s inventory menu. Each weapon (providing it doesn’t already have upgrades installed) has three slots for new upgrades, one of which can be attached ‘for free’ while the other two can only be attached using upgrade tokens which are sometimes dropped by enemies. There are quite a few different upgrades, including speed increases and upgrades that make your projectiles bounce off walls. However, not all of the upgrades are effective for all of the weapons and it does take a bit of experimentation to figure out what works best for which weapons. There are also different levels of upgrades (I’ve seen up to and including three so far) and as you’d expect, the higher the upgrade’s level is the more it improves your weapon.
As I mentioned earlier, there are only six areas in the game. Two of them don’t have enemies, one is a boss fight area and the other three are just ‘regular’ areas filled with all the enemies. There are visual differences between all the different levels as well as some things you only find in certain areas. Every time you play an area the game randomly generates the level so you’ll never have exactly the same experience twice though the levels will look pretty familiar. The reason they aren’t completely random is because there is a story running between the different levels, I don’t want to spoil too much (and to be honest I don’t understand it enough to spoil it anyway) but the game’s story seems to revolve around strange gods worshipped by whatever created the installation you’ve found yourself on. There’s not a whole lot of story in there at the moment but what’s there is most certainly intriguing.
Last but by no means least, controls. For combat and generally moving around they’re pretty good (I played with an Xbox One controller) but they did feel a tad bit clunky for platforming. There were several times in the game where I had to attempt jumps between platforms a few times before I actually made it. It’s not a huge problem (though it’s still pretty frustrating) during regular gameplay but you could quickly end up dead if you run into a particularly tricky platforming section during combat.
MegaSphere is a beautiful game with good gameplay and a mysterious story behind it but the amount of content in the game at the moment, as well as the lack of direction, does, for me at least, let the game down a little bit. I feel that comparisions to the original game is necessary when writing a review for Mass Effect 2, so here it goes:
1. Like Mass Effect, Mass Effect 2 is a story-rich 3rd-person FPS where you play as Commander Sheperd. However, the story was not as captivating as ME1 and it seemed that I spent more time assembling and gaining the loyalty of my crew than on the main campaign, which in retrospect was pretty short and straightforward.
2. The combat system was an improvement from ME1, where it was much easier to utilise abilities (both yours and your squad's) by binding them to the numerical keys. However, combat got really repetitive after a while. The hacking/ bypassing system was also an improvement, although mostly unnecessary and also repetitive.
3. Anyone who played the original game would remember the dreadfully long elevator rides. Thankfully, ME2 had smoother transitioning and also higher quality cut-scenes which were very enjoyable.
4. Like in ME1, it was possible to flirt/ develop relationships with a number of crewmates, although you would have to complete your target's loyalty quest before you could express interest. However, I was disappointed when Liara (ME1 character) could not be recruited into my squad, even though she did make an appearance in the game.
I gave ME1 a rating of 9.5/10 only because of the elevator rides. While ME2 was a good game, it seemed to be lacking in story and also its descent into repetitiveness.

Story – Owlboy stars a young protagonist named Otus who, after a series of events, ventures forth into the floating world to protect it from fearsome pirates. While the premise starts out fairly simple, the plot thickens and turns in a way later on that will leave the player engaged. The charming character designs coupled with their unique personalities (some of which also have backstories to discover through dialogue and environmental interaction) also lend to populating the game with interesting and memorable characters. Late in the game, Owlboy’s story will leave the player with a nice mystery behind the lore of the game’s world, which has already left players coming up with theories on how it ties to the current events happening around Otus and friends.
Gameplay – Owlboy’s gameplay is unique in which the player will spend most of their time flying above ground while carrying one of three companions you’ll unlock as you progress through the game, each with their own unique way of dealing with enemies and puzzles. It essentially comes down to a gunner to shoot enemies/objects at long range, a shotgunner that deals a lot of damage at short range and can be used to burn obstacles, and a companion that can trap enemies and zip the player around the level to avoid hazards.
Unlike most platformers, this game takes a Zelda/Metroid-esque approach where the player explores an open world and will find themselves in dungeon-like areas to progress through the story, rather than progressing right to the next level. Combat in the game primarily consists of the player using the gunner character to shoot at enemies, but sometimes may require timing or melee hits to reveal enemy weaknesses. The first half of the game is relatively easy, with the latter half ramping in difficulty, especially bosses.
There are plenty of unlockables, collectibles and hidden achievements in the game, some of which are hidden behind walls and in plain sight. If you’re a perfectionist, this will add a nice chunk of time to the game’s length which is both a good thing and bad thing. Good thing is there’s plenty to collect, like weapon upgrades for your characters, hats, story bits and an upgrade for Otus himself. Bad thing is, while there are a few shortcuts in Owlboy’s world, the lack of fast travel will make getting those last 3 coins you missed in the second dungeon a bit of a pain.
Music – Owlboy’s music is wonderfully composed as each piece sets the mood and pace of whatever setting/situation you may find Otus and friends in. The overworld music has a feeling of grandeur while escaping harrowing situations has a tense sense of panic and dread. The soundtrack is definitely many will find themselves listening to while the game itself isn’t playing.
Graphics –Owlboy’s graphics are rendered in beautiful pixel art featuring vibrant colors, characteristic animations, night/day cycles and hand crafted environments. Many background graphics are unique in that they rarely share tiles sets and appear as grand set pieces for dungeons, character’s homes, and boss showdowns. Characters are brought to life through expressive poses, subtle sub-pixel animation and character interaction that really leaves the player empathizing with them. This really comes across through Otus, who heavily relies on these animations as he himself can’t speak. Turned eyebrows, cheery smiles and bulging eyes all lend to the character and easily communicate to the player what Otus and other characters are feeling.

Used to play this a lot on Xbox 360, and I snagged a key as a part of their current promotion. It's a pretty competent little arena shooter, here's some quick pros and cons:
Pros:
+Pretty nice looking, especially given it's age.
+Gun mechanics are solid and consistent, a must for any arena shooter.
+Map design is pretty solid.
+Bots are present and provide a decent amount of challenge if you crank the difficulty up.
Cons:
-Not really any players at all. Which sucks, because this game has competitive potential. You'll be playing bots or your friends who own the game, and not really anyone else.
-Menus are bland and often confusing to use, especially so when setting up custom matches.
-Occasional bugs, nothing game breaking however.
Questionable Things:
-The randomized mutators. While they are fun, you have to turn them off to get any true competitive play, because their random nature upsets the game balance more often than not.
So, all in all, it's a competent game. I recommend it because it does have bot play, and it's not too pricey. It'll at least scratch your arena shooter itch until UT4 comes out of Alpha.

Twists and turns are interesting and are somewhat hard to guess so it gets a point from there but at some point you get sick of the amount of the amount of superweapons that the Empire has, at some point it makes you think, do our R&D dept. is sitting twigling their thumbs for years while they build stuff that makes you go, its horribly impractical but i want that. On the name, yes you see you will be surprised how many attractive anime girls and sometimes people that makes you go " WHAT ARE YOU?!" Though it is quite flavorful, the main thing it adds to the genre is cute anime girls, which is a welcome addition to almost anything
Presentation : Graphics are nicely styled and game length is decent it took me about 19 hours to finish main story at least according to my save, i might have gone afk for some time but i felt like the game was really long enough. Music, voice acting etc, were exemplary it never broke immersion, whatever broke it was in the gameplay which brings us toooo
Gameplay: BY GOD, HOW CAN YOU RUIN IT SO BADLY, here is the thing, in game design, you need to have rules and variation to those to keep things interesting, which is nice but in almost every mission that comes to mind , the rules change so much that you need a walkthrough for example,  most missions involve the variations of, go here and capture these camps, which is nice but then you start encountering the kind of units you are not prepared for such as artillery which can 1 shot most of your men and you have no idea, sometimes taking cover uses too much walking points sometimes it doesn't the units level up and change so fast that you have no way of predicting their range unless you replay the mission. All of these complaints come from 2 things, game constantly throwing in new things and the core game mechanics of, when you aim stop getting fired at which completely breaks all semblence of immersion. The other big one is the Orders, in this game you can give orders that use command points which are used to play your units but you never know if that order is useless or overpowered until you use it, it only says it increases defence but by how much? You dont know until you try it.
As such in my opinion as someone who casually watches anime and loves strategy games, this is too much anime too little strategy. If your idea of strategy is replaying missions for 1-3 times ( iplayed final mission 3 times before i beat it ) then go ahead but the whole cutesy atmosphere and cliche characters as well as constantly unfair conditions ( you fight dozens of enemies on average which is fun for the most part). This game is simply not for most western gamers in my opinion but as i said, for me i am torn betwee recommending and not recommending it and went with no but barely.

Listen, I understand why the game isn't perfect. Some people know how to swing a sword in a way physics does not concur with, I can't argue that. But, why I still play it, is because it is the most intense competitive multiplayer game i've ever played. I've played my share of fps's, they're fun and exhilarating, but in the end, a fight consists primarily (if not solely) upon who can click on the other guy the best while attempting to move in a random pattern as to make yourself more difficult to be clicked on. Chivalry, on the other hand is a much more involved fight. You feel like you're actually in a physical fight. The hit detection (while definitely quirky sometimes and hard to pick up on) is consistent and responsive (I know it doesn't feel that way at first, but once you get used to it, it's works). You have to block the tip of the weapon, as it's about to hit you, you have 4 different attack + kick at your arsenal, you can perform fancy legit moves like the 180 swing, jump overhead attack to get over shields, a lot of fun can be had (and this is why it's difficult to deem a move legit or not), looking up and down bends your back, so you can duck under a side attack or lean back out of the way of a stab (it takes practice but its awesome when it happens. Ever watching fight after you die is like watching a fighting match. Granted:
-Blocking a long stab weapon from close range has always been confusing and frustrating. One can stab to the side, the adjust to make their stab into a kind of cheap swing, I would say they need to make stabs very slow to adjust mid swing as stabbing is supposed to be a fine, accurate attack, not some sloppy stab looping.
-One can "drag" their weapon, real time adjusting their swing in the opposite direction to slow down the swing in time to pass their parry. While this is technically legit, I believe a slowed swing should do less damage for obvious reasons.
-One can real-time adjust their swing in such a way that is very spastic and near impossible to predict, this makes them leet. While I know its a video game, it's supposed to at least imitate realistic physics and human movement (not being fantasy(the lore isn't historical, we'll put it that way)). Sporadically swinging a 20 pound iron block on a 4 foot stick like it was a sock em bopper is neither.
But*, despite all that unpolished nonsense, this is a whole new breed of fast paced first person fighter that you can't find anywhere else (it's faster and more organic than war of roses or that viking one).
If you want to get into a fast paced, intense, fun melee, try it, you'll get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes, sure, but it's still a blast.

The premise of this game is simple enough.
In a world of magic and adventure, a town exists around the entrance to a dungeon, attracting the best and the brightest, who try their luck searching for fame and fortune.
You are not one of them. You are the person they buy their equipment from.
So, in Recettear, you play as Recette, an adorable little girl who has to pay off her deadbeat father's debt, or else the fairy mafia will break her little loli legs.
It's an interesting spin on a genre we've all played before, and the mechanics are quite fun - there's nothing quite as enjoyable as buying a solid gold statue in a market where precious metals have nosedived, only to wait out the storm, and sell it for a 230% of it's original price.
A basic understanding of 'Buy low, sell high', is all you need to run a successful business, even if the fairy mob takes a massive chunk of your profits every week. I can't even comprehend the debt left by by Recette's dad.
But the economics is only part of the game, with a procedurally generated dungeon system to add to it. This is where you get the stupid adventurers (that you sell overpriced products to) to risk their lives for your profits.
It's simple enough, with the gameplay reminding me of the Mystery Dungeon series.
In addition, the characters are all somewhat charming, and the game generally makes you feel good, be it from Recette's endless appetite and boundless optimism, Charme's inability to hold her liquor, or Tear's straight man act.
I don't rate things on an x/10 scale, but I enjoyed it, and I certainly think that you should give it a chance.

Disregard the time it says I have played this game for on my steam account. I have played this game since it was in beta, and have streamed countless hours of it. - The first MMORPG to be 2.5D and still have relatively smooth gameplay
Cons:
- Extremely broken PvP (I myself used to non stop do PvP because it was a challenge, and took a lot of skill at the time. As of the past 2 or so years, they continue to remove core features and old skills of characters that made PvP fun and difficult, and give the characters extreme damage buffs and simple and spammy combos instead. Good matches used to last easily over 3 minutes and took a lot of brain power. If you get lucky with the current state of the game, the longest match you'll have will last you just less than a minute.)
- Terrible staff (The staff of the game listens to nobody but themselves, and they believe they know what the community want. The community wants the game to be like it was in 2012-2014. They think the changes they make are actually helping the game mature and get better, but it's doing the exact opposite. The only difference these great weapons made in the past was the damage you did in PvE, it rarely affected your damage in PvP. You could destroy +11 users with a +0 weapon if you were good enough back in the day. Now, they've added up to +13, and people are paying to get easy enhancements to one shot in PvP. Really I'd like to choose neither yes or no to reccomending this because it depends on if you own ETS2 already....
Pros:
It's a new map in ETS2!
New trucks!
Cons:
It's literally just ETS2 but in America. (nothing against America but it would serve better as an expansion to ETS2 rather than a standalone game) The UI is completely the same as ETS2 with very few changes.
The map is scaled down and cities are scaled up compared to ETS2, so you go from one town to the next in nearly no time at all
There are only 3 trucks. Two Kenworth and one Peterbilt. I understand there are licensing issues with adding more trucks but compared to the 12 in ETS2 this isn't worth the £14.99 atm.
Conclusion:
It's not worth the asking price atm. So far there are only two states (Arizona coming soon!), the majority of states will be paid DLC (not a bad thing in itself but...) on a smaller map scale (less bang for your buck). If this were released as DLC for ETS2 (I know, it's not Europe. It's America) with the ability to travel to/from the USA at will OR if it were released with the larger ETS2 map scale and compatability with your ETS2 trucks and save file then I could fully recommend this. Unfortunately, if you already have ETS2 then stick with that unless you desperately need to drive in America. If you don't have ETS2 then choose between driving in Europe and America. All in all it's not a bad game but considering the similarities to ETS2 and the lack of features at the moment it's not worth the purchase, consider waiting until more content is released or the price drops.

Recettear is a JRPG where you play as an item shop owner.  The story is simple compared to most JRPG's, frequently making fun of common JRPG tropes, but it manages to remain a charming tale nontheless, and does have its touching moments.  Some characters seem a little flat, but most of them are well developed, and nearly all of them are memorable.  Gamplaywise- Recettear's mechanics have a solid depth to them, while remaining simple enough for anyone to easily grasp them.  Do you want a game you can pick up and play with little thought once you've learned the controlls?  Recettear is that game.  Do you want a game you can spend countless hours diving deep in to the inner workings of its systems, crunching data as you maximize your odds of success?  Recettear is also that game.  To anyone who enjoys Anime, RPGs, or Business simulations; I can't recomend this game enough.

If you ever loved arena shooters like Heretic, Quake, Duke 3D, etc... then you will feel right at home with Hard Reset. It has a great aesthetic and the fast paced action packed FPS gameplay I loved growing up. There are no chest high walls, just giant robots, little robots, and more giant robots all trying to rip your head off or explode you into gibs. A perfect sci-fi run and gun with massive difficulty on the harder settings, Hard Reset will really test your skills.
My only criticism is that the weapons system is a bit clunky, you have up to 10 available to you, but you never find them, you purchase them in game, and it is impossible to tell which ones you will like using before you've bought them. On the harder modes it takes a LOT of damage to kill enemies, so it makes many of the weapons feel weak by comparison.
If you manage to beat the primary campaign and think it is too easy, the free DLC levels will fix that for you ;o They are brutal, but a welcome addition to a game that is already a good value.

Game is outstanding, if you love RPGs and don't mind turn based combat from an isometric view then getting Original Sin 2 is a must. It offers so much fun roleplaying potentinal and freedom of approach to quests and choices in the game that many modern rpgs today completely lack, the amount of content is staggering and replay value is immense, combined with the fact you can play with a full party of friends online makes the value of this game even better.
The game came out as a surprise for me, didn't even know a sequel was being made for the first original sin [which i did not play but had interest in picking it up in the past] and i gotta say Divinity : Original Sin 2 is easilly one of my favorite games this year and the best rpg of this year already.
Do note, difficulty can at times be kinda unforgiving in the game, don't be ashemed to lower it to explorer if you find yourself never able to progress. Granted, sticking to classic difficult offers the great feeling of winning some really difficult fights so I'd advise trying to stick to classic as best as you can as its more rewarding, once you get the better hang of the game's core gameplay roles and its meta you'll find it's not that hard as it might've seemed first at the start.
There's also a very robust Game Master mode, where you can create your own custom stories [ala pen and paper Dungeons And Dragons] and then play it with other people as you controll everything that's going on in the game world.
Any problems ? Buged quests! They fixed a few with an early patch in ACT 1 but now in ACT 2 near the end i'm stuck with 4 buged quests and it's rather annoying, for an example my quest is to get X's head and deliver it to Y, i do so and the Y takes the head but i get no XP,completion update in the quest log and no reward.  Sometimes a quest is completed but the log just bugs out, which is the best case scenarios in a bugy quest, worst case being when you don't get anything. It's only major main problem the game has atm. other minor issues are, long load times after ACT 1 even on a SSD and annoying stuttering here and there in open world areas when moving arond.
At the end even with the bugs i still wholeheartedly recommend the game because it's so damn good, easilly the best rpg of 2017 and possibly my personal goty for 2017.

Hand of Fate is a good game, the simple brawler mechnics of the combat sequences are fun and challenging enough, like a slightly harder version of the Arkham/Batman games with far fewer variables or moves.  The narrator is amusing, the graphics cartoonish in a lovely way that pops on the screen totally appropriate for a game that is within a game.
The basic conciet of the game though is pretty briulliant - the player is playing cards against the enigmatic narrator who is some sort of dyspeptic frog voiced oracle or wizard. He's fun enough and he has new quips for most new cards, but I could I can see a DLC with a different dealer being profoundly satisfying - say a urbane devil, petulant child or defeatist death.  The card came is itself an adventure, with the randomly selected (you can build the decks though - within certian limits) card laid down and most cards offering a garphic of a charming woodblock image, a paragraph and a choice.  most selections lead to a pick and choose mechnic where four cards representing degrees of success and failure are shuffled monty style and the player picks one.  Other cards lead to combat.  In general when the player is successful with a card they gain a token that's convereted to another card at the end of each game.  Thus as one plays more and more choices are added.  It's fun, and for an "unlock" method of providing content feels very natural.
Despite that praise, I almost gave this gave a thumbs down because even now, long after release (and to the developers' credit the seem to keep adding cards and content) the game seems to suffer from technical issues.  It lags, it slows and it crashes with alarming regularity on my laptop - which while no gaming machine is well above the minimum specs.  This isn't a general set of errors, more a steady degradation of capability culminating in multi minute load times for combat sequences or simply sudden crashes in the combat engine.  Whatever the cause these errors, they make the game frustratingly unplayable - becauase I want to play it and it's a good game.
I'm still giving it a positive rating here because when it does work (and sometimes it's fine) it's a very fun, very smart game.

hand of fate offers a pretty unique experience, melding cards, adventure, combat, and a bit of role-playing. This game does not do one of those things terribly well, my opinion, some may argue. You get a map made up of cards, which are adventures, meetings, shops, curses, and eventually - an exit from the current map. I honestly don't know what to say.
On the one hand, the seemingly decent combat system is kinda jacked, and you just end up spamming the same couple of moves 90% of the time, there are very annoying levels and bosses, the graphics is kind of meh (though in motion it looks better than on the screenshots), and for a parody beat'em up it is not very funny.
On the other hand, you can throw dogs, cakes and soda machines at people, you can also shoot bees and hearts, there are lots of fairly diverse playable characters and a level-up system with perks, you will get showered with achievements for the entire course of the game, and almost every level actually has unique sprites for enemies, props, backgrounds, and bosses.
Despite the mixed bag of positives and negatives, however, the constant introduction of new stuff, coupled with character progression, do make you want to keep playing and just "beat one more level", or "save one more lady", or "level up one more time", or "unlock one more achievement", which was enough for me to get suckered in and beat the whole thing in just one sitting.
So I suppose this makes it a tentative "recommend" if you see it dirt cheap in a bargain bin, and are looking for a game where you can turn off half of your brain completely and just smash a few buttons for several hours.
P.S. I could totally see it being much more fun and replayable as a co-op game, but - alas! - the co-op is only local, which, in my opinion, is a big missed opportunity.

MURDERED: Soul Suspect is the Square-Enix murder mystery blockbuster that you never knew you needed in your life. Or afterlife. Whatever.
I'm writing this after just having finished the main storyline. I'll admit I didn't grab all of the many, MANY collectibles in the game, nor did I ace every investigation with full badge power, whatever that's even supposed to mean (it was never made clear by the game as to what exactly those badges represented, if anything), so maybe I didn't get the full experience from this title. However, I'd like to make a few notes on what little I did have the pleasure of going through.
Much as I'd like to ramble on at length about specific instances ingame, I do think it's poor form to spoil what passes for a plotline in this game... So I'll try and keep this as general as possible.
The investigative portions of the game are awful.
The stealth/combat sections that break up the investigative portions are also awful.
The interrims between major investigations, where you wander around town picking up collectibles and taking on side missions, are probably the most fun... But, ultimately, still awful.
No, really. Investigations are broken up into two main parts, one being "pixel hunt around the room for CLUES(tm) that are either lying on the floor or on top of a table", and the other being "poke inside someone's brain with the correct CLUE(tm) so that they give you the last CLUE(tm) you need to open up the next area".
Pixelhunting is pixelhunting, and for the most part it's pretty tame. The game's nice enough to not require you to find every piece of evidence in a scene before coming to the correct conclusion, but it's also sneaky enough to WITHHOLD further evidence from you until you make a kind of halfway-conclusion. If this sounds confusing, good.
It's the parts where you possess someone and try to kick their memory into gear that things get truly miserable, because I made the dreadful mistake of trying to be clever and think of actual clues, evidence, or events that might stand out in someone's mind and unlock a larger memory. No, that is not relevant to an investigation. What's relevant to an investigation is squeezing into someone's head and straight up asking them "WHO IS KILLER?". Need to work out where the suspect went? Just activate the clue "SUSPECT GOING SOMEWHERE", and you'll get all the answers you need.
It's not so much an exercise in deduction, so much as a quick test to see if you remember why you're in that particular room.  Failing this repeatedly doesn't seem to have any greater consequences than not unlocking some achievement, since you just keep trying things until you pick the answers that the game wants.
Okay, so the investigations aren't all that great... But maybe that's all worth glossing over in the face of an intriguing and suspenseful story?
No, not really. The story is laughably predictable. I spent half the game waiting for the main characters to get on my level regarding an understanding of what was going on.  There were several points where the character was making a frustrated rant about "What does it all MEAN?" and I just sigh heavily because he's literally just read exactly what it all means.  But, hey, I guess that's what you get from the kind of genius who carefully steps over fallen debris as an incorporeal spirit.
Also, yeah, psychics are totally normal and work with the police department, our first encounter with the police force shows an officer picking up forensic evidence and wearing it on his head and the creepy standoffish ghost girl who absolutely doesn't look exactly like Wednesday Addams is TOTES INNOCENT, BRUH.
Oh, right, I mentioned stealth sections... Well, they're bad. Just... Stupid. Unfun. Not even difficult, they're just tedious and blatant padding with completely inexplicable mechanics. Why can our ethereal hero Mr. Fedora McGruffinsmokes banish the zombie goasts by giving them atomic wedgies? Why are they there in the first place? What even are they? Why do you have a set number of floating ghost smears you can hide inside of by rapidly bouncing back and forth between them? These and many more questions add to the mysterious mystery of MURDERED: Soul Suspect.
So, yeah. Do you like sleuthing and crimesolving? Don't get this game. Do you like stealth and/or action? Don't get this game. Compelling story that makes sense and doesn't leave half of the everything unexplained? Yeah, no.
Do you like backtracking repeatedly through cramped environments to pick up a staggeringly huge number of tediously hidden collectibles filled with unrelated backstory? Well then, this might very well be just the game for you!
...but even then, wait for a sale.

-------------------- Warning: Long Review --------------------
Synopsis: You're dead, and you're now a ghost who sees the light on the other side where your beloved, late wife is waiting for you.
Hold up now, you can't pass on until you find out who killed you, and he is a nasty sonofa♥♥♥♥♥ that has eluded the cops, and now has even murdered one - you, Ronan O'Connor.
You need to figure out how this whole ghost thing works, put your detective skills to use, and end The Bell Killer's spree once and for all with the help of an emotional, bratty teen medium trying to find her mom that was somehow connected to the case.
This supernatural-mystery is pretty average all-round. There's nothing it really excels at, story, gameplay, or otherwise. It's a little on the short side, but I will explain why that was a bad thing in the story section. I reccomend that you avoid reading the totality of my review if you want to dive into the game - for which I won't blame you, since any review of a mystery genre media can let things slip that you should have found out for yourself. Go ahead and play it if you're just looking for a game to pass your time.
Gameplay: The core of this game relies on finding clues and piecing them together. This isn't necessarily a difficult task, but it can be frustrating. The clues are kept within a certain area, and it'll tell you how many are left - even if they aren't necessary to the conclusion of your investigation. That's right, you heard me, it provides you with information that doesn't contribute at all to your success. This was actually a smart way of representing how you need to sift through information instead of giving you the answer as soon as you "found it". The downside to this is that the most important clues are the most easily visible, so even if you didn't find the last few clues, you can still "find the answer" while missing information. This was done to make sure the difficulty of the cases wasn't something that would impede your progress, so I can see why it couldn't be avoided, but it still takes away from the experience and makes it more of a point-and-click than a detective or puzzle game. (Also, the badge "mechanic" was utterly pointless. If you aren't able to draw the correct conclusion it's pretty much just trial and error at the sacrifice of meaningless badge "trophies" that are never explained or even mentioned.)
The stealth portions are just plain frustrating. You need to sneak up on demons using various methods like hiding in people or glimmers (They aren't really called that, but I'll be using various terminology like this for the sake of consistency.) as well as avoiding line of sight. Once you're behind them, you destroy them during a short quicktim event. (by dispelling their existence or something, since they never explained it). If you get caught or fail the quicktime event, they will scream for a moment before they begin feeding off of your energy, and you have to move between hiding spots until they stop looking for you and go back to their normal routine. After the first couple of times dealing with them, they aren't really frightening but more obnoxious, as they're just an obstacle that isn't a period of clue collection. It wasn't at all necessary to the story and only provides flavor. I appreciate that they tried to supply a sense of danger, but they didn't put enough effort into it and just made the stealth sequences progressively more [s]annoying[/s] difficult for the sake of having them.
That's about all there is to the gameplay. It was unpolished and didn't feel that engaging, but it still had enough flavor that it succeeded in its purpose.
Art & Atmosphere: Ok, this is where the game hit its mark. The music is great, and it makes getting chased by a demon feel almost scary. The art style makes Salem feel very gloomy and mysterious. The ghasts that litter the place are creepy. You find stories and stuff all over the place that colors the town's terrible history. There's not a lot to say here except: You won't be dissapointed by this game's visuals and atmosphere.
Characters: Ronan is probably the most compelling character I've seen in a while. (In games at least.) He feels genuine. You uncover his personal history throughout the game and through the little scavenger hunts, and it just makes him look badass as a criminal-turned-cop who is looking to atone for misdeeds. His plain-clothes police outfit is also part of his appeal, since it's another homage to Noir that doesn't feel tacked-on or misplaced in the modern setting.
Joy wasn't as polished, but she was enjoyable. It would've helped if they gave her more meaningful interactions with Ronan, but as-is her influence on the story was enough to make her a decent character.
The rest, not so much. Julia is important to Ronan, but she doesn't really feel improtant to the player. If we got more of a direct insight into how she shaped his life or at least what her personality was like, it would make her feel more real. The same goes for Rex, since he's little more than a plot-device as far as the story's concerned.
Baxter just falls flat as a character and has no real depth. He has an irrational "animosity towards Ronan" and plays a small part in the story. Even if we understood a little more about his character, it wouldn't make him any more likable.
Story: It's unfulfilling. It felt rushed. Some characters weren't involved enough for it to entirely make sense, either. They never explain the notes and symbols that Abigail was drawing or why you find them all over the place, or who they were really for. They never explain why Ronan's gunshot wounds are glowing when no other ghost has anything like that. It feels like they skipped more than an hour of story between finding Sophia and finding the Bell Killer's hideout.
Conclusion: I would give it at most a 6.5 out of 10. It's unsatisfying and it wasted a lot of potential, but it's not something you would regret buying (on sale) and playing. Here's hoping we get to see Ronan again, though. I would love to see this story redone as a comic.

Metro builds on the successful formula used in the previous game with advancements to the UI, weapon system and stealth without hurting the essence of its gameplay. I wish there were more games that  made rereleases which actually improve the game like the devs of the Metro franchise have done instead of a poor excuse for a cash grab like many examples out there.
Metro builds a wonderfully depressing post apocalyptic world with a very well designed hidden morality system affected by your ingame behaviour and sense of exploration. You will feel the survivors struggle to survive as they casually go about trying to live their lives. The game is Reknown for being able to create a tense frightening atmosphere and keeping your heartrate up as you immerse yourself into its world. Was the roar of the mutant horde intended for you this time? Maybe, maybe not, but it will keep your trigger finger twitching.
Which is great because your trigger finger has a wide variety of weapons to use. Your choice of weapons and how you modify them is meaningful to your playstyle and to your ability to survive in the game. Resources are scarce and danger is around every corner so maintain your sense of careful exploration if you want to survive future missions.
However, once you get a feel for the game, do try the harder difficulties and adjustments like the Ranger mode. I heavily recommend playing with the UI. Everything you need from the UI is already available ingame. Weapon ammo indicators (such as pressure meters, bullets in your transparent mag, revolver cylinder/ammo belt or for some weapons, just count your shots like a pro), your watch with its breath timer and light detector, your health, your battery charge are all available for viewing ingame and its the best way to play the game. Few other games offer this level of immersion.
And immersed you will be as the strobe like flashes from your auto-shotgun light up a dark corpse filled cave full of a growing horde of mutants clawing you apart as both your blood and theirs splashes across your gas mask and obscures your visibility while your last air filter runs down and your breath grows short.

This game makes me sad. Not because it's an awful game, but because it's just tons of wasted potential. It has great story, good acting, an interesting concept. However, at certain points, it's just annoying.
It could have been a great detective thriller, but it doesn't give you the freedom to actually make your own decisions, to be a detective, take what you could out of a situation. At most it's a puzzle game, not a detective game. In that sense, it's an old-styled point'n'click, where it's not your own choices, but it's a single, RIGHT, choice. I could get over this because the world the game builds is good and interesting.
The other gameplay mechanics (one in particular) is a significant part of the game that's not fun, just annoying. A lot of time is spent not having fun, not enjoying the game, but sneaking (again with a right way to do it) around, waiting to get to the good parts.
In conclusion, while the good parts of the game are really good, the bad ones are really bad. That means I can't "recommend" it. It's not a must have. It's just a game that you, probably, won't hate if you happen to play it. And with the amounts of great game out there I can't say that this one is really worth getting to.

Pros:
It's a new map in ETS2!
New trucks!
Cons:
It's literally just ETS2 but in America. (nothing against America but it would serve better as an expansion to ETS2 rather than a standalone game) The UI is completely the same as ETS2 with very few changes.
The map is scaled down and cities are scaled up compared to ETS2, so you go from one town to the next in nearly no time at all
There are only 3 trucks. Two Kenworth and one Peterbilt. I understand there are licensing issues with adding more trucks but compared to the 12 in ETS2 this isn't worth the £14.99 atm.
Conclusion:
It's not worth the asking price atm. So far there are only two states (Arizona coming soon!), the majority of states will be paid DLC (not a bad thing in itself but...) on a smaller map scale (less bang for your buck). If this were released as DLC for ETS2 (I know, it's not Europe. It's America) with the ability to travel to/from the USA at will OR if it were released with the larger ETS2 map scale and compatability with your ETS2 trucks and save file then I could fully recommend this. Unfortunately, if you already have ETS2 then stick with that unless you desperately need to drive in America. If you don't have ETS2 then choose between driving in Europe and America. All in all it's not a bad game but considering the similarities to ETS2 and the lack of features at the moment it's not worth the purchase, consider waiting until more content is released or the price drops.

What can I say, this game would be awesome if:
1. It was balanced.  Right now even the easiest setting is a blood bath!  You are always out numbered at the start and it seems every encounter has atleast one or more npcs which either summon adds, or the game just cheats and throws more adds in as the battle progresses.
2. NPCs played by the same rules as the characters.  an NPC the same level as your character will always have more HP, will always have more Regular Armor and more Magic Armor (these are two seperate things in this game) will always have more skills and more resists and this is at the easiest setting.  Also NPCs can cheat and shoot arrows and cast spells through things that block your attacks. Like wise human like NPCs seem to have infinite special ammo (like fire arrows and poison bombs) and Monstrous NPCs constantly spam their AOE/status altering attacks.
3. Every battle ground is staged against you.  The enemy always has the high ground for ranged attacks, requiring you to navigate 2 or 3 turns to get on even footing and away from the preplaced barrels of fun that get exploded for your enjoyment er uhm death.  All the while your enemies, enjoying all this carefully placed stuff are wearing you down and spamming the entire battle field with fire / ice / poison etc..
4. Even if you are the kind of person who enjoys reloading and trying the same battle over 10 times or more to figure out how to beat any particular fight, you will still be upset when the game crashes while your doing one of those reloads, or the save you have been reloading over and over again gets corrupted and cant be loaded, Or you finally win the fight only to discover that one of those negative status effects that got applied during the battle, never comes off afterwards, oh and the quest that was supposed to be updated / completed doesnt get updated or completed either.

If you're reading this, you already amaze me. This game is (or was, as of redux) ludicrously obscure.
Simply put, Hard Reset is Bulletstorm done right. Made by 35 people on a budget of less than 5 million bucks, you can see the personality in this game.
The gameplay is a solid case of using the environment to your advantage, and the soundtrack is some of the best cyberpunk-esque you're going to hear in a long, long time.
The graphics put a very large number of triple a games to shame, and all in all the gameplay, sound design and aesthetic come together to make grenading a large group of enemies very, very, very satisfying.
My one and only complaint, as you tend to have with budget titles, is that the story was visibly handled after the rest of the game, being told almost entirely through a comic book style series of cutscenes with voice acting (that sometimes doesn't even match up with the guy voicing the character in gameplay) that doesn't exactly go out of its way to win any awards.
Aside from all this, the developers get major kudos for releasing extension DLC a good 8 months after the game's release completely free.
Hard Reset is a beautiful snack for folks who love retro shooters the likes of Doom, Serious Sam and Duke Nukem, but anyone else should steer clear, as this thing is a hell of an obscure niche title.
Edit: If you're asking whether this or Redux is better, the answer is that Redux nerfed difficulty a fair bit and added a sword weapon straight out of Shadow Warrior.
That's it.

Some first impressions playing in tactician mode.
Safe to say, this is a best of class game.  Addictive and very rewarding.  Challenging and sometimes frustrating, but the game (so far) offers a solution to every problem if you persevere.
Stunning graphics and music.  Lot's of voice acting, some of it excellent (eg. Fane) though the Narrator can be a bit of a ham - which is a pity given it is such a large part and has such a big impact early on.
The environments are amazing.  Beautifully rendered and inventively designed.  Baccus's Labyrinth and Vault are an enormous pleasure to explore and overcome.
The story becomes immersive over time, though I would say the writing is not as strong as other elements and lacks the emotional punch and humour of, say, EOS Online.
A few irritating bugs.  For example, the screen will sometimes stop following your movement if you switch to another character.  The only way to fix this is to talk to an NPC or save and reload.
Combat takes a while to get used to.  There are a couple of key innovations which I initially found very frustrating.  1.  The aoe effects are unpredictable, prevalent and fairly deadly until you get a bit of magic armour.  Over time you get better at understanding what will make an aoe effect spread (or diminish).  However, there remain times when a normal melee attack or ranged attack cause aoe effects to spread to nearby melee characters randomly.  2.  Armour is split into magic armour and physical armour.  Most damage AND crowd control is resisted by one or other type.  This means that if the other side has an armour advantage (as they do in tactician mode), their crowd control is available from the get go and yours is postponed until you have already won the fight.  It also means that emphasising one or other damage type can be a winning strategy if you want to cheese it.
That said, the encounters the game gives you force a constant rethink and require a willingness to adapt.  Fighting the undead particularly the Incandescent mobs is very challenging if you have narrowed your options.  Overall combat is deep and satisfying.  So far there has been no sign that this will be a game where you fall into using the same series of spells every fight.
There are a few things I wish could be fixed.  1.  When you place a spell or other action, the characters affected are highlighted, but sometimes your nearby characters get hit nevertheless.  2.  Melee can sometimes hit you even if you are up on a platform - which seems wrong.  3.
Tooltips could do with some work.  The tooltip for Blind, for example, does not say it is resisted by magic armour.  The tooltip for some spells mention that they hit only enemies.  The tooltips for other spells that hit only enemies are silent.  Maybe past players of the franchise understand these things, but not good to waste gold or upgrade points on something that turns out not to work the way you thought.  4.  Sometimes the game will prevent you from firing a ranged attack because there is no line of sight.  In other cases though it will allow it and the attack fails.  In these cases, there is a small yellow note on screen that the path is obstructed, but it is easy to miss once or twice in a long fight.  Why not just disallow the attack?
Overall, the game seems to offer an enormous amount of depth, and rewards you for trying different combat styles.  So far, the complexity and inventiveness makes each encounter a new puzzle, which I really like.

I once sold a sailor-suit school girls uniform to a man "for his mother-in-law".  Um... yeah.  Another time, I bought a beef bowl off of a woman who "found it in her attic"... and then promptly resold it at a significant mark-up.  I'm sure it was tasty...
I'd recommend this game to someone just off of those experiences, but if you want a more traditional review:
Recetter is a combination time-management game and Zelda-esque dungeon crawler.  Both halves of the game start out seeming pretty simple, but there is surprising depth to be found in each--making the overall experience a unique and enjoyable one.
You start off with a large debt to pay off, and a fairy companion who suggests you do so by turning your house into an item shop that serves the numerous adventurers in town.
There are three ways to earn the necessary money to pay off your debt:
1) Buy items at the local merchant guild or market and sell them off
2) Hire an adventurer to take you into dungeons to find treasure.
3) Use the various monster parts picked up in the dungeon to craft expensive items
The more time spent selling, the better a merchant you become, and the more higher quality goods you can buy from the market and merchants guild.  Conversely, the more time spent adventuring, the more different adventurers you will meet and unlock, the better gear you will find, and the more powerful weapons and armor you can craft (either to sell, or to give to your adventurers to make the next dungeon run easier).
The limiting reagent here is time.  You only have so many turns to sell items in your shop or to adventure out into dungeons.  Use your time well, and you'll pay off your debt... at which point you can keep going, to meet new adventurers, see new dungeons, craft new materials, and try to make obscene profits.
It's an addictive game with fun, cutey graphics, a great sense of humor, and a lot of interesting (and important) choices to make.  And that's besides, the whole sailor-suit incident.  What more could you possibly want in a game?

The Dealer is what makes this game. Considering you spend 95% of your time interacting with him and listening to him, if he was in anyway written terribly, or voiced terribly, then it would kill the game for you because otherwise, all you had was some fun quests and mediocre Arkham combat.
Thankfully, the Dealer is engaging, hardly ever repeats his lines, and even then, his delivery is so snarky and full of personality and flavor, you don't mind occasionally hearing the same line again. He will have up to 3, perhaps even more, different lines for the same card, or same kind of card (like the Helpful Priest line of cards, where he shows his disdain of the clergy).
The Dealer's performance is what sells and buoys this game, especially as the rest of its features and mechanics, while serviceable, really aren't much to talk about. Specifically, the combat is closer I think to Assassin's Creed, where sitting and waiting on the counter indicator to appear is the best way to go, especially if you put it on Hard Mode from the outset (which I recommend, as otherwise the combat pace is even slower and easier).
I would recommend buying this game on sale. I got mind for $10 during 2015's Holiday Sale, and it's completely worth the $10. At its full price, I would have hoped that the combat mechanics be more polished, as they do bring down the whole package and presentation of the game.

I picked this up for cheap and put it on the "do play" pile. After it finaly got to my notice I went through it and was plesently surprised. This game might not be perfect but in some respect it gives plenty of good shooting without most of the modern flaws that plague FPS genre.
Let me get the downsides off first. The game is extremely linear. This is pretty much a coridor shooter with few hidden nooks and crannies that serve as game's secrets. There is very little variety in what you do, you go from one area, flip a switch fight enemies and move on. This in itself isn't a bad thing as long as the shooting is good, which it is. Another issue  (which does have a fix) is the checkpoint system. You can't manualy save, for the most part it works fine but on harder difficulties there are sequences of encounters where there are no checkpoints in between and each encounter requires near flawless execution to proceed. It can be frustrating repeating the same bit over and over, just to die by one small enemy that sneaked past you. Thankfully via console you can bind a key to set your own checkpoint whenever you like. It works but beware, I wouldn't set checkpoints mid fight, do it only between encounters or you might end up corrupting your save file. With this little tweak the game becomes substantially better, because the biggest source of frustration is removed.
*Press ctrl+~ to bring up the console*
-Type: bind *whatever key you want* save //this will make that key set a checkpoint at that moment
-Type: bind *whatever key you want* load//this button will become quick load button to your checkpoint
Difficulty in this game is done right surprisingly. Game's harder difficulties are legitimately hard. They aren't unfair hard, you have plenty of tools at your disposal to deal with anything the game throws at you at any point, but if you are playing the first time and don't know what to upgrade...well you might run into good amount of frustration.
Upgrade system is simple and robust. Killing enemies and collecting nano will "level  up" Fletcher. Then you can spend points upgrading one of your two guns or your suit. The two guns aren't really two guns. Each gun has 5 modes(you start with only one each), and each mode has 2 different fire modes. In essence you have 10 guns, with half of them using one ammo pool while other half the other.You get to pick which gun you get next, and which upgrades for it via the upgrade system. If playing the game the first time that can be a bit unfair because some upgrades are clearly more beneficial over others without the game giving you any sort of hint of what you need.
Every enemy type has simple ways of dispatching it, but the game gives little hint to what you need to use, you have to figure it out yourself. That can be harsh when you never knew you had to upgrade emp blast for the blaster or stasis for the mortar. However once you figure this out, it's a very pleasant skill based shooting experience. Speaking of enemies, beware, even the smallest enemies will rip you to pieces in seconds on harder difficulties. You will die if you let anything get near.
Overall this game was a really pleasant expereince, a little bit of take on Painkiller formula but not quite there yet. Still if you like a skill based shooting where you can get plenty of challange, this is the right game to play.
Game has potential but lacks workshop crews. I'm hoping more maps and challenges surface so we'll see.

MegaSphere is a game with a very dynamic combat system, and randomly generated maps.
The game has a really cool physics system, cables, crates and even pieces of wall get shot up, fall onto you and enemies, resulting in some really fun and constantly evolving battles. The variety of weapons allows you to cause this kind of chaos. You can upgrade weapons as you want, in order to create things like bouncing rockets, or powerful guns that allow you to suck up objects and enemies, and hurl them away.
The fact that the maps are randomly generated allows for good replay value. Maps are huge, and can be traversed through different paths. You can take set ones, or destroy walls and make your own.
There are hints of story every now and again, but nothing incredibly interesting in my own opinion. Although it's nice to feel that there's a purpose to what you're doing, so it's a welcome feature.
Even though this is early access, it feels very well polished and fun!

I saw KY stream this on Vinesauce, and it seemed to control excellently (well, hard to tell when you're not the one playing), plus I really loved the visual style and concept of the game, so I decided to buy it.
I regrettably can't say it was worth it, at least not yet. On the stream, wires could be cut by shooting at them, but for the 15 minutes I was able to play before getting stuck, I only found 2 wires that could be severed. One of the wires almost kept me from completing a tutorial stage as it was blocking a button I had to shoot, but after a dozen attempts I managed to clip through it while jumping and shoot the button. An enemy also spawned within a hanging wire which prevented me to hit it, while it could shoot past the wires just fine.
Wires also turn invisible when I shoot at them, but turn visible again after settling.
The thing that had me get stuck was actually the elevators. A strange bug kept some of them from going up all the way, and instantly switch to going down again just before it reached high enough for me to jump the rest of the way up, so I got stuck down in a pit and could not even shoot myself out through the walls.
The jumping is also highly unresponsive, and more often than not I tend to just fall off the platforms when I try to jump off them, though this may be due to the game just generally being laggy, which also could be the fault of my brand new gaming laptop, maybe. But let it be known that even when putting the graphics on minimal, all of my issues still persist.
So to me, at least, this game is complete and utterly unplayable at the moment, though I don't intend on refunding it as I think it has a lot of potential once thise bugs have been fixed. I still can't recommend it at its current state though.

Ahhh Warframe. A strange love hate freemium game. One of the few Freemium games where they do try to make it better(and the devs do fail,and often with spectactular results)
The game itself? Runs great. It's clear this game has had some effort put in,even with the new Plains of Eidelon update,I still was running fairly well(until the Door of Friendship was a thing)
The gameplay? It's strange,because it fits a few different niches. It's basically a fast paced horde shooter/basher. And it's *fun*. You can mod your weapons to your taste,but DE needs to balance the mods so that way you can have some more flavor or utility instead of the same fit for every weapon.
The art style is a nice mishmash of East meets West. The lore is all over the place,and can easily be ignored,so if you want something you can turn your brain off,hang out with friends and show off how pretty you can make yourself this is it.
But where does this game falter? The grind can be excessive at times. The Hema and Gara are way too hard to get. But everything else isn't too horribly bad.
A few of the major quests are kinda bleh(looking at you Chains of Harrow)
The focus grind,that's horrible,and supposedly DE is gonna fix it. But in all honesty,you can just get one specific skill from the Focus Tree and ignore the rest,you really aren't missing much.
Archwing/Sharkwing/Skywing are all neat ideas,but the controls are wonky and not fun to use,but I like the idea, Taken with a grain of salt. It can be fun,but it's one of those things that is an aquired taste,and most folks won't like it.
Platinum(in game freemium currency) can be made just by trading. Rivens are cancer of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ however and prices range from 1 plat to 15k plat.
Overall? Other than some minor hiccups here and there,this game is great fun when you just wanna turn off your brain have a blast with your friends or even the community. The community is pretty good,and relativley cancer free.
A solid 7.5/10 for me(the grind in some parts and a few other minor issues). With friends? It's a solid 8+. It's got fun,it's got action.

(REVIEW CORRECT AS OF 5/9/15)
If you remember the old Crack Dot Com game ABUSE on the PC or Bungie's port of it to the Mac OSX, then you'll remember what a fantastic game that was. Tight controls, frantic action, great atmosphere and amazing weapons. Megasphere is very clearly taking some lessons from that classic, and this is absolutely a great thing.
Bear in mind though this game is in early access so it's nowhere near as polished as Abuse was. It plays more or less the same, though a touch slower. At first this annoyed me but then I realised it's because with so much flying at you, you need time to strategise as well as react. Because the environments are partially destructable (yes you can actually tunnel through walls... within certain limitations which are fairly logical from a gameplay design standpoint, more on that later), and because there are hazards in the environment that can help or hinder you, you need the additional time to respond to be able to make proper use of them.
There's some great touches here and there, some fantastic spritework and animations, levels are dark and brooding but still clear enough to see what's going on, enemies are lit up rather nicely without glowing like beacons and cluttering up the gameworld, though it would be nice to see some kind of targeting reticule and if the aiming cursor could JUST stand out a little more...  Enemies drop life pickups when they die, but they don't stick around long and other enemies can pick them up too (which is pretty neat actually), so there's a bit of a risk-reward thing going on there, do you get right in the thick of it and risk tons of damage or do you hang back and obliterate them then pick up what remains if you're quick enough?
Given that the only two languages are russian and english, and the english is somewhat dodgily translated at points, I'm gathering the game devs are Russian, but they've done a pretty good job of the translation all things considered. It's certainly not the worst.
If I have any criticisms it's that the game realllly doesn't teach you anything about how to play, making some of the gameplay mechanics ridiculously obtuse, like how am I meant to kill the boss, and how do I upgrade my weapons... The latter point there I managed to work out through fumbling about, but killing Rosyanka-1 still eludes me. I assume it has something to do with those buttons that drop exploding fire...things... which you can grab and throw wiht one of the wepaons I picked up but... I'm still confused as to whether I'md oing any damage or not, could do with more feedback.
Okay so, basic rundown of the destructable environments then. Basically if two rooms neighbour each other, you can tunnel through the walls into them. If there's no room nearby you can "dig" like three or four blocks out in any direction that doesn't neighbour a room before you hit unbreakable terrain. These blocks can occasionally fall down and make steps or block progress, there are cables which are phys-enabled hanging from the ceiling that you can shoot, and yes they will slow your fall, or block your jumping progress, or trap certain enemies to... There's exploding... things that you can shoot to make them pop into firey painful stuff, which I believe can damage enemies too, though not much. OOne gun I found can pick up and throw items like detatched blocks, enemies and explodythings too, which was neat.
The upgrade system is pretty fantastic, you can find modules which you can plug into existing gun-types that you pickup to grant them additional power. Granted once they're set, that's it, you can't pull them back out again so choose wisely.
OKAY, so, pros and cons then:
Pros:
Gameplay is rocksolid, but then it basically plays much like ABUSE, so that's a given.
Nice variety of guns and a great weapon upgrade system keeps things interesting and fresh.
Dynamic soundtrack responds to threats.
Great visual effects when you take damage and are at critical levels of health lets you know when to bug out (if you can) to reassess your situation.
Destructable terrain and phys-enabled objects
Great sprite-based visuals that don't clutter or get massively confusing in huge combats.
Nice wide field of view allows you to tell when combat's about to happen (something ABUSE Lacked, sadly)
Cutscenes are now skippable (hold Space!)
Neat little (semi) hidden hint to give you a clue as to how to beat the first boss (check your map in the first actual level when you enter, should be easy to find).
Invisible-immortal foes/foes in walls bug seems to be fixed!
Devs respond rather quickly to issues!
Relentlessly challenging! (though also could be a downside if you're easily frustrated)
Every run is different! Proceedurally generated levels!
Cons: (REMOVED UNTIL I CAN VERIFY EXISTENCE OF ANY BUGS OR ISSUES)
Only two languages to choose from, English and Russian (Translation to English now appears better!)
(have not tried dying yet with a save point reached so don't know if that bug still happens)
Mouse cursor still kind of tiny.
Brutally, brutally difficult. Though also a plus because it's nice to be challenged by a game, and this game certainly does not handhold you. It lets you make your own mistakes.
Still could do with just something to run you through how to upgrade guns (not what combos are the best or what they do, just how to do it) and maybe something to let you know what level each upgrade module is before socketing it. (also slight b ug with weapon upgrades displaying wrong level and name when you hover over them)
Game ends shortly after first boss, but that's to be expected, we are in Alpha :)
Even at this stage of Early Access, the game is fantastic and well worth paying for and playing! Its difficulty is high enough to make you work real hard for your wins, but not so punishing that it'll drive you away. If nothing else, if you miss the game ABUSE, then absolutely pick this up because it scratches the same itch and then some, and actually is even better than it :D

After dealing with Owlboy for a full video series where I played it, it left a good impression on me as a game itself. Uncertain if I can link that, so here's just the review!
In all honesty, it's hard to rate Owlboy as anything less than 'Amazing' in almost every aspect it tries to touch upon. Gameplay is solid, the map is solid, the characters are great, the art is pretty and stylish, and the story overall is told well... But there are still flaws. In the story itself, there are a lot of things that are hamfisted or simply not explained well enough and most characters come off as negative because of that. Now, a majority of them are still fine and that's why I said they were great, but there are definitely a few I feel have fatal flaws that simply aren't explored in the gameplay. That is my major complaint.
Another major complaint is a build up that never receives a payoff. Something that may hint for things to come now that the foundation has been set, but... It could have been handled better. This game was amazing, there's no doubting that, and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who likes action platformers like this that are very story driven. There's also a lot of hidden things that just aren't really focused on unless you really want to 100% the game, which is a plus. It's nice when a game likes to show you its story through actual work instead of just an hour long cutscene, though there are plenty of small cutscenes through this game as well.
Regardless, this game has flaws and a few major ones too, but it's not a bad game. Gameplay was simple, clean, and overall fun, but ultimately ended up becoming repetitive or just annoying, particuarlly in certain situations. The music was always on point, though, and there were only a few points where the art was an issue, particuarlly when dealing with enemies that have arkward hit boxxes or move a lot. That being said...
.. The information I have states the game took over 10 years to come out. In these 10 years, it got a lot of support and a lot of people were looking forward to it. In no way do I think anyone who did wish for it is disappointed and I am definitely not disappointed either in buying it... But it could have been better and I feel like 10 years was more than enough time to make it better. There's a lot of small things that really make this game just barely reach 'Amazing', but it's still amazing nontheless. I'm looking forward to more from this group and hopefully this game will allow them to see flaws they otherwise missed because of either lack of experience, or simply not trying to focus on fixing them. Hopefully it'll take less than 10 years next time, possibly for a sequel.

This game is the product of nine years of development, and it really shows that the developers crafted every detail of the game with love. Owlboy isn't perfect, but it's definitely a standout title.
Owlboy's strongest attribute by far. The "Hi-Bit" pixel graphics are gorgeous and set a high bar for any future games using a pixelated art style. The soundtrack by Jonathan Geer is beautiful and emotive, making the soundtrack a worthy upgrade if you're the type to listen to video game soundtracks when you're not playing. Animations for the characters are absolutely on point. The characters' expressions and reactions during dialogue are very charming and expressive.
While I had a lot of fun with this game, it's not as polished in the gameplay department as in presentation. The game is often far too easy, with some spikes in difficulty in certain sections. I found myself breezing through the levels, with puzzles, boss fights, and other obstacles doing little to slow my progress. Occasionally, I would get lost in some of the levels if I decided to go hunting for collectibles as there's no minimap, though not much backtracking is required to progress in the game.
I loved the story and spent time talking to every NPC. However, I know the story is hit or miss for some. Owlboy's story pacing is pretty standard, breaking up the action in-between dungeons for narrative development and character dialogue. The characters are likable and distinct, and the story has some unexpectedly emotional turns. If you're not interested in the story, however, you're probably going to get annoyed at the interruptions.
Overall I'd recommend Owlboy to anyone looking for an aesthetically-pleasing game that's light on difficulty but high on charm. If you're an action platformer veteran looking for a challenge, this game will disappoint you. Owlboy is at its best when you just relax and let it pull you in with its story and presentation. I wish the game was longer or more challenging, but I came away from the game without regrets in my purchase, even going back to 100% it and see everything there is to see

SO originally I loved this game and my review was positive, then my Summer holidays ended, at which point I had well over 300 hours (I did not launch the game via steam). The anti archeage hype train actually made me belive archeage is a bad game, that I did not like it. Then I realised something. I am not some Youtuber trying to be the absolute best PVP player in the world, I just want to have fun even if I never progress to the 0.1%
Then I realised that archeage is a great game. The people playing it need to look beyond what they hear and really look at the games issues. Heres a few:
- Patron: The sub fee that is the first reason that causes people to call the game pay to win.This game is free to play remember? If it didn't exist people would bot farm land and every other aspect of the game SO HARD that wouldn't matter if you COULD put down land, there just wouldn't be any to get. If people really want to be that competive you just buy the patron status in-game with gold, is it a big grind to get patron instead of just cashing out? Yes. Does not having it restrict you? Yeah but it is obtainable and it is possible to play free to play more than ever before thanks to bigger public farms. Also it encourages players to group together to make familys where the house is shared. Its not the full patron status but still.
-Apex: You can essentially buy gold and in return the other person gets credits that are most of the time spent on Apex. Is it play to win? EH. It means that people skip a huge amount of time to get things. If they need stone for a house they dont need to spend literal days mining it and can instead just buy it off the auction house. BUT I think that the fact that it is based on the economy, injects gold into the economy, give patron access to those who normally would not have been able to get it, etc the postives out weigh the negatives. Is losing tonce to that guy that dropped thousands of dollars on the game really gonna ruin your life?
-Servers: The 4 day queue times are ridiculous but at the same time I have never experienced it. I think that Trion want to keep costs lower as instead of upgrading a server beyond what will ever be needed they just let the player base trickle in, in a more natural way than the huge DDOS like server spam that happens on launch day. Sad it happens, its avoidable, but at the end of the day..youll have to wait until the end of the day to get in...or the day after...etc.
I wrote this pretty quick if theres anything else you think I should add please comment and tell me. I think this game is an amazing innovation on the industry and just like ESO I think it shouldn't have got the instant hatred that it did.
