This game is... interesting. It wants you to feel out the mechanics but the mechanics are non-obvious enough and they're only ever introduced the moment you need them to solve a larger puzzle. Like, you get to the third area and everything is fine but unless you can work out what the mechanic introduced in that section is you will end up completely stuck; yet once you figure it out the solution is really easy. The game also mixes self-contained areas with the overall game map in ways that are kind of annoying - this is seen again primarily in the third and last areas, with all the other areas being completely self-contained, making it hard to figure out what the game intends when you're not sure if you're stuck because you don't understand the current puzzle or just because you need to do something in a different area. And as well, the final puzzle is... a super tedious and overly long fetch quest that requires no thinking, it's just "find the specific painting you need out of about 10 and put it in the correct room out of 10" about a dozen times. And the ending is very unsatisfying when you do reach it, as a result.
Gripes aside though the puzzles themselves are clever and the game does instill that "aha" moment all good puzzle games should strive to create. Seeing all the pieces fit in to place (when you understand how they work) makes solving puzzles actually feel like an accomplishment (well, again, except for that last one) and due to the non-euclidean nature of the game map it's hard to tell how much is left to explore until you get close to the end (at which point you have basically been everywhere except for the very final room). It's also kind of exhausting to play though, since it requires both logical thinking and working out the game mechanics at the same time. It's not a long game, took me under 5 hours to beat and knowing what you're doing perfectly I bet you could clear this in 10-15 minutes. And the mechanics themselves are kind of clever too, it certainly doesn't feel much like any other game I've played. Yes, it's very aesthetically similar to antichamber, and it's non-euclidean as well, but the games don't have any similarities beyond that.
For the price I'd say it's worth it, it's not a perfect game and can be a bit frustrating at points but it's still pretty enjoyable and doesn't overstay its welcome much. Again, though, that end section is really dumb, I have no clue what they were thinking there.

An excellent game. Murdered: Soul Suspect is a story rich detective game. Your character is murdered at the start of the game, and now as a ghost he has to solve his own murder by following the trail of a serial killer.
The game takes place in a dark urban setting, giving the atmosphere of danger and hopelessness the entire time. In addition to the crime mystery element, it also includes a lot of paranormal concepts, particularly relating to ghosts and mediums. The story is paced very well and does not drag out or include any filler content. Every area you visit is another jigsaw piece in the grand scheme that helps you get closer to uncovering the mystery behind the string of murders happening in town.
Most of the gameplay consists of you searching around the area for clues and then putting them together to finalise on what happened. Most times it's pretty straight forward. It plays like a point & click game, but without overly convoluted puzzles. Everything you find makes logical sense. In addition to that, there are also other collectibles scattered in each level, each of which provide some information on characters or the town's lore. Some also let you uncover special hidden ghost stories, which is a nice reward, as some of those stories are pretty chilling.
At times there are stealth sections where you have to avoid being seen by soul-eating demons. They add a bit of challenge to the game, but overall I was not much of a fan of these sections as they felt unneeded and often got in the way of you exploring. A lot of the time the demons would come in groups of 3 or so, meaning you'd be spending some time trying to figure out how to get past them. You can't fight them, and the only way to kill them is via an execution from behind, if you're brave enough. Gladly these sections were few and far in between. Most times you'd only come across 1-2 such sections per level. So if this aspect is putting you off, I'd still recommend to try the game, since most of the game is spent putting together the clues.
Don't expect challenging gameplay or anything of that sort. This is a story-driven detective game at heart, and I think most critics who have slammed the game have missed this point.
I'd highly recommend this game if you like games about solving murder mysteries or anything with a dark, gripping plot for that matter.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a phenomenal experience anyone who is a classic RPG fan will love.
The overall appeal of Larian studios masterpiece is in its complex RPG systems, dynamic combat and world-changing character choices that synergize together to create an unforgettable experience. There is a ton of replayability because the world dynamically adapts to the choices you make. I think the dev forgot to have their game playtested is the thought I was left with after playing.
You're dropped in without any explanation of how the mechanics work. This leads to trial and error from the get-go and this trend continues upon progression.
Now, I appreciate the surreal look of the game and the unique gamepaly, unfortunately it becomes too abstract for its own good. You're trying to grasp your head around pairing paintings in order to create paths so that you can get a guarded painting out in order to pair it with something else and create an exit, but certain combinations make loops and things can get convoluted. This can be especially seen when there are more than a couple branching paths leading to multiple rooms within a section (by section I mean an area with new music).
The first two sections aren't that bad, but upon entering the third section the difficulty spikes up and you're left to move around trying even more cominations over and over.
To add to injury you cannot run. While the character doesn't move that slow, the feature would of been nice to have. Also, do those hallways in the infinity room really need to be that long?
In essence, as said before, the abstract nature of the game (while nice to look at) ultimately seems to detract from the gameplay. The surreal mechanics along with their combinations can create a mental block which leads to alot of trial and error.
After solving the first two areas I had a slight idea of what I was doing, but when the path opened up I still didn't know how it came to be.
Lastly, I don't know if the gameplay stays the same but it does get monotonous moving paintings over and over after a while with the fact that paintings can only be hung on an empty space. I can only assume the are more colors but that's about it...

FIRST IMPRESSIONS REVIEW:
*I'm writing this review from the stance of a complete beginner, trying to explain how it feels to be a newcomer. I'm sure not all of what I say rings true for every player, however I just wanted to put this out there for anyone looking to join the community as of late 2017. I hope all veterans can appreciate that. Cheers!*
At the time of writing this review, I only have around 3.5 hours on Warframe, however I felt as though there would be no better way to encapsulate my first impressions than to write a review after just beginning my journey. As the status quo for reviews goes, here is my list of pro's and con's.
Pro's:
+ Fluid gameplay (very satisfying and easy to understand game mechanics)
+ Graphically pleasing (While not at the cutting edge, the graphics do much more than an adequate job of engrossing me in the world of Warframe)
+ Unique (While not the first of its kind, the game somehow maintains a refreshing element from the rinse and repeat TPS  games currently out there)
+ Player base (currently one of the most played games on Steam, have yet to not find a squad)
+ Free-to-play! (Seemingly hundreds of hours of gameplay with no other costs than your electric bill)
+ Depth (This, for me, is a double edge sword, but after playing for few hours, I fel as though I've only scratched the surface of the content within this game)
+ Community (Have yet to encounter a toxic player, everyone thus far has been friendly and helpful)
Con's:
+ Depth (While I did add this to the pro's list as well, the game's sheer volume can be a bit overwhelming for a newcomer)
+ Microtransactions (Definitely not game-breaking as far as I know, however I personally believe microtransactions should be purely cosmetic)
+ Learning curve (The game seems to have an economy of its own, that was created by the players. I'm sure as time goes by I will get the hang of it, however this seems a little complex to a complete beginner. I'd like to add that the wiki, as well as YouTube videos, have been a big help thus far.
All in all, I'm very much enjoying Warframe thus far, and can certainly see myself playing this game for a good, long, time. The graphics, game mechanics, depth, lore, and immersive gameplay pull together to create a truly unique, refreshing experience, that you have no reason to not at least try for yourself. Now it's time to force my friends to download it!

You can play as a tank like warframe with high armor and support abilities, as a supporting warframe which helps squad with health/energy boost, as a stealth warframe, as an all out weapon of mass destruction, etc. All depends on what style suits your taste.

Once you've spent over 40 hours into the game, you will stick around for a long time. I recommend this game, it wont cost you any money to play the game for free and decide if you want to invest your time in it.

I'd never heard of role-playing games like this one before. It being free and the concept being something new to me, I decided to check it out. So it turns out that it's kinda like
, where you try to figure out who - among a bunch of other players - the murderer is. You do this primarily by talking to the other players and exchanging items & information.
It basically just told you how to move your character around, and interact with objects. However, upon playing the actual game, I soon found out that interaction wasn't that easy - just writing down the suspect's name proved to be a challenge because apparently you had to click again on the object or something like that.
The game works on the basis that you and the other players you're in the game with, pretend to be the characters the game assigns you. The game made me a random surfer dude on my first attempt, and I was in a yacht with 4 other people - a sexy Chinese lady, a smartly-dressed Caucasian woman, a dark-haired guy who looked like a cop, and another white guy with hipster vibes. It felt weird to role-play at first, but I quickly got the hang of it because thankfully, the other players I was in the game with, were really sporting and all role-played to a tee.
Typically, you need around 5 players (including yourself) to get started. I got lucky - the very first time I played this game, there was no wait at all, because 4 players were already there, so the game started almost immediately. I only realised how
that was when I tried playing again later on, and saw that there were next to no players, even after close to an hour.
Enjoyment of this game fundamentally banks upon the other people who join your game:
- being "serious" about playing, and not there to fool around or troll; and
- fully understanding how to play the game.
Will everyone fulfil the above criteria? Of course not, and that's a risk you must take.
Perhaps this is because the novelty of the concept hasn't worn off yet. But at its current price of $0, I would strongly recommend giving this game a try if you haven't done so already, especially if the idea of playing and chatting with other
, human players in a role-playing context appeals to you.

For one I found the graphics in this game better then what is in the real million dollar (plus) simulaitor I've had the privilage to use on more then one occasion and I like the way this game gives a very small taste of some of the realisticly hard places to get in and out of and a little of what real truckers may encounter during a trip. I'd also like to mention the fact that for what you get in this game I feel is very reasonably priced do to the fact that everything that is left out such as pre-trip inspection, log books, dealing wit dispatchers and brokers and even the creativity involved in finding a place to park in a truckstop after dark would all cost the developers more time and lead to a much higher initial cost to the gamming community. With all that being said, The biggest draw back to this game is that even though it can be played with a keyboard and mouse it is very difficult and somewhat tireing as both hands a kept busy all the time as you are constantly pressing keys to correct steering with one hand and with your other you are ajusting camera angles, operaitng turn indicators, and a ton of other tasks. Breaking is another difficult thing to master with a keyboard as if you leave your finger on the break button a millisecound to long, You will stop dead in the road or sidewalk, whichever you may be driving on at the time. So in closing I just want to say if your thinking about purchesing this game, you may wish to consider the computer hardwear I mentiond first, that is if you can afford the expence, otherwise you may feel a tiny bit disapointed as I do.

What has the gaming world come to when a Truck Simulator becomes fun?
It sounds negative doesn't it? But that was my first thought when I saw this game.
I played it, then I asked myself the same question.
Well, it seems the gaming world is exactly where it needs to be. On the cutting edge of brilliant minds and pushing the limits of incredible technology!
This game hooked me from the start. It's not just a bunch of poorly rendered boxes on wheels floating through an open-world, demolition derby scenario.
I come at this game from two different points-of-view. I am a life-long artist and graphic designer, so visuals are very important to me in a game, but I also have my CDL and spent many years over-the-road in these trucks. After getting in a truck and driving a few blocks, the first thing I noticed was an incredibly detailed world around me! Turns out, this is what is actually keeping me coming back for more. All of the vehicles in-game look incredible, which is what I expected, it's a Truck Driving Simulation game after all! However, the world generated around me, positively blew me away!  I found myself going off the road a few times because I was trying to look over at some of the scenes happening out my window as I'm driving by!
I won't go into any depth about the looks of the game, you just need to see it for yourself. Simply put, visually it's an incredible game and you'll have plenty to look at as the world goes by.
The handling of the trucks seems to be truly accurate, with truck-specific mechanics, right down to the horrible turning radius of the W900! This is truly a simulator, I find myself driving the trucks in-game, the same way I would in real life!
The AI drivers in-game are a little crazy, they randomly ruin your day in a hurry. Stopping on a 80 MPH freeway for no reason or turning right  smack into you at an intersection. I think this is just an AI system in need of  a few minor tweaks, but I found it actually adds to the realism of driving giant trucks around total idiots all day!
Really the only con I have found in the game are the speeding penalties. •	Story
o	The game revolves around Otus, a young mute Owlboy who is lackluster at all things his mentor deems as important to being a proper being an owl. In this game an owl is the protector of the denizens of the floating islands that make up the world. Throughout the game Otus meets new companions who serve as his weapons on his journey to save the floating islands from sky pirates
o	The story told is a familiar take on the Hero’s journey, however it’s done well. Dialogue is well written and character development is well paced. The game is sparse with its NPCs and makes the ones who are in the game pretty significant, if not to the main story then to the side quests that are placed throughout the game.
o	However, even with the side quests mentioned prior, this game is short. I made sure to talk and return to most npcs after each pivotal moment of the game (for anyone interested most of their dialogue changes frequently) and completed all but 2 of the side quests, aand reached the end screen in 7 hours.
•	Technical
o	As Otus is an owl, a majority of the game is navigated via flying. This gives the game a unique feel to its platforming. The levels are designed well around this form of movement and makes exploring the game rewarding.
o	Otus can’t attack on his own, but instead carries his allies around as weapons. His allies hang under him as he flies them around. While this is a cool concept, I found my allies getting snagged on terrain at tense moments as the ally pretty much doubles the size of your controlled sprite. This results in some situations where the controls feel clunky.
o	Every level has its own theme that are visually stunning and every room in the levels are distinct, which assists in preventing the player from getting lost.
o	However, the game lacks a mini map makes it difficult to back track through completed levels. While going through a level the first time is easy and intuitive, the shortcuts opened as you progress make it easy to overlook rooms when returning to collect missed coins. A mini map would fix this.
•	Final Thoughts
o	While there are certain parts of the game that become frustrating due to control issues and the game runs a bit short for the price tag, I would still wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of 2d adventure games and games with touching stories.

I really want to recommend this game, but I can't. It has a lot of good visuals, plays like Fatal Frame, and the music score is excellently brooding. But there are a lot of issues with it, some small and others flat out hair tearingly frustrating. It takes a good concept and then screws it over with poor gameplay designs.
The difficulty is all over the place. While some things are relatively easy, but a lot winds up being luck based in regards to encounters. One such fight (spoiler) agains the infamous Scissor Ghost is essentially all about dumb luck trying to evade an enemy in a tiny room that comes out of the walls with tank controls. In the wrong spot at the wrong time? Too bad, you get stunlocked to death. Respawn back in the room and he gets a free hit on you. They've had forever to fix this.
There's not a lot of direction or explanation to anything as to what you're supposed to accomplish. You'll have to look into your Files section to get some idea, but little is organically explained within the context of gameplay outside of some otherwise nifty Silent Hill style notes that delve into background events. Characterization is more thin than I'd like. You get objects in the game, but it isn't clear if they're supposed to do anything or why you're collecting them.
Controls are tank based... what can I say? Your character runs and turns slowly. She's slow about using her camera against speedy enemies. If you get hit, she recovers like a drunk on downers so enemies can just keep nailing you during your recovery animations. Otherwise, controls are very simplistic.
Graphically, the game is like a late PS2 title. Not a bad thing, really, but it becomes clear more work was put into some things that others. The enemies all look very good and spooky, but human character animations can be choppy. I noticed at one point the heroine's hand clips into her own wrist when bending.
But I WANT to like this title. It sets a great atmosphere even with inconsistent graphics and the way the dust plays across the camera is realistic to actual ghost hunting perspectives. The sound effects are top notch. Play this in the dark with headphones! It does feel like a genuine horror experience. But poor gameplay issues take away from the immersive quality. What should be challenging or scary winds up being nothing else than frustrating as you can get stuck in places with seemingly little to do but wander the same scenes again and again because you either can't figure out what you're supposed to do or it doesn't feel like there was anything you could rationally do... you get by on dumbluck. So it doesn't have that savor of challenge that a difficult title like Darksouls would.
Is it worth $15? Debateable. It feels like some polish is needed throughout. It's not the worst title I've ever played, but it fails to live up to what it could be.
As a final note, the DLC is pretty nice for this game. The comics are interesting and deliver some pretty good wtf moments as well as explains a few things. The music itself is quite sweet too... to access it once you've bought the DLC, check your steamapps!
ACT 2 Comments...
Act 2 was somewhat 'ehh' at first, but ramped up nicely. Things are more lively and story based in the 2nd part, with the end leaving more questions and possibilities. There are a LOT of boss fights in the 2nd part and the location is entirely different. I would in terms of challenge, the puzzles are often harder than the bosses were (there's only a few, but they make only vague amounts of sense), but generally nothing is 'scissor ghost' difficult. The 2nd is definitely darker and more surreal- expect much more direct ghost confrontations but less exploring. The linearity is a little disappointing, but the journey was more enjoyable as a whole. I'm not sure it's enough to say I recommend this title now, but it's not terrible. The experience of DreadOut is reasonably memorable with great imagery and in truth, I'd like to see more despite some qualms with the game. I'm going to say I'm neutral at this point with the recommendation. That said, if it's on sale, just go for it and play in the dark.

As of writing this, only “Act 1” is available, this is worth mentioning since on the steam store page there’s a little note saying “Act 2” will be a free update that comes “later”. Is it fair to review the game when not all the content is out? Then again, is it fair to charge for a game when what’s available amounts to barely anything?
At first I got vibes of a teen slasher film; a group of students on a road trip (with their teacher for some reason?) with a funky sound track and not a care in the world. After a wrong turn they end up at an abandoned town and decide that the sensible idea is to leave the car behind and walk blindly through town, rather than just retreating from whence they came. Eventually they come across a school, and we all know kids love nothing better, so the boys rush inside, presumably to vandalise, but this is basically the last we see or hear of them. It suddenly becomes night and it occurs to everyone that the guys have been gone a while, maybe they should look for them. Upon entering everyone else disappears, and the doors are locked. Hope you like school; it’s all you’re going to see from this point on. While the game doesn’t really say as much, you’re presumably tasked with finding the rest of the suddenly missing field trip posse, though by the end of the act, no real progress is made on that front.
The backstory of the town is explained through the traditional “find the letters” gimmick. However, note “the town”, all the backstory is about the town at large rather than the place you spend all your time in; the school. By the time you’re finished, you’re no wiser as to what was going on at the school than when you started, nor why any of these phantoms are residing there.
Weirdly, once the night time portion starts, you can head back into town instead of going into the school, which reveals a UFO and a couple of other demons, just kind of… there. Sadly it feels like more effort is put into these “secrets” than fleshing out the main plot.
Back in the school, you’ll be aimlessly wandering around looking for puzzles no one asked you to solve. For some reason a pig demon has the keys to the front door around his neck, and it all snowballs from there. It uses the Project Zero gimmick of taking a picture of a scene, only for the image to show to a different place where you go and pick up an item, except there’s nothing explaining why.
If a ghost touches you, then our heroine becomes “stressed”, repeated touching causes her to collapse. Oddly rather than die you appear in “Limbo”, which is to say you wake up in darkness, surrounded by a ring of candles and an eerie source of light in the distance. Sometimes a voice whispers clues, which end up being a lot more useful than the ones Linda keeps in her journal. Sadly why limbo exists and why she’s experiencing it, or whether it’s just something that happens to everyone in this world is left completely unexplained.
Basically, don’t come to this game for the story.
The ghostly crew consists of a phantom pig, a yeti on crack, a businessman, a crossdressing teacher, a giant lady and a lady that likes to sing. After defeating a ghost, you get a little extract in your journal explaining what the ghost’s deal is, but it’s kind of irrelevant and doesn’t really do anything to tie them into the world or explain why they hang out at school.
I was initially impressed with the reserved use of the phantoms, each is a particular character in the world rather than a random spawn, though what exactly that character is isn’t really defined. The second floor contains a ghost that disappears instead of dying, after defeating it, in one of the worst attempts at a jump scare I’ve seen in gaming, you’ll periodically get a image of it going “AAAARGH!” in front of your face briefly appear on screen. This wouldn’t be so bad were it not accompanied by a constant wailing that follows you around the second floor. This completely destroyed the atmosphere. It ended up being a deterrent to exploration since I just stopped going to the second floor until I was certain I’d exhausted every other option.
You can fight the ghosts off via your camera phone, but you can’t actually defeat them, just make them retreat until they feel like attacking again. When you take the picture *something* seems to happen to them, like the pig monster gets smaller and the yeti vanishes, but ultimately it doesn’t seem to mean anything, they’ll happily come back. Also loading screen hints say the camera can be upgraded, but that doesn’t seem to be implemented. The game says that it’s the camera flash that’s defeating the ghosts, but that begs the question; why aren’t they affected by the flashlight?
The game area essentially consists of; four corridors, a foyer, a boss room and a bunch of classrooms, most of which have nothing of interest in, just an array of misaligned desks, chairs and backpacks. Oh, and toilets, a prime place for a spook, right? Not here… In fact, there are very few rooms that contain anything of interest. It feels more like a haunted house; designed to mimic creepy films and rely on the fact you were scared of those, rather than providing any actual frights of its own.
There are a few puzzles, but they don’t have any context, nor make much sense, ultimately the main puzzle of the game is; the pig demon has the front door keys, find a way of getting them. The game just doesn’t have enough content, story, locations, characters… anything.
The idea of DreadOut isn’t entirely bad, neither is the execution, plenty of horror games have clunky controls, I can forgive that. I even enjoyed some of the time I spent with it. But it’s barely a game. It’s an assortment of horror elements, jumbled together with no reasoning behind it resulting in something that completely fails in its object to scare.
Maybe Act 2 will fix that problem, but if it’s anything like the first, the only thing that’ll have me screaming is frustration at the lack of content.

Best feature up front: you can control cats. With that out of the way: this is a detective adventure where you play as a ghost, nothing as fleshed out as Gabriel Knight, think Fahrenheit meets CSI, simplified.
Graphics are not that much to look at, music the same. Voice acting and characters are good.

There are several logical flaws like every log shelter counting as a consecrated building you can't pass but I tolerate that.
Worse are the useless collectable item hunts to add artificial length and distract from the story where you should hunt a terrible serial killer.
Strange design choices like the game world's small hub being filled with collectibles every metre and questing ghosts. They'd better made several small locations accesible by quick travel like most adventures handle it.

The detective part of the game isn't actually that much brainy also and involves some guessing.
Only get this if you like crime and ghost adventures very much and it's on sale. The simple clue clicking and the drive to find out about the killer sees you through.
Barely recommended.

I was excited to try Murdered: Soul Suspect out as it had an interesting concept and Square Enix is one of those publishers whose name is a guarantee for a good game (well, most of the time it is). The game received average scores from critics upon its release, which is probably due to some false expectations. Worry not however, Murdered: Soul Suspect is a very good game, just don't make the mistake of expecting something it cannot provide.
It features an 'over the shoulder' third-person view (as seen in Resident Evil 4 or Dead Space) that might lead you to believe that Murdered: Soul Suspect is an action-oriented game. It isn't. It is an adventure game that focuses on collecting clues and coming to conclusions with a pretty good story unfolding as we progress.
The introduction is one of the most unique in video game history: we witness our own murder. The protagonist, Detective Ronan O'Connor is killed by a masked assailant, who turns out to be the Bell Killer, a serial murderer who's been killing the citizens of Salem (a fictionalized version of an existing town in Massachusetts, USA) seemingly randomly. As a ghost, Ronan meets Julia, his dead wife, who informs him that he is stuck between the world of the living and the afterlife and cannot join her until he solves a mystery connected to his life that binds him there. It isn't hard to guess, that this is related to the Bell Killer case and we'll have to unravel it if we ever hope to leave this passageway between life and death and join our wife.
First we have to get used to what it feels like being a ghost (similar to what Patrick Swayze experienced in the movie Ghost): we can't directly operate objects, can't even open doors, but we can pass through them, if they aren't parts of Salem's Old Town, where houses were christened in order to keep ghosts away (it's a clever way of creating barriers, restricting where the player can travel). There are several ghost specific skills we can use, including the ability to see (and talk to) other ghosts, telekinetic powers and even teleporting (most of these become availabe at certain points of the game). The best and most useful thing however is the ability to possess others, so we can mildly influence them and - even better - read their minds. There are parts where we can also possess a cat (!), which allows us to to reach otherwise inaccessible areas.
There are several cases we can solve throughout the game (these are optional) besides our own and they are worth completing. In these cases we can help other ghosts by uncovering informations about their deaths and these side-quests are responsible for probably the best - both touching and satisfying - moments in the game,
Also there are little ghost tales (basically urban legends) known from horror stories. As soon as we find the given number of related objects (for example 7 pieces of boilers) we can listen to the narrated story related to that specific item (boiler -> A Watery Grave, in which a tenant finds out why the water coming from the local boiler turns brown).
It's a nice little touch and adds much to the eerie atmosphere.
The main story is interesting as well of course (of which I'm not going to tell anything about, for obvious reasons). Besides trying to figure out who the Bell Killer is we can find memories which unfolds the background story of the main characters (Ronan and Julia): we come to know how our hero, who had quite a criminal record, became a police officer and fell in love with Julia, the sister of one of his colleagues. It's like reading through Julia's diary, learning about her feelings towards Ronan, how she struggled with her own mental issues and how she finally said yes, when he asked her to become his wife, despite still not knowing much about Ronan. In the end Murdered: Soul Suspect provides us with a love story as well.
As I mentioned before, the gameplay consists of collecting evidences and clues, crime scene investigations, talking to other people/ghosts (surprisingly the game doesn't punish us for jumping to wrong conclusions) and is occasionally interrupted by action/stealth segments. This is probably what might have confused some people deciding what genre this game is. In these parts we'll have to hide from or dispose of demons who are hunting ghosts like us. They come in 2 varieties: the floor demons (stationary, can be easily avoided) and floating demons. The latter type is far more dangerous, because they can quicky catch and kill us. In order to kill them we have to sneak behind them and press the right combinations of buttons. They can be lured away by possessing nearby crows or we can hide in ghost residue and - as strange as it sounds - inside humans, waiting for the ideal moment to strike. This is the part that received many criticism, because it goes against the regular gameplay of the game. In my opinion though it just gives some thrilling moments to the adventure. If you fail and die, nothing happens, the game lets you retry from the point the demons appeared. The end of the game also contains timed events, you'll have a limited amount of time beating your enemy, something that wasn't common until then, but it does make sense (it would feel odd, running around while irreversible events occur).
The game features some amazingly well designed characters, from which I'd like to highlight Joy, the teenager medium whose facial expressions and acting are almost as real and good as of a real actor. Unfortunately the antagonist is not so memorable and it deducts from the overall value at the final confrontation. I personally also didn't find Ronan that interesting, They tried to made him unique with all the tatoos and extravagant clothing, but for me it just made him distant, someone who is hard to identify myself with.
The visuals of the game are simply amazing: it uses Unreal Engine 3 and it really shows what this engine is capable of. Eveything looks amazingly beautiful and the eerie, foggy and dark (the whole game plays during nighttime) environment is especially noteworthy. You might want to turn bloom off and pick normal AA (anti-aliasing) instead of the other modes though for better quality (something which I figured out late in the game).
The sound is exceptionally good as well: the environmental audio is remarkable, finally a game where it pays off having a surround sound system. I remember playing Baldur's Gate and Thief the first time in 5.1 and the difference in sound was amazing. It applies to here as well. The noises in the cemetery, the owl hooting really makes you feel like you were there. While the music isn't memorable (actually I don't remember any of it) the characters voices are amazingly good, thanks to the great voice actors. Again, I have to mention Joy, whose voice actress, Cassidy Lehrman does an outstanding job.
Overall, Murdered: Soul Suspect creates the impression of a game made with love, by an unknown developer, Airtight Games. It takes you on a memorable adventure, that's certainly not too long (took me 36 hours, but I explored every nook and cranny, something I usually do in good games) and unusual (an adventure game where you have no inventory - you're a ghost after all). Just don't make the mistake of confusing it with an action game (despite the over the shoulder point of view) and you are guaranteed to have a good time. On the other hand 29.99€ might be a bit too much for it (because of its relative shortness), so try to grab it during a sale.
PROS
+ very beautiful visuals
+ good, enjoyable main plot, very good sidequests
+ lots of investigating
+ emotionally moving
CONS
- some underdeveloped important characters
- might seem odd for lovers of classic adventure games
RATING
8/10

Being a fan of RPGs for many years, Divinty: Orginal Sin 2 had a lot to measure up to for me.  What can I say?  This game delivers and more!  I love the character interactions and the various storyline options with voice overs that are diverse and nicely done.  What makes this game superb though is the turn based battles.  Between interacting with the environment and some very diverse skills, your battle options are limitless.  The AI is rather intelligent too, so you wont be facerolling this one through.  The "narrator" voice took a little getting used to, but I find it adds a new imaginative dimension lacking in most games these days.  I rarely buy a game open day, but I am glad I did.  There are some quirks that the developers can iron out (mostly around inventory management), but its very playable and not a "beta" release to make a quick buck like many mainstream shops these days (yeah Ubisoft - talking to you).  Do yourself a favor - if you love RPGs and like strategy game play in battles (think X:COM series), this is best of both worlds.  The storyline itself is compelling and keeps you coming back for more.  Damn it, another 3AM night...

Having over 15 years as a company driver and owner operaitor before retiring I have to say this game brings back a lot of memories. Though I found a lot of things that are not close to being realistic, this game offers a variety of things I have seen that are. For one I found the graphics in this game better then what is in the real million dollar (plus) simulaitor I've had the privilage to use on more then one occasion and I like the way this game gives a very small taste of some of the realisticly hard places to get in and out of and a little of what real truckers may encounter during a trip. I'd also like to mention the fact that for what you get in this game I feel is very reasonably priced do to the fact that everything that is left out such as pre-trip inspection, log books, dealing wit dispatchers and brokers and even the creativity involved in finding a place to park in a truckstop after dark would all cost the developers more time and lead to a much higher initial cost to the gamming community. With all that being said, The biggest draw back to this game is that even though it can be played with a keyboard and mouse it is very difficult and somewhat tireing as both hands a kept busy all the time as you are constantly pressing keys to correct steering with one hand and with your other you are ajusting camera angles, operaitng turn indicators, and a ton of other tasks. Breaking is another difficult thing to master with a keyboard as if you leave your finger on the break button a millisecound to long, You will stop dead in the road or sidewalk, whichever you may be driving on at the time. One really needs a gaming steering wheel and pedel set up. This would defenitly improve a players gamming experiance and I think should be listed as a recommendation under the system requirments. I am currently using a mouse ,Keyboard and Logitech flight stick (to help with smoother steering but even that gets old fast and I am only commpleteing 3-4 trips a day before movig on to a more casual game. So in closing I just want to say if your thinking about purchesing this game, you may wish to consider the computer hardwear I mentiond first, that is if you can afford the expence, otherwise you may feel a tiny bit disapointed as I do.

What has the gaming world come to when a Truck Simulator becomes fun?
It sounds negative doesn't it? But that was my first thought when I saw this game.
I played it, then I asked myself the same question.
Well, it seems the gaming world is exactly where it needs to be. On the cutting edge of brilliant minds and pushing the limits of incredible technology!
This game hooked me from the start. It's not just a bunch of poorly rendered boxes on wheels floating through an open-world, demolition derby scenario.
I come at this game from two different points-of-view. I am a life-long artist and graphic designer, so visuals are very important to me in a game, but I also have my CDL and spent many years over-the-road in these trucks. After getting in a truck and driving a few blocks, the first thing I noticed was an incredibly detailed world around me! Turns out, this is what is actually keeping me coming back for more. All of the vehicles in-game look incredible, which is what I expected, it's a Truck Driving Simulation game after all! However, the world generated around me, positively blew me away!  I found myself going off the road a few times because I was trying to look over at some of the scenes happening out my window as I'm driving by!
I won't go into any depth about the looks of the game, you just need to see it for yourself. Simply put, visually it's an incredible game and you'll have plenty to look at as the world goes by.
The handling of the trucks seems to be truly accurate, with truck-specific mechanics, right down to the horrible turning radius of the W900! This is truly a simulator, I find myself driving the trucks in-game, the same way I would in real life!
The AI drivers in-game are a little crazy, they randomly ruin your day in a hurry. Stopping on a 80 MPH freeway for no reason or turning right  smack into you at an intersection. I think this is just an AI system in need of  a few minor tweaks, but I found it actually adds to the realism of driving giant trucks around total idiots all day!
Really the only con I have found in the game are the speeding penalties. There's not much room for error, if you are near a police officer when the speed limits lowers, you need to be at the correct speed before you pass that sign! I have paid about $20,000 in fines so far just from not seeing the speed limit change soon enough.
The devs seem to be VERY involved in rolling out updates and fixes, and also appear regularly in the forums answering peoples questions and concerns. This is one of the most important details of a game for me, if the devs don't care, then why should I? They sure seem to care in this case.
I would most certainly recommend this game to others. I can't get enough of it! My 12 year-old son was even quickly addicted to this game, after making fun of me for playing a "Truck Simulator" of course!

Game: Kingdom Wars 2 :Battles
Publisher: Reverie World Studios
Still in Early access
Gameplay
Kingdom Wars 2: Battles is a RTS game set in the medieval era with emphasis on battles of epic proportions and managing your kingdom. At first glance, it is a typical run of the mill RTS game which provides players with 3 races : Humans, Orcs and Elves. All the races here are pretty well balanced and none of them feel overpowered in any way. Then there are the undead which spawn when blood has been shed on the battlefield and they have the potential to destroy the army which was remaining on the battlefield. The other part of the gameplay consists of villagers/orcs who build buildings to keep you in control of the battlefield.  There is variation present in the type of soldiers you can build to keep things fresh. You can also upgrade various abilities to make your army better. The gameplay here is fairly basic for RTS otherwise with little to no surprises. Though it does execute the basic things pretty well and is very much enjoyable inspite of the clichéd RTS tropes.
Visuals
Kingdom wars 2 isn’t the best looking RTS out there. It falls somewhere in the lower end spectrum in the graphics category. It reminds me of Lord of the Rings: Battle for Middle Earth II which was a pretty good looking game of it’s time. The water in Kingdom wars 2 is spot on. You can see the waves rushing towards the shore as you make your way through the game. The unit models have some variation but are not as well made as they should have been. Some buildings have some very good design but most of them feel very much rushed out. You can see the buildings, especially the gates being upgraded not only through stats but also visually which brings a really good feeling. Overall, the graphics here are fairly average and nothing exceptional or bad is found here.
Sound
The music in Kingdom wars 2 is really good. It really escalates the feeling of a battle and amps up the sound as the mood changes from peaceful to a more violent nature. The sounds from your units and villagers though interesting at first gets repetitive in not more than 4-5 hours, which is common in most RTS games so it is nothing big of a deal. The battle cries of your soldiers and the grunts of the zombies are good enough to keep you invested in the battle raging in front of you. The music and sound in Kingdom wars 2 is pretty neat to say the least.
Current performance
Kingdom Wars 2 features an episodic single player campaign which is fairly long as of now. The tutorial is actually one of the best tutorials you will find in a RTS games. It is fairly complicated but explains most of the situations to you. I did not find bugs in single player except a couple of freezes and some minor annoyances. The multiplayer though is somewhat of an issue. It did not take me long to connect to a multiplayer game but the lag in the middle of the games were annoying to unbearable. The multiplayer needs to be worked on as it is not in the best condition. Bugs are plentiful too when playing multiplayer ranging from some sound cuts to major lag and crashing of the game. It runs pretty well though when playing an offline game. Since it is still in early access, we should expect to see much more bugs being ironed out.
Overall review
Kingdom Wars 2:Battles is a game which is really enjoyable by the fans of the genre. It’s massive battles and the inclusion of undead really gives a pleasurable experience. The single player campaign is fairly long and there are a lot of options to mess around in a random game. The multiplayer needs some work and there are quite a lot of bugs. It won’t change the mind of the people who don’t enjoy the genre but there are a lot of redeeming qualities which make this a great game.
Rating 7/10

TL;DR - if you like D&D type dungeon crawlers and want something with replayability and a bit of charm, this is a good choice.
I was unsure about this game for a while, but got it during the Winter Sale.  I'm sorry I waited as long as I did, becaause it's a great game.
I'm probably going to repeat what others have said, but it's basically Dungeons & Dragons meets Rogue with cards in a deck used to generate the dungeons and encounters.
The art is pretty good, and the story mode, which I'm currently about 3/4 of the way through, isn't a novel when it comes to the story line, but good enough to capture my imagination.  I've also played some Endless, and the game definitely has replay value.  The main character, who deals the cards, is animated fairly well, and his script is amusing and adds to the atmosphere.
What I find interesting is besides the randomness your choices along the way affect the outcomes.  Maybe even more than the randomness.  And speaking of choices, you get to build the decks that will be put in play.  You build them from cards you have unlocked on previous adventures.
The combat is 3D, and while not the most difficult I've ever played, is definitely adequate enough to give you a challenge and make you earn completion.
I'm really happy with this purchase, and plan to buy the expansion pack before the sale is over.  I think it would also be really cool if they made a sci-fi game based on the same mechanics.

It's not nearly as entertaining as it looks.  A lot of the content is okay to enjoyable, but the structure of the game is deliberately skewed to make single player unreasonably difficult, and they tied the "RPG-lite" system to individual character/controller-slot combinations (as opposed to character or player profiles), so multiplayer is a tedious leveling affair for all players, all the time.  You might cruise along fondly for a few levels, but the seams quickly fall apart as you reach the point where you have to have multiple players actually leveled up to proceed.  I'd be willing to play to the end, but none of my friends are tolerant enough to get there, and honestly, I don't blame them.
It's a shame, because the framework is there for a great beat-em-up game, but they didn't feel to finish the product by correcting poor design decisions and fleshing out the feature set.
My recommendation, if you really want a good beat 'em up, play Castle Crashers instead.  It's got everything present here and a lot more.  If you've already done that and want variety, don't bother here.  You're going to be overwhelmed with the knowledge that it's not nearly as good.

The music is pretty good and you have various environments. Everything to a train that's slowly filling up with poison to riding the streets on a motorcycle. One thing that annoyed me a lot was when flanking a covered unit, they still get the cover bonus even when you are shooting them in the back, requiring the player to somehow destroy the cover or knock the enemy away from the cover before being able to properly damage them.
What made me stop playing the game however was how the enemy could attack you when you are moving your character, while I understand this is a feature of the game and that your units can do the same to the enemy unit, unless you are able to flank, your units will never be able to attack the enemy without getting shot at a couple of times, often causing status effects like lowered defenses or lowered attack damage. Because of this you have to be very fast with your controls to move a unit into position, target the enemy and end your turn because every second wasted is a second your unit is getting shot at. This wouldn't be a huge problem if the same could be applied to the units you controlled, that if the enemy got within your unit's range they would fire back, instead your units require the enemy to get incrediebly close to you and even then they will only get to fire off a couple of shots, unlike the full magazines the opponent will do when you're moving your troops.
There are so many other things wrong with this game and this review is already bloated as it is, it felt good at the start and I really looked forward to playing this game to the end, but with such a huge disadvantage it just ruins the game.

I've had this game in my library for like 3 years now and I haven't bothered to even install it once. Recently I figured that I would play it because I had nothing else better to do and I had seen a few short gameplay videos. It's a game by Square Enix, one of my favourite publishers and it's got moderately good graphics so I'm able to play it Ultra and in 4K resolution.
Firstly the premise seems cool enough, but also pretty simple. You play a detective who's been killed and you have to find out who killed you. No problem there, as I always like a good 'whodunnit' story.
The problem is everything else except the story.
CONTROLS - The controls are so annoying to use. I had to turn the sensitivity down so low to avoid the camera spinning around like a tornado. You also walk so slowly, and are forced to constantly hold run 100% of the time if you even want to get anywhere within a reasonable timeframe; having to always hold shift also made my pinky get sore fast. All of these things make the game quickly feel very cumbersome to play and my patience really started to wear thin...
GAMEPLAY - There's no 'crosshair' but you have to perfectly directly face an object so it is in the middle of your screen in order to interact with it. Due to being a ghost, you can walk through many solid looking objects which is cool until you realise that there is also no kind of map in the game at all. Paths are constantly 'hidden' bethind objects that you have to walk through, and it's very hard to remember where something is. If you missed something way back at the start of the area, you can go back provided you can find your way through the confusing and very narrow/linear path from one area to another. The game is also filled with pointless empty alleyways and dead-ends that I really could not understand at all why the developers didn't bother to make any sort of map. It would have made navigation so much easier. Finding clues and collectables in Murdered: Soul Suspect is a huge part of the game, but sadly it's very hard to spot some mission related clues do to the objects being absolutely tiny, and/or partially hidden.
ENEMIES - There aren't really any except for these 'demons' that lurk around some areas of the game, and 'traps' that just force you to find a way around them. Demons are more of an annoyance than a challenge. Simply hide behind a wall or in a 'safe zone' until they come close enough, then when their back is turned press the right combination to kill them. The combinations are a total pain as you have to keep holding the 'R' button AND then press 2 other buttons at the same time which are often very close to the 'R' button. Getting it wrong means wasting a few minutes whilst the Demon chases you or looks for you. They're incredibly easy to kill as you can spot them through walls and there's often plenty of places to hide. Honestly I found them a pointless addition to the game and just something obviously added to try and increase the overall length of a playthrough.
STORY - The story is good enough I guess. Some of the side missions seem stupid and some of the murder/death mysteries are quite boring really. I found it kind of hard to care about a few of the NPCs but at the same time I guess a couple of them were interesting enough. The main story seems interesting enough so far and so long as it's about the same length as 'The Wolf Among Us' I will be pretty happy. I still prefer TWAU's gameplay and smoothness to this game's by far.
GRAPHICS - Not much bad to say here as graphics are pretty top notch. The game looks really nice in 4K, although I found that some of the floating papers got a bit distracting as I often mistook them for clues that I could interact with. Also the game is capped at 30FPS if you enable Vertical Sync which made it feel really, really choppy for me. A huge part of the game are also pre-rendered cutscenes which are also all capped to 30fps. So if you end up playing in 60+ FPS normally and then move to a cutscene you can end up getting eye fatigure and a general nagging feeling as the game changes framerates constantly. Finally I thought that it was kind of annoying that a lot of the NPCs don't have proper lip movements when they are speaking. This is something that Square Enix usually does really well, but in this game a lot of NPCs just stand there going through their limited behaviour animations with their mouths closed but they are still speaking.
ABILITIES - These are actually pretty boring and feel really lackluster. The first ability you get is to be able to possess people in order to read their minds or try and jog a memory that helps uncover part of the story. Murdered: Soul Suspect has a lot of NPCs in some areas, and using the mind-reading ability shows really how little thought was put into the game. ALL NPCs only have TWO possible dialogues that can be uncovered through reading their minds. Specific NPCs have specific and more 'unique' dialogues however NPCs that do nothing except to just 'populate' the game world almost always all have the same "I don't feel safe here" etc. responses. It's really boring. As for the other features like Reveal, this is just used to uncover small side stories and Teleport is only used to get into 'consecrated' areas that would normally be off-limits.
There's not much else to talk about but all in all I wouldn't recommend the game. The graphics are good and the story is interesting enough but the game quickly becomes a total pain to play. My fingers get sore, my patience runs thin and even the uniqueness of the game and the lingering mystery to uncover doesn't hold my attention for more than a few short hours at a time. More than anything I can't help but feel that a few changes or extra small additions to the game would have yielded a much smoother experience. Things such as a small map, faster walking and running, and increased amount of dialogue in the game would have added a lot of value.

VC is a great experience, and I'm glad the port to PC was so good because I'd been eyeing it for a long time from afar.  Good music, good strategy and to an extent challenge, good character and machine designs, great original fantasy WWI/II setting, gorgeous art direction and style that honestly I'd be okay with other games aping- It's not an accident that this did so well on steam.
There are negatives, too- the tone of the narrative is pretty inconsistent and basically childish, especially in the extra missions, a lot of the later conversations are cringeworthy and the antagonist might as well marker 'evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" on their face.  There's not a heck of a lot of subtlety, at any rate.  Some of the missions kind of suck or drag (There's a pretty strange difficulty curve here), or aren't clear on what you're doing until you've played it a few times to know.  Once you undestand rankings are based almost purely on speed and that spending all of your CP on orders for one person is usually ridiculously viable the game may lose some of that great strategic element.  A lot of the upgrade options aren't really options, like the mortar lances that you should pretty much never ever use.
The flaws, however, are minor compared to the novel strategy and action hyrbrid systems, the underused setting and aesthetic, the satisfying headshot "clunk" noises when you don't screw it up, and the wonderfully exaggerated ragdolling when your characters are shot down.  The main characters are probably likable enough, and as offputting as it is it's also kind of great in a corny way to have the main heroine flash a smile and pump her fist each time she ends someone's life- which she will be doing a lot.
Speaking of which, the many characters you control have a pretty good spread of voices and eccentricities.  The positive and negative qualities like fear of heights or working better when far from the group help give them personality beyond being Engineer # 6.  although most of these being negatives or more trouble than they're worth could have been worked on a bit.
At any rate, Valkyria Chronicles is the kind of game I'd probably try to complete sometime despite the backlog.  Good on sega for bringing this to steam- too bad the newest developing title in the series looks like it might kill it.

Rarely have I felt as compelled to write a review for a game as I have for this one. Dangerous High School Girls in Trouble (DHSGiT) offers a peculiar type of challenge. It's a game of highs and lows. Whether or not you'll find it fullfilling seems deeply personal in a way I've rarely encountered.
At first glance, DHSGiT appears quirky and charming - undeniably unique. A quick look at promotional material suggests 1920's teenage rebels taking on their school and town with wit and verve. I was excited to install the game. Who wouldn't love mouthing off to authority figures and getting into all kinds of period-appropriate debacles?
Unfortunately, I was met with an immediate wall to my enjoyment. Most encounters in DHSGiT are gated with one of four minigames. This has been exhaustively covered in other negative reviews. The four minigames in question are remarkably dull. If you don't enjoy them the first time, I assure you, you'll hate them by the 100th time. They never give way to something more nuanced. No matter what the circumstance, you'll have to taunt, bluff, hangman, or rock-paper-scissors your way to victory. It's disheartening, I must admit. When I realized that they made up the backbone of the game, I almost quit right out of the gate. I was looking for story, not tedious grinding.
Well, as it turns out, my ex adventure gamer instincts eventually took over. I have (if I do say so myself) a rather high level of tolerance for painstakingly hunting down a narrative.  When I became comfortable with the minigame repetition, I started to enjoy myself. The characters are honestly endearing. Over time, I grew to care about my little girl gang. Every hour I spent with them added more affection. I saw my queen Charlotte as dangerously glamorous. Her second-in-command Jean was everything 1920's society found unfeminine, and I loved it. I was hooked.
Unfortunately, my love was not to last. I'm confused by the last acts of DHSGiT, to say the least. The spoiler-free version of this review is that if you care about these characters, prepare to be heartbroken. The story takes an unexpected and extremely dark turn. I'm all for complex narratives, but this felt rushed and disrespectful to what had come before. I've seen many reviews reference "girl power" as a primary theme of DHSGiT. I think the ending puts the lie to that theory rather thouroughly. I've also seen people recommend this game as "family friendly" or an option for children, which I feel could not be further from the truth. At the very least, make sure to play it through first, to understand the conversations you might want to initiate afterwards.

Having over 15 years as a company driver and owner operaitor before retiring I have to say this game brings back a lot of memories. Though I found a lot of things that are not close to being realistic, this game offers a variety of things I have seen that are. For one I found the graphics in this game better then what is in the real million dollar (plus) simulaitor I've had the privilage to use on more then one occasion and I like the way this game gives a very small taste of some of the realisticly hard places to get in and out of and a little of what real truckers may encounter during a trip. I'd also like to mention the fact that for what you get in this game I feel is very reasonably priced do to the fact that everything that is left out such as pre-trip inspection, log books, dealing wit dispatchers and brokers and even the creativity involved in finding a place to park in a truckstop after dark would all cost the developers more time and lead to a much higher initial cost to the gamming community. With all that being said, The biggest draw back to this game is that even though it can be played with a keyboard and mouse it is very difficult and somewhat tireing as both hands a kept busy all the time as you are constantly pressing keys to correct steering with one hand and with your other you are ajusting camera angles, operaitng turn indicators, and a ton of other tasks. I am currently using a mouse ,Keyboard and Logitech flight stick (to help with smoother steering but even that gets old fast and I am only commpleteing 3-4 trips a day before movig on to a more casual game. So in closing I just want to say if your thinking about purchesing this game, you may wish to consider the computer hardwear I mentiond first, that is if you can afford the expence, otherwise you may feel a tiny bit disapointed as I do.

What has the gaming world come to when a Truck Simulator becomes fun?
It sounds negative doesn't it? But that was my first thought when I saw this game.
I played it, then I asked myself the same question.
Well, it seems the gaming world is exactly where it needs to be. On the cutting edge of brilliant minds and pushing the limits of incredible technology!
This game hooked me from the start. It's not just a bunch of poorly rendered boxes on wheels floating through an open-world, demolition derby scenario.
I come at this game from two different points-of-view. I am a life-long artist and graphic designer, so visuals are very important to me in a game, but I also have my CDL and spent many years over-the-road in these trucks. After getting in a truck and driving a few blocks, the first thing I noticed was an incredibly detailed world around me! Turns out, this is what is actually keeping me coming back for more. All of the vehicles in-game look incredible, which is what I expected, it's a Truck Driving Simulation game after all! However, the world generated around me, positively blew me away!  I found myself going off the road a few times because I was trying to look over at some of the scenes happening out my window as I'm driving by!
I won't go into any depth about the looks of the game, you just need to see it for yourself. Simply put, visually it's an incredible game and you'll have plenty to look at as the world goes by.
The handling of the trucks seems to be truly accurate, with truck-specific mechanics, right down to the horrible turning radius of the W900! This is truly a simulator, I find myself driving the trucks in-game, the same way I would in real life!
The AI drivers in-game are a little crazy, they randomly ruin your day in a hurry. Stopping on a 80 MPH freeway for no reason or turning right  smack into you at an intersection. I think this is just an AI system in need of  a few minor tweaks, but I found it actually adds to the realism of driving giant trucks around total idiots all day!
Really the only con I have found in the game are the speeding penalties. There's not much room for error, if you are near a police officer when the speed limits lowers, you need to be at the correct speed before you pass that sign! I have paid about $20,000 in fines so far just from not seeing the speed limit change soon enough.
The devs seem to be VERY involved in rolling out updates and fixes, and also appear regularly in the forums answering peoples questions and concerns. This is one of the most important details of a game for me, if the devs don't care, then why should I? They sure seem to care in this case.
I would most certainly recommend this game to others. I can't get enough of it! My 12 year-old son was even quickly addicted to this game, after making fun of me for playing a "Truck Simulator" of course!

2014 has been shaping up nicely for video games it seems, especially for indie titles with several games I either backed or seen in early development finally coming to fruition. One particular Indonesian title that has already gained a solid fanbase thanks to Youtubers like Pewdiepie, Raedwulf Gamer and Yogcast’s Kim; DreadOut developed by Digital Happiness, was discovered sometime early march 2013 where I instantly backed it and eagerly awaited its arrival.
DreadOut draws its influence mainly from various Indonesian folklore and bears a striking resemblance to Tecmo’s borderline legendary Project Zero series (or Fatal Frame for you Americans out there); the tale follows high school girl Linda and a small group of her fellow classmates when on a field trip stumble across an abandoned village which of course they decide to explore their latest find and hilarity ensues, by hilarity I mean nightfall, and death.
The game follows a very similar formula to Project Zero in that you explore the areas while looking for key items, solving puzzles and fending off against various ghosts and supernatural creatures via your smartphone with camera (which unlike my phone has amazing battery life). Much like in Project Zero, Linda’s camera is key to most of the mechanics of the game including combat and puzzle solving, though interestingly where DreadOut veers off the beaten path is that unlike her Japanese counterparts, Linda cannot naturally see these vengeful spirits. This actually adds a rather interesting depth of gameplay and indeed ups the ante, luckily Linda does react to nearby danger accompanied by a red vignette but until you view through your phone you are effectively blind to your unfriendly apparition.
However taking snaps of your enemies feels rather poor compared to Zero, you don’t charge your attack and you simply take snaps when your phone’s screen starts to act up however since the game tells you to look for weak points you can never be sure if you’re actually doing anything until the buggers have left you alone. This is a small gripe admittedly and does not harm the overall game, along with combat the camera is needed for puzzle solving; similar to the ghosts, certain puzzles or hints are not visible to the naked eye. While it hasn’t been incorporated too much in Act 1, how it was implemented was well done and when you finally figured a certain section out made it all the more rewarding.
Sadly though my biggest gripe with the game is the quality of the visuals, while Linda and her ghostly pals look very nice, the environments are very outdated for a game that had a demo back in early 2013 the visuals are somewhere or par with mid sixth gen graphics (PS2/Xbox/Gamecube). Textures are rather murky with several signs of very low res images used throughout and certain characters animate very awkwardly.
Now while some complain that the game is rather short (which I somewhat agree with), the game is currently presented in two halves where only Act 1 is currently available with roughly 3 hours for a singular playthrough which will probably require a second run just to grab all collectables and achievements seeing as the game promotes a healthy approach to exploring (seeing as you can miss a fair bit of content if you go too far early on).
But considering 3 hours for half a game is pretty standard, so long as Act 2 (which will be given free to anyone who purchases the game) has a similar or longer length DreadOut proves to be a must play for horror fans and if you’re desperate to fulfil your thirst for more DreadOut you can always play the demo which is actually a nicely sized prologue.
Pros:
Great atmosphere,
Creative twist of already established game mechanics,
Balanced gameplay,
Promotes exploring off the beaten path,
Morbid Play is in it :P
Cons:
Rather average story,
Visually outdated,
Little to no punishment for ‘death’,
A lot of empty spaces.

review exceeded Steam's review character limit twofold, so I have published it as a "guide" instead. The full review contains additional sections that explain and analyze the game in more detail:
Hand of Fate is a rare beast indeed - a
genre blend! It is simultaneously a proof of concept and a masterpiece. It is something truly unique and wonderful.
The genre blend is so unusual, that the gameplay is very difficult to explain succinctly. But, I shall try:
Hand of Fate is an RPG card game rogue-lite with an interesting Four Card Monte mechanic and simple, but fun brawl style combat.
Yeah. It's hard to know exactly what that means, but if you'd like to know more, then go ahead and read the Gameplay Explained section below.
Besides the engaging gameplay, Hand of Fate has superb art and animation, music and sound, expertly combined into a highly atmospheric, immersive experience.
In short, I
recommend it.
Yes! Well... probably! It's a bargain at the current sale price, and quite well worth it at full price also.
But, here are a few reasons why you might want to stay away:
* If you really hate reading. You'll have to do a decent amount here.
* If you really, really hate roguelikes. Single sessions are fairly short, except for endgame Endless Mode (there is autosave).
* If you are allergic to repetition. Yes, there will be some repetition per the nature of this genre mix, but I think it's entirely tolerable, and unavoidable given the nature of the genres.
* If you can't stomach the idea that a little grinding may be required to unlock everything and/or 100% the game. If you aren't an obsessive completionist, however, this won't be a problem at all! If you are, it will take you about 50-100 hours to unlock all achievements.
* If you can't stand a video game character occasionally insulting you (masochists, take note).
Otherwise, you have every reason to play the game, especially:
* If you want to try something different
* If you like indie games with high production values and great atmosphere
* If you like card and/or board games
* If you like brawling style combat
* If you like rogue-likes and games with high replay value
* If you like collecting/unlocking mechanics in games

Basically, you don't need it to start with. It's more for expanding endgame possibilities. See full review for more details.

Part two isn't out yet, so count this review only for part one. This is "recipe horror." It follows a structure that will be very familiar to horror game enthusiasts. That certainly isn't a bad thing. The atmosphere is really good. I mean stellar. They nailed the feeling they were going for. The graphics
remind you of your Playstation 2, but in this genre it matters little.
The enemy character models/animations. Oh. my. god. They are fantastic. Typically with smaller productions like this one, you see corners cut, but not DreadOut. There is one exception: the enemy you end up spending the most time around is probably the least scary. His animations are a little stale. After your first encounter or two, he will lose his horror appeal.
On the scary meter I give this a solid 7/10. You won't be thinking about this after you finish it, but I jumped out of my seat a few times. I got the game on sale; I would
purchase it for $15 until part two is out. But, if you consider it the price of a movie ticket, you will not be disappointed.
If I said anything else about the game, I might ruin it for you (part one is not very long), so I'll leave it at that. Overall, I'm pleased. Excited for part two.

A quality single player shooter enhanced by additional levels appended onto the original base game, a.k.a. the extended edition.
Enemy variety could be more varied and the save system is based on checkpoints though they're liberal enough not to cause severe frustration though I have to admit to a couple of F-Bombs and ALT F4s.
The weapon system is based on 2 guns, each with multiple modes.  An interesting attempt to redefine the first person shooter but I think it fails as the system is needlessly clunky.  With the energy weapon in hand, selecting the rocket launcher requires a key press for the host weapon and another for the launcher mode.  Why?  In the heat of battle I felt like a circus performer.  What's worse is that I found the controls to be somewhat unresponsive, no doubt a purposeful design decision to negate any type of weapon mode key press while sprinting.
Despite the flaws, the well realized world reminded me of Blade Runner infused with a bit of Rapture.   The level design, graphics and solid shooting mechanics are enough reasons to play.  Oh did I mention the Quake like rail-gun.  My favorite weapon in the game, though like some of the other weapon modes there is a cool down so spamming anything but the base weapon modes is prohibited.
Weapon upgrades are acquired through upgrade terminals.  This mechanic does enhance the standard fps as the expenditure of the in game currency, called nano, allows for complete customization of your play-through.
The story I thought was well penned but is presented like a comic book.  There are multiple modes once your done with the game though I had little desire to partake.  One mode, called EX allows you to play the game with all weapon and defense upgrades in place.  Another mode, called Heroic allows for one save point at the beginning of the level.  The last is standard Survivor mode where the game throws waves of enemies at you.
I've read that the development team has roots in both BulletStorm and Painkiller.  The quality with which Hard Reset was constructed bears the fruit of that lineage.  It's a great shooter and worthy of your time and slot in your library.

This game was in my Steam library. I have no idea how it got there. Maybe it was a hasty purchase during a sale, maybe it was from a humble bundle, maybe a friend gifted it to me. However it got in my library, I'm glad it did.
This game is a hybrid roguelike and card game. It sounds like a weird combo, but it works well. Your path through the dungeon is randomly laid out cards on the board. When the card is flipped over, sometimes you'll have to battle a monster, figure your way through a short story or even play a mini game. Many cards have a requirement, once you meet that requirement you get a token that unlocks more cards for your deck. Each time you play, you add more and more options for future games.
Some of the cards, however, rely on chance. I personally don't mind that but I know some people might find that offputting. The monster battles are in real time, which is cool. They're a bit on the easy side, however. Those are minor gripes, if you like roguelikes or TCGs or both you should check this game out.

It was pretty good.
The demon evasion "puzzles" were utter filler, though, and felt like they mostly just got in the way of enjoying the game. The takedown QTE's you need to execute to kill them are just weird on the PC. It feels like you're playing finger twister just to reach the keys you need to hold down at the same time, and since they randomize them every time you never know which ones you need in advance. Really annoying.
It was worth going though them though because the story is really good. It's a great murder mystery, and playing as the dead victim puts a novel spin on it as well. The investigations were well made, and it never felt like you were overly penalized for getting it wrong, though frankly once you figured out the games methods almost all of them were pretty easy.
It's a fairly short game, clocking in at about 8-10 hours depending on how diligent you are collecting stuff. There is a veritable TON of collectibles all over the game. In fact, I would go so far as to say there's far too many. It's like the developers didn't think the game would have enough gameplay value with the main story mode alone so they put enough random collectible stuff in it to put assassins creed to shame. If you're into that sorta thing, then great, good for you.
But, for me? By the time I got to the final encounter I pressed "OK" at the entrance to the point-of-no-return without any hesitation at all, despite having completed only a single set.
All in all, I can recommend this game. It's got a good story, and doesn't outstay its welcome. If you like this genre, buy it on a sale and enjoy the ride.
