• Bonus online Labor Point regeneration (10 per 5 minutes)
• Offline Labor Point regeneration (10 per 5 minutes)
• Increased maximum Labor Points cap (5000 maximum)
• 10% bonus to all Experience gained through combat or labor usage
• 10% discount on Marketplace purchases
• 5 Loyalty Tokens per day for use in the Loyalty Store (awarded on first login of the day)
• Ability to claim land by placing farms and houses
• Ability to pay in-game taxes on owned property
• Ability to post auctions on the Auction House by default
Now Lets look at what its like to not be patron.
• Bonus online Labor Point regeneration (5 per 5 minutes)
• Maximum Labor Points cap (2500 maximum)
Yep. you cant own land. you most certainly cant craft anything useful for you to use. all you are left with is a labor cap of 2.5k and a labor income of 5 per 5 mins.. thats 60 per hour. so you're either left with running your PC on all day just to accumulate or you shell out the cash.
Now dont go thinking to yourself that patron will be all sun shine and rainbows... because there are still land botters present in this game that trion is doing nothing about.
Even tho the game is F2P. Free-to-play players are brutaly punished. you either work tirelessly and extremely, EXTREMELY! hard on buying whats known as "APEX" (you need 2 APEX's for 30 days patron) or you shell out the money and do monthly payments for patron.
*Whats APEX* to put it simply: its something you can buy with gold or IRL money and once obtaining it you can either open it for "Marketplace Currency" *CREDITS* or sell it on the auction house.
This game is so unbalanced in terms of PvP and sandbox elements, that free players are hindered in what they can do... people in game will obviously through this statement back at you or dissmiss it and tell you that you can.. but trust me when i say this. from being F2P from the start it was a nightmare just to get 70g to pay for 1 apex. and when i came back to the game it was a brutal nightmare. on my server apex goes for 600-ish gold! and with labor being so crap for F2P. i had no real way of making money other than doing certain in game events in hopes of making 100-ish gold a day.. but even that does not work out half the time!
as someone once said. the rich get richer and the poor get more poor!

Yes, there are indeed tons of people who have given this game positive reviews. And yes, the few negative reviews probably won't do much impact, and fans will not like this review one bit. But I am alright with being one of the black sheep. Below are my very own personal observations and I stand by them:
Just like every platformer lover who also has a soft spot for pixel art, I pounced onto this game. But I am not really happy about what I received.
I really wanted to like this work, which took a whopping 9 years in the making, but I found that not so easy. Without further ado, here is a brief pros and cons list:
Pros:
+Beautiful art indeed
+Smooth controls
+Enjoyable story
+... Nothing else really.
Cons:
-Very little exploration in a vacant world which could have been detailed a lot more than its current state
-Although you get a bunch of allies and abilities, character development is redundant
-No sense of progress
-Too linear
-Upgrades are apparently useless and not even worth pursuing
-No obvious replay value. I don't see any reason to complete this game and ever want to play it again.
-Too many times the game stops you for a long cutscene or unnecessary effects (was it really necessary to halt the game everytime a robot pirate spots you?)
Finally, if I had played this on my 8bit console back in the day, I would have surely fallen in love with it. For a PC game though, I find its sheer lack of depth disappointing. It might be just my nostalgia addiction that led me to the purchase decision. I had been following Owlboy ever since I first stumbled upon the news of its development on some indie website years ago. It stuck in my mind. When it finally came out, I didn't even think twice. Probably I shouldn't have snatched this game so soon. In that regard, the blame is partly mine.
In the end, this game taught me one very valuable lesson that I seemed not to get for such a long while: Don't be hasty about a new game. Wait for reviews to come up. And even if the game has received overwhelmingly positive reviews, go ahead and check whatever negative reviews are out there. Word to the wise. Hopefully you are doing just that yourself right now.
P.S.: I respect long and hard work, and it pains me to write a negative review for this game, but that is just my unpopular personal opinion right here. Take it or leave it.

I move around a small board of cards and each is an event, a battle, a shop, a game of chance. etc. Need food to move, gold to buy stuff, some events reward you with random equipment/ability/blessing. Or a curse, lose equiment, lose health... etc.

Is if you like the concept of a card game, and hack and slash that is not complicated but fun give this game a try.

Tabletop, roguelike, RPG, TCG, third person action RPG... Add it all up and what do you get?
A strange, yet extremely fitting merge of genres, with beautiful use of lighting, shading, art and music.
Not only does it look and sound amazing, but it plays even better, with an amazingly well designed deck building system that allows you to, in a sense, build your own adventure with equipment and encounters alike, all while the dealer throws his own tricks into the mix.
You can take on every challenge, blade in hand, with a battle cry as you rip through your foes, or you can lower your weapon and offer your food and gold to help villagers, and your actions change the outcome, and in some cases, the reward.
Hand of Fate isn't trying to do a lot of things, but what it does, it does well.
Easy to use deck building system, or an automatic option for those not interested in the deck building.
A very basic "map" screen, where your adventure takes place, yet with more than enough depth to keep you engaged and thinking about your actions, with food, gold, equipment, and curses.
A very basic combat area, yet once again, with a surprising amount of depth, and a little planning sometimes, with the use of artifacts, curses, blessing, and enchanted equipment.
If you have any interest in Hand of Fate, and are deciding if you should buy it. Do it.

The game also has a great water-colour-esque graphical style.This game is also note worthy because it is one of the few that explicitly addresses ethnic cleansing. is a real time strategy game set in fictional world with medieval accents. The game plays as you would expect a game of this genre to but a few added mechanics and an online multiplayer mode keep things fresh for players. While this isn’t a genre I am very familiar with I did find the game enjoyable,
as you spend time focusing on micromanaging your units. The game offers single player and campaign modes if you just want to enjoy it on your own.
The story in the campaign mode focuses on the race of humans mainly fighting against orcs. Humanity is on the run from their aggressors, periodically making valiant stands to secure their survival. Each step of the story is told via cutscenes with voice over explaining the battle and what takes place before and after it.
-the result of cannibalism, no doubt committed by desperate war-refugees. The story itself is currently one episode with five chapters.
The game’s mechanics work very well, while I mainly played the campaign mode I also found that the multiplayer mode was a fun option for those wanting to increase the game’s replay value. The game also has a great single player mode where you can play your own adventure or a survival mode. All units in the game are under your control, even down to farm animals. The worker class mines, farms and builds while fighters help protect and progress. Both classes are important to the game as is resource and time management.
requiring both to control the camera and click on areas of interest. Each unit and building have a large variety of actions and options available to players that help to customize gameplay experiences.
The graphics in the game are simple, and even a bit dated. Character models are basic and not overly-detailed and I found some of the buildings hard to tell apart visually. Maps are also standard, nothing is bad but nothing really stands out much either.
The audio in the game is fine, the characters talk when you click on them and there is some voice over as well. The music is fitting, but not memorable.
I found the game to be a good way for novices such as myself to learn about real time strategy, or fans who haven’t played a game in the genre for a while.
offers a lot of options and customizing choices to tailor gameplay to each person as well as three different races to choose from; humans, orcs and elves. No matter what option you pick the game will be fun and challenging, plus
to keep a person coming back for more. With a hands-on development team regularly updating the game, this title is a great addition to any library.

Kingdom Wars 2 provides a brutal but satisfying RTS with a campaign that will carefully beat into your head the importance of slow, careful preparation. Fittingly for a game set in a medieval world, the elaborate fortifications that sprawl across key points of the map are crucial when it comes to holding and expanding your territory, and building up proper defenses first and foremost, both in campaign and multiplayer. Watching a ramshackle palisade grow, bit by bit, into a proper stone castle manned by hundreds of archers and swordsmen never gets old, along with seeing the enemy break on it.
Additionally, the three races within the game all manage to be unique in both mechanics, playstyle, and design. The Humans are the most "standard" faction, training troops from buildings and taking resources from the map. Their workers are fragile, their units work wonderfully together, and their defenses are incredibly strong.
The Orcs automatically spawn workers from their buildings, which are then sent through "training" to become stronger units. Their defenses are lacking, but their troops are strong, with their workers able to fight at range and in melee both, serving as their basic infantry.
Elves are an interesting case, having one of the strongest economies, but otherwise unremarkable defenses and soldiers. The ability of the elves to spend money to make more money, without having to send their workers outside their defenses, is quite powerful, and allows them to build up massively if given the chance. Their greatest strength is their "monstrous" units-massive ents, for example.
The Undead, fittingly, completely change the game once they show up. In Skirmish and Campaign both, they seemingly come across as a minor creep faction that can be dealt with easily, until they swarm you in the aftermath of a major battle and you realize every single corpse can and will become another enemy. Relying on the day and night cycle to combat their spread is crucial, before they turn into an existential threat.
Lastly, while the graphics are seemingly lackluster, they serve well enough and allow the game to throw together truly massive battles with troops in the tens of thousands, with the only limitation being how big you are willing to make your army.

This is a fairly fresh approach to the RTS genre, it throws in a few things which just make the game so much more enjoyable.
It seems to take a few ideas from games such as AOE III, and by that I mean you can use cards during the game for extra resources, a few troops etc, only difference being you will have to craft these cards.
You also have to play the game through a bit before fully unlocking all units and benefits within, as you receive materials for finishing matches which can then be used to craft new techs.
Gameplay is pretty standard RTS, with a few suprises which keep you on your feet. Your base will fortify itself by upgrades, and (this is one of my favourite things in an RTS) you can position your archers on your walls to defend from invaders. There are scattered benefits around the map, such as extra resource deposits for your workers to mine, gold carts (defended by packs of wolves usually), and small forts (defended by bandits) which are good for strategic positions.
The main thing I love about this game, which had me and a friend thoroughly entertained, was that your (and your allies/enemies) troops don't stay dead.. They will rise again as zombies, and at night are even worse to deal with. Essentially, even if you win a fight against your opposition, you'd best get your troops far away from there, or at least hope to god that that fight didn't take place near your base. The zombies swarm, you fight them off with troops and lose more, they gain more zombies, it becomes a losing battle fast.
There is also a survival gamemode, in which you (and allies) defend your bases against zombie hordes. It seems like a normal gamemode, except instead of fortresses they have cemeteries spawning zombies at increasing rates every round. It becomes hilarious and terrifying the longer the game goes on.
Pros:
-Fun gameplay
-Great multiplayer
-Fun Gamemodes
-Interesting advancement with crafting techs for new units
-Collecting materials makes tryharding those slow AI matches worthwhile
Cons:
-Not completelty optimised if your PC isn't fantastic, can get very framey at times (the worst during the survival gamemode)
-Limited to 3 different teams (races)
-A slight lack of unit variety on each time
-Limited amount of maps to play on as opposed to randomly generated maps on other RTS'
Overall, the only cons of the game are things which can be improved over time and in further development/expansions, and I hear a new expansion (free, might I add) is coming in May. If you're questioning whether the game is worth its price, I highly recommend it. You'll get many hours out of the base game alone, plus with the free upcoming expansion I'm sure there's many more hours to pour into it.
Tl;dr - RTS game with many unique ideas/gamemodes, great fun and guaranteed to have a good time.

It's nice to see a throwback to an older horror style, something which I'm always eager for in this day and age, but unfortunately Dreadout is let down by bad game design. The core game does not flow well, player direction is largely vague, and often you're left confused as to how to progress. Even right from the start of the game when your character gets out of the car it can be confusing where you're supposed to go. Most likely while playing this game you'll need to stop every so often and go look it up, which is annoying to have to constantly do. Puzzles, knowing where to go, putting 2 and 2 together, were always a big part of survival-horror games of yore, but in Dreadout's case it's rather vague and things are not clear enough.
Ghosts are cool, but some can be initially frustrating until you work out their quirks. Again, game design is somewhat bad here because you're usually left to die repeatedly until you figure out what the game is demanding from you to beat the ghost.
The game all-in-all is a good effort, the atmosphere is very good, the concept is good, the protaganist has a nice♥♥♥♥♥:P, but it's unfortunately a bad gaming experience because its flaws are more frustrating and immersion-breaking.

Yes, there are indeed tons of people who have given this game positive reviews. And yes, the few negative reviews probably won't do much impact, and fans will not like this review one bit. But I am alright with being one of the black sheep. Below are my very own personal observations and I stand by them:
Just like every platformer lover who also has a soft spot for pixel art, I pounced onto this game. But I am not really happy about what I received.
I really wanted to like this work, which took a whopping 9 years in the making, but I found that not so easy. Without further ado, here is a brief pros and cons list:
Pros:
+Beautiful art indeed
+Smooth controls
+Enjoyable story
+... Nothing else really.
Cons:
-Very little exploration in a vacant world which could have been detailed a lot more than its current state
-Although you get a bunch of allies and abilities, character development is redundant
-No sense of progress
-Too linear
-Upgrades are apparently useless and not even worth pursuing
-No obvious replay value. I don't see any reason to complete this game and ever want to play it again.
-Too many times the game stops you for a long cutscene or unnecessary effects (was it really necessary to halt the game everytime a robot pirate spots you?)
Finally, if I had played this on my 8bit console back in the day, I would have surely fallen in love with it. For a PC game though, I find its sheer lack of depth disappointing. It might be just my nostalgia addiction that led me to the purchase decision. I had been following Owlboy ever since I first stumbled upon the news of its development on some indie website years ago. It stuck in my mind. When it finally came out, I didn't even think twice. Probably I shouldn't have snatched this game so soon. In that regard, the blame is partly mine.
In the end, this game taught me one very valuable lesson that I seemed not to get for such a long while: Don't be hasty about a new game. Wait for reviews to come up. And even if the game has received overwhelmingly positive reviews, go ahead and check whatever negative reviews are out there. Word to the wise. Hopefully you are doing just that yourself right now.
P.S.: I respect long and hard work, and it pains me to write a negative review for this game, but that is just my unpopular personal opinion right here. Take it or leave it.

If you like games along the lines of Rust and ARK, this is a must have.

Having a God to choose at the start of the game adds a very "faction-esque" feel to the game that makes it all the more different.
Being able to choose whether you want to be an Archer or a Swordsman, A club wielding brute, A crafter or a gatherer. NEEDING to work together with other people to get ahead.
Things like this set Conan apart from similar games.
And even though it's in early access, the Devs are in constant communcation and are really listening to the community, being very active in the games development. Staying true to the Early access Model.
Worth the buy, Even if it's just in anticipation for future updates.

Even 16-bit-era fans that are experiencing "pixel art fatigue" owe it to themselves to feast their eyes and ears on Owlboy. The art direction and animation are on a whole other level of polish that will remind you of countless games without ever feeling like style for nostalgia's sake, and the feel of the controls hold up masterfully on a gamepad OR mouse and keyboard.
There's so many disparate elements coming together that Owlboy SHOULD feel like the gaming equivalent of a high concept album; twin stick shooting, ballistics, grappling, platforming, storytelling, and exploration... The fact that it DOESN'T is a testament to how polished and focused this feels compared to many ambitious indie games.
Part of me wishes the mechanics dove deeper and demanded more challening combinations of your abilities, but the length is just about right for a narrative adventure of this scope.
I loved Owlboy, and it left me wanting more without wearing thin.

Hard Reset by Polish developer Flying Wild Hog is an "old school" single player shooter along the lines of Quake, Unreal, Serious Sam and Painkiller.
It features highly destructive environments, upgradeable weapons via a light RPG system and a very sleek and good-looking graphics engine.
The cyberpunk story line and level design is fairly bare-bone, linear and predictable and the style borrows heavily from Blade Runner and similar "sci-fi noir" movies and games, but that does not impede the overall fun of the run and gun gameplay.
If you are looking for some simple entertainment with no complex attachments to weigh it down, this game might fill the void.
With the low price tag and solid value this game offers I can definitely recommend it.
* The "Extended Edition" now includes the DLC and is absolutely worth your time.

Recettear - if I had to sum it up in a couple of words, I would describe it as a concept that
fail, but doesn't. The gameplay is repetitive, the dungeon crawling requires excessive amounts of grinding to gather materials, and the light-novel/anime style is probably a turn off to some.
In practice though, Recettear is an unexpected hit, and a real hidden gem. Recette herself is adorable and everything she does just makes players want to love her more. The concept is fresh and unusual: run your very own item shop, pay off the loan-shark fairy! Play smart, watch for special deals, buy low and sell high to try to maximize your profit! Balance between the general approval of your customers and your profit margins to maximize revenue!
Not only is the concept of running one's own item shop interesting on its own right, but the game can be unexpectedly challenging. Many players fail to pay off the debt and have to use the game's "mulligan" system to complete it (or mulligan by save-scumming) because they got too greedy seeing a deadline approaching, or because they failed to account for a potential drop in an item's value.
Earlier I mentioned that the dungeoneering is pretty bad, and that's true to an extent: there aren't many dungeons, the loot is sporadic and it can take lots of materials to make just one item, and the combat is perhaps too simplistic. Yet there are a slew of characters available, each with their own quirks, and exploring the dungeons can help reward a player with new characters, thereby increasing the amount of interactions.
Speaking of interactions, these characters interact very frequently. The writing is light-hearted, and conversations do not feel like they drag on for any absurd length of time (they can all be skipped as well). Yet at the same time, there are little mysteries about the world that make players want to know more about the world and the people in it. The characters, all in all, are a huge part of what gives Recettear its charm.
Sure, there are a lot of fridge logic moments - areas where a player just wants to say "hey, that shouldn't happen because..." but for the most part, none of these obstruct the game's flow.
Overall, Recettear is a charming little adventure. It's not the most adrenaline pumping adventure, but one can't help but admire how well put together and cute the game is. I highly recommend it for anyone looking for something light-hearted yet difficult enough to warrant paying attention to.
So go - with a little luck, hard work, and the spirit of capitalism, how hard can it be to exploit your friends and pay back the loan-shark fairy?

So, I just have finished playing this wonderful game. I decided that it deserves positive review and I am gonna tell you why.
Story:  It takes place in the year 1935, where two opposing military factions, the Empire and the Federation, wage war against one another on the continent of Europa. You can say that it is some kind of alternate WWII. So, it starts in a small town called Bruhl that belongs to small country Gallia, where a 19 years old girl on town watch, Alicia, encounters accidently the son of a passed gallian general, whose name is Welken Gunther. The two are cast into the military life, where they fight for their lives and lives of their comrades. The plot of the game is very exciting and reveals through the small scenes as a part of the book. You will find a lot of romance, fun and breathtaking scenes here, nevertheless, sometimes you don't believe that just one squad takes the missions where it is required to send full combat company.
Characters: Almost no problems here. All the characters make up a pretty diverse cast. They are well-developed and almost all main and supportive characters have its own chapter telling about their skeletons in the wardrobe. Nevertheless, rest of the crew stories are limited by small notes in the book,  you will find a bit of squad 7 characters development in extras, but it is not enough. If you want to get a little closer to them, you should watch anime.
Music: I will limit myself to one point to which music here is very good. Thats all
Gameplay: Gameplay left a mixed impression and I am gonna tell you why. Battles are quiet challenging and intresting... till the moment you realize that almost any battle can be finished up to 2-3 turns just with scout/*lancer* rushing (except the missions where it is impossible to finish fast due to its specificity *minor spoiler*, like tank *escort*). I can't tell you that I don't like the battle system, but seriously, every f*cking mission where you have to reach point/capture a camp/kill the boss requires just 2(3) things: scout, def order (later +*caution order*). After chapter 9 I've done every mission and got A class for each without problems. Sometimes, you must use lancers. Thus, snipers, shocktroopers and engineers don't deserve a single point of your precious exp point at all (after chapter 9-10 definitly). I understand that it kills fun in the game, but if it allows to use this, why not? From time to time, game tries to convince you that it can't be done this way, although, there is always fast approach to finish the mission, you just have to think a little and I want to tell you that during this thinking and searching, entertaining will come. I can confidently say that despite the uniformity of missions purposes, landscape is different and you always solve a maze as a consequence when you reach the goal it gives satisfaction.
Pumping weapons, tanks and fighters is a good part of the game, I like it. When your fighter grow stronger they get new personal qualities with HP increasing, almost all of them are very useful (especially lancer's and scout's ones)
Summary: I recommend you this game if you like anime style, SRPG, military themes and good stories. The battle system could have been better, but it is entertaining enough I believe.

The wonders that is this game, kinda.
You see, fellow reader, Elsword is kind of a fickle one. It's a 2D MMORPG with some really good aspects that marks the difference between other MMORPG'S.
Right off the bat you will notice something with this game and that is repetition, unlike most other games where you "clear the dungeon, kill the boss and save the princess" in Elsword it's quite different because the princess doesn't want to be saved until you finish the dungeon and kill the boss 3 times. Confusing right? Let me explain from the start and we'll get back to this just keep this in mind.
Elsword starts off with your beta-male mc protagonist Elsword (everyone calls him Elboy, ikr it gets worse) who embarks on a quest to retrieve the pieces of "El" a powerful gem of some sort. In his adventure you meet many characters that join the party known as the "El gang" or "El party" or whatever. It might seem dull but trust me, it's not (kinda) You see, while elsword doesn't have a script written by the masters of literature it gets the job done, it gives a story that you actually give a damn unlike other games.
Characters:
You may be wondering "what, characters? aren't they just your typical sword, archer and shield dude from any other mmorpg?" Well young grasshopper let me elaborate, yes, yes you have. While you do have a certain cliche characters like the sword guy which is Elboy and the waifu spear girl which is Ara you do have backstory to each one of them that you get to learn along the game, and you not only get to learn one of them, you get to know it all. Heck, even some bosses have backstory.
Combat and Gameplay:
Alright, you can't expect much from a 2D Game but if anything elsword does the job good in combat, although with one exception. You see, you have your normal movement (for some reason with the arrows but oh well) your typical ability bar blah blah blah. What frustrates me is the high element of pay to win in this game, unlike most games YOUR ABILITY BAR IS BLOCKED UNTIL YOU BUY AN EXPANSION THAT IS EXPENSIVE AS ♥♥♥♥ UNTIL YOU ADVANCE FURTHER INTO THE GAME. Yes sir, you'll be rocking a strong 4 abilities only through out your entire gameplay unless you coff up 10$ for the sweet 8 ability bar, and guess what? IT DOESN'T STOP THERE. Because you have to pay for another expansion that not only get you up to 10 abilities but the abilities that are in those slots recieve power ups because pay 2 win. But hey, at least the combat is fun amirite?
Enjoyment:
Alright, remember what I said at the beginning with the princess and all that? Let me finally explain, and it's why I almost gave this a negative review despite all the badmouthing I gave it, the game is enjoyable yes, I spent a lot of time in it, upgraded various characters to their last jobs, had a blast with my clanmates but the repetition and grinding was insane. The game literally has ABSOLUTELY NO REPETITIVE VALUE. Because you're forced to play the same dungeon 3 times if you're planning on advancing the story line, and it's 3 minimal dungeons, there were times I had to do it more than 5 times and I wanted to kill myself half way through, the game valued quantity over quality and gave a poor first impression. It's highly pay 2 win although you can somewhat manage without spending a penny in it but it's going to cost you grind and grind. Positive points? Well combat, somewhat decent story, not hard to master the movement (I mean most of the cast are one trick ponies so you can exactly be terribly bad at this game), interesting bosses, Nice character design (Ara and Eve though), interesting abilities and hyperactives but I really wish they could work on the pay 2 win and on the poor repetitive value but I doubt it, core gameplay will never change at the end of the day.

Apparantly I haven't made a review yet, so here goes.
Warframe is about a bunch of cool space ninjas running around space being vigilantes mass-murdering hordes of enemies and grinding bosses so that you can get even more space ninjas to add to your arsenal.
Personally speaking, I'd recommend this as the best F2P game on steam (Even better than TF2), due to the fact that you can obtain about 90~% of the items in the game at absolutely no cost. Although it does have a steep-ish learning curve due to the fact that there is little to no handholding in this game, once you go past that curve you can go solo everything with no problem, no trouble.
It's fun, it's fast-paced, and there's a little bit of everything for everyone, including what weapons you'd like, what colors you'd choose, what capes you'd wear, how you'd decorate your dojo, cats, dogs or sentinels.
The community isn't particularly toxic, and is extremely helpful most of the time, meaning that they'll be happy to hold your hand as you go along.
All in all, I'm happy with all the time I've spent in this game, and I don't regret spending money on the game to support the brilliant devs behind this fairly well designed game.

Fatal Frame, this is not.  My first playthrough clocking in at the 2 hour mark (for Act 1, Act 2 has not yet been released) was underwhelming.  Much like Fatal Frame, the horror lies mostly in atmosphere.  Initially, the atmosphere works well enough.  Musical cues, ambient noises, with the occasional heavy breathing from the protagonist help drill home that the game wants you to know it is 2spooky4u.
Ghost encounters are anti-climatic.  The boar-ghost poses no real threat (hide in a class room, snap photos until he leaves, resume exploring), the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ghost's jumpscare/attack is effective once, and the final encounter is literally a run to the exit repeated three times in a row.  Since you respawn in the same location you "died", you literally have zero reason to fear the ghosts outside of the one or two jumpscares thrown at you.
Oh, and there are really only two puzzles in the game.  Three if you separate getting the photo from getting the key (though the photo flat out tells you where to find it, so I don't see that as a puzzle myself).
The severe lack of ghost encounters, puzzles, and general content is incredibly dissapointing.  There are free horror games which provide many times more content (and are of higher quality) - Phobia 1.5 being a prime example.
Act 2 may redeem Dreadout (once it is released), however Act 1 leaves much to be desired and is not worth it's asking price of $15.  I would, assuming Act 2 does release and does improve, suggest you pay no more than $5 for this game.  Your money can be better spent elsewhere.  Heck, Fatal Frame 1, 2, and 3 are on PSN along with Siren.  You can get Fatal Frame 1 and 2 for 2/3 the price of this.
*Update*
After a quick look to the Steam forums, it seems that you're able to return to the town.  After doing so I can report the following:
-You can fight one more ghost.  It's hilariously easy.  Maybe there are more; I didn't encounter any.
-You can use your camera to see flat / 2D ghosts random float about.  They don't make noises.  They don't attack you.  They are just cardboard cutout ghosts who circle you.
-You'll meet up with a giant ghost (whom you technically meet later in the main game), who flicks you with it's fingers as if you're a booger.
All in all that added 10 minutes to my playtime.

I'm nearly 5 hours in and the graphics continue to wow me, the controls take a bit to get used to at first, especially at the start/intro.
Regarding combat: You're practically thrown headfirst into dealing with some basic enemies, but you are treated to a gradual learning curve by your own admission... without any tutorials about it. I can't explain it, you just seem to slide right on in and your own intuition takes over.
This is NOT a bad thing as it's not too easy or too difficult to work out on your own, you may be defeated a few times and you'll actually eventually learn from your follies, but you won't give up through difficulty-rage; neither will you feel disappointed because it feels like a cakewalk... it feels JUSSST right so far.

It has moments on par with other great story based 2D platformers as I mentioned and referenced in my previous status... and dare I say -- it sometimes shares the same kinds of humour and intriguement as Monkey Island and Final Fantasy respectively when you least expect it.

This is by far one of the best games I've played recently. BEAUTIFUL art, a lovely orchestral soundtrack, fun and well-designed gameplay, and clever level design. For folks who are into completionism and 100%ing, there's a strong collectathon element as well. There are also a few hidden secrets, reminiscent of classic 90s games; however, don't get me wrong, this is overall a modern game despite some classical elements.
I'm a major sucker for nice pixel art, and Owlboy most certainly delivers on this score. Every bit of this game clearly had a lot of love put into it. Color choice, character design, just... unf. Love it, love it, love it. This game is what modern pixel art games should aspire to be. The soundtrack is just as lovely as the art; it gets a little extra appreciation from me given the amount of oboe featured!
The characters and storyline are enjoyable and fun. Our main cast is made up of a mute owl, a friendly (but sometimes a little judgemental) engineer, a poetic pirate, and a wannabe spider; each has their own backstory and character growth. There are quite a few optional opportunities to learn more about each character, in addition to the main plotline. Each one is loveable and quirky in their own way. I also feel as though the somewhat ostentatious and gaudy shopkeeper, Buccanary, deserves an honorable mention in this category. Especially at the end, the game can hit you with a few nice, emotional punches as well. One moment at the very end comes to mind in particular, but unfortunately, it's extremely spoilery.
The gameplay is a nice blend of puzzle-solving, platforming, and Tanooki-suit Mario. While the first dungeon has a fairly simple feel to it, it's clearly meant to be an introduction, as the future dungeons change things up in fun and sometimes novel ways. Everything from grappling puzzles to traditional platforming are featured. Even if it's not revolutionary, none of the gameplay feels "stale" or cliche. Everything is polished and fits well in the context of the game.
I highly recommend this game, overall. Well worth the full price, to me!

Mass Effect 2 is the second installment to the Mass effect franchise. While Shepard’s story can begin here, I recommend that players play the first Mass Effect instalment. It greatly enhances the players experience of the story.
Mass Effect 2 in undoubtedly a great game with reviews to match, but it has to join that list of games I hate, but still believe are great games and would defiantly play them again. I completed my play through on Veteran, since I felt the default was a little too low. The story of Mass Effect 2 definatly is the pinnacle of the franchise, with a strong opening, mid and end game. You decisions are impactful and extensive. The characters are more diverse and each has a story Shepard can partake in. The games complex mechanics from Mass Effect have been simplified for the better. Levels are streamlined and feel more accessible. Overall I'd say Mass Effect 2 provides the greatest story satisfaction. Players will walk out with what they put into the story.
Now, when it comes to gameplay I'm not sure what to say. I want to be somewhat objective about games I play, but still give my opinion. I feel I need to go back a play the game again, but overall I'd say Mass Effect 2 was the most unfair of the three games. What I mean is that I'm one of those people who'll try the game on insanity just to see if I can do it. I couldn't, not because I was terrible at the game, but I felt that Shepard just could do the complex moves he needed to do. Besides that the Squad AI is terrible and dies very quickly putting all the heat on you, which usually mean that you die.
It's the first time I've begun to play on an insanely high difficulty and found it unrealistic and unrewarding. What's weird is that I found Mass Effect 3 was possible on insanity, though it required a lot of restarts. Basically I think Mass Effect 2 is one of the mechanically bad games I've played. Everything works, but higher difficulties reveal that the combat and movement are basically broken and poorly implemented. All this said it’s a fantastic game overall and I highly recommend it along with the entire mass effect series.
Mass Effect 3 (it’s sequel) is only available on Origin which is run by EA Games.

Below are server details so you can get an idea of how I'm playing the game; below that are the pros and cons after about 60 hours of gameplay within the first few days of Early Access release. At the very end I'll include a list of a few glitches that have been very frustrating. However, none of the glitches have made me dislike the game or its core mechanics; they are something that simply need to be addressed.
Sever: Hero's || PvE || Average Online Players: 4-7
-Player Structures are Indestructable
-Equipment is dropped on death
-Only owner can loot player corpse
-No nudity
-Day Time Speed: 10
-Night Time Speed: 1
-Harvest Amount Multiplier: 1.0
Cons:
- Night Cycle is way to dark and makes going out at night almost impossible as you cannot see mobs, cliffs, ect
- Hit Boxes on mobs are decieving for both attacking and being attacked
- Clunky combat system; specifically regarding blocking mechanics
- Lack of information available in game for items, crafting benches, weapon stats, attribute stats, ect
- Map functionality: I like how minimal it is, however, it would be nice if when you discovered an area it would write in the biome type or other simple details (ONLY AFTER you discover the area)
- No weather (other than the very occasional sandstorm)
- Rendering Issues
- Server Rubberbanding
Pros:
- Diverse crafting system (some things should be moved around based on levels you can learn them an item, but not the components to craft the item itself)
- Leveling system, personal character growth, and recipe learning system
- Materials and Gathering
- Weapon and armor tiers
- Graphics
- Developers seem aware and interesting in fixing bugs and balancing the game
Bugs:
- Shallow Waters: We have dubbed this bug "Sacrafices to the Water God" and what happens is if your corpse is submerged in shallow water, you cannot loot your body to get your items back and they are lost
- Bed Bugs......Beds will sometimes not save spawn location and if you die, you end up back in the starting desert
- Crafting stations UIs will show you are creating many of the same item and fill available invenotry space when you only click to create one or a few of said item
- Teleporting mobs, this might be more server based than an actual bug, but mobs have a bad problem with teleporting making it very difficult sometimes to finish a kill
- Wonky Audio Files: Female created characters have the same audio as male characters, hitting small rocks has the same audio sound as hitting a flesh mob

Turn-based crossed with real-time. At this time I am unware of any game existing that has this same mechainc, and it does an alright job of it.
The game starts up and immediately throws you in. The sudden loud music of the title screen only is very startling and there is no volume control, only on/off (same with sound however isn't deafening). Rest of the music is more easy on the ears.
I'm about 2/3rds in and I'm rather torn of a few things.
The level design is alright but is hard to tell what's part of the background and what is an obsticle. There are secrets you need to discover for scientists or health boosts and at times it may be easy to tell if there's a possible secret behind a wall or not.
You aren't given a counter in mid-level of how many scientists there are until you complete the area, which will tell you your total time, turns #'s, secrets and scientists found seperately.
Only way to access the options is when you're in an area AFTER the world map. Also the only effective way to quit the game, otherwise it's (via ESC) Title Screen > Exit.
There is a scientist buddy that comes along with you and talks frequently, but is very easy to ignore and pay little to no attention to him, even if he's giving advice or tips. That could be my impatients as it's not difficult to understand the controls (arrow keys/WASD, 1-3, ctrl to pass a turn or stall, etc.), initial and additional, as you progress in the game; controls are pretty bare basic as they can be.
There is a boss fight at the end of each world, and (so far) one requires a different way than ramming to defeat it.
There are moments you have to react fast while others you have to pause and think of how to get out of a bad situation with the least amount of damage taken.
Unfortauntly, I'm not having fun but I'm not having an awful time either. It's pretty mellow and calm for me.
The game works as it is intended, not noticing any technical issues on my end, controls are responsive, no crashes. There was one time (and this is by pure accident) I couldn't make a move of any kind. A monster was stuck in an air tunnel unable to exit due to a turn-based monster blocking it, so the turn couldn't end. I had to restart the level and make sure I didn't make that same mistake again. Unsure if level design flaw, coding, or what have you, but so far has only happened ONCE.
I would wait for a sale, between 25%-50% off, if you want this game. $9 is asking too much for me after playing 4 hours of it and getting through 2/3rds of it at the time of writing this with little difficulty.

Dangerous High School Girls in Trouble - Oh noes
Believe it or not this is an RPG - a hillarious vintage board game with unique mechanics and a role-playing soul, to be exact/more vague. Set in the early 20th century, you control a group of high school girls trying to solve a mystery murder, which leads them to uncover a darker secret involving the whole city. The skills you invest in are Rebellion, Glamour, Savvy and Popularity. You level up by using those in appropriate 'mini games', which always involve interacting with the townsfolk.
Both writing and the art are superb. While exploring it for 15 hours or so, I encountered some weird things - a talking pony, a split personality, a desk serving as a policeman, a ghost hired to scare unwanted visitors... The story got more ridiculous, more interesting and more serious as I progressed. By the end it felt like Doctor Who, catching you off-guard with messed up revelations & profound thoughts, right in the middle of the laugh. Let's just say I understood why it got banned by Big Fish Games.
If this got you interested at all, try it - a tad repetitive mini games don't detract from this one of a kind experience!

Let me start off by saying, this game is not worth it's full price. This game is alright. Pick it up on a sale.

Secondly, speaking of the demons - these could have been easily left out of the game. I felt that they were tacked on for padding and that all they did was break up the story and hold me up. The system around it was uninspired and just felt like a nuisance every time I faced them. My final quarm with this game is its length. I finished this game in just under 10 hours (not including the credits). It felt short because of this. However, I could've spent longer running around Salem picking up the collectibles if I had felt like they added much to the game. Also, it seemed a little buggy. Despite all this, I had a good time playing this game. The character models and visuals looks very nice, although lacking in the colour department. The story kept me invested enough to see it through to the end. The characters were well thought out and the plot was cohesive and captivating. The gameplay was tight enough to not hinder the flow of the game (mostly). And of course, the collectibles. Oh the collectibles. There are a  l o t  of collectibles. Personally, I only found the ones involving Ronan's wife interesting and didn't pay attention to the rest. These collectibles will add to the length of the game if you feel invested enough to hunt them all out.
Overall this game was enjoyable and concise. But I don't feel it's worth the pricetag because of its quality and length. Originally, I wasn't going to recommend this game, but after writing this, I feel it was worth the effort and time.

Hands down, best strategy game I´ve ever played or seen. It is quite similar to Battle For Middle-Earth II, except this game has more realistic battle mechanics, especially archers - in this game, they are not OP, and you have no chance of succeeding in any battle with archers only. They do make a very useful support though - so, just like they did in actual historical warfare.
One of the things that make this game stand out so much, is how amazingly detailed, scrupulous, and complex its siege mechanics are - there are ladders, belfrys, trebuchets, battering rams, mantlets, and many more contraptions and techniques in which you can break down your enemy´s walls, breach them, or bypass them. On the other hand, you can pour hot oil down from your battlements, or throw rocks, you can install catapults on them to help you defend, build high towers where you can place your archers for a tactical advantage, and more!
I´m not going to lie - my first impression was a mix of confusion, disorientation, and frustration. This game is complex, hard to understand at first, and certainly can pose an intellectual and strategic challenge. And I love that. Once you understand how economy works in this game, and get used to controlling your troops, this game will show itself in its entire greatness.
There are zombies, dragons, mages, mighty heroes, as well as countless other, less fantasy-esque units and foes. You can build a vast army, that will storm your enemy´s city and lay waste to it, or you can level up a few heroes, supported by a mage, who wreaks havoc with his powerful spells, and try taking the entire city on with just a few mighty individuals, much like in Battle For Middle-Earth.
This game is absolutely worth its cost, not just the money, the time spent playing, the initial confusion, the effort you put in learning to play this game, all of it.

The developers have added a lot of content since when I first bought it, which was awhile ago. As a player of RTS style games for many years now, I can safely say this is one of the greatest indie RTS games I have played. In fact it is a solid RTS, for the price, and I haven't really seen anything that was comparable.
It features:
Progressive Gameplay; I.e. upgrade talent tree that is outside of the actual battles. You gain loot and such, then spend it to gain benefits, such as a knight, or spearman, buildings, etc.
Common RTS elements and uncommon RTS elements, all that are good. Base building, troops, management of resources. Uncommon includes choosing to grow chickens vs pigs, to send a cart or not, where to build a farm, how to use the resources. Do I use the wood for this or that, what do I use the stone for, the gold for, do I use food for peasants or soldiers?
Each match (this was awhile ago, sorry if review is outdated), plays out with a strong tactical gameplay set AND elements normally limited to turn based games. The maps are fair sized, and there are plenty of objects to go for. Want more gold, get a cart, some peasants, and send them out to mine. You may need to station soldiers nearby to protect them from enemies, including the undead.
Speaking of the fallen, things that die have a tendency to, well, come back to kill you. If things are left unlooted, which must be done by peasants, they will come back and be an annoyance. At first this seems trivial, but can be abused to cause injury to your foes. Raid the neutral camp near your enemy's base early into the game with a medium sized force. This way if your troops succeed, a large dead force will strike at their peasants and fort, and if not hopefully many die, and the same result may happen to your foe.
Neutral camps, the enemies vary, usually protect resources that you need in order to survive and expand, and are worth looking into.
The game is somewhat complex, and has bugs, but is definitely worth the investment.

DreadOut is a very well designed horror game that draws inspiration from the Fatal Frame franchise. While the developers low budget clearly shows from the outdated graphics, average voice acting and the such - DreadOut manages to nail down the most important thing for a horror game, the atmosphere. Despite some frustrating game mechanics and the short length of the first episode (roughly 2 to 3 hours for a playthrough, although there are plenty of secrets / hidden content which gives the episode enough of replay value for at least couple of playthroughs), I would definitely recommend the game for fans of the genre.

I like to start with the bad first:
I am not a big fan of anime, and a some of the tropes from that culture work their way into the game. Also, the game gives the impression that it may take the Fire Emblem route, and try to flush out the third-tier characters (as opposed to the main characters and the immediate supporting cast) but alas, aside from their brief sound bites and short bios you don't get much. The learning curve is a bit off, and the missions often tell you what you are supposed to do several turns in- after the point when you should already be executing the plan. Controls, particularly tank controls, are wonky on the PC port. There also seem to be characters which are far superior to others, cutting down on the mixing and matching you would normally do. The voice actors/animation for the two lead characters is sometimes cringeworthy.
The good:
A completely unique blend of tactical gameplay that kinda reminds me of Batallion Wars. At its core it is turn-based, but has enough real time elements to keep it interesting. It is also a game that really made me want to 100% it- getting A ranks on all the missions and having fun trying to figure out how to overcome each obstacle. The supporting cast to our two leads is impeccable, with interesting characters and great (albeat sometimes cheezy) acting. I got invested in the story, well, at least the first time through, and there are good moments which subvert the trope of treating warfare lightly in games.
The verdict: Not in my top tier of games, but for the combat system alone I say that this game is a must-play for any semi-serious strategy fan. 8/10

On the surface, this is a fun little platformer game with aspects of twin-stick shooter. Like others have remarked, it has impressive art design. Unlike others, I didn't find myself very compelled by the story and overall game design. Does it have a message? Yes, you can definitely see the parallels it draws between its characters and the hardships that we, as inhabitants of earth, face economically, environmentally and socially.
But, was it fun? Kind of. Will it leave a lasting impression on me? Probably not. Is it worth the $20+US? No...I would say about $15 relative to other games I've played that are similar indie platformers.
I understand this was an indie title that took 9 years in the making - don't really understand why so long - possibly finances? In all honesty, I've played other indie games that were far more enjoyable to play and left a lasting impression - I'm talking about you Environmental Station Alpha, Cave Story and Valdis Story. Opposed to these others, I can't honestly say that I'd come back to play this one. It's very linear. Controls are just ok. There's a section near the end that requires some experimentation with platform jumping. I'll give a hint...if you've been using the analog stick in the flying portions preceding this, you definitely want to switch to the D-Pad during said jumping section near end of game. Something weird convolutes the analog left movement stick with the jumping mechanism, intermittently wonking out and prompting premature flight, loss of hang-time, etc. You'll see. Maybe the devs will fix this.
Anyway, bottom line, it is a fairly enjoyable game that I would recommend...with one caveat. If you don't mind spending the $20+, go ahead and purchase; otherwise, wait for a sale at around $15 or so.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is one of those games who are just a little above average, providing some moments fun while lacking any memorable game or story experience.
The gameplay is extremely simple, resulting in a search for hidden objects, called "clues" in the game experience. While being simle - you find certain hotspots, then "combine" the three most meaningful clues - it has moments of frustration, when you're missing a tiny speck somewhere in the corner of a dark room.
But even worse, little side stories about the key locations you visit can only be uncovered by finding a series of more or less well  hidden objects cluttered around the scene. If you fail to collect all of the items, you won't hear about the sites mysterious past.
It must have dawned on the devs, that such a gameplay isn't really satisfiyng, so they added little skill challenges in form of demons and floor traps, which you have to avoid while maneuvering some of the game locations. While far from being complicated, it's more or less frustrating because there is absolutely no evident reason for the demons or traps to appear.
And that's it: Search more or less interesting locations, avoid demons and find objects hidden around which trigger another story bit.
Graphically the game can't deny it's vintage-console origin as well: Locations are separated by loading screens and rather small, graphics are okay but not mind-blowing and the sound is the typical mix of creak-moan-chime sounds you can find anywhere else.
Characters are unfortunately very clicheed: A dead cop with a doubtful past and a teen-aged, too-cool-to-be-bothered, ghost-seeing medium aiding him.
Fortunately the story is taking a fresh perspective by letting you die right at the beginning, forcing you to find your own murderer. It's told well enough to keep you interested until the end, although it unfortunately never expands on the motivation behind them, which would have enhanced the overall experience greatly.

Mass Effect 2 may be the quintessential example of how to properly do a sequel. Just like its predecessor, Mass Effect is an RPG set in outer space with third person shooter combat, but everything seems far more polished this time. The graphics look much better, the six classes now have their own identity with abilities unique to each, and the storytelling is greatly improved. There are a lot of new and interesting characters, not the least of which is The Illusive Man voiced by none other than Martin Sheen. The roster of squad members is twice as large as in the original Mass Effect and each squad has their own story and loyalty mission. These characters were not just "game characters" to me, they were people. The inventory system is also greatly improved as enhancements armor are researched instead of equipped. Special ammunition can be selected while in combat. Best of all you never EVER have to worry about running out of inventory space ever again. And above all, the story once again is what makes this game so appealing. Bioware went all out in telling a gripping, exciting and emotional story in this game.
If you've played Mass Effect, you can import your custom Commander Shepard from a Mass Effect save file and continue his or her story in this game.

Writing this review sort of breaks my heart.
As I was getting close to completing this game, it was possibly one of the best games I had played so far this year, if not the best.
Excellent art, controls, level design, story and atmosphere.
Then I reached the last stage. And for whatever reason, developers thought it would be a brilliant idea to change the control scheme that worked so well so far (won't spoil how) and use this opportunity to throw a frustrating precision platforming section into player's face. After reading "Stay afloat, Otus!" for the 20th time while failing to reach the corresponding platform, my controller was well on the way to start learning how to fly.
Eventually I got past it - no sense of achievement, only anger.
Then I proceed to try and complete the one optional minigame. Again, a completely different control scheme from the rest of the game. One hour of fruitless attempts before eventually giving up. No less than half the achievements of this game are gated by completing this (not that I care much but it's really a bizarre decision to give so much weight to this ONE optional part of the game).
I am sure I am going to get a lot of flak for this, and yes, I know, "git gut".
But if you are amongst people who can't get good enough, you may want to give Owlboy a pass. You will love it for 95% of the adventure, but the remaining 5% will leave a sour aftertaste...
It makes me really sad - a couple of design decisions that seem inconsistent with the rest of the game in general were enough to switch my opinion from "Highly recommended" to "Not recommended".

Nova-111 is an excellent puzzle game with some really fun innovations to a pretty stale genre. If you like old-school 2D puzzle games like Adventures of Lolo, then this is for you. At first, Nova-111 seems like a typical turn-based puzzle game on a grid. But quickly you learn that some elements in the environment are in realtime. For example, you have to juggle turn-based enemies with realtime laser turrets. This makes for some very fun maneuvering. At first, all your ship can do is bash into enemies, but as the game progresses you gain some additional abilities like a smart bomb and a teleport gun that lets you move two squares in one turn. (And more powers that are better left a surprise.) Overall the game is not very difficult but if you want to save every scientist and find every secret area (while also minimizing your damage and number of moves) then you can make yourself a real challenge. The enemies are fun and varied with interesting patterns to memorize. Not to mention a lively sense of humor and polished art style. Recommended for puzzle lovers!

Do you remember the primitive empire building mechanics in Mount and Blade? Ever feel like they weren't able to cover the real breadth of possible political intrigue? Did you ever think you could have solved a standoff by quietly assassinating a regent, marrying off your sister to a mongolian despot, keeping a rival monarchs heir under lock and key by offering to "educate" them before declaring a surprise war or carefully replacing all your precursors council members with men fiercely loyal to yourself?
Then step right this way my friend, as Crusader Kings 2 is essentially ALL that and a metric tonne more.
On the positive side Crusader Kings 2 is one of those games that benefits from a level of detail that should impress even the most brick-chewing and hardened history buff as the majority of its campaigns are based around the monarchs and clergy of the real middle ages. Paradox has done a laudible job in recreating the insane game of political backsies that these historical figures found themselves living through or dieing in. The fact that it also gives you a quick and easy way to look up more information on particularly interesting characters is a great example of tangential learning used in gaming. Further to this there's a truly dizzying amount of depth to the games mechanics that gives you an idea of just why every ruler had to have a retinue of advisors and counsels to help them manage information and make decisions. The lack of a strong structured narrative also gives the player a lot of freedom in how they tackle problems or exploit oppurtunities. It leads to some rather interesting emergent gameplay scenarios that I suspect people who enjoy the game while love swapping with other players just to compare how they each dealt with unexpected problems.
It all adds together to give CS2 a real sense of atmosphere, refreshingly not in the usual "dark, rainy and miserable" sense that highly atmospheric games often default to. You end up feeling like a man (or woman) with a bit of power under their belt but an order of magnitude more responsibility than you could possibly have been prepared for.
On the other hand...the user interface and tutorial could use a hell of a lot of work. Yes this is fairly par for the course in a Paradox game but it becomes more of a bugbear than usual in CS2 due to the sheer magnitude of information the game is required to communicate to the player.  You open a single figure's profile and you're given their nationality, general skills, specific strengths and weaknesses, religion, marriage/betrothal status, claims to land and title, demense makeup, alliances, honourary titles, family tree, dynastic tree, vassals, retainers, your opinion of them, their opinions of you, their hopes and dreams...AGH! STOP! Look I just want to know who his heirs are so I can kidnap one of them!
Compounding this problem is that the number of possible avenues of play is quite large and, while the tutorial does it's level best to introduce us to all of them, it felt like trying to teach the specifics of circuit design to a confused panda: More difficult than nessecary and ultimately kind of pointless. When I sat down to go through the tutorial myself I had already initiated and succesfully resolved two murder plots by the time the game actually introduced me to the plotting and conspiracy system. Yet by the time my neighbours were marching over my home territory and I was running about in a flap trying to route them the game decided that now, after the invasion of my home had already begun, would be a good time to teach me about building static defences...on my island colony several thousand kilometeres away. Thanks CS2, you couldn't have mentioned this whole "developing technology" thing a little earlier? Perhaps back before my paper thin walls had been breached by a ballistae?
Ultimately though once a player works out the ins and outs of the system, and yes that might take several decades of PHD level research and a small team of interns working around the clock, they'll find themselves immersed in a mechanically deep and highly immersive world that will reward them with... well probbably a poisoned cup of wine carried by your heir apparent but a historically accurate one nonetheless.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 (D:OS2) is a 4-character party RPG. Your game persona is either a customized character or one of 6 origin characters. Origin characters are, basically, more story-rich than customized and self-created characters. However, for self-created characters the players can freely choose some character customization options like talents or backgrounds to pick. During character creation, you can pick one of 20ish existing classes and modify them at your will, independent of you choosing your own character or an origin character.
The overall story is a conflict around who will be the next god, represented by a so-called godwoken - a living being with special powers. As there are several of said beings, conflicts arise and different approaches are taken by them to become the next god. All else is probably spoilers, so I'll refrain from going any further here.
Walking around in the D:OS2 world is real-time. Movement involves, among other things, solving puzzles, clearing dungeons, talking to NPCs, trading, crafting, running errands / quests, or exploration.
As soon as your characters enter, for whatever various reasons, combat, the game becomes turn-based where, based on player or NPC initiative, combatants take turns in which they can spend their available action points on (mostly) movement, casting spells, and attacking enemies. Similar to Divinity: Original Sin there is an elements system where effects from different magic schools can be combined. For example first let it rain and then cast an ice spell on the wet ground to create a frozen surface where enemies and allies can fall over (be knocked down). Or, as another example, cast a fireball into a poisoin cloud for a fiery explosion.
For combat and quests, the player's characters receive experience points which result in level-ups which grant new points for new spells, character stat advancements, new talents, or civil abilities (like bartering, persuasion, thievery, ...).
I cannot review game master mode (where players can create their own quests and story archs using in-game assets) or multiplayer PvP as I haven't played them yet. The game also features co-op for up to 4 players, which I imagine to be pretty hilarious and will try out after my initial playthrough of D:OS2.

As a big fan of the “Fatal Frame” series, I was really anxious to get my hands on “DreadOut”.  I mean, c’mon…fighting ghosts with nothing but a camera?  It may sound silly to the uninitiated, but those who have played “Fatal Frame” know better.  “DreadOut” is a more modern-day version of “Fatal Frame” where the player takes on the role of Linda, a high school student trapped in an old abandoned town.  Equipped only with a smart phone, she’ll (you’ll) be tasked with solving puzzles all the while fending off some really terrifying “creatures”.
Buying the game will grant you access to the first act, with DLC on the second act and a free roam mode to follow.  My biggest gripe is that Act One is only about one and a half to two hours long, once you know what you’re doing.  There’s only a handful of ghosts to boot.  Just as I was getting into the first act, it was over…I didn’t have this problem with “Outlast”, which took between five to ten hours to complete. I was able to confirm with the developer that the second act will be free, though the free roam DLC will have a price tag.  I was also able to confirm with the developer that the second act will contain more content than the first, so that helped to alleviate some of my concerns somewhat with regard to the price.

Besides the “buy Act One now and hope Act Two is more meaty” feeling, I did run into a bug or two.  The game can also glitch out on occasion, forcing you to hard-quit and replay areas already beaten.  One of my save files got corrupted and I had to erase it altogether.  Still, “Dread Out” is an incredible and horrifying experience.  There is a demo available should you wish to try before you buy.  If you can’t get through the first minute of a “Slender” game without screaming like a little girl, then you may want to before dropping the dough.

(edit, I missed a major point and wanted to go over it and explain my reasoning)
Now some of the reviews that are negative because of the absolutly massive amount of DLC there is in the game, and that is true. If you theoretically wanted to buy all the DLC in this game it would run you up 200 dollars, a insane amount. Here is the thing though, Paradox does DLC in a way that is kind of worth it. When a new DLC comes out all the major points are added for free. If the map changes or a vital game mechanic is changed, it is free of charge. The only thing DLCs really do is 1 major point (adding playable factions, flavor events, ect).
My advice is that you buy the vanilla game and just play that, maybe add a DLC of your choosing or two. You really won't need all the DLC they provided. I have never needed such DLC packs like Sunset Invasion (a relatively goofy alternate history DLC) or Sword of Islam (I never found the Islamic caliphates that interesting). If you need help deciding here are some possible DLC I would Highly reccomend you buy if you choose to at all.
Old Gods-Adds pagans as playable factions and a new start date, a major change and it's really fun for vet players.

DreadOut is a call back to the games of the past, it's a old formula revived and updated for the new generation.
The first thing that stands this game apart from any games I've seen lately are the attention to detail in the environments. I spent my first playthrough scanning the landscape and checking each room, great care has been taken in the design of the levels and it's refreshing to have situations where you can get to a lonely dead end that serves little purpose other than to let you explore (but only sometimes are you alone). The controls work well for the game as well and didn't do anything to hinder the gameplay but the lack of a 180 degree turn is sorely missed in some encounters that need some tight turning but it still has tighter controls than Fatal Frame, another game DreadOut takes some ques from. The game also doesn't hold your hand, there's a handy "How to Play" in the menu that I recommend you get familiar with, and get use to using the camera to check things out!
The sound is great as well, I haven't been entranced by atmospheric sound and music since the days of the first Silent Hill entries. Even if there's no immediate threat I found myself on edge just walking around due to the haunting sounds as I explored the game.
I can highly recommend this game and look eagerly forward to the release of Act 2 and the subsequent Free Roam mode. Make sure you check out the demo as well, it's its own stand-alone level that you definately don't want to miss. At the time of this review I couldn't get the download to work through Steam but it should be working on release.
But the game does have some negatives, the first is the length. It's only 2 hours (with figuring out puzzles the first time, I was stumped a couple of them for a good while) if you go in blind so right now there isn't much.. So, it's a negative but when the rest of the game comes out it should pad it more, since I'm more disappointed that there's less game for me to play right now. Second, Death is handled differently in this game, I'll try not to spoil anything but you always get a second chance with more time. There were some technical issues but they've already been fixed by the developer so I won't count those.
Either way, it's great! Might not be too long (for now) but it's an amazing experience!
And remember this when you get the game... when night falls stay outside for awhile before going indoors..

Alright, I just beat Owlboy after 7 hours of play (too much of which was cutscenes for my taste). I did not 100% it, though I did do some of the extra content. It was alright, but highly disappointing. Not a bad game, but only excellent in its use of pixel art. Wait for a sale.
George Weidman (Super Bunnyhop on Youtube) described this game best: "I love you, but sometimes you're a piece of ****"
TECHNICAL PERFORMANCE:
I believe the game at one point exited to desktop suddenly without warning. However, I can't replicate this. What I'm certain it did was minimize itself at points without warning, despite me only using a 360 controller. This happened a couple of times, and may have something to do with using a second monitor.
There were a couple of framerate hiccups that frankly shouldn't have been there considering the style of game, but it wasn't anything harmful to the experience.
You have some options for graphical settings, though not many. Understandable for the style of game.
PRESENTATION:
Lots of wonderful, stunning pixel art that I appreciate thoroughly. Animations are also nice, though there are unfortunately not many of them to see. Characters can emote, and Otus is a precious cinnamon bun, but after the 50th time he gets spooked or looks dead-eyed you kinda wish there were more things they could do. However, what's there is very nice.
Menus worked alright, UI was fairly minimal and unintrusive. You have options to change parts of the UI, which is appreciated.
There was a surprising amount of the screen going a single colour (white or red) due to shooting an enemy or something, and I found that pretty jarring.
GAMEPLAY:
This is where Owlboy just tanked for me. The first couple of hours were enjoyable, even if largely scripted. The ability to fly is nice, though it ultimately may have done the game more harm than good. In Owlboy you can fly indefinitely without consequence, which must have posed many problems for level designers trying to make a challenging 2D "platformer".
It is more of an exploration-based game like Zelda or Metroid, but the only real exploration is done in the game's dungeons. There's some rudimentary puzzle solving, stealth sections, and shooting enemies, standard stuff. However, I never got into a flow like you might in a Zelda dungeon, where you start being unable to do very little to progress and by the end, can do everything in it. It didn't feel like Metroid either; I never felt lost, I never felt I had to explore much more than one or two screens over to find my next path to progress. The level design isn't particularly complex or elegant.
Case-in-point, there was a section where you pass some deadly moving blocks into a room with a giant screw blocking your path. I'd never seen anything like it prior, and couldn't figure out the solution. There was a terminal window in the room, but all it said was a bunch of vague stuff about the story. I tried to leave the area, but found the deadly moving blocks would kill you no matter what timing you used, so all I could do was try the screw again. I did end up progressing, but from what I could tell, nothing prior taught you how to do it, and the solution was not even slightly in-line with anything shown before. That's poor level design, even if I'm just bad at puzzles.
The real boss fights, while good when present, were far too scarce. Several "boss fights" were nothing more than waves of common enemies thrown at you, which was disappointing. This also exacerbated what I feel was the absolute biggest problem: the shooting. It's laid out like a twin-stick shooter, but the weapons at your disposal either don't feel remotely satisfying to use, taking far too many shots to kill, or are just impractical for combat. A shotgun you get halfway through has a preposterous cooldown, which is awful when it's used for several repetitive puzzles. Most of the game you'll be mashing a single button to shoot, just because they found it necessary to give your gun a 3-shot burst if you don't do that.
Combat isn't just repetitive and time-consuming, it's also frustrating. When you get hit, the whole screen stops moving for a fraction of a second and you get flung in a seemingly random direction. If you hit a wall or an enemy, you also slide along that wall for a period of time. This looks good to a viewer, but when you're playing, it just feels like the controls are being yanked from your hand.
CLOSING:
I'm sure you can get something like double the time I spent out of this game, but I'd never want to do so. The game works fundamentally, but it's just not very fun after a while. The art is beautiful, but the game lags behind, trying to compensate by shoving story beats in your face.
If you want pretty art and a bland game that might have you dying more than you expected, but not because it's difficult, go for it. I'd wait for a sale.

Owlboy was an absolutely amazing game. I literally couldn't walk away, I played the my whole first runthrough in one afternoon, and didn't pause for more than 30 minutes that entire time. The story was completely captivating, the visuals were stunning, the music was outstanding, the characters were incredibly well designed, and the combat was unique and challenging, but fun.
I can't help but compare this game to Undertale, as both are simply designed, but still story-rich games that manage to tell a unique and powerful story. Obviously, Undertale saw incredible success and had insane amounts of players, but I absolutely preferred Owlboy. The graphics were glaringly better, the story was even more impressive, and the sheer amount of unique mechanics and ideas put this game all the way over the edge for me.
Some of the later boss fights were a bit challenging for me, mostly as a result of my inexperience with combat in Platformers, but that did frustrate me a little bit because it felt unfair that I had to spend so much time repeating the same battles over and over and had no option to lower the difficulty because there simply isn't a difficult setting. That said, the combat mechanics definitely made that issue a lot more pleasant to deal with. I had never seen anything like the combat in this game, and the aspect of switching between gunners during combat to access their unique abilities was really fun to learn and play around with.
The music in this game was truly great. To go back to my earlier comparison, I know the entire gaming community was raving about Undertale's soundtrack, and I definitely see where they were coming from, but this game was on a completely new level for me. The mixture of orchestral and electronic music was a really good choice for this game. It seemed that every new piece of music I heard throughout the game felt perfectly placed, and did such a good job at setting the tone for the situation.
Overall, this was a great game, absolutely one of my favorites I've ever played.
I give it a 9.5/10, and recommend it to EVERYONE. The only obstacle is that combat may be difficult for players not experienced with Platformers, but the same is true for just about any game from this genre.
