The good: The pixel art and soundtrack are beautiful. The deeper story is interesting.
The bad: There are maybe 10 hours of gameplay here, especially if you spin to move faster, and the game doesn't lend too much to replay value. The cannon mini-game (and to a lesser extent one boss with a related control scheme) do not have well-explained controls, unlike the rest of the game, so they come off as "cheap" or "overly difficult."
The ugly: Unless I'm missing something, there is no way out of "The Loop." The last secret I found involves an eerie conversation about "The Loop" with a dead owl, and that's that. Last year's big indie game had a similar "Loop" style deep story item, but its "True Ending" allowed the player to escape it (and even suggested not playing the game afterwards, as it would negate the premise of that ending). I'm not saying "be more like that game," but it's kind of sad to end with the normal ending knowing what "The Loop" implies.
Was it worth a 9-year development cycle? That's for the developers to decide.
Was it worth $30 and 10 hours of my life? If you have the disposable income, sure. If not, grab it on a Steam Sale.
Update: Nominated for the write-in award "Years of Dev, 10 Hours of Play" for fall 2016 Steam Sale.

Owlboy wants to please you. The game tries it’s hardest to put a smile on your face, and it nearly accomplishes that across the board. Whether it be the stunning pixel art (seriously, this is one of the most gorgeous pixel art games I think there is, period), sweeping soundtrack or the genuinely charming cast of characters, Owlboy’s aim is to please.
After nearly ten years in development, Owlboy has finally released and boy is it great. As I mentioned, the first thing you’ll probably notice is the sublime art direction. You can really feel the love and attention to detail that went into crafting this world and is breathtaking landscapes. Whether it be the dusk sky or an underground cave, the game is simply a joy to look at. On top of the wonderful pixel art are the tremendous animations. Everything here is silky smooth with fluidity that really make everything pop and makes the world feel more alive.
But graphics aren’t everything, right? Luckily, Owlboy is also fun to play and has exquisite controls to boot. While the minute to minute gameplay and standard enemies may not necessarily be that challenging, I still found it quite engaging to traverse and explore the world. The main mechanic of the game is that the character Otus can fly about while holding one of his friends who can fire their respective weapons. I quite liked this wrinkle and by the end of the game during boss battles, I found it quite thrilling to swap between the three friends to mix and match their weapons. Speaking of boss battles, these are some finely crafted encounters that will test your mettle. I found each boss to be tough, yet fair. I don’t think I beat any of them on my first go, but learning their patterns and weaknesses was very rewarding.
While I would not call Owlboy a Metroidvania, it certainly feels like it wanted to be one. The world may seem quite open when you begin but the game is in fact pretty linear. I didn’t find this to be a bad thing, but it’s worth noting. What may alleviate the linearity for some is the excellent level design. The layouts of each area are smart and intuitive so you never feel lost. Going along with the Metroidvania-lite is the fact that there are upgrades, but they range from essential (health upgrades) to useless (hats). While I feel that if the devs fully fleshed this out and made it a true Metroidvania we could be looking at a truly special game, I still greatly enjoyed my time with Owlboy.
If you’re looking for a game that will put a smile on your face and throw in a couple of laughs for good measure, you could do much worse. Owlboy is a beautifully realized world with a standout art direction and just the right amount of challenge to be enjoyed by nearly everyone.

Do you want a game about a ghost trying to solve his own murder while escorting a young woman past various dangers by manipulating objects like some kind of heroic poltergeist? Then play Ghost Trick: Phantom Detective.
Do you want a detective adventure game? Then play Ace Attorney Investigations. Or L.A. Noire.
Do you want both of the above but lack a Nintendo DS? Then get this game.
Murdered: Soul Suspect has all the investigation/logic gameplay of Ace Attorney Investigations with the difficulty dialed back to "negligible", all the poltergeist gameplay of Ghost Trick with the difficulty dialed back to "non-existent", and clumsily shoehorns in some MGS-ish stealth gameplay with the difficulty dialed back to "fish in a barrel".
Fortunately, what it lacks in challenge, it more than makes up for in the strength of its story. For a game that's only 7-12 hours long, the characters resonate very strongly right off the bat, and the mystery is doled out in exactly the right portions at exactly the right time. It might also make you want to take a vacation in Salem, MA, because it makes it look like a fantastically cool and eerie town.
TL;DR: This game is a wonderful visual novel wrapped in a weak stealth adventure game. It would have worked better on a handheld console with the stealth crap cut out, although being a console/PC game did give it gorgeous graphics. If it's on sale, definitely get it. Full price, give it some thought.

As of right now there are too many problems with Conan Exiles for me to recommend it. The official servers have been taken offline until further notice due to lag I'm assuming they were unable to fix even with a server capacity of 40 players.
Major Issues:
* The map is pretty small for 40 players, you will have a hard time hiding from larger clans.
*The weapon and Armor tiers are completely unbalanced. If you are a tier below an enemy you had better hope you are able to run and get away from him because you will not win a fight against him. To expand on this 3 players with iron tier gear cannot beat 1 player with steel tier gear. He will not run from you, he will not fear you, he will simply slaughter you. When these players have steel gear you can safely assume they are higher level which often means their stamina pool is larger so they will out run you and hunt you down.
* The higher tier armor was supposed to slow you down more than lower tier lighter armor but it doesn't, So not only do the higher level players have better armor and weapons, you cannot escape them.
*Melee steel weapons destroy tier one buildings with THE GREATEST of ease. It's like you are in a cardboard box.
*You unlock the higher tier weapons long before you unlock the hightier buildings making level rushers the greatest most unstoppable raiders ever.
* The dancer is the only way to remove corruption but you need a base and supplies to have a dancer, which is insanely hard to do since swords destroy bases. I've had friends lose a quarter of their stats with no way to regain them for a week. It should wear off slowly even without a dancer. Maybe while eating a certain food or something.
To expand upon how unbalanced the weapon tiers are it takes about 20 hits with a stone sword to kill someone, 10 with iron and just 3 with steel. The gap is so large it makes interplay combat impossible, the higher tier just wins automatically.
So no I cannot recommend this game at all for new players, you will not do well.

This game has a lot of polish and attention to detail, but a few things keep it from being a must play.
It seems to suffer from 'I designed the levels so I know where everything is' syndrome. Secret parts of the level that you discover by repeatedly bumping into walls (while every move is counted against your 'grade' at the end). An unknown number of scientists to be rescued. Hit the exit too early? Aww you missed those 4 scientists who were missing and we didn't tell you about.
No checkpoints, no saving. If you want to play a level and not have to repeat any part of it (they are broken into 3 stages), you must play it completely. I suppose this wouldn't be so bad but the levels do feel like a chore after the first time through.
Speaking of which, the absolute worst design choice was the very last level. It took what enjoyment I had found in the game, threw it in the dirt and used its cloven hoof to ground it into non-existence.  Finishing became a chore instead of a goal.
I feel like the game changed its personality mid way through. At the beginning, we learned the mechanics of the game, Everything moved like clockwork, see, plan out your moves well! Then we run into some elements that aren't bound by this rule, hmmm.. curious but we can work around it, and even use it to our advantage. Soon enough, there's  fires raging, enemies exploding, and immunity from step-time seems to be a crutch that the game uses to ramp up difficulty. There are times when they teach you about a elements and enemies and there are others where they kill you to teach you and you restart the level.
There are some clever puzzles that make use of the elements and weapons in the game. I think that was the most satisfying part for me, but as the game evolved it became less enjoyable.
All in all, great graphics, sounds, controls. The levels are well designed and I didn't run into any game breaking bugs that forced me to restart a level. However, lack of checkpoints or free saving and repetition seem to be a way to artificially extend the play time, particularly on the last level.
6/10 - pick it up on sale.

If you’re looking for a game that genuinely feels increasingly rewarding the longer than you play it then I urge you to try Reverie World Studios Kingdom Wars 2: Battles that has been recently released out of Steam Early Access.
Although the game was bundled twice during its Early Access period, meaning many of you may already own the game and therefore have an even greater reason to play it now, the game is definitely worth its asking price especially for those of you who have the time and the energy to make the effort to playing this through to completion. Although I’ve spent four hours playing the game I can already foreshadow that this is the type of game that you could easily sink hundreds of hours in. There are five full campaigns and that’s without even considering the multiplayer. As of writing there are well over one hundred players playing and the in game chat system was vibrant and active so finding a match shouldn’t be a problem for some time.
One of the best things about the game is that there are three playable races. However, unlike a number of other games where each race feels very much alike even though units and buildings may be given different names the play styles of each race feel very different from one another. If not for the graphics then at times you would have a hard time believing that you were playing the same game which is a real boon for a genre where variety can be an important selling point. Another strength of the three race system in this game is that – at least in my experience – none of the races play over or underpowered when compared to the other. Certainly there may be a race that plays to your own individual strengths or against your weaknesses but it is a game where putting in the time to learn to master one or more will give you an advantage in the multiplayer.
There are some weaknesses to the game. My biggest one would be the graphics. The UI, because of the graphics, needs a fair amount of work but I’m not entirely certain as to how I would go to polish it but I do know that it needs work from its present state. At times the screen can be too busy and I found it difficult in these times to know which units – peasants – weren’t being busy. This is especially apparent on the tutorial level where there are just so many different units that bombard you that you can lose track of what is happening all too quickly. I know that I wasn’t the first player to lose at the tutorial level and have this complaint. There are also some bugs that continue to remain in the game. However, to be very fair to the developers, they’ve been great and are removing them from the game at a rapid pace and this has been the case throughout the entirety of the development process.
However, the tutorial level – even if you include the fact that there is a little bit too much going on – is one of the better ones that I’ve played. It’s a welcome introduction to the challenge that you will be experiencing throughout the game. This isn’t a walk in the park regardless of the level of difficulty that you play on and that is as it should be. Some players may well be frustrated at just how tough the challenge can be but if you’re wanting an engaging and challenging game in this genre then you’ve found it.
My favorite aspect of the game is the fantastic skirmish gameplay. This is genuinely the type of game that I would recommend to those who loved the original Warcraft games as well as those of you who play Rise of Nations and other similar games. You’ll be surprised at just how much depth there is to your city/base building while also at the same time how strategically you must be in designing the type of armies that will enable you to be successful. Players of both types of games will be at a distinct advantage as you utilize a combination of the skills throughout the campaign and multiplayer modes.
There is a ton to like about Kingdom Wars 2: Battles. There is potential for the title to become even better. The devs have been great and if they continue working on the title then it could become a classic. If you already own the game thanks to the Damnation Bundle from Bundle Stars or the Be Mine 21 bundle from Groupees then get on board and play it. If not and you’re a fan of the game then you really owe it to yourself to check it out if not right away then when it goes on sale.

Your experience with this game will vary wildly, and 90% of the time, it will boil down to the people you've been paired with, but when the stars align and you get a group of people who play their part, this can be an oddly addicting and unique experience.  You will be placed in one of three weekly situations (or any of the three if you purchase them) as a random member of a cast of characters with a set of different random modifiers and/or items that will determine the general direction of your character's goals.
Or maybe not.  While each round has goals, the game is nearly entirely played out in an almost improv theatre style, with the only interactions open being viewing items in your inventory, trading them, and conversing with players through an at times impressively competent text-to-speech program.  This means that how you act, or rather how your character acts, is entirely up to you and how you want your character to be.  When with the right group, this can make for some great speed roleplay sessions.  However, with the wrong group, it can devolve into one or two people trying to play regularly while the others all see how many dirty words they can cram into the text-to-speech, make awful comments, or create a cult around who they believe is the real murder in a scenario...a sentient thong (yes, this actually happened in a session).
So overall, I'd recommend at least giving this game a try.  While you are always essentially playing roulette with who you'll be in a session with, and sometimes queues can take a while to be ready, the good experiences can make up for it.  And it's free, so there's no harm in dipping your toe in to try.
EDIT: Aparently, there have been some issues regarding the text to speech program since I last played.  The review will be updated once I have more information.

Immediately, it feels like a survival game. You need to build something from nothing, cobbling together scraps to get by, and it's occasionally desperate. Progress therefore, is quite satisfying. The hunger/thirst system is fair and adds to the sometimes desperate "survival" aspect. The combat is up close and brutal. The crafting system is deep and interesting. Putting together outposts and then a full home feels incredible. Similiarly, gearing up to go exploring and returning home with a full inventory after surviving the wilds and occasional NPC attacks is both fun and satisfying. The graphics are good and everything runs well, especially for a pre alpha.
What I don't like: The enemy spawns, particularly crocodiles, can be ridiculous. I chose to build a home on a relatively clear sandbar. There were no crocs at first. Now they spawn seemingly one after another. Archer animations and mechanics really need to be worked out, it's hard to judge distance your arrow can travel, and even if you hit. Some craft recipes are too high. You need 50 branches for the lowest tier campfire for instance. No one wants to pick up resources for that long. It takes a while to get even decent gear. The combat is decent but seems to lack impact and rythm. And most annoyingly, every time you die you need to update your spawn point again by making a new bed. Every time. This is tedious and unnecessary, and if you forget, you spawn way back out at the beginning, making the journey and wasting time.
Overall, I'm excited to delve even further into the games, and see what the devs are going to have in store. Right now, I'd give it a 7.5/10

Not only did I find Hand of Fate very enjoyable, I found it surprisingly challenging as well. Perhaps not entirely in the best way, but it suits the theme very well.
Hand of Fate is all about maneuvering a playing board made up with cards and going through the dangers that lie within. As you complete these challenges, you'll gain additional cards which will unlock additional treasures and additional challenges. Interestingly enough, the game remains very challenging to slightly unfair levels as time goes on. From the beginning, the first three bosses are simple and you'd be forgiven if you think Hand of Fate is an easy game. Not long afterwards more elements are introduced and older cards/challenges get refreshed to be harder so you can't as easily fall back on them for easy rewards. By the end of the game you're scrabbling for every advantage you can get and if you don't spend your time completing these challenges you're going to be absolutely decimated.
But that ends up being one of the game's major weaknesses. While the game is pretty damn strategic and has you fighting a whole lot of different elements in your quest for ultimate ambigious glory (which is told through an interesting way having the various cards represent your character's various memories and experiences), there's a heavy amount of luck involved as well. Especially late game. Smart players will start spotting good cards to stack their deck with, but there are many moments where the game just decides that you aren't going to win and pits you against a boss who makes all enemies of his faction invincible and another that attacks you relentlessly in a very small area. Meaning that if you're fortunate enough to get 200 health - somehow - you can still end up ♥♥♥♥ed by luck so hard that it'll make your head spin. Throw in a slightly slippery control scheme, enemies who love to dog pile on you, various traps that are at times hard to see or avoid (see the control scheme issue), and your victory ends up having a whole lot of luck involved. And one loss can put you back quite a way which means a lot towards the end game.
That said, from start to finish (though I'm very close to finish now, not quite there yet), Hand of Fate is very well set up and excells at telling a story that's all about the adventure. A neverending adventure really. And a whole lot of insanity that occurs along the way. Plus it's just fun, when it isn't deciding that you're not going to have fun.

Your experience with this game will vary wildly, and 90% of the time, it will boil down to the people you've been paired with, but when the stars align and you get a group of people who play their part, this can be an oddly addicting and unique experience.  You will be placed in one of three weekly situations (or any of the three if you purchase them) as a random member of a cast of characters with a set of different random modifiers and/or items that will determine the general direction of your character's goals.
Or maybe not.  While each round has goals, the game is nearly entirely played out in an almost improv theatre style, with the only interactions open being viewing items in your inventory, trading them, and conversing with players through an at times impressively competent text-to-speech program.  This means that how you act, or rather how your character acts, is entirely up to you and how you want your character to be.  When with the right group, this can make for some great speed roleplay sessions.  However, with the wrong group, it can devolve into one or two people trying to play regularly while the others all see how many dirty words they can cram into the text-to-speech, make awful comments, or create a cult around who they believe is the real murder in a scenario...a sentient thong (yes, this actually happened in a session).
So overall, I'd recommend at least giving this game a try.  While you are always essentially playing roulette with who you'll be in a session with, and sometimes queues can take a while to be ready, the good experiences can make up for it.  And it's free, so there's no harm in dipping your toe in to try.
EDIT: Aparently, there have been some issues regarding the text to speech program since I last played.  The review will be updated once I have more information.

I am reviewing as another "sale noob" who got the game, while not for $2, it was still worth my $5 and I would still feel like a charity if I spent $10 on the game. Anything above $10 and you might as well add the DLC that's in the game.
The 'good' stuff about the game;
The game isn't exactly all smooth or running, but it does feel somewhat solid. I usually get the experience I want from the game weather it's the decent sword fighting in the game or the hard to figure out archer where the bows and crossbows aren't easy to compensate for the arrow drop, which there is if you were expecting CoD's hitscan. There isn't any. So the archer is hard to master but fun to use for the most part. The 'for the most part' will come in the bad area.
The maps, while confusing at first, are actually easy to move around and you usually need one play-through to learn them since they look linier, actually have more paths than I expected, though on some maps it's not as branching. The game does do a good job at the sword play though, people can call it buggy or salami but it's not exactly a First-person Shooter. If you go down a narrow hallway and expect to hit someone with your LMB (which is a normal swing) your sword, if it's long enough (E.G. Great sword, battle-axe, war hammer, ect) it will clang off the wall.
But if you were calling salmai where you thought it was salami when you bashed your weapon against the wall and died, you probably didn't check the tutorial, where it's actually useful in this game. There are actually four different kinds of attacks for every scenario that every person I see calls salami on, just spam clicks LMB because, I dunno, pepperoni it? If you scroll up, you will do a straight lunge, where the walls wouldn't effect your attack, or if you have a high enough roof, scrolling down will bash over the top and those walls didn't do a thing to you. It's worth going over the tutorial to get your bearings, or else you WILL have a bad time.
The controls overall are easy to work with but very... Tricky, to learn. I wouldn't say master, but tricky to get a grip of.
Now, the bad part.
When you first jump into the game, you will notice green tabs in the multiplayer server browser, those are low rank servers. Join those for the first time you play the game to get your taste for the multiplayer experience, but don't expect to make friends in there, and don't teamkill your side on accident, will yah? For about the first 2 hours of the game, I called it stupid. Even after the tutorial. I wanted to refund but then I started having fun with the archer, all before I got teamkilled for playing as the archer. Then I started getting more deaths from my team than the actual enemy.
The low rank servers are not to be taken serious, it's hard to take the game serious in some cases, but it's certainly a struggle when you are pushing for the objective in team objective modes and either you get rushed by 16 players or you get 10 teammates attacking the same 2 people, and you happen to be in the middle, even when trying to run away, an axe swing from a teammate to your left cuts your head off. I can't put my finger on why, but it's actually frustrating to die in this game. I haven't been so mad to die in a game since GTA:V Online to a hacker in passive mode.
The mechanics themselves also make me want to tear my hair out, when you swing at someone, putting your crosshair on their head, expecting to cut it off, they look like they were blocking, all before they stab you in the stomach and your sword clearly hit them but they walk it off, I was a Vanguard against a Man-at-arms, which has the least ammount of armour. You will be calling salami on a lot of swings that should of killed a guy that has very low health, but gives them a love tap where they procceed to spam LMB until you can't block anymore and kill you.
This game rewards people for spam clicking LMB with no reguard to a good player fighting back, because the low rank servers have none, at least that I have noticed. I haven't joined other servers other than the low rank so I can get a feel for the game much better, but it's not fun in the low rank servers. As I said, join them in your first play-through, then scroll down and find an official server that's not highlighted in green. Then you can possibly start enjoying the game. Even though, for me, a lot of games that do have players that isn't a low rank server, has really high ping. The lag in this game is incredible.
The low rank server community, isn't all good. Being a PvP game, when you need the community, it's not exactly a community as much as it is people swinging a sword around in the streets until they cut someone's head off. The game doesn't exactly do anything to punish a teamkiller. I've seen people kill 5 teammates on purpose and not get kicked. Even the player vote-to-kick wasn't successful. He had -150 score by the end. The game needs a teamkill limit. If there is one, I haven't seen it. People get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at archers a lot as well, because you were standing next to someone who just joined the game and hits your teammates leg, while you kill the enemy the teammate was attacking. The teammate sword fighting the enemy, who you killed, turns around and kills you, you say "I didn't attack you, the archer next to me did!" he will thus respond "you stole my kill"
Overall, a lot of people look at this game as a First-person shooter, which is unfortunate. I actualyl do like this game and I wish newer players would kinda take it more serious. But until the time comes where people do, don't come into the game with high expectations. The game will reach them. It's the people in the game that will ruin your experience. Nice or not, it's not fun when a teammate behind you tries to help you out in killing the enemy infront of you but cuts your head off instead.
The game feels like Skyrim and I kept wanting to play Skyrim after leaving Chivalry. Because I know I can get a better experience playing that game, both in mechanics and the fact that the game is offline and I can cut heads off without my companions cutting mine off on accident or getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if I was using Archer.

OK here I go:
Dreadout is the first Indonesian game I know that made it to Steam, so this is a matter of national pride, but I will try as much as I can to be objective with the review.
Being a game that comes out of Indiegogo crowdfunding and done in Unity I know there are limitations that the studio cannot cross. Graphics wise it is on par with many PS2 games of the mid 2000s era, with very simple texturing method, animation is also a bit weird at times.
On the positive side: Character design and AI is very well done. I haven't found any critical bugs that would ruin the gameplay. Ghost design is spot on when it goes for the creepiness factor. But what I would give 5/5 stars is the general atmosphere of the game. This game does not rely on cheap jumpscares but more of an unpleasant sense of presence, in that you know there are ghosts and supernatural beings out there to get you and you must get through them to proceed with the story (that is what Dread is supposed to mean I think). Sound effect and music is amazing. It feels like every single step that you make is bringing you closer to another ghost. Gameplay wise some of the ghosts are actually quite challenging to defeat.
Other: If you are not familiar with Indonesian culture you will see many things that are culturally relevant to Indonesians which are subtle but noticeable (sort of an inside joke for me).
Cannot wait for Act 2! and maybe more acts to come!

It looks promising at first, the PS2 level graphics can be excused for more the more important issue of gameplay.
Then comes the first warning sign. 20GB to install a PC port of a PS2 game? That's more than Skyrim needs, even with all the DLC and several content adding mods. That doesn't make any sense for a game that looks like this, even 2GB would be too much. It's a sign that the programmers just didn't care about doing things correctly. I'd actually prefer the other option, that they bloated the size on purpose just to troll everyone, because that wouldn't indicate that I spent money on a terrible port.
Then the part that I regret not looking into earlier. Made by SEGA. Anyone who has played a Sega game on PC knows that Sega has a habit of taking some great original games, and converting them into unplayable crap when it's time to port.
This is no exception.
It's as if Sega does not know what a keyboard and mouse are. Sega, in case you didn't know, keyboard and mouse are what PCs use. If you're going to make a PC game, make it work with those. This is almost as bad as trying to play that Sonic Team Racing game where the first level is literally impossible if you don't spend an extra $50-$60 on a special controller that you'll use for that game and that game only. I suppose it should be considered incredible that Sega actually allows WASD movement at all this time, without having to install keyboard macros in the background. It still doesn't change the fact that there is no "walk" button, so no peeking out from behind corner, and gods forbid your tank runs into a wall and needs to turn in place; watch your movement meter get drained in a second with no real movement being made, forcing you to continue missions with infantry alone or waste turns trying to get unstuck as if you were an invisible mud pit.
Controls aside, how about SKIPPABLE CUTSCENES. If you're going to include cheap surprise gimmicks 75% into a level that force restart after restart while the player tries to figure out how to win with no permanent casualties, don't force me to skip through the same poorly-voiced (In English at least) cutscenes over and over. Especially if following the advice of the in-game help is a great way to lose repeatedly.
And even if you figure out the right tactics, the rest is up to an unfair RNG. Have fun trying to win when some of the recruits have "20% of doing nothing for no reason whatso♥♥♥♥ingever", your Snipers randomly miss your target whenever it's especially important for them to hit their target, and even your story-critical tank sometimes randomly decides to shoot the ground 7 ft in front of it, often missing targets no more than 20ft away.
At least the soundtrack is still good. Apparently the parts that you can't ruin by hiring a random high school kid in their first programming class to do your port will turn out just fine. And I half expected them to convert all the music into 90's era low quality wav files just to waste more space and make my ears bleed.
Conclusion: This is the worst port of a game ever since the last time Sega ported a game.

Owlboy is an amazing game. I can't recommend it more highly. I would describe it as a mixture of Contra, Super Mario, and that it has story telling elements that remind me of the Legend of Zelda (ancient lore behind the story, relics, and such). The overworld feels very alive, and you get a good idea of the personalities of many of the NPCs. The gameplay is stellar, and may be on the challenging end for some people. This game will likely, in my view, go down as an indie classic much like Undertale.
I would be critical of anyone stating that this game is currently 10/10. This game is nothing short of incredible. The artwork, the characters, and the gameplay is so much fun. That said, some aspects feel unrewarding and some levels are going to feel more like memory based platforming as opposed to reflex based. Some people may prefer that, but I get tired of repeating the same scenes over and over again. Some things happen with so little warning that you have to replay from the checkpoint and remember that it is going to happen. This isn't to discredit the game, but just one of my few critiques. When I die in a platformer/shooter/whatever box you want to put this game into; I want to feel like it happened because I made a mistake and not because I just wasn't given any sort of heads up to respond in time.
The only other aspect I would knock is the price range. If this were a $10 game; it would be on the longer end and a huge bargain. $20+ seems a tad steep for how long the game is. I think $15 or so would be far more reasonable. If money is an issue, then I would just keep that in mind. I finished the game in about 8 hours.
I would give this game a solid 8/10.

This game is adorable, clever, full of fun characters, and addictive. There are two major modes of playing: haggling with people and running your item shop, and adventuring in the game's procedurally-generated dungeons.
The Item Shop  is the game's primary mode of play (given that it's part of the title). You control your inventory, the look and feel of your shop, and spend a lot of time haggling about prices with your customers. The tutorials are more than good enough, and the cute characterization makes them worth doing. Playing as an RPG item shop's owner is a creative and refreshing idea (though not totally unheard-of. See Taloon's chapter in Dragon Quest/Warrior IV)
The Adventuring mode is a bit simplistic, but doesn't overstay it's welcome. The easiest way to describe it is a cross between one of the 2D Zelda titles (A Link to the Past comes to mind) and The Secret of Mana. It is responsive and does a good job of breaking up the buying/selling action of the Item Shop mode.
Near the end of my playthrough I did find the buying and selling getting a little repetitive as I'd memorized the preferences of every customer. I was able to successfully finish the game before I got really bored of it, though, and had an enjoyable experience, especiallly for the money.
I never finished all the adventuring dungeons, so there is probably more to the story I never saw. I might go back and do that at some point.
Buy it if you like RPGs or "Tycoon" style games. It's cheaper than a fast food meal, and will entertain you for at least 10 hours.

Not only did I find Hand of Fate very enjoyable, I found it surprisingly challenging as well. Perhaps not entirely in the best way, but it suits the theme very well.
Hand of Fate is all about maneuvering a playing board made up with cards and going through the dangers that lie within. As you complete these challenges, you'll gain additional cards which will unlock additional treasures and additional challenges. Interestingly enough, the game remains very challenging to slightly unfair levels as time goes on. From the beginning, the first three bosses are simple and you'd be forgiven if you think Hand of Fate is an easy game. Not long afterwards more elements are introduced and older cards/challenges get refreshed to be harder so you can't as easily fall back on them for easy rewards. By the end of the game you're scrabbling for every advantage you can get and if you don't spend your time completing these challenges you're going to be absolutely decimated.
But that ends up being one of the game's major weaknesses. While the game is pretty damn strategic and has you fighting a whole lot of different elements in your quest for ultimate ambigious glory (which is told through an interesting way having the various cards represent your character's various memories and experiences), there's a heavy amount of luck involved as well. Especially late game. Smart players will start spotting good cards to stack their deck with, but there are many moments where the game just decides that you aren't going to win and pits you against a boss who makes all enemies of his faction invincible and another that attacks you relentlessly in a very small area. Meaning that if you're fortunate enough to get 200 health - somehow - you can still end up ♥♥♥♥ed by luck so hard that it'll make your head spin. Throw in a slightly slippery control scheme, enemies who love to dog pile on you, various traps that are at times hard to see or avoid (see the control scheme issue), and your victory ends up having a whole lot of luck involved. And one loss can put you back quite a way which means a lot towards the end game.
That said, from start to finish (though I'm very close to finish now, not quite there yet), Hand of Fate is very well set up and excells at telling a story that's all about the adventure. A neverending adventure really. And a whole lot of insanity that occurs along the way. Plus it's just fun, when it isn't deciding that you're not going to have fun.

Nova-111 is an interesting puzzle game in which the world moves when you do. You are able to stop and think how best to deal with any given situation for as long as you need (most of the time), which adds an interesting tactical layer to the puzzle solving. SOME enemies and objects move or activate in real time however, and this can lead to some strange situations in which stopping is not an option.
As the game progresses there are not just enemy creatures to contend with but complex environmental designs and hazards as well. You will also unlock various abilities you can use to move through or manipulate the environment in different ways.
My personal problem with it is that I just simply didn't particularly enjoy the time I spent with it. I found the "stuff moves when you do" idea kind of sucks the life out of the game. Enemies are thoroughly predictable by design - you lure them into moving in a certain pattern to defeat or get past them over and over again. There is variety in this when you encounter enemies in strange combinations, but the whole thing feels somehow stale and dull. As the game progresses the difficulty increases, as you would expect, but an increase in the level of challenge was not really enough to inject any energy into the game.
There are leaderboards for each level, but I have never cared about leaderboards in single player games before and this is not a game in which spending time to place highly seems even remotely worth it.
I appreciate the ideas the game is based around, but for me they do not amount to a fun experience and as such I can't recommend it.

I've played Archeage since release, and I've had a lot of fun with this game. But things to expect:
Pros:
Massive Open World
Mounts (creatures to ride around on)
Vehicles (boats, gliders, longboards, cars, farm haulers, ect...)
Battle pets
Dungons
Pvp
Pve
Game Events & Quests
Ect...
Cons:
Free to play means Pay to win.. and it's heavly geared towards this. You can theoreticlly play compleatly "free" but they seriously limit you.
They do this by using the labor system; anything that you need to gain something in game uses labour free users get 2000 where patron get 5000 labor for free user labor goes up 5 point every 10 mins your on where patron get 10 points when on or offline. So it really requires you to have patron because you run out of labor fast.
Gold if not for the labor system you could aquire gold easily by crafting, trading, grinding mobs, looting, ect... but only having so much labor prevent you as much of these tasks require you to spend labor.
Cash shops they have a couple different types of these shops in game. The main in called the Auction house where users sell items they they have obtained or crafted to sell but this can also include materials. Players set their own prices to bid or sell items oftain you'll find youself paying the gold you made in world to buy items as they are hard to obtain on your own. Selling is another monster without patron you pay 50% more in auction house fee and oftain people will under sell you if they have the same item making it hard to sell a item at a proper price.  The other cash shops are items sold by the game as a special item usually and require real world money however they oftain don't effect the player much so they aren't that good if you want to credit card ninja items.
Not enough quests! They have one main story and after that is done you can finish off mini quests but once your up around leval 50 it's not worth it for experience points. After level 50 your left with doing whatever keeps you from getting bored. Pvp is the next step but again in this world it's Pay to Win a lot of people will have stronger everything.
Overall:
Enjoyed the game. BUT! probably could have bought a couple fallout 4 games and thrown them to the wind with the amount of money I spent. Will be moving on from this game and playing Black Desert Online MMO next once released.

The 'good' stuff about the game;
The game isn't exactly all smooth or running, but it does feel somewhat solid. I usually get the experience I want from the game weather it's the decent sword fighting in the game or the hard to figure out archer where the bows and crossbows aren't easy to compensate for the arrow drop, which there is if you were expecting CoD's hitscan. There isn't any. So the archer is hard to master but fun to use for the most part. The 'for the most part' will come in the bad area.
The maps, while confusing at first, are actually easy to move around and you usually need one play-through to learn them since they look linier, actually have more paths than I expected, though on some maps it's not as branching. The game does do a good job at the sword play though, people can call it buggy or salami but it's not exactly a First-person Shooter. If you go down a narrow hallway and expect to hit someone with your LMB (which is a normal swing) your sword, if it's long enough (E.G. Great sword, battle-axe, war hammer, ect) it will clang off the wall.
But if you were calling salmai where you thought it was salami when you bashed your weapon against the wall and died, you probably didn't check the tutorial, where it's actually useful in this game. There are actually four different kinds of attacks for every scenario that every person I see calls salami on, just spam clicks LMB because, I dunno, pepperoni it? If you scroll up, you will do a straight lunge, where the walls wouldn't effect your attack, or if you have a high enough roof, scrolling down will bash over the top and those walls didn't do a thing to you. It's worth going over the tutorial to get your bearings, or else you WILL have a bad time.
The controls overall are easy to work with but very... Tricky, to learn. I wouldn't say master, but tricky to get a grip of.
Now, the bad part.
When you first jump into the game, you will notice green tabs in the multiplayer server browser, those are low rank servers. Join those for the first time you play the game to get your taste for the multiplayer experience, but don't expect to make friends in there, and don't teamkill your side on accident, will yah? For about the first 2 hours of the game, I called it stupid. Even after the tutorial. I wanted to refund but then I started having fun with the archer, all before I got teamkilled for playing as the archer. Then I started getting more deaths from my team than the actual enemy.
The low rank servers are not to be taken serious, it's hard to take the game serious in some cases, but it's certainly a struggle when you are pushing for the objective in team objective modes and either you get rushed by 16 players or you get 10 teammates attacking the same 2 people, and you happen to be in the middle, even when trying to run away, an axe swing from a teammate to your left cuts your head off. I can't put my finger on why, but it's actually frustrating to die in this game. I haven't been so mad to die in a game since GTA:V Online to a hacker in passive mode.
The mechanics themselves also make me want to tear my hair out, when you swing at someone, putting your crosshair on their head, expecting to cut it off, they look like they were blocking, all before they stab you in the stomach and your sword clearly hit them but they walk it off, I was a Vanguard against a Man-at-arms, which has the least ammount of armour. You will be calling salami on a lot of swings that should of killed a guy that has very low health, but gives them a love tap where they procceed to spam LMB until you can't block anymore and kill you.
This game rewards people for spam clicking LMB with no reguard to a good player fighting back, because the low rank servers have none, at least that I have noticed. I haven't joined other servers other than the low rank so I can get a feel for the game much better, but it's not fun in the low rank servers. As I said, join them in your first play-through, then scroll down and find an official server that's not highlighted in green. Then you can possibly start enjoying the game. Even though, for me, a lot of games that do have players that isn't a low rank server, has really high ping. The lag in this game is incredible.
The low rank server community, isn't all good. Being a PvP game, when you need the community, it's not exactly a community as much as it is people swinging a sword around in the streets until they cut someone's head off. The game doesn't exactly do anything to punish a teamkiller. I've seen people kill 5 teammates on purpose and not get kicked. Even the player vote-to-kick wasn't successful. He had -150 score by the end. The game needs a teamkill limit. If there is one, I haven't seen it. People get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at archers a lot as well, because you were standing next to someone who just joined the game and hits your teammates leg, while you kill the enemy the teammate was attacking. The teammate sword fighting the enemy, who you killed, turns around and kills you, you say "I didn't attack you, the archer next to me did!" he will thus respond "you stole my kill"
Overall, a lot of people look at this game as a First-person shooter, which is unfortunate. I actualyl do like this game and I wish newer players would kinda take it more serious. But until the time comes where people do, don't come into the game with high expectations. The game will reach them. It's the people in the game that will ruin your experience. Nice or not, it's not fun when a teammate behind you tries to help you out in killing the enemy infront of you but cuts your head off instead.
The game feels like Skyrim and I kept wanting to play Skyrim after leaving Chivalry. Because I know I can get a better experience playing that game, both in mechanics and the fact that the game is offline and I can cut heads off without my companions cutting mine off on accident or getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if I was using Archer.
It's a good game, just don't expect the best game if you join the low rank servers. I have not tried modded servers so I can't say anything about them.

DreadOut is an Indonesian survival-horror game that takes inspiration from the Fatal Frame franchise, and pulls a lot from Indonesian myths and folklore.
You play as a non-talkative protagonist known as Linda, who with a few friends is on a car trip. They stumble upon a weird deserted city that isn't marked on their map... The friends go to investigate the town, and soon get wrapped up in some severe hauntings from the strange ghost that start coming out when night falls.
The game has a low-budget, and it shows. Graphically everything looks outdated, with low-res textures, odd character animations, and the like. There's also no real-time shadows. The game also has a few bugs. I didn't encounter anything game-breaking, but a few 'look through the wall with the camera', 'get stuck on an object for a moment', 'that character is levitating,' type of bugs, However, something I found interesting was that they didn't copy and paste many models. There were a lot of posters around town, and each one was legitimately different. Same with pictures, and just small details all about.Outside of a few chairs or piles of garbage, most of the models were unique to each other, and I was surprised the developers didn't take many shortcuts.
Mentioning this, something I noticed about the game is that there were a lot of secrets and original assets used for things that most players would probably not even end up finding or seeing. There's more I have to say on the topic, but I'll get back to this in a bit.
The game has legitimately great atmosphere. There are some fantastic scares, the feeling of unnerve that is caused by the game. It has an atmosphere to it that most horror games these days are missing from the days of old, sort of a combination of dread and excitement for what's going to come next. The atmosphere and scares are more akin to something like Fatal Frame or Kuon than Amnesia or Outlast, I should mention. Recommended at night and in darkness, with headphones.
This is backed by fantastic audio design. The music is great, the sounds are great. Voicing is okay, a bit cheesy but enjoyably so. However, with the music, how it is and how it's used in the game, is really effective, and also I can mention unique. The music is very different than any other horror game I have played, but very effective. And how the music transitions with events going on is very well-done. The audio is also unnerving, and sometimes hearing a weird sound, even without knowing its source or even without it leading to anything, raised the tension. It sometimes gets hard to tell if a sound you just heard is part of the music, or something in the environment, but I say this as a good thing.
And the game does not lie on its laurels. By this I mean a lot happens, and the game never throws the same thing at you twice. I was honestly surprised by the number of ghosts there are in this game, there were a lot more than I was anticipating. Some great enemy variety, and you fight each ghost really only once or twice, there was not a single ghost I think the game threw at you a third time. And the 'events' that happen, like scares or atmospheric additions, were all incredibly varied too. This definitely helped to raise the intrigue as you never knew what might be coming next, and some of what happens really goes into the unexpected.
Combat is similar to Fatal Frame, but a bit more simplistic. There isn't a charge rate like Fatal Frame, or a point system, but the closer enemies are, the more you damage them when you take a shot. And if you attack them right before they attack you, you deliver additional damage.
Even the puzzles are well done and intelligent. Figuring out what to do is fun, and they do a good job at laying out clues to what you need to do to help piece it all together. They have clever hints and details, while not being extremely obvious either. However, it should be mentioned that those with less patience and less of a desire to figure out cryptic clues may not like how they're handled. But if you loved puzzles from horror games in the 90s (which have been notably absent in recent years), then you'll likely be quite happy to see some return to form here.
One of the game's biggest draws is some absolutely memorable moments. Several of the ghost encounters are absolutely fantastically handled and designed, the pacing of the game is wonderful for the most part (though may some end up stuck in the school for a while), and there's good variety with all of it. Some of the moments, such as the sit-down with Ira or the whole Mansion location, are absolutely stellar, and strike me as quality horror moments, something that has been missing from so many horror games, the sort of intrigue, weirdness, and execution that leads these moment to be gripping and chilling.
What they have here is fantastic, it legitimately is one of the best classic-styled survival-horror games to release in the last few years, and I think genre enthusiast who like certain elements of horror games that have been absent since the days of old will really appreciate the game. It's well-paced, well-executed, and well realized. It's low-budget, but those who enjoy the genre likely won't be bothered by this, some absolutely fantastic horror games over the years have been decidedly low-budget. The developers only had $26k to make the game, but they have managed to with that make a very confident horror game, and honestly some of the most fun I've had in a horror game in a while.
The weird thing is the secrets I mentioned earlier. There are complete sections of the game you could miss if you don't do some exploration. There are ghosts you won't fight unless you go off the beaten path. A tip to the wise is when it turns night-time and before you enter the school, don't enter the school like the game suggests and instead head back towards the town you just came from. There are different types of ghosts if you head backwards at this point that you'll never encounter in the main game. And little hidden areas and easter eggs to uncover all about. So on that front, there is some really cool optional content to explore in the game.
There's also a few cool unlockables. Once you complete the game, you unlock additional outfits, all of which are actually pretty well designed, and can be used on a second and later playthrough.
There's also a few side areas you can explore right now that don't really lead to anything, which I can only guess are there right now for the possible future Free Roam Mode (a lot of buildings and side-areas off the beaten-path are currently inaccessible or kind of barren right now, and I assume will be open in the free-roam mode the developers are working on).
I want DreadOut to succeed. I really liked what was here, I'd even go as far to say this is the best attempt at making a 'classic' style horror game to release in the last few years, really having an understanding of those gripping elements that made those games enjoyable (a deeper level of meaning and not just superficially being classic styled with fixed camera angles and tank controls). The whole game will probably take someone 4 - 9 hours, depending on how much they explore and find hidden areas and how long they take on puzzles.
DreadOut is completely worth experiencing. It's tense, sometimes terrifying, has the right amount of weirdness to it, some absolutely stellar moments, and is actually a lot of fun. Its low budget shows, especially in the graphics department, but through clever design, good execution, and variety at hand, manages to be a fun and memorable experience.

Digital Extremes' Warframe is a game that most companies in the F2P gaming business should look up to.
Yes, the game has its flaws as a game (poor story telling, grindy as ♥♥♥♥, bugs, etc.) and in its business model (more in the sense of luring people into spending money for things that are not worth); but what game does not?
For me, the most important thing, is that I DO NOT feel bad if I stop playing for a while and then come back. I CAN keep playing the game without feeling bad for it, without feeling that I have SO MUCH to catch up and I will have to invest money for a boost or a bundle with new content if I cannot invest all the time I should to be able to ENJOY the game again. There are so many things to do and you can choose to do any of them, that you don't feel like there is any kind of barrier to cross in order to enjoy the game.
I have stopped playing a lot of F2P games because I hate the feeling of being forced to play in order to keep up. There are some days that I don not really have a lot of time to play, and playing a F2P because "I have to do my dailies if I want to have enough currency/components for the next piece of content" feels bad. Perhaps that night I felt like reading a book, playing an old game out of nostalgia, watching a movie, go for a late night jog... but that or those games made me feel that I could not.
Games are a mean of entertainment and fun, so I cannot tolerate a game that makes you experience feelings so contrary to those like the burden of having an imposition "You must play constantly if you want to enjoy".
I am most likely going to keep playing F2P, but the moment I drop them, I will be done with them. Warframe has taught me that there is another way of handling F2P games, and I am really thankful for that.

I like this game. Figured I'd put it right up front for people who wanted the synopsis up front. The "Hi-Bit" artsytle brought me back to my childhood of playing snes games but updating the resolution and more frames of animation so the overall effect may be a retro call back but not dated at all.

Graphically I can't express the loving care that went into this, if the artstyle this game uses becomes the next trend sign me up.  Animations are fluid, the interactions between sprite and environment are animated well, and the backdrops are stunning.
Gameplay the game isn't 100% linear but exploration to find addtional coins or rares lore items makes for time investment  outside of the main questline. Combat at first is a little repetative but as you you gain companions and discover some of the nuances that aren't distinctly shown to you things become more managable.  There is a heavy emphasis on puzzles with occasional boss fights peppered in to keep the action diverse so you're not doing the same thing for too long.  There are a couple  frustrating areas that i had to take a break and come back later but overall I think the game is well paced.
In closing this game was a nice suprise that I hadn't heard about even though i follow the indie market pretty closely for the most part. It is good for about 10-15 hours of fun for an average skilled player. I would reccommend to anyone who likes platformers.

*CAUTIOUS recommendation*
It's really easy to recommend this game if you like anime, and don't mind everything that comes with traditional Japanese game design - archetypal characters, long-winded exposition, fairly slow gameplay, and some anime tropes and cliches (although VC does a good job at not going overboard with those).
Now, I did not finish the game precisely because *everything* in Valkyria Chronicles takes about twice as long as it should. The story bits drag on and only occasionally bring something interesting to the table, and the turn-based combat - as good as it is - has no speedup option, which it really needs in my opinion. Each mission can take up to an hour and a half if you tend to take your time and if you screw up, it can be an hour of progress that isn't that much fun getting back. I'm guessing that I'm roughly two thirds in, but I can't bring myself to finish it, because so much about it feels like a chore.
The game is pretty, it is littered with gorgeous understated designs, it has some fun likeable characters (even if the protagonist is a real bore), and the battle mechanics are solid. The third person view really adds to the experience and there are some pretty exciting scenarios. However, chances are that you are also at that point in your life when you say to yourself that life is too short to be playing JRPGs.

Yes, I would reccomend this game. Is it the best thing since the invention of pizza since people are claiming? Not really.
The Good:
- Very Pretty Graphics / Reasonably optimized
- Great Customization
- Fully voiced, great overall quality of acting
- Good world building and lore, main story can be a bit convoluted at times.
- Reasonably Balanced
The Bad:
- I'm not very fond of a couple of combat systems. I think they have overdone the surface system. Every combat , even the tiniest ones end up a swirling chaos of destruction everywhere with burning/poison/shock/blood what have you everywhere.
- Mobs instantly spawn on conveniently placed vantage points to harass you all the time. It's less about organic fights and more like forcing you to reload because you were exploring and not ready for a fight to spawn from thin air. This kinda creates the feeliing that the game is bending the rules against you, cheapening the experience overall.
- Mediocre tutorial overall. Fails to tell you some key details like Lizards don't need shovels and skeletons don't need lockpicks.
- Some bugs, like only half you party entering combat while the other half watches. You have to manually move your characters into combat, even though they are right there in the first place.
All in all, if you're a fan of CRPGs you'll likely enjoy this as I have. but, if you're new to the genre, there are more friendly places to start.

PREMISES AND PROMISES
Being a fan and veteran of RPG-style games, I got excited when I read about this game. Instead of playing a hero, collecting loot and experience, you are a shop owner said hero would encounter on his travels! Very original.
You play Recette , a girl who is left with the family shop after her dad suddenly leaves. He leaves a heavy debt too, and if not paid off, Recette will lose the shop and probably end up under a bridge in a box. She gets help from a fairy named Tear, who wants to see the debt being paid off because it is her company’s money. She is basically this game’s tutorial/faq.
So, how does this all play out? Read on…
TIME FLIES WHEN YOU'RE HAVING FUN… AND ALSO, WHEN YOU'RE NOT
The shop you run can sell weapons, equipment, potions, and sometimes more esoteric stuff. It attracts villagers and heroes both, and keeping them happy is the goal. Well, not the ultimate goal, but if your customers aren’t happy, they’re not likely to return and buy more.
You can make your store more attractive by decorating, and can eventually make your own items when you get certain recipes.
Before you can sell items, you need to buy them yourself from other shops, or you can join a hero on his/her travels in a dungeon and keep the loot that he/she finds (for a price). Then you have to place the item(s) in your shop, open your shop, and wait for customers to come by.
There is a reason why I listed all these actions separately: everything you do in this game takes up time. As you have a limited amount each day, you need to know in advance what you want to do that day.
This time limit forces the player to focus only on the goal of getting enough money to close the current chapter (with more money needed every following chapter). You don’t have time to take it easy: every part of the day must eventually lead to an increase of your cashflow.
Unfortunately, this creates rather frustrating situations. For example, you want some good-selling items, as the deadline for the current chapter is coming up, but cannot buy them from a dealer (not in stock, or too expensive). So you venture into a dungeon, slay enemies, and hope for good drops.
If you’re unlucky, you will only get bad or cheap items. So, you lost time for that day with little or no advantage. Now you need to get lucky in the store while selling the items and hope to haggle in such a way that you gain at least enough money to cover the costs for visiting the dungeon.
This counts more towards having a customer wanting a specific item: he places an order, and you need to get it before he returns. Guess what happens if the item simply won’t drop, or can’t be found somewhere else!
You cannot do anything about this “luck” factor, or plan ahead or around it. This gets increasingly annoying throughout the game, as you start to feel the game is deliberately taunting you. Speaking of annoyances…
WHERE IS THE MUTE BUTTON? OR RATHER, ANY BUTTON THAT WORKS
Recette is an non-assertive girl, has no confidence in her abilities and doubts herself every time something bad happens. This translates to annoying remarks, especially during haggling. For example, a customer comes in and wants to sell you an item you don’t want. The only way to not buy the item is to bid a very low price, have the customer disagree, and leave. Recette will always say something along the lines of “I have no talent” or “Can I really do this?”.
It undermines the action and result of the player’s choice, and I got increasingly agitated with it.
When dungeneering (not a word, get with it), Recette cannot stop asking the hero if he’s all right after he gets hit. Every single time. EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. Why is this necessary? Why does she need to ask?
And boy, are you going to hear it often. The controls in the dungeon feel stiff, and despite seeing your hero hit an enemy, more often than not you will miss the creature, and get hit by it instead. Some enemies have such erratic patterns that it is almost impossible to predict their actions. Some enemies shoot fireballs that track the hero wherever he is, and will almost always result in a hit. Enough hits, and the hero gets incapacitated, you lose the items you collected so far, and you lose the time without getting anything in return.
CONCLUSION: A BROKEN PROMISE, NO CASH RETURNS
Recettear is a broken promise, like finding a shiny, round object on the beach the size of a high value coin, but discover it to be a worthless bottlecap.
Too bad Steam won’t take it back, and now it just sits in my game-list, uninstalled, a constant reminder that an original story combined with a favorite game genre doesn’t automatically make for a good game.

A pretty sweet game. An unusual, but very decent, mix of both real-time and turn-based gameplay. Every move you make (there is a button to 'wait') advances a turn. Enemy movement is also limited to 'when you make a move'. Hazards like explosions, however, are real-time. The result is that this is actually a sort of "fast paced turn based game".
Level design is pretty decent, making most of the upgrades you find along the way. These also tie into the overall goal of the game and help to tackle more complex situations and puzzles (in a way, the game is more a puzzle than a platformer or a tactics game). Still somewhat unfortunate that the game only saves at the end of a zone, so you can't "just" complete a single level. But that's not much of a gripe.
Visual aesthetics and sounds are good but nothing all too special. The story is pretty below-par and even tacked on. There's apparently something with space-time, but the how, what or why is somewhat forgotten about. There's picking up of scientists and some scripted remarks by one of 'em, but the attempted humor falls flat (British humor doesn't work that way) and the game hints feel more like unneeded handholding. But at least it doesn't get in the way.
Still: it's all about the gameplay. And that's very solid: good level design, great AI, good controls. All in all: worth checking out.

: Arche Age is a game the excells in the both the pvp and crafting realms of the MMO Genre. The ability to not only build a home, but choose where to place it along with other crafting plots, and have it be persistant is a fresh take away from most of the MMO rail systems we have today. You can also create ships, and trade convoys that add a very nice in game economy and allows those who don't want to do raiding or pvp, to just focus on crafting and still level up.
The PVP is also very gratifying, with class systems breaking down into whatever 3 different sub classes you decide to combine together.
: The games biggest strengths are inherently its downfall. All crafting and other related actions are done through a labor point system. Unless you subscribe you will never get enough labor to do anything within the game. The cap of 5000 as well means that if you don't log in constently your basically missing out on maximizing any crafting you can do.
Guilds, guilds, guilds. You cannot succeed in many of the crafting aspects of the game without one. And PVP and PVE are impossible without a well organized and active guild. While this isn't the worst thing, it choke holds more solo players from being able to progress, and join in on larger activies if they want to.

Okay, this is the best game i have ever played in my life. It has such an awesome story and characters. All of the things you do, all the thing you say matter. Its not just some random game you can play and don`t care about anything, you get attached to your crew and story by itself feels deep and inspiring. The Music in Mass Effect is utterly awe inspiring. It's music that any true Mass Effect fan has felt empowered by, saddened by, inspired by, and moved by. Even on it's own, out of context of the three absolutely stunning games, it always provokes emotion from me. Mass Effect is the greatest RPG series of all time, and it's OST more than lives up to the story and experience. When it came to the end, when everything came down to the wire, everything that you did in the game came out. You put everything on the line, everything you had, and through sheer willpower, and sacrifice, and tremendous effort, YOU did it. Your team. You. You saw in detail how every choice you made in the game came into play in that final half hour of the game. If you failed, it wasn't some planet you'd never seen, or countless random soldiers you didn't care about, it was your teammates that you'd fought with for hours and hours of gametime, characters you'd built relationships with and honestly come to see as friends. The Suicide Mission is one of the best end-levels in history. The fact that you choose your teammates for each task and aren't told which one is clearly the best made it feel so immersive. You actually had to know them, not just take them for missions as if they are dumb robots. The Mass Effect Trilogy (Mass Effect 2 in particular) is not just one of the great video games ever created, but it's also one of the greatest works of Sci-Fi ever.

Mass Effect 1 was an okay game, it had dull gameplay but a good story and cool characters. Mass Effect 2 does not simply improve everything ME1 did, the devs completely overhauled the whole thing like they build it from scratch, this time with much more budget and a longer deadline. Whats impressive about this is the size of the game and the quality of everything. It is very rare that a big game like this, an open world game or RPG, is so well designed in every area. If you think about it there is always something which is not really fleshed out in some game you think are great, of course they are just small things, but that is the difference between a masterpiece and a very good game. For example look at the trading system and shops in most RPGs. Probably the shops will sell random equipment and you can sell everything you find there, and you probably will get tons of loot you never need.
In Mass Effect 2 you get no loot, except money and resources. There are only some moments in the game where you find an upgrade or an alternative to an existing weapon. Giving the player tons of loot like in other games (also in Mass Effect 1) just doesnt make sense, because it does nothing except wasting your time because you have to compare it to your existing loot to see if its worth it, if not you will sell it. That also breaks the balance of money the players gets in most games and to counter that the developers balance the shops in a way that you rarely find something useful to buy. Because the money you get in ME2 is more controlled and shops have only specific items they sell only once (you only need them once), everything gets better. Exploration and hacking is more rewarding, because the money you get is more useful. Visiting shops is worth doing because EVERYTHING you can buy is worth it, you just need the money for it. And it opens more flexibility for the devs to design their missions, or just small things like giving you opportunities to get discounts which wouldnt be worth getting in other games. All that is just a tiny fraction of the game, I just want to explain to you to how fleshed out and well designed this game is.
Bioware didn't care about genre conventions or did things only because this game is supposed to be an RPG, every decision they made is because it makes sense for the game, nothing else. Another example for that is the inventory system, you have no inventory actually. You only need to find one copy of a weapon, it will be available for all squad members. That removes the really annoying fiddling around with the inventory crap in ME1. They also moved the ammo upgrades from the inventory to the skill menu, which means they are skills now and every crew member has maybe 1 or 2 ammo upgrade available to him, which also gives you more criteria to pick your party-members. There are also other criteria to pick party-members apart from who is the coolest, which was really the only criteria in ME1, skills of your crew didn't really matter. Every party member has set weapon-types he can use, set abilties and strengths which can synergy with others or be redundant.
Also there is a mission every crew member will have for you. Doing these will not only make them loyal, they will also unlock an extra ability for them and also matter for the story (no spoilers), but its not just "doing" these missions, you can fail them and then they are gone and you have to live with the consequences.
In Mass Effect 2 you get your crew members much faster than in ME1, which is good, because it gives you more variety early on and there are more crew members in total, all of them very different and interesting in their own way. There was only 1 character which I hated and is cliche in my opinion (Jack). Actually the conversations with the crew members were the most fun part about ME2 for me, the dialogues were really interesting but not just exposition or alibi character development and all of it is optional, which is great for several reasons. There are many things in Mass Effect 2 which are optional, I think if you do only the must-do things, you could finish this game in 5 hours or so. It took me 25 hours and I know that there were easily 5 more hours I could put into it, but I don't recommend doing everything you can, it could get tenacious. Luckily unlike ME1 where every side-quests was obvious filler, every side mission in ME2 is unqiue and meaningful and you get useful rewards for them. They even managed to make the exploration of planets fun. In ME1 you just clicked on every unexplored planet and you got some text. In ME2 you have a scanner and have to scan the surface manually to find resources. That process is not boring because it is presented very nice and it is very rewarding, because the resources you find are crucial to get upgrades, and the upgrades themselves are also crucial. Still you are not forced to do these scans if you don't want to, there are enough upgrades you can buy and find and you also sometimes find resources on missions.
The combat got the biggest overhaul, it is actually fun and challenging now. The AI is improved greatly compared to ME1, but your party sometimes still does stupid things, but you can control them much more easy now and still more flexbile just with 1 button for each party member, and managing them is more important now, because of their powers. Shephard also has powers now depending on the class you pick, most of them you already know from ME1 (they are still cool), but there are also some new powers. These are not only useful and necessary, they are also really fun to use thanks to really good sound-design, animations and hit-feedback. Bioware also proves that you can make satisfying gunsounds for sci-fi/laser weapons. Enemies aren't bullet sponges anymore, if you know how to bring their shields down, they react to your shots, fall down, scream because you burn them or if they are mechs they loose an arm or something. Your shots just have more impact now which makes combat more fun overall. The only thing which could be improved is the enemy design, the enemies are cool and there are a good number of enemy types, but the tactics you fight them with are not much different. With more diverse enemy types the combat could have more variety, which it does not really need though. I'm not a fan of regenerating health, because it makes the outcome of a fight irrelevant for the next fights, it only matters that you win the fight, but regenerating health makes sense for this game and works.
I don't want to talk much about the story, because I don't want to spoil anything. What really surprised me was the amount of elements which carry over from ME1 and how many choices you have in general, these not only have impacts on small side-stories, but also on the ending of ME2. The ending alone of ME2 is a masterpiece. There are so many variables in the ending it easily surpasses the amount of choices you have in other games, and in most games your choices don't really matter anyway. I'm really eager to see how the consequences will affect ME3. There were parts in the game where I really had to think about my decisions, rarely the choices are black and white, sometimes you might not even notice that something is a "choice". Especially one decision kept me thinking for a very long time, and I still don't know what the right thing to do was (probably because there is no simple right and wrong for that question).
The story is much more engaging and the dialouges much more interesting than in ME1, because they properly animated the cutscenes this time. Characters don't just stand infront of each other like robots, they move around, do things, even Shephard does. I have no more characters left for this review.

Overall, the game is pretty good. The visuals of the 2D pixel graphics over 3D backgrounds are a little jarring at first, but it's easy to get over that. The character designs are pretty well done and create a cohesive visual style. The cliche anime style does well with the dungeon-crawler gameplay.
The gameplay itself is really balanced, giving lots of reward for hard work. The bosses of each level are impressively well designed, implementing technique in a game that feels like there shouldn't be any. It offers a solution to the repetitiveness of the dungeon crawler experience. Some of the adventurers do feel a little unbalanced, but since you're not obligated to use any specific character, it's fairly easy to work around it. Personally, I feel that Caillou's gameplay is too drastically different from any other character for him to be too playable.
The game is very short in terms of the story mode, but the "story mode" is basically just how long it takes to pay back the debt. After that, the game still can be played and still offers whatever content you haven't explored yet.
Given the extra modes available after story mode, the after-game content, the game has what I'd say to be 50~ hours of addictive gameplay.
