Kingdom Wars 2: Battles:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
A kingdom without a king is a recipe for war! Three races are engaged in this devastating conflict and trying to survive. Who is going to have the upper hand? Would it be the Orcs, possibly the Elves or it just might be the Humans?!
Kingdom War 2: Battles is an RTS game which offers several modes of play. In the campaign mode, you will be playing four episodes at this stage (the fifth episode is coming soon), you will be treated with very good cinematics as well as an in-depth story line. This episode with be all about the last stronghold for the human race, the city of “Dagbor.” You will be playing the Humans and then the Orcs. During the gameplay, you will have to achieve all tasks before entering a battle. Essentially, it is like a very good tutorial. You will learn how to gather resources, create buildings and units.
The single player mode is realistically a skirmish; choose your race and up to three others players (AI) to fight against. In the survival mode, you will be fighting against waves of zombies.
There is quite a lot of content here. There is a technology tree for the 3 races and you can unlock upgrade with different resources. If you are missing some, head up to the trade centre and buy what you need from another user. By clicking on the social icon, you will be able to see who is online, become a friend with whoever you want, challenge or engage in a co-op game.
Strategic cards can be crafted and used in a multiplayer game. Select a combination of cards to have the edge against your opponent but be aware, they might have a better combination than you.
The gameplay is good, as are the graphics, although I did experience a couple of flicking screen effects here and there.
The controls are easy to master and follow the trend of this type of game. The only negative here is that I had to click several times to the same points for my units to acknowledge my command, and this can be frustrating.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Good story and cinematics
-	3 races to play with each their specific tech tree
-	Achievements and Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Controls could be more responsive
I really like RTS and Kingdom War 2: Battles show great potential.

We all played the Armored Knight, the Raging Barbarian, the Wise Wizard or the cunning Rogue, going into a glorious quest for honor, wealth or fame. But have you ever wondered what's the life of the regular citizen of the fantasy world, specially the all important Item shops who sell you armor, weapons and potions? Well here is Recettear, a game who will answer just that.
Recettear its a retail simulation game with an RPG twist to it. You'll have to maintain your shop, restock your supplies and go on quests along side adventurers and receive items during the adventure. This is, for me, a pretty fresh new take on the genre.
+ Lots of Items to sell, both generic shop items and special custom made items by you
+ Well implemented crafting system
+ Customizable and upgradable store which directly affects how many people visit and what kind of people visits. (People who are rich and pay more, or people who will haggle)
+ A lot of interesting characters with varying personalities, traits and abilities.
+ Good time management system where you are constantly under-pressure to either open your store or go raid a dungeon.
+ A surprisingly advanced economy involving supply and demand.
+ Easy enough learning curve.
+ High replayability. Different modes are unlocked after the initial story campaign as well as a new game plus.
- Campaign (Story Mode) is short, although New Game+ and other game modes are unlocked later on, it should not be an excuse to totally limit the Story Mode, specially in an RPGish game.
- A bit too simple combat mechanic
- Art Style is not for everyone. This game is clearly made in the Japanese Anime art style which means some people love it while others hate it.
- Character sprites are low resolutions
- No Widescreen Support
- Limited enemy and npc designs: Some of them were clearly just reused and palette swapped
- Restrictive map: There are different areas of the town you can visit but activity in those places are limited and only event triggered. Meaning, visiting a place (ex. Pub) without an event will just be a waste of time.
FUN GAME. Highly recommended to JRPG fans who is looking for a fresh new take on the genre, or those who are genuinely curious what an Item Shop is like.
Although I feel like, given enough time or funding, the developers of this game could have expanded the world and given more complexity on the mechanics that this game is based on. Still, as it is, the game is good and well worth its price.

Alot of people talk about Rogue-likes as these hard-core, unforgiving, all-or-nothing, RNG dependant dungeon crawls... and many of them are. However, if you've played the original Rogue (or Rogue Legacy), you'll find that many game designers who classify their game as a "Rogue-like" have only copied the most sadistic parts of that game and ignored some of the more interesting and rewarding parts.
Hand of Fate manages to replicate some of the progression aspects that the original Rogue utilized that made me actually love that game and reconsider the "Rogue-like" genre entirely. Hand of Fate, like Rogue, is not all-or-nothing. Rather it's a game of incrimental progress. You fight your way as far as you can, gathering tokens (think, card booster packs) along the way, and apon reaching a reset condition (either beating a boss in storymode or dying), those tokens reveal and add weapons, encounters, or armor to your deck which you can then use to enhance your next experiance. That way, you don't feel like you're bashing your head against a wall of RNG spite.
In almost every playthrough of Hand of Fate, you're going to come away with something you can add to your deck to slant the odds ever-so-slightly more in your favor, and that's a motivator to keep on playing.
As for Hand of Fate's drawbacks? I'd have to say it's combat leaves alot to be deisred. It's a watered down counter-system ala Batman Arkham Asylum that offers very little in terms of variety, fluidity or technique. You occationally get abilities to use and dodges to execute but that doesn't save the whole engagment from being awkward. If there were ever a Hand of Fate 2, (which I'd certainly hope for,) I'd say the combat stands to benefit the most from a reassessment.

My initial impression of Warframe was that someone had made a huge mistake, and I'd received a rather expensive game for free. As it turns out, Warframe IS free. Which is incredible considering the polished graphics, and quality as it's presented.
Don't be fooled; Warframe is definitely a time sink. Levelling up a Warframe to use better weapons, to then level them further and unlock better mods for weapons - this cycle continues. There is a serious lack of content aside from the same set of missions. 'Smash 'em up carnage and mindless fun' is a great way to describe the game.
- A huge pull, Warframes, weapons, and ships are
customisable, and the sheer number of each available is insane. While there are real cash transactions, almost everything in the game can be crafted with some effort on your part, barring cosmetic skins/items. I do feel a little miffed that most colour palletes are also locked behind this paywall. I'm not PSYCHED to be a Red Power Ranger, but guess I will be one unless this changes.
- Saying this, the atmosphere and graphics are excellent. It plays and looks fantastic on my GTX1070, with the camera at a third person view, and OTS zooms for scoped or long-range weapons.
- Combat feels seamless in singleplayer, I have had no problems except for my own inadequacy with a gun (which is slowly improving.) With multiplayer, I have noticed a significant amount of movement lag.
- If you're used to being a long-term clicker, like me, your fingers are probably going to ache after CTRL+ SPACE/SHIFT jumping combos (but you do look hella cool.)
There is a LOT of focus on co-op play, and if you suffer from anxiety as I do, I would suggest playing with friends only or changing settings for solo missions. Unfortunately, my experience of the public community is that it is quite a toxic one. Others may not feel this is the case, but for the majority of the time I've played and spent in public groups, there is a ton of verbal abuse over voice chat/nasty trolls, and as a new player it is -hugely- off-putting.  I have learned of the mute option since, but it feels that the longer a game is released, especially of the MMO variety, and the larger player base it gains, the worse the community gets. [Cue group rushed playthroughs, abuse, stress, panic attacks and not wanting to play again for extended periods of time on my part.]
I await the day a majority friendly community lasts in any MMO, but I may as well live in hope of Half-Life 3.
*As to the new Plains of Eidolon update; oh man, THE GRIND IS REAL. It feels as though the developers tried to create a rolling, open world landscape for players to explore and complete missions at their leisure, but the missions are really just repetitive bounties that you have to run all the way back and extract to the main hub to complete. That doesn't fit well with an open world setting.
Repeatable quests and bounties which are required for reputation gain
Feeling forced to grind them for rewards and necessary mats after a relatively 'do whatever you feel kind of vibe,' is odd. It would work well as an increment to a large update, but as the update itself, it feels rather shallow.*

Excellent game! You traverse a dungeon whose rooms are face down cards. Each card has an event or encounter that can lead to combat, treasure, fortunes, or misfortunes. You unlock more cards as you complete events, most of them being a chain (ex. Complete the Ritual event, unlock the Lich boss fight event, complete that and unlock the Druids event storyline). There is luck involved but a lot of it is also in your hands (Do you try to sneak past an enemy or face it in hopes of good loot? Do you really want to get involved in a blood auction?).
There are tons of items that make combat interesting. I'll agree the animations can be a bit clunky at times when compared to something like the Batman games (it uses the basic combat mechanics as those), but it is not as bad as most reviewers will have you believe. Combat gets pretty difficult and intense in the later half of the game, and I pretty much just beat the final boss of the game because I had bought/found just the right items to keep me alive.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of roguelikes or just adventure games. The narrative is well written and the stories, even though they are just text through cards, are interesting and make you want to see them through. Trying to get some of the achievements can also be fun.
The Wildcards DLC adds more variety to the roguelike elements by giving you Fates (classes essentially) that have a buff and a debuff on your character. It also adds Easy and Hard mode. I didn't use any Fates during my initial run, so I can't say much about the DLC, but I don't think it's worth the full price.
I would rather buy WinRar on this point.

Try out the Free2Play version of the game for a few weeks. If you enjoy it, spend the money for a month or two of Patron. Use that time to acquire Apex in game and use it to renew Patron going forward. Expect progress to be a slow build over months and not days. Due to the game’s more brutal RNG nature, I don’t recommend sinking significant money into the cash shop.
The ability to customize properties are amazing. Some of the best I’ve seen on an MMO since SWG. The downside is land is limited and new players will find most open plots are 8x8 (smallest needed for a house is 16x16). The best way to get land is buying it from another player. Patron is also required to own land.
As for PVP, players should expect it. Most lvl 30+ zones cycle through periods of peace, war, and tension. Several zones are always in a state of war. During war and tension, you can be attacked not only by opposing factions, but also by your own faction. No matter you opinion on PVP, assume at some point you will get ganked.
Another issues is the relationship between XLGames (developer) and Trion (NA/EU Publisher). There are pretty regular gaffes that leave players confused (and other more NSFW adjectives.)  Bug fixes can be slow, and the companies do seem to blame each other for “unexpected features and unintended gameplay.” Expect this to impact your gameplay.

I want to start by saying that I don't dislike this game. I wish there was some sort of scoring system as opposed to a yes/no recommendation, because it's not like this is a terrible game, I just simply would not recommend it to most people I know. That said, there's plenty good with the game, but it's also quite flawed. If you take one thing away from this, just remember to
It's definitely not worth the standard price tag, but if you can pick it up for under $10 and this sort of game looks like it's your thing, by all means, have fun. Anyways, on to the review.
I'm gonna start with the negatives and end with the positives, because I just had a particularly irritating play session and more negative critique is on my mind. Granted, I'm not very far into the game, as you can probably tell by my play time, but nonetheless, I think I can offer some valid critique for what we've got here.
Firstly, it's slow. Everything is just way. Too. Slow. Loading is annoying, animations for navigating menus are lengthy, cutscenes seem stilted with how long a gap there can be between characters speaking. Not to mention, in the actual missions, everyone moves really slow, and even there you find annoying animations and the likes in nearly everything you do, artifically increasing the play time. To give you an idea of what I mean, I actually went back and played an earlier mission, timing the amount of time I spent pressing buttons (ergo, playing the game), and compared that with another timer that recorded how much time in the mission was spent during my turns. I kid you not, my turn time was almost
of what my "playing the game" time was. If that doesn't give you an idea of how long all the animations take, just look up some gameplay footage on Youtube and see for yourself.
Second, the story thus far seems very anime. I know that may seem like a bigoted complaint, but if you're not a huge fan of animes, the personalities of many characters will very quickly become grating. The two leads, Welkin and Alicia, are seemingly budding love interests for one another, but their interactions are so cliche that I feel I'll be able to predict the progression of their relationship as I continue through the game. Basically, every overused trope in character development is prevalent in the mains of this game, so if you're looking for a groundbreaking cast, look elsewhere. Not to mention, the plot itself is basically WW2, so if you thought you were avoiding the basic plot of a shooter by playing this game, I must regretfully inform you that is not the case. Who knows, maybe it becomes amazing later on, but for me four chapters in, I'm not interested. "It gets better later" may be good for some people, but if you're like me, such an excuse is invalid.
Third, the movement controls in combat. Maybe it's better with a gamepad, but with keyboard controls, I never felt like I could put my soldiers right where I wanted them to be. It's hard to describe, but when you let go of a key, your character keeps going in that direction for a second. If you're trying to position your character precisely behind a certain bit of cover, tapping the movement keys to inch your way to an ideal spot never works, as your character seemingly has a minimum amount of movement animation required for each key press. Overall, trying to get soldiers from point A to point B while being shot at usually doesn't go well.
And to add on to the previous point. the tank controls.
It's hard to describe just how bad they are, but if you turn the camera a little left or right while moving straight forward, the tank freaks out and starts spinning in place with no logical way to direct the spinning. I suppose what's going on here is a more realistically controlled tank that has to stop and turn in place to change direction, but it doesn't control that way at all. Like I said, there's no way to tell how the tank will start spinning when you turn the camera. For instance, in one mission i wanted to turn my tank 180 degrees to back out of a corner I had gotten in to, so I thought I'd turn the camera all the way around. The tank didn't start turning, so I decided to move forward in the new direction I was facing, which caused it to rotate about halfway to facing the right direction before switching the direction of its rotation, so it took almost twice as long as it should have for the tank to get where I wanted it.
The movement issues (especially with the tank) may not seem like such a big issue, and yes, they wouldn't be more than a minor annoyance if it weren't for the fact that each soldier only gets a certain amount of movement per activation, so trying to right yourself behind cover repeatedly wastes movement time, which could lead to you expending what little you have left only to leave your soldier standing out in the open. With the tank, turning costs movement, so in the previous example I mentioned where it took way too long to face the right way, I ended up using a decent portion of my tank's precious movement for that activation
Perhaps the movement in combat is my biggest issue with the game, and it makes it hard to enjoy sometimes because you end up forming a master plan for how to clear out some enemies while leaving all friendly soldiers in cover, only for that plan to fall apart because of technical issues.
Alright, so that's basically what I think is glaringly wrong with the game. It has maybe a few more minor issues, but honestly, this is what stands out to me. With that in mind, on to what I like about the game.
I'm usually not one to be swayed by graphics or anything like that; I feel that a game should hold up on the merits that it's well designed. But WOW does this game have some great aesthetics. Sure, it's not the most graphically advanced, but the scenery was nice to look at, the music was atmospheric, and the visual design of the characters was distinct and memorable (even if it got a little trope-y at times). If you don't buy the game, get the soundtrack or listen to it online, because it's all got a great feel to it.
Next, I like the diversity offered in character classes and abilities in combat. With such different types of units, each with their own range of mobility and combat prowess against different enemies, coming up with strategies in combat certainly does require some thought and rarely boils down to "shoot them with the biggest guns." Sure, the classes are nothing unique in terms of archetypes, but it's clear there's been a lot of thought put into how each of the classes interacts with one another in combat.
Perhaps my next point ties into aesthetics, but I feel that there's a real sense of weight behind the weapons in this game. Shooting the heads of enemy scouts from the top of a sniper tower
powerful, while firing at a tank with a machine gun
pointless. Not much else to say here, just satisfied that the design and feeling of a game can merge pretty seamlessly in such a case.
Though earlier I said that the characters can be annoying, it's also gotta be said that there's something genuine about their design, and much of the general design in this game. It's clear the developers weren't going for something that would easily have widespread appeal, but rather, a game with some true heart behind it. They put a lot of love into their work, and it's visible through how the characters interact. I personally was turned off from it and you may be too, but hey, I can see the value in a story experience like this.
Lastly, the degree of customization outside of combat is
I won't go too much into depth on it (mostly because I'm running out of space to write this review), but if you look up info on it and like strategy games, I'm sure you'll be impressed.
Good to buy
if you like strategy games.

First of all, starting with the problems, I was unable to play this game without running it in DirectX 9 mode using the -dx9 startup flag. Otherwise, every time I launched the game it would crash immediately. The game still looked fine without the high end graphics settings, and unlike some of the other reviewers, I actually managed to get the game to run at 60FPS with VSync turned on when it was running in DX9 mode.
The game has an intriguing story, and the environments and characters look great. What may be lacking is any actual challenge, asides from the completely unnecessary and frustrating demon sequences that don't really add anything to the game. If you're coming to this game from L.A. Noire or the like, you're probably going to be disappointed in terms of the puzzle/problem solving skills (not) required. In fact, the first few puzzles I tried to solve, I actually tried to be clever and pick a more subtle or interesting answer to the various "questions" that the game poses to you, to find out that the correct answer is ALWAYS the most blatantly obvious one available. There is literally one section in the game when you see a key fall down and you're asked to choose between the key, a fork, and a spoon. You do lose one of your three "police badges" for each incorrect answer you choose, however I didn't see how this had any effect on anything, more of a personal challenge perhaps.
Despite this, the game is still enjoyable, albeit from a more casual "exploring the environment and enjoying the story" perspective. There are a LOT of collectibles, and to the developers' credit, they have a lot of content associated with them, pages and pages of journal about your wife, about the mysteries around the town, and, best of all, the hilariously bad spooky stories you get every time you find a set of objects in a particular location.
The whole game takes place around the small town of Salem, and several outlying locations linked to the town that you are able to enter after a certain amount of time. I like that all the locations are linked to this "town hub", allowing you to get a real feeling of where everything is going on and keeping the immersion going. The game would be considered a horror game, except instead of the horrible things happening to your character, you're finding out about them as you explore the world.
I would recommend getting it on sale if you're into point and click adventure games and you also like an interesting story.

First game was absolutely amazing. For once, a sequel took everything great about the original and kept it, then actually fixed the mechanics that were weak. Then, just for good measure, Larian added a heaping pile of awesome sauce on top of those two points, and built a masterpiece.
Looking for a challenging strategical RPG? Put it on Tactician Mode, and see how every fight can swing rapidly based upon your approach. Some fights are forced to be approached head on, some allow for more... creative approaches. Anything goes, and the AI certainly don't hold back in their own tactics. It's amazingly easy to get overwhelmed until the proper amount of thought is put into each and every fight. Even if you have to 'cheese' some, every conflict is a blast.
Perhaps you're not the best at strategy, and are looking just for the story? Larian still has your back with this masterpiece. Everything is voice acted, even the Omniscent Narrator adding in the expressions and actions NPCs take as you speak to them. Your own replies are more vague, allowing you to fill in what might be said, adding to the Role Playing of the RPG element. There are six unique characters, each with their own stories and specific questlines.
Character customization is amazing, I must have spent nearly two hours upon launch exploring the various options. Not happy with just allowing you to edit your stats, spells, abilities and talents, Larian now introduces unique races, each with their own reactions from NPCs and unique racial abilities, some of which can truly compliment certain builds.
And, wanna play with your friends? It's very easy to start a game, and playing together just makes things all that much more amazing. I am absolutely stunned at how much better multiplayer works in Original Sin 2.
tl;dr - Larian Studios has shown that they know what the hell they're doing. And have made GOTY '17 in the process, in my eyes. All Strategy RPGs could learn quite a lot from Larian's success here.

As a casual gamer with a larger game collection I don't tend to write reviews for products but this title is very different, What you get is a RTS Strategy game that puts Triple A games like Total Wars to shame that on the face of it doesn't look particulary spectacular but the game play is amazing (note I'm not a kid looking for some pew pew - as a older game mid 30's I like to relax after work for a few hours).
Let me get this out of the way straight away:
Cons -
Can't Move the castle - its been my only gripe so far when you start a battle your castle walls are in a pre defined location (one at each side of the map)
Graphics - the textures look like AoE games or games dated around that genre (not a bad thing but the younger gamers wont like it for a 2016 game)

- Gameplay (the battles keep you returning time and again)

All in all a fantastic game... while I look forward to seeing some progression in its current state its well worth a look (just make sure you stick it out for a few hours) - I've sunk 20 hours in so far in just over a week... i petty my gametime in a month

Best RPG I've ever played. Doesn't hold your hand with dozens of quest markers and hints, but instead gives you the tools you need and tells you to do it your own way. Every quest and objective can be completed in numerous ways. Every character can be killed, even plot-relevant characters and companions and you'll have to live with the consequences. If you're into roleplaying, the entire world reacts to you differently depending on your race (human, elf, lizard, dwarf, undead), your background (decided by "tags" you choose on char creation), the things you've done, the people you associate with, etc. etc. etc. If you play as one of the "origin characters" (pre-made characters with defined backgrounds and appearances), you'll have even more role-play potential in unique dialogue and questlines. Origin characters can also be recruited as companions.
Combat is turn-based and quite difficult, even on normal, but this forces you to strategize.There is an easy mode, and it's perfect for those bad at RPG's or just in it for the story. But it''s very satisfying watching your party grow in strength and obliterate enemies who once gave you trouble. Overall, if you have any interest in RPG's, games with deep storylines, or roleplaying, do yourself a favor and buy this. The CRPG genre is most certainly alive and well.

Good, old school FPS game. Reminds me of Quake and a bit of Duke Nukem. Fast paced and hard as balls. Actually am doing an LP on it.

The pros
- truly unique factions that are COMPLETELY DIFFERENT from each other, each requiring a distinct approch to building your base and fight battles. The gameplay of the elves is so different from that of the orcs you would think you're playing a different game!
- very interesting siege defense and battles. There are very few AOE style RTS games out there that♥♥♥♥♥♥such an emphasis on siege elements, and this game does it quite well. Both defending your forts and laying siege on the enemy ones feel exhilarating.
Cons
Note that this game is still in early access stage. I assume and hope that some of the issues below will be fixed/improved. But it is always possible that they won't be. So I think people wanting to try the game should know about them.
- this likely will stay, but it's not too much of an issue for me. The graphics is quite outdated for a 2015 game, even with everything on the highest quality. But for an indie game it's really not bad at all.
- the most serious problem is the constant crashing. 9/10 skirmishes i played ended up CTD. The official solutions did not work. And that's when i have a good rig i7 + gtx 980 ti
- some of the useful features that are omnipresent in RTS games are missing. E.g the game wont automatically redirect to  a unit after you press the number they are tied to, nor are they shown in a specific color on the minimap to tell you where they are.
- your units can be pretty unresponsive to your commands.
All in all it is a very fun game. Just hope the above issues will be fixed.

I'd love to say the game is straight up pay to win, but it's not exactly the truth. It's more like "pay to advance a lot faster than others", so unless you are a complete casual and you want to play single player inside an MMO, you gotta pay. "Patron" a.k.a. "premium" service is pretty much essential. If you don't have it, your ingame progress takes ages. If you have Patron, you generate "labor points" twice as faster as non-patron users AND - more importantly, you generate them even while you're offline.
You can't do anything without labor points, you can't collect crops, chop trees, mine iron, you can't even equip newly found items unless you "identify" them first - which costs labor, of course.
So the first thing you wanna do as a free to play user is get premium - patron. Anyone can purchase "APEX" for ingame gold. Now that sounds pretty good right, just earn some gold, get Patron and roll with the big kids. Oh, also people can purchase APEX for real life money ($10). So it works the other way too - want some quick cash? Buy APEX for real money. That's the first major problem I have with this game - anyone can get really rich really fast as long as they pay.
Oh, did I mention damage and protection boosters? Yeah, you can buy that, too.
The second issue with Archeage is connected to the first.
Imagine you just started playing as a free to play user on a new Archeage server. What's the first thing you want to get? APEX, obviously. Or, in case you don't know what else to do with irl money - quick cash so you can start off real fast. So immediately people start selling and buying APEX. What happens after a couple months ingame? People that were selling APEX early on, don't really need gold anymore. So the APEX that is on market, starts being super expensive, especially since a lot of people stacked APEX early game (because they know the price will rise).
Now if you're a casual sandbox player - you don't pvp that much and you don't sit at auction house all day long and check on prices and ways to earn some extra gold easily, the way that you as a casual player earn more money is by trading trade packs - ingame items that you can craft by spending labor points. The issue here is the fact, that the gold you can earn for trading packs is fixed, while APEX price varies depending on supply/demand. So the longer the game (server) goes on, the more worthless gold becomes and thus it gets even more Pay to Win than earlier.
And this issue is once again connected to the third one.
So like I said, one of the ways of earning gold is having your own farm and crafting trading packs. That's my preferred way of playing - just chill at my farm and trade stuff. Another major way of earning gold is being a d***. The gold you get from trading packs depends on quality of the product AND more importantly - where you deliver it to. The further you travel, the more gold you get. The most gold you can get is by traveling to pvp zones. Now obviously there's a risk that you get killed by the opposing faction. That's completely reasonable. What is not reasonable, is the fact that you can get killed by your own faction as well. Now there's a "punishment" crime system, which is actually not punishing at all and doesn't even matter. So what this leads to is your own people camping near popular trading paths and destroying trading carts with your hard earned packs and potentional money that you earned through lots of work and time spent. You can't even imagine how frustrating is getting your cart destroyed and robbed.
That's not all though! Since having a "land" is a major way of earning money - you can grow crops, trees and build your own house there, it's super important to have one and frustrating if you don't have it. Now for some f-ed up reason, the amount of land available is limited by the game. There're specifically appointed places where you can build your farms/houses and you can't do it elsewhere. Early in the game, people literally hunt the best housing plots and place their houses so they block the largest place possible, just so they can build more stuff later OR sell the plot for mad gold.
Like I said previously, having some land is extremly important. 50% of the game focuses on trading, crafting and housing, none of that is possible if you don't own a plot. Following previous paragraph, after you started playing and spent two weeks ~ish finally earning two APEX (you need two to get Patron), the next thing you look into is probably getting a plot so you can build a house. BUT SURPRISE! There's no more housing space, because the people that wanted a head start spent real life money to buy Patron and took all of the space available. So what does a peasant do? They have to either buy a plot from one of those hoarders mentioned in "3." or they gotta search for an expiring plot - yes, plots expire and get destroyed if you don't pay taxes weekly, tax certificates can be bought for irl cash (obviously) or labor points (a lot of them - if you want more, buy them with irl cash..), so even after people build a farm, they often stop playing because there's the need of playing the game every day so you can buy tax certificates and... be able to keep playing... yeah it doesn't make any sense, I know. Blame Trion, not me. You gotta play so you can play more... If you stop playing for a week and come back later, say good bye to your house. Like I said, people without house plots can find an expiring plot and build their stuff there. BUT SURPRISE! Hackers! Scripters! Waiting an hour for a plot to expire and get it for yourself? Nope! Wild scripter appears and takes it for himself INSTANTLY to add to his collection consisting of 20 other house plots.
...unless you pay. As I said, you need labor points to do stuff, you earn these while playing if you're a f2p user, or both online and offline if you're a Patron. However, even as a Patron the amount of labor you get is not even nearly enough if you want to progress fast. Everything costs so much labor, especially if you wanna craft those sweet expensive items. Oh, also as far as itemization goes - you can upgrade every weapon and armor piece you get for free! But! It can get destroyed in the process... Unless! You can buy a scroll thingy that makes your odds of upgrading the item way higher (but not 100%). Now it is possible that you buy it and the item still gets destroyed. Imagine spending cash for absolutely nothing. That's ArcheAge.
That's probably it as far as the major cons go.

Velvet Sundown doesn't work because of the naiveté of its core gameplay: it puts entirely too much trust on players. The game plays out like Clue without any of the structure that keeps a game like that on track – you’re one of a number of personas with unique backstories and props that inform their actions, and their goals, during the game. There are no voice lines, no rewards, there is no discernable plot, and nothing to incentivize players to stick to the core of the gameplay, which is to find out more about yourself and the other characters, and complete a number of individual goals you’re given at the beginning of the game. You as a character rely on other players to pay attention to who they are and what they're doing and cooperate when your goals intersect. However, when there’s no directive to win, and the game can run its course without anything happening, other people are all too often eager to sit and do nothing, playing instead with the text-to-speech feature to say puerile things to each other for 30 minutes. This game would be cool if played in a more controlled setting, like with a group of people you know would make a sincere effort. But otherwise it goes nowhere.

This is going to be my first review of a game so here it goes. Despite my hours on steam, I have spent hundreds more hours on the official launcher, as well as hundreds more in Void Elsword the private server. So I have played this game for a long time, enough to saftely make an opinion of it.
Pros:
1) The Story is pretty decent. I ussually don't pay attention to the story in MMO's, but something about it is enjoyable especially how each stage tie in with each character. There's also some cutscenes which are nice
2) The cast of characters. Each character has a unique system to them that gives them all seperate playstyles, even amongst job changes! The backstories of each character and their job changes are quite enjoyable as well
3) The PvP. The game has a fast paced combo oriented PvP that's similar to a fighting game. Which makes good PvP matches enjoyable as you test out your skills, and showcase flashy and amazing combos
4) The community. There's some really nice people in the game, and I've made long time friends in my time of playing it. The people all love the game and deeply care for it.
5) The PvE. The dungeons in the game all have unique bosses and stages, and later on into the late game the bosses even get their own gimmicks which are fun and challenging to play with friends.
Cons:
1) Pay 2 Win, and Pay 2 Play. Basically as much as others have said, this game has HEAVY usage of the cash shop. You want more inventory space? pay money. You want more skill slots? Pay money. You want to enchant your gear? Pay money. (this is for +7 weapons and above)
2) The PvP. Yes, I know that the PvP is really good in the game, but at the same time it's really bad. People can bring their end game gear into PvP and absolutely 1 or 2 shot their enemies. This completely breaks the "test of skill" gameplay of a fighting game as people as the heavy gear dependance makes PvP unfair. Long ago in the game, you could beat a max level character with only a level 15 if you were skilled enough. Now, it is completely impossible as with each update PvP gets even worse and worse due to gear.
3) The PvE. Just like PvP the PvE is also bad. The later dungeons it becomes nigh impossible to beat them without either A) having to party, B) having the best gear, or C) both. I can understand the difficulty being raised in the end game dungeons, as they are end game, but the spike just shoots up way too high all of the sudden. This makes it harder not only for solo players, but for the casual players as well, since you will spend all your time grinding for gear just to be able to beat the later dungeons.
4) The community. Just like there's good people, there's also bad people. There are so many toxic players, hackers, cheaters, and even bots in the game that just ruins the community. Even if you report these players and send screenshots of them as evidence, the GM's of the game won't even ban them. They just give them a warning and that's it. They still run rampant in the game.
5) The characters. Yes, although the characters seem cool and fun to play with they are also bad. In both a PvE and PvP aspect, certain characters and job changes are way stronger than others. This is just a balancing issue, but it's enough to put it on here as with each patch all that KoG does is nerf characters down to making them super weak and leaving alone all the characters that needed a nerf as they were too strong.
Conclusion:
Overall I think Elsword is an experience that one must take own their own. Is it a good game? in certain aspects yes. Is it a bad game? Most deffinately. This game had so much potential and it could've been a great 2d fighting game, but over the years through the constant nerfs, and the releasing of new characters that are always more overpowered than the last. I just can't recommend this game anymore. A shame too as myself and so many others love this game and only wished for it to become better and become the game we all hoped for, but that day will never come. As others in the community have said, this is a dying game.

Pros:

Neutral:

Cons:

- Have I mentioned microtransactions?
I have been playing Elsword before it got released on Steam. But back then, it was regional so accounts do not progress the same in different regions (For example: EU servers and Asia servers). Then, they decided to sync all accounts into one international version. KOG gave players a chance to sync their accounts so all player data- Characters, items, levels, mounts, etc- will be saved, which I obviously did. But when the international version went live, all my data was lost. I did all the required procedures and even got a confirmation email. I contacted both local and international Elsword supportbut neither helped getting back my data. So in the end, I lost several lvl 70s and several rare boss drops. After several years, I decided it was fine so I started fresh. I am still disappointed with the game.
Microtransactions are still a vital aspect of the game. Everything, I mean
, can be sped up, improved, enhanced and/or obtained with microtransactions. You are a grinder and your 40 item slot (pretty tiny actually) isn't enough? Too bad, you gotta use real-life cash to unlock slots. You have unlocked skills but don't have enough slots to equip them? Into the Item Mall you go. Starting costume is the best looking costume that follows in-game lore and character design? Ok, actually the item mall doesn't have that. But still, microtransactions are flooding the game in a bad way that actually reduces the fun from playing. Some aren't even permanently available to you after purchase. Several items, after a week up to a month, expire and disappear from your inventory. Well, goodbye precious lunch money.
Don't get me wrong, you can be a pro and get far and progress the game without spending a single cent. But it will be extremely hard and time consuming. It will literally take you YEARS to reach a level where you can beat up everything and have ultra-rare items with epic stats and cool costumes and accesories, assuming you follow every event and play regularly.
Oh the grinding. I absolutely love the grinding. No joke. I used to play with a friend and both of us would party together to clear specific dungeons 100+ times just to get the rare boss drop. Combat is actually fun and satisfying in PvE so the grinding brings more pleasure than exhaustion. That is, of course, if you actually enjoy grinding like I do. If not, then too bad. You are required to grind a HELL LOT to complete several quests and missions, especially in the late-game. "Get 30 monster jaws". Seems simple until you realize that killing the monster that appears only 5 times in an entire dungeon that requires 3-7 minutes to complete only drops a jaw 1/20th of the time.
they said.
I don't go to PvP much; I'm more of a relaxed, play-at-my-own-pace, PvE kind of guy. But the rare times that I do go to PvP, I meet unbalanced, world-level pros or no cooldown, infinite health hackers. Could be just me and my luck. Don't know, don't care.
Overall, Elsword has a great potential to become a great MMO. Fluid combats, character and design are the strong aspects of the game. But the game just has a really big microtransaction problem that most low-level, free players will find discouraging to continue to play. If you are willing to invest a lot of time into this game, fight your way through Pay 2 Wins, and grind like hell, give this game a shot.

It's hard to say whether or not I recommend this. On one hand, the tactics and mechanics are solid and easy to grasp.
On the other hand, the graphical glitches and some missing functionality make me want to suggest you save your money.
Several character models are broken. They have floating bits constantly at least a few inches from their body, and at least a few feet in the case of one Shocktrooper character. The drill sergeant's eyepatch moves from a few inches in front of his eye to in the middle of his face to aaaaaall the way over there. Hell, the main character has a circular object (I'm not sure what it is, exactly), floating about a foot away from his hand at all times.
In addition, the cursor moves unbearably slowly on map screens, taking far too long to go from one end of the battlefield to the other. Also, the enemy turns are long enough that, if I neglect to press any buttons, my laptop's screen will go dark. There is no in-game option to increase the speed of either of these.
Oh, and the main character's lipsynch at the start of EVERY mission is, uh. Well, it's bad. And I'm not going to say charitable things about the rest of the mouth movements in this game, either.
However, you could charitably argue that these are minor details, and I'm honestly not sure if it's just my laptop doing it.
As for the game's actual presentation, well, I had to sit through ten minutes of cutscene (chopped up into three "chapters" for some reason) before I got to actually play the game.
And when the game needs to advance story but doesn't feel like putting actual effort into all the cutscenes the game shows you, the characters will be reduced to talking heads.
While I'm not far enough in the story to safely say one way or the other, I've seen enough anime to smell a dating sim on the horizon, and I'm definitely not looking forward to telling the adopted sister character that I'm not interested in dating her when there are reporter ladies to potentially date.
Oh, and the main character seems a little milquetoast. When told his squad is fighting with each other, his first thought is, "gee, should I really stop these people who are supposed to be acting like a united fighting force from shouting at each other?"
A lot of these are minor flaws, but they add up.
Regardless, the game is still enjoyable despite its flaws, and if you can catch another sale, then pick this game up.

I hate jRPG's. Final Fantasy II was one of the first games I ever played as a child and the format very quickly grew tiresome. When Final Fantasy: Tactics came out it got me hooked again since I was in love with XCOM and the like. Once CD-ROM discs came out and it was possible to have voice actors in games, reading a novel in between every battle became pretty annoying; I played Final Fantasy 7 for about 15 minutes before quitting and I played 8 a bit longer. I haven't played a jRPG since.
UNTIL NOW! Valkyria Chronicles is... I mean it's decent. There's more strategy involved in the battles which is what I enjoyed with Final Fantasy: Tactics. Everything is presented in book format (hence Chronicles, I imagine) so there's no map to explore or anything like that but it still presents you with a lot of lore and backstory via the book you "read" as you play.
It's all superficial though. It may feel like you're playing a strategy game, but you're still just playing a turn based jRPG that lets you walk your characters around as if you were playing a 3rd person shooter. There's a lot of "woe is me" Anime BS going on in between missions and some veiled pedophilia but if you can get over 12 year old girl soldiers wearing cat ears, it can be enjoyable in small doses.

I don't take the time to write reviews often, but this game hit some heartstrings for me. If you grew up in my era and the SNES is what you remember being the best part of being a kid, you need to get this game. I know the price tag is a bit much, but this isn't some cheap SNES clone that you'll mindlessly play through and forget about. Everything from the gameplay, story, graphics, music, and feel of the game will be sending chills down your spine. It's Zelda. It's Final Fantasy. It's Metroid. It's all of those placed into a neat little package that tells a completely new and amazing story that will grab your by your heart and yank it out of your chest. The best part about it all is how it is presented to you. It's not a lot, and it's not a little. It's the perfect amount of detail to keep you wanting more. I also should mention that they get the feels down SO HARD. It's all about little moments that make you teary eyed, or yell, or smile, or cheer. Everything about this game is what I thought it wasn't going to be and it is hands down one of the best games I have played this year. Do yourself a favor and buy it.

NOTE: THIS IS A TRANSCRIPTION OF THE LINKED VIDEO

I pride myself on making brief Show and Tell reviews, but this might be one of the shortest videos I’ve ever made. In the Darkness of the Sea is a 5-10 minute - free - experience. I emphasise “free” because, while this may not be indie game of the year, it’s not a bad way to spend 5-10 of your time on. This game is made up mostly, from what I can tell, royalty free assets and simple shapes, which would often be a red flag for me that maybe this game isn’t worth reviewing - but when I looked at the Steam page something did jump out at me. This game has something, so while I’m going to keep every category here very short, I’m going to try and identify what that is.

Presentation

I mentioned that the game is made up of simple shapes, but I think they have been utilised quite well here.The game certainly has a unique style that looks scrapbook-like; as though someone ripped lots of different pictures out of magazines and turned them into the different visual assets in this game - aside from the sea itself. The sea is a 3D object, but it makes it really stand out against the rest of the game without feeling as though it doesn’t belong; it’s still made up of black and white like everything else. Where the presentation loses balance a bit is in some of the animations - the whales are animated well, but other than that I found them to be lacking a bit - and in some of the assets there are cut corners. In particular I noticed this in the clouds; sometimes there would be unfinished edges that are just floating in space on their own which are hard to spot but are quite ugly when you do.

Mechanics

The actual game itself I think is the weakest aspect of In the Darkness of the Sea. It involves you speeding up and slowing down your boat in order to avoid obstacles or… ducking to avoid jumping fish? It was just a bit weird, and felt tacked on so that people could technically call this a game because it has a fail-state (or any other arbitrary measure that people like to use to decide if a game is a game or not), but honestly it just messes with the pacing of the game and took me out of the experience a little bit. Personally I would have been fine with it being a “walking simulator” type - at the very least it seemed to me that’s what the game was really interested in being. I’m not opposed to the idea of this game having some serious mechanics, but I think if that’s what the developer was going for it needs to actually add something to the experience rather than, in my opinion, taking something out of it.

Story

The Darkness of the Sea has some good moments. I’m not going to say what any of them are due to this being an 8 minute game, but I think this is where I really see promise in this game and this developer. The atmosphere of the game is good, and there was enough in there to surprise me and make me feel something. There’s this beautiful track Fantasia on a Theme that the game uses, though I think in some ways it felt a bit unearned. It’s a really really nice song, but I think sometimes what is going on in the game isn’t as powerful as the music. Music is generally supposed to complement a scene - not overshadow it. - and I think some of what I felt was due to Fantasia on a Theme alone, and not necessarily the combination of the music and the game. Though there were certainly some moments where the combination did work - just not all the time.

Verdict

Again, I don’t think this game is groundbreaking, but it’s free and I think it shows promise for the future of the developer. Forgive me if I’m about to butcher your name here, is it Olivier LeClair? If you are at all interested in his game check it out free of charge, and if nothing else I think this is a developer to look out for in the future. There is something in this game that allows it to stand a head and shoulders above most of the other games that are released daily on Steam.

I have never made a steam review, but this may be the only game that I do one for. I study games art design at university, so I know most of the intricacies and problems that developers face when making a game. Larian is my ♥♥♥♥ing idol. They created a game with so many interesting mechanics, interactions and customisations that I could only dream of making one day.
They not only provided their customers and fans with a great game, they did it through a platform that is notorius for scams and cashgrabs. The fact that Larian managed to do this twice, and go over their expected limit twice, shows you how loyal this community is to them. And if a community is THAT loyal, then it only makes sense that the developers are just as loyal. Larian not only delivers on their promises, but they surpass them. Everyone knew, and even the devs themselves said, that voiceacting would be too much of a feat to include. And yet here we are.
But for me, the best aspect of Larian Studios is their communication with their customers/fanbase. They made update videos throughout their whole development cycle, uploaded patches and continuously fixed problems that were in EA as noted by us the players. I usually wait until a game is released and read/watch reviews before buying it myself. But from watching all the update videos and seeing how passionate this developer was in their game and community, I just had to purchase it.
Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a masterpiece. It adds so much that felt missing in the first game, and the first game already felt wholesome and grand. I used to play a few top down RPGs/cRPGs when I was a little kid on my family's box PC running windows 98. I tried replaying the Baulder's Gate series recently and I just can't get into it. I can't replay any of those games just because of the dated visuals and mechanics. Even most modern RPGs feel slightly dated in how the game plays. DOS2 is the opposite. It not only looks modern..it feels modern. The combat is intellectually challenging, rewards thinking-out-of-the-box, mechanically complex, and satsifying.
That ticks the biggest box for me, because whilst a game can have a great narrative, I'm more of a gameplay-first person. But the other great thing about DOS2 is...that it has an absolutely amazing narrative. I haven't even finished the first act. I've only just escaped Fort Joy, and yet, the dialogue and interactions I've had with each npc I've come across so far has been so immersive and delicately crafted. The writing is superb, and the added voiceacting (which is equally amazing) emphasises it even more.
The only flaws that the game has, in my opinion, are:
- Speed of combat. I don't mind the length of casting animations and whatnot. But I absolutely dislike when it takes years for a character, especially something that usually has a slow walking animation, to move around in combat if its large or open area. I actually haven't looked into the settings all that much, but I really do want a combat speed option or slider.
- The range of customisation in terms of visual aesthetic. The customisation for skills and roles are amazing. But I do feel like there could be more assets for faces and facial accessories. For example, the only human female face I liked was the first one. And I wish there were more hairstyles overall. The colour palletes have good range though. This can be changed with mods I'm guessing.   (Maybe in the next game, we can customise more specifically; eye colour, nose shape, etc. That would be amazing! :D)
Overall, I'm glad that this game has had such a success. But what I'm more glad for is the developers themselves. We would not have this game and the reassurance of its quality without Larian Studios bringing their best. I'm looking forward to countless replays, and creating a few mods myself.

Herein we find all the same lazy tropes we have come to expect from such games. Totally unimaginative world, lifeless characters, unnatural dialogue, and no feeling at all for what another kind of society might think and feel like. Like in most CRPGs, the religion of the inhabitants of the game world was dreamt up by the kind of atheist too small-minded to appreciate paganism, let alone theism. (The dialogue choices for a "mystic" demonstrate conclusively that the game's writers do not know what mysticism is). Its conception of justice is impossibly shallow—after witnessing a character brutally slain for treason on no evidence, the only possible objection the player can give was that the incident was—racially prejudiced! This is poor stuff.
The preoccupation, as so often, is the Death of God. Or in this case, of the Divinity. The whole cult of divinity is, of course, a laughable sham, and those who take it seriously are, invariably, fools. I haven't played very deep into the game, maybe there is some twist coming later? I don't find any of this exciting enough to continue and find out.
A good fantasy universe is informed by a lively interest in the history and philosophy of our own. The writers of this game show considerable ignorance of both. It's like The Witcher 3, but somehow even worse. Don't waste your money.

At its core, Azada is just a collection of video game puzzles (including a few that resemble simple hidden object rooms). But it has a strong, gripping atmosphere that may suck you in and never let you go.
Azada is a unique game. There are many of us who have put dozens upon dozens of hours in it, but it is difficult to explain why. After all, it is nothing more than a bunch of childishly easy puzzles thrown together in a game of very loose narrative.
I know calling a puzzle easy is subjective, but this game will hardly pose any challenge to anyone: most of the levels can be completed under a minute or even less. In exchange, there is a ton of them: if you choose to enter the world of Azada, you’ll be presented with over two dozen types of puzzles totalling over a hundred levels.
A review of Azada cannot be complete without mentioning the photographs. These are similar to simple hidden object scenes, only in this case the emphasis is purely on trying to find a starting item and use that to uncover more, until you solve the entire room. They may not seem like much by reading about them, but most Azada players consider them the best part of the game with very good reason—sadly, one has to experience it to understand this enthusiasm.

Azada is a point-and-click puzzle game. It's a very short game, consisting of ten chapters with nine puzzles a piece. There a handful of basic puzzle forms, including Memory/Concentration, "Move the Matches", Match 3, Sliders, et cetera, that recur throughout the game. The puzzles scale slightly in difficulty as the game progresses, and each chapter ends with a jig-saw-esque puzzle that works toward completing a portrait of a man you're rescuing. (If it sounds very MYST, that's because it is.) It's a short game, there's not a lot to say, so let's get to it!
The Good:
- Visuals are good. The game is older, but doesn't look -terribly- dated. It's a point-and-click game that has since ported over to mobile devices, and its success there is a result of its low-intensity graphics.
- Music might be the best part. The music sounds much higher quality than I expected.
- This is a great game for killing time. None of the puzzles are too challenging, and only took me a couple minutes at best.
The Bad:
- None of the puzzles are too challenging, and only took me a couple minutes at best. A few of the "click to find" landscapes were difficult, but not because the puzzle itself was difficult, but because these games sometimes fall into the trap of making you hunt for individual pixels. Aggravating.
Conclusions?
This game is not especially challenging. I don't know that there's much more to say. I liked it, but it wasn't overly stimulating. Great for your mom, maybe?

As you go along you get a token that will give you the option to bypass any puzzle that you have a problem with. I think there are 5 in total. They help if there is a puzzle you don't enjoy.
There are quite a few different puzzles that test your memory, observation and logic. Some are excellent and a few are poor but generally this is worth what you'll pay for it.

Alright, so what's this game? Well, a post-apocalyptic shooter set in the Russian subway, of course! Well, filled with shady factions and ghoulish creatures too. It's very similar in regards to its predecessor. It plays out like a decent FPS with unique mechanics like a 'breath' one where you'll die if you don't monitor the degradation of your mask's filter and stealth is included too. You've got a cool setting with unique characters and settings. From the subways of Moscow to the dilapidated interior of the Great Library, you'll be on your toes every moment. The storyline is pretty interesting, with twists and turns enough to keep you gripped. This is no Christopher Nolan type of shindig though, but its pretty good. Gotta hand it to the author of the book, though. He has some pretty good source material.
The voice acting is improved on this one too. Don't expect too highly of it, though. It'll come off lacking in some parts but it's passable at least. One possible solution is to fire up the Russian voices and put on English subtitles but sadlly, even though how immersive this is, most of the side dialogs are not subtitled, so word of warning. Oh, and sound design is good for the most part. Mostly. This is a minor gripe though, and it doesn't take away from the experience too much.
So, should you get this? Well, you like to shoot things? And be sneaky every once in a while? Do you like exploring dark interiors and getting spooked by eerie locations? Do you like cursing to yourself as your magazine runs dry as you mow down mutants deep within the Metro? Well, step right up, grab the nearest '♥♥♥♥♥♥♥' SMG and put on that Night Vision Goggles! We're going mutant hunting!
And you're invited. And remember...If it's hostile...you kill it.

Ahh. Speedrunners: the death of us all or as I like to call it, The Friendship Destroyer.
Yes, that's right this game is overwhelmingly competitive and would spark rage into your opponents as you all battle it out on 13 official maps and a variety of workshop maps that are being made everyday by the community via their very own level editor!
What do you mean, "the friendship destroyer"?
Well then my friend, let's just say that continuously blowing them up with rockets and bombs (two of the many item pick ups in the game) didn't really appeal to them as much... Turns out they must've un-installed the game or something... Shame really I would've loved to hear the sweet sound of keyboard smashing :(
But in all seriousness, this game is fun, exciting and unpredictable. Full of intense 1 on 1 situations as the death border comes closing in on you and your rivals masking the map behind it relying on your knowledge of the map to guide your superhero player in the right direction...
Speedrunners is a very easy game to get into..... or should I say, get addicted to; wanting to win just one more game or to just get that final few points to rank up to the next league it's definitely hours worth spending...
The game puts you straight into a tutorial as soon as you load it in teaching you the basics of speedrunners and the controls you're using to jump, slide and swing and all the other jazz such as using your pick-ups... This means that new players will pick up the game quickly and will be soon off to get to their dream league...
I've been playing for at least 74 hours now (in total aha, as addicting as this game is I don't think I'd do 74 hours in one session :P) and I've managed to get up to expert league and I'm in the top 10 in getting to the bronze league... Which is harder than you'd think... The higher league you go the more advanced players will be and the more skilled they will be too. More experienced players would know the best routes and would be quick on their feet to secure their wins using all tactics built up from previous experiences and knowledge built up over time.
This amps up the competitiveness of the game and draws you in.
As you do this, you tend to pick up on some of the tricks other advanced players use and you'll notice tips such as saving your boost and being sure to hit those angle blocks to gain more momentum and speed.. It will be vital that you learn new routes too for the individual maps as going certain routes will be faster than others and some may be more advantageous than others too such as getting into the VIP Area on Nightclub, A tricky route to learn at first (how to get there) but getting there or not can be a great game changer and would definitely score you some easy rounds IF your opponents don't manage to get there.
The artwork/visuals and mechanics of the game are very good and look very pretty (you won't get bored of it too easily is what I mean) and it's being updated constantly; this includes layouts, new characters being added and even secret characters which you'd have to do some digging around to find out how to get them ;) and many more. The animations for all the characters are great and are unique to suit their design and style and they are all fun to play with. Some characters have different skins such as the main Speedrunner can be blue, white, yellow or black for example so you can personalise your favourite characters to suit you..
I would totally recommend this game for anybody who is competitive and/or wants to have heaps of fun in one single session. There are a few bugs scattered around the place which is reasonable for an early access game but with an amazing community and an active team they're being fixed regularly thanks to the wonderful community reporting them and requesting ideas or changes to the game that are always considered by the developers to make the game ready for launch.
And for a game only worth £6.99 It's definitely worth it!

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This is an excelent strategy game for those who want an experience that is totaly different from your conventional strategy title. Rather then taking control of a faction/nation, you take a more personal role as the head of a noble family and after you die, you control your heir. So it really dosen't matter what happens to you politicaly, so long as your dynasty lives on, you can still play on to do something else.
If there's one downside, its the ludacris amounts of DLC this game has (though a significant portion of it is useless junk like portrait packs or additional songs to the soundtrack) and much of it is kind of necessary to make the game reach its full potential (personaly I'd advise getting the Old Gods [pretty much necessary, allows you to play as pagans and makes them far more fleshed out], Sword of Islam [allows you to play as a muslim, a pretty drastic change from the catholic characters with some cool mechanics], The Republic [again, fairly obvious as it allows you to play as merchant republics and create your own republics, completely different mechanics, but fun to play], Ruler Designer/Customization Pack [just fun to make your own dynasty and edit more distant members of your dynasty, though this isn't really neccesary at all], Charlemange [more or less a complete overhaul of the Title system and allows you to more or less fabricate your own titles for kingdoms or empires from scratch, also a new start date], Rajas of India [Allows you to play as a Hindu, Buddhist or Jain]).
All in all a good game, but definately wait for a sale to get it or any of the DLC's.

The combat in VC, where you'll be spending most of your time, is a modern take on the old Final Fantasy Tactics, SRPG except with guns. It does away with the tile/grid based system and makes it into a more open style where your characters can go where they can, with distance restrictions based on class. Instead of overhead camera, it's now third person. Moving is about the only similar thing compared to traditional TRPGs, though. Usually, you can do two things during a characters turn, move and attack. In VC, though, you can move, attack, heal, hide in the environment (tall grass, behind sandbags, from view), and retreat from the battle to call new allies - all in the same turn. While attacking, you can a few things depending on class. While all classes can shoot/launch rockets (normal attack), other classes can use grenades or repair the tank. Engineers can even disarm mines while in movement. Detonating mines can also be done in movement and doesn't end turn, although it's not as effective as when an engineer does it. Healing also works similar to attack whereas you can't heal and then aim for someone. The interesting thing of note is, while moving, there is crossfire. No more will you or your enemy look upon your attacker and say, "Hey, hit me". Now they will say, "if you don't kill me, I will kill you before you get here". Every attack is also a counter attack so it's a very offensive based game with defensive in mind as well. It's the best of both worlds and the combined worlds are great!
There are 19 chapters (including prologue) and about 25 battles. There are also an infinite, although, with loosely pre-programmed AI, number of skirmishes to "grind" exp and money for all those late game weapons and level required potentials and orders. Across these chapters and battles, you meet a diverse cast of characters, some of which are distinguishable from each other as you stop the invading Soviets while defending Estonia (or Lithuania/Latvia).
Storywise, the scenes are short for those who just want to play and not watch but that also means a lot of things get rushed. The love story (as all RPGs have) goes from neutral to love without you realizing it. The game takes place over seven months but you only see 22-24 days over that seven months. I can't but wish a few more reports or other special scenes were included with the game to alleviate some of the rush This is just my nitpick as someone who's really interested in story and character development.
Visually, the game was built on an engine that, as far as I can find, has only been used for the Valkyria Chronicles games that SEGA calls the CANVAS graphics engine. Its whole point seems to be to make everything look like a watercolored wonderland. Assuming you find war to be a wonderland, of course. The only odd/annoying thing about the engine is the border of everything is uncolored and is just an outline. It's not a major deal but it just seems unnecessary. Why not finish it? Characters look anime-ish so typical Japanese video game-ness here.
When it comes to music, it's wonderfully atmospheric. Many of the songs are orchestrated. Sadly, most of the songs aren't even heard. There are really only six or so songs that get any sort of recollection out of me. Fortunately, the whole soundtrack is available in new game plus so give it a listen if you want to. Usually, I like to add official previews or downloads but I can't find any NA versions so here's an
review that's better than anything I can write on music as well as a few previews. Or, ya know, go to unofficial Youtube channels.
I picked up Valkyria Chronicles because I wanted a game like Final Fantasy Tactics that wasn’t a game I've beaten 7 million times. I've tried a few and they ended-up being boring, mundane mistakes. I currently have nearly 60 hours of playtime and I'm still not done with the new game plus and achievement ♥♥♥♥♥ing (although my drive died and my net sucks so 25gigs is painful). Best multiplayer title to pick up a sword and fight, period. Chivalry is the first game to present a truly awesome and original first-person meele combat (and superb archery too) and thus will always remain a classic to me.
It ain't perfect though, the combat mechanics were well designed but abandoned after release, which means competitive players have mastered all kinds of exploits and stupidly unrealistic mechanics while the devs just sat there and said "it's cool that was intended". 360° slashes, accelerating/deaccelerating your attacks to unbalanced and unrealistic speeds (known as dragging) in order to deceive your opponent, facing your opponent backwards while looking up to hit them instantly after pressing the attack button (reverse overhead) and so on. So there's a very high learning curve to this game because one must master such exploits in order to become competitive. Glitches are common too, such as ghost strikes (when a player's attack animation gets desynced and he hits you even though you parried), ranged projectiles sometimes not dealing damage at all, being unable to move after drawing your bow, flags that glitch and can't be captured in Capture the Flag mode etc. It would be simple enough to fix all of these but Torn Banner doesn't care.
I suggest getting this game on discount, it is at least 50% off every month or two and there's an active community of players in North and South America (and probably Europe too) so it's a decent purchase. Or just wait for Mordhau, an upcoming game that aims to build upon what Chivalry did and improve it.

First of all, i'm not a native english speaker so you have to forgive me for any possible confusions. I decided to write a review for this game because the game is marvellous in all aspects with exceptions of a few annoying stuffs which will be summarized below.
Pros:
-Traditional RTS gameplay which consist of base building, economic management and fighting.
-Variation of units and the very distinctive factions not a clone of each others or just a change in skins.
-Each races have different advantages/disadvantages in resources gathering i.e. Humans can do husbandry and collect foods from fatten animals, Eleves instead gather food from picking fruits and let their deer generating supply and lastly Orcs can only hunt wild beasts or breeded animals for food. There are also other resources, gold, wood and stone to manage and each factions have pros/cons. Don't worry though the resource gathering/its technologies upgrade is simplified and cleverly done to not interfere with your fun in mobilizing your troops. These resorces aspect also affect your play style for each races for instance, Elves can generate every resources infinitely from tree symbiosis, alchemy and exchange market. In contrast, Orcs have to find a substitute gold and sone mining in neutral areas.
-Supporting various play styles i.e. turtle, rushing or rogue.
-Zombies, when you leave  corpses both yours and enemy's unattended, they will become the walking dead. Each factions has different corpse sweepers which more or less affect the battle strategies.
-NPCs and creeps, it is very fun to hunt down a dragon for treasury(additional resources which currently incollectible) or kill orges or goblins for dominating forward base/small fort.
-Orcs produce units differently from other factions. If you guys remember the game named Battle Realm a decade back, these orc's units production reminds me of that game. To elaborate, you have to train different types of units by moving them through different types of buildings.
-Sieging stronghold, you have to break through both outer and inner walls before destroying the enemy HQ. You can command various siege units which are vary for each factions.
-Quite steep learning curve which for me is a plus as i'm having fun trying diffrent things.
-Dev is quite active in fixing bugs and adding contents.
Cons:( i will list it down from the most annoying/serious problems)
-Units controls are quite lifeless and a bit clunky, you won't get a feel that you have already ordered your units.
-No hotkeys at the moment particularly "attack move" command which really destroy the fun.
-A few bugs here and there which are mostly under Dev's attention.
-Incomplete contents
Imo, this game deserves much better attention than most AAA RTS game released this year. The game itself have everything you can imagine a very good RTS should have and i definitely won;t regret buying it at full price.

If you are an avid RTS gamer and hunger for a game that has something unique and different to the countless RTS games that have been released in the past, then I would recommend you jump on this developing one. And I'm confident that it will get much better due to the fact that the developers are extremely interactive with the community, asking players what they would like to see included in the game and how they would like it to develop.

I'm happy to stay on the "development ride" and looking forward to see this game achieve the success it deserves.
