TLDR; Conan is,
, so riddled with bugs that either prevent play or dramatically alter play that a player cannot enjoy it as it stands
to Funcom. The future will likely change that, but if wishes were horses we'd all be eating steak.
For a title to be worthy of Early Access for the buyer, it has do at least one thing: be fun in its current state or have working content and mechanics to give feedback on.
At the moment, the number of bugs and genre-inappropriate
in this game defy belief, Early Access or no. It feels like a programming and art team bypassed any sort of QA or game design and uploaded the work-in-progress code of a concept demo to Steam, using a mashup of other title's survival mechanics under Conan-paint. It may, or may not, turn into something worth our time in the future, but right now it is crippled by the density of bugs and its use of temporary, placeholder subsystems.
There's some value to Funcom in us paying for access to bugs and helping them reproduce those bugs (pay to QA) but none for us or Funcom in giving feedback on the play experience when those few areas of play that have not been completely altered by bugs are in fact placeholders, e.g., the entity spawning.
I'm also unable to find anything new or different in the concepts or mechanics of this game. It has the feel of a demo made to show a disgruntled corporate board that, yes, the Funcom team is capable of making the same game other developers have already made time and again.
If you are considering buying now based on positive reviews on Steam, please take a second look at them and notice the number of times the authors say they are "confident" a bug will be fixed or a feature added or that all can be excused by an Early Access banner. Unless they've a special line into the development team, it's not possible for them to know what will come tomorrow; consistent, high-quality updates and patches over the next few months--not hope founded only in wishes--will prove or disprove this team's title.
For now, only buy if you believe in
games, as this absolutely does not yet qualify as Early Access and it remains to be seen if Funcom has the ability
the will
the expertise
the budget
the time to make this into something more than a concept demo wrapped in expensive textures. Put another way, this a good fit for the section "Concepts in Steam Greenlight" and a waste of our time (far more precious than money) as an "Early Access" title.
UPDATE: having read Funcom's embarrassing excuses yesterday--so reminiscent of No Man's Sky (wow so many people)--I want to be clear: connection problems stemming from networking code still wet behind the ears is fundamentally different from what is at issue here, i.e., that once logged in and playing, the game is still full of bugs, broken systems, and placeholder systems.

The things they do ask you real life cash for are either cosmetic or revolve around increasing your allready generous bank space or numerous character slots. GW2 starts you off with five, ArcheAge two. GW2 you can increase to 69 (though why you'd need that many I have no idea) at most here you can have six across all servers. Plus with the upcoming Heart of Thorns expansion, you need only buy that and get the core game too. HESITANT recommendation; Edit at end
You're sitting across from a man with the facial features of an aged Arabian belly-dancer but with the voice of a sophisticated Atheist.
He do fancy floating card tricks. You do choice, luck and basic Arkham-esque combat.
He do menacing. You do persevering.
The Cabinet - the resting place (either dead or in-wait) of Dealer's lieutenants (as it were) - is pretty sizeable with 12 steps towards besting him.
You have Gold, which you can use to buy new Equipment (should you luck out and land on a Merchant) and Food, which you expend one of with every move - heal yourself for a certain amount with each meal.
The random encounters range from a disgruntled wife who needs you to fetch her drunk husband, to a priest asking for charity, to a wounded soldier asking for aid in hunting down his assailants, to an arena with multiple stages, to a devil you can gamble with, to goblins who attempt to steal your loot, to a trap-filled labyrinth... my "Deck Progress" bar isn't a third of the way filled.
The combat is very simple but also quite satisfying; though it mimicks the Batman games, it isn't quite as refined or fast-paced. On controller: X to attack, A to dodge-roll, B to stun (shield-bash), Y to parry (only with a shield) - LB for weapon ability, RB for Artefact.
Your priority is always to get a shield. I had good luck consecutively in obtaining one from the goblin dressed as a man ("Mister Lionel"?); ask him what he wants: Why to help you my boy! Here's a shield!
Once you have a shield, you will get the... iconic (and epic and emotional and cinematic and *buzz-word*) prompts above your head when an attack is about to connect. Best not to button-mash, though HoF is much more flexible in this regard than Arkham is.
The majority of the game is in playing across from the Dealer; the combat sequences never last as long as they should.
My hope for the game:
More extra Cards (read "Decks") added to the game than I could hope to go through.
A mode released later down the line that would allow more of a focus on the third-person action. Maybe not a full campaign, but just the most basic of stringing together the different arenas, with the ability to use any equipment you've previously unlocked, to versus any creature you've previously fought: The most extended Training mode / wave-based survival thing ever... *faints from awesomeness*
The Dealer could be giving voice-overs every now and then, either playing the role of Dungeon Master (more... impactfully(?)) or giving exposition on his past (if it's not further explained later in the game)... so... I guess, yeah, another campaign...
Regarding the game as is, the only faults I have:
The highlighted card isn't always the next face-down one; is the one you just left more often than I'd like. Of course, rage needs to be accounted for in a game (")so based on luck("); in such moments, I'll just spam A to get to the next card, only to exacerbate my anger by inadvertently wasting one (actually two) Food.
The Succeed or Fail challenges; four or five cards shown you, turned face-down, shuffled into one deck (one or two times) in such a way that you can hardly discern. It can easily be argued that we're given a better chance at picking a good card than would be given us IRL, but, with the way this mechanic is presented, I was hoping for more of a "Find the ball in one of these cups," something feasibly able to be beaten (as the Dealer admits that he (")doesn't cheat(")).
There is an Endless Mode in which you have a better chance of unlocking more cards to put into your decks for the Campaings. Upon selecting your target (one of those twelve lieutenants), you can then build your deck. New cards have unknown effects until drawn in the game, so you've several playthroughs ahead of you, aimed at simply identifying all the cards, for to build the best deck for your golden runs.
I absolutely recommend this game and have little doubt it's worth full price. My one bit of hesitation (as applied to all games that aren't open-world sandboxes (i.e. Just Cause 2)) is in how much repetition there is in the text events, in the limited pool of cards and arenas.
EDIT: With (I assume) the game being completely finished (since the sequel is soon to drop), I must say that my absolute recommendation is strained now. SO many of the new cards are extremely archaic in the how you must go about besting them. When I wrote this review, the game was much more reliant on skill, though of course luck(/your perception) was almost as big a part; now, without the aid of walkthroughs, the task of completely beating the game is a ridiculously daunting task. One example of this is when you get lost in the desert and must pick from the four cardinal directions at least four seperate times, in the hope of finding what you're after. Another card actually necessitates that you Fail the first check and Succeed the second. At least five cards seem to be designed solely with the Iron Hunger player character in mind, going so far as to have no (good) effect on ANY other player character that lands on those cards. I still have so much love for the game but there is no denying that the amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t present herein is something to beware of. I don't really enjoy my time while playing any more but am compelled to - progress is a stupid grind, strategy is up to fate, even if you are able to keep up with the shuffles and pick the "right" card each time, there is no telling if that will actually be correct according to the devs apparent "♥♥♥♥-you-lol" mentality (it would be fun, if the game wasn't such a chore to play in situations where you are doing well and two bad hands can kill you) and so much of the game actually plays itself. Without the third-person combat which many seem to dislike, I argue the game would have little substance.

I would like to correct a few things. A big thank you to Firehawk for helping me see the game through the anime. If you haven't read his reviews you really should (someone give that man a job!)
I love this game. However, it does have many, many flaws. Again thank you to Firehawk for helping me acknowledge what i knew but wouldn't accept.
Let's get past the bad part, the gameplay. I won't go into too much detail as others (*cough* Firehawk *cough*) have done a pretty good job, but I shall summarise. Enemies that stand still and take bullets, moments where the AI is incredibly dumb, a very odd leveling system, unbalanced gameplay, some units that respond to incoming fire (scouts, shocktroopers and tanks) and some that don't (all the others) as well as several poorly planned scenarios. Oh you may need to have a certain tolearance for occasional poor dubbing and repetitive soundtracks. There that'll do. For full details see Firehawk.
Now onto what sells this game, aesthetics and writing (though according to some the latter needed work). Beautifully styled anime graphics mean it is the best looking turn based strategy game one can play. Anime fans will instantly be in love with how this game LOOKS.
The best part though, by far, is the setting and characters.

In all my time video gaming I have never seen a game of this type that went to so much trouble, not only to create a great game, but also to craft an intricate plotline and give us great characters that we really want to keep alive. You REALLY feel like you have lost a friend and ally if a unit goes down and you are unable to get a medic to them before they die!  There are at least fifty (though there may be more i have yet to encounter) units All units divided into five classes suited to various combat roles. Each is genuinley an individual with they're own personality, strengths weaknesses and even little things like being a neat freak that can affect combat. All of this together equals a need to really think ahead, plan and use every advantage in order to complete your mission and bring all of squad seven home alive.
So yes if you play this game, play it as a form of escapism, or as a person who simply enjoys anime and beautiful design. If you are a hardcore tactical and strategy fan, you will be dissapointed. I will still recommend this game for people who are strategy/tactical fans or anime fans (or if you are like me, both).

PS3 Classic on PC! Great turn based strategy, mixes squad based tactics with fast paced and decisive movements. Very similar to X-COM but with it's own unique art style and identity.
Story is wonderfully told in a comic book format, with the graphics being colorfully cel-shaded complete with written sound effects ("Poom!") to match.
Squad management is not terribly deep or punishing, which makes this appealing to the more casual gamer while rewarding players who take the time to carefully build a synergetic squad.
Upgrades and equipment is very linear and lacking in creativity, although customisation options for vehicles adds depth and opens up different styles of attack.
The combat system is fresh and unique, and lands somewhere between Jagged Edge's real time system and X-COM's turn based system. Soldier and vehicle movement is very intuitive and encourages risk taking for higher percentage attacks and better field position.
A fantastic game experience now available on PC! Highly recommended for any strategy fan.

Owlboy is a very charming and beautiful game that definitely proves how games can be art. The game was made by D-Pad Studio, a team of only 5 people, during the period of 9 years and it was well worth the wait. Every pixel in this game shows how much of a labor of love this game is. The first thing you’ll notice when you launch Owlboy is the amazingly fitting and atmospheric soundtrack right from the menu screen. Second thing you’ll notice is the most beautiful and detailed pixel art I’ve seen  in a video game since Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. From characters and animations to the game world itself everything looks gorgeous, stylish and unique. The gameplay is simple, but very well made. It’s a mix of flying, dashing, jumping and shooting. You’re Otus, a mute owl from the village Vellie and you fly around the world while carrying your friends to help you on your adventures with their unique abilities. The story is charming, filled with humor, but sad at times and characters are very believable and relatable. The only thing that left me kind of underwhelmed and disappointed is the ending. I really hope that D-Pad Studio will release some kind of DLC to explain the ending and the lore more because me, and I’m sure many other people, would like to know more about the characters and the world at the end. Other than that Owlboy is a phenomenal game that I can’t recommend enough. It’s easily a new indie classic and one of my favorite games of all time.

(Note: this review does contain slight spoilers)
Let’s talk about the positives.
Unfortunately the gameplay is the weakest part of this game. This game is riddled with a lack of polish that prevents it from having a good feel to it.
You cannot remap the buttons for either gamepad or keyboard/mouse (I highly recommend you never attempt to play this game using keyboard/mouse as those controls are inexcusably awful.) The level design often demands a level of precision that the controls do not allow for. Example: You roll with the B (Circle), but aim with the Right Stick. Sometimes you’ll need to roll to avoid an attack while aiming, but can’t remove your thumb from the right stick fast enough.
There are stealth sections that are either tedious or outright terrible. These are often poor with sensible checkpoints and any small screw up results in near instant failure. There are at least 3 of these throughout the game with the last one being essentially a whole dungeon. At least you can fly in that last one.
The main gimmick of this game is that the player can fly. It’s not an original idea by any means. Games like Aquaria, Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet, and others have done similar things, but it’s still uncommon enough to be novel. However there are multiple points in this game where they take away the one unique thing about it and the results vary.
The waterfall sections feel fine. In them you can only jump. The jump is super floaty unlike most other games and takes while to get used to, but those sections are usually very short. A single room or a bit more. You can’t attack other than the little spin attack that does no damage, but combat is usually avoidable or nonexistent in those sections. They’re actually nicely done.
It’s the other times that are extremely questionable. There’s an early stealth section that’s pretty bad but the worst offender is the last area. There you can only fly for a little bit during it. Doing so will cancel all vertical momentum and slow you considerable. This would be fine if flying wasn’t so easy to trigger accidentally. By simply tapping up or jump again while in the air you’ll start flying. For most of the game this is great. You can just hold up and fly around. It feels expected, especially when using the analog stick. However, in that last section, if you start flying when you don’t expect to you’ll likely fall into an instant death trap. This causes you to countlessly restart what should be an fairly straightforward platforming section not because of your own inability, but due to unexpected control issues. It felt like an awful Mario Maker level.
This sort of one-off mechanic that doesn’t quite feel right or is straight up bad is very common throughout the game. There’s a dungeon where everything is dark and you only have a very small radius of light. You have to navigate tight tunnels edged with spikes, but the controls are floaty and the spikes too easy to clip into. Often it doesn’t look like you should have hit them. Later on you’re riding a giant lava snake and moving it up and down to avoid obstacles, but the screen is constantly rotating and it just feels wonky and awful instead of super cool like it should have. There’s not a single area of this game where I could say “Man! That was a really well done and fun!”
Combat in this game is, like so much else, lackluster. It’s boring, slow, and often times unavoidable since enemies will chase you until you’re dead. Boss battles are much the same (expect for the final boss which is actually pretty well done! Though they do make you do it three times). Typical bosses have either a safe area (generally towards the top of the screen) or a simple strategy that makes them a complete non-issue.
Ultimately, I feel like the developers would have better spent their time making a bunch of small games instead of trying to prefect this game. They did not succeed. So much of its issues scream inexperience and stubbornness. Had this game come out a year or two after they had started working on it, it would have been a flawed but alright game that they could have built from. As it stands now, it’s a flawed game that does not live up to expectations. If you want to play game with beautiful pixel art that took 8+ years to make then go play AM2R instead. Owlboy is just not worth your time.

I've been playing Warframe since it's open beta phase in 2013 and I don't ever regret the 2000+ hours I've invested in this game. Starting with gameplay, the mechanics and aspects of gameplay within Warframe are top notch and give paid games of the same genre a run for their money. This is, by far, the best Free-2-Play game I have ever played and it is really free-2-play. Essentially everything that isn't a cosmetic feature can be obtained somehow and even cosmetics are given out as rewards from time to time. In Warframe, there is no true endgame. The game is constantly expanding, constantly updating with new weapons, new systemwide events, new warframes. There is always something for you to do, even if you are a seasoned player. The only true endgame is FashionFrame, a.k.a, who can look the coolest in their frames. Depending on your playstyle and what you are after in th game, Warframe can get a bit grindy, but that is part of the fun. The best part of the game is that no one weapon is the most powerful of them all. All weapons and warframes have the potential to be devastating and powerful, it all depends on how you configure your modules to alter the weapon's damage output and it depends on which enemy faction you are facing, since all factions have different resistances and weakness to different types of damage, so switching your weapons and trying out new builds is encouraged and at times necessary. The most intriguing part of the game is the lore and how it is interwoven into nearly every aspect of what you do. Even the weapons you use have lore behind them that inevitably links to the bigger picture that we can't yet see. I've never played a game with such a great gaming community. Everyone is pretty much helpful and if you are ever lost or need help doing something, it won't be hard to find someone to join your squad and help you out. Last, but not least, the game developers, DigitalExtremes: they are very responsive to the community they serve. They will directly interact with us and push out updates addressing issues we have brought to them. And they have managed to bring Warframe from a game that had one tileset inside of a ship to having an entire open world map on Earth. They keep raising the bar with each new quest, with each new update and they somehow still manage to outdo themselves every time. Warframe is a game, the likes of which I have never played before. It has been updated so many times, gone through so many subtle aesthetic changes that at this point in time, the Warframe that we have now could essentially be called Warframe 2 when compared to Warframe update 2.0. I highly recommend this game.

Loved this first game, kickstarted both. Larian went above and beyond with this game. 16 hours in and i'm hooked in every way.

First game was absolutely amazing. For once, a sequel took everything great about the original and kept it, then actually fixed the mechanics that were weak. Then, just for good measure, Larian added a heaping pile of awesome sauce on top of those two points, and built a masterpiece.
Looking for a challenging strategical RPG? Put it on Tactician Mode, and see how every fight can swing rapidly based upon your approach. Some fights are forced to be approached head on, some allow for more... creative approaches. Anything goes, and the AI certainly don't hold back in their own tactics. It's amazingly easy to get overwhelmed until the proper amount of thought is put into each and every fight. Even if you have to 'cheese' some, every conflict is a blast.
Perhaps you're not the best at strategy, and are looking just for the story? Larian still has your back with this masterpiece. Everything is voice acted, even the Omniscent Narrator adding in the expressions and actions NPCs take as you speak to them. Your own replies are more vague, allowing you to fill in what might be said, adding to the Role Playing of the RPG element. There are six unique characters, each with their own stories and specific questlines.
Character customization is amazing, I must have spent nearly two hours upon launch exploring the various options. Not happy with just allowing you to edit your stats, spells, abilities and talents, Larian now introduces unique races, each with their own reactions from NPCs and unique racial abilities, some of which can truly compliment certain builds.
And, wanna play with your friends? It's very easy to start a game, and playing together just makes things all that much more amazing. I am absolutely stunned at how much better multiplayer works in Original Sin 2.
tl;dr - Larian Studios has shown that they know what the hell they're doing. And have made GOTY '17 in the process, in my eyes. All Strategy RPGs could learn quite a lot from Larian's success here.

This is a conditional recommendation.
The multiplayer is busted on all adversarial modes, the campaign is unfinished and the singleplayer lacks a great deal of enjoyment due to buggy controls and resultant lacklustre gameplay. I recommend either getting this game now and waiting for fixes, or buying it later, so the devs still have an incentive to finish their product.
With all that in mind, here are the reasons you should buy this game:
Units: The units in this game are large scale and yet have plenty of time for tactical diversity. Varying formations and abilities hark back to the good days of Total War, whilst the Stronghold-like maps are utilised well to create interesting battle scenarios. However, the aforementioned lag makes utilising a large-scale army near impossible and the clicks needed to fight most effectively simply cannot be dished out. Furthermore, the movement is basic at best, with units sometimes not moving to where you want to go at the right times. This can be especially annoying when it means losing half your army to someone pouring pitch over them or them walking into spike traps. What remains though is potential - with optimisation and bug fixes the unit system will be enjoyable. Conditional recommendation. Get it once this is better.
Buildings/Economy: The economy system works well. Things are well priced and utilised well, with clear diversity between the races (more on this later). There is a mechanic called "trickle" where you get small-scale income from various buildings/units, whilst gatherers bring in large-scale resources. This provides a multi-tiered system whereby you can manage the short and long term economic needs of your settlement. Furthermore, the design of the buildings is clearly different for all three and provides more clear strategic diversity, with the settlement sieges being truly compelling and enjoyable at the later stages of the game. What's wrong then? Well, the game pre-sets where your walls are going to go, so you don't construct your own elaborate fortifications and they will be the same each time, with the same set-up, regardless of map. This means that in terms of defense, it can get quite samey. Furthermore, for all races but the elves, the ability to snipe resource points from outside the walls can make defending in the long-term impossible.  More needs to be done to ensure fortresses fall and aren't merely starved out in a 2 hour long staring extravangaza. Again though, there is plenty of potential for this to develop as the game goes on.
Other: The races provide good strategic diversity in terms of their late game potential and ability but the cards and tech development is a bit of a sham. For a lot of the cards and techs, they do exactly the same thing but are just reskinned. I can't see this improving.
TL/DR: Poor multiplayer. Broken campaign. Fun as hell mechanics though and plenty of potential. Put this on your wishlist and keep a lookout for improvements.

HESITANT recommendation; Edit at end
You're sitting across from a man with the facial features of an aged Arabian belly-dancer but with the voice of a sophisticated Atheist.
He do fancy floating card tricks. You do choice, luck and basic Arkham-esque combat.
He do menacing. You do persevering.
The Cabinet - the resting place (either dead or in-wait) of Dealer's lieutenants (as it were) - is pretty sizeable with 12 steps towards besting him.
You have Gold, which you can use to buy new Equipment (should you luck out and land on a Merchant) and Food, which you expend one of with every move - heal yourself for a certain amount with each meal.
The random encounters range from a disgruntled wife who needs you to fetch her drunk husband, to a priest asking for charity, to a wounded soldier asking for aid in hunting down his assailants, to an arena with multiple stages, to a devil you can gamble with, to goblins who attempt to steal your loot, to a trap-filled labyrinth... my "Deck Progress" bar isn't a third of the way filled.
The combat is very simple but also quite satisfying; though it mimicks the Batman games, it isn't quite as refined or fast-paced. On controller: X to attack, A to dodge-roll, B to stun (shield-bash), Y to parry (only with a shield) - LB for weapon ability, RB for Artefact.
Your priority is always to get a shield. I had good luck consecutively in obtaining one from the goblin dressed as a man ("Mister Lionel"?); ask him what he wants: Why to help you my boy! Here's a shield!
Once you have a shield, you will get the... iconic (and epic and emotional and cinematic and *buzz-word*) prompts above your head when an attack is about to connect. Best not to button-mash, though HoF is much more flexible in this regard than Arkham is.
The majority of the game is in playing across from the Dealer; the combat sequences never last as long as they should.
My hope for the game:
More extra Cards (read "Decks") added to the game than I could hope to go through.
A mode released later down the line that would allow more of a focus on the third-person action. Maybe not a full campaign, but just the most basic of stringing together the different arenas, with the ability to use any equipment you've previously unlocked, to versus any creature you've previously fought: The most extended Training mode / wave-based survival thing ever... *faints from awesomeness*
The Dealer could be giving voice-overs every now and then, either playing the role of Dungeon Master (more... impactfully(?)) or giving exposition on his past (if it's not further explained later in the game)... so... I guess, yeah, another campaign...
Regarding the game as is, the only faults I have:
The highlighted card isn't always the next face-down one; is the one you just left more often than I'd like. Of course, rage needs to be accounted for in a game (")so based on luck("); in such moments, I'll just spam A to get to the next card, only to exacerbate my anger by inadvertently wasting one (actually two) Food.
The Succeed or Fail challenges; four or five cards shown you, turned face-down, shuffled into one deck (one or two times) in such a way that you can hardly discern. It can easily be argued that we're given a better chance at picking a good card than would be given us IRL, but, with the way this mechanic is presented, I was hoping for more of a "Find the ball in one of these cups," something feasibly able to be beaten (as the Dealer admits that he (")doesn't cheat(")).
There is an Endless Mode in which you have a better chance of unlocking more cards to put into your decks for the Campaings. Upon selecting your target (one of those twelve lieutenants), you can then build your deck. New cards have unknown effects until drawn in the game, so you've several playthroughs ahead of you, aimed at simply identifying all the cards, for to build the best deck for your golden runs.
I absolutely recommend this game and have little doubt it's worth full price. My one bit of hesitation (as applied to all games that aren't open-world sandboxes (i.e. Just Cause 2)) is in how much repetition there is in the text events, in the limited pool of cards and arenas.
EDIT: With (I assume) the game being completely finished (since the sequel is soon to drop), I must say that my absolute recommendation is strained now. SO many of the new cards are extremely archaic in the how you must go about besting them. When I wrote this review, the game was much more reliant on skill, though of course luck(/your perception) was almost as big a part; now, without the aid of walkthroughs, the task of completely beating the game is a ridiculously daunting task. One example of this is when you get lost in the desert and must pick from the four cardinal directions at least four seperate times, in the hope of finding what you're after. Another card actually necessitates that you Fail the first check and Succeed the second. At least five cards seem to be designed solely with the Iron Hunger player character in mind, going so far as to have no (good) effect on ANY other player character that lands on those cards. I still have so much love for the game but there is no denying that the amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t present herein is something to beware of. I don't really enjoy my time while playing any more but am compelled to - progress is a stupid grind, strategy is up to fate, even if you are able to keep up with the shuffles and pick the "right" card each time, there is no telling if that will actually be correct according to the devs apparent "♥♥♥♥-you-lol" mentality (it would be fun, if the game wasn't such a chore to play in situations where you are doing well and two bad hands can kill you) and so much of the game actually plays itself. Without the third-person combat which many seem to dislike, I argue the game would have little substance.

I bought this game with a 90% off discount, which probably seemed quite worthwhile at the time, when the price was something like $30, rather than being free. In retrospect, installing this game for free wouldn't be worth it.
The gameplay itself is an okay matching tile drop thing. You get given blocks of two (or three in some game modes?) symbols, alchemical rune-y things, to drop from the top of the screen wherever you want. Whenever three or more of these matching... sigils?... touch one another, they combine to the next sigil up- the coins become leaves, the leaves become blue illuminati symbols, they become orange magma rhombuses, and so on, as you... alchemically combine these elements into more exotic forms, or something?
The trouble with this is that, logistically speaking, every successful match of three removes two pieces from the board- and every move the player makes ADDS two pieces to the board. Therefore, the player has to make one match every turn to whittle down the board at all. Sure, you can technically match a larger group than three, or make some sort of chain/combo, but in practice, it's a losing battle. Every time you combine pieces, the new piece you created starts to appear in the blocks you get given to drop in. Because the board is only six spaces across, this quickly becomes unmanageable- after around the eighth rune shows up, your ability to progress further is almost entirely down to random chance. It's sort of like, well, 2048? Except in 2048, only the two lowest value pieces are added to the board at a time, whereas in this, wham, suddenly a 256 drops on you out of nowhere.
Surrounding this core mechanic are several different game modes. Unfortunately, most of them are basically the same. The worst mode is "Infinity Mode", because it's just the vanilla game- every time you would lose, it erases the bottom two layers of the screen so you can carry on. There is no end goal and no way of losing, just a meaningless score counter that measures your persistence more than any actual aptitude for the game. "Chaos Mode" is better, because it gives you special pieces which can be used to erase parts of the board (why don't these turn up in Infinity Mode?) and actually has a way for you to lose. "Puzzle Mode" is infuriating, as solving the puzzles requires on foreknowledge you don't seem to be provided with on the first run, as well as suppressing the instincts you used for the other game modes, and understanding the seemingly random behaviour of, say, where the final piece ends up when you combine a flat row of four. Very few of the mechanics of the game are actually clearly explained to you anywhere. "Abyss Mode" is barely distinguishable from the other modes- apparently it's just a game where there's a pre-determined random selection of pieces available to you rather than an individually generated set. Whoopee.
There are also somewhere between two and a dozen other game modes and options that are greyed out on the menu. Bear in mind that this game was released three years ago. Don't get your hopes up for them to be added to the game any time soon.
Also important to note- the music. Each of the currently available, grindy modes, has a single background track- a twangy, mysterious forest sound with faint woodland drums and echoes. This is the most hellish part of the experience. Shortly after playing the game for the first time, I knew I would want to uninstall it- it just wasn't very fun, and my hard drive space is at a premium. So, naturally, I felt- "Oh well! Guess I'll just farm the rest of the cards and have done with it!" This was a mistake. The pennies of value in those trading cards are not worth the hours I have had to spend listening to that mysterious forest music as my computer refused to tab away from or minimise the running game. Faeverse Alchemy has one of the stingiest trading card drop rates of any game I've played.
For the record, Faerie Solitaire, which is set in some sort of shared universe with this game (but since FvA plays completely differently and has literally no story or characters, I'm not sure why), is actually much better.

Owlboy left me wanting more.
I was extremely excited to play Owlboy, and was really looking forward to what the game offered after the demo/first area I had seen on previews before.  A game this long in the making that has so much love put into it, with bright art, compelling characters, and good music too?  Sign me up.
The game pulled inspiration in its mechanics from many other games I've definitely enjoyed.  It's hard for me to say there's anything "bad" about these elements or their execution.
What Owlboy failed to do, for me, was combine the elements to make something unique or interesting, all the while being too short to make use of its by far strongest features; its art, music, and characters.
Ultimately, I ended up with a game that felt like I was simply going through the motions.  Everything is serviceable, but nothing grand.
Because of this, while I can't call the game bad, I also can't reccommend it if you're looking for the same things I am in a game like this.  I'm a huge player of RPGs, I love metroidvanias, Cave Story and Ori are wonderful action platformers that I can get lost in time and time again, and of course I'm always up for whatever twist Nintendo's been putting on their platformers.  Meawhile, the Ys series of Action/Adventure RPGs really works for combat/bosses even though its stories and characters are rather basic.  I have grander story RPGs to fall back on for a compelling story with developed ensemble casts.  If we want to talk about twinstick action gunning, I'll pull out my Genesis and take out Gunstar Heroes.  Close enough.
If you feel you may fall into a similar category, given those quick examples, feel free to read my following thoughts on Owlboy:
-The controls work fine, for the most part, as a 360 controller user, but there are times where your hands need to press multiple things at once, and the buttons needed are all over the face of the controller.  Having to keep a thumb on a second analog stick, an index finger on face buttons, and be ready for all shoulder buttons was probably the cause of this for me.  It didn't cause any significant problems, but felt like they could have been better, and more crisp (Compare to something like Ori and the Blind Forest)
- The combat is very straightforward and very easy.  Something like Cave Story has much more intense fighting sequences, especially on the boss front.  Look into something like Ys that is straight up -made- for its boss fights, and the combat here pales in comparison.  I found the earlier fights more interesting than the latter ones, but it's still not saying much.
- The stealth sequences that augment the combat I personally didn't find enjoyable.  Lots of waiting, and they never really evolved behind "Stay behind cover while enemies move around."  Even with checkpoints after every successful segment, the waiting involved in redoing stealth areas I found tedious.  They were easy, just tedious.
- The puzzles are basic at best.  I'd almost argue there's more to puzzles in Namco's Tales Of series, but that's about the quality I got out of Owlboy's.
- Exploration is not anywhere near as rewarding as a more common metroidvania.  For one, there's very little of it.  This game's world is -small- and most exploration simply leads to a checklist of coins for a relatively unrewarding upgrade system, and it didn't take much effort at all to get "all those upgrades minus the 100% one."  What exploration did exist didn't really feel like it tested skills so much as it tested ability to poke at every wall.  Missing were sections requiring you to execute some cute little tricks to obtain the reward (Platforming, basically).  Entirely missing are *fun* upgrades scattered throughout the game that increase your ability to navigate or perform.  The upgrades obtained through collecting are more akin to stat bonuses, not really changing how everything is approached.  Given, I didn't get the 100% upgrade, so who knows - maybe it's the most amazing thing.
- The dungeons, where you'll spend the vast majority of the time, overstay their welcome a little bit for me, and are quite linear when all is said and done.  I would have preferred dungeons being a bit more compact and getting 1-2 more total areas as a result.
- The art in this game is -very- good, the sprites are detailed, emotional, and the backgrounds are pretty full of life and color, given the art direction of the game.  This is one of the game's strong points, for sure.
- Likewise, some of the music is fantastic too.  My bigger issue with the music is most of the pieces loved are not heard very often, as the game spends most of its time in dungeons with more of an ambience approach opposed to melodic themes you'd hear in every area of a Metroid, or Castlevania, or Cave Story.
- The story and characters are good, but they don't get a time to shine, as everything starts quickly and ends quickly.  These things were very hyped up from many sources, especially considering the main character's status as a literal mute, but ultimately very little was expanded on.  There were many moments of charm, but they passed very quickly, so we could go right back into another linear dungeon.  You may have heard that characters don't do the whole "It's okay, we got this, power of friendship, ACTIVATE!" thing, and the events that happen in the story stick with them.  That's true (to an extent - the friendship-power-buddies thing is still there somewhat), but the weight of the actions upon the characters is never really felt, as there's simply not enough time that passes or dialogue to help facilitate the gravity of everything that's going on.  A short game is not a bad thing, but the other elements must be engaging enough, and in this case, the other aspects of the game simply didn't make up for the lack of time in this story.
Owlboy has a few visual moments that are pretty stunning and awesome, but unfortunately it's almost impossible for me not to compare them to Ori's, which I'd say end up superior in both artistic direction and musical composition.  There's certainly one sequence in Owlboy that completely rocks, though.
If you've stuck with me, I thank you for your time.
At the end of the day, I didn't find myself curious to keep playing, and I just wanted to get it over with so I could see the payoff everyone said I'd get with the characters/story (Again, it ended up serviceable).  The gameplay elements are there, and they work, but I've played so many other games that do each of Owlboy's elements better.  While Owlboy brings them all together, each element ended up mediocre, giving me a very mediocre feeling at the end of this journey, which is a good bit shorter than I had hoped for.
Best of luck to you if you give the game a shot, though I'd personally suggest waiting on a bigger sale - I hope you find it more fun and rewarding than I did.  It's clear many people are enjoying it, and I'm just one person.  Again, thanks for your time.

I've played 25 hours at the time of writing this review. My character just reached level 60.
First of all, don't let the people saying this game is P2W stop you from trying it. Yes, it is SLIGHTLY p2w but only at the top tiers of PVP. Far as a casual PVE game goes, Elsword is just wonderful. The main thing people complain about is the costumes, but from what I can tell so far the buffs they give are not that significant. I've had no trouble finding good sets of equipment to dress up my character with. I even choose not to wear the promotional costumes because I think my character looks cooler with just equipment on.
Since I'm only level 60 so far I haven't really delved into PVP. But I have been looking into how you can upgrade your equipment, what you can grind for, etc. I really like what I've seen, there is a nice variety of equipment, if you just do quests you'll never feel like you need to grind or like you need better gear. A lot of the time I find an awesome set of equipment, only to find another set with better stats a few minutes later that I am reluctant to equip because it doesn't look as cool. The best part is, the advanced sets of equipment have set bonuses.
The game is very generous as far as f2p games go. There is a stamina system, so you can't run dungeons when your stamina runs out, but this resets every day, and if you get a group of players you will barely use any stamina in dungeons. You can easily get free stamina potions though through quests or exchanging hero coins for them. You can also grind a bit to get costumes for free. Quests give you boxes with whole sets of advanced equipment, with sweet set bonuses. You can craft healing items, and quests give plenty of them to you for free. You also get 10 resurrection stones per day, which are basically extra lives in case you die. You can buy more, but I've never used all 10 in a day, even when playing the hardest dungeons for my level, on the hardest difficulty, while undergeared, solo.
The community seems to be very friendly, I was invited to a guild that offers me free stuff (which I don't take because I'm independent) and I always feel welcome in dungeon runs, even when I'm with veteran players who are a lot better than me. Higher level players have no problem steamrolling dungeons and bosses for you, in fact most of them just enjoy showing off their characters. The only negative thing I can say about the community is that I saw a bot one time advertising in a village.
The story isn't that compelling in my opinion. I just skip through all the cut scenes at this point, I play this game for the game play. If you're the type of person who enjoys side scrolling action/combat, and customizing your character, you'll probably enjoy this game. It's free, fun, and simply gorgeous.

This is easily the best shop sim RPG I have ever played. Equip various adventurers with gear you find while dungeon crawling, exploring each floor for loot to use and sell from the store you have to run to pay back your father's debts. The combat is your standard action rpg layout, with a boss at the end of each dungeon. There are a lot of dungeons to explore and many different creatures to fight that will come at you with different strategies as the game goes on.
The game has plenty of rare loot and cool treasures to find, as well as an item fusion system. You will be able to sell these items both to villagers and the adventurers you hire to explore the dungeons. If they buy the gear it will replace their base equipment. The villagers will haggle with you over "hot and cold" items that change all the time. Each week you need to sell enough stuff to pay back a debt, for whatever reasons the payments keep getting bigger until you finally pay the debt.
As you are working to pay off the debt you will be able to spend some money on upgrading the shop as well, this ranges from making more money to just general appearance stuff. After you have paid the debt you will be able to continue and grow your shop, explore a short bonus story, and some extra dungeons. There is a lot of fun to be had here, and it's definitely worth a try.

Best RPG I've ever played. Doesn't hold your hand with dozens of quest markers and hints, but instead gives you the tools you need and tells you to do it your own way. Every quest and objective can be completed in numerous ways. Every character can be killed, even plot-relevant characters and companions and you'll have to live with the consequences. If you're into roleplaying, the entire world reacts to you differently depending on your race (human, elf, lizard, dwarf, undead), your background (decided by "tags" you choose on char creation), the things you've done, the people you associate with, etc. etc. etc. If you play as one of the "origin characters" (pre-made characters with defined backgrounds and appearances), you'll have even more role-play potential in unique dialogue and questlines. Origin characters can also be recruited as companions.
Combat is turn-based and quite difficult, even on normal, but this forces you to strategize.There is an easy mode, and it's perfect for those bad at RPG's or just in it for the story. But it''s very satisfying watching your party grow in strength and obliterate enemies who once gave you trouble. Overall, if you have any interest in RPG's, games with deep storylines, or roleplaying, do yourself a favor and buy this. The CRPG genre is most certainly alive and well.

Archeage was officialy out for 4-5 years, except not international. A game with that much time for development sure is further in its content when introduced to the world. Sadly Archeage isnt, thought as an MMO its still unique in its system regarding gameplay, economy, player housing and etc. Its an MMO where you would truely waste...ehem... i mean... truely spend hours and time exploring and farming around, though its grindy just like every MMO out there is. The problem with Archeage tho is that, its not ment for people who are busy cause its time consuming. dont get me wrong, its fun, but the fun can be eleminated when you just get on to do your daily stuff if you have patreon and then back off because you dont have time.
You can buy gametime with ingame currency and making money through Action house like very other MMO and or another unique thing called going on Trade runs. "This Early Access game is not complete and may or may not change further. If you are not excited to play this game in its current state, then you should wait to see if the game progresses further in development."
It's the year 2017 and a lot of people still don't understand the meaning of early access. Maybe some people are bitter because of previous EA games on Steam. Conan has been out for a few days and people are already complainnig about stuff that is obviously on their roadmap. So far the developer has pushed out several patches adressing the most urgent issues.
Now, to the review part. I have been playing with my friends on our own dedicated server, so I cannot speak for public servers. We have had a blast so far. The game might be one of the best Early Access titles that offer so much after launch.  The standard settings might appear to be too grindy, but having an own server you can adjust the settings (we put the XP gain to 2x and the yield to 2x. The yield was necessary because we are 8 people now and repairing requires a lot of materials.).
The wildlife is ruthless and if you are not careful, you will be killed very quickly.
The building system is pretty solid. There are a few issues that needs to be adressed such as snapping of roofs. It is however already a lot of fun to build stuff because it feels very natural.
Different weapons feels different.
The Thralls system is pretty basic as of right now but the joy of finally finding a blacksmith is amazing.
What surprised us the most is that there is so much to discover already. Quite a lot of hiden lore which adds to the atmosphere.
I will update the review accordingly but so far, if you have the chance to play with friends on your own server, the game gets a definite yes from me. I cannot speak for public servers as I have not played on them yet.
It's good. Buy it.

One thing i didnt liked, is that if you dont go fully "good guy" or fully "bad guy" you will get in trouble later on, as specific dialog is not available.

Wish i could recommend it, but it controls like a pregnant cow on rollerblades. I got the game, because it looks pretty much like an amped up version of Final Fantasy Tactics. There are quite a few interesting mechanics in the game, such as the ability to level up individual enemies by throwing them into other enemies, or a character creation system, by which you select a mentor for the new created hero.
But as much as i want to like this game, i really can't stand the fact that i have to fight the controls more than the NPCs. I tried mouse and keyboard (well mostly keyboard) and i tried a controller, both just don't work right. And while i usually would ♥♥♥♥♥ about it controlling like a RPG from the early 2000... this is exactly what this game is. A game from 2003 and it controls like that. So if you want a journey back in time, and find out what it was like to fight the controls of a game, instead of actually having them not be in the way, this game is for you.
For everyone that thought the Developer would have actually bothered to update the control scheme for their 2016 PC release.. think again. As it stands, i can't recommend the game, because the game actively gets in the way of the game itself.

From its artwork, to its music, to its atmosphere, to its story, to its characters and their interactions, Owlboy is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played.  I didn't want it to end.  As clever, fun, and full of surprises as the main adventure is, perhaps the moments I treasure the most are moments that were entirely optional to the completion of the game.
My dislikes are few and minor.  There are some startling, frustrating difficulty spikes at times.  I had to backtrack through every area in the game hugging every wall and defeating every enemy to obtain all the coins for Buccanary's shop, and even then, there were things that I missed and secrets that were perhaps a bit *too* well-hidden.  But I can forgive this, partly because the coins and secrets are optional, and partly because scouring every inch of the game to find them allowed me to spend more time in its tranquil, rich, whimsical world.
Few games have as much heart visibly poured into every detail as Owlboy, and I'd recommend it to anyone.

I have come across intersections that are single lane turning onto a 4 lane highway. I literally sat there for 10 minutes waiting to turn. Not one jerk would let me in. Very realistic. I eventually just saved it and reloaded so that there was no traffic.

This game is absolutley the greatest in terms of being a 2D adventure game. The pixel graphics is a joy to look at because of the scenery is beautiful, the level designs were put into so much thought, the soundtrack is perfect with each scenario that is playing out, and the character's look can be clearly told in order to display what emotions they are feeling. The controls were simple and easy to control and the combat can be challenging. There were a lot of enemy variety that lets you use different weapons to counter them and puzzles that can be either a breeze to go through or a challenge that makes you think at one point. The story can be a hit or miss for some people but I enjoy the story thoroughly except the ending was a little disappointing in my opinion (I will get back to this). The characters were well thought out and the main character Otus is a joy to watch even though he doesn't talk at all. The ending really did not put the grand finale that I wanted it to be. Sure there is collectables that might unlock another ending (I'm not sure if this information is right or not), but if that is the case they need to have a resolution for the story and the characters you just encountered after the credits roll. I felt the ending did not provide a resolution but instead more questions for the main characters. The pricing might make people suspicious of the game but after playing 12 hours  with fun gameplay and interesting storytelling, I think it is worth it.
The gameplay is solid, the soundtrack is beautiful, the graphics is breathtaking, and the story is interesting up until the last act which takes off a point in my review. I would rate the game a 9/10. Anyone who loves 2D pixel graphics game should experience this game.

I am a big RTS fan, and this game is pretty revolutionary when it comes to the zombie mechanic. (You can turn off the zombies if you don't like them.) The game is basically any other Medieval RTS title, but has zombies! You fortify your castle and upgrade units and structures, there's a whole crafting system in this game, which is weird, but kinda cool. For most new players, like myself it took a few games to realize that I had to craft upgrades from the main menu to actually use them in game. But once I figured it out, the game really came to life.
Basically how it works: You play campaign/multiplayer/singleplayer vs AI. Once you have played a few games, you will get these special resources, now I don't know how to actually acquire them, but it seems like the more games you play, the more you get. Anyway so once you have these resources you can craft certain upgrades that can be used in game. (For the Humans, Halberdier for example.) And after you craft the upgrade you can use it in game. Pretty cool stuff.
All in all this game is pretty awesome. I mean it needs some more refining, and at random times may crash. (Save Often!!!!) It'll get framy and just gucky, so be prepared to have it crash, also sometimes your units won't respond to orders, I've noticed if you stop moving the screen and click it usually works. lol other than that this game is a diamond in the rough, totally worth the money if you wanna support the devs. It's really fun in the state that it's in. One of the best FPS games of all time. If you are tired of boring corridor linear shooters where enemies are just a nuisance to get rid of to continue the story, this is the game for you. Enemies feel real and are actual real threats because they can kill you as easily as you can kill them. And the decision to kill them is not so clear as most of the time you are lacking bullets, want to attempt stealth, or realize that enemies may not be so "bad" as you sneak up and listen to them talk. On the same hand, there are enemies that are pure evil in this game, and it's your choice what you do with them and how you shape your ending.
I would compare this game to Dark souls: Half of the journey in both game series is getting towards the next story point. Some games like COD you just play through levels as fast as possible to reach the next cutscene. In Metro, the journey is just as important as the next areas you reach. The sense of isolation and fear, and anxiety for the next checkpoint. And when you hear a voice down the dark corridor you feel a sense of relief and hope it's a friendly.
Overall, Metro Last Light should be played after Metro 2033, but if you do only play this it won't harm the game much. The game is simply brilliant and feels alive even when there is no life in sight as it's an apocalypse, because the few life forms in the game were carefully created.
The greatest part of Metro is immersion. Graphics are absolutely stunning and better than 99% of AAA games released this year due to the Redux, you can play any style you want and change the ending, the sound quality is brilliant and you are constantly in fear of what you hear, and lastly the thrill and horror of seeing monsters makes an easy emotional response so it's almost impossible to not be in the game. And sometimes, there are even tricks the game makes to psychologically trick you, which was the most scary part for me. Another thing the game does is allowing you to remove all HUDs and make ammo scarce. This was the best thing ever for me. There is no minimap, to tell if you have ammo you have to examine your gun, to see objective you have to physically open your map which doesn't pause the game. And you must try to avoid all gunfights and scavenge as much as possible. This increases difficulty and I was scared to do it, but once again half of Metro is in the way you play. It isn't just about hearing you are in an apocalyptic world, but playing like you are in one.
(wrote this all fast but i feel it's a good summary of what I feel)
10/10 if you played Metro 2033 and enjoyed it, 9/10 easily if you haven't played Metro 2033.

I now have 26 hrs on record in this game, here are my 2 cents.
The game definitely has it's attraction. The strong points are the very entertaining building system, which let's you create mountain fortresses and giant castles, as well as the thrall mechanics, which allow you to capture npcs and use them as guards and assistent crafters (not gatherers currently) in your base.
The graphics overall are nice enough, there is a beautiful day/night cycle and the landscape has a nice wilderness vibe to it.
I'm mostly a builder/crafter/explorer and I enjoy trading with people and fighting npcs, so I played on a pve server and cannot comment on the quality of pvp.
Now to the ugly side - oh  boy :(
This game is exactly how Early Access should not be used. In the Steam Agreement EA is described as access to an ongoing Alpha/Beta development process, which adds features and gameplay, while the community should help with balancing and ideas.
To me this means that the developers should deliver a stable foundation on which to build upon and currently this is not the case with this game. There are several game-breaking bugs and while the developers are releasing patches at a very high interval each patch that fixes one thing breaks another thing, as if several people just added random bits to each patch without proper quality control or changelogs.
The worst part is server stability. As of today several official servers are down for over 20 hours. Some of them are crashing constantly, others are not even responding anymore and from what I read on the forums the cause is a data corruption problem which the developers cannot figure out. The affected servers keep crashing and are inaccessible to the players. In a builder game, this is simply a no-go, because once you dump a certain amount of time into your character and housing, you simply do not want to start over on a fresh server and re-do everything.
I enjoy the concept of Early Access, but as I said before, a game needs a stable core and foundation to expand upon and this is currently not the case with Conan Exiles.
Combat is also not much to write home about, it's mostly about having better armor and whacking your opponent over the head, hoping that your gear and health pool outlasts theirs. Except for a very rudimentary dodge/block mechanic there is very little here.
There is also a long list of stretch goals promising various features and improvements, but considering their netcode and server stability I don't see them adding new content any time soon.
My recommendation: wait 1-3 months before buying and watch the development process. It's a Funcom game, in the past they had good concepts like in Age of Conan and Secret World, but the studio always felt a bit brittle on the technical side and this also shows in Conan Exiles.

Good game, solid storyline with good choice mechanics. Definitely feels like a Mass Effect game.
Pros:
- Interesting story, decent-to-good plot twists.
- Combat mechanics are much better that ME1.
- Insanity feels more challenging but not just because enemies have billions of health like in ME1.
- Choices matter quite a lot; even minute choices from ME1 will carry over to have an effect in this game and in ME3.
- Character development is very good. And the closure in ME3 will be satisfactory, particularly if you get the Citadel DLC.
- Special effects are very nice; superior to ME1.
- DLC is actually pretty awesome and worthwhile. Which is saying something. In order, my favorites were: The Shadow Broker, Arrival, Kasumi - The Stolen Memory, Zaeed - The Price of Revenge, Project Overlord, Hammerhead. In particular, the Shadow Broker and the Arrival not only have fantastic plots but really help set up ME3's introduction so that it is better than it otherwise will be. Kasumi and Zaeed make for interesting characters and Kasumi is overpowered. They also play roles in ME3.
Cons:
- Your character still can't dodge and switching between cover is more difficult than it feels like it should be, meaning you still kind of feel like a walking brick wall.
- Certain parts of the plot feel like bad fan fiction. In my opinion, the last boss is a dumb idea and should have been redacted from the game.
- The game gives interesting hints about the potential endgame and large-scale plan of the enemy, but most of these are retconned or simply omitted by ME3.
- Story quality is dwarfed by ME1. The event at the beginning of the game felt unnecessary but it was certainly interesting and sets up interesting parallels for Shepard.
- If you didn't do a completionist playthrough, one of the major organizations in the game will feel like a complete fabrication. It's not, but its existence was buried in the repetitive side missions of ME1.
All in all, flawed, but only really in comparison to ME1 or in light of some of the greater failures of ME3. It's a fantastic game. Definitely worth a playthrough if space operas and RPG/third-person shooter games are your thing.

Hand of Fate is perfect for fans of card games, deck-building, and role-playing games.   Questlines are randomly generated from a mix of cards owned by both you and the dealer.  Playing through the game rewards you with more cards to add into your decks.  While in a quest, you need to manage your health, money, and food.  You will encounter enemies, allies, and obstacles in your quests and they're always presented to you with choices similar to FTL: Faster than Light.
There's also an element of chance that goes along with your decisions.  An example could be that you're walking along a cliff, and you see a sword at the bottom among some bones.  Do you go on your way or try and climb down? If you try to climb down, you then have to watch four cards, with varying degrees of success or failure on them, be shuffled on-screen.  You pick your card and either get injured on your climb down, or succeed and get the sword (which you can then use in combat).  Combat encounters throw you into a room with enemies and the game turns into a simple version of the Arkham Batman games. The fighting is very similar with it's use of blocking, countering, and combos.
As of the writing of this review, the game is currently 50% off! It's still worth the purchase at full-price though.

Disgaea PC is a port of the original disgaea released on the PS2 on January 30th, 2003. Thirteen years later how does it hold up today? While the story and characters still hold well today, the gameplay isn't the best a turn-based strategy game has to offer.
The story is about a demon prince on a quest to take his fathers place as overlord of the Netherworld after his rather pathetic death. The story is great, but the best thing about it is the overall charming and lovable cast of characters i tended to grow really fond of. Even the highly annoying main character never made me lose my mind, since seeing him fail at times always makes my day. They're filled with such silly and over the top personalities that keeps me connected to the game, which is something not a whole lot of strategy games do for me. (btw Flonne is my waifu i call dibs on her)
While the story and characters still hold well in my opinion, the gameplay however, while not terrible, isn't the most thrilling either. I'll get to that in a bit.
Like I said before it's a turn-based strategy game. You choose a character, move him around a few spaces, can order him to attack, cast spells or use items on himself or other teammates to either heal or buff them untill every character runs out of turns so that the enemy can do the same. The enemie's turns are rather quick so it never slows down the gameplay, but what may slow you down is moving the mouse coursor around trying to click on anything since the in game mouse it uses overlaps very poorly with the game, making it feel very cumbersome to control. I highly recommend using a controller of any kind to play it, it will make your experiance with the game feel a whole lot better. Anyway back to the gameplay. A rather unique mechanic in disgaea is the lifting system, where characters can lift and throw teammates so they can reach places they can't. The lifting system is rather unique as this can be used not only to help teammates reach impossible to reach places, but also to get enemies to back off or hold them for the rest of the turn so they can't attack, but doing this will cause your character to take damage while holding them, creating a feeling of risk vs reward. You can also pick up and throw geo symbols on panels to use to your advantage. Speaking of geo symbols, these are special symbols that give special colored panels different effects on any character who stands on them and ends they're turn. These effects can range from taking damage, one-shot kills, extra experiance, invincibility, tougher enemies, warping towards different locations, or cloneing a character and making them an enemy. These add the best amount of flavor you can add on a strategy game, and even better, the level design makes good use of them, making a lot of the levels feel somewhat creative. But even more creative is something that's kind of a series staple: the item worlds. Each and every item in the game has it's own wave of randomly generated levels that the player can either fight through for special rewards, or skip through by landing a character on a special panel that progresses the player to the next randomly generated level. If it wasn't for this, no matter how good the characters and story was, the game would be completely ruined by one word: grinding.
The game does not do a good job of balancing it's difficulty, making the game really grindheavy. I started out with two of the three main characters of the game, and 3 prinnies which are the weakest monsters of the game, and explode if they are thrown. Later on you can recruit much stronger characters for your team, but they all start of weak, and at level 1, so your still gonna be grinding. It could be a bit more enjoyable if the item worlds had anything unique in them, but the only thing you do in there is fight monsters, go to the next level, fight more monsters, and do the exact same thing again and complete the 10th stage so you can leave, or use a special item to do so. It get's rather tiring and a bit boring, but it's certainly way better than beating the same stage over and over again until your characters are finally strong enough to progress through the 48 1/2 hour campain.
Overall if your a huge fan of the disgaea series and you wanna give this game a go, or if you just want the game and the genuine tf2 cosmetics that comes with it, then i'd say it's worth the 15 dollar pricetag. But if you have not played disgaea and wanna give this series a try, I would start off with the second game. The animations are better, the difficulty is treated a bit better, the characters are just as memorable and the item world is vastley improved. But if you really want to get to know the characters in the first game, then if i were you, i would watch the anime.

I decided to edit my review to add a thing or two I missed before after I grinded out all of the achievements for the game.
Many people will call this a Bejeweled rip-off, but it's actually more of a Puyo Pop clone, with a slight twist in gameplay mechanics.  In Puyo Pop, you drop different colored blocks into the board, and try to match them up in sets of 4 or more to keep the board from filling up all the way.  In this game, the way it works is that you match like sets of 3, and for each matched set, instead of destroying blocks, they build up into a higher level block.  So, for instance, you match 3 green blocks in a row which spawns a yellow block; if you match 3 of those, you spawn a red block, and so on.  The field does get cleared up to an extent as the 3 or more blocks decrease down to 1, yet the board will never be empty after you've placed your first block.
The main issue I have with the gameplay is that as you progress into higher levels of blocks, you'll still receive low level blocks you have to incorporate and work with.  Admittedly, that's where the challenge and strategy comes in, as well as the potential for chains, as setting off one set could net you the next level of block needed to set off the next one and so forth.  However, once you get to 7 or 8 levels of blocks it becomes incredibly challenging, and there's almost nothing that mitigates this difficulty.  At no point do you remove the lowest level once you reach a certain point (and you'll come to hate getting those low level garbage blocks late game), and because the blocks don't go away in the normal sense there's only so much you can do to stave off the inevitable end of the round.
One factor that turns me off to this game I didn't mention the first time was that there are power-ups, but at no point is there any explanation as to what they are, what they do, or how you get them.  You'll just randomly get a power-up, you'll drop it onto a block, and something will happen.  Over time you might learn what a power-up does, but there are still some that I don't understand what they're supposed to do.  There was a glitch/programming error I noticed with the power-ups as well.  Normally when you get one it shows up at the top of the screen like any other block you're about to drop.  However, at times when I went to drop my normal blocks it would just change into a power-up and activate instead.  I also noticed that some rounds that I played, of the exact same mode, I would be dropping block clusters made up entirely of three pieces instead of the normal two and I have no idea why.  This apparantly is a game the developers gave up on half-way (as evidenced by the achievements and unfinished menu screen), and it shows in these simple programming oddities.
I can appreciate that the game goes for a long-term puzzling mindset, instead of a quick reflex Tetris-style puzzle game, but there isn't enough to make me want to keep coming back to this game.  Tetris, Puyo Pop, and Bejeweled all work so well because there's a limit to the number of block types you have to work with, but here it grows beyond what's reasonable for people to manage.  Without anything to mix it up or change what it is I'm doing, and being essentially punished for making progress because I have yet another block type to manage, I have no incentive to keep plugging away.  I can't recommend it, but it's free, so it's worth a quick download and try to see if you like it more than I did.
Don't get me wrong, it sucks, but it is kinda fun and charming.

American Truck Simulator is more of a re-skin of ETS2 but with added detail. People who've played ETS2 will pretty much recognise what they're doing and where to find things due to the game being made using the same engine. If you're new to the Truck Simulator franchise however, you'll find that this game is actually quite fun. The environments are beautiful, the cities are very big and there's a huge variety of roads such as ones that are long and narrow and ones that are more difficult to navigate. If you've played ETS2, I'd say wait till this game is on sale. If you're a newcomer, well worth your money!
All of my reviews are laid out in a particular format that fits the game.
American Truck Simulator [ATS] is a spin off to the popular game, Euro Truck Simulator 2 [ETS2]. Just like the title says, you'll be driving around two of America's states, California and Nevada, in a truck. Since ATS was made using the same engine as ETS2, there are a lot of similarities, most notabley the UI. Just like It's previous games, in ATS you start a company in which you make deliveries for other people to earn money. The more money you get, the more you can upgrade your warehouse, and get drivers to work for you. That's basically it.
Again, gameplay for this game is a lot like ETS2. If you've played ETS2, then this game shouldn't be difficult for you at all. If you haven't played ETS2, It's not hard to get into basics. There are differnet modes for controls, some which are more difficult than others. Just like ETS2, there are radio stations where you can listen to music, you can customize your truck by adding different paint jobs, there are different camera views to view your truck from different angles and have the basis of any other vehicle such as headlights, indicators, windscreen wipers and a horn.
But as I mentioned before there is added detail to ATS. One thing for example is police cars. Police cars pretty much act as moving speed cameras. If you break the speed limit and/or do something that's illegal they'll fine you, plus turn on their sirens and just sit there.... watching you.
Cities and towns are much bigger than the ones in ETS2. There is now an actual good reason to travel through cities and admire the views.
The map in this game is pretty disappointing, I've already discovered at least 80% of it. Yes I know, they're adding a free dlc soon that adds Arizona, but right now, the map is small.
I would say there is a slight better quality when it comes to graphics & design that ETS2.
ATS isn't a hard game to run when it comes to graphics. Just like it's predecessor, there are plenty of graphics options. I can easily run Ultra graphics, so I'm assuming it isn't that hard.
One of the main things the developers were working on this game, was design. The game has much more detail than ETS2. There is much more of a variety of different roads. cities and towns are much larger and are more detailed and there are some really beautiful views. Sometimes at night times you can see shooting stars, and in day time you can easily see planes and jets flying around.
Also I swear I saw a UFO in Nevada...
Like I said before, the UI of this game is pretty much Identical to ETS2's, pretty much nothing has changed, which in most ways is a good thing. If you've played ETS2 then you won't have any trouble on getting to understand where everything is. As for newcomers, just like in the previous games, there are tutorials that tell you where everything is, so I doubt there will be a time where you struggle.
- Beautiful Environment
- So much detail!
- Very relaxing
- It's pretty much what you want in a truck game.
- Much bigger towns and cities.
- Such a small map.
- Very similar to ETS2.
- Some background terrain looks very bland.
More of a reskin, than a unique game. People who've played ETS2 before would probably find this a bit disappointing. But from my experience I've enjoyed playing this. There is much more added detail and many beautiful places to explore, even if It's a small map. Just like It's predecessor, It's a relaxing experience, thats what's important to me.
It isn't perfect, and It's definitely not better than ETS2, but It is worth your money.
Final Verdict - 7.5/10.
