Ronan is a criminal-turned-cop who is killed by the mysterious Bell Killer. Playing as Ronan's ghost, investigate a series of crime scenes (sometimes with the help of teenage medium Joy), searching for identity of the killer. Many supernatural elements come into play – ghosts, witches, demons – and some  flashbacks of the witch trials are pretty gruesome (drowning, burning, hanging).
As the investigation progresses, you'll explore a graveyard, an apartment house, an old mansion, a police station and of course the obligatory asylum level. While the game world is small, it is open, with the ability to just wander around the town of Salem. It's a gloomy place – the game occurs entirely at night – but is well-dotted with NPCs and collectibles. Obtaining collectibles can unlock other stories (usually brief, narrated cut-scenes), and some NPCs will provide side-missions. There's a decent amount of stuff to do, but most collectibles were easily found as I explored the town or a level.
Investigations require exploring a a crime scene, finding evidence (“Press E to analyze”) and sorting through the collected evidence (“Press Q to conclude the investigation”). Walking (or later, teleporting) around as a ghost feels fun;  Ronan can walk through walls, possess people (mind-reading), and turn on random stuff to mess with the townsfolk (poltergeisting). Especially cool were the impenetrable “ghost walls” from past times that can block Ronan from exploring – or even provide new hazards (watch out for the ghost train!). Oh, and you can possess cats, too. This is actually crucial to progress through several stages of the game.
The demon sections, though, dragged the experience down a bit. Demons will sometimes spawn after completing an investigation. Their existence does have a crucial part to play, and they're easy enough to defeat with a little patience. Given that this is a supernatural tale, it would be rather weird if demons of some kind weren't in the game, and having some stealth sections added some variety to the gameplay.  But after a while the demons became annoying distractions from the story.
And the narrative is where Murdered: Soul Suspect stands strongest. There is a lot of backstory to be found about Ronan and his wife (via collectibles). Sometimes collectibles are merely annoying, but they are worth pursuing here. Jason Brooks (as Ronan) and Cassidy Lehrman (as the medium, Joy) provide stand-out vocal performances. The graphics (Unreal 3) are great – murky and dark. Jason Graves' score provides a classic horror-story undertone. Murdered: Soul Suspect is a well-crafted detective game with a few quirks that holds its story aloft as its best attribute. If that sounds good to you, then go ahead and get this one.

First things first, this is a good game: But one that is hardly woreth all the praise it got. I will begin by listing the thing that i dislked and therefore do not allow me to reccomend it:
*No Autosave: This is no primitive title and lack of automated save can give the unaware player plenty of nasty surprises, In a game with permadeath this is almost unforgivable, and there is also no option to restart missions unless you faiL, which coupled with some of the game`s other  flaws can turn it intoa  very frustrating experience
*Clumsy Tank Controls: Despite being WWII inspired, Tank Warare in Valkyria Chronicles  more closely rememble WWI tank warfare: Tanks are sluggish and their primary function is bascally work as mobile cover, Anti-Tank Infantry does a better job at dealing with enemy armor. being as cumbersome as thy are, Tanks are also very difficult to control, and that can prove really inconvenient due to fact that turning also consumes Action Points. That and the fact that losing you main tank commander leads to an auto-fail is perfect mix for disaster
*Unflexible-Uninteresting Soldier Classes: Foot Soldiers in Valkyria Chronicles are divided into Five Classes (Engineers, Scouts, Shocktroopers, Anti-Tank Soldiers, Snipers) all with their own set of abilities which are crucial for battlefield success...or so it would seem. Problem with soldier classes is that they what they suppose to do AND NOTHING ELSE, they have no secondary weaponry, and the game heavily encourage the use of particular set iof soldiers for a certain missions. While you take your pic of grunts to the battlefield, the doesn`t really encourage a combined arms aproach: spamming the right type of soldier can allow to breeze through missions unopposed.
*Poor Teamwork: the above beign said, the also promotes reliance on individual soldiers, circumstances that will require to manuver with your whole squad are rare and chances are that throughout a mission, out of 15 soldiers, you will end up using just 3 or 4. The game has a "comradeship system" as some soldiers like (or dislike) some embers of the squad and can perform team Attacks with their buddies: but your will neraly never use those as all you need to do bring even the stauchest of infrantry if to throw some grenades and then shoot them to the face
The System is broken, given how Anti-Tank Troopers and Snipers donpt participate on team Attacks even with the prople they like which makes this affinity pointless in them.
*Poor cover system: The only thing that offers real cover in this game are sandbags, which will grant you defensive bonuses even if flanked. On the other hand concrete walls, ancient ruins, or even immovile tanks will only stop atacks if they coming from the direction they facing and they not negate flanking attacks: something sandbags for some unholy reason do.
*War Story?: Make no mistake the story is enjoyable but...is no war story, not by a long shot. That, or it is REALLY bad one. The game would greatly benefitted from a slightly darker tone, because it really had grea potential on it`s theme: You are the impromptu commander of hastly assembled Militia Squad of a small country that must repel the overwelming invasion of vastly superior foe.
The problem is...Well, there almost no instances in which you are reminded that you are at war, the game is too bright and colorful for that, the characters are cheerful, way too likeble and lack complexity (except from a moment of bigotry here and there)  There are no visceral moments, which is waste consdering that allegedly most of your grunts were models, Bakery`s workers, Bar workers,  students, teachers, JUST NORMAL PEOPLE  just a couple of weeks ago.  You will not seemthem having  emotional breadowns, no "IT`S GAME OVER, MAN, GAME OVER!" meltdowns or anything of the sort which kinda breaks the immersion: You could tell that you are Militia but because they tell you are, you could be The Expendables of this universe and would still make sense
There is no feeling of dread or that your fighting against a military juggernaut. There is no reaction to casualties or the other realities of war (because they are no really presented in the game) and therefore the characters have to reason to grown up and become more matured, I understand  the angle gameplays: That of common day people who rise to become the reluctant heroes against impossible odds but the mood doensn`t help, characters never mature and there is no transition from zero to hero.
Now, the game do some things right: It`s visually beatiful(speacially if you into Anime), it`s blend of fantasy and technology is interesting,  there plenty of upgrades and customziation you Tank of the Main Character and something that Valkyria Chronicles does better than similar games (such as XCOM) is that it manages to give all the avaible grunts some entity: all of them have perks, les/islikes, that are unique to them and of them have their own character models and backgrounds which is awesome and is nie break from  XCOM geenrical cannonfodder.
But in the end, i cannpt avoid feeling that could have been so much more: The ideas are there, the concepts are there, it has all the minderals to achieve it, but somewhere int he execution fell shot: not too short, but short nevertheles. You should acquire it if youa re willing to appreacite for what it is: a nice turn-based tactical game with a no-so-convencing story which leans more towards idealism rather dirt and blood game, in that case I suggest you Company of Heroes or XCOM 2

Interesting and challenging free to play coffee break game without the hassle and annoyance of "buy this" pop-ups.  Basically plays like tetris with a match 3 twist.  In fact, there are lots more twists then that.  The only part really like tetris is the pieces drop down where one wants them to be placed after rotating the pieces. The match 3 similiarity is 3+ same pieces are required to eliminate those pieces from the gameboard.  Beyond that is where the twists and differences begin.  The first and biggest difference is there is more then one piece to place.  As the game progresses there are more and more different pieces that appear. One new piece per "level" achieved.  Also when 3+ matches are made as the match pieces are eliminated the next "higher" piece will appear in their place.
There will be 7 different modes eventually.  As of Aug 8, 2016 this game is still in early access and not all modes are working.  I will only talk about Abyss and Chaos mode.
Abyss mode is a daily game (one game per day).  What makes this game interesting is the fact the pieces and the order of the pieces appear do not ever change.  Before saying BORING, Abyss mode is a scoreboard game.  So if one can remember just exactly what the pieces are and the order they appear in one can potentially gain a higher and higher daily score.  It is basically a memory game.
Chaos mode is even more challenging but the potential for incredibly high scores is immense.  In Chaos mode the pieces that appear are randomized.  However, the player gets 4 start-up "special" pieces that can be used at will and throughout the gameplay special pieces randomly occur which must be used.  I have not seen all the special pieces yet but some of these special pieces include: addition of a row at the bottom, destruction of all same game pieces (player choice), destruction of a column, one piece only for 4 turns, 3 pieces for 4 turns, 1 random piece added to all columns, etc.  Definitely makes for a challenge.
The other modes are or will be:
Infinity Mode - It is impossible to ever end.
Puzzle Mode - Complete unique puzzle layouts.
Pure Mode - No special pieces are able to drop.
Versus Mode - Play PVP or COOP with a friend locally.
Explore Mode - Go to different FaeVerse worlds and their locations, complete goals, and unlock more.
Recommend to those who like quick little games that have strategy involved, any one who enjoyed Tetris, match 3 enthusiasts, and puzzle solvers.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I recommend this game for the Metro, that's the only reason. All sequences in the Metro itself are tense, atmospheric and interesting. This is all thrown out of the window once you hit the surface, the surface consists of little more than grey and boring landscapes filled with the same enemy type that just isn't fun to fight, there are also periods when you get autosaved when you don't have oxygen meaning you have to replay the sequence.
The game excels in it's Metro, which is the main setting for the book, the stations and their politics is complex and every location feels lived in and different with all sorts of tragic stories and funny moments. I remember sitting by and listening to two women talk about an experience with the Nazi's in which a commanding officer promised the release of one's husband for sexual favours, she complied and once he was released he lashed out resulting in a guard shooting him dead. Another moment came when a fisherman was trying to explain to his daughter what a geiger counter does and where her mother is. These moments are brilliant because you find yourself eavesdropping purposefully and loitering around places that would be purely utilitarian and boring in other shooters. Unfortunately Last Light suffers from "gameplay fatigue" as I call it, many action sequences, whilst the action is well executed, become frustrating because you want to progress the story. This is very very annoying.
The story does have some flaws, for example, it tends to follow a repeating pattern and relies too much on scripted sections. The first half of the game is basically: "go somewhere, get captured, break free, repeat". You first get captured by the Nazis, then the Reds, then you go above ground and Anna gets captured whilst you are powerless. It ♥♥♥♥ing sucks sometimes. You also don't spend enough time at first around the different factions to get a feeling for their ideological motivation, and the Order is weakly explained away.
Combat is fun and rewarding when it's against Humans, you will find yourself wasting ammunition on the beasts that attack sporadically and aren't fun to fight at all. Stealth is too difficult to pull off in most cases and has no real reward that isn't mental. Aboveground combat makes you feel anxious as you have to think about air and ammo conservation, it just isn't fun. Surface levels are ridiculously frustrating because they place water in the way of direct paths without having some kind of reliable system to lead you to these paths, you could say I'm too used to games that handhold your progression, but when you're relying on oxygen that runs out very quickly you can't spare any time fighting to find where you have to go. In an attempt to break up the monotony of constantly running through similar tunnels the surface is ham-fisted into the story to create some sense of change, this completely removes any tension and every time you reach the surface Artyom shields his eyes like it's the first time, spoiler alert, it's just a bunch of ruined brutalist towerblocks with vaguely interesting roadblocks.
I'm recommending this game because the sections in the Metro are superb, like the tense action in tightly packed and cramped store rooms with mad ideologues, the atmosphere of exploring a disused tunnel and the sheer richness of the living environments. The next Metro has been announced and not released at the time of this review, and it seems to be an open world surface game, which means this may be the last time to explore the truly unique Metro and all it's dusty, mutant-spider ridden corners and crevices.

Metro Last Light Redux is the ‘remastered’ version of Metro Last Light which was originally released in 2013. The game is a linear first-person horror survival shooter which was generally based on the novels (Metro 2033 and Metro 2034) written by Dmitry Glukhovsky. This game serves as the sequel to the critically acclaimed 2010 game, Metro 2033.
One year after the events of Metro 2033, Artyom (Артём) finds himself as a full-fledged member of the
who has set up shop in the massive Soviet bunker known as D6. After receiving word that a Dark One survived the ‘canonical ending’ of Metro 2033, Artyom sets out on another adventure in the post-apocalyptic world to capture this last surviving Dark One.
+ Excellent graphics
+ Excellent atmosphere (blend of action, horror, suspense and mystery)
+ Excellent world building
+ Very good sound design
+ Very good map and level design
+ Very good story which is told in a fairly lengthy game time
+ Subtle morality system that will have an effect on the final outcome of the story
+ New game mechanics (ex. Stealth takedowns – lethal or non-lethal)
+ Very fun gunplay
+ Improved enemy AI
+ Improved character animations from the first game
+ Extensive weapon selection and upgrade system
+ Fair but challenging difficulty
+ Very fun and relatively challenging DLCs
+ Lap dances

+/- All weapon mods/upgrades can only be removed if you visit the weapon shops. This means that you cannot remove your silencer at will.
+/- Armor upgrades are now tied to the story and can no longer be purchased, unlike the first original game.

. Metro Last Light Redux is a worthy successor to Metro 2033. Much like the original game, it delivers a unique and very immersive first-person shooter experience while bringing in several game mechanics that add to the atmosphere and immersion of the game. It blends together the atmosphere of narrative driven games, the suspense of horror games, and the heart pumping combat of action games.
The game is worth $19.99 (or your regional equivalent). If you’re new to the Metro series, I would personally recommend that you purchase the
because its only $29.98. If that’s still too expensive, then I suggest waiting for a sale.
This is not an open world Action-RPG game like S.T.A.L.K.E.R or Fallout. The Metro series falls in line with games such as F.E.A.R., DOOM, and Half-Life which are narrative driven games.
Note that the original Metro Last Light (2013) game is no longer available on Steam. As of the time of this review, it has been replaced by the Redux version.

There have been quite a few changes from the wacky, Fable-esque-but-not-insufferable world of Divinity: Original Sin.  New and interesting races have been added, each with their own perks, skill trees have been expanded, and entirely new ones added.  Like Metamorphosis, which lets you grow wings, turn people into chickens, or, to the horror (or delight?) of Japanese school girls everywhere, summon tentacles to slap people with.
Now I’m not the brightest feces-flinging monkey in the Institute for Special Ed Primates, but I still feel like the journal could be a bit less cryptic in its entries, monkey-level intelligence notwithstanding.  There were a few times in my handful of hours playing the full release that I showed up at a quest marker and had no idea what the hell to do.  This is really the only major complaint I have.
Though it retains some of DOS 1’s humor, this game is much darker.  You start the game on the way to a concentration camp, where terrible things are done to “Sourcers” such as yourself.  It’s not a TERRIBLE concentration camp, mind you- there’s long, beautiful beaches, dazzling sunsets, and even the occasional sound of the hideously tortured drifting in on a pleasant evening breeze.
In contrast to the first game, the selection of party members in this game grabbed my attention from the get-go.  From the first interaction, the redhead lady is possessed and fighting for control over her body and mind.  BAM!  Consider me hooked.
Overall, DOS 2 is a very engaging game with strategic combat that can get quite complex, if you’re into that sort of thing.  The story is successful in grabbing and keeping your attention (for as far as I’ve gotten at least), though the journal really drags the game down.  If you like the sound of XCOM meets Dragon Age and the good parts of Fable, it’s absolutely worth the money.

There's a lot of content in this game. There are tons of items and events to unlock, and there's a lot of good combat. I sank over 41 hours into this game, and most of that was probably grinding for trying to unlock specific cards. But it suffers from a couple serious design flaws.
I appreciate the giant random element in the game, but when the difficulty ramps up about 7 bosses in, it makes a very large difficulty spike. Some of the dungeon curse combinations are punishingly difficult.
There are cards which are close to impossible to beat unless you beat them early enough in the game. These can include Devil's Wager and The River.
Too many of the encounters require you to either have  a ridiculous amount of gold or food, or require you to do a lengthy quest chain to unlock new cards. The random chance issues in some of these later encounters can make them ridiculously difficult to complete.
By the end of the game, pain cards can aggregate to the point where you get insta-killed from max HP if you have enough curses. It happens.
Do not ever quit the game in the middle of a run. Normally it will save your spot, but if the developers decide to patch the game, it can delete any in-progress runs you have going. The code to prevent that is simply to hard for them to implement, due to poor design choices. Just don't leave runs in-progress, as the developers should not be trusted.
The dealer is usually funny, tends to get annoying when he runs out of new things to say and just repeats himself over and over. There were also issues with prejudiced and thoughtless dialogue of his which have since been patched out.
The DLC isn't all that expensive, and it unlocks character classes for your protagonist, each which has its own quest chain, but each class has its own benefits and drawbacks. Some of the classes are ridiculously overpowered in certain fields, which kind of makes the DLC "pay to win".
The graphics and controls are okay, usually. A couple of glitches here and there, and sometimes the controller seems unresponsive until a couple seconds after a battle has begun. That's no good.
The developers have an unfortunate habit of "rebalancing" cards, moving around their place in the unlock system or difficulty levels they show up on, and completely changing the way the later dungeons work, and not for the better. This is the sort of negative developer behavior that similarly plagued Dark Souls II.
The overall experience is marred by a couple of bad design choices.

All in all, I give Mass Effect 2 an 11/12, one for every interesting companion.

This includes everything from both versions of the first Disgaea game. Whether or not its the definitive version comes down to your preference. I know I dont have much time logged in this but that's because I am waiting to get my GPD WIN to play it portable which is what I prefer for Disgaea. I played much of it back in the day on the PSP already and wish to revisit it soon. I am obviously a veteran of the series and I'm here to tell you what I love about it and why its so popular!
PROS
-The one version with all the content, updated graphics, menu and layout
-Finally Disgaea comes to PC! Its a great series and now more people can experience it.
-Has achievements and trading cards
-Overall a really solid strategy RPG with endless fun
-Even though mods aren't as plentiful for this title they are still out there if you know where to look.
-It has great action and animations that are fun to watch.
-The ultimate power fantasy game as you can basically infinitely level your units to godlike power.
-The characters are great. They are really funny and comedic and the original Disgaea team from the first game is classic.
-It seems complicated if you watch someone who is well into it play the game but from the start everything is actually very very easy to grasp. Even though its easy enough to understand there is so much you can do!
-You can make and customize your own units from different classes and types. Set their gender, specialties, stats and abilities. Just about everything you could want is here. Supports, ninjas, swordsmen, knights, succubi, gunners, mages, archers, thieves, monsters, demons, angels, and the list goes on and on.
-The item world, a randomized map you play by going into an item.  Each floor you clear upgrades the weapon or item. Its a great system that came from Disgaea!
-Plenty of content!
CONS
-Not portable, I plan on remedying this however when I eventually get a GPD WIN and this is the perfect game for it. I think this series feels best on portable systems for some reason.
-It used to have minor issues at launch date I believe at this point they have updated and fixed just about everything.
-Can get a bit grindy at times, mostly only if you plan on getting all the extra post game stuff.

I've been following Owlboy's development for at least this past year, and was incredibly eager to give it a try for the art and animation alone.
It seems best described as a side-view Zelda-esque game without a lot of extra padding and unnecessary fluff, but it certainly has an identity of its own.
As anyone can see even from the trailer and screenshots, it has a gorgous, incredibly detailed style of pixel art with some impressive animation. It also has some amazing moments of visual spectacle, especially in certain boss fights. The soundtrack also works very well with the game, and has enough standout tracks to warrant listening to on its own.
Owlboy's story is engaging, well-written, fairly unique, and even surprisingly somber at times.There are even several hidden pieces of interesting story and lore to find across the world.
The game's puzzles, while not exactly mind-bending, are still interesting and make good use of your party's abilities and the theme of the area in which they are found.
The Gunners, which function as Owlboy's equivalent of upgrades or "dungeon items," all feel unique and are useful in both combat and puzzles, not to mention being interesting and enjoyable characters themselves.
Owlboy's difficulty isn't especially punishing. I died a fair number of times, but the final boss only defeated me twice. Honestly, the hardest challenge was the Cannon minigame, which is completely optional (if you don't want to be completionist).
Owlboy also does a remarkable job of keeping the player's immersion, both through avoiding breaking the fourth wall entirely and giving contextual reasons for abilities and decisions that in other games often seem arbitrary. For instance, rather than simply being a typical arbitrarily silent protagonist, Otus intead does not speak because he is actually a mute, a trait which the other characters are well aware of.
My one complaint was that the game doesn't convey much of the world outside the little slice of sky you are given to explore. The story is very much contained in this relatively small area, with practically no references to the world outside. And while the characters populating the game's few settlements are interesting, the places seem oddly barren. Even your home village, the biggest explorable populated area, has a grand total of only about 10 houses, 6 of which are only seen way off in the distance, and even fewer NPCs. Don't get me wrong, the area you are given has plenty of interesting details, but the sense of scale of the world is portrayed inconsistently at best.

This game blew me away. After watching Jesse Cox do a fan friday of the game, where he played through only a small amount of it, I had to purchase it and try it myself. The story is beauitful, as is the artwork and music. Some of the boss fights are very difficult, but the feeling of victory when you beat one is worth the frustration. I higly recommend this game to anyone who liked titles such as stardew valley, undertale, zelda and maybe even sonic.
The game also has full compatibilty when it comes to controllers, which is always a plus and I recommend playing it using one, although you'll have a great experience with a keyboard and mouse as well. Personally I played the game with keyboard and mouse.
Theres a few secrets I didn't find or finish, but the game lets you go back before the final bossfight to finish those, even if you already finished the bossfight. Your last save is before the fight.
The end leaves you with a few questions, but the last section of the game may answer a few.
Honestly, the game made me tear up a bit at certain points, and it has a very realistic feel to it, even with awkward silences and arguments that feel incredibly real, making you really connect to the characters. This will definitely go high on my games of the year list. Buy it and play it, it's cheap, it's worth it and it's long, I finished the game in around 11 hours. The story is really something you should see with your own eyes. Also, support the small indie company that spent 9 years developing this, they did a terrific job.

It's not without its flaws, but overall it's a really nice and fun game.

Enough about my first time experience, onto the review.
This is my first written review ever, so bear with me, pelase.
This game is in Early Access. That's FunCom's excuse, and I accept it. I've played far worse games that were full releases.
Early Acces means "not even close to finished", for those of you who are new to the term or who just can't wrap your head around what it means. I see a lot of negative reviews that doesn't seem to take this into consideration, and that annoys me. Being Early Access, it has tons of big and small problems that need to be addressed, but the team at FunCom is working furiously. Already there's been 2-3 patches.
Pro's:
It's a huge map. Lot's of areas to explore, interesting sights to see and so on. I heard there are lots of secrets to find too.
The graphics look good. I mean, it could be better, and some...weird...clipping and movement issues exist, but they are working on it.
It's easy to understand what to do next and how to do it.
The crafting is very self-explanatory, everything is easy to place and it's easy to see what you need.
All monster and character models look very good!
Weapons and gear look good and work fairly well.
THRALLS!!
Clans and clan bases!
Cons:
Server issues, like lag and instability, rubberbanding etc.
Rubberbanding monsters -.-
Crafting menu needs to be optimised. Right now like going through a box of legos, trying to find that one part.
Each craft skill needs to tell you what level you need to be or what you need to have crafted before to get it. I.e. to learn the Sandstone Stairs crafting skill, it seemed I had to have built the walls, floor, roof, doorframe and door beforehand. Skill list didn't say anything about this.
Graphics need improvements here and there.
Combat need loads of improvement.
A.I. is bad. Sometimes enemies won't react or attack even when you're slashing away with your *insert favored weapon*
The bow needs to get fixed. It works and does loads of damage, but you can't tell if your arrow hits the mark as it apparently is invisible.
I don't know how important these things are to other players, but these are my main ares of joy or grief with the game.
I will give the same warning as so many others: don't go in expecting a full game free of bugs etc. this is EARLY ACCES! It's a damned Alpha version at best. If you buy it and play it and think it sucks because you expected another ARK or a full game, don't buy it. Don't even think about buying it. Wait for the full game.
If you buy it, expect problems. Be patient. FunCom is working hard, so just...be patient.

After yet more gameplay, I must admit that Funcom updates this game ALOT. This shows good promise to the game, but there are things that still need to be fixed.
- Skill points, anything outside of health and carry weight is pointless at higher levels. The best weapons doesn’t take Str into consideration.
- Players plant foundations down to stop spawning of Thralls just to stop people from getting any, after they wall (far enough away) off the ones that only they can get to. That needs to be addressed.

The other makes crafting times superbly long, imagine training a thrall for 2 days and they still haven’t completed but constantly takes food. This thrall is not named, and it’s not a lvl 3.
- Player levels are the most important thing in this game, but killing hostile NPCs doesn’t give you much, while Antelope give you a significant amount of XP. “…Whut?”
The game is worth $30 for the hours you’ll put in with friends, but going at this game solo seems sadistic.

The grafics, the animations, the soundeffects, the music, the units, everything is just copypasted from the predecessor.
KW1 was played like an browser game, where you builded one big city and could attack the cities and armies of other players or AI on a big world map. So you had a big city building part, and a big fighting part.
The developers said in KW2, they will focus on the battles. And now you are building a base, gather ressources and fight at the same time against up to 4 players on a small map, just like on every other RTS game.
By abandoning their "city building" part and mixing it to a smaller scaled skirmish together with the battle part, they not only decreased the actual game content, but also their unique feature, that made them standout from the rest of the RTS games.
Another thing is the grinding system. In KW1 you had a gold currency, which you could buy for real money, or earn on the battlefield. From the gold you could buy new technologies and hero-units. It was actually a pretty fair system, since you got a fair amount of gold for defeating enemy units.
Now you dont grind for gold, but for up to 10 ! (or so) different resources-cards, which you get randomly for every fight, and which you need for unlocking new skills, technologies and units. Of course you will always need the right combination of them to progress and some of this cards are very rare. Also mind, that you will have to unlock everything for the orcs/elves/humans separatly.
In the old grinding system, you knew what you get - gold - and you could buy with it whatever you wanted.
Now you get something completly random, that you maybe dont need at all and allready have in large quantities. There is a market where you can trade your resources-cards with others, but of course everyone is trying to sell you his stuff as high as possible, so this doesnt really help.
Except for the new grinding system, the only new feature right now, are the zombies. after some time, the corpses of the fallen soilders will rise as zombies and attack everyone close by. This can be fun, but also quite annoying, depending on the players. You can deactivate the zombies in the options if you want.
Conclusion: The exact same game, but - right now - with less content and a much more tedious grinding system than before.

A Ghostly Murder Mystery in a Town called Salem?
Well, sounds good, but also a bit Cheesy, one could say.
However, this really is a quite enjoyable game. If you like your Crime Scenes (L.A. Noir), your Ghost Stories, some Puzzles and general Detective Work, this could be the right game for you.
The story is really nice, and has you guessing for a while who now might be responsible for all things happening.
There is quite a lot of additional tidbits about the major and some minor characters in teh game as well as the town. Even some Ghost stories apart from the ghost murder mystery to be found. It all really adds to the atmosphere.
It may not have the greatest graphics or mechanics, not even the most challening puzzles/crime scenes, but it is so nicely told, you shall find yourself immersed into the story andwanting to find out more about all the things.
Pro:
- voice acting - I really enjoyed this, as the works for the main characters, but also all those side stories is really good
- atmosphere - the town, the small things you can dicsover ont he side like small "crimes" , stories to be found, lighting, location design and music really adds to it all, and makes this a nice experience
- crime scenes - I found it nice to be checking clues once more, similar to L.A. Noir (though Noir is the superior Game really), as well as then trying to choose the right leads to figure out the actual story.
- Quite the collectibles to be found, though tied to achievements and providing some nice additional info, I was gladly spending a couple more hours to find most of them (only missing 2)
Con:
- it is rather short for the price of 29 bucks. Try getting it in a sale, and if you enjoy the ride you'll have good fun for 8 - 12 hours
- collectibles - the sheer number, and the achievements tied to it might turn peaople away - also they do make up for about 2 or 3 hours of gameplay if you try to get them all
- could be a tad more difficult - puzzles and crime scenes are rather easy to be solved
Long story short:
Looking for a nice ghost story, full of atmosphere, good voice acting on top, some cool detective dude crime scene work with the supernatural touch - if you get for about 7 to 10 bucks - go grab it and have some fun with it.

Owlboy was a wonderous game that had me praising it left and right. While I absolutely adored the game there were some problems we will get to later. You take the form of an owl, an ancient species well known for their intellect, creations, and flight. As you travel you pick up partners that act as your means of combat. This unique concept grabbed my attention enough to give it a go and I will not regret the purchase.
PROS: Above all else I want to praise the visuals. This game is very beautiful. It feels like Rayman Legends in the world of Studio Ghibli. The characters and writing were very funny at times and well put together. Every once in a while you felt really touched by your character's development (without spoiling anything) but I found myself more laughing at all the expressions that they presented. I used a xbox 360 controller and felt like the button layout was very comfortable.Not sure about using a keyboard but you can always change them if you prefer to. The upgrades for the coins were superb. And what do you get for all your hard work of collecting every coin? The ULTIMATE owl cloak that renders you invincible as you zip around at high speed! Totally worth it, and made the final boss battle a wimp haha.
CONS: Achievements at the time of writing this were broken. The creators were made aware of this issue and in the next update (or the early access beta) you will have no problems with them. I feel that the pacing was a little off though. There are certain bosses and "dungeons" *cough* Mechanical Dragon and Floating Continent *cough* that felt so frustrating trying to complete. Which leads me on to the secrets. I love trying to find secrets but many areas hid them to the point of trial and error. Is it here? Nope. Well guess I best slide across every wall now. Small complaint but I wish that the hats you can collect would stay on your head despite being hit. And my least favorite moment? THE CANNON MINIGAME *inner rage*. It took me probably 50 tries to get it right. And I know for some people it may even be near impossible.
The only thing I could wish now is that the game was even more filled with things do to or more story! I finished the game 100% in only 11 hours. Cannot wait to see what they can do with the game in the future, whether a sequel or additions.

You essentially get 2 weapons, BUT those 2 weapons each have 5 different firing modes (so 10 weapons basically...) so switching to one weapon adds the modes to 1,2,3,4,5 on the keyboard and vice versa.  You can upgrade your weapons however you want, so you can make your favorite guns even more powerful and give them new firing modes.  The game also looks extremely pretty since it was developed ONLY for the pc.  No need to worry about the usual console port issues.  The story is pretty bad however, but it is good cheap fun.

SpeedRunners is a game that makes me want to hook my PC to the TV and invite friends over to play. Risk of Rain is a fun romp in the multiplayer universe, but it’s not very competitive. (Unless you’re speed achievement fighting a friend.) I’m fine with Risk of Rain over the net. SpeedRunners makes me want them right there so I can hoot and holler at them and punch them in the arm when they grapple me from downtown.
In SpeedRunners you run around a map with a bunch of obstacles with other players or bots vying for the position of first place. As you run, the border of the screen encroaches in on you making the safety zone from first place smaller and smaller (you need to start catching up!) Last one on screen wins a round. If you win three rounds in a row, you win the game and it starts over at the level select screen.
Even in beta, you can see this game shine. Everything works as it should right now (control wise) other than a few items that are a little OP at the moment. That is to be expected since they are still in the middle of completing the game. That said, it’s common to see the devs visiting the Steam forums and replying and thanking players for their feedback. I know this gets harped on a lot, but if this is done by taking fan feedback with a grain of salt and with the devs ignoring complaints that would change the core of the game into something they don’t want while still maintaining a fun and playable game, victory is assured since the game is already fun.
On the note of adding things, I don’t thing much more needs to be added. I think a few more levels to the basic setup, more aesthetic only different “heros”, an easier way to play imported maps with buds over the net, and if they want to add more items, make them optional would be about it. Others can probably think of more imaginative things while at the moment I’m tapped out. I’m a fan of what they’ve got right now with the bombs, grapple hook and rockets, but adding to many extra items would take away from the core of the game which is racing or speedrunning. You’re supposed to be beating your buds, but it’s not Smash Bros. (Even in tournaments items get turned off there.) There are plenty of smash clones out there, let this be something different.
Fear not, for those of you who are uninitiated in this game, SpeedRunners has a tutorial and a story mode to get you used to how the controls and levels will work. You’ll learn to grapple and wall jump, but there’s something they won’t teach you. “What is that?” you may ask. Well friend, that’s how to deal with the fact that they don’t have a working matchmaking system and you’ll either race against someone who can get so far ahead that he can taunt comfortably or you’ll be destroying the competition. I can’t ding them for this since they said in the forums that this is on the table to be worked on soon. I’m one of those that got paired against a Falcon that could run circles around a first timer like me, but I took it as a learning experience. I’m not a seriously competitive person most of the time so I still had a load of fun. After all, that’s what videogames are for.

Content 6/10
Controls 6/10
Voice Acting 5/10
Graphics: Recycling the same 8 NPC across the *entire* game shows. At least Last Light tried to make it less obvious with masks, but not 2033. Stuttering was easy enough to fix but it was an issue I shouldn't have had to deal with were the game properly optimized. Lense flare is horrible. I hate it. I turn off lense flare, bloom and motion blur whenever I play a game. The lense flare in this game was painfully obvious and did not add to the environment.
Sound: Non-Music is spot on. Though some areas of the game the monster audio plays in the background for ambience and I found that irritating more than scary for the simple fact I use the sound to know what level of alert I should be at and do not play the music while exploring(hate the distraction). Many people would use the music intensity as a crutch for combat readiness. I prefer the monsters for that or at the most your character may hear his own heart beat instead of intense music (just an idea).
Music: Didn't like it. It wasn't worth listening to. The developers tied the audio for the theater show to the music thread as well, so if you didn't have music turned up, you didn't hear any of the theater shows in game.
Animations: Needs improvement. Dead expressions. Literally every single model in the game only had weighting for the mouse and eyelids for talking and blinking. Poor design choice as this is a story driven FPS and if you can't believe the expression on the faces of the people speaking, no amount of voice acting can sell their story. Still better than the model weighting in Mass Effect Andromeda.
Story: The dialogue is contrived. The story is forced. The way the environment was designed coupled with the story suggests the environment was finished long before the story and the dialogue was injected into the game like foam insulation. The poor quality dialogue betrays the over-all integrity of a good idea.
Voice Acting: Mediocre. There were a few choice characters who seemed to be descent voice actors, but 95% of them were emotionally bereft vacuous shells. If a voice actor does not believe they are their character, they can't sell the story. Every line in the dialogue is a sales pitch.
Environments: Top notch. I loved the environments. In fact, they kept me going through the game when the story did not and the dialogue could not. My first visit to the swamp was a blast. Additionally the environments were designed to make borders feel natural instead of contrived. I was able to find invisible walls, but it took a lot of work. You really got an appreciation for the level editors commitment to making the environment feel compelling.
Cinematics: I really appreciated that the game made most of the cinematics seamlessly follow into player control, rather than inject the game with post processed CGI rendered with more detail than the game runs in. This made the game feel fluid and the cinematics were encouraging.
Content: As much as you can customize your weapons, you'll use the same three pretty much from start to finish. Shot gun, Sniper Rifle and Automatic Rifle. The weapons encourage a very specific approach to combat and that is unfortunate. Customization feels like a forced and wasted effort to add something unique to a game lacking content.
There was a large missed opportunity that was only barely brushed over in Last Light to encourage exploration and thats the visions (I won't reveal details). They are worth exploring for and I wish there were more...so much more.
Controls: Game controls feel like a standard keyboard and mouse FPS. I can't complain save to say the walking speed of Artyom is too fast when you're walking behind NPC. I found myself artificially "walking" by shuttering my walk just to keep from ramming into the person I was following. It's a minor issue but pulled me out of the game. In a story driven game, features that pull you out are a bad thing.

The story is gripping and the characters are deep. As well as tactical turn-based combat you can level up your squad, tank and weapons. As the story progresses the characters' relationships with each other develop, but there is a lot of replay value here too as there are a lot of people to choose from who aren't necessarily main characters, but are deep and detailed all the same.
I can't really find a fault with it, but bear in mind that you should save regularly and it also, like many RPGs, requires quite a big investment of your time.

NOTE: This is a shortened review without screenshots.For my full review, please visit
This is the worst game I’ve ever been addicted to.
No, I don’t mean it’s the worst I’ve ever been addicted to a game. I mean this game has the lowest quality-to-addiction rating of any game I’ve ever played.
You play as Recette Lemongrass, a young girl doing her own thing when suddenly, a fairy named Tear (get it? Recettear) pops up and tells you that not only is your dad missing, but he’s also left a humongous debt that you have to pay off. The fairy then comes up with the bright idea of turning your house into a shop, so that you can earn money to pay off the debt in instalments. Of course, the shock of your missing papa and the huge debt does absolutely nothing to dampen your spirits and enthusiasm. You open your shop without any semblance of despair and carry on earning money for the rest of the game.
Throughout your journey, you’ll meet some very odd and annoying characters that will either help or ridicule you, none of which are particularly memorable or likeable. Thankfully, the game gives you the option to skip all the dialogue (or at least scroll through it really fast).
There are two main gameplay modes available in
– the terrible plain item shop simulator and the repetitive randomly-generated dungeon crawler. Let’s examine these two portions separately.
Firstly, the shop. This is
mundane. You display a bunch of items in your shop and throughout the day, assuming you choose to have your shop open (which takes up ¼ of the time you have for each day), people will come in and buy it. A bartering system exists that allows you to adjust the price depending on how much profit or loss you’re willing to take. If your price is too high however, the spoilt morons in town will get unhappy and leave you without a sale. Successfully selling stuff to the idiots in town will reward you with experience that goes towards your “merchant level”, with bonuses experience awarded if you’re able to chain a few successful sales in a row. Increasing your level opens up additional features that you can play around with. For example, whilst at the very beginning customers can only purchase the items on your (limited) shelves, higher merchant levels will allow customers to request an item from your inventory, sell you items or even order multiple items that they want to pick up on another day. Other bonuses include larger shop sizes, wall/floor/counters/layout customisations and even the option to put a vending machine down, to make all the hassle of selling items just that little bit easier on you.
There are several factors that influence which kinds of customers and how many customers enter your shop. The first way is through your showcase display, also known as the “table-next-to-the-window-that-people-can-see-from-outside”. You want people to look at the junk on your table and think “Damn, I wanna go in there!” So your first instinct is to put all your expensive, high-in-demand stuff on that table, but by doing so you risk alienating the poor little girl that can’t afford anything. So in the end I have no god damn clue how you’re meant to attract the most people. The second way to influence everything is by changing the walls, floor, counters and so on in your shop, which is collectively referred to as the “store atmosphere”.  I’m not 100% sure of how it works, but I imagine light and gaudy things attract little girls that can’t afford anything and call you a big meanie poo for marking up the price even slightly, and the more plain and dark ones stores some other weird population. Who knows?
So where do you get the items that you sell? Well there’s two ways to get your hands on some goodies. The first one is to buy them in town, either from the Market or the Merchant’s Guild. It works just like real life – buy low, sell high. Every so often you’ll hear a news bulletin saying that the cost of this is temporarily decreased and the price of this other thing is increased. It doesn’t take a genius to figure out how to approach the situation.
The other main method of obtaining items (which incidentally also makes up the remainder of the game) involves dungeon-crawling. Rather than having your useless little girl go out and magically have the ability to fight, the game allows you to visit the “Adventurer’s guild”, in which you pick from a number of heroes-for-hire who will go do the dungeon-crawling for you. Once you’ve made your choice, you take control of whichever hero you pick and embark on what has to be the most monotonous and tedious dungeon-crawling game in existence. If repeatedly killing incredibly inspired and original enemies such as slimes, bats and bunny rabbits appeals to you in any way then, boy, you’re in for a treat. Each level is set out so that there’s a number of chests, enemies and a goal to get to, which takes you to the next level. Every 5 levels, you’ll generally encounter a boss battle.
Did I say it was monotonous and tedious? Because it is. You’ll encounter the same enemies over and over again (with slight variations from time to time). None of the boss fights are particularly interesting or challenging and although you do eventually unlock a handful of different adventurers to choose from, all of them are limited to a maximum of three abilities, none of which are particularly impressive.
Whilst torturing yourself in the dungeons does reward some goodies for you to sell, the main purpose of dungeon-crawling is actually to collect ingredients, which can be used to craft (or “fuse”) better items or equipment.
Every week or so, you’ll be forced to pay off a part of your loan. This begins at 10,000 pix (the currency used in the game) and increases exponentially for every week that passes. If at any point you fail to pay up, the game is over and you’ll restart. This would be horrible except for the fact that you restart with all of your items and upgrades. As a result, losing the game just makes it infinitely easier next time.
For those that have paid off their debt and want more for whatever reason, you’re in luck – The game allows you to play on in endless mode, start again in New Game + mode or even a survival mode, where the debt keeps becoming exponentially larger until you get overwhelmed.
All in all, there’s a lot of “game” to be had here, although whether or not you enjoy what you’re playing is another matter altogether.
To be honest, the game looks like an early PS2/Dreamcast-era game. There’s no support for wide-screen or any resolution higher than 1280x960. The aesthetic is certainly cute, but otherwise unremarkable. Also worth noting is the fact that alt-tabbing appeared to glitch the games graphics so that one half or more of the screen is completely whited out when selling items. I can’t say for sure if that happens to anyone else though.
The music is adequate but also unremarkable. I’d liken it to a poor man’s version of the music in
games.
Despite crapping all over this game in this review, it’s the intangibles that really matter. For whatever reason, despite all its flaws, Recettear was a stupendously addictive game that I just couldn’t put down. It takes a bunch of repetitive, unoriginal and uninteresting ideas and meshes them into a unique game I both love and hate simultaneously. All that said, I do recommend that
give it a try, because if nothing else, it really is a unique title and one that you should experience for yourself.

Hand of Fate is really something out of the ordinary;
Designed as a card collecting/dungeon brawler game, it tries a fresh, new approach to both genres.
Description to how the game works; (thought I'd put it a bit after the pro and cons, as it's a bit mundane to read.)
At the start of each new dungeon, you'll get to choose, which cards are in your own "equipment" deck and which cards you want to add to the dealer's deck. So you decide whether you want this extra shield or ring, or rather add an extra sword into the deck. The same thing is possible with your dealer's deck, as it's your call to make your game easier and miss out on those card tokens, which you need for new cards, equipment as well as encounters, or choose the cards, which are yet to be beaten and try your best on the way.
The dealer lays out a dungeon with the chosen cards, in which you navigate around with your little figurine, kinda like a board game. From time to time you'll encounter a monster or a trap, from where the game will switch into a Arkam City-style 3rd person combat system, which is debateably the weakest part of the game, in which you can move around a small area, dodge, attack and counter attacks.
I really hope you found this review helpful in aiding your decision towards buying this game.

I had played and mostly finish it on PS2 a butt-load of years ago, and well... Why not try it on PC with the huge sale it got. Is it good, is it bad? As I usually do I'm gonna start with the negative stuff, then move up from there.
First and foremost, the controls. Keyboard and mouse controls are suicide-inducing. It took me less than an hour to tell them to f#ck off and plug the XBOX 360 controller. Way better. I will also say that there's some sort of problem with the mouse controls, at it doesn't seem to respond to some of the clicks for some reason.
Second, parts of the gameplay. Now you gotta understand something, this was the first game of the series, and after having beaten 2, 3 and 4 it shows. Some special attacks are redundant, healers are stupidly useless and will hardly level up (as you need to kill to get experience and healers suck at hurting), monster-type characters are kinda useless compared to humanoids, that kinda stuff. The biggest issue is that the Dark Assembly, the game's government, is just... Harsh. From the start of the game it'll take a few tries to get anything passed on it. The game is build so you just kill the ones that don't agree with you or bribe them, however early on it's nearly impossible to be successful at either. Thankfully most (if not all) of these problems got fixed in future games.
Also, the story has a few stale parts. Scenes that go for too long, mainly. It's not until the mid-game when the story starts to get more interesting. I will also say, the tutorial at the start of the game is forced. Shouldn't you be able to skip it? Sure you can skip it at New Game+, but I mean on your first playthrough. Sure it has some humor on it, but if you already know how to play it then it's just you hitting the A button over and over for a few minutes.
Lastly, the last episodes have a weird raise on enemy levels compared with the others, on which they raised them slowly so your characters could keep up. However in the last chapter enemies start around 50 or so and to the final battle you're suddenly batting against a 90 lvl final boss with a bunch of similar leveled enemies with him. Sure, the game expects you to grind at some moment, after all that's what the franchise was build on, the post-game cool stuff... But it's a raise of levels a bit too sudden and rushed.
That being said, the game is quite fun to play and offers a f#ck-truck of content for a really fair asking price on a sale.
The story, ignoring those scenes that last longer than they should, it's entertaining. Not too many characters, and most of them are well developed (Sadly other characters such as
don't get too much of it). And the humor is actually alright, with the game ocasionally becoming self-aware and laughing it up along with yourself.
The game also has plenty of references and shout-outs that are fun when you actually notice them. Now sure, sequels become an INSANE OVERDOSE of references, but in this game is more tame.
The post-game stuff is is also great. Not only the game has plenty of endings and an extra story that's not really canon but it's fun to play, but the game also has plenty of stages and secret bosses after you're done with the main game. Though expect the grind, as the main story will end with you around level 80 or so and some of the secret bosses are around 1000. There's plenty of spots where grinding can become a breeze (specially during the story, incase you're having issues with a boss in particular), so don't worry too much.
I also find like this game had some of the best characters, no wonder most of them appear in later games over and over. Laharl, Flonne, Etna, Mid-boss, they have better character development than the characters on the third game (which might I add, the third game had a stupidly short story). Sure there's not many choices when it comes to making your own characters as in the future games, but the story ones the game has are quite interesting and fun to keep up with.
Do I recommend this game? Yeah! If you don't mind turn-based strategy rpg games, then jump right in. But remember this: Disgaea 2 is better, as the devs learned from the first game and fixed the problems the game had. This game is good, you'll probably enjoy it, but I suggest you at some moment move to the sequel. It's better in almost every way.
TL;DR Edition: It's a fun PS2 game which has a f#ckload of content, though the keyboard and mouse controls feel as horrible as you would expect. The sequel might be better, but you're still getting your money back on a really long game with plenty of content (and out-of-context sexual comments made by Laharl).

Owlboy does many things right. The most obvious are the GORGEOUS visuals. I do not think the was a background or character I saw that did not scream how much time, effort, and love must have been put into its spritework. The next noteworthy thing is the gameplay. Simple enough to quickly grasp, but engaging enough to keep you involved with only a few breaks in the fun. The last thing I will note are the characters; developed enough to be more than one dimensional, but not developed enough to feel like there is a deep deep deep lore you can find out just by playing the game. The in game lore is there, but it is vague enough so that it doesn't feel like it is pushing itself on you; which leads into what I feel are some of the games weak points.
The first gripe I have with the game; it leaves you wanting more. The game felt short for all it tried to introduce you to, but not quite finish. I found myself wanting more when I would be introduced to a new area or new character. Sadly, very few things are tied up when the story ends. The second and biggest gripe I have with the game; the ending. Without giving away spoilers; the ending feels half full. You never quite resolve a few of the major story points you deal with; some still happening right as the finale is about to begin. I can understand artistic endings, but some people would rather have a full story as oppossed to an artistic ending. I am one of those people. The last gripe is very minor, but still one I feel should be addressed. While I mentioned the gameplay is simple and easily engaging; there are some points, especially late game, where it feels a change or two in mechanics would be appreciatted. Such as including a map to help with exploration, a faster mode of travel (Note, you do get a small form of it, but the distance said mode has isn't particularly long), and the ability to fast travel in the "hub" areas.
Overall; despite the gripes mentioned above, Owlboy does an outstanding job of just being a fun game that is nice to look at, though it is not perfect, it is definitely a good game.

This is one of the most polished simulators you're likely to ever play. It's largely the same feel of Euro Truck Simulator 2 because it's the same company and game engine. You just get to play in California and Nevada instead of England and France. You also get more American style trucks like Peterbilt. The driving itself feels very realistic and I play with a wired Xbox 360 controller on basic controls (accelerate, brake/reverse, automatic gears).
The weather is dynamic so sometimes it will be raining or you'll be driving at night before watching the sunrise. It's a very relaxing game if you want it to be, but I tend to turn on the radio. You can choose from a variety of actual streaming radio stations right inside the game. My favorite is KNAC which is a real life heavy metal station.
Outside of driving, most of the game revolves around you buying new trucks and managing a growing business. You will hire employees and gain experience to deliver more dangerous supplies which grant you more money. A piece of advice is I would save up a little money with quick deliveries and then get a loan from the bank to buy your first truck. The game really opens up once you get your own vehicle as it allows for free roaming.
I would recommend this for those with actual friends, or people who are fine with playing with complete strangers. Mini golf is a blast, and that's true here.

Despite being incomplete / early access, this is a satisfying Tetris-like match-3 game.
The lack of explanations / instructions is a bit frustrating, but once you realize how things work, you get hooked. The sample screenshots show a how to play screen, but I don't actually remember seeing it!
The basic game play is simple:
You have a hierarchy of alchemical ingredients. Each time you match three or more of them, they disappear and are replaced with a single ingredient one step higher. This new ingredient could trigger other combinations.
Like Tetris you are given rotatable pieces to place and you lose if the pieces reach the top of the screen.
Unlike Tetris reaction time is not a factor, the pieces don't drop until you click. Also the pieces aren't actually static. If you have three ingredients in an L shape, you could rotate it into a straight line. If you have a four piece square it can be turned into a diamond. Lastly, when the piece is dropped, each ingredient will drop as far as it can, it will not leave empty space.

Beautiful art, silky-smooth controls, and the charm of a Studio Ghibli film. Although cinematic sequences can feel over-long, they play out like little vignettes and rarely feel cheesy.
Going into Owlboy, I was worried it might come off as cloying or twee, but the tone feels about on par with a Zelda game, and it's got a surprising emotional depth to it. D-Pad studio pushes each pixel to its storytelling maximum, and Otus' animations are stunning in their cartoonish authenticity.
With Owlboy, D-Pad studio has created something that's practically beyond categorization, with elements of twin-stick shooters, shoot-em-ups, platformers, and Metroidvanias all rolled into one cohesive package. The level design never feels cookie-cutter, and each area provides a whole array of new challenges that defy comparison in the hi-bit indie genre.
This game, to me, is a must-play, and one of the finest that 2016 has to offer.

Before I start, I actually have about 6+ extra hours on it already, having played this game previously on my girlfriend's computer, so my current time on time spent playing this game isn't exactly accurate.
I have to say I love this game personally. It's cute, fun, and addictive. It's probably my favorite that I have in my steam library right now. That being said, this is one of those situations where I wish steam had a "meh" button instead of simply recommending or not recommending a game.
So here's the way the game works. (only game mechanics, no story-spoilers) The item shop gameplay is pretty simple. Buy low, sell high, try to make enough to pay off your debt each week. You're restricted on the amount of actions you can do each day. This whole part of the game plays like one of those in-browser flash games. That isn't exactly a bad thing as a whole. The art style is pleasing to look at enough to keep you playing and the game still feels rewarding when you actually figure out how it works. As the game adds more and more to the way the game works, it becomes much more interesting and challenging to play.
There's a kind of dungeon-crawling mode in which you can use to find new items to sell, and I'm betting this is where players really spend 80% of their time. Some commenters say it's too easy, but I disagree. It took me five failed attempts to escape from the first, easiest set of dungeons. You can only escape on certain floors, if you 'die' you can only bring one of your treasures back with you, and the monsters that spawn are very annoying. All of this creates incredibly difficult combat for such a pleasant game. Honestly I love that as well. The maps, simple enemies, and very simple combat system remind me of a top-down version of Dark Cloud. The dungeons are painful to get through, but it's  also nice to see a game that occassioanally throws sand in your eyes, instead of easing up. It's something I'd expect from a 10-20 year old combat game, rather than a modern seemingly-casual capitalism sim. It's still fair and I can't bring myself to blame the game for my failures in the dungeons.
Now for the negatives. Once again, the combat is very basic, your enemies are very basic, and well even the shop management is simpler than it could've been. I think that do it well, but it does leave you wanting a bit more.
A huge issue I have with this game is the translation company, and I originally intended to avoid buying this game for myself at all.
First, the translations are just awful at some points. Maybe I'm just too aware of linguistic issues to overlook it, but there are *so many* moments where the word choices just scream "look at my creative translation, isn't it cool?", when many other translations would've fit better. The point of the translation is to draw attention away from the language use, to forget that the material even came from another language in the first place so you can focus on the story, but when they use obscure words like &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; or made-up words like "yayifications", you're no longer experiencing the story of Recette but having it told to you through an amateur translator. It's really difficult not to get immediately pulled out of the immersion in the story. There's at least one positive aspect of the translations, in that however distracting their translations may be, at least it does fit the characters' personalities. Still, such a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥job makes you struggle to maintain your investment in what's happening in the story.
The second issue is that Carpe Fulgur (the company that translated this into English) has a reputation of changing parts of the story in the translation. The idea of a localization is to best adapt the game to the target region, but the changes they make seem to concern things that have no real legal or social ramifications in the first place. The fact that these changes are unstated makes me lack trust in a faithful, in-tact representation of the game's story and dialogue.
This is why I was content to avoid giving them any of my money. I only bought it myself for two reasons.
1: It was on sale.
2: I'm learning Japanese so I might as well practice using this game on my own computer. I don't really plan to run it in the English version at all.
To sum it all up
+addictive, fun
+challenging yet simple and fair
-shoddy translations work
-questionable business practices of the distributor, thus untrusting that the game was localized as intended.
If it sounds like fun, more power to you. But the negatives, at least in principle, are enough for me to warrant a downvote. At least until Steam adds a "meh" button.

Hand of Fate is really something out of the ordinary;
Designed as a card collecting/dungeon brawler game, it tries a fresh, new approach to both genres.
Description to how the game works; (thought I'd put it a bit after the pro and cons, as it's a bit mundane to read.)
At the start of each new dungeon, you'll get to choose, which cards are in your own "equipment" deck and which cards you want to add to the dealer's deck. So you decide whether you want this extra shield or ring, or rather add an extra sword into the deck. The same thing is possible with your dealer's deck, as it's your call to make your game easier and miss out on those card tokens, which you need for new cards, equipment as well as encounters, or choose the cards, which are yet to be beaten and try your best on the way.
The dealer lays out a dungeon with the chosen cards, in which you navigate around with your little figurine, kinda like a board game. From time to time you'll encounter a monster or a trap, from where the game will switch into a Arkam City-style 3rd person combat system, which is debateably the weakest part of the game, in which you can move around a small area, dodge, attack and counter attacks.
I really hope you found this review helpful in aiding your decision towards buying this game.

I have enjoyed Conan Exiles so far.  After an almost-ragequit when my bedroll disappeared (it's one-use only), I settled in and have had a great time collecting, crafting, and building.  The building is a ton of fun, and it's easy to spend hours just building the next room onto your castle.
Pros:
- Intuitive building
- Lots of crafting to do
- Brutal setting (if you're into that sort of thing)
- Looks great
- Not sure how deep it goes yet, but the lore seems interesting
Cons:
- Servers have had their issues, though they seem much better on day 3
- Can be very grindy (though this can be changed in server settings)
- Combat is pretty weak at this point, hopefully improves quickly
- Every once and awhile the snap function gets a bit wonky while building, but it always seems possible to get it right with a bit of patience
Overall, if you're a fan of survival games and crafting/building, there's a ton to get into here.  Recommended for fans of survival games.  Not currently recommended for those who prioritize combat.

Currently the most enjoyable game I've had the pleasure of playing. At first there's a lot of trial and error involved. It can be difficult to get the whole feudal paradigm of medieval Europe. Normally in strategy games one is used to be some sort of an illicit and unseeable god-like creature making decisions and having the gameworld react to them in a hivemind fashion. This game really stands out because it actually places you as a locatable, almost real life character inside of a world full of other people that will react to you depending on your actions, status and traits. This simple novum ends up defining the entire gameplay in a very appealing and unique way, engrossing you for hours and hours in intrigue, misery, joy, luck, and all kinds of very human emotions and reactions.
Despite all this whimsical nonsense it still is a true strategy. And even though the 'art of war' in itself may not be the most challenging part of the game, once you get the hang of it. Managing an empire and your ability to produce a eugenically stable line of succession is! Be prepared to see your hard earned empire fall into chaos, only to re-emerge on the other side of Europe as a freefought vassal in a newly established kingdom.
And above all this unique gameplay, historical content, loads of DLC, dark intrigue and nice sound & visuals: the game is actually very funny and 'light'. With lots of funny remarks and meta-jokes to make you enjoy the many hours of game-addiction that will follow.
Furthermore: these games are always in development. Lots of new DLC coming out every couple of months inclusing bug patches and rebalancing work.
Extra kuudos when you consider yourself something of a history freak.

The biggest single merit of Murdered is likely that the conclusions it frequently prompts the player to draw are actually quite sensible, which alone unfortunately puts the game head and shoulders above most detective games. The game rarely feels like a pixel hunt, and the protagonist's psychometric ability provides means of intuitively verifying the conclusions, instead of them simply remaining educated guesses, as is often the case in detective stories, both those found in games and other media.
If there's one gripe I have, it's the fairly obscene amount of collectibles, which have been scattared across the game world for no reason given. Some of these relate rather closely to the story, but are hidden well enough to cause furstration for anyone who wishes to experience the story in full. Others seem to have little to with anything at all, and appear to only be in the game to add to its otherwise quite short length -- despite what some reviewers have states, the game world is definitely not "vast", and even a casual completionist like myself who checks every nook and cranny and walks everywhere finished it in under 10 hours. The story is focused enough to by no means feel rushed, however, and while the dialogue is nothing much to write home about, the character arcs all draw to a satisfactory close and the story in general holds together very well.

Crusader Kings II is one of the best grand strategy games I have ever had the pleasure of playing. The game has beautiful graphics, execellent gameplay mechanics, an engine that is heads above other competitors, and challenge that keeps bringing players back for more. Add on the dozens and dozens of modifications and DLCs this game brings Grand Strategy to a whole new level.
This being said, it is worth mentioning that there is somewhat of a learning curve and the instructions, at least for me, seemed more difficult and confusing than simply jumping in to the game. As well, some of the events and other parts of the game are difficult to fully appreciate without knowledge of the time period. This being said, the game does  simply some very interesting and dynamic developments from the period that could be interesting. These shortcomings also only really matter for those who studdy the subject.
Another personal desire/qualm is the fact that one cannot play as the Papacy or any explicitly religous vassal. This comes despite being allowed to play as such powerful characters as the Caliphs of the Near East. The problem is that it would add a whole new level of replayability.
Yet despite these few minor gripes, it is a funj dymanic game you can spend many hours in creating your own stories. The replayability of it is fantastic and it offers a diverse and interesting experience for anyone into either history, grand strategy, or both. As well, if you are a EU IV player you can actually import your CK II game if you have the DLC (which is best bought during a summer sale or anytime you don't need to play full price. All in all a magnificent game and a must own if you enjoy the period.
