You’ve been murdered, it’s a real bummer. But now you get the chance to find out who it was and seek justice from beyond the grave. Or you would if you played this.
Enter Ronan a bad guy turned good trying to stop a murderer on a killing spree but wouldn’t you know it you wind up just another one of their victims. But with unfinished business to attend to you hang around for a while and haunt the halls of Salem city searching for clues that could lead you to solving your own murder and ascending to heaven.
Or at least that’s the plan but as the recently departed not many people will talk to you. Enter the one witness to your death Joy who also happens to be psychic, after a lot of convincing the duo team up and take down the evil together. The story is certainly an intriguing and unique one. I have not seen a murder mystery from a dead person’s perspective before and with the amounts of twists and turns that come flying at you as you progress it will get you enthralled right to the end.
The game is stacked full of collectables, over a hundred of them to be precise, each with its own story. They all fit seamlessly into the town of Salem with its terrible past and not too stellar present. The world is more or less open world with you being able to travel from one location to another through the hub of the down town area. Each part of the world is beautifully designed and looks great mixing an old ghostly past with the present to make something new.
The game also features a huge amount of side quests and cases to solve. Speaking of which the detective mode is also something of an oddity, find a crime and solve it with clues found in the environment and placed together like pieces of a puzzle, I found a lot of pleasure recreating crimes to try and figure out what had happened and who the culprit was.
Now onto the main meat of the game combat…. There is none. Well that’s not true, there are a few enemies and by few I mean around 12 in the whole game and the only thing that happens is when they see you a QTE begins, win and you can proceed, lose and you have to start a short ways back. I would classify this more as an interactive novel than a game. Not that it’s a bad thing, but just be sure that’s what you are looking for before you delve in.
This game offers a lot and is a great distraction if you are looking for a unique experience that’s heavy on the narrative but light in most other places. At full price I can’t really recommend it but on sale you should pick this up and just enjoy your time in purgatory.

Overall i highly recommend getting this, the price is justified for the content and the countless hours you will spend cruising across america, and with the Arizona DLC to come, then many more (will we see all 50 states? i hope so) this game will just keep on giving.

Hard Reset represents everything that used to be good about FPS games. It comes to us by the grace of some of the folks behind Painkiller, and is comparable to games like that and Serious Sam in its sensibilites. Numerical health, hordes of enemies, very big guns all with alternate fire options and no need to be reloaded, gigantic bosses and lots of secret areas to find. It even has a new game plus function, so you can keep on buying upgrades and try out weapons you missed. The story is a bit thin, being the tale of a gruff, alcoholic enforcer who rebels against his corporate overlords, but that's not what games like this are about. It's a game about fun, and blowing up robots in the most graphically pleasing way possible. All of the weapons are useful, and you will have to switch between them quickly. Luckily, switching your CLN firearm or NRG weapon's modes does not reset their cooldowns, so you can to keep up a sustained fire rate, which you will need to do to keep up with Hard Reset's incredibly aggressive enemies. It's also extremely affordable. So if you dare, then let Hard Reset take you back to the golden days when men were men, cover was for amateurs and pulling the trigger made things go boom. I recently replayed this game and enjoyed it even more then the first time I played it, as I also had the chance to play the free Exile DLC, which adds several new levels to the campaign. It seriously beefs up the game's total length and adds a more satisfying conclusion, as well as another boss fight. If you didn't play Hard Reset when it first released, or you did and found it lacking, you'd be doing yourself a favor to give it (another) shot.

I would like to start this review by saying that this game took 9 years to make.  9 years that were totally worth waiting for.  This is what game developers should aspire to.
Owlboy is a short, metroidvania-style game made by D-Pad Studio.  I stumbled upon this game shortly before its release, because Savant: Ascent (A previous title by the same studio) was such a fun game, I wanted to try it out again.  When I reinstalled Savant, I noticed a small news article on the game page talking about Owlboy's upcoming release.
D-Pad Studio has, in my opinion, the best pixel art style out there.  And Owlboy is no exception.  Througout the entirety of the game, I was amazed simply by how beautiful every area was.  This game has no map, but it's not needed, because the great art style lends itself to some gorgeous landmarks, to help you find your way.  Sadly, there is no form of fast-travel, but it isn't necessary, due to the speed at which you can traverse to a new area.
Savant: Ascent really had done gameplay well.  Owlboy kept to these tight controls and fun gameplay, while adding a short, but powerful story.  While sometimes difficult, no part of the game ever felt frustrating, and I always kept coming back.  This was mostly due to the varied cast, all of whom had well written dialouge.  As such, many of the game's characters were some of the most relatable characters I've come across in recent years.
Owlboy may be a short game, but there are a decent amount of collectables, and I could definitely play through the game again, to experience some of the emotions this game will bring out.
This is one of the best games I've played in years.  Do NOT let this one pass you by.

Alot of time has gone by since I first made a serious review of this game, so I think, as it has made significant steps in the right direction, I should update my review of it.
Kingdom Wars 2 has all the makings of a classic, aswell as a few things that make it definately stand out, some things seem like poor choices... i don't know why there's a progression system in an RTS, or why its next to impossible to get any of the high level crafting objects, but those are just nitpicks, so lets tear into the game as a whole shall we? I'll be judging it as if it was a finished project so anything that ends up being ironed out when you read this may no longer be applicable.
The game features the standard 3 factions, a faction with expensive troops, a faction with tankish troops, and a faction with cheap troops, however each faction works in very unique ways such as how they gather their resources and how they build their armies, which is a neat thing to see in an RTS.
Kingdom wars 2 is also the first RTS I've seen to feature zombification as a mechanic, and its more or less clunky, it really just makes sieges more of a hassle and slows the game down, but it has its high moments, there's a lot tension when a massive army of your troops or an enemy's army has been defeated near something important, and you need to clear the area of corpses before either: your enemy arrives again or the sun sets.
The strategy side of this game seems fairly weak, sad to say, this hasn't changed at all in the past year, no doubt this is because the community for this game is fairly small, and the armies themselves aren't balanced ESPECIALLY orcs. The people who play this game regularly seem to play it exclusively for the survival mode, which is kinda a shame for me.
I'm happy to see the majority of glitchs have been ironed out, and the remaining lag is probably just the fault of my own computer or internet, i'm not sure.
This game is still not finished, though it is finally ready for release, I suppose. The units are grossly unbalanced, but and the devs do seem very invested in the community around this game, so I'm actually going to go ahead and recommend you support them still.

First off, though it had a rough release with a lot of nasty glitches, these have been since corrected. The voice acting is still cringe-worthy, but the writing is epic. So with the only real two issues out of the way, let's get into why Disgaea is amazing.
First off, Disgaea understands its audience intimately. People who played FFT and similar games loved the in-depth story arcs, the incredible customization, the complex tactical combat and having so much extra stuff to do that playthroughs which take over one hundred hours still allow for immense replay value anyway. Disgaea takes all of these concepts and expands upon them to absurd levels.
So, story-wise, the story itself is absurd, yet amazing. The specific dialogue is exceptionally self-aware and knows just how silly it is - for example, at one point the "protagonists" (honestly, it's more like you're playing the antagonists), are attacked by obvious power ranger wannabes... and then during the ranger's attempted stereotypical transformation sequence, they just get shot. With a gun. And then throw a fit because you're not allowed to do that during a heroic transformation sequence. The end-of-chapter previews are... useless for knowing what will happen in the next chapter as they usually have little to no relation whatsoever, yet are amusing as hell, so yay anyway.
The gameplay's amazing, with puzzles to solve in-combat, particularly within the item world sections. Being able to throw characters and objects allows for some surprisingly complex tasks and unique level design, and your choice of abilities and characters allows for a lot of customization in how you play.
Disgaea's greatest strength, though, is its replay factor. It's a grindy game. That's the point. If you like these types of games, you generally also enjoy maxing out characters in a wide variety of tasks and classes, teaching them to be amazing at everything they do. The level cap is 9999, and you can even specialize weapons and armour, or even health potions if you want, by going into the item itself and battling your way through such to increase the stats or to defeat special hidden characters in the items which give bonuses and can be transferred to other items, allowing for rather ridiculous levels of customization and augmentation. It's a game that's fun to play, and it goes out of its way to give you excuses to drag the game on longer, such as a wealth of hidden bosses and extra story arcs to be unlocked well after the base game is beaten. Given how surprisingly long the base game is, and that much extra content being available, it's easy to spend literally hundreds of hours playing Disgaea.
Basically the story is ridiculous and epic, the characters are interesting and well-defined in personality, the gameplay's great and it goes out of its way to make sure you have every excuse to keep playing. It's basically the perfect tactical RPG custom tailored to be exactly what that player base enjoys.
That you get to play as the villains is really just a bonus. =P

I had already played Metro 2033 back in 2010 but I could never finish it as my copy was pirated and a game breaking bug prevented me from doing so. Well, as it turns out, Metro 2033 was far worse than I had it in my memories. So, I didn't expect much when I started playing Metro Last Light. Boy, I was in for a pleasant surprise.
Once again you step into Artyom's boots, who has now become a ranger in the Spartan Order after the events of the first game. Khan, a dude that helped you kill the Dark Ones in the first game, shows up and tells you that there is one of them left. A child so-to-speak. He tells you it was a mistake, that the Dark Ones only wanted to help and so on. So now, you set out on a mission to save the last of the Dark Ones. At least that's what you think you'll be doing. But just like in the first game, you embark on a journey in- and outside the Metro while stirring up the sinister plans of the Reds, the Nazis and all of the other scum.
Story and characters have improved enormously in comparison to Metro 2033. Now, you as Artyom have a real motivation: a personal vendetta that ties in perfectly with the overall objective to save the Dark One. This time around, the Dark One doesn't get out of focus like in the first game. Instead, it plays a massive role in the second half of the game. I'm not going to tell you anything about that, find out for yourself.  All of the new characters are very interesting and are finally fleshed out. Characters from the last game that show up again however aren't. They're still the dull, boring cutouts of characters.
In Metro 2033 it kind of went like this: here's a horror level, here's an action-packed level, here's a sneaking level, here's a level to explore a peaceful station. This time around, the different aspects of the metro: the horror, the disgust, the sparks of hope have been balanced out more properly. Save from the very beginning, you feel way more invested into the story than in Metro 2033, because it has much better flow. It feels more complete, while the first game felt like a collection of short stories, which was due to the writers trying to adapt the novel as accurately as possible.
Overall, it feels that the writers managed to overcome the source material and finally started to do their own thing. Metro Last Light isn't as accurate of an adaptation and damn, it feels fresh. Virtual copies of the Metro books also don't show up as frequently as in the previous game. Last but not least, the singleplayer is noticeably longer (Metro 2033: ~7 hours/ Metro Last Light: ~10 hours).
Less fights inside the Metro, more fights outside the Metro. Damn, that's exactly what I wanted. However, no major changes considering the FPS - typical gameplay. AI hasn't changed much. Once you're noticed, they'll charge at you until they're all dead. A few new weapons, new type of mines, but still almost all weapons feel alike. Get a shotgun, a semi-automatic gun, a revolver, put a silencer on all of them and you're good to go. Which leads me to...
The levels have become bigger and more open concerning what you want to do first (because objectives are still very linear). Sadly, Metro Last Light doesn't exactly put this to a good use. It forces you to sneak by everyone (even more so than in the first game), not killing a single person, unless it's a cutscene. Or else you won't get the good ending. Really stupid decision, for a FPS. However, if you don't give a damn about which ending you get (good or bad - they are almost exactly alike save for a narration in the good ending) that's not that bad. Well, it only is, if you want to get all of the achievements.
Metro Last Light runs noticeably smoother than Metro 2033. Even on my system, I managed to play on high settings without any framedrops whatsoever. It isn't perfect though, there are some chapters where the game will keep crashing for no reason at all if you die only one time. So, either don't die at all or you'll have to restart the chapter.
Metro Last Light perfectly shows what the developers are aiming for with Metro Exodus. Namely: an open-world  approach (kind of) and more fleshed out characters. Sounds good in theory but if they don't fix the obvious flaws (like the forced sneaking) I don't think I'll be as satisfied as I am now, comparing this game to Metro 2033. So, obviously I hope that Metro Exodus will be an improvement as big as this one.

Overall, I think Metro Last Light is a pretty good game. It's not an excellent game, it's not a great game. It's simply a good game. The enviroments are very enjoyable scenary wise, and the graphics are pretty good all things considered, however, the story line is a little diluted. It feels rather slow and uninteresting, at least, in my opinion. I didn't feel invested in the character's lives or outcomes. I didn't care if they lived or died, I just wanted to shoot up Metro Nazis and Communists as well as mutated beasts of the surface.
There were times when I was playing where I felt extremely immersed yet get stopped by the characters to run around the city aimlessly, or I'm running through the sewers yet can't proceed until the slow moving NPC catches up to me. This may not bother you, but as a person who games for instant action and fun, this was an issue.
Additionally, the game mechanics felt clunky at times. There is no ingame FOV editor. You have to go access your .ini file and edit that manually. Even when you do that, status effects (like damage, blood)  will not apply to the entire screen. Only to the area where you FOV is "supposed" to be. The gunplay was pretty well done but your movement is a little awkward sometimes.
The game has a very linear path it wants you to follow, and on numerous occasions, I'd see rocks and boxes I tried to jump on only to be completely blocked by an invisible wall. These piles of rocks and boxes didn't lead anywhere, most of the time it was just a single rock and a single box. There's no reason you shouldn't be able to get up there, other than the game simple didn't want you to. It was very cumbersome. Yet, make a bigger jump that's actually apart of the path you're suppose to be taking and there's no issue. I just don't understand what the game creators acomplished by this.
So overally I feel like the game is definitely enjoyable, definitely fun for the five dollars you will probably buy it for on a Steam sale, but I couldn't imagine dropping the full retail price on this. It's really just too cumbersome to be called a masterpiece, but not cumbersome enough it fails to be enjoyable.

I am a huge medieval RTS fan. It's been a very long time since we have another good medieval RTS, I can't remember the last good one released in recent years. All we have these days are those futuristic ones with guns and mechs yawn...
Then I stumbled upon this game.
+ Beautiful graphics. Nothing outstanding for 2015 but for a RTS game it still looks very good.
+ The three factions in this game are very different from each other. Can we have more factions though? Why every RTS game these days has exactly 3 factions? I know it's quality over quantity but still!
+ Great wall defense mechanics. Pouring oil down to the invaders!
+ Fire arrows. Archers in this game have much more impact than just being some low-HP fire support.
+ After a battle, you can send peasants to loot corpses for gold and wood. Nice.
+ Interesting crafting system, with different cards for different factions.
+ Good price for a game like this. Look up other recently released RTS games on Steam, they are very overpriced despite just being clones of Starcraft, C&C etc.
- Variety of buildings and units, hope more will get added.
- Not really a fan of the zombies. More polishing would make this a + instead of a - though.
- Bugs & optimization, but not really a con here since the game is still in early access.
I'm excited to see new patches and content added to this game.
As of right now I cannot not consider this one of the great medieval RTS games yet, but lots of potential here, don't screw it up guys.

This is one of my favorite games of all time. Why the negative review?
The game is broken in so many ways. I bought the most expensive EA pack back before the game was released. Actually, my whole guild bought EA packs. So that was $200.00 I spent. Long story short, I probably spent over $1000.00 ingame. It's really easy to do. That, in fact, is the games biggest flaw. The devs want your money. I feel like they want your money before they want you to have fun. That's a huge problem. From the get go they didn't want to open more servers. They opened one after another very slowly even thought it took hours upon hours waiting in line to get into the game at launch. Then eventually all of that was fixed. Then came the hackers and bots. You could walk around and see when a house was going to expire due to unpaid taxes. Then you could camp that spot once the timer was about to run out. Low and behold... it would get sniped. Plot sniping was a problem that developed due to hackers. They could be ANYWHERE in the map and somehow snipe up that plot you were stalking faster than you could say, "Ya.... NOOOO!"
Then came Hasla. Don't even get me started on Hasla. So Hasla had some of the best weapons in the game. You had to grind mobs who dropped these stone things then turn those in to create a weapon. every mob dropped one. There were about 7 different types. You generally had groups big enough so that 2 people were assigned to each type of stone. 7 stones, 14 people. So you had a 1 out of 7 chance of getting your stone from a mob and then a 1 out of 2 chance of actually getting the stone if yours dropped. Also, you needed 150 of them. Then a month or 2 after that, the devs released Hasla tier 2 and 3 AT THE SAME TIME. We were all sick and tired of grinding and all FINALLY finished grinding out weapons out when BOOM. Now we had to brind all over again for about 3 times the amount of stones. I think they were actually called runes. But thats not the worst part. Hasla was also contested and the reds ALWAYS seemed to own the area that you needed to turn the stones in. SO yeah. You had to grind for like 15 hours to get all your stones. Then shortly after that I think they released chrystal shores. Yeah, you guessed it. Better weapons than Hasla. More grinding. FML.
But the bots. The Land Snipers. The Hackers. It never ended. Whenever you wanted something, someone was there to take it from you.
But didn't I say this is my favorite game of all time?
Yep. Because I also murdered, plundered, raided and conquered. We once attacked a fortress for no reason. The guild called in all their people to hold up there turf. They couldn't hold it. We pushed them COMPLETELY out of there fortress and into the spawn area. They couldn't leave it if they wanted to. Good times. I mean, we couldn't take the fort from them or anything, but it was a lot of fun to do it anyways. They looked like fools after that. We did that to them. And that is what is awesome about this game. You wanna visit pirate island and take it over for a couple hours and kill all the pirates? Go ahead. You wanna run around enemy territory and murder people for no reason? Go ahead. Do you wanna go into the starter zone of an enemy faction and shoot off fireworks? You can do that. Do you wanna attache your ship to a blimp and learn to fly? Yes? Well you can do that.

Currently the most enjoyable game I've had the pleasure of playing. At first there's a lot of trial and error involved. It can be difficult to get the whole feudal paradigm of medieval Europe. Normally in strategy games one is used to be some sort of an illicit and unseeable god-like creature making decisions and having the gameworld react to them in a hivemind fashion. This game really stands out because it actually places you as a locatable, almost real life character inside of a world full of other people that will react to you depending on your actions, status and traits. This simple novum ends up defining the entire gameplay in a very appealing and unique way, engrossing you for hours and hours in intrigue, misery, joy, luck, and all kinds of very human emotions and reactions.
Despite all this whimsical nonsense it still is a true strategy. And even though the 'art of war' in itself may not be the most challenging part of the game, once you get the hang of it. Managing an empire and your ability to produce a eugenically stable line of succession is! Be prepared to see your hard earned empire fall into chaos, only to re-emerge on the other side of Europe as a freefought vassal in a newly established kingdom.
And above all this unique gameplay, historical content, loads of DLC, dark intrigue and nice sound & visuals: the game is actually very funny and 'light'. With lots of funny remarks and meta-jokes to make you enjoy the many hours of game-addiction that will follow.
Furthermore: these games are always in development. Lots of new DLC coming out every couple of months inclusing bug patches and rebalancing work.
Extra kuudos when you consider yourself something of a history freak.

This is one of the most polished simulators you're likely to ever play. It's largely the same feel of Euro Truck Simulator 2 because it's the same company and game engine. You just get to play in California and Nevada instead of England and France. You also get more American style trucks like Peterbilt. The driving itself feels very realistic and I play with a wired Xbox 360 controller on basic controls (accelerate, brake/reverse, automatic gears).
The weather is dynamic so sometimes it will be raining or you'll be driving at night before watching the sunrise. It's a very relaxing game if you want it to be, but I tend to turn on the radio. You can choose from a variety of actual streaming radio stations right inside the game. My favorite is KNAC which is a real life heavy metal station.
Outside of driving, most of the game revolves around you buying new trucks and managing a growing business. You will hire employees and gain experience to deliver more dangerous supplies which grant you more money. A piece of advice is I would save up a little money with quick deliveries and then get a loan from the bank to buy your first truck. The game really opens up once you get your own vehicle as it allows for free roaming.

Great FPS that manages to incorporate some innovative concepts within the "old school" formula. Weapon management in particular feels both unique and practical as you have to manage two basic guns/weapon trees. Those guns "branch out" to various others when upgraded in certain stations that are scattered throughout each map. Transition between firing modes/guns is instant (accompanied by a weapon morph animation a-la Vanquish) . Each difficulty lvl feels just right. A check point system is utilized (and well implemented imo as each point is well placed). New Game + mode is available (allowing you to start a new campaign with all your upgrades equiped). 45 upgrades in total. Visuals are incredible and interaction with the environments is encouraged. Short length (3 full progressive playthroughs on nrml,hard, insane approx 17hrs), a weird sprint mechanism (takes some time to get used to) and an out-of-place score (sounds like the Inspector Gadget theme at times) are its main drawbacks.

This game is an anomaly. Basically, if you think you will like it, then you probably will. If you aren't sure, don't. It's a much safer bet to get Euro truck sim since it is much more fleshed out.
In ATS the scaling is a bit wonky. It takes no time at all to get from las angeles to reno, which is stupid becuase that drive is like driving the entire map in ETS. Granted, the US is HUGE and would take forever to traverse if the scaling was bigger.
The start of the game is quite shakey, since there are only two states and two truck companys. I know that eventually the liscencing will come around and all will be good after more states are added. However I think DLC is terrible for video games and I personally would rather of waited a year or two more to get a super fleshed out game, rather than 30% of the content.
Lastly, the police are like, WAY to picky. I realize that trucks are slower and I get that speeding is bad, but still. It's nowhere near that bad in reality.
Now that my major beefs are out of the way, let me break down everything else
PROS
+Pretty realistic, true to real life scenery
+Overall good gameplay
+Good graphics (although very rarely glitchy)
Cons
+"Small" map (to scale).
+Incredibly small amount of trucks.
+Over reacting police.
+Slightly messed up AI.
+Accidents are either always for fault, or when they aren't you don't get money to help recover from the wreck.
+Hud is exactly the same as ETS
+Gui is nearly identical to ETS
As you can see my list of cons is larger than my list of pros, howeve I like the game to much to let that waiver my opinion. In all, Most of my issues will be patched in time, but like I said earlier, I would much rather have a fully fleshed out game a little late rather than have a half crap one where you have to wait to get the full experience. It loses it's awesomeness when you have to wait like that, after you bought the game.
TLDR: All in all, it's a solid enough game, and I really do enjoy it. If you think youd like it, then you probably will. If not then don't get it/

Early Access: It's interesting. I look forward to seeing the polished final product. This is not an MMO, you have to scour through a server list. You also have to hope the server will be there tomorrow if you wish to progress from where you left off. Even when the ping is great, like under 90 there is rubber banding, enemy glitching all around and you can't fight them very well. There is a lot left to be done to optimize the game. There might be a memory leak, it takes a huge amount of cpu to run, 68% of my CPU, I got the most current nvidia driver which was 'optimized' for this release, but at the end of the first session I got a nvidia kernel error and had to reinstall. This has never happened with a finished game. I have over 16 gigs of ram, this was using up nearly 6 gigs by it self.
There have been a few patches since then and no more nvidia crashing after reinstalling the driver. I hope this gets stabilized soon. The official servers are broken out by play style which I DO LIKE A LOT. They have the PVP servers, they have Roleplay Servers and they have PVE servers. I opted for PVE since it's hard enough to get started and learn the game without having someone rushing out of new spawn zone and pking taking all you've worked for over the course of an hour and having to start over again.
At this point I've learned to stay alive for quite some time. Have not ventured inland. Just spent time looking for a place to call home. I discovered that people can join a server, put down a bed roll and maybe never come back, but that spot of ground is taken and is inaccessible. I hope those bedrolls eventually decay?
So anyway, people have been helpful and the crafting is pretty simple to work out, easy to get the first gear put together once you figure it out.
I say it has lots of potential and people should definately expect to do this with friends, it is a lot easier that way. But it is also possible to solo play at least for a little while before joining a clan just to learn the basics.
There is supposed to be a single player mode, I tried it, it leads to a 'create a server menu' so it's not a solo game that just starts up. I don't know anything about servers but I expect you can just make the population set to 1 and lock it so no one can join in to make a solo game or just a simple family co-op game.

I do like you can select your own tolerence level so no matter what the other guy can see you can decide to have a modesty setting, partial modesty or full nudity enabled client side. I guess the full nudity is for the roleplayers later down the line when they add in the capturing of other players...ok so maybe some funny business for the roleplayers...giggles for the rest.

Conan Exiles has made a great first impression on me as well as many other people.
Unlike many other games these days, be it; Ark, Rust, and other similar Survival Games, Conan Exiles takes a fresh, not-yet seen take on the Survival World genre.
I will open with the Cons the game has at this current point in time.
Cons
- Glitchy Enemies, Creatures, Mobs
- Some broken Animations
- (with two monitors) The mouse doesnt stay in the games window and when looking around will drift to the other monitor and in the event of using the mouse to click/attack, will tab out of the game.
- Sub-par combat. No real skill needed to click your mouse and hit something.
This is all I have had a problem with currently though Early Access is usually riddled with bugs. It is to be expected!
Pros
- High Quality Graphics
- Immerisve Introduction
- Crafting System works in a way that makes sense (different times for more complex tools)
- Unique world type. (No other game I know of has really gone with the mythological side to a survival game)
- More to do than just build and level up! (Worship religions, enslave people, start empires!)
At this point in time, I do recommend Conan Exiles! The game has a good deal of features as well as very responsive developers and a good community. The game has great potential and I would recommend people support this team of developers to make a one-of-a-kind game that will be like no other!

A lovely skill-based coffee break game that follows the rule of fun to a tee. It combines the best of 'quick fix' games from teh '80s and '90s with the sleek aesthetics, polish, and indie quirkiness you'd expect from today's market. It's really a delightful thing and I'm a fan, most definitely. It feels a little like a runner, in execution, as the name implies. So it's got a touch of Canabalt to it, but without the randomisation. Instead of that, it has hand-designed levels which make for some sublime gameplay, and quite a bit of verticality to it as well, so in that respect it reminds me of N.
There's a bit of a karting design ethos in there, too. If you've played Sonic & All Stars or Mario Kart, then you'll understand what I mean when I say it has power-ups that can be used to♥♥♥♥♥♥with the other players in a variety of entertaining ways. As each super hero races toward the goal, the other heroes can use those power-ups to even the playing field. I think the only one that feels a bit cheap is the golden grappling hook, but I actually think that's more on me than the devs because I have bad sight. So I would like to be able to turn power-ups on/off individually, but that's all I can think of that comes even close to a complaint.
And it really shouldn't mar your opinion of this game, either. You should get this even if you have no one else to play it with as the bots are well done (with difficulty levels), and there are a bunch of single-player levels which introduce you to the mechanics as well. All in all, I really can't see anything wrong with this game. And since I'm not the sort to worry about offending the sensibilities of people who believe that only games with huge budgets deserve big scores, I'd give this one a [whatever implies a perfect score to you].
For what it sets out to do, it does it with aplomb. And what it is, it is sublimely so. This is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be and doesn't let anything stand in its way. There's no baggage, there's no drama, it's just a fun game to play to kill an amount of time in one of the most entertaining ways with. I even want to praise it for the depictions of its characters, I won't say too much, but as a disabled person I'm finely attuned to prejudices and there's really none to be found, here.
Could I give this a more glowing review? Probably, but you've likely already stopped reading by now and rushed off to buy it. Good for you!

Positives:
The game has a lovely concept regarding deathmatches and the like, and the feeling of swinging a sword and keeping a shield up to ward off a folley of arrows is rather fun. The graphics are prettty good, and the lighting and texture work seems to be the key feature in regards to graphics. If you're also into medieval-based games that aren't over-the-top with fantasy designs in armor and weapons, and more towards historical accuracy, this game would be for you. Since characters have a battle-charge dialogue, lots of servers are full of players who like to do some light-hearted role-playing for poops and giggles, and surprisingly few speak in childish L337 text. For a game with a low profile, the community is still large enough to find populated servers to join.
Negatives:
It's a rather small game. The content itself is rather limited. For example, there aren't enough things to customize your class with. Sure, there are helmets and weapons, but there's maybe, at the most, 10 or so helmets to choose from, maybe three shields, if you class can use them, and virtually no body armor or tabards to apply, aside from the two meger DLC pieces for every class. It would be nice to have a lot more, even if it's merely cosmetic. Who doesn't love to customize?
Although the lighting and texture work is rather well-done, the map meshes, such as houses, towers, walls, etc. are clearly used in an older version of UNREAL, and look rather simple, especially if you fly around in spectator mode. If you've ever played a game like Unreal 2004, Cube2: Sauerbraten, Red Eclipse, etc. you'd know what I mean. Good texture work is slapped on rather basic geometry.
The music is rather dull. It's not envigorating enough for the battlefield and is almost like elevator music, or an idle theme, not even atmospheric for an open world RPG. This is surprising coming from an Unreal-inspired game, which usually has heart-pumping soundtracks. Other than that, the soldiers shouting in a battle charge make up for that, and gets the in-game text chat really into sarcastic role-playing.
Overall:
I'd rate this game an 8/10. The gameplay highly makes up for the little nit-picked flaws, and has a rather stable core. On the brighter side, the community, including the modding community, is still active, and there's a chance for this game to evolve in the near future, even if it's a few days away from 2016.

TLDR:
Gameplay - 7/10
Graphics - 7/10
Audio - 9/10
Controls - 7/10
Overall - 7/10
I WOULD Recommend.
Hand of Fate is an interesting title from Defiant, a hodge-podge group of Australian blue bloods and potential filled greenhorns. After launches of games on multiple platforms with varrying degrees of success this group turned to kickstarter to help get one of their more ambitious games released. After a Succesful funding of $54,095 AUD the game was released to steam with very positive reviews.
GAMEPLAY - This game offers a wide variety of different aspects. At the surface it is an RPG-like linear adventure game following a random itteration of card placements that the player picks almost at random. As the game progresses the player is introduced to both Hack-N-Slash fighting reminiscient of the Batman games which comes across somehow as both novel and trivial. Finally the player is also introduced to what lies at the heart of this game: deckbuilding. While the game appears to be centered around this aspect it is just as easy for the player to never have to do any of their own building to progress through the entirety of the game. This allows for the player to choose how they would like to play the game and allows for a game that is more immediately approachable by a wider audience. 7/10
GRAPHICS - Upon first glance of the title screen with our singular character floating and shuffling his deck of cards by magic it is easy to think the game is beautiful. The atmosphere of the games setting feels volumisically appropriate and well designed. The cards artwork is appropriate, but lacks the subtleties of a physical card game such as Magic or Munchkin. The games biggest graphical downfall comes from the animations. It is first noticed on the initial dealings of the cards that the cards aren't quite as fluent as you would want them to be from a magical card shuffling man, and that is even on the highest of settings. It is also quite apparent that the hits and strikes during the combat portions of the game seem to miss entirely but still do damage. Despite the issues with animations the graphics don't feel poor. 7/10
AUDIO - The audio in this game is very subtle. The voicework of the Dealer is well casted and recorded, and despite some repeats in dialogue feels varied enough to keep the player interested in the storyline. Background noises and sound effects always feel in place but do lack the instant recgonizability that all developers would like to obtain. The voice work however in this game is done masterfully and used in conjuntion with the simplistic soundscape and effects the audio deserves some praise. 9/10
CONTROLS - This game doesn't ever feel out of hand. I am not sure as to whether or not they recommend that you use a controller, but that was the preferred method during my playthrough. The game feels fine under keyboard and mouse as well, despite a few issues with selecting cards, the game still feels intuitive. Any control issues come down to the combat once again where the controls feels both too simplistic and without force. 7/10
GAMEPLAY - The game excels in its script. The Dealers dialogue is both humourous and insightbul at times as well as a pleasant driving force through out the game. An action RPG that lets you play through a trading card game feels new and different, however the action part of the game does feel hampered. It is easy to play the story mode through without touching the endless mode at all. Endless mode, while fun and different, feels like a remnant of Defiants IOS past. 7/10

What drew me towards this game was the aesthethics and atmosphere shown in the trailers, and I was not disappointed.
The game is presented as you, the protagonist, sitting across from the dealer, a mysterious hooded figure, to play game of cards.
Everything in the game has a representation as a playing card.
The playing field is a bunch of cards, laid out in small mazes.
Your equipment is made up of cards like weapons, helms, shields and a plethora of rings.
Your enemies are cards in 4 suites (dust, skulls, scales and plague), each of which is a theme (e.g. the card "2 of dust" is a pair of bandits).
The cards are sorted into various stacks and decks, the most important two are the equipment deck, from which you draw your rewards; and the encounter deck, from which the playing field is drawn.
The encounter deck shapes the way the game plays out, which is a mix of "choose your adventure" style events, and combat situations.
Between encounters you move your figure between cards, one per turn. As you step onto a card it is revealed, and the dealer narrates the events that ensue, while you decide how you act in the situation.
There is a wide range of different situations presented here, some result in combat, some might draw you cards from the pain deck (punishments, if your decisions or luck are bad) or the gain deck (food, gold, health, equipment).
On some encounters you play for a token, which represents one (or more!) cards to unlock for future rounds.
Aside from your inventory, you have health, food and gold as resources, all of which are important. On each turn, you consume 1 food, which heals you, unless you have no food, in which case you begin to starve. This quickly results in death, and means that you should plan a few turns ahead. And maybe not spend all your gold on shiny rings, but good instead.
Whenever you enter combat mode, you enter the world in third person mode and do battle against the monster cards the dealer has drawn for you.
Controls are fairly simple, left stick to move around, and the actions at your disposal are "attack", "counter" (if you have a shield), "weapon ability" and "use artifact" (usually buffs or area effect attacks)
While this may appear shallow at first, it becomes rather taxing once there are more than a few enemies on screen, some of which may have ranged or special attacks, or block your attacks.
I played with a controller and felt the game controlled very smoothly. I did not try mouse/keyboard at all, so cannot make a statement about it.
After you beat the tutorial, the dealer reveals to you that there are 12 champions (the "royal" cards of the suites, Jacks, Queens and Kings) for you to defeat. As you progress through the game you unlock many new equipment and encounter cards.
Out of these you build 2 decks which the rounds are based on.
But as you gain more cards, the dealer also inserts his own cards into the encounter deck, the pain deck and of course the monster deck from which your opponents are pulled.
In one session you will usually accrue a number of items making combat easier for you, but to balance it out, you will also take damage, consume resources and later might be struck by one or more of the dealer´s nasty curse cards.
These serve as a means of hampering your progress, to not make it too easy for you. They range from basic debuffs (e.g. starvation causes more damage) to severe restrictions (e.g. you can not sell items, or "the more gold you carry, the slower you move"), putting you into interesting predicaments.
Death is permanent, but especially in the beginning of the game you will mostly emerge from a round with several newly unlocked cards, as such, frustration is kept to a minimum.
Unlocking new cards is a strong incentive to keep playing, as many of the cards are interesting, and the encounter cards often form little story arcs.
I beat the game after about 20 hours, meaning I defeated all of the champions.
After beating the main game, there is also an endless mode, in which you dont construct a deck, but have all of your unlocked cards available (and so has the dealer, that sinister man.)
There were a few difficulty spikes (mostly the Jack of Scales and the King of skulls for me), but nothing too bad.
As mentioned before, the art style and graphics, as well as the beautiful music (with an oriental touch) serve to craft a very nice atmosphere.
The sinister musings of the dealer are often interesting (tough they repeat after a while, but not to the point where they are annoying)
While I can heartily recommend the game, there are a few gripes & nitpicks I have, which I will list here, in case they are a show-stopper to you:

Crusader Kings II is one of the best grand strategy games I have ever had the pleasure of playing. The game has beautiful graphics, execellent gameplay mechanics, an engine that is heads above other competitors, and challenge that keeps bringing players back for more. Add on the dozens and dozens of modifications and DLCs this game brings Grand Strategy to a whole new level.
This being said, it is worth mentioning that there is somewhat of a learning curve and the instructions, at least for me, seemed more difficult and confusing than simply jumping in to the game. As well, some of the events and other parts of the game are difficult to fully appreciate without knowledge of the time period. This being said, the game does  simply some very interesting and dynamic developments from the period that could be interesting. These shortcomings also only really matter for those who studdy the subject.
Another personal desire/qualm is the fact that one cannot play as the Papacy or any explicitly religous vassal. This comes despite being allowed to play as such powerful characters as the Caliphs of the Near East. The problem is that it would add a whole new level of replayability.
Yet despite these few minor gripes, it is a funj dymanic game you can spend many hours in creating your own stories. The replayability of it is fantastic and it offers a diverse and interesting experience for anyone into either history, grand strategy, or both. As well, if you are a EU IV player you can actually import your CK II game if you have the DLC (which is best bought during a summer sale or anytime you don't need to play full price. All in all a magnificent game and a must own if you enjoy the period.

As the game begins we find Ronan exploding out of a shattered 4th story window after a confrontation with a shadowy figure.  He awakens to find himself temporarily disembodied but that state soon becomes permanent upon the arrival of the Bell Witch Killer.  Shot 7 times with his own gun, Ronan must now solve the mystery of his own murder and in the process uncover dark secrets that have haunted Salem for centuries.
Quite a build up eh?
It is and it's worthy of it.  The story is intriguing with twists, turns and dead ends to thrill any devotee of the mystery genre.  Add in a tastefully done horror component supported by an eerie backdrop of a dark and gloomy Salem complete with lost souls, haunted houses, and frightful demons.
The game is gorgeous even on my creaky old gaming laptop ( circa 2008 ) and the controls simple.  You're led on a path similar to the Call of Duty campaign modes on the hunt for clues to your own murder.  On the way you'll find ample opportunity to complete side quests but be warned if like me you seek to earn all of the Steam achievements you must be methodical in your approach.  For me it took 2 playthroughs as there is no quicksave nor any way to go back once you've completed the final chapter of the game.
It's a casual game but it can be maddening at times.  For one, you have no onscreen map nor any way to mark your progress toward achievements.  Meaning you'll spend a lot of time running in circles to find the way forward and backtracking for that one elusive clue.
Then there's the demons.  I understand that a game in the horror genre has to have some kind of threat but they're all over the place.  It breaks the flow of the narrative and it's jarring to go from a casual detective story to a flurry of button mashing every 10 minutes.
Still, even with the more "gamey" aspects, it's still more ghost story than game which explains some of its mechanical shortcomings.  My first playthrough was simply for the sake of taking it all in.  The second was purely for my own desire to see everything and in the process earn every Steam achievement.
All tolled I've spent a bit over 30 hours and enjoyed every minute of it.

Being very well read in medieval history, I was first intrigued by this game as it offered an immersive approach to feudal law and politics. While many rts type games allow city/empire building and detailed battefield control, CKII provides a rewarding experience from the necessity of developing and maintaining dynastic bloodlines.
The necessity of developing technology in order to unlock building progression helps maintain a realistic evolution of your demesne. And while many games allow attrition to become an achilles heel, you will be hard pressed to churn out massive amounts of troops - making your strategies far more consequential. Throwing all your troops into the fray unwisely will result in catostrophic results, as the time required to rebuild levies may take longer than the time your enemy needs to defeat you.
Education, Marriage, Technology, and Councilors become your greatest weapons in acquiring new fiefs and solidifying your dynasties chances of survival. CKII effectively allows expansion through both martial or political means.
I highly reccomend this game to fans of the historical time period and those wishing to master the destiny of dynastic rule.

It pains me to write down that I don't reccommend purchasing American Truck Simulator.
American Truck Simulator (ATS), created by SCS responsible for legendary titles like Truck&Trailer, Extreme Trucking, German and UK Truck Simulator, Euro Truck Simulator and Euro Truck Simulator 2, should've been a slamdunk shoe-in in all and every aspect and it just isn't.
The AI is a definate step back from the AI in ETS2 and it will slow down and/or brake violently where it isn't needed. Traffic-rules AI is over-zealous and will issue fines upwards of $700 ingame currency for the minorest of mistakes.
The map is tiny and the two states provided (Cali and Nevada) are so condensed that a trip from LA to Oxnard is in length comparable to Rotterdam-Amsterdam in ETS2. Time flies so fast that your fuel-tank is always empty and your trucker is always yawning.
The two brands of trucks the game starts with are legendary and speak to the imagination, Peterbild and Kenworth, the Adidas and Puma of the truckingworld. But they're weaksauce dinkytoys that can't even pull a load up a hill without losing steam and are hardly the monsters they ought to be.
The highway-system portrayed in the game, which is a simulator, does in no way reflect the actual highway system in use in America today and is in that aspect worse than the  German Autobahn portrayal in ETS2.
The handling of the trucks feel floaty or loose which gives the whole experience a very arcady feel.
ATS is however a beautiful game, much of which a follower of SCS has come to expect. But beautiful graphics do not make a simulator. Realism (as much as possible anyway) and depth of simulation is. ATS is an arcade trucking game, much like Big Motha Truckers, but without the fun.
I would suggest that you buy Euro Truck Simulator 2. It has more depth of simulation, more destinations, less absurd time-compression, more trucks, more jobs, more different trailers and a more diverse landscape.
It's also cheaper, both in the meaning of the word and in what you get for your money.

A lovely skill-based coffee break game that follows the rule of fun to a tee. It combines the best of 'quick fix' games from teh '80s and '90s with the sleek aesthetics, polish, and indie quirkiness you'd expect from today's market. It's really a delightful thing and I'm a fan, most definitely. It feels a little like a runner, in execution, as the name implies. So it's got a touch of Canabalt to it, but without the randomisation. Instead of that, it has hand-designed levels which make for some sublime gameplay, and quite a bit of verticality to it as well, so in that respect it reminds me of N.
There's a bit of a karting design ethos in there, too. If you've played Sonic & All Stars or Mario Kart, then you'll understand what I mean when I say it has power-ups that can be used to♥♥♥♥♥♥with the other players in a variety of entertaining ways. As each super hero races toward the goal, the other heroes can use those power-ups to even the playing field. I think the only one that feels a bit cheap is the golden grappling hook, but I actually think that's more on me than the devs because I have bad sight. So I would like to be able to turn power-ups on/off individually, but that's all I can think of that comes even close to a complaint.
And it really shouldn't mar your opinion of this game, either. You should get this even if you have no one else to play it with as the bots are well done (with difficulty levels), and there are a bunch of single-player levels which introduce you to the mechanics as well. All in all, I really can't see anything wrong with this game. And since I'm not the sort to worry about offending the sensibilities of people who believe that only games with huge budgets deserve big scores, I'd give this one a [whatever implies a perfect score to you].
For what it sets out to do, it does it with aplomb. And what it is, it is sublimely so. This is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be and doesn't let anything stand in its way. There's no baggage, there's no drama, it's just a fun game to play to kill an amount of time in one of the most entertaining ways with. I even want to praise it for the depictions of its characters, I won't say too much, but as a disabled person I'm finely attuned to prejudices and there's really none to be found, here.
Could I give this a more glowing review? Probably, but you've likely already stopped reading by now and rushed off to buy it. Good for you!

Disgaea, a game that I cautiously recommend since you will either enjoy it greatly or look at it with disgust, depending on your taste in humor, tolerance for rather mediocre writing, and how crazy you like your game's mechanics to be.
Disgaea PC in terms of color and sound is fine, but suffers the obvious problem of originally being a PS2 game. The music is energetic and gets more somber and serious when it needs to, the voice acting is nothing horrible, and the sound effects give everything the impact it needs to fit how crazy this game gets. Do you want to go from a sword slash that attacks a couple of enemies to launching an enemy to the sky and beating the daylights out of them? If you like those crazy shenanigans, then Disgaea has got a lot more of that.
Being rather abruptly woken up, prince Laharl of the Netherworld finds himself in chaos since apparently he had been poisoned and was asleep for two years with his dad passing away via chocking on a pretzel. Of course, everyone is fighting for the throne and Laharl fades away from the public mind, absolutely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥him off. From there, his quest to secure the throne as the rightful takes off and antics ensue.
The story of Disgaea is simple, predictable, and bounces around from having some amount of focus to seeming like fanfiction. Disgaea's big problem with its focus is that it also tries to slap in some humor, but that ends up hurting the game's plot. Granted, when Disgaea gets its shoes on right, the writing isn't half bad. It is nothing life changing, but characters do develop and grow which does give the game's story some charm. The characters are all bombastic and all stand out from the loud and bombastic Laharl to the devious Etna, the way-to-innocent Flonne, and group of earth-defenders from space acting like super heroes from old cartoons featuring a robot named Thursday. However, if you must play a game with a serious story or can't stand a story that focuses on being fun and crazy, then you will struggle to enjoy Disgaea unless you end up greatly enjoying Disgaea's gameplay.
This is the reason why you consider playing this game. Disgaea offers you a playground of tools, classes, items, and god knows what to make your gameplay something incredible. Outside of combat you can call the senate to raise and lower the prices of items, min/max the hell out of characters you make and bring them to level 9999 and then shoot them down to level 1 with better base stats to make them even more comically strong. Don't want to level characters to crazy lengths? Then why not dive into an item and explore it to level the item itself up. you can have your characters get into a T formation and juggle the enemy around and deal crazy amounts of damage. If you want to get somewhere on map, then you can get your units into a tower and have them toss each other all over the place. The only problem is that Disgaea can be rather difficult to get into. Thankfully there isn't a whole lot in this game compared to others in the franchise and you can grind if you ever need to. Disgaea gives you the tools you need to play how you can imagine and if you do struggle, Disgaea makes it incredibly easy to power-level to your hearts content.
Disgaea is a rather tough recommendation since you will either have a blast with this game or struggle to enjoy it. If you are in the mood for a crazy time or just love being surrounded by numbers for you to manipulate to your hearts content, give Disgaea a shot. But there is no shame in refunding this or not picking it up again for some time since this is not a game for everyone.

This is an early access review so take it with a grain of salt.
I really enjoy this game for a multitude of reasons.
One of those reasons is the addition of zombies as a game mechanic in the game. It is something that isnt done in the RTS genre, and it really opens up different avenues of strategy in taking down the enemy base. Another consequence of this game mechanic is that it forces you to make sure that you have enough troops when exploring or else you will be overrun by your -former- soldiers as they die off.
There are many other reasons why this game is great but they are commonplace in the RTS genre.
Now, for the reasons why this game sometimes annoys me.
- You need to unlock the tech tree for each race individually using items and other things found during your campaigns. This makes it feel grindey just trying to get the tech.
- There are a multitude of bugs such as units getting stuck and units not following orders
- Siege rams are way too op right now. I shouldnt be able to take down three gates with a single ram against a fully defended castle
However, despite these cons (most of which can be fixed by either game balancing or bug fixing) this game is a definite buy.

I've been playing Warframe since it's open beta phase in 2013 and I don't ever regret the 2000+ hours I've invested in this game. Starting with gameplay, the mechanics and aspects of gameplay within Warframe are top notch and give paid games of the same genre a run for their money. This is, by far, the best Free-2-Play game I have ever played and it is really free-2-play. Essentially everything that isn't a cosmetic feature can be obtained somehow and even cosmetics are given out as rewards from time to time. In Warframe, there is no true endgame. The game is constantly expanding, constantly updating with new weapons, new systemwide events, new warframes. There is always something for you to do, even if you are a seasoned player. The only true endgame is FashionFrame, a.k.a, who can look the coolest in their frames. Depending on your playstyle and what you are after in th game, Warframe can get a bit grindy, but that is part of the fun. The best part of the game is that no one weapon is the most powerful of them all. All weapons and warframes have the potential to be devastating and powerful, it all depends on how you configure your modules to alter the weapon's damage output and it depends on which enemy faction you are facing, since all factions have different resistances and weakness to different types of damage, so switching your weapons and trying out new builds is encouraged and at times necessary. The most intriguing part of the game is the lore and how it is interwoven into nearly every aspect of what you do. Even the weapons you use have lore behind them that inevitably links to the bigger picture that we can't yet see. I've never played a game with such a great gaming community. Everyone is pretty much helpful and if you are ever lost or need help doing something, it won't be hard to find someone to join your squad and help you out. Last, but not least, the game developers, DigitalExtremes: they are very responsive to the community they serve. They will directly interact with us and push out updates addressing issues we have brought to them. And they have managed to bring Warframe from a game that had one tileset inside of a ship to having an entire open world map on Earth. They keep raising the bar with each new quest, with each new update and they somehow still manage to outdo themselves every time. Warframe is a game, the likes of which I have never played before. It has been updated so many times, gone through so many subtle aesthetic changes that at this point in time, the Warframe that we have now could essentially be called Warframe 2 when compared to Warframe update 2.0. I highly recommend this game.

I have very mixed feelings about this game.  Over all I'd recommend it.  Here are my thoughts:
Positives:
The story was absolutely awesome.  The whole concept of solving your own death on its own was great, but then the actual mystery behind your murder is rather compelling.  I played this with my girlfriend watching and she was never ready for me to stop for the night.  So I'd recommend the game just for the story alone!
Throughout the game, there are collectable items that give some insight into the history of Salem and the Witch Trials as well as random little stories about certain events relevant to the area being explored.  These add a cool dimension to the game taking away from the story and adding some cool information.
Playing as a ghost and getting to use ghost abilities was pretty sweet.
Negatives:
The BIGGEST flaw in my opinion is the use of demons in this game.  I think the game is good enough on its own to just be a mystery without the demons in there to give a "horror" feel.  Truthfully, the demons didn't seem to serve a real purpose to the game and were only in a few spots to take up your time and add just a bit of difficulty to the game.  In such a story-driven game, I think leaving this out would have made the game even better because you wouldn't have to go through buildings wondering if a demon is going to pop out or not; you could have just gone on wondering about the story and exploring every facet of the city.
Another big flaw, as I've read in several other reviews and agree with, is that you get really awesome ghost abilities, position, for example.  When possessing a person, you can do several things.  However, you can really only do something cool or useful with possession on major characters; on background characters, you can only mindread and for a vast majority of these characters, their thoughts are recycled (so you get the same thought from several characters throughout the city).
Overall, I'd absolutely recommend this game.  While there were a couple things that bothered me, the story really was enjoyable.  Honestly, this could even make a movie.  Definitely worth a play-through.

Don’t purchase this game if you expect a lot of gameplay. It’s a narrative gaming experience which involves looking around for clues and solving a few simple puzzles. Overall I had fun and when I wanted a break from action-packed games I played Murdered Soul Suspect. Let’s see the pros and cons.
* The game engine: the game was developed using Unreal Engine 3, one of best engines there is. The game never crashed and I was able to play it with maxed settings and 60fps.
* Visual: even though the textures aren’t exactly top notch, the motion (especially the particles) and the lightening are great.
* Original concept: a detective solving his own murder, passing through walls and talking to other ghosts and mediums. That’s gotta be enticing.
* The “mind reading” feature: I was expecting that every NPC would have unique thoughts and a lot of embarrassing things would be exposed to the players. That’s not what happens. By using the “mind read” in several different NPCs you might end up hearing the exact same thoughts. It appears they are randomly generated and distributed amongst the NPCs. That was definitely a disappointment for me. What’s the point of mind reading if they don’t appear to be real people, but rather randomly generated walking robots that spurs platitudes?
* The linearity: it is not possible to leave an area and return to the investigation later. I reckon this is a game based on narrative, but other developers managed to create narrative games without recurring to such strict storytelling (for instance, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter).
* Looks like the developers tried too hard to make the game “PG-13”. The NPCs don’t do anything interesting. You never see them doing anything out of the ordinary (unless you find a ghost. Apparently everyone who is naughty ends up dead too). It’s like the whole town of Salem is composed of boy scouts.
Other than that the game is fun. I hope to see a sequel that will address the abovementioned flaws. There’s a lot of potential for a series.

It pains me to write down that I don't reccommend purchasing American Truck Simulator.
American Truck Simulator (ATS), created by SCS responsible for legendary titles like Truck&Trailer, Extreme Trucking, German and UK Truck Simulator, Euro Truck Simulator and Euro Truck Simulator 2, should've been a slamdunk shoe-in in all and every aspect and it just isn't.
The AI is a definate step back from the AI in ETS2 and it will slow down and/or brake violently where it isn't needed. Traffic-rules AI is over-zealous and will issue fines upwards of $700 ingame currency for the minorest of mistakes.
The map is tiny and the two states provided (Cali and Nevada) are so condensed that a trip from LA to Oxnard is in length comparable to Rotterdam-Amsterdam in ETS2. Time flies so fast that your fuel-tank is always empty and your trucker is always yawning.
The two brands of trucks the game starts with are legendary and speak to the imagination, Peterbild and Kenworth, the Adidas and Puma of the truckingworld. But they're weaksauce dinkytoys that can't even pull a load up a hill without losing steam and are hardly the monsters they ought to be.
The highway-system portrayed in the game, which is a simulator, does in no way reflect the actual highway system in use in America today and is in that aspect worse than the  German Autobahn portrayal in ETS2.
The handling of the trucks feel floaty or loose which gives the whole experience a very arcady feel.
ATS is however a beautiful game, much of which a follower of SCS has come to expect. But beautiful graphics do not make a simulator. Realism (as much as possible anyway) and depth of simulation is. ATS is an arcade trucking game, much like Big Motha Truckers, but without the fun.
I would suggest that you buy Euro Truck Simulator 2. It has more depth of simulation, more destinations, less absurd time-compression, more trucks, more jobs, more different trailers and a more diverse landscape.
It's also cheaper, both in the meaning of the word and in what you get for your money.

23 hours in at the time of this writing and I'm still not out of what is regarded as "chapter 1." I love this kind of game.
You can pick a pre-made character that you can freely edit in terms of skills and stats, or make your own from scratch. Those you do not play as end up as your companions. It adds a degree of replayability to experience the story from multiple perspectives, though you do get to see a lot of the companions' motives and personalities even if you aren't playing as one.
There's a lot you can do, too. There is usually more than one way to solve a quest or puzzle, and even the combat encourages you to get creative. Drop oil barrels on enemies to ignite them, or burst them open in front of you and create a wall of flame to protect your backline. Electrocute anyone standing in water. Wager risk vs. reward when you factor in the inevitability of friendly fire. Every encounter is sure to leave the player thinking, "What if I handled that differently?" And this, to me, is the mark of a great game - something that makes you want to go back and try it again.
The story is present and much more solid than the first game, though I would say the NPC interactions and pushing the limits of what you can do are the real draws to the game. If you enjoyed old-school CRPGs like Baldur's Gate, Arcanum, or Planescape, you'll definitely enjoy this. Well worth the money spent.

After 70+ hours of game time I think that's enough time invested to give a quick review of this game. I'll lable out the pros and cons I've witnessed during my time playing.
The story is rich and very easy to get into. Almost every NPC you meet has their own background and/or problems that you can either get a taste of or even involve yourself in. It goes so far as to make you feel bad for killing a magister when you find out later that you could've avoided the fight and let them live on to see their family.
Combat is what you'd expect from Divinity. Tactical and makes you think about your moves just like if you're playing a game of chess. Enemies won't fall for easy to see traps and they will create their own combos on you switching the tide of the battle at a second's notice.
The voice acting is well played out and makes you actually listen to majority of the conversations that are going on around you. Though you can tell the devs had a limited funding as a lot of the NPCs have the same "voice" but they va's do their best to make that NPC seem different then another one they did earlier
With the ability to combine two seperate spells from different schools it allows you to craft a very powerful skill for your team. This is great and I've hardly ran into many NPC's using the same combo spells that I have making you have a decent advantage.
There are so many quests to do that you might end up spending over 12 hours just on the starting island! There is always something to do and if you have pet pal in your team, which you better have, you'll get even more story and quests than you to dance in your computer chair to.
I know the game is very new but there are glitches/bugs I've ran into that should have been dealt with in the beta versions. I don't know how many times my screen has gone black during combat forcing me to reload, NPCs I need to speak with spawning in the ground or just a part of them was rendered. The latest is a graphical bug where my portraits of my team look like they took a time warp back to the 90's and using 16 bit color scheme!
This one took me awhile to consider. I understand that the game is suppose to challenge you but majority of the fights I have engaged with after the starter island seems to give the AI complete advantage. I've had NPC's run into buildings or behind walls where I couldn't hit them but they sure as hell could land their shots on me. I've had melee NPC's run to platform I'm high up on and some how whack away at me despite me being 3-4 tiles high. My favorite though is how I have a 95% accuracy to hit before I attack and I miss ALL OF MY ATTACKS, then the NPC runs a marathon to reach me and still has enough AP to use 3 attacks/skills before their turn is over.
In conclusion the game is a must if you want to enjoy a game for it's story and challenge yourself like games use to do before the industry went to "gimmie all your money plz". The biggest flaw for me is the unfair advantage the game tends to have but I'm chalking it up that it needs to be tweaked and it's just some bugs that'll be raided out in the next month.
~Cheeky

This game has been getting a lot of needless flak in my opinion. Folks, the game is Early Access and it literally JUST came out. There are going to be some issues.
That being said, I didn't start my experience on day one which, based off of what I read, had a lot of issues with lag and servers being poorly optimized. I didn't pick up the game until day 2 and by then they had already released a patch which must have fixed most of those server issues because I haven't experienced a shred of bad connection. So, I hope negetive reviewers that spent most of their time on that would consider revising and updating their review as things get fixed.
Anyways, how about a nice pros and cons list?
Pros:
-Nice character customization
-Excellent graphics for the genre
-Related to graphics: character models are nice and detailed and they wear the armor nicely
-Armor models and aesthetics
-Singleplayer/co-op is fantastic (co-op has a slight con which I'll list later)
-Crafting system; similar to Ark and Rust but with better UI I think
-Building system; again very similar to Ark and Rust combined but I think improved
-XP/Leveling; seems pretty much a copy of Ark but that's not bad. If anything it's streamlined and better. I also feel like you get more bang for your buck. Unlocking a recipe usually nets more than one crafting recipe which is nice.
-Combat; pretty easy to get the hang of and incredibly satisfying in my opinion. Love seeing the gore and dismemberment.
Cons:
-Co-op; an awesome feature that doesn't require getting your own server but I like to define it as advanced shared screen co-op. You and your mate/s are confined to a certain area, albeit a rather large one, and can move on as a group. As soon as someone pushes that limit they get pulled back within the confines. A small nag if anything at all and I am sure it all has to do with reducing the power required by the host to generate everything that the different people are seeing.
-Rock inconsistencies; again, picky, but some rocks crumble into pieces as you mine them which is rather satisfying but some just fly out of the ground spasmodically once they've been depleted.
-Aggro; &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥WTF WHERE?!" is what I found myself saying time and again when a random little goblinoid type monster came running out of the bushes towards me. Seriously, the aggro range is pretty large and sensitive with some NPC's and it can get irritating.
-Building; I love the building but I wish there was a way to choose the highth of the foundation when placing them
That's all I have for the moment. I intend on editing this as the game progresses. As a final note I would like to say that I have a lot of faith in Funcom and their ability to complete the game. I am really impressed initially that within the first day they could release a patch to fix some of the glaring issues people were giving it a thumbs down for. This game has a lot of potential and I think the devs will exceed the expectations as the project goes on.

I don't recommend this game in it's current state.
Whilst it's a good game, it just feels too rough around the edges for a purchase at the moment. I've been interested in this game for a while and after seeing the developer behind it I expected even Early Access to be a little more polished than it is at the moment.
The combat feels really clunky, dodging feels like it makes no difference, getting absolutely shredded by pretty much every NPC within a matter of a couple hits even after changing the server settings heavily to fix this issue. It feels extremely unbalanced, I've played my fair share of Rust and Ark, while both are unforgiving they're nothing compared to this.
The server settings though are excellent, some require a bit of research to understand what they do exactly (does the slider increase or decrease certain things etc). So this game can be playable if you can stomach the combat and you can balance it yourself.
Another issue I'm having is the size of some of the building blocks, they're about 25-50% the size of those in Rust or Ark. To get a large enough base for a sleeping back and box you need atleast 4 foundations in this game opposed to 1 in other games. This doesn't help that again the amount of materials required is massive although due to the excellent settings you can also increase the amount gathered to circumvent this issue.
Something I'm actually a bit concerned about though is the quality of some of the texture maps, in a lot of cases Low looked much cleaner and polished than Ultra. The only way I can describe this (those in the game dev industry will understand) is they've used dirty normal maps on some of the ultra textures to add more detail but all it's done is reduced the overall quality. To top that off on Ultra a lot of the texture maps still looked very low res which was disappointing considering how heavy it was hitting my 1060 6GB (30FPS near water).
It is definitely a game to keep an eye on though and over the next few weeks I'm sure these issues will begin to getting resolved or atleast improved a bit. I will update this review after a few major updates if these issues have been resolved.
