Okay I love this game. Highly recommended. I've got about 4 hours logged in the game and this is the first game in a long time that I want to continually revist. So here's what I like about the game sprinkled with some opportunities I think the developers might consider:
- the musical score in this game is absolutely wonderful. It can be delightful, brooding, somber, exciting, uplifting, everything. It's so wonderful, I don't know how else to describe it. I can't really go into depth about it since I'm no audiophile, but lemme say it really greatly adds to the mood and setting of the game at any given point.
- this is a 2D game of course, but as far as 2D games go, this game looks absolutely gorgeous. I will say here that sometimes the environments feel somewhat empty, and the lack of a map or map hotkey makes navigating somewhat difficult but it's not unbearable and never really feels like it's a huge hinderance. I think it may make collecting all the extra stuff a little hard but I think not spoonfeeding stuff to players isn't a HUGE problem.
- the game is really responsive, I never find myself doing something I didn't want to do, same with the aiming and all. The whole concept of carrying different gunners to do and accomplish different things is really cool and it's a clever gameplay mechanic. The puzzles are pretty fun, not too difficult though, but again, no hand holding here and it's great.
- I leave this one up to you guys. I really enjoy the story line, I know some of you out there will say it's a tried and true story, done plenty of times before. But that doesn't stop me from really enjoying the story. My only wish is that the game doesn't end quickly. I'm only 4hours into it, I hope theres a lot more of the story left.
I'm not going to assign a number value but I'm going to say this game is great. I really love it. I hope the game lasts quite a bit longer, but I'll append this Review when I'm done to give a good idea of how long it takes. Highly recommended, if you need a new story driven game that doesn't hand hold you through every single piece of it, look no further, speak no more.
Edit: I finished the game, I have 9 hours logged and I could've finished it a lot faster honestly. I really love this game, the ending is memorable and I look forward to what the creators have next in store. I wish the game was longer though, that's probably my only gripe.

What to say about this game? I have played this game on four different platforms, PS2, PSP, DS, and PC, and I have more than 500 hours put into this game in total. I'm not sure whether it tells more about me or about the game, but still. And I know I'm not the only one.
It takes something special to have the players want to not only revisit the game again and again after (multiple) completions, but to actually have the players want to play all the different versions of the game.
Because there is something very unique about this game that almost all its successors have sought to replicate, but have never quite hit the mark as well as this one. It's a special combination of character dynamics done just right, the pacing and the warmth of the story, and a healthy dose of quirky humour. Also, if you are a friend of endlessly tweaking stats and levels (be they character or weapon or equipment stats and levels), or planning complicated master-pupil character creation chains for optimal end results, this is the game you are looking for. If that isn't your thing, well, you can pretty much ignore all the nittygritty fiddling with the stats and just concentrate on the story.
Though I have to say, there is nothing quite as satisfying as having your fine-tuned mage throw a kick <3ss spell that nearly wipes out all resistance from the field. There is no such thing as tactical overkill, after all ;)

A review huh?
Out of respect for the developers I will write one,
Now KW2 is a great game, some may not agree because it is an "Unfinished game". But as a player who has joined many of these said same games, I cannot stress how different this one is. The developers are EXTREMELY ACTIVE! Don't believe me? Look on the forums and click a random topic and you will see how.
Now I remember when this game was first launced and how buggy it was, haha those who are vets know what I am talking about and all the glitches we all used to take advantage of. But the thing is, all the people in the player base post on the forums explaining in detail about these same bugs. Depending on how bad it affects gameplay depends on how much priority the developers give to fix it. When I say priority I mean those with a huge effect, developers try to fix it with the next patch, Those with low priority get fixed within a few weeks. Now those of us who were here since beginning had fun PVP and with campaign, but the game changers that EVERYONE mostly LOVES was the zombie feature. Haha I cannot tell you all how much fun I personally had in matches online with the zombies.
The times in a FFA where 4 players are going head to head trying their all to take one another out, but alas due to all the deaths and carnage in the midst of the ruined battlefields undead would arise. Now in the beginning this was a major issue, personally I ♥♥♥♥ING LOVED IT!!!!!!!! Nothing more thrilling than that first player finally getting his base destroyed by your forces and wondering how the other 2 players are doing in their battle. Just as you are finishing up mopping uphis building in his base and of course handling the undead that appeared during your battle. As you are taking it all in you see either your base or the rear of your units taking damage. seeing it is a few steady stream of undead coming from the other 2 players side of the map. You cannot help but notice that the stream is getting larger and larger slowly forming into a horde, thus you must reorganize your troops before they die and add to the already large undead horde. Only once that you FINALLY (Ya those of you that had been in that situation know what I mean when you finally get them under control like an infestation) get the undead under control you decide to send a scout to see how the others are doing because these undead came from their end. Only to discover a massive horde beseiging both of their bases and them fighting for their lives against the AI. Ahhhhh haha I will never forget those beautiful games where all players put aside their differences of humans, orks, or elves and team up to exterminate the undead on the map before they completely take us all out.
Those were proud memories I have of this game, memories that years from now as I get older I can talki video games to others my age or younger and tell them of a game that I really and honestly had alot of fun playing. Kind of like I do with Age of empires from when I was kid.
Zombies now are a joke from what they used to be, they do not give that rush of a feeling but i guess in some instances it is possible to get that horde feeling even if it is just for a few minutes.

Kingdom Wars 2: Battles is probably the most unique and entertaining medieval RTS I have played in a really long time. The developers have continued to do a fantastic job of making changes big and  small  through communication with the players in the forums, as well as there own creative expertise, and its going to be a really really fun game when its all said and done. The graphics as of now are not the best, BUT its running on DX9 and it will be running on DX11 in the future, and it will look really good! Any complaints about no AI for the AI :p sound they like they are gonna dealt with in this next lineup of pathces and updates. All in all the zombies are a really fun addition to the battlefield, and seeing them wander around and do there thing is pretty cool, and alot of people bash them, but they add a whole different strategy to the game! you can lead a horde to the enemies gates and watch it attack the front gates and mob in through the mangles doors! Or my personal favorite: building a huge army and just charging over the walls and getting wiped out, but doing enough damage to let the corpses rot, and then wake up and start burning there town down from the inside! Honestly my only qualm so far is the peasents! They are SO stupid lol, and when you're playing against AI players that sit in there fortress its one thing, But I can imagine it would be very frustrating being in the middle of multiplyer game and all of the sudden have to divert all of your attention to stopping your peasents from being slaughtered in droves by a dragon, or the zombie hordes, or a HUGE pack of wolves for some reason, because they got bored doing what you wanted them to do. I'm not really sure what to write, since I don't generally write reviews, but do make exception for things i find above and beyond. That being said, then of course, I find this game above and beyond. First, I had originally played it on the ps3, so I knew what I was getting into to a degree, though I never completed it on the ps3. So first for technical issues, let me say as far as a port goes, I couldn't even tell it was one.
The game itself is almost like its trying to reference world war 2. It has emotional pull if you like that. It has a beautiful story. You can to a degree customize your characters. About the characters, there is a set list (a decently large list) and so many for each type of unit. each of these characters have "potentials" that change what they are good at somewhat, and specific people on that list they like, that can change the way you play a lot. Now there sadly a few from each that are obviously just much better, as well as some of the characters dont really have much personality (one i thing was specifically designed not to though). For the list of people they like, it will make them assist in combat without it being their turn.
the battle is interesting, you start out as if you are looking at a map, and you can see your units, your base(s), and generally the enemy base(s). You also see any enemies in line of sight of your units. These are all displayed on the map. on your turn you can (generally) issue orders that are like buffs, or select one of your units to take control of. When you do this, it zooms in on your unit, and you start playing in a sorta neat mostly turn based style. You move your unit around a (I think) beautiful hand drawn scenery (well, besides the desert, thats just desert lol). You find the spot you want to place your unit, generally in some form of cover (at least at the beginning, just a nice tip, shocktroopers can pretty much headbutt the front lines when done right, ROSIE DONT NEED NO COVER, lol, for reals though, gotta do it right). and then if an enemy is in line of sight, you can press to aim, and then line up your target and shoot. After you shoot, it goes back to allowing you to move if you have any more AP to do so. During the time you aren't firing however, any enemy that can see you and is close enough, gets to auto fire at you (works with your units against enemies too though), and they only stop nicely when you are trying to aim.
The story is about mainly about welkin gunther, and how with his nature boy knowledge, manages to gain the trust of his allies, and lead them through some pretty neat victories. The game really focuses on trust and friendship in a way with that. This happens after a small village is attacked by another nation, (if I recall the beginning story says its over their fuel sorce, which weklin's nation has a huge supply). They then pretty much get listed into the militia, as welkin's nation has this thing where everyone has military training through their school years.

The problem is that the game gets very repititious, very quickly, and the strategies that you employ in the early- to mid-game completely unravel when facing the last stage. I am honestly surprised at how many glowing reviews this game has.  Maybe it is because the port was well done, which I can agree on, since it felt like it was made for PC.  I did not like the game itself.
The story is horrible.  It's the most sophomoric thing I've ever seen.  It's like watching a really bad anime.  It's completely naive, unrealistic, and makes me truly hate the main characters.  It's like Michael Jackson got together with the creators of Barney and the Teletubbies, each chewed up lithium and Prozac, and then collaborated on an anti-war picture book for dementia patients.
Let me explain.  I really don't mind a bad story -- FFV had a bad story, my favorite pvp games have NO story, etc.  The problem is that Valkyria tries to have a good story, they take you away from the gameplay to show you slide after slide of the story, and the stupidity of the story makes you feel truly insulted as a human being.
The gameplay doesn't make up for it.  The first few encounters that you try may impress you, there are some interesting mechanics in play and somewhat interesting character stats, but you tire of it quickly.  The AI is either terrible or way too good, the combat has bugs, some mechanics don't make sense (dodging a sniper bullet?), and when you fail a mission due to one tiny bug or bad mechanic the rage monster takes over your body.  This is because you have to start over from the beginning, and some battles can take 1-2 hours.
There is one battle in particular reviewers have mentioned here, where some super-being enters the fight towards the end of the battle and immediately wipes your team.  I did not know that I was supposed to let a huge tank drive through my camps and destroy everything in order to make its radiators pop up so that I could kill it.  I was defending my camps, which made the tank impervious, and as a result I lost 2 hours of my life because I didn't quite kill the super tank by the final turn.  As a gamer I really like doing the best job possible, I like to apply strategy and to apply min-maxing, and so to be punished for doing a good job, in my mind, is unforgivable.  It's either bad design, or worse, it assumes that its players are incompetent or stupid.
The art style is awful.  I wouldn't even call it a style, it's just a Photoshop filter over the rendered graphics.  It's disgusting.  I really mean it.  If the story didn't insult you, this will.  It doesn't go away, ever.
There was a period when I first started playing the game where it was exciting.  I wanted to level up my classes, recruit new snipers, see what challenges lie in the next battle.  But I soon learned that this is a really bad strategy game.  I barely used my brain, and when I did, it didn't seem to matter.  Eventually it all turned into "whatever."  Line up a bunch of shock troopers because they can fire on advancing enemies?  Never mind, the AI goes from point A to point B asap and immediately fires, which means you rarely fire back, so "whatever."  Use 3-4 snipers on an open-field map?  Oh wait, there are invisible walls blocking half the shots, so "whatever."
If I had to choose between either bringing this game with me to a deserted island or a stash of diapers, I would pick the diapers, make little lancers out of my own poo, and play with those instead.

First and foremost, this game is amazing in so many aspects.  The best part of it is definitely the story.  There's no doubt that the plot is very compelling with well developed characters and an insane mystery that is just too addictive to ignore.  Once I started this game, I HAD to know what happened.  I just HAD to know.  And when I did, I was extremely satisfied.  Gosh, the story is brilliant - in fact, I will go so far as to say it's one of the best mystery/thriller stories in a game I've ever experienced.  Truly.
Now on to the gameplay, it's a mixture of adventure with some point and click elements and a little bit of action.  If you take investigation aspects of LA Noire, mixed it in with some supernatural elements, and added a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of interesting collectibles, you have a gist of the gameplay.  It's fairly simple with movement.  It just gets a bit annoying when you have to angle the camera "just" right at times to perform certain actions.  Speaking of action, it's mostly exploration but you face demons which you can either sneak past or fight.  Either way, those things were terrifying to say the least BUT not terrifying to prevent me from playing.  And this is coming from someone who is a pansy with jumpscares and whatnot.  Just if you're playing with headphones or have particularly loud speakers, you might want to turn them down a bit at times.
Now though this is a mystery game, there aren't really any puzzles so to say but there are times where you have to piece together evidence - sometimes in order, sometimes not - and sort out what information is most relevant to your investigation.  So in a detective sense, I find the pacing to be well done.  It's very realistic and definitely keeps the mystery solving at a decent pace.
If you happen to be an achievement hunter, this game is definitely enjoyable in that sense but it is also a bit challenging especially if you're aiming for collecting all the collectibles.  Some are fairly simple with 8 objects or so and others have 20+ objects to collect and can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to find.  Fair warning: beating the game will not allow for you to explore the map freely.  In fact, you will have your very last chance to do so right at the end of the ♥♥♥♥ing game right before you reach the finale.  Of course, little me was very tempted to know the ending so I just said "Screw collectibles!  I want answers NOW!" and rushed to the last location in a jiffy.  If you have self control which I clearly lack, this probably won't be a problem for you.
The music soundtrack is...creepy to say the least.  ♥♥♥♥ the music in this game sometimes.  I was paranoid enough about ♥♥♥♥ing demons and then the suspenseful music just made me more twitchy!  Eh, it's not too bad but it's still ♥♥♥♥ing creepy.
Visually, this game is pretty nice.  It's not absolutely gorgeous.  This is murder and ghosts we're dealing with here after all.  But for what it's worth, the atmosphere is very fitting without being too overwhelming with horror.
Overall, I'd give this game a 9/10.  It'd be perfect but the demons nearly gave me a heart attack at some points.  Plus, angling things when you're trying to perform actions like demon exorcisms can get tricky and can be a little inconvenient when I'm a second away from exorcising those ♥♥♥♥ers but I'm a little notch off from succeeding and a second too late.  Then, I deal with a very♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off demon and I'm shrieking like a little ♥♥♥♥♥.
9/10 would shriek like a little ♥♥♥♥♥ again.
10/10 would definitely give this game another playthrough in the long run because the story is just that great.
0/10 would not want this soundtrack to play in the background of my life.
10/10 would definitely replay just to get all the achievements and collectibles.

Time Mysteries 3: The Final Enigma is the final chapter in the Time Mysteries series and does a good job at wrapping up all three stories and connecting them while also tying up loose ends.
The game itself is nothing special and is a little dated, as are the previous two games, but if you like the Hidden Object genre, then all three games will probably satisfy you. No bugs, reasonable voice acting, plenty of puzzles, and lots of HO scenes.
Time Mysteries 3 also has a bonus chapter, as had Time Mysteries 2, but while the bonus material in TM2 was mostly original, the bonus chapter in TM3 is mainly re-used HO scenes (with the same objects) from TM2 and TM3 which was a little disappointing.
Overall, the trilogy is a decent, if not spectacular, journey through time with the Ambrose family that is perhaps on the easy side for experienced HO players, but still worth making.

This is a bold game - a game that's all about dialogue. Not action, not progression, just dialogue. For those who love immersing themselves in different worlds as different character and aren't scared off by a chat system - this will be one of the greatest games you'll play. For those who aren't really excited by what I just said, this game is probably not for you. That's okay.
A big problem at the moment is the crappy community that's usually around. Sometimes, someone will disconnect on you in the middle of the game (Hindering progress for all players) or not care about the goal of the game at all and just ruin and distract everyone.
If you can get a group of friends to play this game with, or you trust the community enough, this game will deliver some of the most thought-provoking experiences you had in a video game. Otherwise, steer clear. It's not a perfect game, but at least it's an interesting one.

I just barely recommended this game, and my opinion is subject to change as the game progresses; but as of now, my review is as follows.
I am an American trucker. I have been for a while now. I own my own rig. I run all 48 states, plus Canada and Alaska. I played ETS2 more than any other game in the past 30 years. (even more than super mario) I loved that game. It was the first simulation game for trucking that came anywhere near the real thing. Now, I do not live in Europe. I cannot say how similar it actually is to true Euro Trucking. Well, this is American Truck Simulator and I am an American trucker, so certain things do stick out to me. For one, no where in the USA, will you have an interstate with a state road just turning into it. You'll never find that. You will have a long on ramp and off ramp for these. Every single time. There are no splits in the interstate. Also, the layout of the truck stops is way too similar to ETS2, and nowhere near similar to true American truck stops. Yeah, I see that there are some legal issues dealing with naming the big truck stops (Loves, Petro, Pilot, Flying J, TA), but don't take something that is never a truck stop (Chevron) and turn it into one. Also, you'll never find a truck stop that just turns off of the interstate. You'll always take an exit, go a few blocks down and then it will be all by itself or surrounded by other buildings. I was really hoping that this would be more accurate. Some truckstops are challenging, while others are a cake walk. However, you will never find a truck stop that pulls off of the interstate like a rest area, and you will never find a truck stop with parallel parking. It will always be back in parking.
Now onto the trucks. I get it, the game is new. But why only 2 trucks to start out with? Maybe I'm playing it wrong, but maybe not. I'm not going to touch too much on this; but I will say I hope to see more trucks appear very soon. (Not just models, but other makes also)
My biggest beef, besides the interstate shortcomings, is the fact that the game devs decided to put this in California. (Or as some truckers call it, Commiefornia) This is the single worst state to drive a truck in. It is far from the "American spirit" in regards to trucking. It has the slowest speed limit, the highest emissions laws, and the most corrupt state Department of Transportation in the country. If this game were to really see the heart of American trucking, they should have started it off in the Midwest or the South. Anywhere from Kansas to Texas would have been best. Something with a high agriculture outport, high manufacturing, and even high livestock. But no, we had to go with California, who imports most of what they ship from China. Oh well, I can only hope that more states will be added, and soon. I see that Arizona is next on the list to be released, and I am just curious as to what cities they are planning on introducing, and what they believe actually ships out of Arizona. Should be interesting to see.
I really also wish that the backing in the game was harder. I see that it has gotten more difficult from ETS2, but it is FAR from being accurate with some of the shippers and receivers around this country. How about some 90 degree blind side alley backs? Or how about some blindside parallel parks for flatbeds? These are what truckers have to deal with daily here; so why not throw a few, or a ton, of them into the game? It would add more of a challenge while, at the same time, becoming a bit more realistic.
Now, I did give this a "yes I would recommend" vote. It is a fun simulation, and for what it's worth, the simulation is fairly accurate. You won't find a better trucking simulator out there. Hell, even trucking schools have worse software to teach people how to drive a truck. This is a cheap game, at only $20, but it has amazing potential. I hope to see this game live up to my expectations, especially after having waited so long to get it.
If you are not a trucker, this game will be great for you. If you are a trucker, you'll find the same gripes about it as I did; but you'll still play it.

My first run through this felt jubliant, so excited was I to continue the saga. As such, I gave this tremendous benefit of the doubt. I assumed that my myraid choices from the first game would eventually be reciprocated in the finale, if not this game. My, how naive was I?
Upon reflection, it became vividly clear that I did not enjoy this game at all. My excitement was the product of my own imagination, not the endless series of pop-n-cover gun fights that literally make up the entire game.
Forgive my candor, but the gameplay is garbage. All the rpg from the first game was stripped out, and now this game necessiates cover, meaning that the wild skirmishs of ME:1 no longer exist. Your class doesn't matter anymore. Just sit behind a block of concrete and shoot whoever pokes the head out from their respective block of concrete. I didn't have to leave Earth for this dreck. Now you have to reload your gun (they do have a reasonable lore explanation), so this game has very little to distinguish itself from other lifeless 3rd person shooty smut.
But what about the story? The story for ME:2 is almost entirely just build up for ME:3, the idea being that you are marshalling forces to deal with some mysterious threat. This is a brilliant concept for a party oriented rpg, but it's hard for me to make myself care about my comrades when the end result is the same no matter what you do, and whatever happens here doesn't really matter for ME:3.
The difference between ME:2 and New Vegas in this context is that your choices actually matter in New Vegas, and the companions are completely and utterly optional, nobody is trying to make you care about them. Please just play New Vegas.
So why even play this, if the gameplay is so bland and story choices are so inconsquential? Even if you like the Mass Effect story, you could probably skip this game entirely. Nothing of significance occurs in this game.
If you want to see the correct way to carry over player decisions to a sequel, play Golden Sun and Golden Sun: TLA. If you want to see the correct way to involve the player in the plot, play New Vegas. The Mass Effect series attempted to do both and failed miserably.

Oh boy, I was blinded sided by Owlboy.  Over the 8 or so years this game had been in development I somehow managed to avoid hearing a single thing about it until I saw it on the front page of steam. I bought it on a lark and have had a hooting good time.
The first thing you notice is that the game is pretty, every aspect of the game looks great and is a joy to look at, from backgrounds to enemies, and most of all the main characters, especially our mute avian hero Otus. His small sprite is highly expressive and very cute that instantly endears you to him.
The writing is also top-notch. The story is interesting and all the characters involved make you want to learn more about what is going on. The game is a touch ruthless on hammering home the fact that our hero is a low bird on the totem pole, many characters in power are dismissive of you and actively blame the little owl for things way beyond his control. From this arises one of my problems with the game, and fair warning this paragraph will contain some slight spoliery things. The problem with the writing I have is that come the last leg of the game you get the feeling that you in fact have just made things worse than if you stayed home. The first few missions of the game you get beaten down for failures that Otus had no control over and this instills in the player a feeling of proving that you are right and can save the world so we cheer on Otus and the gang through their hardships.  This falls apart in the last segment of the game, it’s revealed that you have in fact been getting in the way of the character really trying to save the world and almost blow it completely and doom all of creation. That is to say you get a feeling that had you just stayed home then things would have played out similarly in the grand scheme of things. This could be a damning ending for a game but the rest of the experience was so wonderful and the characters you get to interacts with make it more of an annoyance than ruining the whole thing.
The game is also very good as, well, a game. The controls are tight and flying with Otus feels great as you traverse the world around you. Once you can pick up your friend Geddy (and a few others later) the game becomes a two stick shooter, you move with one hand and, aim and shot with the other which feels great. The game feels fun and rewarding to play though it is admittedly not that difficult. I don’t mind the casual feeling of the game though for some it is a valid strike against it. The game ramps up the difficulty at a fair pace though it never gets too hard that one should be stuck because of combat for too long. The puzzles also aren’t that hard but I feel that it helps the casual pace of the game where focus is more on having fun with the good controls and keeping the narrative flowing at a decent clip.
.  The one point of contention I have seen many bring up is the price and I understand it, I feel that 25$ for the 9-10 hours you get from beating the game is worth it to me, I feel that each of those hours is so jam-packed with lovely visuals and fun gameplay that the quality makes up for the quantity. Some people evaluate the price of their own time differently than I do so may not feel that it is worth it for the amount of game play so I would keep how highly you value hours per dollar in mind before buying the game.
Overall I feel Owlboy is worth a play, it’s a delight to control as well as look at and the characters are fun and interesting as is the writing, for the most part. The game left me happy with the time I spent with it though a bit hungry for more content. I also want to pay kudos to the Devs who are active on the discussion board and even helped me when I did encounter a (now patched) game breaking bug within the game. I say take wing with Owlboy and friends and explore this colourful world!

Build a deck with helpful items and events. A dealer adds some of his own including a boss which has some overall rule like "lose gold every turn" or "shop prices are low but you get cursed for buying anything". Start at point A and hop onto face-down cards to flip them and try to find point B. Most will be random events with a x-card Monte minigame to determine whether it resolves positively or negatively. You get a token the first time you complete a challenge correctly, which typically but not always is by getting the positive result. Manage food, gold, and health, win equipment and blessings to strengthen your character for battle challenges (typical negative event result plus every round ends with an boss fight, at least), and avoid curses which are basically just negative blessings. If you beat the boss your collected tokens turn into new cards. If you die at any point you lose your tokens from that round and start over.
Each round of the game is pretty short, and at least working through the story the first time there's a solid sense of progression from the deck building. I also really like the voice acting for the Dealer, he's a pretty charming character. On the base difficulty at least, if you're familiar with how Arkham combat works then you really can't lose a combat event. There's some challenge modes I can't vouch for yet.

The real problem is that the game uses two modes (keyboard/mouse) of input when only one was necessary. -The tank is in EVERY mission, sure the tank can kick some major butt in most situations, but when it's not useful, the tank simply becomes a huge escort mission (One that can be killed with a single shot or within a single enemy turn pretty easily.) You can try to use the tank as mobile cover in this scenario, however the buggy controls will often cause you to run your teammates over, not doing any damage, but still frustrating.
-Unskippable cutscenes during missions, this is only frustrating when you fail and retry a mission, normally this isn't much of a grievance, but they sure can drag on and on, repeating something that was at one time useful, but is now rage inducing to be said again.
-Sometimes you just miss, maybe it's some kind of RNG element at work here, but sometimes you just miss a target literally a meter or two in front of you. It's frustrating, but it is a strategy/FPS hybrid, I'm sure for those who have played enough of it, can work with it, but for those of us not willing to put in the amount of time, just go ahead and avoid snipers. And forget about any Lancer (anti-tank) skill shots either, unless you're completely masochistic.
All in all, the game is still interesting, it's worth $10, however I'm only saying that because it's too late for a refund, I'd rather just have my $10 back.

Before Elsword was incorperated into Steam, I was a regular player who had been within the game since the Beta was officially released. The game itself is interesting, especially for a side-scroller, and the graphics are curiously-entertaining. As far as the community goes within the US servers, most people are polite (aside from those who, naturally, become irritated upon being defeated in PvP) and are willing to help you if you ask. On the negative side, as with any MMORPG, there are bots within every major city or town that spam the chat with their currency-scamming tactics, which makes for a rather annoying encounter.
Game-wise, the controls are relatively easy to understand; the game gives you an approximation of how hard a character will be for you to play. Classes are also available within the game, and there are a few of them to choose from for each character. Hacking isn't really an issue from what I've seen; since the beginning, there hasn't really been many of them unless they make it blatantly obvious within PvP, such as non-draining Mana or never-ending HP. (Your only major "concern" are the currency-scamming bots, honestly).
When it comes to their in-game currency, K-Ching, it is a bit over-the-top how much they make you pay for it. For example, if you purchase approximately 1500 K-Ching in game, that will get you maybe 4-5 items; give or take. The costume pieces are very expensive, and take a lot of KC to buy from their in-game store. They charge quite a bit. making it nearly useless to purchase K-Ching unless you're willing to spend a lot of money to get what you want.
Overall, the game is fun to play and offers a unique side-scrolling experience. I would recommend it for anyone looking for a game that will take time to play, and anyone willing to invest a lot of time into their different characters.

Time Mysteries 3: The Final Enigma is a sequel of Time Mysteries 2: The Ancient Spectres.
You play as Ester Ambrose to save the world of an evil cataclysm that a hooded face wants to happen. She will need to time travel in order to be able to save the world and prevent the cataclysm to occur. And then begin a new journey for her.
As every Artifex Mundi game you can move freely in different area and need to solve some puzzles and find all objects in hidden objects scenes. The game has (different difficulties?) and a guest feature: every one of the family can play an independent save and resume the game where they left it. When you first play the game you’ll have a notebook where you have all your objectives as well as all your notes. You’ll also have a time travel device showing a map that allow you to fast-travel. Adding to that you’ll have a hint button that will help you in many ways but be warned that you may not use it in any puzzle or hidden object scene (HOS)or investigation scene (IS). Hints can be used to know where you need to go, where is the next interaction or to show an object or clue in an HOS or IS or to skip a puzzle. To conclude this part, you’ll also have an inventory to store useful items through your journey.
Puzzles are good and different. Hidden objects scenes (HOS) have only the classical one (as far as I remember): find objects hidden with the help of their name. Orange names mean that you need to interact directly with the scene or use an item in the scene.
One of the very good thing of this game is that there are 2 unique features you won’t find in any other Artifex Mundi game (except Time Mysteries):
•	You’ll be able to freely move through time (and space) with your time travel device.
•	You’re able to play a unique mini-game instead of the HOS. (I don’t really suggest it if you’re going for achievements though.)
To do so (to time travel) you’ll first need to find it (?) and to retrieve every token to be able to travel to specific dates.
And for the mini-game, as far as I recall I think that’s a matching game: you need to click on a chain of three or more adjacent balls to remove them. (The aim is to let some kind of token to fall out of the screen or to remove adjacent balls?) Each time you remove a token you remove also an item in the hidden objects list.
(*) :
In addition to no skip or use any hint while playing every puzzles and Hidden objects scenes, there are a few more missable achievements. Two of them requires you to complete a puzzle and a hidden objects scene under one minute. And 2 other hidden objects achievements ask you to find 3 objects within 3 seconds or to finish a scene with less than 4 misclicks.
Finally if you missed anything while finishing your first playthrough, you’ll need to play the game again. I guess but I’m not sure that you need to play on the same profile to get the “One of a kind” achievement.

Hidden objects were not cheaply placed for the most part, as in placing objects that blended together.  I did not need to pixel hunt a few inches from my screen.  Hidden object scenes were also of good enough quality and resolution that I did not stress out when doing them.  There were also not a lot of clutter and objects were not too small.
Graphics are stretched, even though cutscenes were in widescreen.  That can't be helped though; it is the nature of the genre.
There were a minor aesthetic/visual glitch and a major gamebreaking bug though.  The major bug involved using objects on environments.  When I used the objects, my cursor disappeared and I couldn't close the pop-up interaction scene.  I had to exit to the main menu and then go back into the game.  Luckily, the game saves the exact location and the activities you have done.
The story is a good wrap-up of the first two games.  It connected the first two games of the series, whereas the second game had a new story, completely disconnected from the first.  Story was still cheesy though.
There is fast travel and helpful hints on what to do next.  Those helped cut down the amount of time wasted going back and forth; nobody wants to do that.
Overall, the game was decent to below decent.  Hidden object scenes were not frustrating.  This game is fine for HOG fans, but passable for everybody else.

The first game in this series was a disaster.  The second was passable but had a few notable flaws.  The third time is evidently the charm.  This final outing for the series still didn't seem quite as good as some of AM's other offerings, but the blatant weaknesses of the previous two are not to be seen here.  It's a solid HOG with nothing much to complain about.
Regrettably for those who enjoy a challenge, as QA stepped up in this game, difficulty took a step down.  But Artifex Mundi fans should already be familiar with AM's emphasis on aesthetics and storytelling over challenge.  Playing on Expert typically helps in an AM game, but I don't recommend it in the later two
games because of the time-travel mechanic -- without the helpful "something to do" icons on the Portable Time Device, you'd be stuck rewandering every time era over and over to find where HO scenes have become reactivated.
In the final analysis, this is a decent HOG on its own, though having played the other two first does give it more context, and it's definitely the best of the trilogy.  The trilogy as a whole, however, is decidedly sub-par for this publisher.  If you haven't yet played much of Artifex Mundi's catalogue, you'd do better to start elsewhere.

The investigations are easy but the findings are not trivial and kept adding real new information throughout the game. Only when I was very close to the end of the game was I able to figure all the pieces, meaning the game keeps the tension very well.
However, Murdered: Soul Suspect also has linear progression, too trivial investigations, many collectibles which I did not find interesting and sort of bland side investigations and strange stealth combat.
For me the game really picked up when I stopped trying to collect everything and doing every side mission. So, I recommend this game with a suggestion to stick with the main story.

I got a 90% off coupon for a crafting reward for another game and I figured that, since I am fond of puzzle games, I'd add another to my library - for three bucks, what's the risk?  The puzzle game in question is, of course, FaeVerse Alchemy.
The controls are very simple - one mouse button rotates the patterns, the other button drops the pieces and the mouse slides the arrangement from side to side.  Basically the overall gameplay feels like Dr Mario from the old NES with elements from Tetris thrown in (three symbol patterns).  What's interesting is that as you match alchemical symbols, new symbols get added making the game more difficult than Dr Mario ever was.  All in all, I like the game, I like the music, and I like the whole premise of the game.
The only thing I
like?  The $30 price tag slapped on this game.  Okay Subsoap, I get that you are proud of yourselves for making this game.  It's great fun, very stylish and slick looking, and has a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack;

Most people might dismiss this as another Rust or other survival along those lines and they're not very far off at the moment, but there's plenty there that suggests there'll be lots more to this game than most others. It's also the first game I've seen that lets you adjust the size of your character's assets (both male and female) and lets you run about unapologetically flaunting them if you so choose, though keep in mind everything can kill you. As far as visuals and gameplay now, it is basically Rust with more threats and the crafting system is identical to Ark as you need to level up to unlock crafting recipes, and you're mostly gathering materials from the ground, rocks, trees and the occasional animal. One of the biggest things, for me anyway, is that you're able to set up private games for playing alone or with friends without needing to worry about the worst people in the world inhabiting your server, and you can do it in-game without tools or renting a server (I'm pretty sure it works like 7 Days to Die). After that there isn't much else but don't forget this is a newly released early access game, there is more to come.
All in all, if you enjoy survival games this one's okay but $30 is probably too pricey for it really be worth it right now, but keep your eye on it as it will doubtless get better with time and hopefully justify that price tag a little better. Personally, I like it and will definitely keep playing around with it as they update it more.

My minor gripe about the game is it's asking price of $30 which seems high for a game that competes with other casual puzzle titles that are sub $10.  The overlay is supported, as is a single steam achievement, making this game ideal for Perfect Game hunters and puzzle enthusiasts alike.  This is definitely a title to keep an eye on.

It seems odd to have mixed feelings about a game I have spent so much time on, but the good outweighs the bad.  First, the good.  The world is well-drawn and looks good for the most part.  The combat is much better than ME1, which I found unplayable for the most part.  The choice of male or female, paragon or renegade, and different classes gives the game quite a bit of replayability.  I even played through ME1, which I hated, just to have different choices to carry over into this game.  The look of the armor is fun to customize.  Most of the characters are interesting and I wanted to do their loyalty missions because they are worth caring about.  The best part was the spam emails, odd conversations to overhear, and the overall lore of the ME universe.  I may even check out some SF books based on this playground.  And the game made me laugh out loud many times, which was unexpected and great.  "But all haggis tastes like♥♥♥♥♥anyway."  "True, but in the right hands, it can taste like mighty fine♥♥♥♥♥"  Priceless.
Unfortunately, things that were not so great in the first game were not fixed, they were discarded.  Convoluted and over-complicated inventory, gone.  Mako, gone.  Scanning for resources gets boring, but it was quicker than running around with the Mako, but I wish these things could have been improved instead of lazily scrapping them.  Elevator simulator replaced by load screens.  Fish that are impossible to keep alive.  Most of the extras included in the DD edition I didn't care for.  Zaeed mission was okay, but the character seemed to be a concept piece discarded in the original then just tossed in to grab some case in DLC.  The cerberus and collector armor that is part of the DD edition I didn't like and never used.  The godawful ugly armor from the first game is just gone, leaving your squadmates in the same slick outfits on the ship as in combat.
The biggest problem, however, is the DLC.  Digital Deluxe seems to describe a comprehensive collection, containing all of  the expansions.  Not by a long shot.  Romance Liara in the first game?  Shepard gets a only a kiss, since you have to buy Shadow Broker.   Submachine gun is useless.  Buy Kasumi, etc.  These DLC cost much more than I paid for both complete games I bought on steam, thanks to the unholy trinity of EA, Bioware, and Origin.  Now either get ripped off or find a pirate copy, and still have to deal with Origin for the third game.  Oh, smeg!

Owlboy is simply one of the most impressive indie games I've seen the last years, and I'd say the overall experience makes it equally worth playing as the likes of Shovel Knight, Braid, Cave Story, Undertale and Hyper Light Drifter (not to say that these other games don't have strengths this game doesn't have). The pixel art is stunningly good, perhaps the best I've seen in any hi-bit game. Especially the multiple layered backgrounds look amazing. It contains a very charming cast of characters, who are well-written and highly likable. The OST fits the game perfectly, and some of the tracks will hit you right in the feels.
The gameplay is fairly simple, but with an intersting blend of mechanics for the combat. You fly around freely, though you can only stun enemies with Owlboy; for dealing damage you need to use other characters you encounter in the game, and their respective attacks are effective against different set of mobs. The combat works as a twin stick shooter where you can freely aim and fire in all directions irrespective of movement or the direction Owlboy is facing. The gist of it is dashing to dodge mobs while aiming and firing with correct timing, as well as swapping efficiently between your different characters depending on the specific weakness of the mob(s). Your are pointed to the main dungeons in a mostly linear fashion, interspersed with cutscenes and dialogue that drives the story. But there's also metroidvania-like exploration for collectibles (coins and golden disks) and simple puzzles, and the game handles the dungeons well by keeping them fresh and unique, often revolving around gimmicks specific to the abilities of the most recently acquired character.
Owlboy doesn't have the same replayability as Shovel Knight with its speedrun achievement or Undertale with its multiple endings, and it's not a hard game to beat. But as an aesthetic experience it's superior to both. This is a masterly handicrafted game, a labor of love, and the most comfy 10 hours you're likely to spend this year.

The game sure is a strategy RPG. It gives so much options to the players to pick, choose, and apply them to the players playstyle. Not only the usual walk and whack system, it allows you to lift units (yes including enemies), combine and capture enemy, stealing their items, utilize map elements (that capable of insta killing units), and many more.
Story wise, compared to disgaea 2, it does a good job in balancing the serious and comedic moments.  I find that the angel and demon dynamic/chemistry were handled well; however, Laharl power level was not really defined; making the story attempt in creating stake and danger seems misdirected. While we are at it, the most questionable part of the game is when they introduce what seems like a throwaway silly characters
and let them stay for more than a chapter. They also have a dramatic chapter dedicated for them, which I cannot care/take seriously because of their nature. In addition, that chapter had a quite high difficulty spike; resulting a bad experiance, grinding just to proceed to a story that I couldn't care about. In conclusion, it has a passable story; the weak near end section can be covered by the fun first-half of the story
Next, other reviews mention/complain about the grinding; however, in my opinion you should grind as little as you can afford to for two reasons. First, there will always be a better method/better place to grind that simply renders the 5-10 levels that you just gained by grinding for 1 hour useless, because you can fnish a map in 5 minutes and gain the same result, or even better later on. Secondly, as mentioned earlier in this review; there are just many options that you can do to alleviate the need of grinding:
- Fight with small party (1-3 units) and let them get more levels
- Use ranged spell attacks to kill strong enemy (even if you have to cast it 20 times)
- Use ailment to weaken/kill enemy
- Steal enemy's equipment so that they do less damage and take more damage
- Use disposable units as a bait/healer
- Lure enemy, separate them, and gang them near the base panel
- Have 1 character tank the damage, while others can pop up from base, attack, and then retreat
- Let enemy waste their MP by constantly taking hits and heal
- Throw enemy/ally to a disjointed side of map
- Arrange geo panels to kill enemy
I am sure I miss other viable strategies, but the point is that I did not grind much for most part of the main story section. Admittedly, the last few chapters require you to grind. (which if you grind enough to pass that chapter, you are good until the end of the game)
One last thing, endgame content are also worth mentioning. This is a game that, if you feel like it, you can play endlessly. There are multiple endings to pursue, secret stages to complete, ultimate weapon to get, overpowered/sily party to build,  secret stats and tid bit that you can learn and exploit. Just don't be afraid to read FAQS and you are good to go (else you'll waste a lot of time doing stuff inefficiently).
Edit: Honorary mention to the PC port for adding keyboard shortcuts, mouse support (even if I did not use it), resizable windows, and general graphic improvements.

The biggest problem I have with this game is the balancing. I immediately started the game in hard mode and I still beat every boss in my first try until the last row of bosses. Here it started to get hard, but only because of randomness and chances. Either the game gives you crazy curses or just some tiny things which dont really make it more challenging for you, there is not much inbetween. Also the blessings you get are nowhere near as powerful as the curses you get, most of the blessings are simply useless. Later there will be many encounters which outcome is either you get to draw 3 equipment cards or something like that, or you loose 50% of your maximum health. Again there is nothing in between. Why not loose 5% maximum health? Why maximum health? Why not normal health? Ah because the game lets you regenerate tons of health every step so making you loose health isn't a problem, but when you are out of rations you loose TONS of health with every step. They should reduce both of these values and make the punishments less ridiculous.
At this part of the game it's not about "do I want to take this event with me or not" but more about "just try to pass every card without getting into trouble". What makes this more problematic are the rewards you get. Most of the time it's just things like "+5 max health" (WOW!), "+5 gold" (WOW!) and after you found a good weapon or good armor all other armor or weapon drops you get are useless. At least you can wear many rings at the same time, so those are always useful, but the rings don't have good effects at all, some totally useless. And even worse, every reward you get is meant for combat, but not the game itself, like there is nothing which gives you better chances or I don't know more vision of the map or something like that apart from 1 or 2 items maybe.
And this is a problem because the combat in this game is extremely easy, I beat 90% of the fights without loosing health, and if I loose health it's just because I got careless because it's so easy. So if the game gives me stuff which makes combat even easier I'm not really feeling rewarded.
The combat itself is solid, but they throw in so many unnessary and random slow motions during the fight which are annoying and bad for the pacing. There aren't that many different enemy types but enough I guess. Whats nice is that the different weapons and armors do not simply have better or worse stats, but unique effects like "cast an explosion", "freeze everyone", "damage everyone who hits you" and stuff like that.
My problem with the combat is that it doesn't fit the theme of the game in my opinion. This is a card game, so I thought it is the perfect situation for a combat like in other card games like Hearthstone, Yu-gi-oh or whatever. Or make a turn-based fighting system which happens on the table with the cards. Everything is better than what we have here, especially because this Arkham combat system is only as good as its presentation, you need nice sound effects, lots of great animations and stuff like that.
The biggest selling point is the presentation of the game, I especially like the "gamemaster". Unfortunately he starts to repeat himself very fast and very often which gets annoying. But the voice actor does a good job. Also the music fits the game and creates a nice atmossphere, but you will hear the same music all the time. The card texts are written very well and there is a good amount of variety. I like that they want to tell small sub-stories within the game, after beating a card you get its symbol which unlocks a new card which continues the story of the previous card in some way. But they could do more with that, because these cards still work individually and tell smaller stories than I expected. I think what would be nice is that you could have like 4 cards for the same story which you could all put in your deck, then the game would scatter them in the world in order and you get better and better rewards for each of them. This would give you more decisions as the player, do you put the beginning cards of the story in your deck which is safer or do you put more story cards in your deck to have like more synergy. Currently the deck building is bare bones. I just put everything in my deck where I haven't unlocked the symbol yet and the rest I fill up with the cards where I know the game won`t screw me over, because some cards are just useless. The chances of winning for some is ridiculous and the rewards are not good enough at all to make this risk worth it.
The game is still fun because of the nice presentation, exploring the different cards and their stories and the combat is not terrible, but doesn`t fit the game. Some design flaws and some wasted potential makes this just a "good" game though, but it could easily be a fantastic game.

To cut straight to the chase, this is my favorite strategy game to date, and that is not due to lack of variety. I have played a large amount of RTS such as Sins of a Solar Empire, Age of Empires, Total War, and Star Wars: Empire at War, and various others.
Yet none of the above gave quite the satisfaction that Kingdom Wars 2: Battles does, and that is not due to cheap gimmicks or repetitive game play.
Just to give a brief bullet point list of some of the features that I find quite enjoyable:
- Faction Diversity
- Unit Specialization
- Fire, lots of fire
- Size of maps allow many forms of combat
- Zombies
- Unit Diversity
Now, to go over each piece individually.
Faction Diversity
Each faction quite simply plays very different from each other, and while there is a slight bit of overlap, as there is in every RTS, each have their own tricks and techniques to master. For example, the Orc Faction has the highest number of soldiers per unit as well as the ability to mass produce weak units such as goblins, which can win wars of attrition if you play your cards right. On the other hand, the Human Faction has some of the tankiest units in the game but is more of a balance between Elves and Orcs than anything else. Other than their durability, their units do not stick out too much, but it is quite pivotal if you are able to compound on such. Finally, the Elves, have the lowest soldiers per unit, but also have the highest quality of units, which allow them to defeat superior numbers more often than not. Despite all of this though, each faction has balanced counters and maneuvers to use against each other, with no one strategy being undefeatable. For each move, there is a counter move, for every counter move there is another counter. In essence, balance is maintained for the most part, with no one Faction getting too far ahead of the others. Each can be phenomenal in the right player’s hands.
Unit Specialization
Quite simple really, but each unit has 'levels' that they achieve when they have gained enough experience from combat. This in turn, allows you to distribute stats for that unit as you see fit, meaning that a full blown army can be as unique as you deem fit. It could be as simple as maxing out the defensive stats, or going for full out mobility... Yet each is viable in different situations, with no one configuration being the end all be all. Diversity is the word of the game.
Fire
This one is much simpler than the previous item, in that it is quite self-explanatory. Archers and siege equipment can make use of fire to damage buildings, do extra damage to units, or even light the battle field itself on fire. In short, just as in real life, fire is one hell of a weapon.
Map Size
There are four castle plots, one taken by each player unless there are less than four of course. Each one is in a corner of the map, with defensible positions dotted all over the place, including bridges, ruins, quarries, and npc forts. The time it takes to travel across the map isn't too long, but just long enough to make you think before emptying your garrison. Caught without an army at home, you will suffer the consequences.
Zombies
A relatively new addition, these buggers form up large hordes outside your castle and in essence prolong the game unless you can circumvent them. You used to be able to direct them against your opponents with clever sacrifice of units, but they are more a field threat these days. Every unit that dies and is not looted... Well... Expect to see them again. Not only does this add some threat to the general map to consider when moving about, but it also being key to use scouts to avoid them or funnel enemies towards them. While they are destructible, they can still wreak quite a bit of havoc before being put down.
Unit Diversity
Each Faction has some basic units similar to another, but even then, each have their own defining characteristics. Take spearmen for example, orcs have Impalers, elves Sentries, and humans Halberdiers. The Halberdiers lack special abilities, but have higher base stats and are able to cut down monsters and Calvary quite efficiently. Impalers on the other hand are slow and lower damage, as well as health, but have an AoE ability that can one shot a large charging Calvary force, as well as stun them, not to mention it works decently against other infantry as well. Sentries on the other hand have a stun ability, which allows them to combat Calvary and monsters while taking little damage. What we have here, are three different units designed for the same task, yet go about doing it in completely different ways. Nor are they only type to have such differences.
In short, KW2 is a great RTS that gets you in the action, gives you the tools to create the army you always dreamed of commanding, and to proceed however you want. Want stealth based combat? Elves have plenty of that, and the Orc's Goblins can do such as well. Want to take a tanky approach? All three have their own methods, such as Slayers, Knights, and Grandmasters. Archers? Most definitely. Another interesting thing, is the siege equipment... But I might as well not spoil it for those who have not played yet, but suffice to say, they can be used in a variety of situations.
Don't believe me on half of what I said? Try it for yourself, and you are sure to find something you enjoy here.

In Hand of Fate, from what I can surmise, you are in some sort of netherworld or afterlife and have met with a dealer who plays a card game with your life at stake. This game is beautiful in a lot of ways, from the narration, to the environment and visuals, to the overall presentation. Early on, the game is very balanced, growing in difficulty as you progress. It also features a roguelike element, in that if you lose, you start at the beginning of the floor again. The roguelike comparison mostly ends there, besides luck being an element, but there is also a choose your own adventure feel to the game that adds longevity and a breath of fresh air!
In this card game, you have cards that both you and the dealer place into the deck. The deck is then laid out like a dungeon, and you traverse it. Each step, or new card, costs food, but there are gain cards that you can draw that can give food, money, or equipment. There are also pain cards that will make you lose resources or health, too. So there is in almost all things an element of risk vs reward, and this is good. There is also resource management: You will have to be wise with your spending. The right or wrong gear can save or cost your life.
This game features real-time rhythm-based combat, in an interesting mix. You can attack at any time, but if you wait and time your button presses, you can dodge, or parry enemy attacks automatically. With every update it seems to get smoother, allowing for a fun and engaging flurry of attacks that flow together with bliss.
There is also an element of stacking the deck, as you gain more powerful equipment, and more situations in which you know the outcome to pit yourself against, you can make sure to load the deck with only encounters and equipment suited to the floor ahead. In this way, early on, success can be guaranteed, but later on, it will become very beneficial and perhaps required.
Other gameplay features include and endless mode, mini dungeons complete with traps and treasure, a card-based mixup game where you can actually track the cards, and inventory management in the form of being able to buy/sell extra cards at shops.
The graphics in Hand of Fate can be as simple or immersive as you want, ranging from murky at the lowest settings to absolutely gorgeous when maxed out, although this can be quite performance intensive. The use of color, light, shadow, cartoonish and realistic aspects are all outstanding. There is also a great use of special effects. Everything feels immersive and hand-tailored to perfection.
The environments are gorgeous, from the dealer's room to the mini-dungeons to the encounter fields and even the cards themselves. Everything in this game drips quality and polish. This game is obviously a labor of love for the developers.
I should also mention that the animations and transitions, which can be jittery at times, are really well done!
If you've heard the dealer speak, then you likely know how nice the audio in this game is. Everything is crisp, with a good recording quality, and here too, drips polish. The sounds of weapons slicing, clashing, and bouncing off of shields are all quite nice, and probably some of the most common you will hear aside from the dealer.
The music is good, although I find it blends into the background sneakily most of the time. The large majority of the game is made up of the various sound effects, all of which, again, are nice. Unfortunately, I can't say much specific about the audio that would convey to you just how it all sounds when you're actually playing the game.
Hand of Fate is more of an indie goldmine than an indie gem. It oozes polish and is a glorious mashup of TCG and roguelite featuring rhythm-based combat that still allows for real-time as well. It features quality music, an outstanding voiceover, flowing combat, a wonderfully refreshing choose your own style, and good resource management qualities. You owe it to yourself to pick this game up and enjoy!

"Hand of Fate" could have been a total mess, a hybrid of a collectible card, board, choice, hack & slash, rouge-like and various other game elements, with an "opponent" who is sitting opposite of a table to you and just insults you most of the time.
But somehow, it isn't a mess. On the contrary, all it's aspects are put together in such a smart way, that it makes for an interesting, engaging, fun game to play.
At the core of the game is a "deck of cards", packed with various encounters, events, vendors, monsters and equipment. Here a big part of it already starts, because as you progress through the game, you mostly become responsible for which cards are in the deck and you form your own adventure. Though, at the same time, the role of your "opponent", the dealer, becomes obvious soon, when he includes some cards himself into the deck and deals the cards to you, taunting you, looking down on you when you fail and showing his spite on your success.
This theme and the dynamic presented by the only one who actually gets some character, which is the dealer, already creates an intriguing setup.
Then, when the cards are dealt, you have to continue over a kind of "board" made of the encounters, which are usually revealed as you step on each card. Sometimes something mandatory happens, but most of the time a choice will follow, how you want to deal with the encounter and as you progress through the game, you will learn about the consequences of those decisions. And sometimes, through the encounters, you will have to play in a completely different setting, where a lot of the actual action and fighting happens, which requires your skill to overcome those chellenges, though sometimes it feels somewhat unprecise.
And like that you progress through the game, board by board, gaining new cards, events, equipment, but also new monsters and other chellenges.
And so the weird mix turns into this game, which you can influence in a lot of ways, the way you want to play, with which cards and how to act upon encounters, spiced with some chance and skill, delivered through an awesome theme, underlined with some story, which just makes it awesome.
10/10 would play again and again and again...

Kingdom Wars 2: Battles is an incredibly interesting concept in todays view of rts strategy games. It takes mechanics from all over, with resource nodes from games like age of empires or empire earth; huge scale combat from the total war games including the batallions of x amount of units per squad. It's so nostalgic and at the same time thrilling to play a game like this. As much as I'd like to praise it up to the stars and call it the new messiah, I can't do that fairly. So let's look at some of the negatives I've noticed during gameplay.
- Archers: These guys are useful, but good god can they not aim at times. If you stick them on a wall, sure they'll aim as well as they can, but when you have about 3 orcish marauders (orc archers) left in a squad firing at your 5 squads on a wall, and killing them like flies while hundreds of arrows rain down upon the orcish invaders, and not a single one is hitting them, it's a little bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's not even a case of them having godly luck by dodging, the archers just don't aim at them. They aim a bit to the left, or a bit to the right, and every single arrow aims in that spot instead of where the enemy is actually standing! It's infuriating! The siege is the same too, missing countless shots and wasting ammunition to try and flatten the ground next to the invader. AGH!
- Terrain: This is a little bugbear of mine, but it still counts in this. On some maps you play singleplayer, I've found that if I try to play humans, and have stone walls defending the core of my city, I can't place anyone on the outer layer. By outer layer I mean the humans have a kind of bastion style design. If intruders break through the outer walls, they have to break through the inner gates. But the inner gates are broken into two parts. I won't fully explain it since I'd sound like an utter moron trying to explain something I don't know about, but look it up. I'm sure there are a few images flying around of the human castles by now.
- Balance: As of the current release of the game, I've found that the elves are insanely overpowered. Now, in a lot of games I've played over the years, elves can be quite dangerous, but if you try enough, they'll fall over flat on their pretty little faces. In this game? Good god. They're the same as all others, don't get me wrong. Push enough and they'll still die. But in terms of resources, they will outlast you. How? They get a building called a symbiosis tree, which allows them to CREATE resources. Yup, I really mean that. They can create gold mines, stone mines, even more berries if they so fancy. This means they can keep pumping out entire armies of powerful troops, while you're scrounging around the map desperately trying to find some gold for another squad of knights.
- Walls: Useful, correct? well, not when the wall is blocking all your arrows trying to murder a single zombie battering down your damn gate, and you can't open that gate because the zombie is hitting it. Infuriating, especially as an orc, since you only get one exit out of your plateau. Truly infuriating. It's made even worse when you watch your archers arrows hit thin air way above the barricades and the enemy on the other side is perfectly safe. Worst bugbear ever.
Now, I know that a lot of these problems should be solved during the next couple updates, and admittedly they'll take a while. I'm an impatient person so I want them as soon as possible, so I can enjoy this game even more. But on the whole, for the feel this game gives you when you play this, it's totally worth it in my opinion. Especially for the price right now. £10.99? I'd pay £20 for this game, just because it's brilliant, and brings back the main thing I love in games like this; strategic options. Rush them, or defend. It's your choice.

I have 3 drives on my PC (1 ssd and 2 WD black HDDs that I use to store games)  and this game runs like trash on one of the HDDs. No idea what causes it, but I was only getting like 20-30fps on when I had it on that drive and it wouldn't even start on that drive unless I changed the compatiblilty to Windows 98/Me. I switched it over to the other hard drive and it runs much better, I'm now getting 200-130fps depending on where I am and I didn't have to change the compatiblity at all. The drive I originally had it on runs games like The Witcher 3 and Shadow of War just fine, so I don't know why this game has such a problem. 23 hours in at the time of this writing and I'm still not out of what is regarded as "chapter 1." I love this kind of game.
You can pick a pre-made character that you can freely edit in terms of skills and stats, or make your own from scratch. Those you do not play as end up as your companions. It adds a degree of replayability to experience the story from multiple perspectives, though you do get to see a lot of the companions' motives and personalities even if you aren't playing as one.
There's a lot you can do, too. There is usually more than one way to solve a quest or puzzle, and even the combat encourages you to get creative. Drop oil barrels on enemies to ignite them, or burst them open in front of you and create a wall of flame to protect your backline. Electrocute anyone standing in water. Wager risk vs. reward when you factor in the inevitability of friendly fire. Every encounter is sure to leave the player thinking, "What if I handled that differently?" And this, to me, is the mark of a great game - something that makes you want to go back and try it again.
The story is present and much more solid than the first game, though I would say the NPC interactions and pushing the limits of what you can do are the real draws to the game. If you enjoyed old-school CRPGs like Baldur's Gate, Arcanum, or Planescape, you'll definitely enjoy this. Well worth the money spent.

"Hand of Fate" could have been a total mess, a hybrid of a collectible card, board, choice, hack & slash, rouge-like and various other game elements, with an "opponent" who is sitting opposite of a table to you and just insults you most of the time.
But somehow, it isn't a mess. On the contrary, all it's aspects are put together in such a smart way, that it makes for an interesting, engaging, fun game to play.
At the core of the game is a "deck of cards", packed with various encounters, events, vendors, monsters and equipment. Here a big part of it already starts, because as you progress through the game, you mostly become responsible for which cards are in the deck and you form your own adventure. Though, at the same time, the role of your "opponent", the dealer, becomes obvious soon, when he includes some cards himself into the deck and deals the cards to you, taunting you, looking down on you when you fail and showing his spite on your success.
This theme and the dynamic presented by the only one who actually gets some character, which is the dealer, already creates an intriguing setup.
Then, when the cards are dealt, you have to continue over a kind of "board" made of the encounters, which are usually revealed as you step on each card. Sometimes something mandatory happens, but most of the time a choice will follow, how you want to deal with the encounter and as you progress through the game, you will learn about the consequences of those decisions. And sometimes, through the encounters, you will have to play in a completely different setting, where a lot of the actual action and fighting happens, which requires your skill to overcome those chellenges, though sometimes it feels somewhat unprecise.
And like that you progress through the game, board by board, gaining new cards, events, equipment, but also new monsters and other chellenges.
And so the weird mix turns into this game, which you can influence in a lot of ways, the way you want to play, with which cards and how to act upon encounters, spiced with some chance and skill, delivered through an awesome theme, underlined with some story, which just makes it awesome.

Rougelike, CCG, brawler, with a dark and interesting antagonist.
It's an indie title that's tried something new, and nailed it in my opinion. on't be everyones cup of tea.
But the game is laid out fairly simply enough, it's a rouge like where each card is an encounter of some sort either won by luck, prior knowledge, or through brawling. There are a 3 decks, your deck of cards that you can select to put into the pile, the antagonists deck which he picks from to screw you over as you play the game, and the static cards put into the pile based on which boss awaits you at the end of that run. Each time you play you can earn new cards by successfully beating an encounter for the first time, this will give you more cards to pick from when you play the next round. Will you make your deck challenging with higher rewards for those risks, or easier with less rewards which will leave you less capable of fighting the boss at the end of that run...?
