So this game is really good.
I have a few complaints, but most of those were answered in the sequels (from what I can tell). There are a lot of little hang ups and problems with shoving turn based strategy and third person action shooter together, but honestly the combination is more interesting than it is flawed.
What this game does accomplish is a cool setting with a cool aesthetic, seriously the art is super well done. Unlike a lot of tactics games, this one keeps the game fun while still dealing with the reality of warfare, that is to say there isn't an Advanced Wars 1 and 2 style 'lawl fighting is great' after losing literally hundreds of troops and combat machines. Unlike a lot of WW2 games, there are a lot of little touches on the not so great side of war, like that civilians often get caught up in the conflict with nowhere to go when they're between two armies other than hoping that joining one of them will give them some control over their lives (or deaths), that the worst in people can show up (like prejudice against certain people) and that not everyone in the military gets preferential treatment like a lot of the 'heroes' in games usually set in this era (as you're technically a militia rather than a regular army even though you fight just as hard and are given missions that even the regular army doesn't want to do).
The absolute coolest thing about this game though is that every trooper has a personality. You get this in both the fact that each has individualized voice acting (which is ♥♥♥♥ing cool enough, like wow) and that each soldier has individual ways in which they both have traits and represent them in combat. Some of them have a pretty decent effect on how that combat goes too: If your engineer prefers the company of women you'd better shove her in with your women troopers so that she fights harder, if your trooper is prejudiced against darcsens you might want to pair them up with non-darcsen troopers so that they fight better overall. Soldiers will have people they like and pairing those people together will mean they'll probably fight a lot better and work to protect their friends. Soon your fighting unit starts to work in certain ways because of your troops preferences, even if on paper a lot of them are largely the same. You can totally replace them if they actually die in battle too: you level up troopers by class instead of on an individual basis, so if you level shocktroopers to level 4, all your shocktroopers, the ones in your squad now and ones you might add in the future, are level 4. That said, there have been more than a few missions I've delayed to med-evac troops even though it would honestly save time to just let them die, because a. I know how they work as individuals and b. this game honestly makes it easy to get attached to them.
That last part, right there, alone, makes this a good game. The rest of it paired with it is just icing on the cake. Really, this game is phenomenal and I hope we get to see the sequels on steam soon.

Have you ever played Final Fantasy and thought to yourself "I wish I could be that guy behind the counter" when you walked into an item or weapon shop?   Yeah... me too.  Now your dreams can become reality!
This game is a pretty unique idea and it's reasonably well executed, for what it is.  It's a very simple game, but the mechanics of it make it addictive enough to warrant my purchase.  I honestly didn't expect much out of it, and bought it on sale, but I am plreasantly surprised - it's entertaining.
The game is about a slightly mentally handicapped girl named Recette, and her loan shark (who happens to be a fairy) forcing her to run a small business in order to pay her father's debt or ultimately reposses her house and everything this owns.  Recette, not being the brightest girl, decided to combine her name and the name of the person trying to take everything she has (Tear) into one word for the name of the shop - Recettear.  Unfortunately, the poor girl doesn't quite understand her circumstance and even though I've not played the game too much yet, I am doubtful she ever will until of course, you can't pay the debt back and the game over screen shows her living in a cardboard box with her name on it.
Yeah, I lost.  I didn't make the first payment.  But I had a pretty good time.  There are some decent pro's to this simple game that make it more entertaining than the summary of it's plot makes it sound.  Recette's stupidity is adorable, of course, and there's a good deal of other humor that at least got a chuckle out of me.   Like say.. the name of her store being absurdly close to "Racketeer".   The dialogue will probably make you giggle a little bit, if you like the cute brain-dead loli personality.
The game's mecahnics are not complex, but they are pretty fun.  You buy low from a a wholesaler or find good deals at the market, and sell as high as you can without♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your customers.  You set up the shop to appeal to people walking by the window by placing your best items in the window displays.  People come into your store, and browse, and get stuff.  You haggle with them based on their reactions and try to make the sale.  You can upset people, or you can get loyal customers, depending on your success.  People will often come in and tell you they're looking for a sword, or dinner, and you then have to suggest something in your stock to them and try to get them to buy it.  People will also sometimes offer to sell you an item, which follows the same rules as buying, but in reverse.   You can upgrade, re-arrange and expand your shop, once you suck a little less.
One neat aspect of the game is that you can go adventuring in a dungeon and you will have adventurer friends - whom will come in and buy items from you.   They will then use those items in the dungeons and have a higher chance of success - at less cost to you.  The dungeon gameplay is fun as well.  Think Zelda / Secret of Mana, and it feels satisfying.  There are special attacks, to add a little variety, though most of the time you'll just be attacking normally - it's still pretty fun.
It's cute and good natured, and is an easygoing experience.  It's worth a couple dollars - on sale the price was definitely right.  I might have even paid a couple more for it - maybe.   It's not a game that will keep you coming back for more indefinitely, but what can you really expect?  The sprites and backgrounds have a lot of character and detail, and the characters are not bad, for the most part.  I have a few issues with the localization, but it's not that much of an issue.
I'd buy it.   It's a different kind of game and is pretty entertaining. Capitalism Ho!  ...as Recette would say.    Great game!

The artwork is very pretty.  That's about the only positive thing I have to say about this game.
It is *intensely* boring.  If you want to make a card game, make a card game.  If you want to make an action combat game, then do that.  What you have here is a very mediocre card game and an extremely mediocre action combat game put together.  If they had given up one concept they might have had enough resources to devote to the other to make it good.
Here's how it works, you build a deck of equipment, bonus cards and encounters.  And then the game master lays some encounters on the table face down and your game piece "walks" across them, you pick the next card to walk on, and frequently you have only one choice.  Each encounter is either a choose-your-own adventure style multiple-choice question with a bit of random chance thrown in, or a "battle" if you can call it that.  Each battle is a mouse mashing clickfest.  The mechanics are stunningly bad and you can't even rotate the camera which is very annoying because some of your opponents will run off camera where you can't see them.
That's pretty much it.  Card after card after card, monotonous battle after monotonous battle, all accompanied by the narration of the game master, whose mouth is masked but unfortunately not gagged.  The lines are delivered by a capable voice actor, but they are so vapid, uninspired, and ultimately irrelevant that eventually they just become annoying noise that you have to sit through.
Sadly, there is no "shut up" button in evidence, maybe somewhere in the options?
In any event I only played about a half hour or so... if you're bored in 30 minutes it's a really bad sign I figure.  Anyway, I guess it's not a game for me, and listening to other people rave about it, I am clearly in the minority. You may enjoy it, I recommend going on youtube and watching someone else play it for an hour.  If after that you are still interested, you'll probably love it.

I picked this up on a sale for 1,99€ and it was worth the money.
It's a point and click detective game with a supernatural story.
It's not much to the detective part in the game, you mostly answer questions by clicking on clues you have found.
The game have some kind of system where if you guess something wrong you lose a "badge" and you have three badges for each mystery but it will not effect anything in the game as far as I could tell.
It feels like it was meant for a achievement but they never put it in or that the detective part was supposed to be more complex but got scratched later on.
The game have a nice old detective movie feeling to it and the story keeps you interesting.
The story is about a detective that have to solve his on murder as a ghost to move on. The two main characters are good written and works well together. It's a nice spooky feeling throughout the game even tho it's not a horror game.
In addition to the main story you can solve a handful of side cases for lost spirits around the world to give them peace and in addition to that there is a lot of collectables scattered around.
The collectables tells you about the town, the murderer, your character and ghost stories. The ghost stories is a really nice addition, I appreciated them a lot.
It took me around eleven hours to finish and I did most of the side stuff, I missed some collectables.
If you see this game on a sale I would recommand you to pick it up but not for the current pricetag (29,99€).

Well, I'm not gonna give a lengthy description of this game like a lot of other players have, however this is a game I suggest.
I had personally been wanting to play this since it came out, mostly because I'm a fan of murder mysteries -I've played several of the Sherlock Holmes games and enjoy them alot- so solving a murder mystery appealed to me, especially my characters murder.
Not counting all of the extra items, collectables and stuff, the game is pretty short, I beat it in about 11 hours.  I'm sure that grabbing all the collectables would take a bit longer, but on my first playthough, I always focus on getting through the plot, then I grab extras.
I enjoyed challenging myself and trying to guess who the killer was, while getting a reminder of a darker side of American history in the process. The ending was about 50-50 predicable, in my opinion, in a completely good way. I figured it out a little ahead of Ronnan, but not by too much. The final culprit practically surprised but left me interested.
The most annoying thing that I found about the game was the 'demon' hunting.  The multiple button pressing at the same time often ended in failure for me, and I was often frustrated with them -since they pit you against groups of 3-4 usually. Failing to take them out quickly ususally either gets you killed, or alerts at least one other and you get two of them hunting you. As a result, I was often frustrated and running from the demons several times before I would finally kill them.  The buttons could have been a bit better for dispatching them, I think, since in my case, pressing R and then either Q, W, A, S, D with a mouse button often did not end well.
'Demons' Aside, I quite enjoy this game and its an entertaining mystery that also helps give a somber reminder of history with it.

"A, B, C. Always Be Closing."
If it weren't for
with Alec Baldwin, I probably would've never heard of this film. Even though much of what his character claims can be
in the face of newly developed sales strategies, nothing alters the true impact that both the audience and the surrounding characters feel during those first 15 minutes. A change in motivation for said characters isn't easily accomplished by one mere speech though, and with everyone's job on the line in spite of all the years they've worked at the agency, things get a bit stingy in the Big Apple.
Being a faithful recreation of the play, Glengarry GlenRoss dedicates much of its time to the characters and their reactions to the conflicts that arise in the film. And as expected, the main cast conveys these emotions flawlessly, with every line of dialogue hinting at something relevant and meaningful to the film. Jack Lemmon goes above and beyond in his portrayal of Shelley Levene, and truly shines when conversing with Kevin Spacey's character, where we get to feel Levine's innate desperation to protect his job at any cost and regain his pride as a salesman.
Much of the underlying subtext is brilliant as well; at the conclusion of the "closing" scene, Baldwin's character walks back into the main office with the camera positioned in a way that emphasizes the "Salesmen are born, not made" banner above the office window. That message comes largely into play later, and can arguably explain why the characters in the office didn't exactly heed Baldwin's advice. The thunder & lightning in the first half also does justice in escalating narrative tension, notably in Dave Moss's monologues about his attitude towards Mitch & Murray (Owners of real estate agency that sent Baldwin's character to "motivate" the salesmen), and almost all of the scenes with Jack Lemmon.
Jack Howard Newton is an unknown name to me as far as the music department goes, but when music does play, it captures the noir-rich atmosphere of the film's setting just right, with New York-style saxophones & bass guitars dominating the score. My only gripe is that the guitar was a little hard to hear during Al Pacino's scenes in the second half; I didn't like how his voice kept drowning it out, but that's probably just me.
On behalf of the estimated
that the filmmakers lost during theatrical release, it's safe to say that Glengarry GlenRoss isn't for everyone, regardless of the film's all-star cast. Sales jargon is practically omnipresent, so talk of "leads" and "pipelines" can easily throw off viewers whom aren't acquainted with the jargon beforehand. No marketing research required, but this is definitely one of those "Ah schucks, I've gotta watch this turkey again to understand it better" movies.
All in all, Glengarry GlenRoss is a cinematic classic, and a film I recommend to anyone who loves movies with great characters, well written dialogue, and A-list actors.

Continuing the story from the second game (and marginally attempting to include bits of the first game), this concludes the Time Mysteries series of hidden object games. Like the first two, the puzzles are straightforward and it shouldn't take you long to finish the game and get all the achievements. The voice acting is still bad, but the writing has improved a bit for this one and sends you in better time-looped circles than the first two.
Improvement in the graphics is sadly offset by typos in the main menu and game text, and some explanatory text which doesn't make sense (have a look at the chess game puzzle). To top off the 'we rushed this' attitude, the trading cards still have the Time Mysteries 2 logo on them.
After being a bit more impressed with the Nightmares hidden object games, playing through all three of these games I keep coming back to the same thought - there's a really neat concept here with the time travelling family with its roots in the Merlin mythology that's been butchered and given poor, rushed execution. While this continuation of the story is an improvement, the series still leaves a bitter aftertaste in knowing it could have been done so much better.

I don't even know where to start. At first I thought I'd get a typical space adventure with laser beams and stuff, but what I actually got was beyond all my expectations. First of all the story is great. It keeps gradually developing between the games and keeps the player intrigued at all times. We all have played at least one of those games that keep you wide awake through the whole night, and this truly is one of those. Even after finishing the game there are loads of fascinating lore waiting to be read and trust me, it's worth it.
Sadly if you're not interested in talking to people wholeheartedly or just don't care about the dialogue that much, you'll miss most of the game's charm since most of the important stuff happen during conversations. Some things tend to get complicated really fast if you decide to skip even a few important dialogues. And sometimes just listening to random NPCs was enough to keep me entertained, even if it didn't have anything to do with the mission itself. The amount of work that has been put into the dialogue really pays off, and I barely remember times when talking with someone didn't put a smile on my face.
Probably the thing that made the game for me were the characters. I found something intriguing in all of them (even if Kelly Chambers deserves death for "you have new messages" when there are none) and I couldn't wait for getting to do their loyalty missions and actually making them my friends rather than just comrades during the war. Only some of them started to grow on me. The more I talked with them the more I started to love them to bits... especially Tali, Garrus and Mordin. I actually started to feel like I wanted to keep them alive and protect them at all costs, and that's when you know they're well made.
After playing the first game the controls feel so smooth and not complicated at all, so there's nothing to complain about. During combat the only flaw I found was that at times Shepard seemed to be unable to follow the instructions and just died without jumping over a simple obstacle, but those things happen. Also the AI might seem a bit idiotic, but that probably can be corrected by choosing a higher difficulty setting.
And oh god, the replay value. The possibilities are almost endless when it comes to how you want to play. Different classes, gender, decisions, romances... everything can be played differently and affects things in different ways. In most games the only thing you can affect is whether you want to be the good samaritan or not, and that's it. This is the first time I've ever felt that by replaying I might actually achieve something I didn't the last time I played, even if it'd take another 30 hours of my life.
The graphics were really good too, even if Bioware still tends to overuse the blur effect. Overall the game is pretty and really pleases the eye. There simply aren't reasons why someone shouldn't at least try the game out - except if you aren't ready for the bumpy ride Mass Effect 1 first wants to offer you.

Owlboy is a beautiful, retro-inspired platformer that delivers fun and emotional story telling, a neat twist on platforming, and wonderful roster of characters. The gameplay is reminiscent of a more linear Metroid. This game does SO much right with just a few minor, albeit annoying, flaws slipping through the cracks. First off, this game is gorgeous. It totally captures the snes age, retro feel but with modern day pixels. Sprites are well designed and the landscapes are intuitive and fun to explore. The gameplay is very fun and pretty unique and discovering hidden areas feels very fulfilling. The buddy characters add a lot of dimension to exploration and combat and the teleportation mechanic is very well done. Iinitially, I was a little disappointed with the runtime. I beat this game from start to finish, while in no particular rush, in 7 hours. However, those 7 hours were so packed with content and fun I really can't complain. The pacing is top notch. There were multiple times where I intended to play for 30-45 minutes and ended up playing for 2 or more hours. The story really chugs along and gets you invested right off the bat. I highly recommend this game!!

The ones who liked Euro Truck Simulator for its qualities will also like the American Truck Simulator.
Technically, it is to 90% the same game, the difference in the 10% are the following:
1) Instead of European Trucks you're driving the American ones of cause.
2) You can design your own driving route now on the map just like e.g. in Google Maps on your smartphones with waypoints.
3) Instead of just parking your trailer manually and autoparking it you now can chose between a medium/hard way to park it manually, an easy way to park it manually and the alrdy known autoparking. For the medium/hard way you get the most XP (40/90 XP-Points))
4) The game world is filled with life to a higher degree, there are more peasants walking on the pedestrian walks, there are workers working on the delivery/reception sites, there are security men standing in front of supermarkets etc etc.
5) There are more different delivery sites, instead of just delivering to company yards and building sited you can now also deliver to gas stations.
6) The game is set in America (Cpt. Obvious strikes again).
The game is available for a fair price of 20€, for which you get the US-States of California, Nevada and Arizona (That's still in the pipeline).
But California and Nevada for themselves are alrdy highly detailed, there are about 10-15 cities in California and about 10 in Nevada, so, if you compare it with the Old 18 Wheels of Steel Games from SCS, where California had two cities, a huge increase!
Arizona is coming for free too, what States in which Quantity the other DLC's will deliver is subject to the future, I don't know that.
I think, that SCS, as they alrdy did with ETS2 and its DLC's, will deliver a reasonable amount of DLC's for a fair price and with a fair content in it.
As I've read, relying on that this wasn't a joke, they plan to eventually map the whole of North- and Latin-America atleast down to the equator, but of cause this is a work for years to come.
All in all, this game, just like his older brother ETS 2, is a shining juwel in the simulation genre and I can recommend it from the bottom of my heart.
Update #01: Another positive thing: Just days after release they alrdy added the third truck the legendary Kenworth W900, a truck the community asked for. Another reason to recommend the game, because of the consumerfriendly policy of SCS, thumbs up!

I got this while it was on sale not long ago but it has proven itself to be rather fun. It's a weird cross of solid action fueled combat (similar to the Batman Arkham series or LotR: Shadow of Mordor) and text based choose your own adventure/games of chance with a tid bit of card game deck building thrown in.
It's got a decent amount of replay ability admittedly it does get kind of repetitive especially if you don't like the aforementioned combat style or get sick of listening to certain dialogue/reading certain text over and over again. However the battles are challenging usually and the types and number of enemies combined with the different environments is random enough to often keep it interesting especially when the possibilities regarding your own equipment and state of well being is added in.
Combat is pretty much where the game really shines, the controls are easy and fairly fluid (at least with a controller not sure how KB&M does). The graphics are decent, the terrain is ever changing and often offers unique challenges of it's own on top of the enemies themselves. The only real issues is a somewhat fixed/bad camera angles (though no where near unplayable levels) and a lack of a lock on which can at times be frustrating when combined with the camera as it is occasionally possible to lose track of a single enemy.
The numerous choices in both encounter and equipment cards allows for a diverse and interesting deck all your own which has significant impact on your overall game session. Which brings me to another nice thing the game doesn't really punish you for losing or to be blunt while you are likely to lose and feel bad about doing so the simple fact is you can start up a new game with no fuss and no muss and you gain whatever card tokens you win, allowing you to edit your deck and give you a chance at changing the overall outcome. Also a really nice feature is you can stop at almost any time and come back to where you left off (as long as you weren't in the middle of battle) which makes it extremely nice for those with time constraints or who might need to stop quickly.
One kind of bad point against the game (at least for me) is that I've experienced numerous game crashes, which can get annoying at times but since you can literal start it up again and be pretty much where you left off turns it for a serious issue to a mere annoyance. However I think this might have been due to the fact that I got it shortly after the release of their free update and as any gamer knows whenever  new content is added in an update a game has a tendency to get buggy, however they have patched it a number of times since and while I do occasionally still get a crash it's no where near as bad as before.
In short it's a good game but one that won't appeal to everyone, however I would recommend it to/for those who are interested in the game play it offers. To be blunt you get what you see in the trailer video and most of what is in the game's overall description. Though I would suggest waiting til it's on sale as while good it's not worth $24.99 + 4.99 for the Wildcards DLC (which while not required to play or enjoy the game would I think make it a lot more fun and interesting, mind you I do not own said DLC as of the writing of this review but do have plans to purchase it the next time it goes on sale) unless you got that kind of cash to spare regularly in which case go for it otherwise wait for at least a 33% or more sale price drop.

The final boss is a complete joke. I problably spent half of my gameplay hours on him. It ramps up the dificulty, but not in a good way. The dificulty of the final level is that it slowly chips away at your health and abilities with a curse at every stage and the inability to aquire blessings (this can be changed if you're lucky and has the proper cards).
The final boss is a gauntlet of all previous bosses, separetad by enemy type. This woul be easy if the three plague bosses wheren't so OP. The king and the jack have a small window of vulnerabillity and they usually stunlock you and take a lot of health, the king specially. The problem is not defeat them, but to do so without loosing much health.
Between matches with the previous bosses the Dealer unleashes some magical attacks and there's a QTE. The last one is my main death reason because it's really hard to dodge all of them. It can easilly hit you for 40+ hp and with your health already chipped away by all the previous bosses... you got the picture.
The cheap way around it is to kill the game before dying. The game saves just before the fight for crash prevention purposes. That way you don't have to pass through all the maze again. Hell, if you're feeling particularly cheap you can do that every time  something bad happens to you so you arrive at the last battle in better condition.

I feel like this game has so much potential, but it just doesn't manage it.  For one thing, of course, there just aren't enough people playing it to get into a game in a reasonable length of time.  And because of that, there's usually no way you'll have the max number of people in a scenario.
And that's a shame, because it ensures that in a game where complexity is a bonus, every session will be as simple as possible.  And the plots of the missions aren't even as complex as they could be.  Instead of walking around the boat and letting things happen naturally, the mission usually consists of everyone forming a group, and talking at eachother until the mission is done.
And this all assumes, of course, that you end up in a session with other people interested in roleplaying and fulfilling their objectives.  More often than not, you'll just end up with three other people typing random♥♥♥♥♥♥ uninterested in the actual gameplay.  This wouldn't be a problem if we had more people.
It's free of course, so what I'd recommend is, if you have five interested friends, maybe try it with them for a night.  Otherwise... no go.  I'd like to see something done with this concept, because it really is an interesting idea, but as presented it just doesn't work.

I rather enjoyed this game. I enjoyed the story, and the level of player engagement seemed spot-on for this quick, story-driven game.
On the other hand; I did encounter some repetitiveness in the dialog after a bit. The puzzle solving felt a little forced, and didn't have alternative scenarios if you chased down the wrong lead.
I usually don't like the over-the-shoulder gameplay style. I found it gave me some issue when trying to interact with some objects, but it wasn't
obtrusive.
The enemies were laughable, all you had to do was sneak up behind them and perform an action - a random button/mouseclick which is a direct port over to the button/paddle on the console. I found these enemies to be more of an obsticle than an actual challenge. But I belive this is intended, as to keep the game story focused and not combat driven. I actually salute the developers for remaining story focused and not bogging down the player with ubsurd mechanics or prolonged battles... or health bars for that matter (You're already dead! No health for you!)
Many players have complained that they were unable to go back and complete the collectable achievements, as this has a very linear progression in the story. This will often require a second playthrough, stopping at each location, and clearing the zone to ensure you have collected everything. I kept catching myself thinking in normal gameplay rules, where I would walk around walls and objects. Just remember, you can walk through that. There are still barriers - ghostly walls and santified buildings - that prevent you from passing through everything.
Due to a bug in the final fight, I didn't finish the game. After many many attempts, I kept starting the scene in a void zone, where I couldn't escape, or didn't have enough time to complete my objective after I escaped. I have not read of this bug happening to other players. YMMV. I did see alot of weird, creepy stuff in this game, but this is the only only thing I would call buggy.

On first impression you'll feel like you just bought a port of the iOS puzzle game for about 30x more than the portable version costs. The game has awkward menus that one must click and hold with the mouse to slide them around. The menus feel broken, as it seems like things are off screen and there isn't any intuitive way to access the off-screen menu items with the mouse.
Even in early access, the developer talks so highly of his game that I thought perhaps it would blow me away. I imagined never before seen mechanics and gameplay but found myself let down by the hype. I would recommend waiting until the price is reduced to at most $15.
It's interesting to find a game in early access where feedback is highly censored and not welcome from experienced fans of the genre. What is the point of making your game early access if you aren't willing to hear constructive feedback?
The gameplay itself is limited to one mode at the moment where you play until the gamespace fills up. This is quite challenging and fun. As you play you match 3 elements and each match creates new elements. These new elements then start to appear in the pieces you are given to make creating new elements easier. It's exciting to try and see what new element comes next and it makes for that "just one more game" feeling.
Sound effects are minimal and nice, just right for this kind of game. The music is a bit repetitive with only 3 similar (short) tracks. The music has the same low quality mono sound that Faerie Solitaire has. Hopefully the music will get an upgrade in quality as game development goes on.
You will find that the developer for this game has an interesting "my way or the highway" type personality. When the game was first released as early access the forums filled up with potential customers wondering why the price for this game is 3x higher than any other puzzle game on Steam, including the best selling games in this genre. They were still interested, just wanted to know the story behind the price. By their play time and achievements you could see many of them love puzzle games and own his previous game on Steam and were genuinely interested in purchasing and playing this game.
The developer started deleting price topics and making rules that comments are welcome as long as they are not about the price. He would then say that if you don't like the price then you must not be a true fan of quality puzzle games because he loves this game he is creating. He even started telling the gamers that this game isn't for you if you think $30 is too much. Requesting an explanation of what makes the game so unique results in a pasted copy of the match 3 concepts that are in this game, nothing unique or exciting about it.
Next up the developer created a sub forum called "Price Topics Go Here" and started closing and moving topics. You would think having so many topics about the price would give a clue as to what action is needed next for a healthy community. The sub-forum became too much of a hassle and was closed. Now he has one pinned (and locked) topic about price being something he will not discusss, even if it is questions about what makes the game worth 3x more than the competition.
I would definitely wait on this title--you won't have much of a chance to give input. If you don't like how things are--then, as he would say, "This game isn't for you."

TL; DR: Good game, but the pricetag is a way too high. Steam won't let me post without giving it a thumbs up/down, so thumbs down because I didn't really enjoy the game, the price is too high, and the average score is too high.
Virtually everything about Owlboy is good. The art, music, gameplay, presentation, and writing are all well done. It's clear that a ton of love and effort has gone into the game. Like anything, there are a few rough spots here and there (the platforming in one of the final areas was particularly frustrating) but overall, each part of the game is great. That said, I can't really say that I loved the game.
For whatever reason, the whole never really came together as something greater than the sum of its parts (despite those parts all being individually decent). The gameplay is decent enough, but it wasn't quite mechanically engaging enough to pull me along. The checkpoint system is incredibly forgiving, so there isn't really any challenge. The whole idea of having companions never really plays out to be more than just having different weapons equipped, which feels like a bit of a missed opportunity. On top of that, the puzzles aren't very mind-bending nor the gameplay particularly exciting. Likewise with the story and characters. They were interesting enough, but I usually didn't really feel super interested in what was around the next corner. The music was uniformly well composed and performed, but often felt out of place. The world is very pretty and well-connected, but there isn't really enough going on to encourage a ton of exploration. Ultimately, it feels like you end up with the worst parts of a Metroidvania game (excessive backtracking through areas) without the good ones (the feeling of excitement to use a new skill/ability to open new areas and find secrets). I realize the game isn't necessarily meant to be a Metroidvania, but the style of the world is reminiscent of one.
All that said, the quality of the individual components of the game gives it a bit of charm that settled in by the end of the 8-10 hours I spent with it. I can't give it an outright recommendation because of the price and the lack of cohesive greatness, but it is by no means bad.
Edit: The more I've been thinking about it, I just didn't really find the game to be fun. Plain and simple. And because none of the other elements really stuck out to me as being really exceptional, I wasn't left with a great impression overall. If you find the game fun, I think it will feel really, really great but I didn't because the gameplay didn't really grab me.

This is the closest I've come to giving an Artifex Mundi title a thumbs down. It's presumably one of their more dated projects, and it shows. Not only is the game short (I beat it in 2 hours, including the bonus story, though I'll confess to skipping two or three puzzles in addition to about two-thirds of the cinematics), but it's just a little clumsier than what I'm used to seeing from them. The hidden object segments are hit and miss, but mostly miss thanks to lower-res images and a tendency to hide the most identifiable part(s) of some objects so that you can't even tell what they're supposed to be when you're looking straight at them. (An inevitable few confusing labels - "handle" for a knob, e.g. - are old hat, but still annoying when they happen.) The usual nonsensical "keys" and progression items are at play, which is forgivable but not ideal, and it definitely has one of the weakest and least well-integrated plotlines in the library. My biggest gripe, though, is that this game only offers two difficulty options, basically divided into a kiddie mode that holds your hand constantly (this is what I settled on, contributing to the brevity of the playthrough) and an exasperating mode that forces you to find and remember every detail of the often unintuitive environments if you wish to progress.
That said, the successful AM formula - a good balance of puzzles and hidden object scenes, nice visuals accompanied by good voice acting, etc. - manages to keep the overall experience positive.

This game was released with a few problems but most of those are fixed now and I'm more than happy to write a review for it.
This game will absorb hours of your time with it's endless amount of content and the game ends when you decide it does rather than the game forcing you to dosomething else. So you could realistically keep playing this game for years and keep progressing your characters.
The story is pretty funny but I somewhat wish that the voice acting was a little better but overall it was pretty decent.
As for the gameplay itself it starts off sluggish and slow but the more your progress the more avenues you have open to you. For example, it probably took me around 25-30 in-game hours to hit level 100 for the first time.  When I respeced my MC it only took me an hour to reach that point again and being even stronger than previusly and learned a new move when I hit level 100 as well. So you definitely have the option to keep leveling your characters and it should not take forever after you play through the story and unlock some of the better levels.
The assembly can be a pain as each character has seperate senators and it took a very long time just to get one of mine to have a good standing with all of them to pass the things that I wanted.
As for the cast there is a very diverse amount of characters that you can use and you can seriously vary your team compositions to your liking. Want to have a squad full of ninjas? Well go for it, nothing is stopping you other than having to fight the class once and unlocking it for creation. And if you save up enough mana to make the character a genius it'sthat much easier to level them and they are that much more powerful as well.
The concept of the item world was really interesting and very difficult. One thing that you will have to learn is how to use the difficulty setting and when to turn it up or down. Usually when you are doing the item world you want the lowest setting possible so you can get to the lowest floors. Some items are better than others because they have more floors so the more you level them the more powerful the item becomes. You can also move and combine specialists making items even stronger.
The visuals are nice for a handheld game (which is what you should expect since this is a port of a handheld game) and while they may eventually get boring you do have the option to turn them off and on to your leisure which is a major plus in cutting down grinding.
Overall I'd give this game an 8/10 and if you are into turn based RPGs then this is one of the best ones out there so give it a shot and see if you like the game for yourself.

Excellent turn-based action/strategy game. If you love oldschool turn-based RPGs you'll probably love this game.
This game twists the old turn-based formula and makes units reactive outside of their turn, units attacking and counterattacking each other within a certain range. It really makes you plan your assaults.

That being said, there are only two real downsides for me.
1) Lots of cinematics between battles. Most of them are only 30 seconds to a couple of minutes long, but there are a lot of them. They set the story before battles.

2) This game is hard as balls if you're rusty on the strategy front, the tide can turn quickly for either side. You may find missions drag on until you get that one break in the enemy's defenses. It can be merciless, and you will lose units (permanently if you don't put another unit in danger to call a medic to the downed soldier).

Example: 3rd move into my turn, my scout turns a corner and just gets mowed down by a tank and two machine-gunners. He didn't stand a chance. If the enemy isn't in your line of sight their position and movements are unknown to you. Makes for some really hilariously bad situations.

Graphics: 10/10 - You can play in 1080p 60FPS
Audio/Voice Acting: 9/10 - A decent variety of voice actors, though some are a bit too quiet. There isn't much talking outside of the cinematics or radio chatter while on the battlefield.
Gameplay: 8/10 - Moving around some terrain is difficult with a mouse and keyboard. You clip edges of various things and get stuck, wasting a portion of your AP you need to move at all. However you can control the same unit multiple times (though with further reduced AP each time you control them) to advance them quickly. This helps to get machine-gunners and snipers with low AP caught up with the rest of your troops, at the cost of your command points each time. Plan accordingly
Storyline: 7/10 - The story is pretty neat. There's a lot of storytelling cinematics if you're into that. You may get annoyed by it if not.

Kingdom Wars 2: Battles (which I will refer to as KW2B in this review) is a bold approach to RTS strategic simulation games that focuses on the building and destroying of massive medieval citadels. The battles are intense and the strategy is unlike most other simulations out there so most players can expect a challenging experience unlike any they have faced before. That is, unless you happened to play the original Kingdom Wars. What gives this series its unique flavor is Reverie World Studios, INC's strong focus on siege warfare, making it unlike anything else being developed.
Players will naturally need to gather resources, build structures, research technologies, and train armies just like in most other RTS sims of this nature. However, the economy and techs have all been streamlined so the player doesn't have to micro-manage their progression and can devote most of their attention to the battles themselves. Currently there are three races to choose from: Humans, Elves, and Orcs. Each race has its own unique units, structures and styles. Since the game is still Early Access, its possible that more will be added later but I cannot say for certain.
Players can choose between single-player story mode played out in episodes, skirmish mode, and Multiplayer mode. There is only one episode available now but current plans include five in total and these additional episodes will be released as Free DLC's. Other features in the works include a crafting system based on rewards earned during battles for a variety of advancements, an intricate card system used for powerful bonuses during games, a trading market where players can trade crafting items with other players, and a guild system that will allow players to create or join a battle clan for shared strength. At this time, some of these things are still in development so its not easy to elaborate on them, but they sound pretty cool.
The graphics are very rich but older systems struggle to keep up on moderately high settings so this may change in order to accommodate more players, especially for Multiplayer PvP. There is an in-game chat system so players can communicate during gameplay without the hassles of using the Steam overlay. A level editor is included for the mod community can get a jumpstart on their own creations. The sound effects are a bit troublesome currently and being sorted out. Nothing new for an Alpha version though. Also, there are still a number of bugs scattered about so don't be alarmed. This is typical of an Early Access game and the devs welcome any information on them so they can work to correct the problems. Still, the game is very stable and entertaining. Being part of the Early Access phase gives players the opportunity to help shape the future of KW2B and help the developers build the best game possible. However, if you're one of those gamers who has little patience or prefers only finished/polished projects, then i suggest holding off a while longer. Unhappy gamers do nothing to help the community, the developers, or the game.
KW2B has all the promise of a great game and I have no doubt the developers will see this game all the way through to a polished gem. Siege warfare is often a neglected aspect of RTS strategy sims and its rarely done properly so this game offers a fresh experience for most players. Strategy players will definitely want to grab a copy and strap in for battle. This game isn't the best choice for impatient people or those who expect to have a smooth and complete experience since its still Early Access Alpha though.

Kingdom Wars 2: Battles review
KW2 has some very impressive graphics that sadly require one meaty boss of a computer to even go on medium settings. However the game's still beautiful even on the very low settings. So all that it would take is some improved optimisation to make the game more playable. I can play 99% of games on maxed out setting, but this game only runs on 25fps, so that will make KW2 to lose a few points. Apart from poor optimisation, the game is a masterpiece, no questions needed. Although you don't always get to just stare at this work ofart for too long as there is always action to be seen.
This game is like the Total War series (the good games of the series), Clash of Clans (for a giant amount of things you can build) and Company of Hereos had a marvelous baby. You can build tons of different thigns (each race has different buildings), there's a campaign mode, a gigantic variety of classes (every race has different classes), different ways to gather up resources (races have different ways to get them), different advantages and disadvantages throughout the races, multiplayer, singleplayer, and so, so much more content. So to tum this topic up, if you like a lot of content in a game, this is will fullfil your expectation even more than you could wish for it to.
There's currently 3 classes. Humans, Orcs and Elves. Humans are the most basic class (and the most boring)... why would you want to choose them? Well, maybe if you're new to the game you will choose them. The second class is Orcs, just as you might think, some really cool guys who are violent, much like the Vikings but in a beast form. SCS software has pulled out another epic simulator for the trucking community with American Truck Simulator.
If you're familiar with the software background of ETS2, you're covered. However, theres a few things to keep in mind with these differences.
1. Truck geometry (size) is entirely different from ETS2, you'll have to relearn your truckspace and angle points. If you're new to it, you won't have an problems learning the geometry.
2. Speedzones are tricky, especially in California (now I see why some of my professional trucking friends try to avoid driving through there). [Corrected - v1.1.1 Allowing time to change to different speedzones]
3. Cops are not very forgiving in CA, so watch your speed and traffic light timings. [Nerfed by v1.1.1 - Alot of folks were verbal, figured ya learn from driving in an area. Guess not for many folks]
4. For now, work on your ADR certs and high value cargo for now until they expand further out of Cali and Nevada.
5. There are weird easter eggs and hidden gems to seek out in the game, you'll easily spot them so I won't spoil them.
A biggie:
1. It is a solid simulator/game with many new goodies that will be coming along the line over the progress of updates/upgrades.
2. It is 64-bit native, so you need a 64-bit machine to run it properly. They still have 32-bit floating around but keep in mind that they stress that it is "NOT SUPPORTED" in the event you have tech problems. They're slowly phasing out the 32-bit flavor to allow the game to have more flexibility on machines with decent resources handy and not choking on limitations.
The only hiccup I've seen sofar (as of this posting) is that the AI vehicles are hovering on the roadways.
Wishlist for the game (which would liven the experience a little more):
1. Dynamic construction areas (changes to a random location every 30 game time days).
2. Electronic road boards (the type the DOT uses, not the roadside adverts [though, thats also not a bad idea too]).
3. Signs that read "Reduce Speed Ahead" and "Construction Zone Ahead". May help prevent trailer damages in the event an AI plows into the back end when you slam on the brakes due to sudden speedzone changes (coughcalicough). [fixed via Ver 1.1.1 - Time allowance to reduce speed applied. Cops nerfed based on Driver's Level]
Note: In any situation where you see a Prius make a right turn into your right of way. You will crash if you don't catch up on the brakes. For some odd reason, the Prius is suicidal. Sofar, I've seen this happen 7 times in Cali.

This is an interesting game. Its not for everyone, but if you like cute light-hearted storylines then this has that. If you like sim games that let you manage things then this has that. If you like simple dungeon crawlers with phat loot at the bottom, then this game has that also. If you like tower defense... this no, thats not in this game, no tower defense.
In many ways, this game remindes me of Persona 3. The option to go to the "dungeon" or skip going to the dungeon to do other things is an interesting mechanic. Sure you can go buy supplies at whole-saler prices, then mark them up for a profit, thats easy and safe... Or u can gamble on a dungeon run and sell all the things you pick up in the dungeon. You need an adventurer to dive that dungeon for you, and you can even give them the best equipment you can find... Or you could sell that equipment for a hefty price, the choice is yours. Equiping your adventurer well makes diving the dugeon easier, but it also means that they can carry less and thuss cut into your profits. Diving the dungeon a lot can give lots of goodies to sell, but going to the dungeon takes a lot of time, and you cant run your store while out at the dungeon. Like Persona 3 you have to decided how you will spend your time each day of the week. Manageing this time well is the key to success.
Choices, this game is about choices, you can make your store interior look a certain way, this affects the "vibe" of your store. You can sell all sorts of things, you can specialize, selling the finest foods, the best weapons/armor, excellent jewlry, or a mix. You get no special bonuses for stocking a specific arangment of items, but again its a choice.
The games characters arnt super original, but theyre well presented the pair of female leades are charming with their goofball and straightman act. The supporting characters are kind of 1 diminsional with very small character arcs if any. Still the game is one of my favorite, and its not very offten you get to run a fantasy world item shop.

Conan Exiles is another victim of the Steam community and its reaction to early access titles.  Outside of those waiting for this game and understanding the meaning of early access, it has recieved unjust criticisms that lack consideration of its current state.
The first day was rough but was very far from being a terrible launch.  To paint a picture:, I'll elaborate on how some people around me reacted. Multiple streamers I enjoy, and collaborate with, felt very mixed towards the end of the first day.  One did not recommend anyone buying it for another month or so; however, he kept playing. Through the rubberbanding and all -- he stuck through with the understanding that it is in a very early state. Now, he's continuing a Conan Exiles marathon and has totally changed his suggestion while also giving away a copy or two.
Today, I joined the playerbase and am very happy with the multiple patches released just today.  The game has improved more in less than 24 hours than many of its competitors have in months. Nevertheless, I am very excited about the potential this game has.
I haven't touched the content, graphics, sound, and mechanics yet -- and I'll save those for another day.  I will say I am impressed with how optimized the client is on launch. Those with aging systems may very well be able to join in on the fun.  If you cannot deal with bugs and a game with ongoing development -- then heed the warnings clearly stated in the disclaimers and steer clear for a while.
Back to more grinding.  I'll re-review when it is appropriate.

This game could be awesome, if only it would have been better executed. It's a third person adventure game about ghosts with elements of stealth, bearable QTEs, nice graphics, good voice acting and choice-based investigation mechanics. It's spooky at times, but mostly peaceful.
The main story is interesting, and although the concept of ghosts among the living is borrowed from the "Ghost" film, and many game mechanics are borrowed from some other games, the whole idea is original enough to keep you interested. However, the game is filled with side quests, side stories, non-essential dialogs, action elements, "detective" mechanics - and all that filling is at times depressingly mediocre, which lowers the overall quality.
Sometimes it feels like cliches were roughly stiched together to make up soap opera mini-dramas of people around you. The dialogs are full of lousy writing and stylistic inconsistences. The stealth mechanics are buggy (you press the key and nothing happens, "enemies" suddenly see through walls, etc). Investigation mostly requires you to guess the choice the game expects from you, or so dumbed down you just pick the most obvious choice and that's it.
It feels that less significant details were delegated to either not imaginative, or simply not enthusastic (or both) people, which resulted in an uneven experience of intriguing story progression diluted with clumsy products of forced attempts to do something original by people who are stuck in the ways of formulas and cliches, A bit of humour would have helped, but it's very seldom.
If the right people were chosen to make this game, who'd be creative and inspired by the subject, it would be awesome, but unfortunately the small but plentiful amount of flaws downgrade the experience and makes it just a bit above average. Still, it deserves to be noted for originality of its general concept and bravery of producers to come out with an original game instead of milking an established franchise. When I say it could be awesome, I must also say that it could have been much much worse. So I recommend this game with a discount. I mean, guys, where else can you possess a cat? :)

I gave negative reviews to the first two games in this serious.  And I was very tempted to do the same to this.  This is the best game of the three.  The mechanic is similar to the second, the story ties everything together nicely, the artwork is the usual for Artifex Mundi.  But this game is not without its problems.
The main reason to give it a negative is that it commits one of the cardinal sins of hidden object games.  Unclear objectives, or multiple objects that fit the goal.  In one puzzle in particular, it asks you to find a feather.  There are no fewer than three feathers in the puzzle, only one of which is the "proper" one.  This is not the only example.  This is something that should never happen in a hidden object game, under any circumstances.  That was the only major problem I have with this game itself.
The story is tied up in the previous games, to a degree.  You certainly can pick this one up and play through it, without getting the references.  But it's meant to pull the whole thing together.
However, I cannot judge the single game by the whole trilogy.  On its own, this game is decent enough, but Artifex Mundi fare.  I probably should give it a negative just based on the problem with the hidden object puzzles, since that's the core of the game, but I will be lenient this time out.  But do not pay full price for this game.  If the developers don't care enough about their game to fix flaws like that, they most certainly do not deserve to get full price for their shovelware.

The Final Enigma; Artifex Mundi's last installment in the Time Mysteries Trilogy. As a pretty avid Hidden Object Gamer, I love Artifex Mundi and all their work. If you're familiar with them, you already know that many of their games share a similar engine and similar play styles. This usually makes it easy for one to write a review about, but Time Mysteries is a difficult series, one which I believe I may find myself split on with a
Time Mysteries is probably the single trilogy that seems to not get the positive ratings that Artifex games always get. I can tell particularly, several reasons why. It is hard for me to speak on this series, given that I have only played 75% of the way through of this particular game, which happens to be the last. Therefore, I didn't want to judge too quickly, but I've noticed these several things enough that I feel I can speak as to the pros and cons of
installment. I have sunk maybe an hour or two into it, which if you know Artifex Mundi, you know that their games are short, but never lacking in content that truely makes the game. Artifex Mundi is known for its' great puzzles, HOGs, and storylines. These are the issues that I find are excellent and poor points of The Final Enigma...
- As always, beautiful scenery and great artwork
- The time travel element of the game is great. Using the special time clock you have is almost like using the map in other Artifex games, but something about it is just different and fun! :D
- The story is very solid
- Dozens of areas in the game to go to, more so than past games
- The cutscenes can be amazing (at some points. It seems that AM has possibly changed up their cutscene style??
- The voice acting in AM games can be a bit corny, but we deal with this because we love AM! But, this game, barring the protagonist, has a fair amount of poor voice acting.
- Sometimes, the voices can sound overdriven or not mixed so well.
- The puzzles difficulty level vary rapidly. I've found extremely easy and difficult ones just as well. This is probably a game to play on the Expert mode.
- The cutscenes can be poor (at a minimal level, only sometimes).
- Sorry Artifex, I love you, I really do. The Final Enigma wasn't all that I expected. the mixed and negative reviews made me think that they were people who just weren't that into HOGing or Artifex in general. Upon playing this game, I realized why the reception was so mixed.
The first Time Mysteries is about to be released on Steam (after a reconstruction process, this is why some of the first games from the AM trilogy are currently missing). Before I write this series off as a sub-par trilogy, I would like to play through the entire series. The second and third (this one) have often recieved a thumbs down or negative reviews. It is probably for the above reasons that I am truely split on this game. For the first time I actually do wish Steam had a "Neutrul" Button. I
recommend this for the time being. Why? Because it has a bold, newer style to it. The way that you travel throughout time and space is very cool. Also, the concept of the entire game (and probably series) is an interesting one.

is a typical Hidden Object Game by Artifex Mundi. At its core, it's a relatively easy point-and-click adventure, featuring (rather) beautiful scenes, attractive Hidden Object screens and some small puzzles. Both puzzles and hidden object screens are quite easy, so that even complete strangers to this kind of game will find something to their liking here. The story of the game, still the core of any adventure, is however rather bland, especially during the first third of the game. Featuring the same female protagonist as in the earlier two games in this series, the game tells about the need to "save the world" and how Esther manages to do so by altering the past, in order to save the future. With the help of Time Crystals, she can travel to different dates in the past and search for clues in order to avoid the upcoming catastrophy. It's nothing original, but the story picks up after some time and kept me interested during the latter part of this (rather short) game.
This edition also contains a bonus chapter which tells the same story from another point of view: a neat touch that added not only an hour of extra gameplay, but an original view on the game a well. While the visuals are up to Artifex Mundi's high standards, the sounds certainly are not. The voice-acting is one of the worst I've yet heard in a game by Artifex Mundi: completely artificial and never giving any character something like a personality. The music is too repetitive: I muted it very early in the game. As ususal, Steam integration is perfect, complete with trading cards and a series of easy-to-get achievements which should give you another "perfect game" without much as a hassle.
All in all, I'd like to give this game a "neutral" recommendation, but since the quality of Artifex Mundi does shimmer through even in one of their weakest game, I will still give a "thumbs up" - but there are many other, more recent, Artifex Mundi-games  out there that offer much better quality.
Overall score: 6/10.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a fun if not somewhat linear detective adventure game. The premise is as eerie as they come. You must solve your own murder. I have toyed with the notion of death and the afterlife on more than a few occasions. One might say I have even become obsessed with it. I lost my father in 2009, and more recently, I was reminded of my own premature death at birth. It lasted only seven seconds, but it gave me a lot to think about. What if I had not been revived? I would not be sitting here writing this review right now. I would, for all intents and purposes, be dead. Having never experienced this world at all. I would have no distinction between life and death, and having never played a video game, why I must now collect everything in sight. Murdered: Soul Suspect is filled with such collectibles. Shiny objects which dot the area. They are optional between crime scene investigations, but you know you want them. They shed further light on the town of Salem and its inhabitants. My only real gripe with this game is that, once you reach the climax, you cannot backtrack for the remaining items. You are effectively locked in for the final act. A warning beforehand would have been appreciated. I am, however, still giving this game a recommendation for its foreboding atmosphere and chilling soundtrack. Check it out when the game is on sale.

I've been playing Warframe since it's open beta phase in 2013 and I don't ever regret the 2000+ hours I've invested in this game. Starting with gameplay, the mechanics and aspects of gameplay within Warframe are top notch and give paid games of the same genre a run for their money. This is, by far, the best Free-2-Play game I have ever played and it is really free-2-play. Essentially everything that isn't a cosmetic feature can be obtained somehow and even cosmetics are given out as rewards from time to time. In Warframe, there is no true endgame. The game is constantly expanding, constantly updating with new weapons, new systemwide events, new warframes. There is always something for you to do, even if you are a seasoned player. The only true endgame is FashionFrame, a.k.a, who can look the coolest in their frames. Depending on your playstyle and what you are after in th game, Warframe can get a bit grindy, but that is part of the fun. The best part of the game is that no one weapon is the most powerful of them all. All weapons and warframes have the potential to be devastating and powerful, it all depends on how you configure your modules to alter the weapon's damage output and it depends on which enemy faction you are facing, since all factions have different resistances and weakness to different types of damage, so switching your weapons and trying out new builds is encouraged and at times necessary. The most intriguing part of the game is the lore and how it is interwoven into nearly every aspect of what you do. Even the weapons you use have lore behind them that inevitably links to the bigger picture that we can't yet see. I've never played a game with such a great gaming community. Everyone is pretty much helpful and if you are ever lost or need help doing something, it won't be hard to find someone to join your squad and help you out. Last, but not least, the game developers, DigitalExtremes: they are very responsive to the community they serve. They will directly interact with us and push out updates addressing issues we have brought to them. And they have managed to bring Warframe from a game that had one tileset inside of a ship to having an entire open world map on Earth. They keep raising the bar with each new quest, with each new update and they somehow still manage to outdo themselves every time. Warframe is a game, the likes of which I have never played before. It has been updated so many times, gone through so many subtle aesthetic changes that at this point in time, the Warframe that we have now could essentially be called Warframe 2 when compared to Warframe update 2.0. I highly recommend this game.

SCS software has pulled out another epic simulator for the trucking community with American Truck Simulator.
If you're familiar with the software background of ETS2, you're covered. However, theres a few things to keep in mind with these differences.
1. Truck geometry (size) is entirely different from ETS2, you'll have to relearn your truckspace and angle points. If you're new to it, you won't have an problems learning the geometry.
2. Speedzones are tricky, especially in California (now I see why some of my professional trucking friends try to avoid driving through there). [Corrected - v1.1.1 Allowing time to change to different speedzones]
3. Cops are not very forgiving in CA, so watch your speed and traffic light timings. [Nerfed by v1.1.1 - Alot of folks were verbal, figured ya learn from driving in an area. Guess not for many folks]
4. For now, work on your ADR certs and high value cargo for now until they expand further out of Cali and Nevada.
5. There are weird easter eggs and hidden gems to seek out in the game, you'll easily spot them so I won't spoil them.
A biggie:
1. It is a solid simulator/game with many new goodies that will be coming along the line over the progress of updates/upgrades.
2. It is 64-bit native, so you need a 64-bit machine to run it properly. They still have 32-bit floating around but keep in mind that they stress that it is "NOT SUPPORTED" in the event you have tech problems. They're slowly phasing out the 32-bit flavor to allow the game to have more flexibility on machines with decent resources handy and not choking on limitations.
The only hiccup I've seen sofar (as of this posting) is that the AI vehicles are hovering on the roadways.
Wishlist for the game (which would liven the experience a little more):
1. Dynamic construction areas (changes to a random location every 30 game time days).
2. Electronic road boards (the type the DOT uses, not the roadside adverts [though, thats also not a bad idea too]).
3. Signs that read "Reduce Speed Ahead" and "Construction Zone Ahead". May help prevent trailer damages in the event an AI plows into the back end when you slam on the brakes due to sudden speedzone changes (coughcalicough). [fixed via Ver 1.1.1 - Time allowance to reduce speed applied. Cops nerfed based on Driver's Level]

It's hard to sum in in just a few sentences.
On the surface it is fairly simple. The game consists of about a dozen missions (each with a different boss encounter at the end, each taking about 10-30 minutes). You have a deck of cards that represent the items you might find during each mission and another deck that represents the encounters you might come across during the mission. The encounter cards also form the 'dungeon' in that they are placed face down in a pattern and you need to walk over them to activate them.
At first you only have a few basic items and a few encounters, but each time you 'beat' an encounter card, you get new cards, either new items, new encounters or both. This happens even if you don't beat the boss at the end. Thus even an unsuccessful mission rewards you with more gear for the next time you play the mission.
The neat thing is that you choose the set of encounters in the deck yourself, meaning you can stack the deck towards a certain type of encounter.
The other thing is that the encounter unlocks themselves tell a story, for example there is one encounter chain where you first come across to lovers who want to run away together, you will later unlock further encounters that tell you what happened to them afterwards. This unlocking of quests gives you another progression axis, so instead of just running the missions and progressing that way by beating the bosses you also progress on this encounter-unlocking axis which makes failure much less frustrating and runs much less repetitive than it would otherwise have been.
The narrator is absolutely awesome and really pulls you in to the game.
The combat is ok, it's a low prodction values version of the Arkham system. I see some people complain about it not being that great, but it is perfectly functional. The combat sections generally are quite short, and for that the way it works is fine. I have not had any complaints.

This is an interesting game. Its not for everyone, but if you like cute light-hearted storylines then this has that. If you like sim games that let you manage things then this has that. If you like simple dungeon crawlers with phat loot at the bottom, then this game has that also. If you like tower defense... this no, thats not in this game, no tower defense.
In many ways, this game remindes me of Persona 3. The option to go to the "dungeon" or skip going to the dungeon to do other things is an interesting mechanic. Sure you can go buy supplies at whole-saler prices, then mark them up for a profit, thats easy and safe... Or u can gamble on a dungeon run and sell all the things you pick up in the dungeon. You need an adventurer to dive that dungeon for you, and you can even give them the best equipment you can find... Or you could sell that equipment for a hefty price, the choice is yours. Equiping your adventurer well makes diving the dugeon easier, but it also means that they can carry less and thuss cut into your profits. Diving the dungeon a lot can give lots of goodies to sell, but going to the dungeon takes a lot of time, and you cant run your store while out at the dungeon. Like Persona 3 you have to decided how you will spend your time each day of the week. Manageing this time well is the key to success.
Choices, this game is about choices, you can make your store interior look a certain way, this affects the "vibe" of your store. You can sell all sorts of things, you can specialize, selling the finest foods, the best weapons/armor, excellent jewlry, or a mix. You get no special bonuses for stocking a specific arangment of items, but again its a choice.

Unfortunately I have to give this game a thumbs down, for now.
tl;dr - It does a lot of things well, and starts off fun, but the difficulty gets extreme enough to make the game unplayable as anything but a suicide simulator.
It frustrates me that I have to give a negative review to this game, because it was really fun when I started playing.  The animations were nice, combat was fun, the voice acting was great.  It was a really well polished random adventure generator game.
The basic mechanic of the game is that encountering cards generates an encounter, whether combat, puzzle, story, what-have-you, and completing the card will unlock that card's token, which will in turn unlock more cards to add to future decks.  It gives a good incentive to try to encounter many cards and figure out how to unlock more.  Quite cool.
As you progress in the game, unlocking more cards, you will also encounter bosses.  Beating them unlocks the next boss card, and after you beat enough bosses you will unlock an artifact that gives you some bonuses but will also make the game harder.
This is the point where the game goes wrong for me.  The difficulty increases introduced by the artifacts make the game virtually impossible by the end.  It was not unusual for me to start a game and the very first card would be a combat against a prior boss, 9 of their minions, on a trapped battlefield with an accompanying totem.  There were so many high powered threats my brand new out of the box adventurer had no chance to win.
What makes it worse is that there's no going back.  Once those difficulty spikes are unlocked, they affect the whole game, retroactively.  If I go back to the very first boss of the game, my first encounter on that level might be the aforementioned impossible fight (and was, the time I tried).  The fun of the game, of running around kicking bandits in the face and solving problems for townsfolk became overshadowed by a constant string of deaths brought on by unwinnable fights.
There's an easy mode that gives the player some benefits, but activating it disables achievements (gotta punish those filthy casuals) and you can't access any of the other character archetypes in the game, which locks out almost all of the games replayability.
Currently the only solution to get rid of the difficulty spikes is to use the 'Erase Progress' feature, which you don't realize until it's too late.  Now, after playing for 12 hours, I'm forced to decide to either erase everything I've accomplished or give up because the game is unplayable.
Neither of those choices make any sense, and are a big part of the reason I can't recommend this game.  There's a great premise here, and the underlying system is really, really cool, but it becomes difficult to the point of impossibility and I've got better things to spend my gaming time on than dying forever.
Should the devs put in a way to disable the artifacts, or otherwise customize the difficulty of the game in a way that doesn't lock out every other character option, I will revisit this review and hopefully change it to a positive.

Time Mysteries 3 was yet another excellent foray from Artifex Mundi. Unlike Time Mysteries 2, this game had a great variety of puzzles, so that it wasn't a non-stop parade of the same hidden object scenes over and over again. None of the non-HOG puzzles were obtuse, another welcome change from TM2. Also, there was an adorable puppy right at the start of the game, and numerous other cute animals sprinkled throughout (yet another thing TM2 lacked).
I didn't play through this game on Expert mode due to my poor experience with the second game, so if you prefer playing it on that mode I can't vouch for how the constant time-hopping would make it tedious via having to manually hunt through every room for a new hidden object hotspot. There were far fewer HOG scenes in this game than in TM2, though, and the game's design is so much better than its predecessor that it shouldn't be that onerous of an experience.
The weakest part of the game was the storyline. I had just come off the confusing Time Mysteries 2 (and I've never played the first title), so I didn't understand what was going on early on in the game. I soon got a handle on things, though, and the story was an enjoyable experience until close to the end. The ending itself was quick and unexpected, and there were still a few loose ends that hadn't been tied up. Like, why was the Terminator trying to destroy the world? And why was Rasputin going along with it? I suppose it's possible that these answers might lie in the side story which I haven't completed yet.
All in all, I can easily recommend this game to anybody, from those with a casual interest in HOGs to the hardcore superfan. Definitely a much more pleasurable experience than Time Mysteries 2.
