The Final Enigma is the final installment of Time Mysteries series by Artifex Mundi. Previous installments as follows: Inheritance and The Ancient Spectres.
Game Menu Option: Two section – Volume and Miscellaneous settings. The volume section has the following: Music and Sound. The miscellaneous section has the following: Custom Cursor and Full Screen.
Game Difficulty Modes: Two game difficulty modes – Regular and Expert.
Cinematic Scenes: All cinematic scenes can be skipped if you do not want to watch them. They can be watch over again under the video section the extras.
Dialogues: There is an option for skipping the entire dialogue scene without having sit through it.
Voice Overs: Nothing much can be said about the voice overs asides from that they are well done.
Game Music/Sounds: Nothing much can be said about the music/sounds asides from that they both fit well with the game.
Game Graphics: Nothing much can be said about the graphics asides from that they are nicely drawn with a painted feel to them.
Inventory Panel: There is no option to lock the inventory panel in place.
Map: In a form of a time traveling device. The map interactive with useful indicators; map icons/markers. The legend on the map explains the function for each of the map icons. The ability to fast travel to another location and back.
Notebook: Two section – Notes and Objectives. Notes section is for the story and clues from the game. Objectives section is for all the objective from the game and the completed ones are checked off.
Hidden Object Gameplay: Traditional word list, Find “X” amount with some and/or no interaction required. For the traditional word only, the sonar feature show you the shape of the item. Most of the hidden object scenes can be replayed in the extras.
Match 3 Mini Game: This is optional mini game to play instead of looking for items in hidden object scenes.
Puzzle Gameplay: Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve. There is a skip button if the puzzle(s) becomes too tasking to solve.
Game Ending: The ending of the main portion of the game is complete. The bonus chapter somewhat overlaps the main portion of the game.
Game Extras: The game’s extras are locked. Completing the main portion of the game will unlock the bonus portion of the game. Completing the bonus portion of the game will unlock the other extras.
Game Bonus Chapter: Can be access after the main portion of the game is completed.
Game Achievements: Steam achievements. There 11 different achievements to earn from the game but they also comes with certain requirement into order to unlock them.
Game Wallpapers: Six wallpapers in total.
Encyclopaedia Temporis: Information on all the characters in the game.

Just go buy this game. It's the best thing created by a human ever. Except for Breaking Bad. Both are amazing...not convinced? Damn. Well, let's review Mass Effect 2 then.
A hundred and fifty years in the future, humanity has figured out FTL travel and has found their place in the galaxy among the numerous alien races. A rogue Spectre nearly brings on the end times by summoning giant robots that wipe out all life called the Reapers, barely being stopped by another Spectre (yes, that is you and yes, this took place in the last game), proving humanity's worth. You play as Commander Shepard... until he or she gets spaced. This isn't really spoiling since it happens in the first five minutes. But a group called Cerberus decides to bring Commander Shepard back to life to fight the Collectors, a mysterious race of aliens who have been abducting human colonies. Shepard agrees to work for it, though he or she is a bit hesitant since Cerberus is barely a step above a terrorist organization. The story then follows you recruiting numerous people with various talents for a Suicide Mission against the Collectors, where your decisions there and your team decides whether everyone lives or everyone dies. Good luck, Commander.
Gameplay is fantastic. The combat is a lot better than ME1, instead of the overheat system, you get the traditional gun system, and I like this more than the overheat system. There's also now a reason to use powers, even if you have awesome guns, you'll still need to use them on some enemies, compared to ME1 where once you got some good guns, it didn't really matter if you used powers or not. Squadmates are also a lot more useful, the 6 in ME1 (5 in the end... sometimes 4... spoilers?) gets boosted up to 10 (12 if you have the DLC), all of which are very good and have distinct personalities. Plus you can bang some of them, so that's nice.
There is also a good upgrade system, although in order to get the materials to do so, you have to do a kinda boring scanning minigame, which is not that fun to do. There are six classes (Soldier, Adept, Engineer, Sentinel, Vanguard, and Infiltrator), all of which are a lot more distinct than in ME1. I for one prefer Vanguard, but all classes are overall decent from what I hear. There are multiple conversation branches, a Paragon/Renegade morality system that is affected by dialogue and interrupts that you take, and loyalty systems, which once you do a mission for a character, they become loyal, making them more likely to survive the Suicide Mission and gets that squadmate a new loyalty power. Gameplay is fun, that's all that matters.
Characters are likeable for the most part. Shepard is customizable, letting you choose his/her looks, gender, and backstory. The squadmates you'll get, Miranda, Jacob, Garrus (returning from ME1), Jack, Grunt, Mordin, Tali (also returning from ME1), Thane, Samara, Legion, Zaeed (if you get the Cerberus Network DLC) and Kasumi (if you get the Stolen Memory DLC.) Your pilot Joker, played by Chris Griffin (Seth Green, but I call him Chris Griffin), is basically comic relief, however he and the banter with the AI is actually pretty funny. You'll encounter your previous ME1 squadmates who won't join you, Liara, Kaidan/Ash, and (if he's alive) Wrex. Wrex and Liara have some good scenes, but Kaidan or Ash... don't. The Illusive Man, who's the head honco of Cerberus and awesomely played by Martin Sheen, is probably one of my favorite villians of all time. All the characters are well written, are well voice played, and I can't really hate these characters. My personal favorites are Garrus and Tali.
Criticisms? There are some kinda baffling plot details, Shepard's revival making no sense being my biggest complaint. The scanning minigame I mentioned earlier isn't very fun. There's hacking, which I hear a lot of people hate, I didn't... that much, at least, but I see where people come from when they say it's lame. Also, there aren't very many weapons, which is kind of lame, to be honest.
Still, this is an awesome game that everyone should play in their lifetime. 10/10, if you have the money, buy it. Now. Get the other two games in the trilogy as well, ME1 is on Steam as well, but you have to deal with Origin for ME3.

This game....what an experience.
Metro 2033 was already a great game, but LL has fixed pretty much every flaw and added more positive features to boot. By far this is one of the best games, let alone sequels, I've ever played.
Just like 2033, the truly oppressive, claustrophobic atmosphere of living in metro tunnels beneath a bombed out, radioactive ruin hasn't lost its bite one bit. The debris-strewn and dirty maintenence and train tunnels, the wild and well-animated enemy creatures, the wide open and windy ruins of surface Moscow--all of it is top-notch and perfectly executed.
The survival-horror gameplay is still as great as it was in 2033. The weapons are varied and have great animations, design, and impact (though I still argue that Ranger mode's two-weapon limit is unwelcome and needlessly restrictive in a game like this). Whether you're fighting humans from the shadows in dimly-lit train tunnels, or battling for survival against mutated abominations on the rainy Moscow surface, the gameplay is highly varied and not a single level feels derivative or uninspired. The most welcome change of all is the vastly improved ending. The ending in 2033 was good for its narrative, but the last third was underwhelming from a gameplay perspective. In LL, that is not the case at all. From beginning to end the story and gameplay are well-paced, with tons of great characters, twists, and deeply emotional moments. Be warned: tears will ensue many times throughout the campaign.
And unlike 2033, there are DLCs here, and they're an unfortunate mixed bag. Many are well done (Spider Lair being a very spooky survival-horror experience, and Pavel providing great gunfights), but others focus way too heavily on combat at the expense of everything else that makes the Metro games so unique.
In summary, the strengths of this game are immense and the weaknesses are nitpicks. If you love FPSs, survival, or story-driven games, buy this. You'll have no regrets.

The combat is the strongest part of the game, but it's also the hardest to get into; I had to restart the game multiple times to get the right party structure to tackle the game's challenges.
If you don't have the right party makeup, skills, and items, then it's going to feel like the game is cheating you. Enemies will constantly be inflicting status conditions (usually turn-skipping ones) if your armor isn't up to snuff. A lack of skills means that enemies will be able to out-maneuver and out-damage you. And, of course, having a party of all mages isn't a good idea when archers can just sit and take potshots at you three times a turn. If you're not sure what you're doing, there's no shame in playing on the lower difficulty setting. Trust me.
The other two major selling points of this game are the story and the exploration, both of which are a bit weaker in terms of originality but are just as great as the combat system. The dialogue is your standard Neverwinter Nights affair, made a bit spicier by the Tags system. Simply put, each character has Tags (related to aspects of their personality, history, or appearance) that give unique dialogue options. You can even acquire new tags as you play, making the system versatile as well. The dialogue itself is well-written and hilarious at times, giving the game a comedic twist and elevating it from a drab, boring fantasy adventure. I won't spoil the story, but I'll say that after 30 hours I've only brushed up against what the story has to offer. The thousands upon thousands of dialogue trees are backed up by some impressive voice acting, which makes reading through the game's story (which might as well be novel length, if not longer) actually fun and engaging instead of a slog.

I really enjoyed this game. It took me roughly nine hours to finish, and that includes finding over 150 artifacts, completing all the cases where you help other ghosts cross over, and exploring the town. Oh, and my game got erased about an hour in, so I guess it was really about eight hours to complete all that.
This isn't a particularly difficult game; in fact, there's a certain element of hand holding. You always know where you need to go next - there's even a tracker telling you how close you are to the next destination and an arrow to follow to get there. So there's a bit of hand holding.
That's okay, though, because I was in this game for the story, and it had a great one. The main character's backstory is interesting, and although the side characters weren't particuarly well developed, it was enjoyable finding artifacts to learn more about their backstories.
The voice acting was excellent. Some of the best voice acting I've ever heard.
It's not a perfect game by any means. You have an option to do certain ghostly skills, which is a major reason I was interested in this game, but that was a letdown. I thought maybe you could develop some skills or have your own unique skills, but no, not really. It's all pretty generic.
One of the skills is possessing other people, and although it's fun at first to possess the random passerby on the streets, that gets old pretty quickly. There's a lot of repetition in their thoughts and nothing particularly interesting to think about. It would have been better to find some of them holding secrets or something, in my opinion.
Another letdown was the demon fighting. The mechanics are simple, it's also repetitive, and there's basically  no challenge. It just serves to slow you down for a bit.
That said, I did enjoy this game and I'm glad I got it. I would definitely recommend for those looking for a game with a great story that isn't too intensive to play.

For a game that's 5 years old, it still is one of the best in the Mass Effect series.
You step back into the shoes of Shepard and embark on a quest to defeat another evil that threatens the galaxy. Everything is taken a giant leap towards being awesome with characters being some of the most unique and interesting characters you'll ever meet in any video game. The combat is also refined to be relatively good as well, clearing a bit of room on the Power Wheel. And obviously the story is what brings it all together.
Here's the thing with ME2. In ME1, your decisions didn't really affect anyone so much that it would affect you personally. Many of the side missions weren't required and were more for killing time.
This time in ME2, you HAVE to do side-missions (a.k.a Loyalty Missions) for your crew, in order for everyone to survive the Suicide Mission. Every time I play, I ALWAYS make sure everyone is loyal so that everyone lives. Someone died in the final mission? Then their gone. Per-Ma-Death. They. are. dead.
It's this requirement of doing these missions and collecting resources that makes ME2 so enjoyable. It adds on the game time, so you really have a lot of stuff to do and it affects you personally, making sure that everyone is loyal. This simple game mechanic is probably the exact reason (probably others, but I think this one.) why Mass Effect 2 was voted THE BEST GAME in 2010.
And you know what? It still is. BioWare really hit the nail with this. Everyone should play it. Even if you're not combat-heavy, the characters will surely have you wanting to talk to them more. This game is a MUST for everyone.

I love almost every aspect of this game. This game is beautiful.  I absolutely love this game's concept.  It's like Nidhogg, but in an old Japanese tapestry.  Sadly, Online Multiplayer is dead.
I love this game's art design, it's as if you're fighting in a painting.  The challenge levels are what they say they are... Challenging.  Some challenges may be difficult for people who are hard of hearing or have a tough time distinguishing similar sounds.  Most of the challenges are enjoyable and I feel that the challenge levels and Local Multiplayer are the main selling points to this game, since there is never anyone online to play with.  It's enjoyable and took be about two hours just to beat the challenges.  It takes awhile to get used to, but once you understand the controls and start to figure out what you're doing wrong, it's easy to correct your mistakes and become decent at this game.
Once in a blue corn moon, somebody else is online searching for a game and you finally get to play online multiplayer.  In all honesty though, you can have just as much fun playing Local Multiplayer or even Singleplayer.
Even when going against AI in singleplayer, it's pretty enjoyable.  It's a fun game, but can be a bit rage inducing.  Most of the time the controls and movement are accurate, but very seldomly something glitches out and either you kill them, or they kill you in an abnormal way.
The options menu is well made and I love the audio in this game.  It sounds so authentic.  There are presets for the controls, however you have the option to fully customize your controls.
I recommend this game, however, if you want a game like this for online multiplayer, look elsewhere.

SCS software has pulled out another epic simulator for the trucking community with American Truck Simulator.
If you're familiar with the software background of ETS2, you're covered. However, theres a few things to keep in mind with these differences.
1. Truck geometry (size) is entirely different from ETS2, you'll have to relearn your truckspace and angle points. If you're new to it, you won't have an problems learning the geometry.
2. Speedzones are tricky, especially in California (now I see why some of my professional trucking friends try to avoid driving through there). [Corrected - v1.1.1 Allowing time to change to different speedzones]
3. Cops are not very forgiving in CA, so watch your speed and traffic light timings. [Nerfed by v1.1.1 - Alot of folks were verbal, figured ya learn from driving in an area. Guess not for many folks]
4. For now, work on your ADR certs and high value cargo for now until they expand further out of Cali and Nevada.
5. There are weird easter eggs and hidden gems to seek out in the game, you'll easily spot them so I won't spoil them.
A biggie:
1. It is a solid simulator/game with many new goodies that will be coming along the line over the progress of updates/upgrades.
2. It is 64-bit native, so you need a 64-bit machine to run it properly. They still have 32-bit floating around but keep in mind that they stress that it is "NOT SUPPORTED" in the event you have tech problems. They're slowly phasing out the 32-bit flavor to allow the game to have more flexibility on machines with decent resources handy and not choking on limitations.
The only hiccup I've seen sofar (as of this posting) is that the AI vehicles are hovering on the roadways.
Wishlist for the game (which would liven the experience a little more):
1. Dynamic construction areas (changes to a random location every 30 game time days).
2. Electronic road boards (the type the DOT uses, not the roadside adverts [though, thats also not a bad idea too]).
3. Signs that read "Reduce Speed Ahead" and "Construction Zone Ahead". May help prevent trailer damages in the event an AI plows into the back end when you slam on the brakes due to sudden speedzone changes (coughcalicough). [fixed via Ver 1.1.1 - Time allowance to reduce speed applied. Cops nerfed based on Driver's Level]
Note: In any situation where you see a Prius make a right turn into your right of way. You will crash if you don't catch up on the brakes. For some odd reason, the Prius is suicidal. Sofar, I've seen this happen 7 times in Cali.

Armed and armored brave companies of soldiers ride out to meet those fell beasts. The hordes of teeth and claws fall before a volley of arrows and crash upon stalwart shields. As the soldiers break open the gate they swarm over fortress slaying the brigands and cutthroats. At the end of the day, when the banner of the new kingdom flew from the tower the settlers knew they had the grace of the gods.

Upon the field they assembled a legion of shields and steel... to the north they marched... to their destiny.

Oh Sega. You have made a fantastic TBS game. To me, it's on par with Fire Emblem. Okay enough gushing for now. Best to give this a proper rub down.
Pros:
The first time you play this game [given if you don't skip the intro bit after the Sega Logo shows up] is that the art style that the game has is beautiful. It's like watching drawings come to life with how the effects work. If you ever get the chance, you could make a pretty awesome screenshot in the game that's wallpaper worthy for your computer. The story really gets to you as you play through it. You begin to form bonds with the cast of likable characters as soon as you begin playing the game, which is a great way to start any game. With characters in mind, you wouldn't believe how colorful they can be. You'd be surprised by some of them when you begin forming your version of Squad 7 when you, for example, pick a buff guy and heard his voice and personality shows he's more than meets the eyes. I'm looking at you Jann. Don't ever change. Gameplay's pretty good, save for one, but I'll get onto that later. It's a Turn Based Strategy game, but it has a bit of a twist. You select a character, and you go into third person with him/her and move them around, where which way you go and when has immediate consequences because you won't take back what you do, and the enemy [and your forces] will fire at the active soldier moves into range. This makes you really need to think about every move, or you will have a fallen ally on your hands. However, unlike the Fire Emblem games before Awakening, when an ally soldier's down, they don't die instantly. You can save them when an ally touches them before three turns pass. I loved that feature because I ALWAYS wanted to keep everyone alive. There's so many features that I loved about this game, but the good will have to end for now because of the...
Cons:
Back to gameplay, there's one feature I didn't like and that's the tank controls. I don't know if it could be the default controls for keyboard and mouse or what, but there were times where moving around makes it a struggle to get it in the right spot. It drove me nuts. The second, and last bad point is the music. Nothing seems to stick with me when I listen to them, but then again, it's my opinion. I bet there's fans that loves the music. [3/18/16: One song finally sticks with me. If you ever get the chance, listen to "A Love Passed On"]
Extra Bits: Now already, this game's a great game for those that love strategy games, and want a great story with great characters. What could make it better? The free DLC that comes with the game. You get more skirmish missions that focus on the various classes. A mission where you play as Edy's Edy Detactment, which is a pretty tough mission due to the characters you're stuck with. Some are great, good, or ugh... I'm looking at you Susie! You want a harder time? There's EX Hard Mode after you beat the game, which is really hard [which is a guess. I've yet to touch that yet. An update later?]. And for those that like to see the other side of a story, look at Behind Her Blue Flame, which you take command of the Selvaria's forces and learn more about her and her newest engineer.
3/22/16: I got around with playing with the EX Hard Mode DLC, and here's the thing, it only counts for the Base Game's Skirmishes. After beating the game once, you unlock two more difficulties for the nine missions: Hard and Expert. Hard Mode, you're learn REAL quick that positions and/or the entire map gets altered. I bet with enough time and careful planning, you can clear it with no problem. Expert Mode kicks it up a notch and then some. First of all, You have no tank, which means Welkin will be on foot this time. This also means no Orders. It's just pure thinking and making each move count with this mode. Best of luck to you all if you play that mode and may the Valkyrur protect you.
Final Thoughts: This is a must have if you don't have this game on PS3 or PS4 since it'll be getting a re-release as well, which is really neat. My only regret is that the series went onto PSP and we will most likely never see those games on Steam or the consoles. Then again, who knows what the future will hold.

So I walked into a bar and a guy in a hood asked me if I wanted to play his hipster version of DnD. I went "sure, why not, I'm bored", and promptly started to hallucinate while he dealt me cards, and I was left wondering why I'm even in a bar, considering I don't drink...
Hand of Fate is a rather story-vague game that puts you into the place of some kind of wandering adventurer. Our status is unknown (alive? dead? neither? both?), and we've crossed what's known as "The Thirteen Gates" to come and meet... whoever this is, we'll call him The Dealer (not that kind). The Dealer seems to be offering the adventurer a chance to get whatever they want, be it riches, eternal life, answers or what have you. Honestly, I'm not entirely sure what's happening, all I know is that I don't trust him and that whoever he is, he's going to give me what I want. Bit like a Djinn if you will.
Although that's a point in the game's favour; it allows the player to make up their own little story and figure out what's going on while getting hints of a past life from the cards that are played against them.
The gameplay itself is surprisingly well done; the first portion of the game is a DnD style card game, where the dealer acts as a sort of Dungeonmaster to explain what occurs on each card, then gives you the necessary tools to resolve them. Cards can either give you Health (self-explanetory), Gold (ditto mark), and Food (required to explore and continue in the game), Armor/Weapons (more self-explanatory terms), Special items and other assistances. Cards can also be negative, and punish you with loss of any of these above subjects, or even summon monsters to fight you.
Upon drawing a monster card we're placed into the Brawler aspect of the game, wherein the game takes an adequately presented 3D perspective to let you physically fight your opponents, which change based on card suit and number (3 of Dust for bandits, a 2 of Skulls for undead, so on and so forth). Your weapon and armor cards become actual weapons and armor to use, and special items can be activated to change the outcome of the battle if necessary. It's well presented and flows excellently, allowing fluid dodging, countering and attacks to whittle down enemies for success. There's very little to complain about.
It's not an extroardinary game, mind. It feels more like something you'll flick on every few hours to kill 10-30 minutes, something to occupy you for a bit while you wait. Almost like a mobile game effortlessly intermingled with a dungeon brawler game. It's impressive in its own way, and rather enjoyable.

One of the most entertaining gems to come out of steam. One part rogue like, one part Fable-esque hack-n-slash, one part deck builder, add in some truly wonderful monologues from the Dealer, and you arrive at Hand of Fate.
The combination of deck building and roguelike allows for a unique choose your own adventure style of play. With the release of the Wildcard dlc the replay value skyrockets by adding in new "Fate" cards (essentially new player characters) that come with thier own unique challenges.
The game starts out reletively easy, with a limited number of cards and shorter dungeons. But as you progress you unlock upgrades that improve your abilities but also thte abilities of your enemies, creating a more traditional roguelike experience (i.e. hard as hell). While not overly difficult with thte default Fate, it becomes increasingly more difficult when playing as the Warlord (hard mode) or the Monk(no gold!!). Top it off with some real nasty curses and this game would appeal to the most masacistic roguelike fans.
On the downside, and it really is the only downside I can see, the combat gets a little stale after a while. It boils down to more or less hit and run strikes, although with the right equipment this ceases to be a problem.
Highly recomended, one of the best additions to the steam catalogue. With the simple addition of new cards the potential for expansion is nearly infinite. 9/10

I honestly don't know how I feel about this game; that's still the case after 12.2 hours, and at this point in my review, I haven't decided whether this is going to be positive or negative.
Firstly, the images you see in the slider above are not reflective of the graphics in game at the moment. The water from above looks reasonably nice, but dip your head under and it's a different story.
The servers are laggy with FPS issues, and the loading bar that says "this may take several minutes" should actually say "this may take several hours".
The 'monsters' in the game consist of a selection of about 10-15; crocodiles can't swim, and the AI is absolutely horrendous. The fighting in general doesn't shout skill to me; you hit something in front of you, then it rubberbands 3 metres behind you, and then you hit your tribe mate that's popped up in front of you out of nowhere. That's my experience so far.
So much of the 'learn recipes' (skill tree) doesn't make sense to me; being a stonemason is a prerequisite to being able to use a
Yet, you can destroy a base with a few arrows at level 5.
The NPC's are derpy as♥♥♥♥♥♥ They can't swim, they often stand and look blankly at you, and then comes insta-death. Oh, and then 7 wolf/dog/hyena things pounce on you.
The building is fairly simple; I like that the walls show the outer wall face, as opposed to placing one down, then realising it's wrong and having to destroy it. You can make some fairly decent looking buildings with the resources available, but they'll only last a few minutes before the rust fan boys come and raid you out of house and home.
You don't have the ability to build a bed until level 13 (off the top of my head) which means you have to constantly craft bed rolls in order to not lose all of your stuff every single time you die (which is often).
I haven't had the luxury of reaching a point where any of the temple stuff comes into play (I don't even know if the game is capable of this at the moment).
People are comparing this game to ARK, but I can't make that comparison myself; I'd feel like a dirty lying cheat if I were to say that. ARK has it's issues, yes, but it's beautiful, and there's a game to play, a point to it. This honestly feels like a worse version of Rust. I liked Rust at first, but the more I played the more I came to realise there wasn't really much point to it. I want the motivation to survive in a survival game for a reason. This game currently doesn't give me that.
So I guess on that note, I'm going to stamp this as negative for now. I believe the game has potential, but this should not have been released in its current state. Whoever tested this game... I want a word with you! It's a little embarrassing.

I often call Owlboy the "Undertale of action platformers", and that's exactly what it is! Owlboy is a beautiful 2D adventure set in a world floating in the sky. You'll explore ancient ruins, fight monsters, aquire friends with unique abilities, and battle challenging bosses. Everything here is so carefully crafted, from the balanced difficulty to the design of the levels. You'll never be truly lost in any dungeon, and you'll always end up going in the right direction anyway. The art itself is so beautiful, even if I got lost somehow, that I was in disbelief. The sheer effort that went into the animation and pixel art is ASTOUNDING! The story alone is incredible and compelling. There is nothing better than a group of friends going up against overwhelming odds! What a classic tale full of tension and hope! For this review, I am not going to do my usual summary of the positives or negatives. Because there really isn't a single negative to say about Owlboy. Maybe the odd stealth sections are a minor flaw, because they do a good job breaking up the usual gameplay, but everything else is so well made. In fact, if you don't care about collecting everything or finding all the secrets, the collectable coins are designed exactly to give you the upgrades you need just by playing normally. That is polish and care on a higher level! Owlboy is another "indie darling" that deserves to sit next to Shovel Knight and Undertale!

At first view this seemed kind of cringy, with bad voice acting and repetitive music. The protagonist also seems to be... well... kind of dumb, discarding objects after one use for seemingly no reason, when they could easily come in useful again later. However, so far i'm finding it oddly addicting. I've played hidden object games before of course, however it isn't a genre i'm usually interested in. This is different though, adding in the very interesting mechanics of being able to time travel and see your changes in the past reflected in the future. There's also sometimes quite a delay between finding an item and being able to use it, or vice versa, giving that lovely eureka feeling of "OH I remember what I do with this". The puzzles aren't too difficult, just enough to make you think but not enough to frustrate you, with lots of variety in the types of puzzles you have to solve, ranging from simple "find these items" to connecting fuses in a way that reminds me a little of Bioshock's pipe puzzles. This game ended up surprised me in being a lovely game to play casually to wind down in the evenings.

No i don't mean that against the game at all, there's just a game each year that fans oversell massively leading to many arguments online, I believe Owlboy is this year's game for that.
The obvious draw to this game is it's immaculately detailed pixel art style with 9 years to create and refine and I will agree along with the many others and say it delivers. The world is vibrant and interesting consistently with beautiful environments throughout. The audio and soundtrack also come in to enhance the art style in order to build a very enjoyable experience. The game is absolutely worth a purchase for it's artistic work in itself(or even grabbing the game + soundtrak bundle).
The main overarching plot isn't impressive nor bad, you will probably roll your eyes when you discover it has 'that' story, I won't spoil but you've heard it before. the world however does have enough interest and intrigue to easily keep you invested throughout. Characters however is where the game does start to shine, each one is enjoyable and is interesting enough that you want to hear what they have to say or press the interact button till they run out of lines and you can find yourself caring about their fates. The over the top animations also do a great job of giving a much greater personality to the sorts of characters that would generally be uninteresting.
All up Owlboy has successfully done what few games manage to do and that's create a complete package that oozes with charm and is in general an experience that's just enjoyable to experience and be in from start to finish.
Gameplay is unfortunately where Owlboy starts to struggle.
The main idea behind the gameplay, of Otus being fairly limited in how he fights but can carry objects carries a nice novelty and gets you to think a little differently. Each companion has a unique set of abilities to assist Otus in navigating the world and defeating a handful of creatures littering the world, some unique others are a new skin on classic platformer enemies. Unfortunately these concepts are burdened by the games levels having a clear "use this character here" vibe and very quickly becomes "plant wall, shotgun", "bomb creature, there must be something breakable nearby" some sections of the game do get you to think but unfortunately most of the time you're just absent mindedly running through the motions to progress, there's little room to play. With most of the gameplay then just falling into fairly standard platformer puzzles there's little to impress in the gameplay in that regard, nothing much is terribly done, but there's nothing amazing either, all up it's consistently 'okay'.
Controls can also be a little fiddly with many cases of struggling to interact with a specific item, having to pick up a character and throw them away to get to something or pick up something a few times before you get its position right, all up it's a minor annoyance most of the time and can be ignored.
The game could also really do with a decent map, with the world being large with a short view distance it becomes very easy to become lost and i worry about anyone who's a real completionist as finding out the last few areas you haven't been to i can imagine will become a pain to figure out.
Late game became slightly less enjoyable with slow tedious time based puzzles where accidentally tapping the jump/fly button a second time ruins everything. Yes, it also does the slowly rising screen where you jump on breakable objects with a split second to jump on the one that's just appeared at the bottom, is there anyone that enjoys that? Especially when it's happening so slowly you're not getting that rush that comes from having to jump at a million miles an hour.
Finally, I found bosses, particularly late game to be genuinely unenjoyable with short cutscenes breaking the flow and unclear weaknesses that lead you to blindly shooting till you spot the weakness. the worst of which involving a pirate switched your character, showed a cutscene and then instantly jumps at you giving you some less than fair damage as you try to get out of the way and switch characters before projectiles start flying at you.
If the art style doesn't interest you i would not recommend this game, there's nothing else here for you. Everyone else however the world, visuals and sound track all easily compensate for any gameplay shortcomings and it's absolutely worth playing through if you’re after a game you can just relax and enjoy.

First the TL:DR version: good HOG, it's a good buy for like 2$/€ or in a bundle. Mechanically stable, playeable without problems.   BUT!  It's an incredible letdown and disappointment for an Artifex Mundi game. If you want to get a fantastic HOG, not only an "okay" one, check out other Mundi titles, as Time Mysteries is incredible weak compared to their other games.
A little longer:
Time Mysteries: The Final Enigma is the third and final episode of the Time Mysteries series. I really hoped that the game will improve compared to the second title, but sadly it didn't succeed. They used almost (completely?) same sound track as in the second one, the bonus chapter recycled who HO scenes - it's not a big problem, but foreshadows other issues.
I just can't believe that this is a Mundi Game.  This came out in January 2013. Enigmatis 2 maybe in August, same year. The quality difference between the two games is like they were made  DECADES apart from eachother.
I'm not joking - while Enigmatis titles and Grim Tales features the most beautiful animations I've ever seen in HOGs, Time Mysteries' character animation is much closer to Fallout 2's talking head animations than other recent Mundi titles.  I just don't know - they piled all funds for Enigmatis? Or had serious deadline-issues with the (whole!) Time Mysteries project, or it was designed to be a lower-budget game? I'm really curious about this.
Although it's quite common in HOG that they feature strange logic or storytelling sometimes, sadly T.M: t.F.E. also features one of the weakest plot I've seen in HOGs. The antagonist literally tells you that you wouldn't get his motivation, so he don't tell you anything why he did what he did - the act that set the whole 3-episode saga into motion.
Also there were lots of puzzles that's design was quite flawed. I've seen 4 (!) puzzles that required you to guess the correct order of 3 things without any clue, and one "play back the notes" game that was so fast and started instantly that you couldn't see the original order, and there was no option to repeat it. So, back to guessing again.   Also the gameplay was greatly elongated by "cheese mechanics": you found a key besides a safe, only to open a door in the precious room to find the safe's handle there. I know, this is base HOG-mechanic: but there was so many place when you could feel that item placement makes no sense, they just wanted to insert another item to make the game longer. Somehow the game missed the atmosphere and logic that usually makes you believe or at least okay with this "inflated gameplay time" - here there was no such thing.
If you're still with me:   I really do love Mundi games, I think they are one of the best HOG in terms of quality, I would rate them differently from the most other HOG games because of their exceptional graphics and content.  But it would be a lie to say this game is exceptional - besides the still quite beautiful graphics, this is not more than an ordinary HOG.   But as a Mundi product, the quality of ordinary is sadly a big-big negative adjective. This game could be so much more  :\
Final verdict: Okay-good HOG, but a big letdown if you ecpect Artifex Mundi quality.

Time Mysteries 3 corrected almost everything that was wrong in the previous game at the cost of play time and puzzle difficulty. A solid ending to a hidden object game trilogy.
One of the largest problem with Time Mysteries 2 was the lack of story and continuity with the first game. Final Enigma chose the opposite path: not only it’s completely plot-focused, but it features characters and places from both previous games. Sure, it’s basically a huge rip-off of Terminator, but fits well into the established canon.
It seems the story was such a priority that the development team forgot to work on the puzzles; they pose absolutely no challenge. Even the hidden object scenes are a letdown with only a few dozen items per scene. The contrast is even more apparent in the bonus chapter, which reuses parts of the second episode. (It also lacks any original content, making it possibly the laziest bonus episode we have seen in a hidden object puzzle game.)
To sum it up, if you have been along for the ride since the Inheritance or if you would like a nice and easy HO game for a change, then it’s more than recommended to get this one.

Oh Sega. You have made a fantastic TBS game. To me, it's on par with Fire Emblem. Okay enough gushing for now. Best to give this a proper rub down.
Pros:
The first time you play this game [given if you don't skip the intro bit after the Sega Logo shows up] is that the art style that the game has is beautiful. It's like watching drawings come to life with how the effects work. If you ever get the chance, you could make a pretty awesome screenshot in the game that's wallpaper worthy for your computer. The story really gets to you as you play through it. You begin to form bonds with the cast of likable characters as soon as you begin playing the game, which is a great way to start any game. With characters in mind, you wouldn't believe how colorful they can be. You'd be surprised by some of them when you begin forming your version of Squad 7 when you, for example, pick a buff guy and heard his voice and personality shows he's more than meets the eyes. I'm looking at you Jann. Don't ever change. Gameplay's pretty good, save for one, but I'll get onto that later. It's a Turn Based Strategy game, but it has a bit of a twist. You select a character, and you go into third person with him/her and move them around, where which way you go and when has immediate consequences because you won't take back what you do, and the enemy [and your forces] will fire at the active soldier moves into range. This makes you really need to think about every move, or you will have a fallen ally on your hands. However, unlike the Fire Emblem games before Awakening, when an ally soldier's down, they don't die instantly. You can save them when an ally touches them before three turns pass. I loved that feature because I ALWAYS wanted to keep everyone alive. There's so many features that I loved about this game, but the good will have to end for now because of the...
Cons:
Back to gameplay, there's one feature I didn't like and that's the tank controls. I don't know if it could be the default controls for keyboard and mouse or what, but there were times where moving around makes it a struggle to get it in the right spot. It drove me nuts. The second, and last bad point is the music. Nothing seems to stick with me when I listen to them, but then again, it's my opinion. I bet there's fans that loves the music. [3/18/16: One song finally sticks with me. If you ever get the chance, listen to "A Love Passed On"]
Extra Bits: Now already, this game's a great game for those that love strategy games, and want a great story with great characters. What could make it better? The free DLC that comes with the game. You get more skirmish missions that focus on the various classes. A mission where you play as Edy's Edy Detactment, which is a pretty tough mission due to the characters you're stuck with. Some are great, good, or ugh... I'm looking at you Susie! You want a harder time? There's EX Hard Mode after you beat the game, which is really hard [which is a guess. I've yet to touch that yet. An update later?]. And for those that like to see the other side of a story, look at Behind Her Blue Flame, which you take command of the Selvaria's forces and learn more about her and her newest engineer.
3/22/16: I got around with playing with the EX Hard Mode DLC, and here's the thing, it only counts for the Base Game's Skirmishes. After beating the game once, you unlock two more difficulties for the nine missions: Hard and Expert. Hard Mode, you're learn REAL quick that positions and/or the entire map gets altered. I bet with enough time and careful planning, you can clear it with no problem. Expert Mode kicks it up a notch and then some. First of all, You have no tank, which means Welkin will be on foot this time. This also means no Orders. It's just pure thinking and making each move count with this mode. Best of luck to you all if you play that mode and may the Valkyrur protect you.
Final Thoughts: This is a must have if you don't have this game on PS3 or PS4 since it'll be getting a re-release as well, which is really neat. My only regret is that the series went onto PSP and we will most likely never see those games on Steam or the consoles. Then again, who knows what the future will hold.

There are good games, life FIFA 15.
There are great games, like Tomb Raider.
Then there are games that I can't wait to play. Games that I think about when I'm far away from my computer. Games that make me realize that the quality of the game has nothing to do with how many hours it takes to finish the campaign. Games that make me want to play them, not out of obligation because everyone else played it, but because it is truly extraordinary. Games that make you realize it's okay to be bored by assembly-line games like Far Cry, Destiny, Halo, and Call of Duty, all of which have good game mechanics but poor lore. Games that make me want to play all the prequels just to undertand the lore better. Games that are just as good without friends as they are with friends. Games that somehow manage to be as beautiful on the inside (content-wise) as they are on the outside (graphics-wise). Games that make me want to replay them even though there are other games I haven't tried yet. Games like Mass Effect 2, which firmly established the Mass Effect series as one of the best series of all time.
I haven't played a game this good in years and maybe I won't for years to come. Bioware have other good games, but nothing that rivals the Mass Effect series. This game is a phenomenon. The Mass Effect series has the potential to become a legacy, like the Final Fantasy series or Pokemon series (both of which are so popular that they have been able to make games long past their expiration dates).

Something else I'd like to mention first, is that this is a game you'd typically play during a short break or when you don't have time to play your time-consuming bigger games. Hence why the average playtime on this game would never be as high compared to other games in general. It's really a 'quickie'-game.
Now on to the problem. After several months of bug fixing, there are still several really major bugs within the game which will definitely ruin game-play experience often enough. When you queue up for a game, you'll disconnect or receive error messages about half of the time. But that's not the worst part. The worst part is the bugs still going on when it comes to races and custom-made maps. As you'll likely know, you're losing a match if your opponent manages to outrun you and gets you out of the screen due to that. But there are bugs within the game that causes the winning player to actually lose. The winning player runs too fast, gets out of the screen, and loses. That is not how it's supposed to work. The same counts for catching up with your opponents. It's possible that when you catch in too fast, that you, the winning player, loses the game as you get out of screen. When it comes to custom-made maps, you'll often find out that the game totally breaks due to the automatically generated starting point of a race being out of the map. Players either fall into an endless void, or get to see a blacked out screen until someone automatically loses or wins after some time. Now, mind you, for the majority of the time you won't experience this issue. But you will experience those bugs often enough (especially the queuing bug) that it will make you hate the game. Those bugs aren't occurring rarely, no, those bugs are occurring way too frequently. Whenever I play the game for about 30 minutes, I'll experience at least a couple of those bugs. These bugs have been in the game for months, and have never been fixed even though there were several hotfixes for other bugs.
Now, you might say ''how can you downrate the game due to bugs while it's still in the beta phase?''. That is because the developers just announced that the game is almost in its final state (nothing major going to happen anymore) while those bugs still haven't been fixed over the course of months and several fixes. Therefore it's very unlikely that they actually will fix those bugs before they will release the game soon. If they actually do fix them before they launch the game officially, I'll come back and request it, as it's an amazing game. But as they still haven't fixed months-old bugs and are about to launch the game in this state, I can't recommend it. None likes to play a racing game and lose because they were actually too fast or because of other bugs.

This is my 3rd review on this game as it is constantly improving.  My original review was a "not recommend" and they have already fixed most of my original gripes.  I highly recommend this game for anybody that is competitive that enjoys a tough challenge.
PROS:
Very competitive online
Skill depth (look up Taters McShit on youtube)
Fun and Addictive for any skill level
CONS:
Items Ruin Ranked - This is a biggie for me.  Basically the cheesier you play, the more you'll win and the saltier your opponent will be.  I think this is cancerous for the community and probably why so few people play this game.
Small Community - I find myself playing the same people every day. A lot of the time, nobody's online so I get mis-matched with players that are either way better than me, or way worse than me.
Join Lag - If you're in a race and someone joins, the game lags out and will usually cost you the round.  Very frusterating.
SUGGESTION:
Make ranked matches without items.  Or atleast make it to where people can choose their own item settings and item options are randomly chosen between player's preferences each game.  Or you could reward people with extra rank up points for using no items.  It would also be great if there was a way to tech hitstun from an item (kinda like smash) to get up faster if executed properly.  Either way, their should be a way to offset the items.  Look at any game that has items/pickups (smash bros, mario kart, Halo, TF, etc.).  All of those games competitive ruleset is to play without items/pickups.  By forcing people to play with items on, you're closing the door to more potential players.

One of the most entertaining gems to come out of steam. One part rogue like, one part Fable-esque hack-n-slash, one part deck builder, add in some truly wonderful monologues from the Dealer, and you arrive at Hand of Fate.
The combination of deck building and roguelike allows for a unique choose your own adventure style of play. With the release of the Wildcard dlc the replay value skyrockets by adding in new "Fate" cards (essentially new player characters) that come with thier own unique challenges.
The game starts out reletively easy, with a limited number of cards and shorter dungeons. But as you progress you unlock upgrades that improve your abilities but also thte abilities of your enemies, creating a more traditional roguelike experience (i.e. hard as hell). While not overly difficult with thte default Fate, it becomes increasingly more difficult when playing as the Warlord (hard mode) or the Monk(no gold!!). Top it off with some real nasty curses and this game would appeal to the most masacistic roguelike fans.
On the downside, and it really is the only downside I can see, the combat gets a little stale after a while. It boils down to more or less hit and run strikes, although with the right equipment this ceases to be a problem.
Highly recomended, one of the best additions to the steam catalogue. With the simple addition of new cards the potential for expansion is nearly infinite. 9/10

Along with it's elder European brother, ATS is a truly wonderful Sim. And improves on many features of ETS. Mainly, the amount of detail in the world; whereas ETS felt a bit too much like a copy-paste when strolling through all different towns, you never really knew if you were in Paris, London or Milan, other than a different backdrop, this was one of the biggest changes into ATS. with a clear difference between states (currently only 2, but plans suggest CSC will expand nearly all states over a long period of time), now it feels as if you're actually entering Los Angeles, seeing known landmarks, the sloped streets of San Fransisco and not to mention the large array of hotels and casino's in Las Vegas. Though some of the smaller towns feel more like a street than a town, it doesn't feel less filled or detailed.
however. my main concerns with ATS are the following:
- Cops, good on paper but a huge pain in the game. Too large fines (1.000 dollar for driving 22MPH in a 20MPH zone (right after a weighing station)) and TOO, MUCH TOO fast in fining, trucks are heavy and increase in momentum when going downhill, but unless your breaking constantly without dropping once, you'll be fined.
- Ambulances and Cop cars never really do anything, like an emergancy call forcing you to make way for them. This would add another level of realism in my opinion.
- Customization is a lot less than before. Keep in mind the Game only has 2 trucks at the time of this review. with a £rd on the way, there is just very little to do on both the outside and inside of your truck, no airhorns, no beacons, 2 bullbars only, no cabin-accessories. It all just feels a bit underwhelming. but hopefully we'll receive more and more features as the game progresses into more states and more trucks.
- And last, the trailers, though a 53ft trailer is impressive and surely isnt simple to handle, more massive hauls would be welcomed any day of the week. Have some special cargo, have difficult cargo, anything that asks more of us as sim truckers would be great, we like to be challenged!

This is a game that seems strange at first, but then after the first game, I realized I was playing something inspired.  You make your deck, then the dealer adds his own cards to it.  These cards make up the "dungeon" and are placed face down (mostly) randomly.  You move your avatar from one card to the next to explore each dungeon, turning the cards face up and resolving their events or encounters as you go along.  Maybe it's a shop, maybe it's an ambush, maybe it's an event where you get lost in the swamp, or goblins steal your equipment and you have to kill them before they escape.
The variety and depth is impressive.  Some events rely on skill (beating down goblins who just stole all your weapons, for example), while others rely solely on chance/luck of the draw (picking from 3 success cards and 1 failure card to climb safely down into a ravine, for example).  As the game goes on, it introduces more and more facets, all of which give another layer of chance and strategy.  Combat takes place like the Batman: Arkham Whatever games, where you just smack enemies until they fall over and counter when it tells you to, but it's still fun, and the enemies provide enough challenges to keep from being boring/easy.
Absolute recommend.  This is one of those rare times where a game tries to do a little of everything, and manages to succeed at it fantastically.

First impressions here;this game needs honest reviews.
The game has a story, voiceovers, and grants a very pleasing welcome in detailed character creation. Races of Hyperborea are well described. I started with a redheaded Aesir.
Contrary to ARK which requires a lot of RAM, loading time etc here you can host your single play (or coop) server and get inside within seconds. Considering this, I just do not understand all the fuss about online servers. I have yet to welcome other players to my server before checking more about the netcode. Here I had no lag during my game and could play with no crash and no issue.
Crafting was also "fast enough" to leave room for exploration here and more neatly packaged than in ARK. Note that when you create your server you are invited to customize crafting rate etc in a neat UI, and there is also a creator mode where you can drop anything to your character like in Minecraft creator mode. I don't use this but I am sure plenty of others would find this attractive.
The game begins just like one of Conan the Barbarian scenes, where you are hung and left to die on a wood cross amid vast arid lands. This was a situation Conan lived. The context, once you leave the first dunes and get landscapes in sight, shows you wild animals and other survivors often just trying to kill you, which feels very consistent with the situation.
Most of the following gameplay is cut and pasted from ARK, which itself deepened other gameplay I have seen on a few MMORPGs (but added its fantastic lore, taming and dinosaurs). You find resources in the exact same way than in ARK, making this game a "MMA" of sorts (massively multiplayer Ark).
As opposed to ARK, you here are opposed to various giant creatures and savage humans and ave a more "completed" gameplay. It is also easier to get your situation (and not get stupidly lost) as there are less jungles and more mountains.  There are statues I see afar and certainly many places to explore in Conan Exiles.
However at times I also felt it was not as deep as ARK taming and mysterious islands to explore. I believe I am fond of both games. I have yet to prospect the size of the world, the randomness in it, to get the full extent of the game.

At one point, I had fun with this game (as evidenced by my playtime). However, that changed, and at the same time, I also realized that Elsword just wasn't a good game. Now, it's been a long time since then, but I can't imagine the game's gotten any better, and there's a reason for that. For now, the review....
The main problem with Elsword, in my opinion, is that the combat is very, very repetitive. Going through dungeons will comprise a large portion of your playtime, and those dungeons require minimal skill, as you can simply mash Z and kill everything. No skill, forethought or strategy required. Unfortunately, this also applies to many of the game's bosses-- the only difference is that you might have to jump over an attack or two.
The second problem is the shameless cash grabs. When I was playing, I would occasionally get some sort of container with excellent items inside that could only be opened with a specific key-type item. Where would one find those items, you ask? Why, the cash shop, of course.
Look, it's standard P2W crap. I don't think I really need to go into detail here.
The third issue I took with Elsword, and the reason I don't think it'll ever improve, is that the game had a bad case of power creep. Every so often, a new character would be released, and those new characters were invariably better than all of the other ones. This was a complete disaster for the game's balance, as these new characters would dominate the PVP, and everybody else (Myself included; I played Rena, one of the game's oldest characters) suddenly had a very difficult time competing.
To wrap things up, the PVE isn't interesting, and the PVP isn't balanced. Neither is particularly fun after a certain point. So, what's left? Please think about that before you play the game.

~Pros~
-PvE Dungeons are fun at early levels.
-Various Characters have different gamestyles and backgrounds storywise.
-Job System, Class Advancement and more skills.
-Ability to party and chat with friends pretty easily.
-Guilds, Guilds, and most of them are friendly and very welcoming and most of the PvE Communtiy.
-You can customize your character and don't have to look the same the whole game.

-You have the ability to skip Dungeon areas if you are a high level enough or are overleveled by being able to go to the next town in the game.
~Cons~
-Some Characters are more powerful than the others, And can have very BS worthy skills.
-You have 8 skill slots, and 4 are locked and you need to purchase a skill slot medal to unlock.
-You have to buy an extra item space, aka consumable items. (see above ^)
-Later Dungeons just become tedious and hard to accomplish on your own merits.
-PvP Community is very salty, and they are rude and will say anything to try to degrade or hurt you.
-You are restricted a lot during the early levels from things high level players can do which is unfair.
-The Korean version recieves earlier updates, and usually get different events that are rewarding even though some are good here too.
-Lag, Lag, And Lag are just those certain days and SOME Updates cause lag. But not all the time.
-A Stamina System that prevents you from doing more than 10-15 Dungeons a day.
-Characters are genderlocked, except for a few.
All in all it sucks that you need to buy a "medal" to get extra skills, and also one for extra consumable items, and as the list of cons are long enough there is also Invetory Expansions you need to buy if you want a larger inventory for each section.

This game is a hit or miss, it's up for you to decide.

Good writing, good storytelling, and an interesting twist do not save Murdered: Soul Suspect from its boring and simplistic gameplay. I understand that this is a story-driven experience, but this is almost the bare minimum of what one can even call a game.
In Murdered: Soul Suspect the player will follow the path of a convict-turned-cop as he attempts to solve his own murder. The story follows the traditional detective story arc, right up to the 'big twist' at the end. The characters are interesting enough. And by that, I mean the other characters. The protagonist himself is unfortunately a stereotype, and not very interesting at all. Just your generic ChisledFace McBadass tough-guy cop, who somehow manages to continue smoking the same cigarette long after his death. He's witty, he's sarcastic, he doesn't play by the rules, nobody understands him, and he's exactly the same disgruntled detective we've seen a thousand other times before.
Despite this, the story is somewhat enjoyable and does have interesting ties to real historical events. Namely, the Salem witch trials. However, once again, getting through the story is a chore and this really is a figurative point-and-click game. Yet it is lacking the thing that saves genuine point-and-click games: puzzle-solving elements. Murdered: Soul Suspect has almost no such elements, which is misleading considering that this is supposed to be about solving a crime. No brainpower is required here, and you simply need to follow the convenient onscreen prompts to get through the entire story.
To top it off, this is a game that was very clearly designed with a 'console first' mentality, and a PC port thrown in as an afterthought. A bit of a warning, you cannot remap any of the keybinds. Matters are made worse by the face that the default keybinds feel clunky, especially when navigating menus. You'll definitely want to have an Xbox 360 controller to connect to your PC. In addition to the poor controls, I noticed several FPS drops throughout the game. The performance is not awful, and I have seen much worse, but it's just another example of this game's PC port being forced to the backseat.
My final gripe with this game is that it is quite short. I only took about five hours to finish it. Knocking off the time I spent in the pause menu, I'd estimate it's roughly a four hour campaign. All I can say is that I'm glad I bought it on sale. I would recommend this game as a rental on consoles. As a purchase on PC, unless on super-sale, it's simply not worth it.

No magic, no ridiculously overpowered sword swings, no 9000 HP. This game is about simplified samurai swordsmanship, one strike, one kill. This game is about timing, precision and your own fighting psychology, just like Kendo (way of the sword).
As a Kendoka, I personally I like how this game peresents samurai swordsmanship: You have 3 stances, jodan/chudan/waki-no-kamae. Jodan is a very offensive stance, but you can't block. Chudan is the ambivalent stance, where you can attack and block. Waki is the most difficult stance, because it is a counter-strike and therefore must be very well timed (execute the strike when the enemy raises his sword for a attack).
Unfortunetly this game lacks hiki-waza (striking while going backwards). That would make taiatari more fun.
What I really don't like about the game mechanics is, you can only use certain strikes in a certain kamae. For example you can't strike a do-uchi (strike to the stomach) from chudan, but only from waki. There is only one oji-waza (counter technique) and that is nuki-waza. It would be really nice if there were sureage, kaeshi or uchiotoshi in this game.
All in all a great game, that would be even more awesome if there were more features (maybe a campaign/storymode?) and a working multiplayer.

One of the best games I've ever played. Apparently the PC port is based on the PSP version which is (suprisingly) inferior to the original (PS2) in terms of quality of life features. NISAmerica, despite of being masters at creating incredible strategy games, is a lazy company. The buttons are remaped to PSP so you don't have L2/R2, instead you have to use combinations like square + L/R to perform what should be assigned to L2/R2 (and this can't be changed). You can't choose resolution (the game will snap to fullscreen at 16:9, which is very strange and as I said, lazy). They didn't add the option for text and walk speed, the game feels incredibly sluggish. This is unaceptable for a 2017 remake. Still, the game is a mandatory introduction to the series. I recomend playing it first if you plan on playing other games of the series, because it will feel very slow in comparison, but even so it is a classic and should be experienced by everyone in my opinion.

This feels like a stripped down 2d Bushido Blade. While that's not an entirely bad thing. Kiai seems to be missing a lot of the elements that made BB so damn fun.
There is no variation in the (only)2 characters you get to choose from. Sure that helps with balancing, but only because balancing isn't a thing when everyone is the same. However it kills the player's individuality & stymies gamer's creativity.
There are only 3 attacks & no options when it comes to fight or flight. Sure you can dodge back, but full on running away to lure the enemy into a disadvantageous position, makes for some crazy interesting battles. No projectiles, to throw your opponent off guard for a quick strike.
No limb damage, no jumping or using the terrain to your advantage, etc.
Content is lacking in Kiai also. Only 3 stages & like the characters, they're just aesthetic differences.
Online seems to be dead.
Look, I know Kiai isn't Bushido Blade & never pretended to be. My point is that Kiai is in the same vein as BB & while it does some things right, Kiai comes up a little short. The mind game & the quick twitch is there, but the variation in gameplay & content are lacking.
A good example of a 2d game that got a lot of this right is Nidhogg.

As much as I like this game, I can't recommend the game in its current state. Something else I'd like to mention first, is that this is a game you'd typically play during a short break or when you don't have time to play your time-consuming bigger games. Hence why the average playtime on this game would never be as high compared to other games in general. It's really a 'quickie'-game.
Now on to the problem. After several months of bug fixing, there are still several really major bugs within the game which will definitely ruin game-play experience often enough. When you queue up for a game, you'll disconnect or receive error messages about half of the time. But that's not the worst part. The worst part is the bugs still going on when it comes to races and custom-made maps. As you'll likely know, you're losing a match if your opponent manages to outrun you and gets you out of the screen due to that. But there are bugs within the game that causes the winning player to actually lose. The winning player runs too fast, gets out of the screen, and loses. That is not how it's supposed to work. The same counts for catching up with your opponents. It's possible that when you catch in too fast, that you, the winning player, loses the game as you get out of screen. When it comes to custom-made maps, you'll often find out that the game totally breaks due to the automatically generated starting point of a race being out of the map. Players either fall into an endless void, or get to see a blacked out screen until someone automatically loses or wins after some time. Now, mind you, for the majority of the time you won't experience this issue. But you will experience those bugs often enough (especially the queuing bug) that it will make you hate the game. Those bugs aren't occurring rarely, no, those bugs are occurring way too frequently. Whenever I play the game for about 30 minutes, I'll experience at least a couple of those bugs. These bugs have been in the game for months, and have never been fixed even though there were several hotfixes for other bugs.
Now, you might say ''how can you downrate the game due to bugs while it's still in the beta phase?''. That is because the developers just announced that the game is almost in its final state (nothing major going to happen anymore) while those bugs still haven't been fixed over the course of months and several fixes. Therefore it's very unlikely that they actually will fix those bugs before they will release the game soon. If they actually do fix them before they launch the game officially, I'll come back and request it, as it's an amazing game. But as they still haven't fixed months-old bugs and are about to launch the game in this state, I can't recommend it. None likes to play a racing game and lose because they were actually too fast or because of other bugs.

This is my 3rd review on this game as it is constantly improving.  My original review was a "not recommend" and they have already fixed most of my original gripes.  I highly recommend this game for anybody that is competitive that enjoys a tough challenge.
PROS:
Very competitive online
Skill depth (look up Taters McShit on youtube)
Fun and Addictive for any skill level
CONS:
Items Ruin Ranked - This is a biggie for me.  Basically the cheesier you play, the more you'll win and the saltier your opponent will be.  I think this is cancerous for the community and probably why so few people play this game.
Small Community - I find myself playing the same people every day. A lot of the time, nobody's online so I get mis-matched with players that are either way better than me, or way worse than me.
Join Lag - If you're in a race and someone joins, the game lags out and will usually cost you the round.  Very frusterating.
SUGGESTION:
Make ranked matches without items.  Or atleast make it to where people can choose their own item settings and item options are randomly chosen between player's preferences each game.  Or you could reward people with extra rank up points for using no items.  It would also be great if there was a way to tech hitstun from an item (kinda like smash) to get up faster if executed properly.  Either way, their should be a way to offset the items.  Look at any game that has items/pickups (smash bros, mario kart, Halo, TF, etc.).  All of those games competitive ruleset is to play without items/pickups.  By forcing people to play with items on, you're closing the door to more potential players.
